host_range: C. rolfsii infects more than 500 species of monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants, but is especially severe on legumes, solanaceous crops, cucurbits and other vegetables grown in rotation with beans (Hall, 1991).
potential_eco_desc:
Disease caused by C. rolfsii occurs on a broad range of crops and can be of economic importance in tropical and subtropical regions of the world.
Stem and pod rots caused by C. rolfsii affect groundnut in many countries, reducing yields by 10-25%. Pod yield losses may reach more than 80% in heavily infested fields (Mehan et al., 1995). A yield-loss study of groundnut in Alabama, USA, during 1983-89, showed that yield yield was increased by an average of 10.6% and disease incidence was reduced by 52.6% in plots protected by fungicide compared with untreated plots (Bowen et al., 1992). In a survey of betel gardens in different localities in India, C. rolfsii was found to be responsible for plant losses of 42-62% (Singh and Chand, 1972).
In August 1990, soyabean plants with characteristic symptoms of southern blight caused by C. rolfsii were found in south-eastern Kansas, USA; the disease affected 10-50% of plants in localized areas (Appel and Jardine, 1992). In southern regions of the USA, losses in soyabean of 20-30% have been reported, but the disease is generally considered to be minor (Aycock, 1966). The disease has been reported as a minor problem in soyabean in Zimbabwe (Smartt, 1960).
Corticium rolfsii ear rot has been reported on maize only in the Himachal Pradesh region of India, and in Pakistan, where it has causes significant losses (Sharma et al., 1976, 1977). A sunflower disease survey in the mid-west of the USA during 1989 detected S. rolfsii wilt in 6% of surveyed fields (Gulya et al., 1991).
management_info:
Chemical Control
Control of C. rolfsii has been obtained on several crops by fungicide applications, as foliar sprays, soil drenches or seed treatment. Successful control by spray applications has been reported for tebuconazole on groundnut (Grichar, 1995). Quintozene, chloroneb and tridemorph applied as soil drenches gave good control of sugarbeet infection in field plots inoculated with sclerotia of C. rolfsii (Sharma et al., 1990). Other effective soil drenches include carboxin on sweet potato (Sivaprakasam and Kandaswamy, 1983) and benodanil on wheat (Hagan et al., 1991). Granular application of quintozene or flutolanil to soil controlled the disease in groundnut (Hagan et al., 1991). The insecticide chloropyrifos reduced stem rot by C. rolfsii by 17% in groundnut (Kucharek and Edmondson, 1991).
Fungicide seed treatments are effective for control of C. rolfsii diseases on several crops. The most commonly cited fungicides include captan (Fahim et al., 1984), quintozene, thiram and carbendazim (Singh et al., 1982), triadimenol (Sharma et al., 1994), benomyl (Prasad et al., 1987), mancozeb (Singh et al., 1985), guazatine (Kulkarni, 1980) and oxycarboxin (Reddy et al., 1976). Biological Control
Several fungi have been investigated extensively as biological control agents for S. rolfsii. Application of a wheat bran preparation of Trichoderma harzianum enriched with nutrient solution at 10 g/m2, soil at the same time or 1 year after soil inoculation with C. rolfsii at 1.5 g/m2, significantly reduced sugarbeet root rot and increased yield. The same preparation retained its protective effect against C. rolfsii the following year, but a second treatment with T. harzianum increased the protective value (Ciccares et al., 1992). The mechanism of control by was investigated by examining the hyphal interactions between T. harzianum and C. rolfsii in vitro. Thin hyphal branches of T. harzianum grew towards and along those of C. rolfsii, forming several short branches and coils. Neither of these structures was formed in the absence of C. rolfsii. Penetration sites on the host hyphae were observed after removal of T. harzianum. Following penetration, granulation and vacuolation of the host hyphae occurred (Sariah-Meon, 1991).
T. viride and T. koningii gave some control of C. rolfsii on barley under greenhouse conditions (Olivos and Mont, 1993) and tomato under field conditions (Ristaino et al., 1994). Gliocladium virens has shown potential for biological control of C. rolfsii on groundnut (Sreenivasaprasad and Manibhushanrao, 1993), Phaseolus vulgaris (Lewis et al., 1993) and tomato (Ristaino et al., 1994). Various vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been examined for control of C. rolfsii in chilli (Sreenivasa et al., 1992) and wheat (Harlapur et al., 1990). Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods
Crop rotation has a strong influence on survival of C. rolfsii. Populations of viable sclerotia were highest in soil in a field in which tomatoes were planted for 3 successive years before sampling and in one in which tomatoes followed groundnut in the 2 years prior to the study. Lowest sclerotial numbers were recorded in fields in which groundnut followed maize or in which maize or sorghum was the last crop before sampling (Chima Wokocha, 1988). In another study, no sclerotia were detected in fields under maize which had been under groundnut the previous year, while 3.33 sclerotia/250 ml soil were found in groundnut fields which had been under maize the previous year (Rodriguez Kabana et al., 1974). Other crop rotation studies on groundnut have shown that the incidence of C. rolfsii infection was lower in rotation with crops such as cotton or soyabean than in goundnut monoculture (Rodriguez Kabana, 1991a, b).

management_info: 白绢病是一种土传病害。在防治上应以农业防治为主，并结合进行化学防治。慎选茶苗种植地是一项重要的防病措施。尽量避免在感染过白绢病的植物地上种植茶苗，当在熟地栽种茶苗以前，应用70%五氯硝基苯粉剂15~35kg/ha，混入细土200~300kg，撒施在土面，并进行浅耕，可以杀灭土壤中的白绢病菌。加强对茶园苗圃的检查，如发现有茶苗萎蔫并出现早期症状时，可用0.5%CuSO4液，或50%托布津500倍液，或50%多菌灵500~800倍液灌施茶苗茎基部以及土壤中，以防止病害继续蔓延。间隔7~10天后在灌施一次，效果更好。对于死苗，立即拔除，并将周围土壤一并挖出，换以新土，在病树穴中以及病土中同样施入上述杀菌剂进行消毒后，方可补植茶苗。挖出的病土应携出园外。此外加强田间管理，增施有机肥，改良土壤可以提高茶树的抗病力。
author: 张希玲

description: 春季或初夏，温湿度适宜时，菌核萌芽形成吸器或菌丝体，呈匍匐状沿着土隙蔓延至邻株。夏季降暴雨时，病菌可随雨水冲流而传播。此外，通过中耕以及移动土壤等农事操作也可传播病害。还可随苗木调运传播。

potential_eco_desc: 花生白绢病主要分布于长江流域和南方各花生产区。一般为零星发生，严重的发病率也可高达30%以上。该病菌寄主范围很广，能侵染60多科200多种植物。受害的主要作物有烟草、番茄、茄子、马铃薯、甘薯、大豆、棉花、甘蔗等。
management_info: 收获后及时清除病残株和深耕深埋病残株和菌核，轻病地与禾谷科作物轮作1年，病重地轮作2~4年均可减少菌源而减轻病害发生。注意防涝排渍，改善土壤通气条件，不施用未腐熟的有机肥也可减轻病害。美国常在花生下针期施用五氯硝基苯（PCNB）和萎锈灵颗粒剂或喷雾，有效地控制病害发生。

description: Incidence^p^pAs an ear-rotting fungus, infection levels of up to 100% have been reported in maize (Sharma et al., 1977). C. rolfsii was detected in nine out of 32 seed samples of groundnut (Mridha and Fakir, 1978). Other seeds on which the pathogen has been detected include lentil (Rajendra Prasad and Chaudhary, 1987), Phaseolus vulgaris (Akem and Dashiell, 1991), wheat (Epps et al., 1951), lettuce (Silveira, 1947), jute (Mandal, 2001), periwinkle (Ou Yang and Wu, 1998) and watermelon (Ikediugwu, 1980).^p^pC. rolfsii was reported in kernels of lodged sunflowers that had contact with infested soil, but the pathogen was not recovered from seeds from non-lodged plants (Lakshmidev et al., 1991).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pC. rolfsii rots kernels on the ears of maize (Sharma et al., 1977).^p^p^Seed Transmission^p^pThere is no evidence for seed transmission of the pathogen.^p^p^Seed Treatments^p^pFungicide seed treatment is effective for control of C. rolfsii diseases on several crops. potential_eco_desc: The disease was recorded in North Carolina, USA, in 1904, and remained localized and of little importance until the late 1940s when, concurrent with the intensification of chrysanthemum flower and pot plant production, it began to cause serious losses throughout the range. It is now considered the most serious fungal disease of chrysanthemums in Florida. In 1975, in Connecticut, the disease was reported to be particularly important on chrysanthemum cuttings in propagating benches under mist; 50% losses occurred.^p^pThe increasing intensification of chrysanthemum production, with all-the-year-round cultivars, mist benches, use of dark covers, etc., favours spread and development of the disease. In addition, the fungus can develop under a wide range of conditions and, once established, is both difficult and costly to eradicate. The fact that the disease is recorded in California shows that it will persist even in areas with apparently unfavourable climatic conditions.

remark: D. ligulicola is an A2 quarantine pest for EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1982); it also has A2 quarantine status for IAPSC. In the EPPO region at present, ray blight is of significant economic importance in countries where it occurs. Widespread establishment of the disease within the EPPO region could cause considerable economic losses to propagators and growers of chrysanthemums. Some countries (Finland) maintain an eradication programme. Only chrysanthemum plants for planting are concerned. In countries where the disease occurs, growing-season inspections should be carried out, especially during rooting of cuttings, but also on mother plants and at flowering. Rooted or unrooted cuttings should come from rooting beds or plants, respectively, which were found free from D. ligulicula during the last growing season (OEPP/EPPO, 1990). ^p^pSymptoms may develop in transit on blooms which are apparently healthy when cut.
author: CPC2006

management_info: In Europe, the disease has been controlled successfully with benomyl. However, the repeated and excessive usage of this fungicide over a number of years has led to resistance build-up and a consequent increase in ray blight importance (Grouet, 1974). More recently dicarboximide derivates have been successfully used for control (Engelhard, 1984).^p^pCurrently there is no biological control method available. However, certain cultivation and phytosanitary requirements can reduce infection by D. ligulicola, especially during the rooting of cuttings (Hahn and Schmatz, 1980).

description: 菊花疫病是stevens, F.L.于1904年在美国北卡罗来纳州首先发现并报道的。由于此病主要侵害花部，因此对菊花生产具有很大的危害性。但在此后很长一段时间内，在美国其余各州及其他国家均未发现，直到1932年在密西西比州发生此病，随后在马里兰（1947），佛罗里达（1954），纽约（1956）也相继报道。日本（1952）也发生了菊花疫病。从1904年后40多年中，北卡罗来纳州主要是从外地调入菊花种植材料，后来随着菊花生产的发展，大量的种植材料、切花才从北卡来纳州调运、销售到其他国家与地区。显然菊花疫病也随着病区带菌的种植材料和切花而外传。1959年英格兰南部地区在从美国引进的菊花上发生此病，德国也是在从美国、荷兰、丹麦引进的插条上发生，捷克斯洛伐克1967年10月从荷兰引进菊花插条时带入此病。我国迄今未发现此病。

在病区内主要由病株残体上的子囊孢子通过气流传播先侵染花部，在发病季节，大量分生孢子通过雨水飞溅传播，栽种密集时，可通过相互接触直接传播到附近植株上。另外露水、雾滴、携带分生孢子的昆虫、气流也起一定传播作用。

management_info: 此病是菊花生产上的一个重要病害，尤其在欧洲各菊花产区。因病菌在整个菊花生长季节都表现很强的生活力与致病性，因此一般措施难以控制此病的发生。病菌一旦立足，就很难将其根除。1962年联邦德国颁布的植物检疫条令，就规定菊花疫病为检疫对象，1972年民主德国将之列为内检对象，以防止病害的进一步扩散。此病也是苏联、挪威的检疫对象。一旦发现病区，应将病区内的病株全部烧毁或腐烂，并对曾栽种过发病菊花苗的土壤进行严格消毒，可用三氯硝基甲烷（氯化苦）或蒸气灭菌处理。

potential_eco_desc:
刺茄为多刺的灌木，常分布于热带和亚热带地区，耐干旱，在温暖湿润的肥沃条件下生长最好，生境包括：灌木林、森林空旷地，岩石山坡，牧场，沼泽，路边，废弃地等。高1~3m，有时可达5m，传入美国佛罗里达州后，在牧场形成密集灌木丛。植株具刺，易形成密集的单一物种，侵占林地、牧场，影响生态环境和林木业生产。
刺茄是美国有害杂草。目前已普遍定植在毛伊岛（夏威夷群岛中的第二大岛），主要归化于牧场和农业区低洼的干扰地，在夏威夷州发现它是地中海实蝇的寄主之一。
该物种的根和叶片产生3-氨基螺旋甾碱烷组（3-amino-spirosolane group）的类固醇生物碱。叶片、果实和根的主要成分为非生物碱以及生物碱和皂苷。根含圆锥茄次碱（jurubidine），是一种3-氨基螺旋甾碱烷（3-amino-spirosolane）的生物碱。在印度将其成熟果实作为蔬菜食用。在加纳它的果实用于做汤和炖煮。在印度和缅甸等国家种植，将其浆果用作调味，在斯里兰卡种子已被用于制作咖喱粉。在印度刺茄可以单独或其他药用植物组合使用，浆果用于治疗胸痛，叶片用于治疗蛇和昆虫的叮咬，果实和根治疗胃痛，根用于解毒，树皮用于治疗疟疾，浆果还能治疗夜盲症和牙齿感染。Lu（1986）记载，在中国发现该物种的根含生物碱，可用于散淤血，缓解疼痛，减轻咳嗽。果实具祛痰和止痛的功效。刺茄和茄子间作可用于抗假单胞菌、根结线虫属、轮枝菌属、根串珠霉属烟草黑胫病菌、疫霉菌和茄镰刀菌复合体。它还能抗茄二十八星瓢虫，但对炭疽病菌易感。
description:
自然扩散通过食用果实的鸟和蝙蝠，也可通过水流、土壤等传播。人为传播通过引种、农作物的调运。
长距离传播主要通过园艺贸易。植株本地扩散通过种子，它的种子依靠食用果实的鸟和蝙蝠，也可能通过车辆或污染土壤。
management_info:
（1）物理方法：由于刺茄很难根除，因此新的分布地应尽早进行控制，防止进一步扩散。当小范围发生时可使用清除的方法，由于植株多刺，需注意安全。但根据巴布亚新几内亚的调查，机械控制方法（切断或拔除）不像化学方法那样有效。
（2）化学方法：可使用草甘膦进行处理。幼株（主茎基部直径0.5~1.0mm）也可使用50%的2,4-二氯苯氧乙酸丁酯（2,4-D丁酯）每亩50~70ml进行叶面喷洒，而成株（主茎基部直径1~6cm）和老的植株（主茎基部直径大于6cm），清除植株的上半部分，留下高度为10~15cm的草桩使用2,4,5-涕酸丁酯（2,4,5-T butyl ester）0.5%~1.0%水溶液喷洒可控制蔓延。
（3）其他方法：在美国夏威夷州发现，该物种的传播与来自分布区的设备或土壤有关。因此，对来自分布区的车辆和设备进行清洗有助于减少在毛伊岛的蔓延。

host_range: As a perennial species, S. torvum is unable to survive to maturity in annual crops and, as such, is most commonly a weed in perennial crops. In pastures it can be a major nuisance as it is woody, prickly and probably both unpalatable and poisonous. It is
potential_eco_desc: S. torvum is an invasive weed of pastures, roadsides and open native vegetation, and is occasionally found in cassava and other perennial crops in which it is not exposed to cultivation. It has been suggested that the plants are poisonous to stock, but no conclusive evidence is available.^p^pS. torvum is relatively resistant to Meloidogyne spp., and is used as a rootstock for grafting tomatoes in susceptible areas (Shetty and Reddy, 1985). It is also resistant to Pseudomonas solanacearum (Hebert, 1985) and phomopsis fruit rot of aubergine (Datar and Ashtaputre, 1988).^p^pThe species is a natural host for many insects and pathogens (see Natural Enemies section).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pSeedlings may be hand pulled when the soil is wet, otherwise the plants need to be dug or grubbed out to remove the upper root from the soil either by hand or mechanical cultivation.^p^pChemical Control^p^pSeedlings can be controlled in pasture with 2,4-D (Henty and Pritchard, 1975; Chadhokar, 1976). Australian registrations for the control of S. torvum are restricted to 2,4-D + picloram (Hamilton, 1997).^p^pBiological Control^p^pNo work has been attempted to establish biological control agents for S. torvum, since it is too closely related to many useful crops and ornamentals.

host_range: D. abyssinica is a weed of many crops, including large- and small-grain cereals, fibres (cotton, flax and sisal), tree crops (coffee, forestry nurseries, tea and wattle) and plantation crops including pineapple, pyrethrum and sugarcane.
potential_eco_desc: D. abyssinica is the most troublesome weed in the crops of Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania (Ivens, 1989). It is reported as the most important weed of coffee in Kenya and of cotton in Uganda (Holm et al., 1977). The growth and yield of crops is greatly reduced in the presence of D. abyssinica. Heavy infestations can kill coffee bushes (Ivens, 1989), reduce sisal yields by 2 t/ha (Richardson, 1965) and cotton yields by 50% (Prentice, 1957). This may be caused, in part, by toxins released from the roots of D. abyssinica which have an allelopathic effect on the crop (Wallis, 1959). Serious mechanical damage can occur when trying to remove rhizomes entwined in crop roots.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Mechanical Control^p^pA forked hoe will remove many rhizomes, however, this method is very labour intensive and total eradication of all viable fragments left in the soil is virtually impossible (Terry, 1974). Where high densities of D. abyssinica are present, ploughing with draught animals is impeded. The increased traction can cause injury to the shoulders of draught animals. Mechanical tillage with tractors can expose rhizomes to desiccation on the soil surface, but can also spread the fragmented rhizomes. In laboratory conditions, desiccation of rhizomes for four days at temperatures of 7°C to 27°C led to complete kill (Mshiu, 1978). Field trials with cover crops have shown that noug (Guizotia abyssinica) and linseed (Linum usitatissimum) considerably suppress D. abyssinica in coffee with no significant effect on the crop (Dubale, 1987). Rotation with noug (Guizota abyssinica) is also regarded as a useful control measure in Ethiopia.^p^pChemical Control^p^pHerbicides that have been tested and used against D. abyssinica include alloxydim, amitrole, asulam, butylate, dalapon, glufosinate-ammonium, glyphosate, haloxyfop, hexazinone, metribuzin, MSMA, sethoxydim, sulfosate (glyphosate-trimesium) and TCA - sodium. Dalapon was a standard treatment to young foliage (Ivens, 1989) but this has largely been superseded by glyphosate (Terry, 1974; Baguma et al., 1995).
author: CPC2006

potential_eco_desc: CoRSV is present in the main coffee-growing states of Brazil. The disease has not been of major importance since 1938 when it was first detected. However, in important coffee-growing regions of Minas Gerais State, 80-100% plantations were affected with this disease resulting in 20% yield losses (Figueira, 1995). The severity of the disease was attributed to ecological disturbances associated with expanding coffee areas and chemical pest control favouring the vector. Mutation of the virus is another possibility (Figueira, 1995).

management_info: So far, no control of coffee ringspot has been employed as the disease has not been considered significant. Nevertheless, this disease poses a phytosanitary risk (see Phytosanitary Risk). As CoRSV is not seedborne, proper seed selection is a desirable step towards limiting the spread of the disease. Coffee growers in Brazil select seeds from their own trees, or use certified seeds from coffee research stations.^p^pThere is no phytosanitary regulation specifically against CoRSV (in Brazil). Strict quarantine and regulatory control will be necessary to limit spread if the disease becomes a serious problem in the future. Countries (and parts of any one country) free of this disease presently could apply phytosanitary control methods to protect their coffee cultivation. This will be mainly in the form of preventing importation of coffee plants and plant parts from countries (or parts of any one country) where the disease is endemic.

description:
咖啡环斑病毒(CoRSV)自然地通过紫红短须螨（Brevipalpus phoenicis）传播，它是一种在干燥的月份大量繁殖的杂食性螨虫(Oliveira, 1986)。到目前为止，不同的虫龄传播CoRSV的效力是未知的，虽然成虫非常的有效(Chagas, 1973, 1978)；个别地传播到咖啡幼苗中去的带病毒的雌性螨虫能以24.24％的比率传播该病害，但不能通过卵巢传播(Chagas, 1978)。咖啡环斑的散布机制由通过风和植物运输分散的媒介的散布机制所决定。此外，咖啡植物和其他的媒介的多年生寄主生产叶片。
在菲律宾，Valdez (1966)发现在埃塞尔萨咖啡（C. excelsa） 中16.9％以及阿拉伯咖啡（C. arabica）中25.7％的种子传播比率。然而，在巴西种子传播被否定的证明；来自感染咖啡干种子的1149棵阿拉伯咖啡（C. arabica）幼苗中，在播种后的18个月后没有一棵显示症状(Chagas, 1978)。这证实了Silberschmidt and Bitancourt (1965)先前在巴西说该病害不是种传的报道。
超微结构的研究指出：咖啡环斑是一个非系统性病害(Kitajima et al., 1972; Chagas, 1980)。这事实排除了该病害种传的情况。在菲律宾，在来自感染树木的幼苗上的症状从5个月到1年和九个月中出现，这是一段允许可能媒介传播的相当长的时期。如果媒介是在巴西发现的同一个螨虫品种，那种传应该在菲律宾作检查。 Coffee rinsgspot virus (CoRSV) is naturally transmitted by the false spider mite Brevipalpus phoenicis, a polyphagous mite which multiplies profusely in dry months (Oliveira, 1986). To date, the effectiveness of different instars in transmitting CoRSV is unknown, although adults are fairly efficient (Chagas, 1973, 1978); viruliferous female mites, individually transferred to coffee seedlings, could transmit the disease at a rate of 24.24% but were unable to transmit it transovarially (Chagas, 1978). The dispersal mechanism of coffee ringspot depends on that of the vector which is generally dispersed by winds and by plant transportation. Furthermore, coffee plants and other perennial hosts of the vector bear leaves.
In the Philippines, Valdez (1966) found 16.9% seed transmission in C. excelsa and 25.7% in C. arabica. Nevertheless, seed transmission in Brazil proved negative; none of the 1149 C. arabica seedlings from affected coffee berries showed symptoms l8 months after sowing (Chagas, 1978). This confirmed what Silberschmidt and Bitancourt (1965) had reported previously in Brazil, that the disease was not seedborne.
Ultrastructural studies indicated that coffee ringspot is a non-systemic disease (Kitajima et al., 1972; Chagas, 1980). This fact strongly precludes a seedborne condition of the disease. The symptoms on seedlings from infected trees in the Philippines appeared from 5 months to 1 year and 9 months, a sufficiently long period which could permit possible vector transmission. If the vector is the same mite species as that found in Brazil, seed transmission should be reviewed in the Philippines.
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: 在菲律宾，Reyes (1961)报道了在埃塞尔萨咖啡（Coffea excelsa [C. liberica]）上8.7％的种子传播比率，Valdez (1966)发现了大果咖啡（C. liberica）上16.9％以及在阿拉伯咖啡（C. arabica）上25.7％的传播比率。 In the Philippines, Reyes (1961) reported 8.7% seed transmission in Coffea excelsa [C. liberica] and Valdez (1966) found 16.9% in C. liberica and 25.7% in C. arabica. The disease has not been of major importance since 1938 when it was first detected. However, in important coffee-growing regions of Minas Gerais State, 80-100% plantations were affected with this disease resulting in 20% yield losses (Figueira, 1995). The severity of the disease was attributed to ecological disturbances associated with expanding coffee areas and chemical pest control favouring the vector. Mutation of the virus is another possibility (Figueira, 1995).
author: zhangjianjun

management_info:
到目前为止，没有咖啡环斑的防治被应用，因为该病害不被认为有重要性。然而，这病害具有一个植物检疫的危险（见植物检疫危险）。因为CoRSV不是种传的，所以适当的种子挑选对限制该病害传播是一个理想的方法。巴西咖啡种植者从他们自己的树木中挑选种子，或使用来自咖啡研究机构的经鉴定的种子。
没有针对CoRSV有特定的植物检疫规程（在巴西）。如果该病害在将来成为了一个重大的问题，那就需要有严格的检疫和常规的防治来限制病害的传播。目前没有这病害的国家（和任何一个国家的一些地区）可通过应用植物检疫防治方法来保护他们的咖啡栽培。这主要是以防止咖啡植物和植物部分从该病害在当地是地方性病害的国家（和任何一个国家的一些地区）的进口的这种形式。 So far, no control of coffee ringspot has been employed as the disease has not been considered significant. Nevertheless, this disease poses a phytosanitary risk (see Phytosanitary Risk). As CoRSV is not seedborne, proper seed selection is a desirable step towards limiting the spread of the disease. Coffee growers in Brazil select seeds from their own trees, or use certified seeds from coffee research stations.
There is no phytosanitary regulation specifically against CoRSV (in Brazil). Strict quarantine and regulatory control will be necessary to limit spread if the disease becomes a serious problem in the future. Countries (and parts of any one country) free of this disease presently could apply phytosanitary control methods to protect their coffee cultivation. This will be mainly in the form of preventing importation of coffee plants and plant parts from countries (or parts of any one country) where the disease is endemic.

host_range: This is the first report of Orchid fleck virus infecting Liriope spicata.
description: In April 2015, lilyturf (Liriope spicata) plants with bright yellow flecks on the leaves were observed in landscape plantings across the St. Lucia campus of the University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia. These symptoms were reminiscent of those observed on leaves of orchid species infected by Orchid fleck virus (OFV). Symptomatic leaf samples were collected and analyzed. Based on the observed symptoms, particle morphology, N gene amplicon using OFV primers, and high sequence identity with other OFV sequences, we conclude that the lilyturf plants were infected with OFV. This is the first report of OFV infecting Liriope spicata.  This alternative host of Liriope spicata may play a possible role in Orchid fleck virus (OFV) spread to orchids or other ornamental species that are colonized by its Brevipalpus sp. mite vector.
reference_name: First Report of Orchid fleck virus in Lilyturf (Liriope spicata) in Australia

host_range: The natural host range of SCV is restricted to cultivated Fragaria spp. but the virus can be transmitted experimentally by grafting and by viruliferous aphids to a narrow range of wild Fragaria species including F. chiloensis, F. vesca and F. virginiana (
potential_eco_desc: SCV and other aphid-borne viruses such as Strawberry mottle virus (SMV) and Strawberry mild yellow edge-associated virus commonly occur together in infected plants and, when in complex, their symptoms and economic effects are often additive. Moreover, infected strawberry cultivars differ significantly in their levels of tolerance to SCV and virus complexes. For instance, in Washington State, USA, in comparison with healthy plants of the same cultivar SCV alone, decreased the marketable fruit yield of cv. Hood by 26% but together with SMV reduced yield by 64% whereas in cv. description: Crinkle disease of strawberry was first reported in Oregon, USA by Zeller and Vaughan (1932), but has since been shown to have an extensive geographical distribution.
author: CPC2006

description: Vector Transmission^p^pSCV is transmitted from infected to nearby healthy plants in the persistent, propagative manner by the strawberry aphid, Chaetosiphon fragaefolii, and in certain local areas by C. jacobi (Prentice and Woolcombe, 1951; Engelbrecht, 1967; Frazier, 1968; Zamfirov, 1978). Aphids can acquire virus from infected plants within 24 hours and, after a latent period of 10-19 days (C. fragaefolii) or 14-59 days (C. jacobi), remain viruliferous until they die (Frazier, 1968). The virus multiplies in C. jacobi (Sylvester et al., 1974) and probably also in C. fragaefolii, but is not transmitted transovarially (i.e., in the eggs of viruliferous aphids). The virus is also experimentally transmissible by three other aphid species (Hyperomyzus lactucae, Macrosiphum euphorbiae and Myzus ornatus) injected with infective, partially purified SCV preparations Sylvester and Richardson, 1981, 1986; Sylvester et al., 1987).^p^pThe virus has undoubtedly been disseminated inadvertently in virus-infected planting stock. SCV is not seedborne (Kacharmazov and Kristov, 1976).
author: CPC2006

remark: SCV has been reported to occur wherever strawberries are grown commercially so does not have quarantine status.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Introduction^p^pSCV is best controlled by the production of virus-free plants, their propagation in locations remote from unsprayed strawberry fields, the annual planting of certified virus-free stock and control of the aphid vector of this virus.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pSignificant differences exist in the levels of tolerance to SCV among infected strawberry cultivars. For instance, in Washington State, USA, SCV alone decreased the marketable yield of cv. Hood by 26% and SCV + Strawberry mottle virus (SMV) by 64% in comparison with healthy Hood plants, whereas in cv. Northwest there was no significant difference in marketable yield between healthy plants and those doubly infected with SCV and SMV (Barritt and Loo, 1973).Shanks and Barritt (1974) demonstrated strong resistance to colonization by Chaetosiphon fragaefolii in some clones of wild F. chiloensis, a parent of the modern cultivated strawberry. They recommended that this kind of germplasm be incorporated into the strawberry breeding programme to develop strawberry cultivars immune to C. fragaefolii colonization. However, recent strawberry breeding programmes have put more emphasis on selecting genotypes for virus tolerance than on incorporating resistance to C. fragaefolii colonization.^p^p^Vector Control^p^pThe principal vector of SCV, the strawberry aphid (C. fragaefolii), feeds and lives entirely on strawberry. Both wingless (apterous) and winged (alate) forms can spread SCV. Some common insecticides such as diazinon and azinphos methyl effectively reduce aphid populations when sprayed on plants, provided that coverage is thorough and timing coincides with the beginning of aphid population increase in the crop. Growers should consult local agricultural authorities for recommendations about choice of insecticides, timing of sprays, and required days to harvest after application of the insecticides. The first spring application of insecticide should be made when 0.5-1 aphids are found per leaf sample. This is usually in mid-April in the Pacific Northwest of the USA, but the timing will vary with geographical location and should be determined on-site. Repeat applications are made at 2-4 week intervals until the disappearance of the vector aphids, usually in mid-summer, and an additional application is made in late September or when vector aphids again appear. The use of a regular aphicidal spray schedule on nearby, established strawberry fields will help to control the spread of SCV by aphids into new fields of certified plants.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pVirus-free plants can be obtained from infected plants by heat therapy (Posnette, 1953; Posnette and Cropley, 1958), meristem tip culture (Miller and Belkengren, 1962), a combination of heat therapy and meristem tip culture (Sobczykiewicz, 1980; Paulechova and Maliarcikova, 1988; KonDakova, 1995) or by regeneration of small (0.8 mm) stem apices grown on a medium for organogenesis containing 2,4-dioxohexahydro-1,3,5-triazine (Kondakova and Schuster, 1991). Plants so produced can be used for the subsequent production and use of virus-free certified stocks.^p^p^Regulatory Measures^p^pSCV does not have quarantine status because it has already been reported to occur in many geographical locations. However, stringent efforts should be made to avoid international dissemination of uncertified stock. Certification is an important control measure that needs to be carried out by government officials or by state-recognized certification services operating under government control according to rules and standards set by legislation.

description:
SCV由草莓蚜虫，草莓钉蚜（Chaetosiphon fragaefolii），及在某些局部地区由C. jacobi从感染的植株以持续、增殖的方式传播到附近健康的植株(Prentice and Woolcombe, 1951; Engelbrecht, 1967; Frazier, 1968; Zamfirov, 1978)。蚜虫可以从感染的植株中获得病毒在24小时内和在10-19天(C. fragaefolii) 或 14-59 天(C. jacobi)的潜伏期后，在它们死亡以前都是带病毒的(Frazier, 1968)。病毒繁殖于C. jacobi (Sylvester et al., 1974)且也可能在C. fragaefolii繁殖，但并非传染地传播的（如，在携带病毒的蚜虫的卵中）。病毒也可能由其它的三种蚜虫种类（茶蔗苦菜蚜（Hyperomyzus lactucae），马铃薯长管蚜（Macrosiphum euphorbiae）和饰瘤蚜（Myzus ornatus））注入具传染性的、部分纯化的SCV制剂实验上传播。（Sylvester and Richardson, 1981, 1986; Sylvester et al., 1987)。
病毒的确已经被不注意地散布于被病毒感染的种植的根砧木中。SCV非种传的(Kacharmazov and Kristov, 1976)。 SCV is transmitted from infected to nearby healthy plants in the persistent, propagative manner by the strawberry aphid, Chaetosiphon fragaefolii, and in certain local areas by C. jacobi (Prentice and Woolcombe, 1951; Engelbrecht, 1967; Frazier, 1968; Zamfirov, 1978). Aphids can acquire virus from infected plants within 24 hours and, after a latent period of 10-19 days (C. fragaefolii) or 14-59 days (C. jacobi), remain viruliferous until they die (Frazier, 1968). The virus multiplies in C. jacobi (Sylvester et al., 1974) and probably also in C. fragaefolii, but is not transmitted transovarially (i.e., in the eggs of viruliferous aphids). The virus is also experimentally transmissible by three other aphid species (Hyperomyzus lactucae, Macrosiphum euphorbiae and Myzus ornatus) injected with infective, partially purified SCV preparations （Sylvester and Richardson, 1981, 1986; Sylvester et al., 1987).
The virus has undoubtedly been disseminated inadvertently in virus-infected planting stock. SCV is not seedborne (Kacharmazov and Kristov, 1976).

Moreover, infected strawberry cultivars differ significantly in their levels of tolerance to SCV and virus complexes. For instance, in Washington State, USA, in comparison with healthy plants of the same cultivar SCV alone, decreased the marketable fruit yield of cv. Hood by 26% but together with SMV reduced yield by 64% whereas in cv. Northwest there was no significant difference in marketable yield between healthy plants and those doubly infected with SCV and SMV (Barritt and Loo, 1973).

description: S. perseae was first noticed in California, USA in July 1996 when it was discovered damaging fruit in a Saticoy avocado orchard in Ventura County. management_info: Cultural Control ^p^pA novel method of controlling avocado thrips pupating in the soil beneath host trees (approximately 78% of second-instar larvae drop from the trees to pupate in the soil) is the use of coarse composted organic yard waste. Composted material that is prepared correctly is devoid of pathogenic diseases and pestiferous arthropods. Small field trials have demonstrated that 50% fewer thrips adults emerge from mulch laid under avocado trees in comparison to non-mulched trees that have leaf duff (litter) and branches under them. It is probable that the mulch suppresses the pupation of avocado thrips because it harbours a more diverse fauna of natural enemies (including entompathogenic fungi, nematodes and generalist arthropod predators) that opportunistically feed on microarthropods living in the mulch. This diverse fauna is lacking in avocado leaf duff in California, USA. Consequently, these generalist natural enemies attack avocado thrips larvae that fall from the trees to pupate. Interestingly, about 98% of Franklinothrips orizabensis (a common predatory thrips in avocado orchards) larvae drop from the trees to pupate in the soil. The organisms living in the mulch do not adversely affect F. orizabensis, probably because they pupate within protective silk cocoons, something avocado thrips does not do. It is unknown if the mulch can provide orchard-wide suppression of avocado thrips; if the reduction of thrips emergence is great enough to prevent economic damage to fruit; if the level of suppression seen is consistent year to year; or how regularly the mulch needs to be reapplied as it decomposes (Hoddle et al., 2002a). ^p^p^ Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThis area has not been studied for S. perseae.^p^p^ Chemical Control^p^pIn developing a strategy for managing avocado thrips, a grower should consider a large number of interrelated factors including tree size and vigour (which may affect the amount and timing of leaf flushes that avocado thrips prefer), the past history of avocado thrips population dynamics, and fruit scarring experienced in the grove and surrounding regions. Also the amount of leaf flush and/or small fruit present; whether these fruit are the major set or additional fruit sets are expected; avocado thrips levels; natural enemy levels; grove topography; spray equipment availability; the grower's tolerance for fruit scarring; and an interest in preserving avocado thrips pesticide susceptibility. One should also consider that the weather, and the timing and amount of leaf flushes and avocado fruit sets, can vary tremendously from year to year. Just because avocado thrips caused significant fruit scarring one year or in a particular grove, does not mean that this or other nearby groves will have economic avocado thrips levels in subsequent years. Many groves do not need to be treated for avocado thrips and as a general principle, if practical, it is best to withhold treatments as long as possible to maximize the negative impact of the weather and natural enemies on avocado thrips levels. management_info: Cultural Control^p^pEnvironmental conditions are important for disease management, as discussed earlier. Soil temperatures should be favourable for the growth of the host. In addition, avoiding overwatering and soil pHs above 5.6 limit disease development. In controlled studies, herbicides have been demonstrated to increase black root rot (Lee and Lockwood, 1977; Lewis and Papavizas, 1979).^p^pCrop rotation is important to prevent the build-up and maintenance of high soil populations of the pathogen. Anderson and Welacky (1988) in Ontario, Canada, reported soil populations were related to frequency of soyabean production and frequency of tobacco and soyabean in rotation. Holtz and Weinhold (1994) in California, USA, found higher populations in soil planted for three or more years to cotton than fields rotated to other crops (safflower, wheat or barley). Fields having crop rotations of sorghum or small grains or fallow had less blackhull on the subsequent peanut crop than rotation of cotton or peanut (Hsi, 1966). Weed control may be important for reductions in populations of the pathogen (Gayed, 1972; Klimova 1979; DeVilliers, 1987). The pathogen can be recovered from plant species that are showing no symptoms and are not considered hosts (Wills and Lambe, 1978; Yarwood, 1981). Incorporation of hairy vetch as a green manure reduced black root rot on cotton as a result of reductions in the population of the pathogen from the release of ammonia from the decomposing residue (Rothrock et al., 1995; Candole and Rothrock, 1997).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pVariation in susceptibility of cultivars or lines has been reported for a number of crops including: cherry (Pepin et al., 1975), chickpeas (Bowden et al., 1985; Bhatti and Kraft, 1992b), holly (Merrill et al., 1986), lettuce (O'Brien and Davis, 1994), pea (Lloyd and Lockwood, 1963), soyabean (Anderson, 1984) and groundnut (van der Merwe et al., 1993). In tobacco, resistance is well characterized with complete single dominant gene resistance from Nicotiana debneyi and a number of sources of partial resistance (Clayton, 1969; Shew and Shoemaker, 1993). ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pSoil fumigation has met with mixed results for the control of black root rot and should be combined with other management practices (Shoe and Shoemaker, 1993). Soil solarization with clear polyethylene tarps has been shown to be effective in reducing or eliminating C. elegans soil populations in fields (Pullman et al., 1981). Soil flooding also has effectively reduced pathogen populations (DeVay and Garber, 1997). Sterol-inhibiting fungicides have been shown to be effective in disease control. Flusilasol and triadimenol reduced black root rot on tobacco (Prinsloo et al., 1989). Black root rot on cotton was reduced by triadimenol and myclobutanil (Davis et al., 1994). Similarly, blackhull on groundnut was reduced with propiconazole and etaconazole (Labuschagne and Kotze, 1996).^p^pIn greenhouses, sodium hypochlorite and captan were effective disinfectants, reducing the viability of C. elegans, but other disinfectants containing bromine or quaternary ammonium were not effective (Copes and Hendrix, 1996).^p^pThe postharvest disease of carrot is controlled by reducing wounding, storage at 7-10°C, and postharvest and posthandling dips of calcium propionate at a pH 4.0 or potassium sorbate or sodium hypochlorite, especially at pH 6.8 (Punja and Gaye, 1993).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pPseudomonas fluorescens strain CHA0, isolated from a suppressive soil, has been shown to be very effective in controlling black root rot on tobacco (Stutz et al., 1986; Stutz et al. 1989; Haas et al., 1991). Other strains, RD:1, of P. fluorescens have also been reported to control black root rot (Reddy and Patrick, 1992). The predation of chlamydospores and hyphae of C. elegans by mycophagous amoebae have been reported in soils (Anderson and Patrick, 1978).

host_range: This species is widely distributed throughout tropical and subtropical regions where palms grow. Movement of P. blanchardi into new areas has commonly been from the importation of infested date offshoots. It was accidentally introduced to the USA in 1890
potential_eco_desc: P. blanchardi is considered a serious pest in several countries. The primary hosts of this species are palms. It was found to be the most abundant pest of date palm in Libya (Bitaw and Ben-Saad, 1990). This species may infest all parts of the date palm with heaviest infestations at the base of the leaves and crown (Khoualdia et al., 1993). The primary feeding site on the host is the succulent white tissue at the base of the leafstalk (Boyden, 1941). A discolored area of injured tissue develops where individuals settle and feed. If the population is allowed to develop unchecked, P. blanchardi may become a serious pest. Significant damage to the leaves results in the pinnae becoming withered and eventually dying. Heavy infestations weaken the tree by inhibiting transpiration and photosynthesis. Carpenter and Elmer (1978) noted that date palms in commercial plantings were seldom killed by P. blanchardi, primarily due to the implementation of control programmes against it. However, feeding damage by the scale directly affects plant vigour and often results in reduced yields. Infestations of the fruit results in not only an unsightly appearance, but physical damage too. Smirnoff (1957) reported fruit losses of 70-80% resulting from direct feeding by the scale.
author: CPC2006

management_info: P. blanchardi has been eradicated in the USA and distribution of the date palm scale has been limited through quarantine and control procedures. Foliar applications of a variety of oil-based compounds have proven effective against the immature stages of the pest (Al Hafidh et. al., 1981). Although several insecticides have provided effective control, some are considered too toxic for use (Siddig, 1975). Use of cultural techniques of providing undergrowth to protect predators of this pest has been effectively used to reduce infestation levels and maintain infestations below the damage level. Mechanical methods of pruning and disposing of infested limbs followed by application of chemical sprays is effective against light infestations (Siddig, 1975). Inspection of transplant shoots before transporting into new areas also restricts outbreaks. Some plant varieties are tolerant to infestations by this pest (Swaminathan and Verma, 1991). The implementation of an integrated control programme has resulted in successful control of P. blanchardi (Kehat et al., 1976). Implementation of an integrated pest management strategy basically involves developing an educational system for the involved personnel, establishing a survey system for the pest, restructuring the farm management of the crop, reduction of pesticides, and enhancing the beneficial agents. Such programmes have been highly successful in significantly reducing P. blanchardi populations in Israel (Kehat et al., 1976).^p^pThe effectiveness of biological control agents against P. blanchardi appears to be dependent upon the predators ability to adapt to the region, fecundity and consumption rate. Predators have been recorded to provide up to 45% mortality in the pest populations (Gharib, 1973). Release of the predators Chilocorus bipustulatus and C. bipustulatus var. iranensis into date palm grooves in Mauritania, Niger, and Tunisia, respectively, provided an acceptable level of control for P. blanchardi (Stansly, 1984; de Montaigne et al., 1986;Khoualdia et al., 1993, 1997). Muralidharan (1994) reported a consumption rate of over 1300 diaspidids over the lifespan of the predator, Chilocorus nigritus. In a comparison of three predators, Pharoscymnus horni was the most effective against the pest in India (Swaminathan and Verma, 1991).

management_info: Sanitary Measures^p^pInfested host fruits should be plucked or those that fall on the ground should be collected and buried deep in the soil. Proper sanitation in fields and orchards is essential. After harvest no fruit should be left unpicked because they become the source of later infestation.^p^p^Physical Control^p^pWrapping or bagging individual fruit to prevent oviposition by females is also effective.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe use of chemical control based on bait sprays and relatively less hazardous insecticide such as malathion seem to be the most convenient and efficient control methods available (Roessler, 1989). The insecticide is usually mixed with protein hydrolysate to form a bait spray. Individuals of both sexes are strongly attracted to a protein source from which ammonia emanates. Practical details have been summarized by Bateman (1982).^p^p^Male Annihilation^p^pMethyl eugenol is an effective attractant to the males of B. zonata. It can be mixed with insecticide (preferably malathion) and protein bait and can be used in traps. Male annihilation by using attractant would be effective in reducing the population to a very low level if carried out on a large scale.^p^p^Plant Quarantine^p^pPrevention of B. zonata from establishing in fly-free areas may be achieved by strictly enforcing quarantine regulations. Import of host fruits and vegetables from areas of infestation without postharvest disinfestation treatment should not be allowed. Travellers may also carry infested hosts in their baggage and thorough checking at entry ports is essential.^p^p^Postharvest Treatment^p ^pMany countries, such as the mainland USA, forbid the import of susceptible fruit without strict post-harvest treatment having been applied by the exporter. This may involve fumigation, heat treatment (hot vapour or hot water), cold treatments, insecticidal dipping or irradiation (Armstrong and Couey, 1989; Armstrong, 1997). Irradiation is not accepted in most countries and many have now banned methyl bromide funigation. Heat treatment tends to reduce the shelf life of most fruits and so the most effective method of regulatory control is preferentially to restrict imports of a given fruit to areas free from fruit fly attack.

potential_eco_desc: This pathogen could have a great impact on olive production in southern Spain, especially in susceptible cultivars when wounds occur in the branches due to hail, frost damage, or mechanical harvesting of fruit.
description: During the springs of 2011 to 2014, we observed surface and rounded branch cankers (0.5 to 3 cm in diameter) and dieback of twigs on olive (Olea europaea) cvs. Arbequina and Picual in southern Spain. The test results demonstrate that Neofabraea vagabunda is pathogenic on olive twigs and that wounds are necessary for infection. To our knowledge, this is the first report of N. vagabunda causing cankers in Spain, having been previously registered only in Italy.

host_range: Primary hosts are wild and cultivated species in the family Rosaceae, primarily Malus spp., Crataegus spp., Sorbus spp., Pyrus spp. and Cotoneaster spp.; occasionally Cydonia spp. and Mespilus spp.; but rarely, if ever, Prunus spp. Secondary hosts in the
potential_eco_desc: R. insertum is an economic pest of apples in Europe and North America. Damage is due to direct feeding on the young leaves, shoots and buds. Most damage is caused in spring, when the flower buds are opening. Considerable crop yield losses can occur due to the constant sucking of sap, which decreases fruit set and can cause the premature fall of fruitlets. R. insertum is one of several aphid species responsible for considerable loss of crops annually, particularly in orchards that are not regularly sprayed (Rogerson, 1947; Evenhuis, 1968).^p^pR. insertum is also a pest of cereals, due to its ability to transmit the persistent barley yellow dwarf luteovirus (BYDV). All the major cereal aphids are vectors of BYDV, including Rhopalosiphum padi, Sitobion avenae and Metopolophium dirhodium, in addition to R. insertum. Yield losses due to early season inoculation with BYDV can be as high as 35-44% in wheat, 35-51% in barley and 67-81% in oats (Vickerman and Wratten, 1979). R. insertum can also transmit potato Y potyvirus N (PVYN) (Van Hoof, 1980).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pIn apple orchards, chemical washes have been used in winter against eggs and contact insecticide sprays applied after egg hatch, for control of R. insertum. Evenhuis (1968) questioned the effectiveness of treatments against eggs, which may be unnecessary and damaging to natural enemies. Aerial spraying in spring with methyl-demeton-S [demeton-S-methyl], azinphos-methyl or fenitrothion controlled R. insertum, even at ultra-low spraying rates (Cooke et al., 1976). Nordlander (1977) and Bonnemaison (1972) evaluated insecticides for aphid control in apples, with regard to their effect on natural enemies in integrated control programmes. Sato and Sasaki (1995) described insecticide treatments used on apples in Japan.^p^pThe insecticides demeton-S-methyl, monocrotophos, pyridaphenthion, beta-cyfluthrin, bifenthrin, deltamethrin, esfenvalerate, imidacloprid, cypermethrin, chlorpyrifos and pirimicarb have been effective at controlling cereal aphids, including R. insertum, transmitting barley yellow dwarf luteovirus in cereals (Igrc, 1990).^p^p^Early Warning Systems and Forecasting^p^pThe abundance of autumn migrants (gynoparae) caught in suction traps, while migrating from Poaceae to Rosaceae, has been correlated with numbers of oviparae found on apple leaves, in southern England, UK. Suction trap catch data has been used to predict the likelihood of attacks on apples in the spring (Vickerman and Wratten, 1979). The presence of anholocyclic clones in Southern Europe, living year-round on grasses, makes forecasting more difficult.^p^p^p^Biological ControlCarroll and Hoyt (1986) described Praon unicum as being a significant parasitoid of R. insertum on apples in Washington State, USA, where it contributed to the biological control of R. insertum. P. unicum was found on apple, peach and hawthorn (Crataegus). On apple, the presence of attending ants may interfere with biological control agents (Baumgartner et al., 1985).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pDifferent levels of resistance to R. insertum have been recorded in cultivars of bluegrass (Poa arachinfera and P. compressa) (Crocker et al., 1992).^p^p^p^IPM^p^pControl of R. insertum within integrated control programmes has been described for apple orchards in Sweden (Nordlander, 1977), the former Czechoslovakia (Stary, 1975) and France (Bonnemaison,^p1972).

host_range: Aleurothrixus floccosus can be regarded as a polyphagous whitefly species, having been recorded on more than twenty different plant genera of various families (Mound and Halsey, 1978). However, in the Mediterranean region where the whitefly was introduced
potential_eco_desc: As with most whitefly species, A. floccosus affects the host plant by the suction of sap from the infested young leaves. High infestations can be detrimental to young plants. Indirect damage is also caused by the large amount of honeydew produced by the nymphs. Nymphs of A. floccosus also produce large amounts of waxy filaments which stick to the honeydew, thus forming a continuous coat on the underside of the leaves, hardly permeable to insecticides and giving some form of protection to the whitefly nymphs. Another type of indirect damage is the formation of sooty moulds on the honeydew which impairs the photosynthetic process of the plant part affected.^p^pIt is difficult to assess the economic impact of A. floccosus where it has been introduced as a pest on Citrus spp. During the initial introduction of the pest in the new geographical regions the damage caused was substantial. This was mainly the result of dense populations of insects on the leaf undersides producing copious honeydew and waxy filaments on which black sooty moulds grew. This interfered with the normal physiological activity of the host plant, and in the case of nurseries, young citrus trees were severely affected. However, the establishment of a number of introduced natural enemies effectively controlled the pest and the economic impact was very much reduced.
author: CPC2006

remark: Aleurothrixus floccosus is mainly transported via infested plant material and it is thus recommended that phytosanitary measures should be enforced to limit further spread of the insect.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Biological Control^p^pThe most important contributions to controlling Aleurothrixus floccosus have been through biological control programmes. In several Mediterranean countries where the pest was introduced, two species of hymenopteran parasitoids, Amitus spiniferus (Platygasteridae) and Cales noacki (Aphelinidae), were introduced. In the northern regions A. spiniferus became well established and showed appreciable parasitic activity (see, for example, Arzone and Vidano, 1983). C. noacki was better able to adapt itself wherever it was introduced, reaching high parasitization levels on the whitefly nymphs everywhere (see, for example, Longo et al., 1985). In citrus groves where chemical control was not applied, C. noacki was found to parasitize 99% of A. floccosus young stages, thus depressing the whitefly populations to very low levels throughout the year. C. noacki development may slow down with the high temperatures and low relative humidities of summer in such a way that high infestations of the whitefly may occur towards late summer-early autumn. This increase of the pest whitefly population is, however, controlled again as conditions favour the development of C. noacki. However, C. noacki does not attack populations with heavily pigmented nymphs and pupae (see comment under Taxonomy and Nomenclature).^p^pIn 1996 an attempt was made to control A. floccosus in Uganda by introduction of C. noacki. It was successfully imported and was reported to be established in field cages (IIBC, 1997).

host_range: The host range of P. lilacinus is extremely wide. Comprehensive lists of alternative host plants may be found in Williams (1982), Cox (1989) and Ben-Dov (1994). P. lilacinus attacks cocoa, guavas, coffee and other tropical and sub-tropical fruits and shad
potential_eco_desc: P. lilacinus is a pest of cocoa throughout the Oriental Region and South Pacific area (Szent-Ivany and Catley, 1960; Pillai, 1987; Cox, 1989), causing severe damage to young trees by killing the tips of branches. It also occurs on and causes damage to a wide variety of economically important crops such as coffee (Sekhar, 1964; Chacko and Sreedharan, 1981), tamarinds (Butani, 1978), custard apples [Annona reticulata] (Butani, 1976; Shukla and Tandon, 1984), coconuts (Fernando and Kanagaratnam, 1987), Citrus (Cox, 1989), grapes, guavas and mangoes (Tandon and Verghese, 1987). It has increased and spread to most coffee-growing areas, attacking roots and shoots and causing serious damage to the plant (Sekhar, 1964). The importance of the species has warranted its control using chemicals and biological control agents in several parts of India, mainly on coffee, cocoa, custard apples and mandarins (see Control).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Biological Control^p^pIn India, the ladybird Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, from Australia, reared in the laboratory on pumpkins and released on a coffee plantation, virtually eliminated the mealybug (Chacko et al., 1978; Prakasan, 1987). Mani and Krishnamoorthy (1990) demonstrated that the predators Spalgis epeus and C. montrouzieri cleared P. lilacinus on fruits in pomegranate orchards around Bangalore, Karnakata in India in 1986-88. The release, recovery and efficacy of C. montrouzieri on P. lilacinus in India have been described (Anon., 1978).^p^pOn the other hand, although Leptomastix dactylopii, an encyrtid parasitoid of Planococcus citri, was found to be responsible for the suppression of P. lilacinus in lime orchards, mass releases of either L. dactylopii or C. montrouzieri did not have any impact in guava orchards in southern India (Mani, 1995a). Again in India, L. dactylopii released in 49 coffee estates in Karnataka established better in 19 estates where P. citri, rather than P. lilacinus, was the predominant mealybug (Reddy et al., 1992). Another field trial in India on mandarins and coffee (Nagarkatti et al., 1992) showed that L. dactylopii appeared to be specific to P. citri in the field. ^p^p^Chemical/Integrated Control^p^pIn Tamil Nadu in India, a field trial conducted to evaluate seven insecticides and coconut oil showed that monocrotophos was the best, followed by coconut oil treatment (Dhandapani et al., 1992). In Kerala, India, soil application of dimethoate was the best of several systemic insecticides tested (Kumar and Prakasan, 1992). Other compounds found to be effective against P. lilacinus in India were a combination of kerosene and parathion-methyl, kerosene alone (Kumar et al., 1989) and monocrotophos (integrated with the release of C. montrouzieri). The insecticides fenthion, phosphamidon, quinalphos, dimethoate, phosalone and endosulfan, in descending order of effectiveness, also gave good control. In another report from Karnakata, India, isofenphos was effective against P. lilacinus on roots of both robusta and arabica coffee (Chacko and Sreedharan, 1981), whilst the same insecticide together with one or both of the fungicides triadimefon and oxycarboxin gave complete control of both the mealybug and an associated fungus (Diacanthodes sp.). The mealybug species involved, however, might be a misidentification of Planococcus fungicola later described by Watson and Cox (1990). ^p^pIt should be noted that, where hymenopteran parasitoids are important in regulating P. lilacinus populations, use of insecticides may well cause a population increase of the mealybug by eliminating its natural enemies.

description: A disease with typical LBVD symptoms was first observed in Israel in December 2010 in two commercial fields in the Besor region in the southwest of Israel. Further surveys for LBVD and assays for the presence of associated pathogens were carried out in three lettuce growing cycles during August, October, and December 2011 in two commercial fields in Sde Nitzan (N31°1308.03, E34°2503.32) and Ein HaBesor (N31°1554.74, E34°2814.33) in the southwest of Israel. Sampling and analysis confirming that Olpidium spp. was present in the lettuce roots. Associated viruses were identified, the results show that LBVD caused by Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus (MLBVV) and Lettuce big-vein associated varicosavirus.  LBVD is associated with a complex of two viruses, lettuce big-vein associated virus (LBVaV) and Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus (MLBVV), which are transmitted by motile zoospores of the soil-borne fungus Olpidium spp.
reference_name: First Report of Lettuce Big Vein Disease Caused by Olpidium spp., Mirafiori Lettuce Big-Vein Virus, and Lettuce Big-Vein Associated Virus in Israel

host_range: 莴苣Lactuca sativa
description: Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is a common vegetable in Saudi Arabia, being cultivated on more than 4000 ha either in open fields or in greenhouses. In March 2014, field lettuce crops were surveyed in the Riyadh region and around 40% of plants were observed to have virus-like symptoms including vein clearing, stunting, deformed leaves and thickening of the main veins . These symptoms resemble those caused by Lettuce big-vein disease (LBVD), an important disease of lettuce worldwide. Lettuce big-vein associated virus (LBVaV) and Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus (MiLBVV) are associated with LBVD. Nineteen samples (17 symptom-bearing and two symptomless) were collected from the fields, Based on molecular detection showed that 16 of the 17 lettuce samples showing symptoms were infected with LBVaV, nine with MiLBVV and eight with both LBVaV and MiLBVV. To our knowledge, this is the first report of the occurrence of LBVD-associated viruses LBVaV and MiLBVV in Saudi Arabia.  Lettuce big-vein associated virus (LBVaV) and Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus (MiLBVV) are transmitted by the soil fungus Olpidium brassicae.
reference_name: First reports of Lettuce big-vein associated virus and Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus infecting lettuce in Saudi Arabia
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

potential_eco_desc: Lettuce was observed displaying mild to severe mosaic, leaf deformation, reduced growth, slight thickening of the main vein, and plant death. At the beginning of the epidemic there were just a few plants with visible symptoms and 7 days later the entire crop was affected, causing a loss of 93% of the plants.
description: From March to May 2012, a disease on lettuce was observed in the south region of Mexico City. It was estimated by counting the number of severely affected or dead plants in three plots. No thrips, aphids, or whiteflies were observed in the crop during this time. The samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was Lettuce big-vein associated virus. To our knowledge, this is the first report of LBVaV infecting lettuce in Mexico. Further surveys and monitoring of LBVaV incidence and distribution in the region, vector competence of olpidium species, and impact on the crop quality are in progress.  Mirafiori lettuce big-vein virus (MiLBVV), Lettuce big-vein associated virus (LBVaV), both transmitted by the soil-borne fungus Olpidium brassicae.

host_range: BWYV has an extremely wide host range including legumes, crucifers, lettuce, and many weed species and can cause diseases in several crops worldwide. Epiphyllum spp.  can serve as a reservoir for BWYV.
description: In 2015, an Epiphyllum hybrid with chlorotic spots was found in California. Twelve more Epiphyllum hybrids (six with chlorotic ring spots, mottle, or mosaic and six asymptomatic) were obtained from a commercial nursery in New York. BWYV was detected in three different hybrids of Epiphyllum spp., an observation validated by RT-PCR, sequencing, and graft transmission. To our knowledge, this is the first report of BWYV in orchid cactus. It remains unclear whether BWYV causes symptoms in either single or mixed infections in other species and hybrids of Epiphyllum spp.  BWYV is an aphid-transmitted species.
reference_name: First Report of Beet western yellows virus Infecting Epiphyllum spp.

host_range: In most of the early luteovirus descriptions, host range studies were based on symptomatology only. Furthermore, researchers mainly used test plants that are common hosts for TuYV and beet mild yellowing luteovirus (BMYV), such as Capsella bursa-pastoris,
potential_eco_desc: In the UK, Walsh et al. (1989) detected no significant differences in seed yield between TuYV-infected and uninfected plants that were removed from oilseed rape fields or grown under glass. When grown in a gauzehouse, only one of three cultivars tested showed a yield reduction due to TuYV infection. Smith and Hinckes (1985), however, reported that plots with high levels of natural infection showed a 10% reduction in seed yield compared with plots in which the infection level was reduced by spraying with aphicides to control the vector. Artificial inoculation of rape plants in field plots in the autumn, resulted in a 7-14% reduction in plant height from April to June and a 12-13% reduction in dry weight in May and June when compared with uninoculated control plots (Jay and Smith, 1995). Final seed yields were decreased by 26% and average seed size was also reduced.^p ^pIn Germany, yields from single plants of one breeding line and one cultivar, inoculated with TuYV at the 4- to 6-leaf stage, were reduced by 40 and 53%, respectively (Schroder, 1994).^p^pIn yield loss studies on two cultivars artificially inoculated with one TuYV isolate in the autumn and monitored for 3 years (1992/93 to 1994/95), significant reductions in seed yields were recorded (Graichen, 1997). In 1993, both cultivars yielded 12% less seed; in 1994, seed yields were reduced by 19 and 34% and, in 1995, by 18 and 22% when compared with virus-free plots. In the third year, a second TuYV isolate was used for the inoculation of trial plots. This isolate reduced yields by 22 and 28% in the two cultivars. The average reduction in seed yield over the 3 years was 20%; this is approximately equivalent to 8 dt/ha. In tests on seed quality, TuYV infection did not reduce the oil and protein contents, but did result in higher glucosinolate levels.

management_info: Resistant Crop Cultivars^p^pResistance to TuYV (as beet western yellows virus (BWYV)) under field exposure was detected by Thomas et al. (1990) in forage brassicas, including Brassica napus subsp. napus, B. napus subsp. napobrassica, B. oleracea var. viridis and B. rapa subsp. rapa.^p^pIn glasshouse and field experiments, 652 genotypes of summer and winter oilseed rape cultivars, actual breeding lines and resynthesized rape forms were screened for resistance to a highly virulent TuYV isolate from oilseed rape (Graichen, 1994; Graichen and Peterka, 1995). All of the rapeseed genotypes were susceptible to TuYV except for a single resynthesized form. Crosses of susceptible oilseed rape cultivars and breeding lines with the resistant resynthesized form resulted in progenies with different levels of TuYV resistance. Individual plants with high resistance to TuYV were selected. Experimental inoculation of these plants in the field produced no virus symptoms, very low infection rates and very low virus concentrations. This successful transfer of TuYV resistance to susceptible oilseed rape cultivars and breeding lines shows the future potential for developing resistant oilseed rape.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pIn the UK, applications of insecticides to control the aphid vectors of TuYV (Myzus persicae and Brevicoryne brassicae) in winter oilseed rape have produced unsatisfactory results (Hill et al., 1989; Walsh et al., 1989). Read and Hewson (1988) concluded that repeated treatments were necessary for sufficient vector control to reduce virus infestation. However, these repeated chemical applications are unacceptable to growers.^p^pIn the future, it may be possible to control virus vectors by treating seeds with insecticides to prevent early virus infection. This method is already used against aphid virus vectors in sugarbeet and winter barley crops.

potential_eco_desc: 在秋天的田间田块中芸苔的人工接种导致从四月到六月7－14％的植物高度的减少，而在五月和六月与非接种防治田块相比有12－13％的干燥重量的减少(Jay and Smith, 1995)。最终的种子产量减少26％而且种子的平均大小也在减少。 Artificial inoculation of rape plants in field plots in the autumn, resulted in a 7-14% reduction in plant height from April to June and a 12-13% reduction in dry weight in May and June when compared with uninoculated control plots (Jay and Smith, 1995). Final seed yields were decreased by 26% and average seed size was also reduced. 在两个在秋天被人工接种一个TuYV分离种以及监控3年(1992/93 到 1994/95)的品种的产量损失研究中，记录了种子产量的一个明显的减少(Graichen, 1997)。在1993年，两个品种都减少种子出产12％；在1994年，与无病毒的田块相比，种子产量减少19％和34％，和在1995年，种子产量减少1 8％和22％。在第三年中，第二个TuYV分离种被用于实验田块的接种。这个分离种在两个栽培品种中减少了22％和28％的产量。种子产量的平均减少在3年内超过20％；这大约相当于没公顷8 dt。在种子质量测试中，TuYV侵染不会减少含油量和蛋白质含量，但会导致较高的硫苷水平。 In yield loss studies on two cultivars artificially inoculated with one TuYV isolate in the autumn and monitored for 3 years (1992/93 to 1994/95), significant reductions in seed yields were recorded (Graichen, 1997). In 1993, both cultivars yielded 12% less seed; in 1994, seed yields were reduced by 19 and 34% and, in 1995, by 18 and 22% when compared with virus-free plots. In the third year, a second TuYV isolate was used for the inoculation of trial plots. This isolate reduced yields by 22 and 28% in the two cultivars. The average reduction in seed yield over the 3 years was 20%; this is approximately equivalent to 8 dt/ha. In tests on seed quality, TuYV infection did not reduce the oil and protein contents, but did result in higher glucosinolate levels.
author: zhangjianjun

management_info: 在英国，对冬芸苔的防治TuYV媒介蚜虫(桃蚜和甘蓝蚜)的杀虫剂的应用产生令人不满意的结果(Hill et al., 1989; Walsh et al., 1989)。在未来，很可能会通过杀虫剂处理种子来防治病毒媒介来防止初期的病毒侵染。这方法已经对甜菜和冬大麦上的病毒媒介蚜虫使用。 In the UK, applications of insecticides to control the aphid vectors of TuYV (Myzus persicae and Brevicoryne brassicae) in winter oilseed rape have produced unsatisfactory results (Hill et al., 1989; Walsh et al., 1989).In the future, it may be possible to control virus vectors by treating seeds with insecticides to prevent early virus infection. This method is already used against aphid virus vectors in sugarbeet and winter barley crops. 在温室和添加实验中，652个夏芸苔和冬芸苔品种的基因型、实际育种系和人工合成的油菜形式为抗来自芸苔的高毒性TuYV分离种的抗性进行筛选(Graichen, 1994; Graichen and Peterka, 1995)。 In glasshouse and field experiments, 652 genotypes of summer and winter oilseed rape cultivars, actual breeding lines and resynthesized rape forms were screened for resistance to a highly virulent TuYV isolate from oilseed rape (Graichen, 1994; Graichen and Peterka, 1995).

host_range: EMDV causes damage in important vegetable crops such as cucumber, eggplant, tomato, potato, and pepper. To our knowledge, this is the first report of EMDV infecting Podranea ricasoliana.
potential_eco_desc: EMDV infection in Podranea ricasoliana and other ornamental species seems to have a low impact but might be epidemiologically relevant since EMDV can be transmitted by several species of leafhoppers from these natural virus reservoirs to susceptible vegetable crops.
description: In September 2015, plants of Podranea ricasoliana (Tanfani) Sprague showing chlorotic mosaic or apical intervenial yellowing on leaves were observed in several private gardens in Náquera, Valencia, Spain. The samples were collected and identified. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays of extracts of these plants showed a positive reaction for Eggplant mottled dwarf virus (EMDV) with polyclonal antisera. Diagnosis was further confirmed through molecular identifications. To our knowledge, this is the first report of EMDV infecting P. ricasoliana.  EMDV can be transmitted by several species of leafhoppers from these natural virus reservoirs to susceptible vegetable crops.
reference_name: First Report of a Natural Infection of Eggplant mottled dwarf virus in Podranea ricasoliana Showing Leaf Intervenial Yellowing
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: EMDV was first reported from eggplant in Italy in the 1960’s and is endemic in the Mediterranean basin. It is mainly found in solanaceaous vegetables but was also identified occasionally infecting ornamentals of the genera Hibiscus, Lonicera, Pelargon ium and Pittosporum. This is the first report of EMDV infecting Hydrangea macrophylla. Whether the observed symptoms are caused by EMDV alone or by synergistic effects with HdRSV remains unresolved.
description: In May 2013, an unknown disease was observed in hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) in a nursery in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Symptoms observed consisted of flower breaking and vein clearing/banding. The samples were collected and identified, the causal agent was identified as Eggplant mottled dwarf virus (EMDV) by electron microscopy, RT-PCR and ELISA. This is the first report of EMDV infecting Hydrangea macrophylla. Whether the observed symptoms are caused by EMDV alone or by synergistic effects with Hydrangea ringspot virus remains unresolved.
reference_name: First report of Eggplant mottled dwarf virus causing flower breaking and vein clearing in Hydrangea macrophylla in Germany
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 百子莲属Agapanthus sp.
description: A survey to identify the presence of Eggplant mottled dwarf virus (EMDV) in cultivated and wild plants in Latium region, Italy, was conducted during September 2012. In the same area, potted plants of Agapanthus sp., with symptoms suggestive of virus infection were observed in a private garden of Minturno. The test demonstrated the identity of the virus isolated from diseased Agapanthus as EMDV. To our knowledge, this is the first report of natural infection of Agapanthus by EMDV. EMDV continues to be an economically important viral pathogen of several crops in Europe and this report of EMDV infection of an ornamental plant suggests its increasing host range and that infected Agapanthus might act as a potential reservoir for EMDV.
reference_name: First report of natural infection of Agapanthus sp. by Eggplant mottled dwarf virus (EMDV)

description: 在营养繁殖作物中，特别是在观赏性植物中，EMDV是通过感染的繁殖材料散布的。在不存在种子传播的情况下，到蔬菜作物中的再侵染可能是以一个媒介作媒介的，这媒介需要从自然的储存场所中获得病毒，可能是野草(El-Maataoui et al., 1985; Lockhart, 1987)。感染蔬菜再田间的分布型说明了一个效率低的空气中的媒介的活动(Martelli, 1990)，然而，它还未被鉴定出。通过蚜虫和叶蝉传播茄子和海桐花分离种的再三尝试是失败的(Rana and Franco, 1979; M. Conti, Istituto di Fitovirologia Applicato del CNR, Turin, Italy, personal communication, 1997)。 In vegetatively propagated crops, especially ornamentals, EMDV is disseminated through infected propagating material. In the absence of seed transmission, the recurrent infections to vegetable crops are likely to be mediated by a vector that acquires the virus from natural reservoirs, possibly weeds (El-Maataoui et al., 1985; Lockhart, 1987). The distribution pattern of infected vegetables in the field suggests the activity of an inefficient aerial vector (Martelli, 1990) which, however, has not been identified. Repeated attempts to transmit the eggplant and Pittosporum isolates by aphids and leafhoppers have failed (Rana and Franco, 1979; M. Conti, Istituto di Fitovirologia Applicato del CNR, Turin, Italy, personal communication, 1997).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: EMDV在它侵染的观赏性植物中没有很大的影响。相比之下，该病毒对蔬菜作物有严重和高度的损害。然而，它的经济影响是较小的，因为在茄子上和其他作物，如番茄(El-Maataoui et al., 1985; Castellano and Martelli, 1987)、辣椒和黄瓜(Roggero et al., 1995)上田间侵染的发病率是非常低的，在茄子上它很少超过1％(Martelli and Cirulli, 1969; Martelli et al., 1984; Cherif and Martelli, 1985; Martelli and Hamadi, 1986)。 EMDV does not appear to greatly affect any of the ornamentals it infects. In contrast, the virus is very severe and highly damaging to vegetable crops. Its economic impact, however, is minor because the incidence of field infections is very low, both in aubergine, where it rarely exceeds 1% (Martelli and Cirulli, 1969; Martelli et al., 1984; Cherif and Martelli, 1985; Martelli and Hamadi, 1986), and in other crops, such as tomato (El-Maataoui et al., 1985; Castellano and Martelli, 1987), pepper and cucumber (Roggero et al., 1995).

potential_eco_desc: It is not clear how widespread TaVCV is in American Samoa, it should now be possible to investigate the incidence of TaVCV in the territory.
description: In August of 2016, taro plants (Colocasia esculenta cv. Samoa red 2) exhibiting leaf-vein chlorosis and streaks along the petioles, similar to the symptoms caused by Taro vein chlorosis virus (TaVCV), were observed on the extension plot (14.319176°S, 170.740749°W) of the American Samoa Community College’s Division of Agriculture, Community, and Natural Resources. Only a few (<5%) plants exhibited symptoms, and no symptoms were observed at two nearby taro farms. Based on molecular diagnostics confirming TaVCV was presented in the symptomic taro plants. This is the first report of TaVCV infecting taro in American Samoa and only the second report in the U.S.
reference_name: First Report of Taro vein chlorosis virus on Taro (Colocasia esculenta) in the U.S. Territory of American Samoa
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 芋头Colocasia esculenta cv. Iliuaua
description: In March 2013, taro plants (Colocasia esculenta [L.] Schott cv. Iliuaua) with leaves displaying veinal chlorosis and necrosis were observed on the island of Molokai. These symptoms were similar to those of taro vein chlorosis, a disease of taro caused by Taro vein chlorosis virus (TaVCV; family Rhabdoviridae, genus Nucleorhabdovirus). The test demonstrated that the pathogen was TaVCV. These findings, representing the first detection of TaVCV in Hawaii and the United States.
reference_name: First Report of Taro vein chlorosis virus Infecting Taro (Colocasia esculenta) in the United States

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pMeasures to control V. nigrum in conservation areas and biological preserves have significant costs in herbicide and labour. Records of impact on crop production are not available.^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pV. nigrum and V. rossicum successfully dominate susceptible natural areas, which can lead to loss of biodiversity. Change of habitat structure affects fauna populations. Cover of native plant species is greatly reduced where V. nigrum is dominant. ^p^pThe ability to dominate the woodland herbaceous layer raises concerns about forest regeneration.^p^pIn Europe, Vincetoxicum species are important alternate hosts for cronartium rust and resin-top, Cronartium flaccidum, in conifer trees, although no information is available on the susceptibility of V. nigrum to the rust (Kaitera, 1999).^p^p^p^Social impact^pPersistent, intractable infestations of V. nigrum have discouraged gardeners in some cities of the northeastern USA. Large infestations have interfered with management of, and access to, amenity areas.^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pAt least one endemic species, Astragalus robbinsii var. jesupii, is under pressure by an expanding population of V. nigrum. ^p^pBoth V. nigrum and V. rossicum may have negative impact on monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus) reproduction, as empty eggs have been found in the field. Experiments in field cages and in the laboratory indicate that larvae hatched from eggs oviposited on stems die in early instar stages (Casagrande and Dacy, 2001; DiTommaso and Losey, 2003).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; environment; forestry production; human health; native fauna; native flora; rare / protected species; tourism
description: The earliest herbarium record for North America is from 1854, and was collected in Ipswich, Essex County, Massachusetts, USA. The next, collected in 1864 from the same county, indicates that the plant escaped from a botanic garden in Essex County, Massachusetts. The first herbarium record in New York State was 1874. By the twentieth century it was known from 9 states, and is currently in at least 16 states of the USA (Sheeley, 1992). The first herbarium record in Canada was from Montreal, 1949, near the arboretum of Notre Dame College (Pringle, 1973). Regional flora, such as Gray's Manual of Botany (1868 edition), indicate that the plant escaped from cultivation in gardens.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pSeeds are wind-dispersed, bearing the tuft of hairs, or coma, typical of the milkweed family. Seeds of the related species Vincetoxicum rossicum travel up to 18 m at an average wind speed of 11.2 km/h from their release point, with 50% falling within 2.5 m (Cappuccino et al., 2002).^p^pVector Transmission (Biotic)^p^pVincetoxicum spp. can be transported by man, through garden cultivation and possible decorative use of dried fruits on the vine, as witnessed in an infested tourist area in New York, USA. Presence on transportation corridors suggests enhanced wind dispersal. Seeds have been observed in trouser cuffs of hikers and hunters.^p^pAgricultural Practices^p^pVincetoxicum seeds can be moved via hay sales from infested hay fields, sale of nursery stock and Christmas trees.^p^pAccidental Introduction^p^pPossible new introductions by seed travelling with agricultural commodities are possible.^p^pIntentional Introduction^p^pSeed appears to be available on the internet in The Netherlands and Sweden.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: .^p - Fruits (inc. remark: Further spread of V. nigrum is ongoing by wind-dispersed seeds. Accidental introductions will continue via agricultural commodities, contaminated soil and vines/seeds caught on equipment. The attractive flowers and pods invite collection by an uneducated public.^p^pThe state of Vermont, USA, has included V. nigrum in a noxious weed quarantine list. It is included on invasive plant lists for New York State and the New England states, but the lists have no regulatory power.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pThere are no reports of cultural control of V. nigrum. Grazing of V. hirundinaria by sheep has been investigated with mixed conclusions, from no grazing, to nibbling young plants, to voracious feeding ( Haeggstrom, 1990). The closely related species V. rossicum has been suppressed in cattle pastures in New York State, USA, with release when cattle were removed. ^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pMowing, pulling and other top destruction methods have poor long-term success for control of V. nigrum, as there is rapid regrowth from perennating buds. Effective timing of cutting, as fruit begin to enlarge, will prevent maturation of the seed crop and prevent successful recovery to form a new seed crop. Digging must remove the rhizomes and root crown.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pTriclopyr has been more effective at reducing the related species V. rossicum than has glyphosate (Lawlor and Raynal, 2002). A systemic herbicide must be used against this perennial plant.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pPossibilities for biological control of V. nigrum are being investigated (Tewksbury et al., 2002). The chemical signature of Old World Asclepiadaceae may separate Vincetoxicum spp. from Asclepiadaceae species of the New World for effective host specificity.^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pPrevention and early eradication are the best control strategies for V. nigrum. Seed crops from upwind infestations must be managed to successfully prevent new infestations.
