remark: Further spread is highly likely due to contamination by seed of N. trichotoma of agricultural seed and wool, which could lead to long-distance or intercontinental dispersal, and by farm animals (externally or internally) and machinery for in-country spread. Its potential distribution in Australia is calculated at 32 million ha, currently it infests just over 1 million ha (McLaren et al., 1998).^p^pN. trichotoma is a proclaimed noxious weed in South Africa, and subject to all provisions of the Weed Act of 1937 (Wells, 1978). It is a declared noxious weed in New South Wales (1938), Victoria (1954), South Australia and Tasmania (1959) (Campbell and Vere, 1995; McLaren et al., 1998). An action plan, funded by the State government, has been enforced in Tasmania to isolate and contain N. trichotoma (Goninon, 1998). Government Committees in New South Wales oversee the control of N. trichotoma, and special low interest loans are available to landholders to implement recommended control measures. N. trichotoma was designated as a Federal Noxious Weed in the USA in 1983 (Westbrooks and Cross, 1993). However, in a somewhat bizarre case, N. trichotoma was intercepted in eight shipments of tall fescue grass seed from Argentina by USA quarantine in 1988, but no action could be taken because legislation was not in place to prevent onward distribution. By the time a recall order was granted, Festuca seed totalling over 24,000 kg, heavily-infested with N. trichotoma, had already been sold in the states of Illinois, Kentucky, Missouri and both North and South Carolina (Westbrooks, 1991; Westbrooks and Cross, 1993).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pGrazing by cattle and sheep cannot control N. trichotoma; however, at low weed density (10% of an improved pasture), goats can help to restrict weed population density (Campbell, 1982). Nevertheless, most reports claim that N. trichotoma is unpalatable and that animals will not readily graze it (Wells and de Beer, 1987). N. trichotoma burns readily but is quick to recover, whilst associated species are killed (Healy, 1945). Thus, ideal conditions are created for massive weed infestation because of the large seedbank (Campbell, 1982; Wells and de Beer, 1987). In general, therefore, burning can increase rather than decrease weed populations.^p^pAfforestation has been used in both Australia and New Zealand to control N. trichotoma, especially with Pinus radiata (Healy, 1945; Campbell, 1982). However, it can take up to 6 years to shade-out the weed and prevent flowering, and a further 4 years before the tussocks die (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992; Miller, 1998). The planting of hedges or living windbreaks to trap windblown panicles has been practised in both Australia and South Africa (Campbell, 1982; Wells and de Beer, 1987).^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pChipping, or severing the root system, has successfully been practised in New Zealand, following-on from other control measures, but is mainly used to kill isolated plants (Healy, 1945; Denne, 1988).^p^pPloughing can also have an impact but only in combination with other techniques (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pBoth glyphosate and flupropanate have proven to be effective against N. trichotoma in Australia and, despite its slow action, flupropanate has been favoured until recently because of its ease of use, low mammalian toxicity and selectivity, especially when applied in late spring (Campbell and Ridings, 1988). In addition, it was found that herbicide residues in the soil killed the next flush of N. trichotoma seedlings (Campbell, 1998). Glyphosate has recently been shown to be effective in preventing seedhead production, if applied in spring, 2-8 weeks prior to seedhead emergence (Campbell et al., 1998).^p^pOn non-arable land in Australia, aerial application of flupropanate, pasture seed and fertilizer has been used: control depends on replacing N. trichotoma with a strongly competitive pasture (Campbell, 1998). Spot-spraying with flupropanate has been favoured by landholders in New South Wales but this involves frequent inspection.^p^pLong-term trials have continued with flupropanate for management of N. trichotoma and initial results suggest that boom or aerial application at 3- or 10-year intervals could economically control the weed over large areas (Campbell et al., 2002). Unfortunately, flupropanate has since been withdrawn from sale in Australia and glyphosate now remains the only herbicide option (Campbell and Nicol, 2001).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pGrasses are difficult targets for classical biological control, particularly using arthropod natural enemies, because of the uniform, simplistic architecture which favours polyphagy (Evans, 1991). Moreover, N. trichotoma was considered to be too closely-related to native Australian Stipa spp. 'to allow the introduction of agents' (Wapshere, 1990). However, this changed when the Australian tussock species were found to be so phylogentically distinct that they were accommodated in the new genus, Austrostipa (Jacobs and Everett, 1996). Several fungal pathogens, including the rust Puccinia nassellae and the smut Ustilago hypodytes, are currently being assessed in Argentina as potential biocontrol agents of N. trichotoma in Australia (Briese and Evans, 1998; Briese et al., 2000).^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pNone of the methods outlined above can be used in isolation, and the management focus has now changed from trying to kill millions of seedlings, per hectare, up to 3400 million (Healy, 1945), by blanket coverage with herbicide, to promoting pasture competition and the strategi

host_range: V. persica is principally a weed of cereal crops, beets and oilseed rape in temperate regions of the world. It is also commonly reported as a weed of vegetables, plantation crops, orchards, vineyards and leguminous crops (Holm et al., 1997).
potential_eco_desc: V. persica has been reported as a weed of 27 crops in 45 countries (Holm et al., 1997), and according to Holm et al. (1991) is a serious or principal weed in 10 countries. In a survey of 2359 fields growing either winter wheat or winter barley in the UK, V. persica was one of the four most common broad-leaved weeds (Whitehead and Wright, 1989). Although V. persica has been shown to compete with crop plants for nitrogen (Welbank, 1963), its effect on crop yield is slight. In the UK, densities from 45 to 3685 plants/m2 did not effect the yield of wheat (Wilson and Wright, 1990). Lutman et al. (1993) reported similar findings in oilseed rape with V. persica having no effect on crop yields at all densities tested. The application of urea-based herbicides for grass control can lead to an increase in the density of V. persica, and in some instances this may result in lodging of crop plants.^p^pV. persica has been reported as an alternative host for a range of crop pests and pathogens. Alternaria linicola is able to survive on the weed between successive linseed (Linum usititassimum) crops (Vloutoglou et al., 1995). It also acts as a host for beet western yellows luteovirus (Stevens et al., 1994), clover yellow vein potyvirus (Okuda et al., 1992), Verticillium dahliae (Mesturino, 1990) and the melon aphid, Aphis gossypii (Natazo, 1988). Roots of V. persica may be colonized by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. lini (Lacicowa et al., 1987) and Myzus ascalonicus may overwinter on the weed in strawberry fields (Karl, 1983).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pThe ability of V. persica to root at the nodes makes it difficult to control mechanically (Herrmann et al., 1986), as disturbed plants are able to reroot following surface cultivation (Roberts and Stokes, 1966). The emergence and density of seedlings may be affected by the timing and nature of cultivation practices. In trials in New Zealand, emergence of V. persica was stimulated by autumn cultivation (Hartley and Popay, 1992) and in Germany, cultivation between one hour after sunset and midnight greatly reduced densities of broad-leaved weeds, including V. persica (Hartmann and Nezadal, 1990). Shallow tine cultivation without ploughing kept freshly shed weed seed in the upper 5 cm of the soil and resulted in an increase in the density of V. persica (Knab and Hurle, 1986), indicating that shallow depth or minimal cultivation is not effective for its control.^p^pV. persica does not grow well in shade and establishment of a dense crop population is an effective method of reducing population densities. Fitter and Ashmore (1974) found that a dense tobacco canopy could reduce growth of V. persica by 90%.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pA wide range of herbicides have proved successful for controlling V. persica. Dithiopyr resulted in excellent control in wheat and barley (Parrish, 1993). In field trials conducted throughout Europe, thidiazimin controlled V. persica in cereals (Weiler et al., 1993). Efforts to exclude G. aparine from conservation headlands in cereal fields in the UK by spraying with quinmerac also achieved successful control of V. persica (Boatman, 1991). In oilseed rape, pyridate and benazolin + clopyralid gave good control and metazachlor applied both pre- and post-emergence adequate control of V. persica (Makepeace and Turner, 1990). In sugarbeet, phenmedipham + ethofumesate gave good control (Bonin and Heckl, 1988) as did autumn applications of chlorsulfuron and metsulfuron-methyl in winter cereals (Selley et al., 1985). A mixture of trifluralin + linuron successfully controlled V. persica in spring peas (Daniau, 1981), trifluralin was also effective in runner and dwarf beans (Roberts et al., 1974).Mamarot and Rodriguez (1997) list recommended herbicides for crops in France, including dimethenamid for maize; aclonifen for legumes, potato and sunflower; alachlor for soyabean and maize; atrazine for maize and sorghum; fluchloridone for peas and sunflower; hexazinone for lucerne; metolachlor and metribuzin for soyabean; prosulfocarb for cereals and potato; sulcitrone for linseed; trifluralin for cereals, soyabean and sunflower; also many herbicide mixtures and combinations.^p^pV. persica is tolerant of chlortoluron (Gonneau et al., 1988).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pNo attempts at biological control are reported in the literature.

description: One of the major diseases that affect figs is the fig mosaic disease (FMD), which was reported in China in 1935. A causal agent of this disease is associated with the Fig mosaic virus (FMV), a negative-strand RNA virus with six RNA segments. In 2013, and later during a survey in 2014, fig plants in several orchards in Xinjiang displayed symptoms of a virus-like disease, which was characterized as FMD. These symptoms included chlorotic clearing as well as banding of leaf veins along with various patterns of discoloration, severely distorted leaves, and deformed fruits. The test demonstrated that the causal agent was Fig mosaic virus (FMV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of FMV in fig trees in China.

potential_eco_desc: In the spring of 1989 in the USA, bacterial fruit blotch of watermelon first occurred in commercial watermelon fields in Florida and, as the season progressed, the disease was observed in South Carolina, North Carolina, Maryland, Delaware, and Indiana (Somodi et al., 1991; Latin and Rane, 1990). In some fields, losses were more than 90% of the total marketable fruit. Since then, the disease also has been found in Alabama, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Iowa, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma, Oregon and Texas. Bacterial fruit blotch of watermelon has continued to be a threat to the watermelon industry in the USA. In most years, the disease has occurred in relatively few fields but has been devastating in many of these, sometimes resulting in the loss of all marketable fruit. Losses to individual growers have been over $100,000 in many of these cases (D. Hopkins, University of Florida, USA, personal communication, 1997). Fruit blotch was prevalent in Georgia in 1992 and was especially widespread in 1994, causing losses in thousands of hectares distributed over at least 10 states.

description: Incidence^p^pThere are very few reports of the incidence of A. avenae subsp. citrulli in commercial seed lots. However, the infection level generally has been low, because in heavily infected seed lots the bacterium would have been detected and seed would not have been sold. One commercial seed lot was reported, in a grow-out test, to have one infected seed in 9000 (Rane and Latin, 1992). Sowell and Schaad (1979) reported disease incidence on USA plant introductions of watermelons to be over 50% in some cases, however this was based on only 25 seeds. Seed samples collected from symptomatic fruit have had infection levels over 80% (Kucharek et al., 1993).Walcott et al. (2003) investigated the role of watermelon blossom inoculation in seed infestation by A. avenae subsp. citrulli.  Approximately 98% (84/87) of fruit developed from blossoms inoculated with 1 x 10(7) or 1 x 10(9) c.f.u. of A. avenae subsp. citrulli per blossom were asymptomatic. Using immunomagnetic separation and PCR, A. avenae subsp. citrulli was detected in 44% of the seed lots assayed, despite the lack of fruit symptoms. Furthermore, viable colonies were recovered from 31% of the seed lots. Of these lots, 27% also yielded seedlings expressing bacterial fruit blotch symptoms when planted under conditions of 30°C and 90% RH. A. avenae subsp. citrulli was detected and recovered from the pulp of 33 and 19%, respectively, of symptomless fruit whose blossoms were inoculated with A. avenae subsp. citrulli. The ability to penetrate watermelon flowers was not unique to A. avenae subsp. citrulli, because blossoms inoculated with Pantoea ananatis also resulted in infested seed and pulp. The data indicate that watermelon blossoms are a potential site of ingress for fruit and seed infestation by A. avenae subsp. citrulli.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pThere does not appear to be any effect of A. avenae subsp. citrulli on seed quality. Seed appearance, germination and seedling vigour are unaffected.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pThe 1989 outbreak of bacterial fruit blotch of watermelon in the USA appeared to be initiated by contaminated seed. Disease symptoms appeared in Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Maryland, Delaware and Indiana, all within a few months. In Indiana, initial symptoms in diseased seedlings in commercial greenhouses were limited to distinct foci (Rane and Latin, 1992). Many of the fruit blotch infected greenhouses and fields were associated with a seed lot that was later shown to be infested with A. avenae subsp. citrulli. Laboratory and greenhouse tests have demonstrated transmission of the bacterium from infested seeds to as high as 80% of the seedlings from these seeds (Kucharek et al., 1993; Hopkins et al., 1996). Other studies have corroborated transmission of the pathogens by seeds. A. avenae subsp. citrulli was detected in 44% of the seed lots assayed using immunomagnetic separation and PCR. Viable colonies were recovered from 31% of the seed lots. Of these lots, 27% also yielded seedlings expressing bacterial fruit blotch symptoms when planted under conditions of 30°C and 90% RH (Walcott et al., 2003). In Australia, tests showed A. avenae subsp. citrulli  was readily seed transmissible from naturally infected rockmelon and honeydew fruit for at least 3 months after seed extraction (O'Brien and Martin, 1999). ^p^pInfested seed is the primary way in which A. avenae subsp. citrulli has been introduced into the transplant house or into watermelon fields (D. Hopkins, University of Florida, USA, personal communication, 1997). Alternative hosts can also serve as the source of inoculum into cucurbit fields.^p^p^Seed Treatments^p^pSeveral studies have been conducted on the control of bacterial fruit blotch of watermelon with seed treatments. management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pFruit of some cultivars are more susceptible to bacterial fruit blotch than others. The susceptibility of fruit appears to be related to rind colour. The most susceptible fruit are those with a light green rind, more tolerant are those with light and dark green stripes and most tolerant are those with a solid dark-green rind (Hopkins et al., 1993). Triploid watermelons are less susceptible to A. avenae subsp. citrulli than diploid watermelons (Rhodes et al., 1996). However, the level of tolerance currently available in commercial watermelon cultivars will not guarantee freedom from fruit blotch under conditions which favour disease development.^p^p^Exclusion of Pathogen^p^pThe ideal control is to prevent the introduction of A. avenae subsp. citrulli into the field (Hopkins, 1997). Plant seeds that have been tested for the presence of the fruit blotch bacterium. A negative assay is not proof that the seedlot is free of the bacterium, but does indicate that disease was not detected in a representative sample of the seedlot. Use transplants from houses in which there were no seedling symptoms of the fruit blotch disease.^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pCultural practices in the transplant house should include minimal manipulation of plants; decontamination of hands, plant containers, and tools after contact with plants; closing sides of the transplant house during storms or windy periods; and destroying discarded plant material. Spread of the bacterium in the greenhouse can be minimized by low humidity, low temperatures, and bottom watering (Hopkins, 1994; Latin et al., 1995). Irrigation with an overhead boom may result in splash dispersal of the bacteria throughout the greenhouse. Spread of the bacteria may be reduced by practices that minimize or eliminate long periods when leaves are wet. It would also be advisable to segregate different seed lots in the transplant house to reduce the chance of cross contamination. Decontaminate a transplant house that had infected seedlings and wait at least 2-3 weeks to plant cucurbits in it again. A 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution, as well as commercial bactericides, may be used for decontamination.^p^pThe possibility of A. avenae subsp. citrulli being introduced into the field from contaminated volunteer watermelons can be reduced by ploughing under debris, including watermelon culls, from an infected field (D. Hopkins, University of Florida, USA, personal communication, 1997). The current field should be planted as far as possible from the previous crop. Volunteer watermelon seedlings from previous crops should be destroyed immediately to eliminate potential sources of the fruit blotch bacterium. In northern growing areas, fruit blotch affected fields should be planted subsequently with crops that utilize herbicides that will kill volunteer watermelons. Eliminate wild cucurbits and volunteer cucurbits near transplant houses and production fields. Do not work in an infested field if the foliage is wet. Decontaminate irrigation or mechanical equipment before moving it from an infested field to a noninfested field.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pApplications of copper-containing fungicides at the full recommended rates have reduced the incidence of fruit blotch symptoms when applications were initiated prior to fruit set (Hopkins, 1991; Hopkins, 1995). If fruit blotch symptoms are observed, applications of copper-containing fungicides should begin at first flower, or earlier, and continue weekly until all fruit are mature. As a preventive treatment, biweekly applications of the full rate of copper or weekly applications at half the recommended rate of copper-containing fungicides may be used.
author: CPC2006

description: The fruit blotch bacterium may be introduced into a field from infested seed, infected transplants, contaminated volunteer crop cucurbits, or infected wild cucurbits. In the field, symptom development and spread of A. avenae subsp. citrulli on foliage and fruit is most rapid during periods when the weather is hot and humid, with thundershowers (Hopkins, 1993). These conditions are common during the summer. In addition to wind-driven rain, the bacterium can be spread by contact with farm workers, irrigation, and other cultivation equipment (D. Hopkins, University of Florida, USA, personal communication, 1997). The bacterium does not appear to spread as rapidly during cool, rainy weather. With favourable weather, a few primary infection sites in a field can result in infection of all plants by the time of harvest. Leaf lesions in the field do not result in defoliation, but are important reservoirs of bacteria for fruit infection. Under some environmental conditions, foliar symptoms may not be very conspicuous and the watermelon grower may not realize that there is a problem until fruit symptoms render the crop unmarketable.

potential_eco_desc: D. lycopersici occurs sporadically in Europe and New Zealand. Modern techniques used in tomato production (culture in nutrient solutions and rockwool) have eliminated soil as a source of inoculum and have, therefore, reduced disease incidence. Despite this, localized outbreaks do occur: in one glasshouse in West Sussex, UK, 105 basal lesions (affecting 12% of the tomato plants) were recorded in June 1985, 6 months after the plants were established on rockwool (Fagg and Fletcher, 1987).

management_info: Cultural Practices^p^pAvoid wounds and high rates of watering. Remove diseased plants. Debris from the previous season's crop should also be removed and destroyed. In glasshouses the humidity should be kept below 90% RH and the temperature above 15°C (Verhoeff, 1962; Fagg and Fletcher, 1987; van Steekelenburg, 1988). Solarization of soil and of the reed canes (Arundo donax) or Eucalyptus stakes used to support tomatoes reduces disease incidence (Besri, 1983; Cartia, 1989; Besri, 1991). ^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pResistance to D. lycopersici on F3- and Bc1-lines from interspecific crosses of L. esculentum with L. hirsutum and with L. hirsutum f. glabratum is not monogenic and is inherited in a dominant fashion (Boukema, 1982). Tomato grafting on the hybrid KNVF has shown resistance to D. lycopersici (Ginoux et al., 1978) but there is no tomato cultivar with complete resistance to the disease (Fagg and Fletcher, 1987).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pPreventive measures include spraying or drenching with iprodione, procymidone, dichlofluanid, maneb, folpet, captan, nabam and benomyl (Knight and Keyworth, 1960; Phillips, 1961; Channon, 1972; Cheah and Soteros, 1983; 1987; van Steekelenburg, 1988; Cheah et al., 1992). Following infection, satisfactory control can be achieved by painting isolated lesions with a mixture of benomyl or iprodione and a mineral oil (Fletcher and Sharpe, 1978; van Steekelenburg, 1988). In systems using the nutrient film technique, a combination of etridiazole or ethyl phosphonate and carbendazim or benomyl placed in the nutrient solution controls the disease (Staunton and Cormican, 1980). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pTrichoderma harzianum strain VKM F-2477D gives good control of D. lycopersici and results in yield increases (Grin'ko, 1997). Favaron et al. (1993) demonstrated inhibition of D. lycopersici polygalacturonase by Allium cepa and A. porrum extracts.

description: A survey to identify pathogens causing peony diseases in southern Chile (37°95′ to 40°58′S) was conducted from 2008 to 2011. A noticeable symptom consisted of small red spots on peony leaves, stems, sepals, and first petals of the bud. The samples were collected and identified, based on morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity test showed that the causal agent was Mycocentrospora acerina. This is the first report of M. acerina on P. lactiflora globally.

potential_eco_desc: E. crus-galli is reported to be among the three most serious weeds of rice in many countries in Asia, and is a major weed in a wide range of crops throughout the tropical and subtropical world (Holm et al., 1991). It competes with crops for nutrients, water and light. In India, Varghese and Nair (1986) concluded that it competed with transplanted rice for N and K during days 11-50 and for P during days 21-40 after planting. There is also some evidence for further effects via allelopathy on maize (Bhowmik and Doll, 1980).^p^pMost evidence for the economic effects of E. crus-galli are from rice, and a range of studies have measured the losses caused in this crop. In transplanted rice in Sri Lanka, the threshold density of E. crus-galli for season-long competition was 5 plants per square m, at which level grain yield losses were 8-17% (Senanayake et al., 1986). In Brazil, season-long infestation reduced yields by 45% (Velez, 1982). In Malaysia, it was estimated that using a scale of 1-10 (10 = complete weed cover) there was a 7% rice yield loss for every unit increase of E. crus-galli infestation compared with no infestation (Lo et al., 1992). In China, Gu and Zhao (1984) note that E. crus-galli infests seedbeds and is often transplanted with the crop. It may then grow faster than the crop and compete for light. One E. crus-galli per 3 rice plants per hill reduced yield by 38%. When the weed only germinates after transplanting, damage may be much less. Chisaka (1977) showed losses of 16% when 20 E. crus-galli per square m germinated soon after transplanting but no reduction if germination was delayed for 12 days. In other studies in Japan, Chisaka (1977) showed that E. crus-galli was much more competitive than Monochoria vaginalis - 50 E. crus-galli per square m caused a 23% yield loss while M. vaginalis caused only 6% loss. He also showed that competition was for both nutrients and light and that additional nitrogen in the top-dressing could result in increased competition (12% loss compared with 9% loss with basal fertilizer only) presumably due to more luxuriant growth and increased competition for light.^p ^pIn direct-sown rice damage may be more consistently serious. In India, unchecked weed growth of E. crus-galli in direct-seeded lowland rice can cause a 53% reduction in grain yield (Ali and Sankaran, 1984). Also in India, Paradkar et al. (1998) recorded 30% yield loss from 15 E. crus-galli per square m and 40-61% loss from infestations of 30-120 per square m. In Malaysia, Azmi et al. (1992) reported that in direct-seeded rice, competition with the weed during the first 15 days after sowing had no significant effects on yield, whereas competition beyond this caused severe reductions in yields; only 10 plants per square m were required to cause yield reductions of approximately 18.7% (representing 1 t/ha). In Colombia, weeds which emerged with the crop, including E. crus-galli, were the most damaging to yield, and rice yields increased with longer weed-free periods up to 70 days after emergence (Fischer et al., 1993). In water-sown rice in Korea, the number of plants, panicles per plant, spikelets per panicle and yield showed highly negative correlations with the growth rate of E. crus-galli, and a weed-free period for the first 30-45 days after sowing was required in order to avoid any yield loss (Huh et al., 1995). In Cuban rice fields, a yield reduction of 70% was recorded at E. crus-galli densities of 200 weeds per square m (Antigua and Armenta Soto, 1993). In Brazil, de Andrade (1982) reported losses of 16, 25, 70 and 80% from infestations of 5, 10-20, 40-60 and 80-100 weeds square m, respectively. In the USA, Stauber et al. (1991) recorded 50% loss from about 20 E. crus-galli per square m. There was further yield reduction up to 40 plants per square m, but no greater loss at higher infestations.^p^pRecent studies demonstrate that not all rice varieties are equally affected by E. crus-galli. management_info: Cultural Control^p^pHand weeding can be effective if adequate labour is available, but when young, E. crus-galli is hard to distinguish from young rice, making hand weeding very difficult.Bhatia et al. (1990) found that high populations of E. crus-galli in rice fields were due to new seed added every season. Pot and field studies revealed that 97.7% of the seed reserves were exhausted in one season, and by the third season the soil was free of viable seed. Farmyard manure and other organic fertilizers can be major sources of weed seeds, including E. crus-galli, but these lose their viability after being subjected to anaerobic fermentation for one month (Sarapatka et al., 1993).^p^pDeep water flooding (up to 22 cm) can provide good control of E. crus-galli in rice (Williams et al., 1990). Water-sowing, a method of direct-broadcast sowing of rice, began in California, USA, during the 1920s as a cultural method to control E. crus-galli var. crus-galli by continuously-flooded water management (Seaman, 1983).^p^pThe use of Azolla in transplanted irrigated rice failed to suppress E. crus-galli var. hispidula, which increased by 226.4%, whereas some weeds were suppressed (Janiya and Moody, 1984). Field and laboratory studies in Asia have indicated that some rice cultivars exhibited strong allelopathic effects against E. crus-galli (Olofsdotter et al., 1996; Chung et al., 1997).^p^pChung (1995) found that dried lucerne residues inhibited germination and seedling growth of the weeds E. crus-galli, Siegesbechia viridis and Portulaca oleracea, as well as several crops.^p^pDifferent tillage systems in soyabean and maize fields in northern Italy have been shown to profoundly alter the weed community, with species linked to increased disturbance being annuals, such as E. crus-galli (Sarapatka et al., 1993).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pTsukamoto (1997) describes using virulent isolates of Exserohilum monoceras (anamorph of Septosphaeria monoceras) and Cochliobolus sativus to achieve an approximate 80% reduction in dry matter of different botanical varieties of E. crus-galli. Zhang (1997a) studied optimal temperature and dew-point for the development of E. monoceras on E. crus-galli and E. colonum after inoculation.^p^pA zearalenone derivative extracted from Drechslera portulacae, a pathogen of purslane (Portulaca oleracea), inhibited root length of E. crus galli and Abutilon threophrasti in pot experiments (Kim, 1994; Kim et al., 1994).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe use of herbicides against E. crus-galli has been widespread and it is susceptible to a wide range of herbicides used in rice cultivation, including butachlor, butralin, cinmethylin, chlomethoxyfen, fenoxaprop, glyphosate, molinate, oxadiazon, oxyfluorfen, paraquat, pendimethalin, piperophos, pretilachlor, propanil, quinclorac and thiobencarb (Ampong-Nyarko and de Datta, 1991).^p^pField trials in the Korea Republic showed that 2 applications of herbicide using butachlor or thiobencarb 3 days after sowing and followed by tank-mixed bentazone + quinclorac 50 days after sowing were necessary to control E. crus-galli (Seong et al., 1991). Studies in the USA showed late-season control with pendimethalin + quinclorac was more effective than pendimethalin, quinclorac, thiobencarb, or pendimethalin + thiobencarb. Control using pendimethalin, quinclorac and pendimethalin + thiobencarb exceeded that with thiobencarb. Propanil + molinate controlled E. crus-galli more effectively than propanil (Jordan et al., 1998).^p^pThe introduction and spread of E. oryzoides and E. phyllopogon in California, USA, have caused rice farmers to rely on herbicides such as molinate or propanil to protect the crop from serious losses in yield and grain quality. host_range: 该病毒的寄主范围尚不十分清楚，可能在栽培的香蕉种中没有抗病品种。目前已知在自然条件下，该病毒主要侵染野生蕉（Musa acuminata ），此外还可侵染其他栽培蕉类，包括Musa textilis、Musa ornate和大蕉Musa sapientum。在实验条件中，纯化病毒可通过机械接种而系统侵染本氏烟（Nicotiana benthamiana）。没有鉴别寄主和繁殖寄主的报道。
potential_eco_desc:
在菲律宾，由病毒引致的产量损失在栽培种Cardaba和Saba(ABB)上高达40％。许多小型蕉园都可见受侵染的植株，病害严重影响甜蕉基因型“Cavendish subgroup” （AAA）品种，在1988年病害在General Santos City 几乎达至流行的程度，至少使25000个发病中心区的香蕉植株完全失收。在菲律宾的种质资源收集圃中许多栽培种的植株都可见BBrMV危害的症状。
在印度喀拉拉邦，BBrMV引致的症状在栽培种“Nendran”（AAB）上随处可见，在其他的栽培种植株上也可见病害症状。在品种“Yenugu Babtha” （ABB）上果束重量与正常果束相比减轻达47％，而且，受病害危害的果束，由于不正常的外观而使商品价值率大为降低。
在斯里兰卡栽培种‘Embul’(AAB)上随处可见BBrMV，经常易与香蕉束顶病毒（Banana bunchy top virus）和香蕉线条病毒(Banana streak virus)混合侵染，其产量损失也是巨大的。
description: 病毒在田间可由棉蚜（Aphis gossypii）、玉米蚜（Rhopalosiphum maidis）和香蕉交脉蚜（Pentalonia nigronervosa）以非持久性方式传播，但香蕉交脉蚜的传毒效率可能低至10％。偶尔通过汁液接种也可实现从香蕉到香蕉的病毒传播。病毒的主要传播方式之一是通过侵染的无性繁殖材料传播，这些无性繁殖材料包括组织培养种苗、吸芽苗、以及种质保存材料等。

host_range: The host range of Banana bract mosaic virus (BBrMV) is not known, but no resistance has been reported in cultivated banana clones. Musa textilis (abacá) has been found to be naturally infected in the Philippines (Sharman et al., 2000). Musa ornata is another known natural host of BBrMV; this wild species was growing in a germplasm collection at the Kerala Agricultural University Station, India, and was infected naturally from nearby plants (D.R. Jones, INIBAP, Montpellier, personal communication, 1995). Other Musa species may be susceptible.Nicotiana benthamiana has been systemically infected with BBrMV after mechanical inoculation with purified virus particles (M.L. Iskra-Caruana, Montpellier, France, personal communication, 1995).Primary hosts are banana cultivars derived from Musa acuminata and M. acuminata x M. balbisiana, and abacá cultivars selected from M. textilis.
potential_eco_desc: In the Philippines, yield losses have been estimated to be as high as 40% in the popular Cardaba and Saba (ABB) cultivars (Magnaye, 1994). Many plants have been observed to be infected in smallholdings in Mindanao. The disease also affects commercial plantations of cultivars in the Cavendish subgroup (AAA) on Mindanao Island and, in 1988, it reached epidemic proportions around General Santos City where 25,000 mats were believed to be destroyed. Many cultivars in Musa germplasm collections in the Philippines have been seen with symptoms of BBrMV.In Kerala, India, symptoms of BBrMV are commonly seen on cv. Nendran (AAB, syn. ‘ French Plantain‘ ) and losses are understood to be substantial. Symptoms of the disease have also been seen in many other cultivars in AA, AB, AAA, AAB and ABB subgroups. Bunch weights were reduced by up to 47% in Yenugu Bantha (ABB), but in addition, fruit loses its market acceptability because of its immature appearance and occasionally discoloured peel (HP Singh, National Research Centre on Banana, Trichirappalli, India, personal communication, 1995).BBrMV is common in the banana cultivar ‘ Embul‘  (AAB, syn. ‘ Mysore‘ ) in Sri Lanka and double infections with Banana bunchy top virus and Banana streak virus are often found (Anon., 1995). Yield losses have not been determined but are believed to be substantial.
reference_name: Banana bract mosaic virus (banana bract mosaic disease)
author: CPC2006

remark: BBrMV is the cause of a very serious disease of Musa and great care must be taken to ensure it does not spread beyond its present areas of distribution. As the disease can be carried in tissue cultures, all germplasm should be indexed for BBrMV as recommended (Diekmann and Putter, 1996) and observed for symptoms before release from quarantine. Plantains are seriously affected and the disease would probably cause considerable damage if introduced to West Africa and Latin America where cultivars in this subgroup are widely grown by smallholders.

author: CPC2006

management_info: Experience has shown that aphid-transmitted viruses of Musa cannot be completely controlled by the use of aphicides or biocontrol agents that are effective against banana aphids. However, these methods may reduce inoculum levels and slow the rate of spread. The disease may be kept in check by the destruction of affected plants in plantations and smallholdings. Suckers arising from diseased mats would also need to be destroyed. This can be achieved by physically removing the affected corm or by treating the pseudostems and suckers with herbicide. Spraying the diseased plant with an aphicide before treatment would prevent infectious aphids carrying Banana bract mosaic virus to nearby plants.All plants used as sources of meristems for propagation in tissue cultures should be indexed for Banana bract mosaic virus or partially purified leaf sap examined by electron microscopy for filamentous particles.

management_info:
实践已显示芭蕉科的蚜虫传播的病毒不能完全被杀蚜虫剂和有效抵抗香蕉蚜虫的生物防治剂的运用控制。然而，这些方法可能降低接种体水平且减慢传播速度。该病害可能被在大农场和小农场中受感染的植株的毁灭制止。产生于感病的覆盖物的吸根也必须会被毁灭。这可以通过完全地清除受感染的球茎和通过用除草剂处理假茎和吸根而完成。在处理之前用杀蚜虫剂喷雾感病的植株会防止有侵染性的蚜虫携带香蕉苞片花叶病毒到附近的植株。
在组织培养中作为分裂组织繁殖原料的所有植株应该被表明为香蕉苞片花叶病毒或用电子显微镜检查部分纯化的叶片汁液的线状微粒。 Experience has shown that aphid-transmitted viruses of Musa cannot be completely controlled by the use of aphicides or biocontrol agents that are effective against banana aphids. However, these methods may reduce inoculum levels and slow the rate of spread. The disease may be kept in check by the destruction of affected plants in plantations and smallholdings. Suckers arising from diseased mats would also need to be destroyed. This can be achieved by physically removing the affected corm or by treating the pseudostems and suckers with herbicide. Spraying the diseased plant with an aphicide before treatment would prevent infectious aphids carrying Banana bract mosaic virus to nearby plants.

All plants used as sources of meristems for propagation in tissue cultures should be indexed for Banana bract mosaic virus or partially purified leaf sap examined by electron microscopy for filamentous particles.

Attempts to transmit BBrMV by sap inoculation to herbaceous indicator plants have so far been unsuccessful (Magnaye and Espino, 1990; Mu馿z, 1992; S. Cohen, Montpellier, personal communication; Diekmann and Putter, 1996). However, occasional sap transmission from banana to banana has been achieved (L.V. Magnaye and L. Herradura, Davao, personal communication, 1998). The virus can be transmitted through vegetative planting material including suckers, bits and corms and via micropropagated plantlets.

potential_eco_desc: RGSV is one of the major diseases of rice (Ling, 1976). The importance of RGSV has increased since 1970 due to the high population of the brown planthopper, Nilaparvata lugens, in central tropical Asian countries, mainly in South, East, and South-East Asia (Dyck and Thomas, 1979; Hirao et al., 1985). N. lugens is also a vector of Rice ragged stunt virus (RRSV) (Ling et al., 1978; Hibino et al., 1979) and causes feeding damage known as hopperburn (Mochida, 1979; Mochida and Suryana, 1979). ^p^pActual yield losses are difficult to estimate because the damage caused by viruses cannot be distinguished from that caused by N. lugens (Palmer et al., 1978). In 1971, RGSV and N. lugens affected 8000 ha of rice in central Java, Indonesia, causing an estimated yield loss of 77.8% (Tantera et al., 1973). By 1974-1977, RGSV was considered the most damaging and widespread rice virus in Indonesia especially in Java, Bali, Sumatra and Sulawesi, wherein a total of 1.2 million ha was affected by the vector and virus. Combined yield losses exceeded 3 million tons of paddy rice amounting to more than US $510 million (Mochida and Suryana, 1975; Palmer et al., 1978; Palmer and Rao, 1981). ^p^pA major outbreak of RGSV was reported in 1973 in Laguna (IRRI, 1973) and in Mindanao (Ou, 1985), the Philippines; estimated yield losses due to virus and planthopper was about $26 million (Dyck and Thomas, 1979). In Kerala, India, 15,000 ha were affected by RGSV (Gopalakrishnan et al., 1973; Anjaneyulu, 1974; Kulshrestha et al., 1974; Santhakumari et al., 1982) and yield losses due to the virus and planthoppers were estimated at $20 million (Dyck and Thomas, 1979).

management_info: RGSV is relatively difficult to control as the insect vector must be also be considered.^p^pHost Plant Resistance^p^pRGSV has been successfully controlled in Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Vietnam by planting resistant varieties of rice (Ling et al., 1970; Kush and Ling, 1974; Nuque et al., 1982). These varieties carry sources of resistance derived from Oryza nivara, a wild rice species. However, O. nivara became susceptible when RGSV2 arose in the 1980s (Cabauatan et al., 1985; Hibino et al., 1985a). There are currently no rice varieties resistant to both RGSV1 and RGSV2 (IRRI, 1993).^p^pChemical Control^p^pChemical methods are usually used to control the insect vector of RGSV. Carbofuran and disulfoton reduced the incidence of grassy stunt disease by about 50% when applied at two dose levels in field trials in India (Pillai and Nair, 1982). A mixture containing buprofezin and fenobucarb, formulated as a driftless dust, is also effective in reducing the planthopper population and incidence of grassy stunt (Hirao et al., 1983). The application of insecticides is not always successful in controlling vector populations, especially in regions where rice is grown throughout the year (Hibino, 1986b). The insect has a tendency to adapt to the extensive use of insecticides. ^p^pBiological Control^p^pNeem seed oil (from Azadirachta indica) was highly effective in reducing the survival of Nilaparvata lugens, and in suppressing the transmission of RGSV and rice ragged stunt oryzavirus (RRSV) to rice under laboratory conditions (Saxena and Kahn, 1984; 1985).^p^pCultural Control^p^pCultural control methods contribute to a reduction in the planthopper population and the elimination of the virus inoculum source (Oka, 1987; Mochida, 1979). Methods used include: simultaneous cropping rotated with secondary crops; immediate destruction of rice stubble and ratoons of harvested rice crops; raising the water level in the field or complete drainage over a few days; and plant spacing which allows sunlight to reach the basal portion of the plant.^p^pIntegrated Pest Management^p^pThe integration of host plant resistance, chemical, biological and cultural control measures is the most effective approach to the control of both RGSV and the planthopper vector (Mochida, 1986).

potential_eco_desc: Rice stripe disease was first recognized in the Kanto district of central Japan, where it caused severe damage and yield loss in rice Kuribayashi, 1931a,b Amano, 1933; Toriyama, 1986b). Since the 1950s, the extension of early planting of rice promoted the occurrence of the disease in Japan (Yasuo et al., 1965; Iida, 1969). Damage was most severe during the years 1963-68, when ca  100,000 ha  (ca 20% of total rice paddy acreage of Japan) were infected each year. Disease incidence in Taiwan was also severe in the early 1970s when in 1973 ca 1045 ha was infected (Lee, 1975). In Korea, about 40% of hills were infected in 1965 (Lee, 1969). Stripe disease was prevalent over the rice zone in China and resulted in rice yield losses in several provinces (Cheng et al., 1988; Lin et al., 1990).
author: CPC2006

description: Vector Transmission^p^pThe natural vector of RSV is the small brown planthopper, Laodelphax striatellus Kuribayashi, 1931a,b, but Unkanodes sapporonus (Shinkai, 1966), U. albifascia (Hirao, 1968) and Terthron albovittatum can also transmit the virus (Shinkai, 1970).^p^pMechanical transmission^p^pRSV can be experimentally transmissible by mechanical inoculation, but with great difficulty. The virus is thus insufficiently infectious to be so transmitted in the field.

management_info: Strategies for the control of RSV were reviewed by Xie et al. (2001).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pResistance to RSV has been studies extensively in rice-growing countries (Sakurai and Ezuka, 1964; Yamaguchi et al., 1965;Washio et al., 1967, 1968a,b,c; Lee, 1969; Toriyama, 1969; Chiu et al., 1986). Most Japanese paddy varieties (japonica-type) are highly susceptible, but Japanese upland varieties and indica-type varieties are resistant. A 'seedling test method' was devised for the first-step evaluation of varietal resistance (Sakurai et al., 1963; Sakurai, 1969). In Japan, the highly resistant hybrids Chugoku 31 and St No1 were bred by crossing cv. Norin No 8 (japonica) and cv. Modan (indica), and then back-crossing with cv. Norin 8. These hybrids have been used as mother lines for breeding new varieties resistant to the virus Toriyama et al., 1966, 1972; Toriyama, 1972) and many practical resistant varieties have been bred using these lines in Japan (Ezuka, 1985). Elite line BL1 is very resistant to RSV but not to the vector (Ise et al., 1999).^p^pBreeding and selection of resistant varieties for rice production has continued in rice-growing countries and several practical varieties have been bred in Japan (Ito et al., 1989; Sakai et al., 1989; Shinoda et al., 1989;Shumiya et al., 1991, 1994; Narizuka et al., 1994; Orimo et al., 1994; Ando et al., 2004; Imbe et al., 2004a,b ), Korea (Lee and Kim, 1968;Lee et al., 1989a,b; Lim et al., 1989; Koh et al., 1992; Choung et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2003; Ha et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2003; Shin et al., 2003) and China (Xing et al., 1985; Chiu et al., 1986; Lu et al., 1992). Hayano-Saito (2002) reviewed the coding strategy of RSV and genetic analysis of resistance.^p^pThe inheritance of resistance is governed by multiple alleles with various levels of resistance: gene St2 in Japanese upland varieties and gene St2i in indica-type varieties. Another gene, St1, in addition to St2, is essential for resistance in Japanese upland varieties (Washio et al., 1968 a,b; Toriyama, 1972).^p^pWhen the resistant rice cv. Musashikogane and two other varieties, which were bred by introducing the St2i gene, were infected at the 1.5 leaf stage, the virus concentration was the same as that of a susceptible variety, cv. Nipponbare (Noda et al., 1991). However, the virus concentration in resistant varieties infected at the fifth-leaf stage was much lower than that in susceptible varieties (Sonku, 1975). Resistance to the virus in cultivars Musashikogane and Minamihatamochi was distinctly enhanced by the introduction of the resistant gene(s) against the vector, L. striatellus, from cv. IR50 (Nemoto et al., 1994).^p^pRice resistant to RSV has been genetically engineered by introducing the coat protein gene into two japonica-type varieties (Hayakawa et al., 1992; Yahiro et al., 1994), and by transferring to rice constructs that produce dsRNA (Upadhyaya et al., 2001).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pAn epidemic of rice stripe disease in Japan followed the widespread adoption of planting rice earlier in the season (Yasuo et al., 1965; Kiritani, 1983). The immigration date of the vector, Laodelphax striatellus, which had multiplied in wheat fields, probably coincided with the transplanting season for rice seedlings. Thus, the transplanting or seeding date has a significant affect on the incidence of the disease (Yasuo et al., 1965; Cheng, 1974; Kim, 1985; Bae and Kim, 1994). Extensive cultivation of resistant rice varieties favours a decrease in the density of viruliferous insects in fields, making it possible to cultivate susceptible varieties (Takayama et al., 1987; Nakazawa et al., 1991;Gao et al., 1993, 1994).^pGlobal warming could affect the incidence of RSV by changing the degree of synchronization of vector and susceptible stage of crop development; using Global Climate Models, areas of Japan have been identified that might be so affected (Yamamura and Yokozawa, 2002).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pInsecticides ha

potential_eco_desc: 1963—68年间损害是最严重的，约每年100,000 ha，相当约日本的稻田的总英亩数的20%。在台湾病害发生率在1970年左右是最严重的：1973年损害约1045 ha (Lee, 1975)。在韩国，约40%的山丘被侵染于1965年(Lee, 1969)。条纹病害在中国水稻区广泛流行，导致几个省的水稻产量损失(Cheng et al., 1988; Lin et al., 1990)。 Damage was most severe during the years 1963-68, at about 100,000 ha per year, corresponding to about 20% of total rice paddy acreage of Japan. Disease incidence in Taiwan was most severe around 1970: the damage was about 1045 ha in 1973 (Lee, 1975). In Korea, about 40% of hills were infected in 1965 (Lee, 1969). Stripe disease was broadly prevalent over the rice zone in China and resulted in rice yield losses in several provinces (Cheng et al., 1988; Lin et al., 1990).
description: 水稻条纹病第一次被认识是在20世纪在日本中心关东地区，那里产生严重的水稻损害(Kuribayashi, 1931a, b; Amano, 1933; Toriyama, 1986b)。直到20世纪50年代，水稻早期种植的普及增进了在日本病害发生的频率(Yasuo et al., 1965; Iida, 1969)。 Rice stripe disease was first recognized in the 1900s in the Kanto district of central Japan, where it caused severe damage in rice (Kuribayashi, 1931a, b; Amano, 1933; Toriyama, 1986b). Since the 1950s, the extension of early planting of rice promoted the occurrence of the disease in Japan (Yasuo et al., 1965; Iida, 1969).

management_info: 大量杀虫剂已被用于RSV媒介昆虫灰飞虱的防治，包括蚜灭磷，残杀威，乙拌磷，二嗪哝和克百威 (Yamada et al., 1955b; Hirao, 1973; Ryu et al., 1977; Bae et al., 1992)。S-氰戊菊酯对媒介昆虫灰飞虱有很高的穿透性(Umeda and Hirao, 1990)。 A number of insecticides have been used for control of the vector planthoppers of RSV, including vamidothion, propoxur, disulfoton, diazinon and carbofuran (Yamada et al., 1955b; Hirao, 1973; Ryu et al., 1977; Bae et al., 1992). Esfenvalerate has high repellent activity against the vector Laodelphax striatellus (Umeda and Hirao, 1990). 抗病性的遗传被多种有着不同水平抗病性的等位基因控制着：基因St2日本内陆地区品种和基因St2i穗型品种。另一种基因，St1，除St2之外，是日本内陆地区最重要的抗病品种(Washio et al., 1968 a, b; Toriyama, 1972)。水稻对RSV的抗病性已被基因工程引进两种日本型品种里的外壳蛋白(Hayakawa et al., 1992; Yahiro et al., 1994)。 The inheritance of resistance is governed by multiple alleles with various levels of resistance: gene St2 in Japanese upland varieties and gene St2i in indica-type varieties. Another gene, St1, in addition to St2, is essential for resistance in Japanese upland varieties (Washio et al., 1968 a, b; Toriyama, 1972).Rice resistant to RSV has been genetically engineered by introducing the coat protein gene into two japonica-type varieties (Hayakawa et al., 1992; Yahiro et al., 1994). 水稻条纹病害在日本的流行通过广泛采用水稻在季节早期栽培而被引发(Yasuo et al., 1965; Kiritani, 1983)。这可能是媒介昆虫——灰飞虱（已在麦田繁殖）迁飞的日期，与水稻苗期移植季节同时发生。这样，移植或播种日期在病害发生率上有重大影响(Yasuo et al., 1965; Cheng, 1974; Kim, 1985; Bae and Kim, 1994)。水稻抗病品种的大量栽培使田间带毒昆虫的密度得到减少，使栽培易受影响的品种成为可能(Takayama et al., 1987; Nakazawa et al., 1991; Gao et al., 1993, 1994)。 An epidemic of rice stripe disease in Japan was triggered by the widespread adoption of rice cultivation earlier in the season (Yasuo et al., 1965; Kiritani, 1983). It is probable that the immigration date of the vector, Laodelphax striatellus, which had multiplied in wheat fields, coincided with the transplanting season for rice seedlings. Thus, the transplanting or seeding date has a significant affect on the incidence of the disease (Yasuo et al., 1965; Cheng, 1974; Kim, 1985; Bae and Kim, 1994). Extensive cultivation of resistant rice varieties favours a decrease in the density of viruliferous insects in fields, making it possible to cultivate susceptible varieties (Takayama et al., 1987; Nakazawa et al., 1991; Gao et al., 1993, 1994).

potential_eco_desc: RHBV is found throughout most of tropical America and causes sporadic epidemics in rice (Morales and Niessen, 1985). Although often found as isolated infected plants in ricefields, when epidemics occur significant yield losses of up to 100% have been reported (Jennings, 1963; Vargas, 1985).^p^pRHBV has caused serious production losses in rice in Latin America. In 1956, yield losses in Cuba and Venezuela were about 25 and 50%, respectively (USDA, 1960). Jennings (1963) observed slight to almost complete grain losses in commercials fields grown with susceptible rice cultivars in Cuba, Venezuela and Colombia. Following two separate epidemics in the 1950s and 1960s (Jennings, 1963; Galvez, 1969), the disease virtually disappeared from most of the regions in Latin America for nearly 15 years (Zeigler et al., 1988). In 1981, serious widespread outbreaks recurred in Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela, causing losses of up to 100% (Vargas, 1985).

management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe Rice Program of the Centro Internacional de Agricultura Tropical (CIAT) has developed management and control strategies directed at both the planthopper, Tagosodes orizicolus (name changed from Sogatodes oryzicola), and RHBV (Zeigler et al., 1994; Zeigler et al., 1988). Resistance sources against RHBV originate from rice japonica germplasm and have been transferred to indica backgrounds, suitable for use in Latin America breeding programmes. Resistance in rice to RHBV is controlled by two or more dominant genes (Lamey, 1969; Zeigler et al., 1988). Resistance also increases with plant age in both susceptible and resistant plants (Zeigler et al., 1994). A field screening method, based on mass rearing of viruliferous insects and the development of stable vector colonies, was developed to screen rice breeding lines for resistance to RHBV (Zeigler et al., 1988). However, a better understanding of resistance is needed in order to use it effectively (Zeigler et al., 1994).^p^p^p^Integrated Pest Management^p^pFarmers in Latin America often apply insecticides to prevent hopper burn, caused by direct feeding damage from high populations of the planthopper, and outbreaks of RHBV (Vargas, 1985). However, there is no evidence that this is effective. If there are significant numbers of RHBV active vectors in the field, the threshold of an epidemic can be crossed when insect levels are well below any damage threshold estimated for insect feeding damage alone. An IPM strategy aimed at reducing pesticide applications, which target Tagosodes orizicolus (name changed from Sogatodes oryzicola), must be accompanied by a resistance breeding programme for RHBV that eliminates the risk of occasional RHBV epidemics (Zeigler et al., 1994).

management_info: Control of MSpV is largely dependent on chemical control of Peregrinus maidis. Cultural control methods, such as removing infected plants from the field, can greatly reduce the secondary spread of MSpV. Besides the possible use of resistant varieties, the most logical approach to control is vector control. potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pIn its native country, Australia, P. semipunctata occurs throughout Eucalyptus forests, but its damage is usually restricted to dead and dying trees. During severe droughts, beetle outbreaks may occur, but the populations normally appear to be limited by a complex of natural enemies, including predators and parasitoids. In the majority of other regions where P. semipunctata is found, however, tree death occurs in woodlot plantings, especially when subjected to periodic moisture stress, and includes apparently healthy trees.^p^pIn the Mediterranean basin, rapid spread of P. semipunctata was favoured by the poor state of many plantations, mainly due to drought and poor soils along with the great dispersal capacity of the beetle (Cadahia, 1986). The pest caused very serious damage to plantations in Tunisia in the years following its introduction in 1963. The first focus in Morocco was eradicated, but a later outbreak in 1981 caused an estimated loss of 2 million trees, approximately 1.18-1.47% of the area of Eucalyptus plantations (about 170,000 ha) (El-Yousfi, 1982). The average tree mortality rate in the province of Huelva in Spain, since P. semipunctata was first detected in 1981 until the end of 1983, was estimated to be between 2.23 and 3.88%, equivalent to a loss of 6207 ha, despite the high economic and labour cost of control measures (Gonzalez Tirado, 1986).^p^pThe economic impact appears to be greatest in regions of the world with Mediterranean climates. In the absence of supplemental irrigation, the hot dry summers associated with these regions potentially place the trees under moisture stress at the time of year when the beetles are most active. Although present, the beetle does not seem to be as much of a problem in parts of the world where there is abundant summer rainfall (e.g., coastal portions of eastern Australia, Hawaii, portions of Brazil).^p^p^Environmental impact^pP. semipunctata is endemic to all six biogeographic ranges in Australia. Although it kills eucalypts in its native range, it is primarily a scavenger of dead, stressed or dying trees, broken branches, or material that has been damaged by fire or other natural disturbances. The beetles can, however, cause significant mortality in areas where the trees have been introduced. There are few records of the beetle attempting to colonize non-host trees, particularly in areas where it is an introduced species. Consequently, it has little direct impact on the natural environment in these areas. Ironically, the detrimental impact of the beetles on introduced trees is perceived by some individuals or organizations as a positive environmental impact as eucalypts planted in novel geographic regions are viewed as invasive weeds.^p^p^p^Social impact^pMortality of plantation-grown eucalypts, caused by P. semipunctata, may have a significant impact on the local economy because the beetle reduces the production of wood fibre from these plantations. This reduced economic benefit has an impact on local jobs and social welfare. In some parts of the world, eucalyptus plantations and woodlots provide grazing and firewood that benefit the local communities. Tree mortality reduces the long-term social benefit derived from these secondary uses.^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pP. semipunctata colonizes only eucalypts, which are now widely planted outside their native ranges in Australia and Papua New Guinea. The beetle has very little impact on biodiversity in novel habitats because their host trees are also introduced; however, plantations of eucalyptus trees or trees that have become naturalized in the new environments have an impact on the native flora and fauna. The beetle is perceived by some individuals as a potentially beneficial insect as it causes a reduction in eucalypt populations.
description: P. semipunctata was first reported as an introduced insect problem in South Africa in 1906. The widespread movement of the insect did not occur until the later third of the twentieth century when eucalypts were widely accepted as a major source of cellulose for paper production and plantations were established in many parts of the world with a Mediterranean climate. For example, the beetle was present in Tunisia before 1969, in Italy, Spain, Egypt, France, Portugal and Turkey by 1983, and in California, USA, by 1985. Populations were established in South America by the early 1990s.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pLiving Eucalyptus trees are not easily protected by pesticides, as the beetles' behaviour limits their exposure to the chemicals; the beetles hide during the day under loose bark and do not feed on leaves or bark.^p^pIt does not appear likely that chemical control in the forest could be achieved. The adults are active during the greater part of the year and it would, therefore, be necessary to use pesticides with long residual effects or to make frequent applications to kill beetles landing on the tree. Also, viable eggs can be laid on sprayed areas before the pesticide can kill the female beetles. Eggs are usually protected from exposure to pesticides, because they are laid under layers of loose bark. Once the larvae are inside the bark, they escape pesticide applications.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pIn Spain and Morocco silvicultural measures are used as the most effective and ecologically sound methods of control. Curative measures include clearance and felling of all attacked and dead trees, followed by their removal from the forest. Freshly cut trap logs, treated with 2% lindane, are placed in woodlots to attract adult beetles. Female beetles lay their eggs on the sprayed logs which are replaced every 2 weeks with fresh ones. The old logs are destroyed within 2 months to prevent beetle emergence. Recommended preventive measures are concerned with managing the forest in such a way that trees are kept in good health. Weak and declining trees should be removed. Selection of the appropriate tree species for each zone is the main preventive measure (Gonzalez Tirado, 1986; El-Yousfi, 1989).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pThe parasitoid Platystasius transversus was obtained from eggs of P. semipunctata in Morocco (Fraval and Haddan, 1988). Although described from specimens collected in Italy, the encyrtid egg parasitoid Avetianella longoi, is native to Australia and has been widely distributed around the world. It provides excellent biological control of P. semipunctata in some areas (Hanks et al., 1995a; Paine and Millar, 2002), but may contribute to the replacement of P. semipunctata by P. recurva in areas where both species have been introduced (Luhring et al., 2000).^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pEPPO recommends that only debarked wood of Eucalyptus should be traded. It recommends also that wood of Eucalyptus (including wood chips larger than 4 x 0.5 cm) should be kept in storage under supervision for at least 6 months after debarking or must have been fumigated by an appropriate method (OEPP/EPPO, 1990). In general, dry logs older than 9 months can be considered free from larvae and pupae.^p^pMethyl bromide fumigation at the rate of 125 g/m3 for 48 h was established by the Spanish Department of Agriculture as the quarantine treatment of wood against P. semipunctata. Mean internal temperatures of the wood piles in the affected areas are, in general, higher than 10-12°C, which are the effective temperatures for methyl bromide.

scientific_name: East African cassava mosaic Malawi virus
host_range: 木薯 Manihot esculenta
description: Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) is a major constraint to sustainable production of cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) in Zambia and other sub-Saharan African countries. During a survey conducted between April and May 2014 in six (Western, Northwestern, Northern, Luapula, Lusaka, and Eastern) provinces of Zambia, 226 symptomatic cassava leaf tissue samples were collected from CMD-affected plants in 214 farmers’ fields. The causal agent was isolated and identified as East African cassava mosaic Malawi virus (EACMMV). The results provide definitive evidence for the occurrence of EACMMV in Zambia and represent a first report of the virus in the country. It also indicates an expanded geographical distribution of EACMMV in sub-Saharan Africa.
reference_name: First Report of East African cassava mosaic Malawi virus in Plants Affected by Cassava Mosaic Disease in Zambia

description: Incidence^p^pThe incidence of infection of seed by TBRV has been reported in more than 24 species in more than 15 plant families and can occur through both the pollen and the ovule (Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967). ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality ^p^pIn some weed seed, TBRV infection delays germination (Lister and Murant, 1967).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission ^p^pAt least 15 species in 12 plant families are known to be infected by TBRV through seed, although most infected seedlings show no obvious symptoms (Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967; Murant, 1983). In commercially important plant species including lettuce, beet, tomato and soyabean, seed transmission rates of 3, 3-7, 20 and 83% , respectively, were reported (Murant, 1983). Seed transmission of TBRV is an important feature in the epidemiology of the disease because the virus is retained for only a few weeks by its nematode vectors. TBRV therefore relies on its persistence in the seeds of wild plants for survival over winter or through periods of fallow (Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967; Murant, 1983; Harrison and Murant, 1996). ^p^p^Seed Treatment ^p^pNone. ^p^p^Seed Health Tests ^p^pNone reported.

description: TBRV是由自由生活的寄居于土壤中的线虫品种长针线虫属传播的(Brown et al., 1996)。属于苏格兰血清型的TBRV的分离种由伸展长针线虫（L. elongatus）传播最为有效(Harrison et al., 1961; Taylor and Murant, 1969)，英格兰血清型的分离种则是由渐狭长针线虫（L. attenuatus）最为有效的传播(Harrison, 1964)。然而，这些品种中每一个的传播效率是相当低的(5-25%)。来自英国和德国的G血清型分离种在它们通过一个来自英国的渐狭长针线虫（L. attenuatus）的单一种群的传播上非常的不同(Brown et al., 1989)。媒介特异性由该病毒的RNA-2上的遗传因子控制，可能是病毒的衣壳蛋白(Randles et al., 1977)。线虫的幼虫和成虫都传播病毒，但该病毒不能在媒介体内复制，而且不能在蜕皮后保留，或传播到线虫后代去。当在休耕土壤中存活时，伸展长针线虫（L. elongatus）能保持侵染性超过9个星期(Lister and Murant, 1967)。在携带该病毒的线虫的超微结构研究中，类似的病毒粒子在媒介线虫的齿坚针和探针中(Taylor and Robertson, 1969)。在苏格兰，TBRV的S血清型的分离种与悬钩子环斑病毒拥有共同的线虫媒介(伸展长针线虫（Longidorus elongatus）)，而且这些病毒能在土壤中一起发生。 TBRV is transmitted by species of the free-living soil-inhabiting nematode, Longidorus (Brown et al., 1996). Isolates of TBRV belonging to the Scottish serotype are transmitted most efficiently by L. elongatus (Harrison et al., 1961; Taylor and Murant, 1969), and isolates of the English serotype by L. attenuatus (Harrison, 1964). Nevertheless, transmission efficiency by each of these species is relatively poor (5-25%). Isolates of the G serotype from England and Germany differed greatly in their transmission by a single population of L. attenuatus from England (Brown et al., 1989). The vector specificity is controlled by determinants on RNA-2 of the virus, probably the virus coat protein (Randles et al., 1977). Both larvae and adult nematodes transmit the virus but the virus does not multiply in the vector, and it is not retained after moulting, nor is it passed to nematode progeny. L. elongatus retained infectivity for up to 9 weeks when maintained in fallow soil (Lister and Murant, 1967). In ultrastructural studies of nematodes carrying the virus, virus-like particles were associated with the odontostyle and the stylet guiding sheath of vector nematodes (Taylor and Robertson, 1969). In Scotland, isolates of the S serotype of TBRV share the same nematode vector (Longidorus elongatus) as raspberry ringspot nepovirus and the viruses can occur in soils together.

management_info:
在缺乏抗性材料的情况下，健康的种植材料应在不受TBRV侵染的作物品种的种植区域中和在没有带病毒的长针线虫属品种存在的土壤中使用。
TBRV爆发的防治最好是通过允许休耕间隔来达到，通过不种植休耕或通过种植病毒免疫寄主。倘若该病毒没有被疏忽的再传入田间中去和维持良好的野草防治来防治任何存活的线虫重新获得病毒的话，在这段时期内线虫媒介逐渐失去侵染能力。选择性地，防治能通过土壤消毒来杀死线虫或适当的土壤消毒剂开达到(Murant and Taylor, 1965; Harrison and Murant, 1996)。
该病毒能从一些品种的感染植株的生长的枝尖中根除，包括马铃薯和葡萄，分别或联合通过热处理和分生组织顶端培养(Stellmach and Gartel, 1973; Kaiser, 1980)。 In the absence of resistant material, healthy planting material should be used in planting areas of the crop species free from known TBRV infection, and in soil free from viruliferous Longidorus species.
Control of TBRV outbreaks is best achieved by allowing a crop-free interval, either by bare-fallowing or by planting virus-immune hosts. During this period the nematode vectors gradually lose infectivity, provided the virus is not inadvertently re-introduced into the field and that good weed control is maintained to prevent any surviving nematodes from re-acquiring the virus. Alternatively, control can be achieved by killing the nematodes by soil fumigation or suitable soil sterilants (Murant and Taylor, 1965; Harrison and Murant, 1996).
The virus has been eliminated from developing shoot tips of infected plants of some species, including potato and grapevine, by heat treatment and meristem tip culture, either alone, or in combination (Stellmach and Gartel, 1973; Kaiser, 1980).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc:
在自然爆发当中，TBRV侵染在作物中通常引起不均匀的小块侵染，这反映着媒介线虫的分布。在感染植物中，叶片症状如果存在的话，那通常由病毒分离种、植物基因型和不清楚的环境条件决定的(Murant et al., 1996)。
在一些作物植物品种中，该病毒引起严重的活力衰退，引起生产数量和品质的重大的损失(Hollings, 1965; Murant, 1987; Murant and Lister, 1987; Murant et al., 1996)。 In natural outbreaks, TBRV infection is usually associated with patchy infections in crops, reflecting the distribution of the vector nematode. In infected plants, leaf symptoms, if any, are often dependent on the virus isolate, plant genotype and ill-defined environmental conditions (Murant et al., 1996).
In some crop plant species the virus induces severe decline in vigour causing significant losses in productivity both quantitatively and qualitatively (Hollings, 1965; Murant, 1987; Murant and Lister, 1987; Murant et al., 1996).

description: GRAV不能机械传播。蚜虫传播的GRV、它的卫星RNA和两者的辅助病毒的GRAV，这三者一起引起花生丛生病害。整个的复合，和于是推断起来的GRAV本身，是由蚜虫苜蓿蚜（Aphis craccivora）以一个持久（循环、非繁殖）的方式传播的(Storey and Ryland, 1955; Watson and Okusanya, 1967; Dubern, 1980; Misari et al., 1988)。有丛生病害（可能包括GRAV）通过棉蚜（A. gossypii）传播的一个单一的报道，但蚜虫在田间不是一个重要的传播媒介。关于丛生复合传播方面的更详细的的内容，见花生丛生病毒的数据。 GRAV is not mechanically transmissible. GRAV acts as a helper for the aphid transmission of GRV and its satellite RNA, the three components together being responsible for groundnut rosette disease. The entire complex, and therefore presumably GRAV itself, is transmitted by Aphis craccivora in a persistent (circulative, non-propagative) manner (Storey and Ryland, 1955; Watson and Okusanya, 1967; Dubern, 1980; Misari et al., 1988). There is a single report (Adams, 1966) of transmission of rosette disease (presumably involving GRAV) by A. gossypii, but this aphid is not important as a vector in the field. For further details on the transmission of the rosette complex, see the data sheet on groundnut rosette virus.

host_range: MaYMV was recently identified from maize (Zea mays) in China. MaYMV has also been reported to infect sugarcane (Saccharum spp.) and itch grass (Rottboellia cochinchinensis). description:
CaRLV不能人为地传播。它作为CMoV（可人为传播）蚜虫传播的一个辅助，两个病毒一起造成胡萝卜的斑驳矮化病害，也会侵染一些其他的伞形花科作物。CtRLV（和因此混合体）是以一个持久的（循环的、非遗传）的方式通过蚜虫伞形花二尾蚜（Cavariella aegopodii），而不能通过郁金香西圆尾蚜（Anuraphis tulipae [Dysaphis tulipae]）、豌豆蚜（Acyrthosiphon pisum）、欧洲防风二尾蚜（Cavariella pastinacae）、肖鲍尔德二尾蚜（C. theobaldi）、茴香明蚜（Hyadaphis foeniculi）、桃蚜（Myzus persicae）或两个未经确认的长管蚜属品种传播(Stubbs, 1948; Watson et al., 1964; Murant, 1974; Waterhouse, 1981)。胡萝卜微管蚜（Brachycolus heraclei [Semiaphis heraclei]）被报道是来自日本的胡萝卜病毒分离种的一个另外的媒介(Komuro and Yamashita, 1956; Ohki et al., 1979)。
Elnagar and Murant (1978a)发现，C. aegopodii需要一个大约30分钟的最小获取时间来获得CaRLV/CMoV复合，和大约两分钟的最小获取时间来接种病毒。最小的潜伏时间大约是6－8个小时(Watson et al., 1964; Elnagar and Murant, 1978a)。蚜虫在蜕皮之后(Stubbs, 1955; Watson et al., 1964; Elnagar and Murant, 1978a)和至少12连续的每天传播后(Elnagar and Murant, 1978a)继续传毒。没有证据说明病毒在蚜虫内的繁殖或病毒能传播到带病毒蚜虫的后代去(Elnagar and Murant, 1978a, b)。该病毒通过注入带病毒蚜虫的汁液的蚜虫传播(Elnagar and Murant, 1978b)。 CaRLV is not manually transmissible. It acts as a helper for the aphid transmission of CMoV (which is manually transmissible), the two components together being responsible for motley dwarf disease of carrot which also affects a few other umbelliferous crops. CtRLV (and therefore the complex) is transmitted in a persistent (circulative, non-propagative) manner by the aphid Cavariella aegopodii, but not by Anuraphis tulipae [Dysaphis tulipae], Acyrthosiphon pisum, Cavariella pastinacae, Cavariella theobaldi, Hyadaphis foeniculi, Myzus persicae or two unidentified species of Macrosiphum (Stubbs, 1948; Watson et al., 1964; Murant, 1974; Waterhouse, 1981). Brachycolus heraclei [Semiaphis heraclei] was reported to be an additional vector of carrot virus isolates from Japan (Komuro and Yamashita, 1956; Ohki et al., 1979).
Elnagar and Murant (1978a) found that C. aegopodii require a minimum access time of about 30 min to acquire the CtRLV/CMoV complex and a minimum access time of about 2 min to inoculate the viruses. The minimum latent period is 6-18 h (Watson et al., 1964; Elnagar and Murant, 1978a). The aphids continue to transmit after moulting (Stubbs, 1955; Watson et al., 1964; Elnagar and Murant, 1978a) and after at least 12 serial daily transfers (Elnagar and Murant, 1978a). There is no evidence for multiplication of the viruses in the aphid, nor are they transmitted to the progeny of viruliferous aphids Elnagar and Murant, 1978a, b. The viruses were transmitted by aphids that had been injected with extracts of viruliferous aphids (Elnagar and Murant, 1978b).

management_info: Introduction^p^pAs winged Myzus persicae cannot be prevented from entering sugarbeet crops and feeding on individual plants, crops are potentially at risk from virus infection every year. To minimize the development of initial foci of infection and subsequent virus spread, growers are encouraged to adopt an integrated control programme. This should include removing sources of infection, the use of cultural practices to reduce the risk of infection, the application of insecticides to seed, soil or foliage and the use of virus-tolerant varieties.^p^p^Reduction of Infection Sources^p^pSugarbeet crops should be sited away from known sources of infection wherever possible and up-wind of clamps, seed crops, brassicas or other aphid sources.^p^pSeed crops can be important sources of virus infection. In England, UK, the Steckling Certification Scheme was introduced in the 1950s and required that seed crops were subject to strict controls (Hull, 1954). Currently, the few seed crops grown in England are situated away from the main sugarbeet-growing areas. They are drilled to stand, usually under barley, with a granular systemic insecticide. Further aphicidal sprays are applied during the autumn, and the crops are regularly inspected for virus and other diseases.^p^pTo reduce the risk of infection from mangold and other fodder beet clamps, roots should be closely topped at harvest so that there are few shoots on which aphids can feed and multiply during the winter. Clamps should also be well ventilated to minimize aphid reproduction and cleared before the new sugarbeet crop emerges (Hull, 1961; Smith, 1986). Groundkeepers, root remnants on soil heaps and roots not sent to the factory can also act as potential sources of infection.^p^p^Cultural Practices^p^pGrowers are advised to sow early to achieve maximum yields; older plants are less physiologically attractive to aphids (Williams, 1995), therefore by sowing early there is a greater chance that plants will have matured before peak aphid migrations. Late-sown crops are more susceptible to infection because winged Myzus persicae are attracted to the yellowish-green leaves of young sugarbeet plants.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pA selection of different chemical products is available to prevent the build up of virus-carrying aphids. Carbamate insecticidal sprays such as pirimicarb have a fumigant effect but are not systemic and do not prevent the initial aphid colonization of plants. However, unlike organophosphates, pirimicarb does not kill beneficial predators, such as coccinellids, and is more effective against resistant aphids. The granular carbamate aldicarb was introduced in England in 1974 primarily for the control of nematodes and other soil pests. When applied to the seed furrow it is rapidly taken up by seedlings and also gives protection against aphid attack for up to 9 weeks (Dewar and Cooke, 1986). Synthetic pyrethroids rapidly intoxicate aphids and can also act as repellents, preventing probing and virus transmission. As direct contact is necessary for the chemical to be effective, aphids protected by the canopy remain unaffected. This problem can be overcome by mixing two aphicides with different properties, for example a pyrethroid with either a carbamate or organophosphate compound. ^p^pThe seed treatment imidacloprid has become increasingly popular throughout Europe during the 1990s for the control of the aphid vectors and other economically damaging soil pests. The granular carbamate aldicarb was introduced in England in 1974 primarily for the control of nematodes and other soil pests.Synthetic pyrethroids rapidly intoxicate aphids and can also act as repellents, preventing probing and virus transmission.a pyrethroid with either a carbamate or organophosphate compound. imidacloprid　works by slowly poisoning the aphid during feeding. 种植者被建议提早播种来到达最大产量；较老的植物对蚜虫的生理上的吸引力较少(Williams, 1995)，于是提早播种能给植物有较大机会在蚜虫移植高峰期之前就成熟。迟播种的作物对于侵染更加敏感，因为有翅的桃蚜（Myzus persicae）被幼嫩甜菜植株上微黄绿的叶片所吸引。 Growers are advised to sow early to achieve maximum yields; older plants are less physiologically attractive to aphids (Williams, 1995), therefore by sowing early there is a greater chance that plants will have matured before peak aphid migrations. Late-sown crops are more susceptible to infection because winged Myzus persicae are attracted to the yellowish-green leaves of young sugarbeet plants. 因为不能防止有翅桃蚜（Myzus persicae）进入到甜菜作物和在个别的植物上取食，因此作物每年都有可能存在被病毒感染的危险。为了将最初的侵染集中点的发展以及后来的传播减到最少，种植者被鼓励采用综合的防治程序。这应该包括清除感染来源。降低感染危险的农艺操作的运用、种子、土壤或树叶上杀虫剂的应用，以及耐病毒性品种的使用。 As winged Myzus persicae cannot be prevented from entering sugarbeet crops and feeding on individual plants, crops are potentially at risk from virus infection every year. To minimize the development of initial foci of infection and subsequent virus spread, growers are encouraged to adopt an integrated control programme. This should include removing sources of infection, the use of cultural practices to reduce the risk of infection, the application of insecticides to seed, soil or foliage and the use of virus-tolerant varieties.

description: BMYV是由蚜虫传播，并与蚜虫具有持久的（循环的，非繁殖的）关系。桃蚜（Myzus persicae）是BMYV的主要媒介。蚕豆蚜（Aphis fabae）的角色到现在还是不清楚的。马铃薯长管蚜（Myzus euphorbiae）被认为是BMYV的一个不重要的寄主(Heathcote and Cockbain, 1966; Jadot, 1975)；其他的被显示为BMYV传播媒介的蚜虫包括Myzus ascolonicus、茄沟无网蚜（Aulacorthum solani）、Rhopalosiphoninus staphyleae tulipaellus(Heathcote, 1988)以及忽布疣额蚜（Phorodon humuli）和杏圆尾蚜( Brachycaudus helichrysi )(Thornhill and Hinckes, 1986)。 BMYV is transmitted by aphids and has a persistent (circulative, non-propagative) relationship with the vector. Myzus persicae is the principal vector of BMYV. The role of Aphis fabae remains unclear．Myzus euphorbiae has been regarded as a poor vector of BMYV (Heathcote and Cockbain, 1966; Jadot, 1975);Other aphids that have been shown to be vectors of BMYV include Myzus ascolonicus, Aulacorthum solani, Rhopalosiphoninus staphyleae tulipaellus (Heathcote, 1988) and Phorodon humuli and Brachycaudus helichrysi (Thornhill and Hinckes, 1986).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: 甜菜植物受BMYV感染引起中断光合作用、呼吸作用和其他的代谢作用的叶片的褪绿。这些变化增加了氨基氮、钠和钾在根部的水平，这会相反地在处理中影响糖分的可提取性。 Infection of sugarbeet plants by BMYV causes chlorosis of leaves which disrupts photosynthetic, respiratory and other metabolic processes. These changes increase the levels of amino nitrogen, sodium and potassium in roots which adversely affects extractability of sugar during processing. 当植物在早期生长阶段受到感染，BMYV引起超过30％的最大的产量损失， (Smith and Hallsworth, 1990)。当植物有超过20片叶片时，后期的感染普遍的被认为其对产量的影响不大。在英国英格兰，在考虑处理的功效后，由黄症病毒（主要是BMYV，但也包括甜菜黄化病毒）引起的损失估计会损失糖类产业每年24,700公吨的糖。这相当于1.8％的国家产量和五百万的经济损失；缺乏防治方法的条件下，损失大约是这的两倍(Jaggard et al., 1998)。 BMYV causes greatest yield loss, up to 30%, when the plants are infected at an early growth stage (Smith and Hallsworth, 1990). Later infection, when the plants have more than 20 leaves, is currently thought to have little effect on yield. In England, UK, losses due to virus yellows (predominantly BMYV, but also including beet yellows closterovirus) after taking into account the efficacy of treatments was estimated to cost the sugar industry 24,700 tonnes/year of sugar. This is the equivalent to 1.8% of the national yield and a financial loss of ?.5 million; in the absence of control measures the losses were approximately double (Jaggard et al., 1998).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pSpecies of Xylosandrus and related genera are known pests of various forest and agricultural plants. X. discolor could become an important shoot borer if imported outside its native range. Its apparent preference for non-indigenous trees should be noted. ^p^pX. discolor and other ambrosia beetles have the potential to transmit pathogenic fungi to their hosts.^p^pLePelley (1968) records the species as a primary, though not an important pest of coffee in Java, Sri Lanka and Vietnam. Entwhistle (1972) also records the species as a primary borer of twigs and shoots, but notes that its occurrence in cocoa in West Irian was sporadic and in not entirely healthy trees. Speyer (1923) found the species only in diseased branches of rubber trees. Browne (1968) notes minor injury to Mesua ferrea in Pakistan, and its occurrence in unhealthy crowns of several forest plantation trees in India and Sri Lanka. It is clear that the economic impact of the species to date has been small.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>crop production; forestry production
