description: Natural Dispersal^p^pThe adult females fly readily, and flight is one of the main means of movement and dispersal to previously uninfected areas. Of more importance for long distance movement, however, is the transport of infested seedlings, saplings or cut branches.  X. discolor is unlikely to occur in wood packing or crates and similar material, because it normally attacks stems of small diameter (not more than 5 cm diameter).^p^pVector Transmission^p^pThe female has a mycangium, a pouch used to carry spores of the ambrosia fungus on which both adult and larvae feed, opening between the pronotum and mesonotum, and extending below the pronotum (Beaver, 1989). 'Contamination ' of the mycangia by the spores of pathogenic fungi is possible, and the ambrosia fungus itself may be pathogenic in some cases, although there is currently no evidence for this in X. discolor.  The spores of pathogenic fungi could also be transported on the cuticle of the beetle, although their chance of survival there is much less than in the mycangial pouch.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Adults; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Wood: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. Pods)^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx^p - Leaves^p - Roots^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain).

remark: Three other species of Xylosandrus, Xylosandrus compactus, Xylosandrus crassiusculus and Xylosandrus morigerus, with similar habits to X. discolor, have become important pests of tree crops, ornamental and native trees in tropical and subtropical areas where they have been introduced. The risk of introduction for X. discolor must be considered high, most probably in the twigs and small branches of imported plants, although other pathways are also possible.  Once established, such species are difficult to eradicate, and are likely to spread with the movement of infested plants, as well as by normal dispersal of the adults. X. discolor is not currently known to be specifically listed as a quarantine pest.
author: CPC2006

management_info: When Xylosandrus species are detected in plant material, it is necessary to immediately destroy all of the infested material. When they are detected in traps, plant material in the vicinity of the trap should be actively inspected, with special attention directed towards imported woody products such as crating, dunnage and lumber milling scraps. If an active infestation is detected, control using insecticides is possible but of limited effectiveness. Chemical control is not generally effective since the adult beetles bore deep into the host material. The following insecticides were found to be effective against a species of Euwallacea destructive to tea: fenvalerate, deltamethrin, quinalphos, cypermethrin and dichlorvos (Muraleedharan, 1995); these insecticides may also be effective against other ambrosia beetles. Bambara and Casey (2003) suggest the use of permethrin for the related species, Xylosandrus crassiusculus, but multiple treatments may be required during a season. They also suggest the use of some attacked trees as trap trees, which need to be removed and burned before the life cycle of the beetle is completed. ^p^pThe concealed habitats in which these species feed and reproduce, the difficulties and high costs of insecticide application, and environmental concerns all limit the effectiveness of chemical control.

host_range: The natural host range of the virus is limited to species of the Fabaceae; crop hosts are mainly Glycine max (soyabean) and Phaseolus spp. (beans). The weed species Desmodium paniculatum and D. canadensis are natural perennial hosts of BPMV (Moore et al., 1969; Horn et al., 1970; Krell et al., 2003). BPMV is experimentally transmissible to a few other species of the Fabaceae, including Glycine spp., Lespedeza striata, Phaseolus lunatus, Trifolium incarnatum and Vigna unguiculata (Krell et al., 2003).
potential_eco_desc: BPMV was first found in the southern USA in the late 1940s (Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1948) and is now widespread in soyabean producing states. Surveys in Arkansas, Kentucky and North Carolina showed the disease to occur in 100, 66 and 30% of fields, respectively (Walters, 1970; Ross and Butler, 1985; Ghabrial et al., 1990) at incidences ranging from 1 to 100% (Walters, 1970; Pitre et al., 1979; Mueller and Haddox, 1980). Crop loss studies, in which yields of inoculated plants were compared with those of healthy controls, estimated yield reductions ranging from 3 to 52.4% (Myhre et al., 1973; Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Windham and Ross, 1985a; Ross, 1986b). Another report estimated that the incidence of infected plants above which economic loss could occur was in the range of 20-40% (Horn et al., 1973). Individual soyabean plants, growing adjacent to infected plants, yielded 50% more than healthy plants adjacent to healthy plants, suggesting that yield compensation effects occur in infected fields (Windham and Ross, 1985b).^p^pA severe outbreak of BPMV in the north central and northern Great Plains states of the USA in the late 1990s is currently causing serious concern to soybean growers and to the soybean industry in this region (Giesler et al, 2002).
reference_name: Bean pod mottle virus (pod mottle of bean)
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence ^p^pBPMV was established as seedborne on soyabean by Lin and Hill (1983) and Ross (1986b). Daniels et al. (2001) detected incidences of infection on soyabean seeds to 13%. Krell et al. (2005) showed that delayed planting is not a consistently effective management tactic for controlling BPMV. ^p^pEffect on Seed Quality ^p^pMottling and streaking of seed may occur (Brunt et al., 1996). A dull sheen was evident on the seed coat of seeds harvested from inoculated plants, but field emergence was not affected (Quiniones et al., 1971; Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b). Seed samples harvested from BPMV-infected field plots in Nebraska, USA, showed mottling ranging from 59.3 to 91.7% and the average seed quality rating ranged from 2.0 to 4.0 (Ziems et al., 2001). In addition to reducing the yield of infected plants infection also has a deleterious effect on the oil and protein of infected seeds. ^pYield losses induced by BPMV differ according to cultivar, growing conditions and earliness of infection. Losses of 10-40% have been reported (Horn et al., 1973). Yields losses in soybean are much greater if plants are infected with both BPMV and Soybean mosaic virus. ^p^pPathogen Transmission ^p^pSeed ^p^pBPMV was transmitted at a rate of 0.10% by seeds harvested from infected plants, and plants in the greenhouse in sterilized soil in the absence of other inoculum sources (Lin and Hill, 1983). A similar study reported a transmission rate of 0.013% (Ross, 1986b). These low transmission rates have recently been confirmed (Giesler, 2002). ^p^pOther means ^p^pBPMV can be transmitted to soyabeans from Desmodium paniculatum and D canadensis, perennial hosts of the virus, a perennial host of the virus (Moore et al., 1969; Horn et al., 1970; Krell et al., 2003) by the bean leaf beetle (Ceratoma trifurcata), the main vector of the virus (Walters and Lee, 1969). A study of the spatial and temporal distribution of infected plants in a soyabean field indicated that the ability of C. trifurcata to transmit the virus was greatest between the second and third population peaks, about 12 weeks after planting (Hopkins and Mueller, 1983). C. trifurcata transmits BPMV to soyabean plants at growth stages V1 to V6 but not at V9 (Patel and Pitre, 1976). Other vectors for this pathogen include the striped blister beetle (Epicauta vittata) (Patel and Pitre, 1971), the banded cucumber beetle (Diabrotica balteata), the spotted cucumber beetle (D. undecimpunctata howardi), grape colaspis (Colaspis florida) and soybean colaspis (C. lata) (Horn et al., 1970). More recently, western corn rootworm (Diabrotica virgifera virgifera) and soybean leafminer (Odontota horni) have been identified as potential vectors (Werner et al., 2002). ^p^pSeed Treatments ^p^pDaniels et al. (2001) showed that seed treatment with imidacloprid significantly reduced bean leaf beetle damage in the first month after planting, but had no effect on insect damage when leaves were assayed on 21 July. Hunt and Echtenkamp (2001) indicated effective control of the bean leaf beetle on seedling soyabean studies with seed-applied imidacloprid and thiamethoxam. In earlier work, the application of dimethyl sulfoxide, a potential antiviral agent, to healthy seeds before planting did not control field infection (Pitre et al., 1972). ^p^pSeed Health Tests ^p^pGrow-outSeeds were planted in steam-sterilized soil in a greenhouse fumigated at weekly intervals. No other legumes infected by BPMV were present in adjacent greenhouses. Seedling infection was confirmed by testing sap against antisera in agar gel plates, and indexing on bean cv. Royalty Purple Pod and soyabean cv. Williams (Lin and Hill, 1983). ^p^pSerological tests ^p^pBPMV can be detected by ELISA and Ouchterlony gel diffusion assays in bean leaf beetles (Ceratoma trifurcata) and leaf tissues (Ghabrial and Schultz, 1983; Hopkins and Mueller, 1984a). ELISA is still used widely for BPMV detection (e.g., Krell et al., 2005; Di et al., 1996). ^p^pIowa State University Seed Health Testing Laboratory has adapted a diagnostic kit manufactured by Agdia Unc, Elkhart, Indiana, USA, to test for this pathogen in seeds. The method is available at the USDA National Seed Health System web site, www.seedhealth.org. ^p^pMolecular methods ^p^pPolymerase Chain Reaction. A PCR procedure has been shown to be very efficient and highly sensitive for the detection of BPMV (Gu et al., 2002). A degenerate Reverse Transcription Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (RT-LAMP) has been used successfully for the detection of BPMV in seeds (Wei et al., 2012). The virus can also be detected by Western Blotting (Krell et al., 2005).

management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pNo resistance was found in 169 soyabean cultivars and PIs (Scott et al., 1974) or 70 soyabean lines and cultivars (Walters, 1970). Another study showed that no cultivars were immune, but some displayed a high degree of resistance (Schwenk and Nickell, 1980). Four soyabean germplasm lines were registered as resistant to BPMV in 1986 (Ross, 1986a) but no resistant cultivars were commercially available as of 1990 (Ghabrial et al., 1990). Higher levels of infection reported in tall rather than short genotypes probably resulted from larger numbers of the vector, Ceratoma trifurcata, preferentially feeding on taller plants (Windham and Ross, 1985b). Resistant transgenic plants have been produced (Srinivasa et al., 2001; Di et al., 1996) but their possible practical use has yet to be fully tested.^p^p^Disease Management^p^p Delayed planting^p Disease incidence increased more rapidly in June than in May plantings in North Carolina (Windham and Ross, 1985b). Another report from the same state showed that the pathogen caused significant yield loss for both early and late plantings (Ross, 1986b).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe application of dimethyl sulfoxide, a potential antiviral agent, onto inoculated seedlings, had no effect on disease development under greenhouse conditions (Pitre et al., 1972). Carbaryl sprays reduced populations of the vector Ceratoma trifurcata (Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Ross, 1986b). A good correlation between BPMV infection levels in leaves and C. trifurcata within the same rows in a soyabean field suggested the possibility of using beetle assays to predict plant infection and the need for insecticide sprays (Ghabrial et al., 1990).

management_info: 一种可能的抗病毒的物质二甲亚砜在接种苗上的应用在温室条件下对病害发展没有效果(Pitre et al., 1972)。西维因（Carbaryl）喷雾能减少媒介Ceratoma trifurcata的种群数量(Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Ross, 1986b).。叶片上BPMV的侵染水平与在大豆田内的同一排中的C. trifurcata的良好的相互关系揭示了利用甲虫化验来预测侵染水平和喷洒杀虫剂的需要的可能性。 The application of dimethyl sulfoxide, a potential antiviral agent, onto inoculated seedlings, had no effect on disease development under greenhouse conditions (Pitre et al., 1972). Carbaryl sprays reduced populations of the vector Ceratoma trifurcata (Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Ross, 1986b). A good correlation between BPMV infection levels in leaves and C. trifurcata within the same rows in a soyabean field suggested the possibility of using beetle assays to predict plant infection and the need for insecticide sprays (Ghabrial et al., 1990). 在169种大豆品种和PIs(Scott et al., 1974)或70种大豆系和品种(Walters, 1970)中，没有发现抗性。另一份研究显示，没有品种是免疫的，但一些显示高度的抗性(Schwenk and Nickell, 1980)。1986年四种大豆种质系被登记作为BPMV抗性(Ross, 1986a)，但在1990年没有抗性品种是在商业上采用的(Ghabrial et al., 1990)。较高水平的侵染在长的而不是短的基因型上被报道，这可能由较大数量的媒介Ceratoma trifurcata优先在较高的植物上取食而引起的(Windham and Ross, 1985b)。 No resistance was found in 169 soyabean cultivars and PIs (Scott et al., 1974) or 70 soyabean lines and cultivars (Walters, 1970). Another study showed that no cultivars were immune, but some displayed a high degree of resistance (Schwenk and Nickell, 1980). Four soyabean germplasm lines were registered as resistant to BPMV in 1986 (Ross, 1986a) but no resistant cultivars were commercially available as of 1990 (Ghabrial et al., 1990). Higher levels of infection reported in tall rather than short genotypes probably resulted from larger numbers of the vector, Ceratoma trifurcata, preferentially feeding on taller plants (Windham and Ross, 1985b). 在北加州，6月种植比5月种植的病害发生率增长得更加迅速(Windham and Ross, 1985b)。另外来自同一个州的一份报道显示，该病原物引起早期和后期种植的重大的产量损失(Windham and Ross, 1985b)。 Disease incidence increased more rapidly in June than in May plantings in North Carolina (Windham and Ross, 1985b). Another report from the same state showed that the pathogen caused significant yield loss for both early and late plantings(Windham and Ross, 1985b)
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: 调查显示，阿肯色州、肯塔基州和北加州在病害发生率从1％到100％的范围(Walters, 1970; Pitre et al., 1979; Mueller and Haddox, 1980)内病害发生率分别为100％、66％和33％(Walters, 1970; Ross and Butler, 1985; Ghabrial et al., 1990)。比较接种植物和进行了健康防治的植物的产量的作物损失研究估计，其产量减少范围从3％到52.4％(Myhre et al., 1973; Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Windham and Ross, 1985a; Ross, 1986b)。另一份报道估计，感染植株在经济损失之上的发病率能在20％到40％的范围内发生(Horn et al., 1973)。生长在感染植物附近的个别的大豆植物比邻近健康植物的健康植物要高产50％，这显示产量补偿作用发生在感染田地中(Windham and Ross, 1985b)。 Surveys in Arkansas, Kentucky and North Carolina showed the disease to occur in 100, 66 and 30% of fields, respectively (Walters, 1970; Ross and Butler, 1985; Ghabrial et al., 1990) at incidences ranging from 1 to 100% (Walters, 1970; Pitre et al., 1979; Mueller and Haddox, 1980). Crop loss studies, in which yields of inoculated plants were compared with those of healthy controls, estimated yield reductions ranging from 3 to 52.4% (Myhre et al., 1973; Hopkins and Mueller, 1984b; Windham and Ross, 1985a; Ross, 1986b). Another report estimated that the incidence of infected plants above which economic loss could occur was in the range of 20-40% (Horn et al., 1973). Individual soyabean plants, growing adjacent to infected plants, yielded 50% more than healthy plants adjacent to healthy plants, suggesting that yield compensation effects occur in infected fields (Windham and Ross, 1985b).
description:
BPMV在美国南部于20世纪40年代后期被第一次发现(Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1948)，现在已经广泛分布于生产大豆的州。BPMV于20世纪90年代后期在美国大平原州的中北部和北部的一次严重的爆发，普遍引起了这个地区的大豆种植者和大豆产业的重大的关注(Giesler et al, 2002)。 BPMV was first found in the southern USA in the late 1940s (Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1948) and is now widespread in soyabean producing states.
A severe outbreak of BPMV in the north central and northern Great Plains states of the USA in the late 1990s is currently causing serious concern to soybean growers and to the soybean industry in this region (Giesler et al, 2002).
author: zhangjianjun

description: BPMV能以0.10％的比率通过来自感染植株和种植在温室没有其他接种体来源的消毒土壤中的收获种子来传播(Lin and Hill, 1983)。BPMV能通过该病毒的主要媒介菜豆叶甲(Cerotoma trifurcata)从该病毒的一个多年生寄主Desmodium paniculatum (Moore et al., 1969; Horn et al., 1970)传播到大豆中去(Walters and Lee, 1969)。这个病毒的其他媒介包括北美豆芫菁(Epicauta vittata) (Patel and Pitre, 1971)、the banded cucumber beetle (Diabrotica balteata)、黄瓜十一星叶甲(D. undecimpunctata howardi)、葡萄肖叶甲 (Colaspis flavida)和豆肖叶甲(C. lata) (Horn et al., 1970)。更为最近，玉米根萤叶甲 (western corn rootworm)和大豆斑潜蝇(soybean leafminer)被鉴定为可能媒介。 BPMV was transmitted at a rate of 0.10% by seeds harvested from infected plants, and planted in the greenhouse in sterilized soil in the absence of other inoculum sources (Lin and Hill, 1983).BPMV can be transmitted to soyabeans from Desmodium paniculatum, a perennial host of the virus (Moore et al., 1969; Horn et al., 1970) by the bean leaf beetle (Ceratoma trifurcata), the main vector of the virus (Walters and Lee, 1969). Other vectors for this pathogen include the striped blister beetle (Epicauta vittata) (Patel and Pitre, 1971), the banded cucumber beetle (Diabrotica balteata), the spotted cucumber beetle (D. undecimpunctata howardi), grape colaspis (Colaspis florida) and soybean colaspis (C. lata) (Horn et al., 1970). More recently, Diabrotica virgifera virgifera (western corn rootworm)and Odontota horni (soybean leafminer)have been identified as potential vectors (Werner et al, 2002).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: The incidence rate are approximately 65% in a commercial field.
description: During June 2014, approximately 65% of hot pepper (Capsicum annum) plants in a commercial field in Multan district of Pakistan showed symptoms of curling, deformation, and interveinal leaf yellowing. The symptomatic leaf samples were tested by double antibody sandwich (DAS)-ELISA and RT-PCR showed the presence of Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of PeVYV from Pakistan.
reference_name: First Report of Pepper vein yellows virus Infecting Hot Pepper in Pakistan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: It has been reported that PeVYV could infect pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) and black nightshade (Solanum nigrum) under natural conditions. This is the first report that tobacco is a natural host of PeVYV.
description: In 2016, 21 tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) plants showed viral-like symptoms of interveinal yellowing and leaf puckering in a field in Guiyang, Guizhou Province, China. Based on molecular diagnostics confirmed the presence of Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV). This is the first report that tobacco is a natural host of PeVYV.  PeVYV is transmitted by aphids in a nonpropagative manner.
reference_name: First Report of Pepper vein yellows virus Infecting Tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) Naturally in China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: Sweet pepper (Capsicum annum).
potential_eco_desc: In the greenhouse, symptoms were evident in about 35% of the plants.
description: In October 2015, severe symptoms not previously reported by growers in the horticultural area of the province of Trapani (Sicily, Italy) were observed on sweet pepper plants in eight different greenhouses. These symptoms were reminiscent of those caused by poleroviruses. The samples were collected for analysis. Based on sequences analysis confirmed the pathogen was Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of PeVYV in Italy. PeVYV has the potential to cause significant to pepper crops.  PeVYV is a member of the genus Polerovirus. Poleroviruses are transmitted by aphids in a persistent (circulative) and non-propagative manner.
management_info: Anti-aphid treatments were done to prevent the spread of disease to other areas.
reference_name: First outbreak of Pepper vein yellows virus infecting sweet pepper in Italy
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: In Europe, PeVYV has only been reported on Capsicum spp. in Spain (Villanueva et al., 2013). This is the first report of PeVYV in Italy where it has been detected in three of the major species of cultivated chilli: C. annuum, C. chinense and C. frutescens. With the simultaneous findings of PeVYV in two distinct areas, and in different varieties, it is possible that the virus has a wider distribution in Italy.
description: In 2015, 2% of plants from two fields located in different provinces of the Lazio region (Viterbo and Roma) and used for germplasm maintenance and seed production of chilli varieties and species, were observed showing interveinal yellowing or yellow patches, and brittleness of leaves. Total RNA from samples of diseased leaf tissue, the presence of Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV) was confirmed using RT-PCR. In Europe, PeVYV has only been reported on Capsicum spp. in Spain (Villanueva et al., 2013). This is the first report of PeVYV in Italy where it has been detected in three of the major species of cultivated chilli: C. annuum, C. chinense and C. frutescens. With the simultaneous findings of PeVYV in two distinct areas, and in different varieties, it is possible that the virus has a wider distribution in Italy where the cultivation of chilli is increasing for its ornamental, food and nutritional value, as well as posing a threat to sweet pepper production in the region.
reference_name: First report of Pepper vein yellows virus infecting chilli pepper (Capsicum spp.) in Italy
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 辣椒 Capsicum spp.
potential_eco_desc: The disease incidence was estimated at about 75% based on visual symptoms.
description: A routine inspection of a field planted with hot and sweet pepper (Capsicum spp.) in South Texas was undertaken during late summer of 2014. Plants showing symptoms consisting primarily of interveinal yellowing and vein clearing were observed and disease incidence was estimated at about 75% based on visual symptoms. The samples were collected and identified, based on molecular diagnostics showed that the causal agent was Pepper vein yellows virus(PeVYV). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of PeVYV in the United States, thus adding the nation to the areas of occurrence of the virus, and highlighting further its potential as a worldwide threat to pepper and related crops.
reference_name: First Report of Pepper vein yellows virus Infecting Pepper (Capsicum spp.) in the United States
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 辣椒 Capsicum annuum
potential_eco_desc: The disease incidence was estimated to be 5 to 10%.
description: In the summer of 2014, pepper plants in Juxian, Shandong Province, China, showed symptoms of leaf curling, vein yellowing, and stem internode shortening, which are similar to those caused by species belonging to Polerovirus. The samples were collected and identified, based on molecular characteristics the causal agent was identified as Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of PeVYV infection in pepper plants in Shandong Province, China.  PeVYV was first reported in Japan in 1995 and is known to infect plant during grafting and by aphids.
reference_name: The First Identification of Pepper vein yellows virus in Shandong Province, China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: Our finding supports other findings that Pepper vein yellows virus threatens pepper and other Solanaceae crops across the globe. It has been reported infecting pepper and nightshade (Solanum nigrum) in several districts and countries in Southeast Asia, Africa, and Europe in 2013. This is the first report of pepper vein yellows virus infecting red pepper in Mainland China.
description: In June 2013, six samples of red pepper (Capsicum frutescens L.) were sampled in three greenhouses in Changsha city, Hunan Province, China, for viral-like symptoms. Of these, three of the sampled red pepper plants displayed symptoms in common, which were similar to those that infected by Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV), also designated as Pepper yellow leaf curl virus (PYLCV) and Pepper yellows virus (PYV) at one time. Based on electron microscopy and RNA sequencing confirmed that the pathogen causing was PeVYV. The spread of PeVYV in Hunan Province, China is evidence that this virus is spreading from the field where it was first discovered in1995.
reference_name: First Report of Pepper vein yellows virus Infecting Red Pepper in Mainland China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 辣椒Capsicum annuum In addition to hot pepper (Capsicum annuum), PeVYV has recently been identified in seven other countries and on one new host, Solanum nigrum.
description: In two successive winters (2009 and 2010), 14 hot pepper (Capsicum annuum) samples showing unusual symptoms were surveyed in permanently irrigated seasonal vegetable gardens along the Blue Nile in central Sudan (specifically in Gezira State). Symptoms included leaf curling, leaf deformation, reduced leaf size, leaf puckering, interveinal yellowing, vein clearing, or yellow patches. The samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was Pepper vein yellows virus（PeVYV）. The presence of the recently described Polerovirus PeVYV is the first report of detection in pepper in Sudan.
reference_name: First Report of Pepper vein yellows virus Infecting Hot Pepper in Sudan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: In Ecuador, tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) disorders caused by potyviruses have been reported in the past. In 2013, leaves from tamarillo plants showing severe virus-like symptoms (mosaic, mottling, and leaf deformation) were collected from orchards in Pichincha and Tungurahua. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) was extracted from three independent batches and used to generate cDNA libraries to screen for RNA viruses by shotgun cloning. Sequencing revealed the presence of the potyviruses Potato virus Y (PVY), Potato virus V (PVV), and Peru tomato mosaic virus (PTV), and the polerovirus Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV). To determine the occurrence of the viruses, leaf samples tested by RT-PCR. Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription was done. For symptomatic plants, PVY and PLRV were the most common with 64% and 30%, respectively. PVV and PTV were found in 8% and 10%, respectively, with only 4% of the plants coinfected by both viruses. Plants coinfected by PVY and PLRV were the most common with 22%, followed by plants coinfected by PVY and PTV (10%). PVY has long been considered the most common virus in tamarillo in Ecuador. This communication reports for the first time in tamarillo the presence of PVV and PTV, two potyviruses once considered strains of PVY. Further studies are needed to determine the significance of PVV and PTV in single and mixed infections in tamarillo.
reference_name: First Report of Potato virus V and Peru tomato mosaic virus on Tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) Orchards of Ecuador
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 长蒴黄麻Corchorus olitorius (cv. JRO524)
description: In June 2013, symptoms suggestive of a viral disease were noticed on jute (cv. JRO524) in an experimental field of the CRIJAF research farm, Barrackpore, India, and the incidence of the disease was less than 2%. Although initially the incidence was low, it may spread to larger areas in subsequent years. Because the jute fiber is extracted from the stem, stunted growth and short height would badly affect the fiber yield and quality. The samples were collected from the field. Based on molecular detection showed that the causal agent was Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV). PLRV is a small isometric RNA virus with worldwide distribution belonging to the family Luteoviridae whose natural host range is mainly restricted to solanaceous plants and few plants of other families. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of PLRV naturally occurring on jute (C. olitorius).  The aphid Aphis gossypii was often noticed in the jute field. Cucumber mosaic virus, Bean common mosaic virus, Cowpea mosaic virus, Papaya ring spot virus, Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV), Potato virus Y, and Watermelon mosaic virus were common aphid transmitted viruses.
reference_name: First Report of Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV) Naturally Occurring on Jute (Corchorus olitorius) in India
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 马铃薯Solanum tuberosum
description: A survey for potato viruses was performed between mid-August and the beginning of September during the 2009 and 2010 growing seasons. Tubers or leaves were sampled from plants showing virus symptoms of rugosity and dwarfing from some farms in the agricultural region of southern Greenland. The test demonstrated that the following viruses were presence: Potato leafroll virus, Potato virus A, Potato virus X, and Potato virus Y. To our knowledge this is the first time that potato viruses have been recorded in Greenland.
reference_name: First report of Potato leafroll virus, Potato virus A, Potato virus X and Potato virus Y in potato in Greenland
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: Natural hosts are mainly species in the Solanaceae (Sousa-Diaz, 1993), although Ullucus tuberosus in the Basellaceae (Lizarraga et al., 1996) and Sisymbrium altissimum and Capsella bursa-pastoris in the Brassicaceae (Fox et al., 1993) have also been repor
potential_eco_desc: PLRV is considered to be the most serious and damaging virus of potatoes. It causes severe yield losses (up to 90%) and in some cultivars also reduces the marketable quality due to internal net necrosis (Jeffries, 1998).
author: CPC2006

description: PLRV is transmitted by several aphid species in a persistent, circulative manner. The green peach aphid (Myzus persicae) is the most efficient vector in nature although the potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae), the foxglove aphid (Aulacorthum solani) (Stevenson et al., 2001) and Aphis gossypii (Singh et al., 1988) are also important vectors under some conditions. The efficiency of transmission increases with prolonged acquisition, incubation and inoculation times and the size of the vector population is important in increasing the incidence of PLRV in the crops.^p^pLong-distance dissemination of PLRV occurs mainly through the distribution of infected potato seed tubers.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: borne internally; invisible.^p - Fruits (inc. Pods): borne internally; invisible.^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx: borne internally; invisible.^p - Leaves: borne internally; invisible.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: borne internally; invisible.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; invisible.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - Roots^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain).

remark: PLRV is not considered a pathogen of quarantine status because of its wide distribution.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Seed Certification^p^pControl of PLRV is based primarily on the use of virus-free or certified seed potatoes (Slack and Singh, 1998). Tolerance levels to PLRV in certified seed planted in several countries differs. In most stringent programmes, tolerances are not usually higher than 0.5% although in others up to 3-5% is considered to be the threshold level.^p^pEarly warning systems for increases in aphid vector populations exist only in a few developed countries. These systems are especially helpful in detecting late-season aphid migration in seed production programmes.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pTwo approaches have been used to develop resistance to PLRV: resistance to the virus (resistance to infection and multiplication) and resistance to the aphid vectors (Harrewijn, 1986; Barker et al., 1994; Franco Lara and Barker, 1999). In addition, transgenic resistance to the virus is being studied, alone or in combination with natural resistance (Derrick and Barker, 1997). Natural resistance sources have been described at the International Potato Centre in Lima, Peru (Jayasinghe and Salazar, 1998). However, due to the multicomponent nature of the resistance to PLRV, cultivars with high overall resistance to PLRV are not easy to develop.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pRoguing of infected plants and the elimination of weeds and volunteer potatoes are common practices used to prevent or minimise the spread of leafroll. Control of aphids in the field by the application of insecticides also helps to reduce or prevent the spread of PLRV.

host_range: This is the first report of grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) as a natural host for SCYLV.
potential_eco_desc: Sugarcane yellow leaf virus can caused yield losses up to 20% in susceptible sugarcane cultivars. If this virus continues to be spread by Melanaphis sacchari in grain sorghum and across sorghum-growing states, yellow leaf could become a new emerging disease of this plant in the United States.
description: Since late 2013, severe infestations of grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) by Melanaphis sacchari were observed in several southern U.S. states (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, and Texas), and also more recently in southern Florida. In summer 2015, numerous aphids (>100 individuals per leaf) were seen on plants in two grain sorghum trials at Belle Glade, near sugarcane fields and Columbus grass (S. almum) known to be infected by SCYLV. From September to December 2015, stalks of S. bicolor cultivar were collected from these trials and tested for SCYLV using tissue blot immunoassay and molecular method, results confirmed the samples of S. bicolor with SCYLV. To our knowledge, this is the first report of grain sorghum as a natural host for SCYLV.  SCYLV is transmitted by at least four different aphid species (order Hemiptera, family Aphididae) in a persistent, circulative, and nonpropagative manner: the sugarcane woolly aphid, Ceratovacuna lanigera; the white sugarcane aphid, Melanaphis sacchari; the corn leaf aphid, Rhopalosiphum maidis; and the rice root aphid, R. rufiabdominalis. Among those, M. sacchari has been reported to be the most widespread and efficient vector of SCYLV.
reference_name: First report of Sugarcane yellow leaf virus infecting grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) in the United States
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of Columbus grass (Sorghum almum) as a host for Sugarcane yellow leaf virus .
potential_eco_desc: Columbus grass(Sorghum almum) is widely distributed in sugarcane-growing areas in Florida and may constitute an alternative host and previously unknown inoculum source of Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV). Transmission of the virus from Columbus grass to sugarcane needs to be verified to investigate the importance of this potential secondary host in the epidemiology and control of sugarcane yellow leaf.
description: During spring 2015, leaves or stalks of several grasses growing near sugarcane fields were collected and tested for Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) using tissue blot immunoassay. A total of 170 of 489 samples (35%) of Columbus grass (Sorghum almum) tested positive for SCYLV. Molecular diagnostics showed Columbus grass as a host for SCYLV. This is the first report of Columbus grass as a host for SCYLV.  Transmission of Sugarcane yellow leaf virus from Columbus grass to sugarcane needs to be verified to investigate the importance of this potential secondary host in the epidemiology and control of sugarcane yellow leaf.
reference_name: First Report of Sugarcane yellow leaf virus Infecting Columbus Grass (Sorghum almum) in Florida
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 除侵染甘蔗外，人工蚜虫接种还可以侵染玉米、水稻、高粱、大麦、小麦、燕麦等。
potential_eco_desc: 是一种严重危害甘蔗生长的世界性甘蔗疾病，发病率在10％～96之间。我国各植蔗区也相当普遍和严重。  该病的发生导致甘蔗产量下降，品质变劣和种性退化，严重时甘蔗产量减产高达40％～60％。巴西的高糖品种SP7卜6163，种植面积曾占巴西圣保罗州30％以上，但是其对甘蔗黄叶综合症非常敏感。最大减产高达40％～60％[1]。甘蔗YLS引起美国路州主栽品种LCP82-89产量减产15％～20％，糖产量减低6％～14％[2]，曾为夏威夷和佛罗里达的主产品种H65-7052和CP72-1210，因严重感染该病使甘蔗减产25％～50％。美国报道所有CP系列的甘蔗品种均感该病。
description: 自1990年Schenck等第次报道了有关在美国夏威夷群岛上甘蔗大面积出现的一种有别于营养缺乏的甘蔗黄化现象，世界甘蔗主产区先后报道该病。2001年我国广西区南宁市第一次出现甘蔗黄叶综合症类似症状，当时未引起人们的注意。2002年，广西区大面积出现甘蔗黄叶综合症类似症状。  病原可由带毒种茎或种苗做为初侵染源．田问经蚜虫传播进行再侵染，主要传播蚜虫有：高梁蚜(Melanaphis sacchari)、玉米叶蚜(Palosiphum maidis)和红腹缢管蚜(R. rufiabdominalis)传播，但不能通过机械摩擦传。
author: cpqis.liangxinmiao

description:
由甘蔗黄叶病毒引起的甘蔗黄叶病1989年首先发现于美国夏威夷，现已证明在世界多个蔗区均有发生，近年我国台湾及广西已有该病发生的报道.  该病毒分布于寄主韧皮部伴胞中，可经高梁蚜(Melanaphis
sacchari)和玉米蚜(Rhopalosiphum maidis)以持久性方式进行传播。甘蔗绵蚜(Ceratovacuna lanigera)也可携带该病毒。

description: In June 2014, viral symptoms of interveinal green mottling, initial chlorotic legions of younger leaves, and bright yellowing and thickening of older leaves were observed in melon (Cucumis melo L., Cantalupensis Group, ‘Cantalupo’) plants in Eum-Seong, Korea. Effective controls of aphid vectors are a good strategy for CABYV management in melon as well as in other cucurbit crops since CABYV is a persistently transmitted virus.

description: In January 2014, interveinal chlorosis and yellowing symptoms were observed in cucumber (Cucumis sativus) and in squash (Cucurbita pepo) plants in two greenhouses and two open-field crops, respectively, in the Al-Kharj area of the Riyadh region, Saudi Arabia. At least three viruses are reported to be involved in cucurbit yellows disease: Beet pseudo-yellows virus (BPYV), Cucurbit yellow stunting disorder virus (CYSDV), and Cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus (CABYV). A total of 56 symptomatic samples (27 cucumber and 15 squash leaves) as well as 13 symptomless weed samples (three Malva parviflora, seven Chenopodium murale, two Sonchus oleraceous, and one Solanum nigrum) were collected and subjected to total RNA extraction. RT-PCR results revealed the presence of CABYV in both cucumber (8/27) and squash (10/15) plants as well as in C. murale (1/7) and S. nigrum (1/1). CYSDV was also detected in cucumber (11/27) and squash (6/15) and appeared in mixed infections with CABYV in cucumber. To our knowledge, this is the first report of CABYV infecting cucumber and squash in Saudi Arabia, while infected weeds may play an important role in epidemiology of CABYV as potential reservoirs.

potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pBaYMV is regarded as a major pathogen of winter barley in Belgium, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Korea and the UK. It is restricted to barley and occurs only on autumn-sown crops, but within the countries named it occurs throughout the regions where the crop is grown. Because the virus survives in soil within its fungus vector, it causes disease every time that a susceptible crop is planted but the intensity of symptoms and the degree of yield loss varies, depending upon the barley genotype, sowing date and winter weather conditions. The disease is most severe on crops sown early in the autumn (Watanabe et al., 1989; Adams et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1998; Overthrow et al., 1999) and when the autumn is mild and wet but the winter is especially cold (Kusaba et al., 1971). Like other soil-borne diseases, the distribution of the pathogen in the soil is rarely uniform and this complicates the measurement of yield losses. Where appropriate resistant varieties exist, these are immune to the virus and suffer no yield loss. Their increasing use in Japan and Europe has decreased the national losses, and the disease is now reckoned to be less damaging on a national scale than in the 1980s, although concerns remain about the development of resistance-breaking strains of the virus.^p^p^Crop Losses^p^pIn China, it has been estimated that the disease causes yield losses of 10-30% in infested fields, but as much as 50 to 100% where infestation is severe. The average yield loss approximately 10 years ago was estimated to be 0.45 t/ha, which, at 2000 prices, represents an economic loss of 450 yuan/ha. In field experiments, 10-80% of plants were killed, the number of tillers was reduced by over 10%, the numbers of grains per ear were reduced by 30-85% and the thousand kernel weight by 15-51%. The total land area affected throughout China was estimated to be 12M ha (Ruan and Chen, 1991).^p^pIn Japan, barley cultivation is decreasing and in many areas deployment of resistant two-rowed cultivars (containing the ym5 gene from Mokusekko 3) has overcome the disease. However, in some areas, especially Tochigi and Ibaraki Prefectures where the resistant cultivars have been grown for more than ten years, the BaYMV strain III, able to infect cultivars with the ym5 gene, has become widespread (Sotome et al., 1997). In field experiments with susceptible cultivars (for example, Akagi Nijo) in 1984-1990, it was shown that when 64-66% of plants were affected, the yield was reduced by 48%, and when 88% of plants were affected, the yield was reduced by 61%. In more recent work using the ym5 resistant cv. Misato Golden infected by BaYMV strain III, 10-25% yield reduction occurred when the disease incidence exceeded 90% (Iida et al., 1992). In 1998, barley was planted on ca 56,000 ha in Japan, and 3802 ha of them (mostly two-rowed barley) were affected by BaYMV (surveyed by the Plant Protection Division, MAFF, Japan; Ohto, 2000). There are no official figures for economic losses from BaYMV in Japan. In a rather old estimate for Ibaraki Prefecture in 1985, Ogawa (1986) estimated the affected area as 4050 ha, grain losses as 3900 t, and the economic damage about 700 million yen. It seems probable that the current economic losses in Japan are similar to this.^p^pIn Italy, BaYMV is only known to occur in association with Barley mild mosaic virus (BaMMV). The two viruses are very widely spread in central and northern Italy, especially in the regions of Emilia-Romagna, Lombardia, Friuli and Veneto. About 180,000 ha of winter barley is grown in these areas and the disease is serious where barley is grown intensively but there are no estimates of the land areas affected. potential_eco_desc: 在比利时、中国、法国、德国、意大利、日本、韩国和英国，BaYMV被作为是冬大麦上的主要病原物。它被限制在大麦上而且只发生在秋季播种的作物上，但在这些国家内它在所有作物种植的地区发生。因为病毒存活于土壤内的它的真菌媒介中，所以它在每一次种植易感作物时引起病害，但症状的强度和产量损失由于大麦基因型、播种日期和冬季天气条件的不同而不同。这病害在于初秋播种的作物上(Watanabe et al., 1989; Adams et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1998; Overthrow et al., 1999)以及当秋季是温暖和潮湿的但冬天特别的寒冷时(Kusaba et al., 1971)最为严重。 BaYMV is regarded as a major pathogen of winter barley in Belgium, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Korea and the UK. It is restricted to barley and occurs only on autumn-sown crops, but within the countries named it occurs throughout the regions where the crop is grown. Because the virus survives in soil within its fungus vector, it causes disease every time that a susceptible crop is planted but the intensity of symptoms and the degree of yield loss varies, depending upon the barley genotype, sowing date and winter weather conditions. The disease is most severe on crops sown early in the autumn (Watanabe et al., 1989; Adams et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1998; Overthrow et al., 1999) and when the autumn is mild and wet but the winter is especially cold (Kusaba et al., 1971). 在所有的地区，除了直接损失外，因为土地的感染可能限制了在冬大麦是主要作物的地方的作物或品种的选择，以及抗性品种可能比最好的敏感品种有更低的产量可能性，因此还存在间接的经济影响(Gouis et al., 1999)。大麦轻型花叶病毒是相当普遍的，特别在欧洲，它与大麦黄花叶病毒有相同的传播媒介。两种病毒通常在同一块田内发生，并且可能在同一棵植株上发生。大麦品种可能对这两个病毒作出不同的反应，所以田间侵染是复杂的。 In all regions, apart from direct losses, there may also be indirect economic impact because infestation of the land may restrict the choice of crop or variety in areas where winter barley is the preferred crop and resistant varieties may have a lower yield potential than the best susceptible ones (Gouis et al., 1999). Barley mild mosaic virus is fairly common, especially in Europe, and has the same vector as Barley yellow mosaic virus. The two viruses often occur on the same fields and may occur together in the same plants. Barley varieties may respond differently to the two viruses, so yield effects are complex.

description: BaYMV是通过感染根部真菌禾谷类多粘菌（Polymyxa graminis.）传播的。这个真菌是一种专性根部寄生菌，它在谷类的根部非常的普遍，但很可能只造成较小的损害，除非它也传播细菌。它的休眠孢子在孢子堆内形成（通常叫做休眠孢子堆），它存留在作物收获后的根部残骸中并在土壤中保存多年。该病毒只有在真菌在大麦根部里生长的情况下才能被获得或传播，它被携带在孢子里面，并由于这个原因该病害是土传的。干燥空气的土壤能保持侵染能力超过5年(Inouye and Saito, 1975)，但这几乎是肯定地低估了它在田间接种体内的寿命。 BaYMV is transmitted by the root-infecting fungus Polymyxa graminis. This fungus is an obligate, root parasite that is very common in cereal roots but which probably does little damage unless it is also transmitting the virus. Its resting spores are formed in clusters (often called cystosori), which remain within root debris after the crop is harvested and can persist in soil for many years. The virus, which can only be acquired and transmitted while the fungus is growing within a barley root, is carried within the spores and for this reason the disease is soilborne. Air-dried soil retained infectivity for more than 5 years (Inouye and Saito, 1975), but this is almost certainly an underestimate of the longevity of inoculum in the field.

description: In November 2016, cassava fields were inspected in Ituri Province, northeastern DRC. Fields were selected at 10- to 20-km intervals in the surveyed area. A total of 360 (10 per field) leaf samples were collected from 36 fields. Using molecular diagnostics showed, eleven of the 36 fields were affected by CBSD, and average incidence in affected fields was 90.3%. Of the 360 leaf samples, 108 tested positive for cassava brown streak ipomoviruses (CBSIs). Species-level identifications using real-time PCR, made on a subset of these positive-testing samples, revealed that 55% had mixed UCBSV + CBSV infections, whereas 45% were only infected by UCBSV. There were no single CBSV infections. To our knowledge, this is the first report confirming the occurrence of both UCBSV and CBSV in the north-eastern part of DRC.  CBSV and UCBSV are spread through infected stem cuttings and by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
reference_name: First Report of Mixed Infection of Cassava Brown Streak Virus and Ugandan Cassava Brown Streak Virus on Cassava in North-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo

description: In 2014, symptoms of yellowing on leaves and brown necrotic rot on tuberous roots on different cassava landraces on the west coast of Mayotte (Maoré) were associated with Cassava brown streak virus (CBSV) and Ugandan cassava brown streak virus (UCBSV). Similar symptoms were observed in April 2015 in the north of Mayotte and in July and September 2016 in the three other islands of the Comoros archipelago: Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Anjouan (Ndzuwani) and Mohéli (Mwali). To evaluate the disease epidemic in the south-western Indian Ocean islands and to verify the identity of the causal agents, symptomatic leaf samples were collected and tested. The test results demonstrate that CBSD epidemic has reached the four islands of the Comoros archipelago and as in East and Central Africa. Cassava brown streak disease (CBSD) is caused by two ipomoviruses, CBSV and UCBSV. This is the first report of CBSD in Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli which demonstrate the expanding epidemic of CBSD in the south-western Indian Ocean islands.

management_info: Introduction^p^pCBSD has received such limited research attention that current control recommendations are largely based on general pathological principles and experience rather than on extensive research (Hillocks, 1997).^p^p^Phytosanitation^p^pCassava is usually propagated vegetatively from hardwood stem cuttings, and CBSD is perpetuated and disseminated in this way. There is a considerable traffic in plant material within and sometimes between countries and inevitably CBSD is disseminated in this way. Selected 'virus-free' planting material is seldom available except when produced specially for official introductions using meristem-tip therapy and/or heat therapy in order to meet quarantine requirements. It is important that such requirements are strictly enforced because of the present limited distribution of CBSD in parts of eastern and southern Africa.^p^pA basic approach to control should be the use of virus-free planting material, but little attempt has been made to develop and apply this approach with CBSD or other virus diseases of cassava (Thresh et al., 1994). With CBSD there are difficulties in selecting virus-free material because the symptoms of infection can be vague and indistinct, and more effective means of detection were not previously available. However, it is likely that considerable improvement could be made in the present unsatisfactory situation by selecting cuttings for propagation only from plants that have been inspected during growth and also at harvest and found to be free of leaf, stem and root symptoms. Foundation stocks could be established in this way for subsequent multiplication and distribution to farmers. There are also advantages in farmers selecting propagating material only from unaffected plants at the time they collect cuttings. Unfortunately, however, farmers are not familiar with the whole range of CBSD symptoms, and cuttings may be collected at times when the source plants are almost leafless or severely affected by the cassava green mite (Mononychellus tanajoa), cassava mealybug (Phenacoccus manihoti), leaf spot or bacterial blight. Further studies are required on the most effective means of selection and on the ways in which simple procedures can be introduced to farmers.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe differences between varieties in their sensitivity to infection are already being exploited by farmers who tend to discard those severely affected by CBSD and retain those that grow and yield satisfactorily even when infected. There is certainly a high turnover in cassava varieties as recorded in many parts of Africa and influenced by various pests and diseases (Nweke et al., 1994).^p^pEarly experience in Tanzania showed the scope for breeding resistant or tolerant varieties. Moreover, in crop improvement programmes there is a need to evaluate the response of introduced genotypes before they are released for use by farmers in areas where CBSD is prevalent^p^p^Integrated Pest Management^p^pThere is a general acceptance of the need to develop overall IPM programmes for the whole range of cassava pests and diseases (Thresh et al., 1994). However, little progress has been made in developing such programmes, even though there are likely to be important interactions between CBSD and other diseases, and also with cassava mealybug and green mite.

description:
有间接证据证明CBSV的自然传播发生。因此，幼苗后代在排除种子传播的情况下有时候会受到侵染，当被种植在马拉维、坦桑尼亚和肯尼亚的受感染地方时，西非品种和来自不发生CBSV的地区的其他引入也会受到感染。有少量的关于传播速率的公开证明，但在一些情况下，这被已知是快速的。
传播的方法是未知的，但粉虱被长期暗示作为传播媒介。用烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci ）(非洲木薯花叶的媒介和在非洲最普遍侵染木薯的粉虱)来传播CBSV的尝试是不成功的，用桃蚜（Myzus persicae）的测试也同样不成功。非洲伯粉虱（Bemisia afer ）(以前是B. hancockii)被暗示作为CBSD的传播媒介但没有传播实验被进行。这个品种在发生CBSD的地方的木薯上是普遍的，它在较低的叶片上有最大的数量，这个位置有显示侵染的最显著症状的趋势。
有少量关于CBSD的传播速率和方式或关于侵染的野生或野草寄主的作用的的病害流行信息。 There is circumstantial evidence that natural spread of CBSD occurs. Thus, seedling progenies sometimes become infected in circumstances which preclude infection by seed transmission, and West African varieties and other introductions from areas where CBSD does not occur have also become infected when grown in infected localities in Malawi, Tanzania and Kenya. There is little published evidence on rates of spread but, in some circumstances, this is known to be rapid.
The means of spread is unknown but whiteflies have long been implicated as vectors. Attempts to transmit CBSD using Bemisia tabaci (the vector of African cassava mosaic and the commonest whitefly infesting cassava in Africa) were unsuccessful, as were tests with the aphid Myzus persicae. Bemisia afer (formerly B. hancockii) has been implicated as the vector of CBSD but no transmission tests have been carried out. This species is quite common on cassava in areas where CBSD occurs and it is most numerous on the lower leaves which tend to show the most conspicuous symptoms of infection.
There is little epidemiological information on the rates and pattern of spread of CBSD or on the role of wild or weed hosts of infection.

management_info:
品种对侵染的敏感性的不同已经被丢弃严重受CBSD侵染的品种和保留生长和产量即使受侵染仍令人满意的品种的农民所采用。在非洲的许多部分记录的木薯品种的确有高的销售量，销售量受到不同的害虫和病害所影响(Nweke et al., 1994)。
坦桑尼亚早期的经验显示了育种抗性或耐性品种的机会。此外，在作物改良程序中，在CBSD流行的地区，它们被释放给农民使用之前需要估计引进的基因型的反应。 The differences between varieties in their sensitivity to infection are already being exploited by farmers who tend to discard those severely affected by CBSD and retain those that grow and yield satisfactorily even when infected. There is certainly a high turnover in cassava varieties as recorded in many parts of Africa and influenced by various pests and diseases (Nweke et al., 1994).
Early experience in Tanzania showed the scope for breeding resistant or tolerant varieties. Moreover, in crop improvement programmes there is a need to evaluate the response of introduced genotypes before they are released for use by farmers in areas where CBSD is prevalent. 木薯通常从硬木茎插条中营养地繁殖，CBSD以这种形式永久的存在和散布。有相当多的植物材料中的贸易在国家当中和有时候在国家之间进行，不可避免地CBSD在这种情况下散布开来。经挑选的‘无毒’植物材料很少是可利用的，除了当为官方采用而利用顶端分生组织疗法和/或热疗法来面对检疫要求的特别生产时。重要的是，因为CBSD在非洲东部和南部的一些部分中当前的有限分布，这些要求受到严格的强迫。
防治的基本方法应该是使用无病毒的种植材料，但对于发展和应用这防治CBSD或木薯上其他的病毒病害的方法，人们只做了少量的尝试(Thresh et al., 1994)。因为侵染的症状可以是含糊的和不清晰的，而且更有效的诊断方法先前没有被采用，所以对于CBSD，很难去筛选无病毒材料。然而，在当前令人不满意的情况下通过只从在生长和收获阶段经检查发现没有叶片、茎和根部症状的植株中筛选繁殖插条，这样相当大的改进很可能实现。基础砧木能在这种方法下为后来的繁殖和分配给农民而建立。在农民收集插条的时候，他们只从不受感染的植株上筛选繁殖材料，这也是个有利条件。然而不幸的是，农民们不熟悉CBSD症状的整个范围，插条可能是在来源植株大多数无叶或严重受到木薯绿螨(Mononychellus tanajoa)、木薯粉蚧(Phenacoccus manihoti)、叶斑或细菌枯萎病的侵染的时候来收集的。进一步的研究必需在最有效的筛选方法和在简单的程序能介绍给农民使用的方法上进行。 
人们普遍赞成的是，需要对木薯害虫和病害的整个范围有全面的IPM程序(Thresh et al., 1994)。然而，在发展这些程序当中只有少量的进展，即使CBSD和其他病害，以及木薯粉虱和绿螨之间，很可能有重要的交互作用。 Cassava is usually propagated vegetatively from hardwood stem cuttings, and CBSD is perpetuated and disseminated in this way. There is a considerable traffic in plant material within and sometimes between countries and inevitably CBSD is disseminated in this way. Selected ‘virus-free’planting material is seldom available except when produced specially for official introductions using meristem-tip therapy and/or heat therapy in order to meet quarantine requirements. It is important that such requirements are strictly enforced because of the present limited distribution of CBSD in parts of eastern and southern Africa.
A basic approach to control should be the use of virus-free planting material, but little attempt has been made to develop and apply this approach with CBSD or other virus diseases of cassava (Thresh et al., 1994). With CBSD there are difficulties in selecting virus-free material because the symptoms of infection can be vague and indistinct, and more effective means of detection were not previously available. However, it is likely that considerable improvement could be made in the present unsatisfactory situation by selecting cuttings for propagation only from plants that have been inspected during growth and also at harvest and found to be free of leaf, stem and root symptoms. Foundation stocks could be established in this way for subsequent multiplication and distribution to farmers. There are also advantages in farmers selecting propagating material only from unaffected plants at the time they collect cuttings. Unfortunately, however, farmers are not familiar with the whole range of CBSD symptoms, and cuttings may be collected at times when the source plants are almost leafless or severely affected by the cassava green mite (Mononychellus tanajoa), cassava mealybug (Phenacoccus manihoti), leaf spot or bacterial blight. Further studies are required on the most effective means of selection and on the ways in which simple procedures can be introduced to farmers.
There is a general acceptance of the need to develop overall IPM programmes for the whole range of cassava pests and diseases (Thresh et al., 1994). However, little progress has been made in developing such programmes, even though there are likely to be important interactions between CBSD and other diseases, and also with cassava mealybug and green mite.

The growth and yield of sensitive varieties are severely affected as there is extensive dieback of the stems, and the tuberous roots develop extensive necrosis and rot to such an extent that they are virtually worthless. Thus, field trials have shown that CBSV can decrease root yields of the most sensitive varieties by 70% and induce necrosis of roots which renders them unsaleable (Hillocks et al., 2001).Tolerant varieties are much less severely affected and there is little effect on root yield or quality; cv. Nachinvaya, a local cultivar in southern Tanzania has a form of tolerance in which leaf symptoms are produced but the development of root necrosis is so delayed that the full potential yield is obtainable (Hillocks et al., 2001).

host_range: CVYV occurs naturally in several major cucurbit crops including cucumber, melon, squash, watermelon and courgette (Cohen and Nitzany, 1960; Yilmaz et al., 1989; Mansour and Al-Musa, 1993;Cuadrado et al., 2001a,b; Jannsen and Cuadrado, 2001; Anon., 2001; L
potential_eco_desc: The cucumber disease caused by CVYV was first observed in the late 1950s in the Jordan valley area of Israel during the warm autumn growing season where it was reported to be severe and damaging. At that time, it had not been recorded in the cooler regions of Israel or during other seasons in the Jordan Valley (Cohen and Nitzany, 1960). In 1985, CVYV was recorded as present in the Jordan Valley in Jordan, but no indication of damage in this country has been given except that the virus stunted parthenocarpic cucumbers grown under plastic and that it was the most frequent viral disease of that crop (Al-Musa et al., 1985; Mansour and Al-Musa, 1993). Mansour (1994) reported that, in 1992, CVYV was detected in 43% of tested samples collected from cucumber crops grown under plastic. Similarly, the presence of CVYV on cucumber and melon in Turkey was not accompanied by information on crop damage other than a description of symptoms (Yilmaz et al., 1989). However, CVYV has been described as a widespread and severe disease of cucurbits in the eastern Mediterranean basin (Lecoq et al., 2000) and considerable losses were reported from Spain during the first outbreak (Cuadrado et al., 2001b). In autumn 2000, CVYV was considered important enough for the Spanish authorities to destroy affected plants covering 70 ha of glasshouses in an attempt to suppress further spread (Cuadrado et al., 2001a). In 2001, occasional splitting of watermelon fruits has been observed in Spain (Janssen and Cuadrado, 2001).
author: CPC2006

description: In international trade, CVYV is most likely to be carried by infected vegetative host material, such as seedlings. B. tabaci will spread CVYV locally. Internationally, CVYV is semipersistent in its whitefly host and is retained for less than 6 h, so B. tabaci is only likely to introduce CVYV if it is carried on infected host material. B. tabaci carried on non-host plants may not remain viruliferous long enough to transmit the virus.^p^pNo work has been reported to determine whether CVYV is seedborne. Although Sweet potato mild mottle virus, which is the type species of the genus Ipomovirus and the only Ipomovirus species recognized by van Regenmortel et al. (2000), is not seedborne (Brunt et al., 1996), other viruses in the Potyviridae can be seedborne.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: borne internally; invisible.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - True Seeds (inc. Grain).
author: CPC2006

remark: CVYV is not recorded from several regions where cucurbit crops are grown. It is present in countries of the eastern Mediterranean area and, with the report from Spain, one country in the western Mediterranean area. It is likely to become established in areas where Bemisia tabaci, its whitefly vector, is established. B. tabaci is present outdoors in many southern European countries and is a glasshouse pest in some northern European countries. Therefore, CVYV has the potential to become a serious disease of cucurbits in the EPPO region. Cucumber is grown throughout the EPPO region, while melons and watermelons are most commonly grown in Mediterranean countries.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pCare should be taken to protect cucumber or melon seedlings from infection before transplanting in the field or under plastic. This requires raising the seedlings in a whitefly-free environment. In protected crops in Spain, control relies on preventive and cultural practices (use of pest-free seedlings, adequate glasshouse window screens, double doors, treatment of infected vegetable residues and the introduction of a rest period of at least one month between two cucurbit crops, monitoring of Bemisia tabaci populations). ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pWhen preventive and cultural methods are not sufficient, control of CVYV centres on the control of its whitefly vector B. tabaci. Regarding chemical control, B. tabaci appears to develop resistance to all groups of plant protection products that have been developed for its control. A rotation of insecticides that offer no cross resistance should therefore be used to control B. tabaci infestations. ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pThe parasite Encarsia formosa is used as a biological control agent to control Trialeurodes vaporariorum, but it is less efficient against B. tabaci. Repeated introductions of larger numbers of E. formosa than B. tabaci are necessary if eradication is required. The predatory beetle Delphastus pusillus, however, is very effective against B. tabaci (Anon., 2000).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThere is no information on resistant cultivars of cucumber or melon. No data are available on trials that may have been undertaken to reveal yield losses in the non-parthenocarpic (symptomless) and parthenocarpic cucumbers. ^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures ^p^pCVYV was added to the EPPO A2 action list in 2003, and is thus recommended for regulation as a quarantine pest by EPPO member countries. International trade in young cucurbit plants for planting seems the main pathway for introduction, but little information has been found on movements into or within the EPPO region. It is not clear how likely it is that seedlings would become infected, but they should presumably be protected from infection before entering trade. Visual inspections of export material may not detect the virus since it is latent in some hosts and may take some time to express symptoms in others. Suitable measures would ensure, for plants for planting of cucurbits from areas where CVYV occurs, crop or place of production freedom from the virus and exclusion of the vector Bemisia tabaci.

management_info: To minimize SPMMV-induced crop losses, it is often essential to grow virus-tested stocks; in cultivars that are totally infected, these can be obtained by meristem-tip culture followed by multiplication and eventual commercial use of plants in which no virus can be detected under insect-proof conditions. Methods for meristem-tip culture, either alone or combined with thermo- and/or chemotherapy, have been well described (Frison and Ng, 1981; Love et al., 1989; F Wambugu, University of Bath, Bath, personal communication, 1991). Levels of natural infection in parts of Uganda are often unusually low; under such circumstances, it is possible to simply select disease-free cuttings for subsequent planting (Gibson et al., 1997).^p^pThere is currently great interest in the possibility of producing virus-resistant transgenic plants, although none is yet available for sweet potato production (F Wambugu, University of Bath, Bath, personal communication, 1991).

description: In November 2016, cassava fields were inspected in Ituri Province, northeastern DRC. Fields were selected at 10- to 20-km intervals in the surveyed area. A total of 360 (10 per field) leaf samples were collected from 36 fields. Using molecular diagnostics showed, eleven of the 36 fields were affected by CBSD, and average incidence in affected fields was 90.3%. Of the 360 leaf samples, 108 tested positive for cassava brown streak ipomoviruses (CBSIs). Species-level identifications using real-time PCR, made on a subset of these positive-testing samples, revealed that 55% had mixed UCBSV + CBSV infections, whereas 45% were only infected by UCBSV. There were no single CBSV infections. To our knowledge, this is the first report confirming the occurrence of both UCBSV and CBSV in the north-eastern part of DRC.  CBSV and UCBSV are spread through infected stem cuttings and by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
reference_name: First Report of Mixed Infection of Cassava Brown Streak Virus and Ugandan Cassava Brown Streak Virus on Cassava in North-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo

description: In November 2013, symptoms of yellowing on leaves and brown necrotic rot on tuberous roots were observed on different cassava landraces (Manihot esculenta) in Dembeni on Mayotte Island, a French Overseas Department in the southwest Indian Ocean. The symptoms, similar to the cassava brown streak disease described in East Africa, suggested the possible involvement of cassava brown streak viruses. The expanding cassava brown streak disease epidemic in East Africa is caused by two ipomoviruses, Cassava brown streak virus (CBSV) and Ugandan cassava brown streak virus (UCBSV). To verify the identity of the causal agent, symptom-bearing leaf samples of 17 affected plants were collected in March and June 2014. Based on molecular detection showed follow results: the sequences showed the highest nucleotide identity (86%) with isolates of UCBSV from Uganda and Malawi and 85% with an isolate of CBSV from Mozambique. A phylogenetic reconstruction with publicly available complete genome sequences of cassava brown streak viruses confirmed that the Mayotte isolates are genetically more related to UCBSV isolates than to CBSV isolates from East Africa, and represent a separate lineage that appears to be almost intermediate between current isolates of CBSV and UCBSV. This is the first report of cassava brown streak disease in Mayotte.
reference_name: First report of cassava brown streak disease and associated Ugandan cassava brown streak virus in Mayotte Island

management_info: NLV, usually in complex with other viruses, is prevalent in older commercial cultivars of ornamental bulb species, especially those of Narcissus and bulbous Iris. Minimization of virus-induced crop losses is therefore best achieved by selecting or producing virus tested (putative virus-free) plants and their rapid multiplication to obtain elite stocks which, thereafter, should be protected as far as possible from re-infection. Where it is not possible to select virus-free plants from existing stocks, healthy plants can be obtained by meristem tip culture. Effective procedures for virus testing, production of virus-free plants and for their rapid propagation are available (Baruch and Quak, 1966; Stone et al., 1978; Brunt et al., 1984; Mowat et al., 1986; Van der Linde et al., 1988; Bertaccini and Bellardi, 1991).^p^pVirus-free stocks should be propagated in gauze houses before substantial quantities are available for outdoor commercial production. Reinfection of field-grown virus-free bulbous irises can be reduced by spraying crops with insecticides (synthetic pyrethroids) or with mineral oil (Asjes, 1985). Although such treatments reduce potential bulb yields, treated crops produce higher bulb yields and better quality flowers than those of infected stocks (Asjes, 1988).^p^pCertification schemes for major flower bulb species have been developed for use in the Netherlands and the UK (Ebbels, 1986).

description: In April 2014, several rice fields in Dedza District in Malawi showed diseased Oryza sativa plants with an incidence of 20 to 30%. The disease caused leaf yellowing and mottling, delayed flowering, and plant stunting. These symptoms suggested the presence of Rice yellow mottle virus (RYMV, genus Sobemovirus), the main viral pathogen of rice in Africa. Subsequently, a survey was conducted in Karonga (two sites), Khanta Bay, Nkhotakota and Dedza districts, four major rice-growing regions in Malawi. Symptomatic leaves were collected randomly on O. sativa variety Kilombero. Based on biological detection, ELISA assay and molecular identification, RYMV was confirmed in the samples.
reference_name: First Report of Rice yellow mottle virus in Rice in Malawi

potential_eco_desc: The severe nature of rice yellow mottle disease poses a serious threat to the cultivation of susceptible rice in the wetlands of Africa. The disease mainly affects irrigated rice production of lowland rice in sub-Saharan countries (IITA, 1978; Fomba et al., 1989). However, it may occur sporadically in highly susceptible exotic varieties under rainfed, upland production systems (Raymundo et al., 1979; Awoderu et al., 1987). ^p^pIn inland swamp regions, disease incidence may reach up to 80%, most probably due to the regeneration of new stems from existing stubble (Raymundo and Konteh, 1980). In irrigated paddy, 5-25% infection was found on many farms where a long duration variety was cultivated in the eastern province of Sierra Leone. Deep flooded or floating rice showed 10% incidence of the disease. ^p^pThe disease was also observed in farmers' fields in areas around Bida in the Niger flood plains and at Badeggi in Niger State, Nigeria (Rossel et al., 1982a) and in rice project areas of the former Anambra and Imo States, Nigeria (Rossel et al., 1982b). ^p^pTraditional African rice varieties, adapted to upland conditions are significantly more tolerant and appear to possess a higher level of resistance to RYMV, regardless of origin, than exotic lowland cultivars (Raymundo et al., 1977; Raymundo and Konteh, 1980; Okioma and Sarkarung, 1983). Most of the indica cultivars showed 20-25% height reductions when infection occurred at the panicle initiation state (Raymundo and Konteh, 1980). Attere (1981) reported that RYMV affects plant height, but not to the extent of stunting growth and reducing tillering capacity.^p^pSevere outbreaks of RYMV have occurred in Kenya (Bakker 1970, 1975), Niger (Reckhaus and Adamou, 1986), Sierra Leone (Raymundo et al., 1979; Raymundo and Konteh, 1980) and Liberia (Raymundo and Buddenhagen, 1976). More recently, RYMV has been reported from Madagascar, where it is considered a serious disease (Reckhaus and Randrianangaly, 1990). Taylor (1989) reported yield losses of 84-97% due to RYMV infection in three susceptible cultivars in Sierra Leone: PN 623-3, TOX 516-12-SLR and ROK 3.Fomba (1986) reported yield reductions due to RYMV ranging from 19.6% in cv. Angkatta to 95.8% in cv. ROK 5. Reckhaus and Adamou (1986) reported yield reductions ranging from 58 to 68% in Niger following RYMV infection.^p^pAlthough the effect of RYMV on rice production in Gagnoa, Cote d'Ivoire, was insignificant in 1976, the spread of the disease in this region is currently very high and many ricefields have been abandoned (Yoboue, 1989). In Kenya, extensive yield losses of up to 60% have been recorded in some places, especially where infection occurred up to 30 days after transplanting (Okhoba, 1989).^p^pThere is no evidence that RYMV incidence increases in successive seasons under continuous cropping, rainfall or wind speed (Heinrichs et al., 1997). ^p^pThe incidence of RYMV is very high in the Sahel followed by Sudan Savanna, Guinea Savanna and tropical rainforest in that order (Awoderu, 1991a).

remark: Although RYMV is not transmitted through rice seeds, leaf debris and spikelet contaminants have been implicated in the transmission of the virus. Purity of the seed to be exported or transported to new areas should therefore be emphasised. Insects also transmit the virus.

management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe use of natural host-plant resistance is an appropriate way to control RYMV (Fomba, 1988; Thottappilly and Rossel, 1993). Exotic varieties of rice are generally highly susceptible to RYMV whereas traditionally grown, African upland varieties are usually moderately resistant or tolerant to the virus (IITA, 1979; Raymundo et al., 1979; Raymundo and Konteh, 1980; Rossel and Thottappilly, 1985; Fomba, 1988; Taylor, 1989; Awoderu, 1991b, Thottappilly and Rossel, 1993). Among indigenous African Oryza species like O. glaberrima and O. barthii, several accessions were identified as highly resistant (Attere and Fatokun, 1983; Thottappilly and Rossel, 1993). Breeding for resistance to RYMV was initiated in many countries (Masajo et al., 1988; Paul, 1992; Masajo and Rasoafalimanana, 1995; Paul et al., 1995a, b; Vales et al., 1995;John et al., 1985, 1986b;Ahmadi and Cisse, 1995a, b; Singh, 1995; Fomba et al., 1995a; Alluri et al., 1995; Bouet et al., 1995).^p^pRYMV resistance has been found to be under polygenic determinism and 15 quantitative trait locus (QTL) have been detected on seven chromosomal fragments (Loriuex et al., 1996; Ghesquiere et al., 1997; Albar et al., 1998).Paul et al. (1995a, b) studied the inheritance of RYMV in O. glaberrima. The genetic analysis of the crosses revealed that two recessive genes conferred RYMV resistance. Also studies on the inheritance of resistance/tolerance to RYMV disease were conducted by Mansary (1995a) and Kumwenda et al. (1995). The former reported that resistance in O. sativa is controlled by partial dominant genes and that variety CT 19 possesses excess recessive genes conditioning resistance to RYMV. The latter indicated that 1-2 recessive pair of alleles confers resistance to ITA 235 and 3 dominant pairs of alleles confer resistance to RYMV for LAC 23. Two dominant genes condition resistance in LAC 23 (IITA, 1980); TOS 3554 has excessive dominant genes conditioning resistance to RYMV and other plant characters. However, Ahmadi and Singh (1995) indicated that resistance to RYMV in O. sativa is weak, bi-directional and conditioned by partial dominant genes. Ndjiondjop et al. (1999) produced results consistent with the presence of a single recessive resistance gene common to Tog 5681 and Gigante varieties of rice. Resistance of japonica cultivars has been introduced into indica cultivars in some instances (Singh, 1995). Also, transformed lines encoding the RNA dependent polymerase of RYMV are resistant to RYMV due to post-transcription gene silencing (Pinto et al., 1999). Resistance is also affected by a morphology dependent mechanism and significant epistatis (Pressoir et al., 1998).^p^pStudies have been carried out to characterise the genetic basis of RYMV resistance and to map resistant genes in rice (Albar et al., 1998; Pressoir et al., 1998; Ioannidou et al., 2000; Pinel et al., 2000). One RAPD marker is already linked to RYMV resistance (Albar et al., 1995). Efforts are concentrating on developing non conventional virus resistance using genetic engineering by incorporating viral genes into rice (Baulcombe, 1995; Kouassi et al., 1995; Pinto, 1995).^p^p^Integrated Pest ManagementReckhaus and Andriamasintseheno (1995, 1997) advocate an IPM strategy for control of RYMV in Madagascar. This strategy includes the destruction of crop residues, delaying planting time where irrigation facilities are available, the use of tolerant varieties, and chemical control of vectors. Important factors in the spread and management of RYMV in Africa have been advanced by Abo and Alegbejo (1997), Abo et al. (1998), Abo and Sy (1998), Imolehin et al. (1998) and Nwilene (1999). description: 属于叶甲科的甲虫成虫，如Sesselia pusilla，跳甲属（Chaetocnema spp.），趾铁甲（Dactylispa spp.）和Trichispa sericea被认为是RYMV的天然媒介昆虫(Bakker, 1971, 1974, 1975; Raymundo and Buddenhagen, 1976; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 1998, 2000a, b; Nwilene, 1999; Banwo et al., 2000, 2001a, b, c)。刺吸式和咀嚼式口器的昆虫如长触角的蝗虫（Conocephalus spp.）已经被发现是传播RYMV的媒介(Bakker, 1974, 1975; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2001b; Banwo et al., 2001b)。一种食植物的coccinelid在筛选测定试验中被发现可传播RYMV(Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2000b)。RYMV的低传播通过老鼠获得在肯尼亚(Aceria bankerii and Stereotarsomus spinkii)。甲虫能够从病害水稻植株获得病毒，获得后保存病毒，而且随后接连不断的几天侵染健康试验植株在获得后(Bakker, 1974; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2000b)。从受侵染的水稻植株中观察得是没有种子传播的(Bakker, 1974, 1975; Fauquet and Thouvennel, 1977; IITA, 1985; John et al., 1986a; Abo, 1998; Konate et al., 2001)且通过采集于田间周围病害植株土壤中的生长中的水稻发现没有传播。病毒容易通过机械传播(Bakker, 1970)。病毒传播可能通过由风引起的叶子接触发生(Bakker, 1970)。当感病植株的水稻根部与健康植株缠绕在一起时，RYMV可以被传播，这已经被设立，源于附近空间植株的叶子接触，源于不完整腐烂植株残骸的稻茬和源于感病水稻植株的空稻穗(Abo, 1998)。RYMV可以通过胶液和在重感染稻田的灌溉地区传播(Bakker, 1974, 1975)。农具如用于丰收水稻的镰刀已经被发现可以传播且增加田间病毒发病率(Tsuboi et al., 1995)。移植水稻比直接播种水稻更容易受RYMV的袭击。水稻的修剪和截根苗增加田间RYMV的发病率(Abo, 1998)。在稻田RYMV的侵染一般开始于田的沿岸和苗圃床。栖居于土壤的线虫已经在筛选试验测定中发现不传播RYMV (Abo, 1998)。 Adult beetles belonging to the family Chrysomelidae, such as Sesselia pusilla, Chaetocnema spp., Dactylispa spp. and Trichispa sericea are thought to be the natural vectors of RYMV (Bakker, 1971, 1974, 1975; Raymundo and Buddenhagen, 1976; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 1998, 2000a, b; Nwilene, 1999; Banwo et al., 2000, 2001a, b, c). Insects with biting and chewing mouthparts such as the long horned grasshoppers (Conocephalus spp.) have been found to transmit RYMV (Bakker, 1974, 1975; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2001b; Banwo et al., 2001b). A phytophagous coccinelid was found to transmit RYMV in screening tests (Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2000b). A low transmission of RYMV was obtained with mites (Aceria bankerii and Stereotarsomus spinkii) in Kenya. The beetles were able to acquire the virus from diseased rice plants, retain the virus after acquisition, and subsequently infect healthy test plants for several consecutive days after aquisition (Bakker, 1974; Abo, 1998; Abo et al., 2000b). No seed transmission was observed from infected rice plants (Bakker, 1974, 1975; Fauquet and Thouvennel, 1977; IITA, 1985; John et al., 1986a; Abo, 1998; Konate et al., 2001) and no transmission was obtained by growing rice in soil collected from around diseased plants in the field. The virus was readily transmitted mechanically (Bakker, 1970). Transmission of the virus possibly occurs by leaf contact caused by wind (Bakker, 1970). It has been established that RYMV is transmitted when rice roots from infected plants become intertwined with healthy plants, leaf contact from closely spaced plants, rice stubble from incompletely decomposed plant debris and empty rice spikelets from infected rice plants (Abo, 1998). RYMV could be transmitted through guttation fluid and in the irrigation water of heavily infected rice fields (Bakker, 1974, 1975). Farm implements such as the sickle used in harvesting rice have been found to transmit and increase the incidence of the virus in the field (Tsuboi et al., 1995). Transplanted rice rather than direct seeded rice is more vulnerable to attack by RYMV. Trimming and ratooning of rice increases the incidence of RYMV in the field (Abo, 1998). The infection of RYMV in the rice fields normally starts from the edges of the fields and nursery beds. Soil inhabiting nematodes have been found not to transmit RYMV in screening test (Abo, 1998).
