description:
线虫传播：
　　所有的测试的隔离种，包括来自啤酒花(Humulus lupulus)和大麦的血清学变种，由自由生活的土壤寄生线虫裂尾剑线虫（Xiphinema diversicaudatum）传播的(Harrison and Cadman, 1959; Jha and Posnette, 1959; Valdez et al., 1974; DJF Brown and AT Jones, unpublished data, Scottish Crop Research Institute, Invergowrie, UK)。这种线虫也传播草莓潜隐环斑病毒(SLRSV)，这两种病毒可一起在土壤发生。它还能通过X. madierense.用实验方法传播，但成功率不高(Brown et al., 1992)。它还被报道由柯克斯剑线虫（X. coxi） (Fritzche, 1964)传播，但这些数据被认为是不确定的(Trudgill et al., 1983; Brown et al., 1996)。
种子传播：
ArMV在许多的自然和实验寄主上能通过种子传播，通常有较高的种传频率(Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967)。虽然多数感染的幼苗不表现明显的症状，但至少有12个科的15种植物是已知通过种子传播的，(Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967; Murant, 1983)。
该病毒还可通过菟丝子传播(Cuscuta spp.) (Schmelzer, 1962; Eppler, 1992)。 Nematode Transmission
All tested isolates, including the serological variants from hop (Humulus lupulus) and barley, are transmitted by the free-living soil-inhabiting nematode, Xiphinema diversicaudatum (Harrison and Cadman, 1959; Jha and Posnette, 1959; Valdez et al., 1974; DJF Brown and AT Jones, unpublished data, Scottish Crop Research Institute, Invergowrie, UK). This nematode also transmits strawberry latent ringspot virus (SLRSV), and the two viruses may occur together in soils. It is also transmitted experimentally, but with low frequency, by X. madierense (Brown et al., 1992). It is reported to be transmitted by X. coxi (Fritzche, 1964) but these data are regarded as not conclusive (Trudgill et al., 1983; Brown et al., 1996).
Transmission through Seed
ArMV is seedborne in many natural and experimental hosts, often to a high frequency (Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967). At least 15 species in 12 plant families are known to be infected through seed, although most infected seedlings show no obvious symptoms (Lister and Murant, 1967; Murant and Lister, 1967; Murant, 1983).
The virus is reported to be transmitted by dodder (Cuscuta spp.) (Schmelzer, 1962; Eppler, 1992).
author: zhangjianjun

management_info: 该病毒能从产生几个品种的感染植物（包括carnation, daphne 和 grapevine）的枝条顶端培养(2 mm)上被消除，通过加热处理或分裂组织顶端培养，或者两种方法一起来实现(Stellmach, 1973; Stone, 1973; Schmidt, 1974; Oertel, 1977; Sweet et al., 1979)。 The virus has been eliminated from developing shoot tips cultures (2 mm) of infected plants of several species, including carnation, daphne and grapevine, by heat treatment and meristem tip culture, either alone, or in combination (Stellmach, 1973; Stone, 1973; Schmidt, 1974; Oertel, 1977; Sweet et al., 1979).   在抗性材料的缺乏下，健康的种植材料应被应用到没有已知ArMV感染的作物的种植地和没有带病毒的裂尾剑线虫（X. diversicaudatum.）的土壤中去。 In the absence of resistant material, healthy planting material should be used in areas free from known infection with ArMV in the crop species planted and in soil free from viruliferous X. diversicaudatum. ArMV在啤酒花上的防治能通过间隔两年休种啤酒花来很好的实现，这可以通过休耕或种植免疫寄主来实现。在这段期间，倘若病毒不能偶然地重新传入田地中去，媒介裂尾剑线虫（X. diversicaudatum.）会逐渐地失去其侵染能力。如果两年的啤酒花休种间隔不能实现，那间隔期应尽可能的长并且要在之后进行土壤消毒。同时这个处理不可能是完全成功的，因为它有可能延迟严重的ArMV再侵染超过5年(Pitcher, 1975; Harrison and Murant, 1996)。 Control of ArMV on hop is best achieved by allowing a hop-free interval of 2 years, either by bare-fallowing or by planting virus-immune hosts. During this period the vector (X. diversicaudatum) gradually loses its infectivity, provided the virus is not inadvertently re-introduced into the field. If a 2-year hop-free interval is not practicable, the interval should be as long as possible and followed by soil fumigation. Whilst this treatment is unlikely to be fully successful, it may delay serious re-infection with ArMV for up to 5 years (Pitcher, 1975; Harrison and Murant, 1996).
author: zhangjianjun

description: In 2016, we sampled grapevine leaves from 16 individual grapevine plants representing 12 different grapevine cultivars. Except for a Shine Muscat (Vitis labruscana Bailey × V. vinifera) plant sampled from a vineyard in Okcheon, all 15 grapevine plants were grown in the Grape Research Institute. Based on molecular diagnostics confirming diverse Vitis spp.(including V. labruscana and other Vitis hybrids grown in the Grapevine Research Institute except imported grapevine cultivars belonging to V. vinifera) have been infected by GFabV. The results revealed a high prevalence of GFabV in important grapevine cultivars in Korea.
reference_name: First Report of Grapevine fabavirus in Diverse Vitis Species in Korea
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: During a sweet cherry resistance screening greenhouse experiment (July 2018) against Little cherry virus 1 (LChV-1) and Little cherry virus 2 (LChV-2), branches and leaves from 10 non symptomatic trees, representing propagation material from different cultivars grafted on Gisela 5 rootstocks, were collected and pooled as a single composite sample. Total RNA was extracted from samples. The presence of Prunus virus F (PrVF) was confirmed both in the composite sample and individual trees by high-throughput sequencing. The PrVF-infected trees also harboured other co-infecting Prunus viruses, such as LChV-1 and Cherry virus A which is considered a latent virus in Prunus. This is the first report of PrVF infecting sweet cherry in Belgium. The detection of this graft-transmissible latent virus in trees collected from nurseries may indicate a long-term occurrence of fabaviruses in Belgian germplasm.
reference_name: First report of Prunus virus F infecting sweet cherry cultivars using high-throughput sequencing in Belgium
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: During a survey for Prunus spp. viruses in the Czech Republic carried out in June 2008, three asymptomatic samples of sour cherry (P. cerasus) cv. Amarelka chvalkovicka were collected (among others) in a germplasm collection in Holovousy. The presence of PrVF in all three trees was confirmed by RT-PCR. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PrVF infecting sour cherry in the Czech Republic. The repeated detection of PrVF in samples collected from the same trees in 2008, 2013, and 2016 indicates the long-term occurrence of this virus in the germplasm collection.
reference_name: First Report of Prunus virus F Infecting Sour Cherry in the Czech Republic

potential_eco_desc: The incidence from 16 to 30% in the field.
description: Ageneral virus-like symptom of mosaic leaf had been observed on nonheading Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa L. var. chinensis [Linnaeus] Kitamura), with a high incidence ranging from 16 to 30% in the field. From March 2010 to December 2016, the nonheading Chinese cabbage was tested for Broad bean wilt virus 2 (BBWV2, genus Fabavirus, family Secoviridae), Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV, genus Potyvirus, family Potyviridae) and Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV, genus Cucumovirus, family Bromoviridae) in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. The leaf samples showing mosaic symptoms were collected and tested, the results showed that BBWV2 was presence in samples. This is the first report of BBWV2 infecting nonheading Chinese cabbage in China.  Nonheading Chinese cabbage plants are widely infected by BBWV2, the crop may serve as an overwinter host, posing a potential risk for other host crops, e.g., tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), broad bean (Vicia faba), pepper (Capsicum annuum), eggplant (S. melongena), and kidney bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), in coming season.
reference_name: First Report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 Infecting Non-Heading Chinese Cabbage in China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: A survey of sesame viral diseases was conducted in July 2016 in Jiyang, Shandong Province, China. Symptoms of mosaic, chlorotic mottle, distortion, and puckering symptoms were observed on leaves of approximately 30% of the sesame plants (cv. Zhongzhi No. 13) in fields. Based on molecular diagnostics, the result revealed the presence of Bean common mosaic virus (BCMV) and Broad bean wilt virus 2 (BBWV2). BCMV had already been reported in sesame. To our knowledge, this is the first report of BBWV2 in sesame.
reference_name: First Report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 Infecting Sesame in China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: BBWV has previously been found on Veronica scutellata in New York though it was not specified whether BBWV-1 or BBWV-2 was present. BBWV-2 has been previously detected in Digitalis and Salvia officinalis in the UK. This is thought to be the first confirmed finding of BBWV-2 in Veronica in UK.
potential_eco_desc: Symptomatic plants were widespread throughout the nursery which could affect their marketability.
description: In August 2016 a sample of Veronica gentianoides cv. Tissington White was submitted to Fera Science Ltd. from a nursery in West Sussex. The sample was submitted with symptoms of severe distortion and mottling and these symptoms were widespread throughout the nursery which could affect their marketability. The pathogen was identified as Broad bean wilt virus 2 (BBWV-2) by molecular diagnostics. BBWV-2 has been previously detected in Digitalis and Salvia officinalis in the UK. This is thought to be the first confirmed finding of BBWV-2 in Veronica.
reference_name: First report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 in Veronica gentianoides in the UK

host_range: 薯蓣Dioscorea opposite.
description: In May 2015, to examine Broad bean wilt virus 2 (BBWR2) incidence in Chinese yam fields in Korea, two open fields were randomly selected in Andong City where Chinese yam has been cultivated intensively. Chinese yam plants were easily found at a relatively high incidence of 10 to 15% in the surveyed fields. The leaf samples were collected and identified by DAS-ELISA assay and molecular diagnostics result showed that all the samples were infected with BBWV2. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of BBWV2 in Chinese yam (Dioscorea opposite) in Korea. As a high incidence of BBWV2 in Chinese yam was found in this study, the effect of BBWV2 infection on yields of Chinese yam production needs to be evaluated by further studies.
reference_name: First Report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 in Dioscorea opposita Thunb. in Korea
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 花毛茛Ranunculus asiaticus cv. Elegance.
description: During 2013 to 2014, about 20% of Ranunculus asiaticus cv. Elegance plants in a commercial greenhouse in Campania, Southern Italy, were found showing leaf deformation and mosaic. Leaves from twenty-five symptomatic plants were tested by double-antibody sandwich (DAS)-ELISA and Istituto per la Protezione Sostenibile delle Piante (IPSP) tests, all twenty-five symptomatic buttercup plants tested positive for BBWV-2,  twelve of them also tested positive for RanMMV, a virus previously reported on this species in Italy. The pathogenicity test further confirmed the results. To our knowledge, this is the first report of R. asiaticus as a natural host of BBWV-2 and the first report of RanMMV infecting this species in Campania, Southern Italy.
reference_name: First Report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 and Ranunculus mild mosaic virus in Ranunculus asiaticus in Southern Italy
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 细叶益母草Leonurus sibiricus
description: Leonurus sibiricus is a widely distributed subtropical weed in Southeast Asia, it has been commercially cultivated on a small scale in many geographic areas of Korea. In August 2012, field-grown L. sibiricus plants showing mosaic, yellowing, and stunting symptoms were collected near a pepper field in Andong, Korea. Since L. sibiricus is only consumed as a raw material of traditional medicine in Korea, symptomatic plants lose commercial value entirely. The molecular detection demonstrated that the causal agent was Broad bean wilt virus 2 (BBWV-2). Currently, BBWV-2 is epidemic in pepper fields in Korea. Because BBWV-2 is easily transmitted by various aphids, and L. sibiricus is widely distributed in both wild and cultivated fields in Korea, this host might serve as a potential source of BBWV-2 to other crops such as pepper. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of BBWV-2 in L. sibiricus.  BBWV-2 is easily transmitted by various aphids.
reference_name: First Report of Broad bean wilt virus 2 in Leonurus sibiricus in Korea

potential_eco_desc: Until 1987 P. cervinus was generally considered to be a relatively minor pest of Citrus. Larvae feeding on roots generally caused no economic damage and it was rarely necessary to apply a treatment for control of adults feeding on foliage. However, the move by Japan in 1987 to declare P. cervinus a quarantine pest dramatically elevated its pest status on Citrus, particularly in the major exporting countries of the USA and Australia (Haney et al., 1987). In the USA alone, ineffective control of P. cervinus on Citrus threatened fruit exports to Japan worth more than $187 million in 1987 (Haney et al., 1988). Despite the now confirmed presence of P. cervinus in Japan (Masaki et al., 1996), quarantine restrictions are still in force, maintaining the high pest status of P. cervinus on American and Australian citrus fruit grown for the Japanese market (Smith et al., 1997).^p^pThe economic impact of P. cervinus on other crops (for example, deciduous fruit, vegetables and ornamentals) is generally small. Economic injury levels are exceeded infrequently and outbreaks are usually confined to small areas.
author: CPC2006

remark: P. cervinus is a quarantine pest in Japan affecting Citrus exports to that country. Fruit is required to be 100% free from egg masses of P. cervinus (Anonymous, 1986).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control is rarely required. In Citrus orchards where fruit are grown for export to Japan, it is recommended that the lower branches be removed from trees and weeds are controlled, to minimize weevil access to tree canopies (Smith et al., 1997). Sticky polybutene bands applied to tree trunks, directly (with copper to minimize trunk disease problems) or indirectly (on a plastic or cloth substrate), are effective in preventing weevils from climbing trees (James, 1991). Trunks can also be treated with a recommended pesticide, such as lambda-cyhalothrin, deltamethrin or bioresmethrin (Magarey et al., 1992; Sale, 1997), but there is no advantage in treating the trunks with a combination of sticky band and pesticide (James, 1991, Smith et al., 1997). Foliar and soil insecticide treatments have also been used to control P. cervinus in Citrus (Bullock, 1985; Elmer, 1986; Bullock et al., 1988) and other crops (Myburgh et al., 1975; Hely et al., 1982; Prestridge et al., 1989).^p^pFollowing the emergence of P. cervinus as a zero tolerance quarantine pest of citrus fruit entering Japan, research on control has also focused on the removal of eggs from fruit through post-harvest fumigation (Soderstrom et al., 1991), heat disinfestation (Jessup et al., 1993; McCoy et al., 1994), cold storage (Haney et al., 1988, Jessup et al., 1993), irradiation (Johnson et al., 1990; Jessup et al., 1993) and insecticide treatment (Coats, 1990).

description: For the past two years, we have noticed plants showing disease symptoms including severe mosaic and yellowing of leaves and severe fruit deformation and color cracking in pumpkin and squash in all the cultivars grown in Trinidad. The infection was suspected to be caused by Zucchini yellow mosaic virus (ZYMV). Detailed surveys to record the severity of disease were conducted during dry and rainy seasons for a two-year period in farmers’ fields in six different locations (Barrackpore, Macoya, Las Lomas, Moruga, Waterloo, and Orange Groove) representing all the major cropping zones of the country. Virus infection was noticed at all growth stages of the crop and a maximum disease incidence of 74% was recorded in the dry season during 2014 and 2015. The molecular diagnostics indicates that there were present of ZYMV in pumpkin and squash plants and Squash mosaic virus (SqMV) in pumpkin and watermelon plants in Trinidad.
reference_name: First Report of Zucchini yellow mosaic virus and Squash mosaic virus Infecting Cucurbits in Trinidad

potential_eco_desc: Economic losses caused by SqMV are probably most common in the Western Hemisphere because of the common occurrence of cucumber beetle vectors which are responsible for secondary spread from the initial seed source or from overwintering weed sources (see Biology). The extent of symptom development depends on the specific host species or variety affected, the environmental conditions and the isolate of virus present. The variants of SqMV have been grouped into two serotypes which differ in host range and pathogenicity. The melon strain (SqMV-I) induces severe symptoms on melon but mild symptoms on squash, while the squash strains (SqMV-II) induce conspicuous symptoms on squash but mild symptoms on melon. Some isolates of group I can infect watermelon.^p^pIn cantaloupe-type melons, SqMV infection results in reduced yield per plant without affecting fruit quality (Alvarez and Campbell, 1976). In Charentais-type melons, SqMV infection results in severe mosaic on the fruit rind resulting in reduced marketability.^p^pIn seeds, the virus infects the embryo. Middleton (1944) and Middleton and Bohn (1953) reported that poorly filled seeds from infected fruits carry a higher percentage of virus than normal seed. However, Powell and Schlegel (1970a) did not find a significant difference between seed lots fractionated on the basis of weight and the percentages of SqMV transmitted.

description: Incidence^p^pSqMV was first reported as a seedborne virus of melons by Kendrick (1934) in California, USA, and later by Freitag (1941, 1956) and Middleton (1944). It was also reported from Michigan (Mahoney, 1935) and New York (Rader et al., 1947). The virus was detected in seed of three of 29 muskmelon cultivars commercially available in Ontario in 1973 (Kemp et al., 1974). SqMV serotype I is seedborne in squash, melon and watermelon, whereas serotype II appears to be seedborne only in squash (Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1969). ELISA readily detected SqMV antigen in extracts from seed coats, papery layers and distal halves of embryos from individual cucurbit seeds. Antigen presence in the embryo was independent of that in the seed coat or papery layer (Nolan and Campbell, 1984).^p^p^Effect on Seed QualityMiddleton (1944) and Middleton and Bohn (1953) reported that poorly filled seeds from SqMV-infected fruits carry a higher percentage of virus than normal seed. However, Powell and Schlegel (1970a) did not find a significant difference between seed lots fractionated on the basis of weight and the percentages of SqMV transmitted.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pSeed^p^pCucurbit plants produced from the germinative halves of the same embryos were observed for embryonic transmission. Many infected embryos produced infected plants, but several embryos that contained antigen detectable by ELISA produced virus-free plants. No embryos judged virus-free by ELISA produced virus-infected plants (Nolan and Campbell, 1984). Seed transmission rates usually range from 0.1 to 10%, with commercial and experimental seed lots yielding about 10% infected seedlings (Grogan et al., 1959). Up to 94% transmission has been reported (Rader et al., 1947). Some isolates of SqMV from Morocco are known to be seed-transmitted in Chenopodium quinoa and C. murale (transmission rates of 20-25%) (Lockhart et al., 1985). Serogroup I strains are transmitted by seed in melon, squash, pumpkin and watermelon Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1973a, b. Serogroup II (SqMV-II), the squash strain, causes conspicuous symptoms on squash and pumpkin but mild symptoms on melon. No strains of Serotype II infect watermelon. Seed transmission for this group is limited.^p^pThe main method of widespread dispersal of SqMV in most cultivated cucurbits is through the exchange or trade of infected seeds from one country to another. SqMV can be found in areas where cucurbit seeds are produced (Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1973a; Alvarez and Campbell, 1978). Seed producers are well aware of the seedborne nature of SqMV and have taken steps through the years to limit the presence of the virus in their melon and squash seed stocks. Certification of virus-free seed still remains an effective means of limiting the virus.^p^pOther sources^p^pSqMV is transmitted by at least 14 different species of chewing insects, mostly beetles. The beetle vectors belong to the Chrysomelidae (Acalymma sp., Atranchya sp., Aulacophora sp. and Diabrotica sp.) or the Coccinellidae (Epilachna sp.). The main vectors in the Western Hemisphere are the western striped cucumber beetle (Acalymma trivittata) and the spotted cucumber beetle (Diabrotica undecimpunctata). In the Mediterranean basin, the principal vector is Epilachna chrysomelina [E. elaterii]. A grasshopper (Melanoplus differentialis) is also reported to transmit the virus (Campbell, 1971).^p^p^Seed Health Testing^p^pSerology^p^pDAS-ELISA, with a sensitivity varying from 5 to 20 ng, is an appropriate technique for the routine testing of large numbers of leaf samples and for indexing seed lots. management_info: Seed Certification^p^pSeed producers are well aware of the seedborne nature of SqMV and have taken steps through the years to limit the presence of the virus in their melon and squash seed stocks. Certification of virus-free seed still remains an effective means of limiting the virus.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe development of varieties resistant to SqMV would be an advance. Although there are claims of virus resistance in some lines of Cucurbita pepo and C. moschata, these reports have not been confirmed. Some virus tolerance has been reported in some Cucurbita spp. as well as in some accessions of Cucumis melo from India and China (Provvidenti et al., 1978). Resistance has been reported in Cucumis metuliferus and Lagenaria siceraria Provvidenti, 1977, 1981; Provvidenti and Robinson, 1974). No information is available regarding resistance in watermelon or cucumber. The transgenic approach to breeding resistant cultivars is possible since the coat protein genes for SqMV have been cloned and sequenced.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pIn the field, virus spread can be reduced by the application of insecticides to control the beetle populations.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pOnce the plants are infected there is no cure, but occasionally the infected plants may recover making diagnosis difficult. The new developing leaves may look almost normal although the plants remain potential sources of virus. Thus, as soon as infected plants are discovered, the infected seedlings should be removed to prevent additional spread. This may not be completely successful, however, because initial symptoms are apparent only after an incubation period of 1-2 weeks, during which time virus replication has occurred and virus spread may have occurred by mechanical transmission from plant to plant or by vectors. Because of the threat of mechanical spread, especially in crops grown under glass or in plastic tunnels, disinfection of pruning and harvesting tools with a 5-10% solution of trisodium phosphate reduces the risk of mechanical transmission. Weed sanitation should also be practised to remove this reservoir of virus.

description:
SqMV能够被发现于生产葫芦种子且葫芦种子在生物学和在栽培葫芦里病毒的传播扮演着关键的角色的地区(Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1973a; Alvarez and Campbell, 1978)。在多数栽培葫芦里大范围传播的主要方法是通过一个国家到另一个国家感染种子的交换或交易。
SqMV血清型 I 已经被报道为是种传的在南瓜，甜瓜和西瓜里，而血清型 II 似乎仅在南瓜里是种传的。西瓜矮缩株系被报道为比普通株系更经常通过种子传播(Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1969)。种子传播比例范围常常为从0.1到10%，商业的和试验的种子大量产量约10%侵染苗(Grogan et al., 1959)，而高达94%传播已经被报道(Rader et al., 1947)。SqMV的一些摩洛哥分离种也通过种子传播在蓖诺藜和墙生藜里。
一旦病毒被引进在成批受污染的种子上，病毒能够通过修剪，收获和植株之间的直接接触机械传播。
SqMV通过至少14种不同种类的咀嚼式昆虫传播，大多数为甲虫。甲虫媒介昆虫属于叶甲科(Acalymma sp.，Atranchya sp.，守瓜属（Aulacophora sp.） 和叶甲属（Diabrotica sp.）) 或瓢甲科 (Epilachna sp.) (Campbell, 1971)。在西半球主要的媒介昆虫是西方条纹黄瓜甲虫(Acalymma trivittata) 和斑点黄瓜甲虫(Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi)。在地中海港湾，主要的媒介昆虫是Epilachna chrysomelina [E. elaterii]。蝗虫(Melanoplus differentialis)也被报道为传播病毒。 SqMV can be found in areas where cucurbit seeds are produced and plays a key role in the biology and dissemination of the virus in cultivated cucurbits (Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1973a; Alvarez and Campbell, 1978). The main method of widespread dispersal in most cultivated cucurbits is through the exchange or trade of infected seeds from one country to another.
SqMV serotype I has been reported to be seedborne in squash, melon and watermelon, whereas serotype II appears to be seedborne only in squash. The watermelon stunt strain is reported to be transmitted by seed more frequently than the common strain (Nelson and Knuhtsen, 1969). Seed transmission rates usually range from 0.1 to 10%; commercial and experimental seed lots yield about 10% infected seedlings (Grogan et al., 1959), but up to 94% transmission has been reported (Rader et al., 1947). Some Moroccan isolates of SqMV are also transmitted by seed in Chenopodium quinoa and C. murale.
Once introduced on contaminated batches of seeds, the virus can be spread mechanically through pruning, harvesting and direct contact between plants.
SqMV is transmitted by at least 14 different species of chewing insects, mostly beetles. The beetle vectors belong to the Chrysomelidae (Acalymma sp., Atranchya sp., Aulacophora sp. and Diabrotica sp.) or the Coccinellidae (Epilachna sp.) (Campbell, 1971). The main vectors in the Western Hemisphere are the western striped cucumber beetle (Acalymma trivittata) and the spotted cucumber beetle (Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi). In the Mediterranean basin, the principal vector is Epilachna chrysomelina [E. elaterii]. A grasshopper (Melanoplus differentialis) was also reported to transmit the virus.

description: In an Ohio survey in March to April of 2016, plants with virus-like symptoms, including stunting, chlorosis, and mosaic were collected from both planted soft red winter wheat fields and nearby volunteer wheat at 40 locations across 20 counties. Total RNA extracted from symptomatic plants, RT-PCR tests detected AgMV in only volunteer wheat in Wayne and Putnam counties and only production wheat in Huron county. This is the first detection of AgMV in Ohio (at multiple locations) and in the Midwest United States.  AgMV was transmitted by the cereal rust mite Abacarus hystrix.

host_range: M. carolinensis attacks members of the genus Pinus including P. banksiana, P. resinosa and P. strobus (Linsley and Chemsak, 1997). In addition, M. carolinensis adults have been reared from P. echinata (MacRae, 1993) and P. sylvestris (Pershing and Linit,
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pEconomic impact tends to be directly related to the presence of the pine wood nematode (Bursaphelenchus xylophilus) as vectored by M. carolinensis. Economic loss within North America is difficult to quantify because local losses tend to be to individuals who plant exotic pines on their property and small businesses such as Christmas tree farmers and nurseries. For lumber producers, timber quality can be diminished by beetle presence because of larval galleries and the infestation of blue stain fungi that often accompanies the beetle's presence in wood. Well-managed forests or logging operations would reduce or eliminate cosmetic damage from the insect. ^p^pTranscontinental trade losses are more substantial. Economic loss due to the ban on softwood products from infested countries to the European Union is difficult to estimate because environmental, regulatory and supply issues come into play. One company has estimated a $20 million loss due directly to the embargo (Dwinell, 1997). British Columbia (Canada) has an estimated potential loss of $700 million in unseasoned softwood lumber exports (Anon., 1991). Five million m3 of sawn lumber is exported from North America to the European Union, and Canada also exports $3 billion (CAN) in forest products. These industries are threatened by the embargo. Multi-million dollar wood chip markets that were developed in Europe in the 1980s have been lost due to the restrictions on wood imports (Bergdahl, 1988).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe environmental impact of M. carolinensis is negligible in North America because the pine wood nematode Bursaphelenchus xylophilus, which is vectored by M. carolinensis, only kills exotic pines or stressed pines planted outside of their natural range, and the beetle causes very minor damage to healthy trees.
description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pMonochamus beetles are generally poor fliers, though in flight mill experiments, female M. carolinensis beetles have flown a maximum distance of 10 km with a flight duration of 115 minutes (Akbulut and Linit, 1999). In mark and recapture studies of the closely related beetle, M. alternatus, most beetles were recaptured within 100 m of the release site in one study and 800 m of the release site in another study. Although no such studies exist for M. carolinensis, flight performance in the field is probably similar.^p^pVector Transmission^p^pThe propagative form of the pine wilt nematode Bursaphelenchus xylophilus develops and reproduces in both susceptible healthy and dying pines (Mamiya, 1984). Monochamus beetles are attracted to dying trees where the beetles locate mates and copulate. Females deposit eggs underneath the bark, and the nematodes exit the beetle's trachea and enter the wood through the oviposition wounds. M. carolinensis matures in dead pine, and B. xylophilus enters the beetles following the beetles' moult from pupae to adults and just prior to the beetles' emergence from the trees. A specialized life stage of the nematode, the JIV dispersal juvenile, is the nematode stage that is vectored. B. xylophilus are then carried to healthy trees, where they enter through beetle feeding wounds.^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pPine wilt disease is not spread through seeds/pine cones.^p^pSilvicultural Practices^p^pPine wilt disease might be spread directly from wood chips chipped from nematode-infested trees to healthy trees through contact with the roots, although conflicting evidence exists for the transmission of the disease in this manner. Pine seedlings with wounded roots are susceptible to infection from nematode-infested pine wood chips (Halik and Bergdahl, 1990). However, a study by Mamiya and Shoji (1989) suggested that transmission through soil to roots is negligible. Tomminen and Akar (1990) showed that four species of Coleoptera can be infested with the pinewood nematode from wood chips.^p^pDead trees left standing, stumps of logged trees, and the logged trees themselves, if left for substantial periods of time in the field, are subject to infestation by M. carolinensis. ^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pThe presence of nematodes in pine bark chips destined for Scandinavian countries prompted Sweden, Norway and Finland to ban raw pine wood products imported from the USA, Japan, and other regions where B. xylophilus is present (Dwinell, 1986; Kinn, 1986). The European Union considers the nematode and its Monochamus beetle vectors, including M. carolinensis, A1 quarantine pests (Directive 77/93, EEC) and consequently bans importation of pine wood products, except kiln-dried lumber, from infested countries. Although infested beetles could conceivably be transported to new areas in pine wood timber or chips, the nematode is a much more likely candidate for accidental transportation in trade. Various species of longhorn beetles have been intercepted in pine wood pallets and crates (Dwinell and Nickle, 1989).^p^pPortugal recently detected and eradicated a nematode infestation as the possible result of an accidental importation of infested wood, though the actual mechanism of introduction has yet to be established (Sousa et al., 2001). In 1988, the pine wood nematode was accidentally introduced into Korea from Japan in infested wood containing Monochamus alternatus (a close relative of M. carolinensis) and the nematode (La et al., 1998). The wood was used to package imported goods from Japan. In the past, M. titillator has been intercepted in timber imported to Europe from North America (Duffy, 1953). To date, M. carolinensis has not been implicated in the spread of pine wilt disease to uninfested countries.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; invisible.^p - Wood: Larvae, Pupae, Adul
management_info: Prevention is the best method of control. Logs should not be exposed during the egg-laying period of the beetle, from approximately July through September (Dwinell, 1997). The removal of bark immediately after felling will also prevent beetle damage. ^p^pIn North America, control is minimal, usually limited to removal and burning of infested trees and calendar spraying of insecticides on vulnerable exotic pines such as Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) in commercial settings (i.e., Christmas tree farms). The rapid progression of pine wilt disease generally results in diagnosis after tree death. The recommendation to individuals in North America who have susceptible exotic pines is to remove infected trees, burn them, and plant resistant native conifer species.^p^pAccidental transportation of the beetle to Europe or Asia can be prevented through a variety of means. Wood chips should be free of insects (but not the nematode Bursaphelenchus xylophilus) because the act of chipping the wood kills the larvae and pupae. Wood chips also can be treated with fumigation, irradiation, elevated temperatures or chemical dipping to kill both the insects and the nematode. Heat-treating (pasteurizing) and kiln-drying (to 56°C internal temperature for 30 minutes) kill all organisms present in sawn lumber. Heat-treating is also effective in sterilizing logs.
remark: The Monochamus vectors of the nematode Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (including M. carolinensis), as well as the nematode itself, are considered A1 quarantine pests by the European Plant Protection Organization (Directive 77/93, EEC). Consequently, all coniferous wood chips, sawn wood, and logs are regulated and/or banned for importation to the European Union and other countries.

potential_eco_desc:
以种子和根状茎繁殖，具化感特性和较强的竞争力，迅速定植并产生密集的植株，一平米内可产生100~300棵植株，是所有杂草中最具竞争力的。
叶具苦味，牲畜不喜欢食用。植株含毒素，长期食用可能造成马大脑永久性损伤，患上“咀嚼病”，不能咀嚼或唇肌失常。种子同样有苦味，混入谷物会带来令人不愉快的味道。植株易积聚锌，植株周围土壤中锌含量是通常的8倍。
能危害几乎所有的冬季作物，与作物争夺水和养料，在澳大利亚引起谷物产量损失超过75%。20世纪初传入北美洲，目前已成为重要杂草，广泛分布在加拿大和美国西部，并扩散到加利福尼亚州南部和亚利桑那州，加利福尼亚州许多农田因它而被废弃。在阿根廷和南非危害葡萄园和谷物，在原产地——伊朗、土耳其和前苏联地区南部是大麦、小麦、玉米和甘蔗重要杂草。曾在俄罗斯蔓延成灾，是俄罗斯南部旱作最严重的杂草之一。
description:
随种子和地下茎的延伸进行近距离传播，种子成熟后通常保留在头状花序中，大部分种子跌落在母株附近1m处，随灌溉水沿着沟渠转移，也能粘附在动物皮毛、农机具、交通工具等上进行传播。
远距离传播为种子和地下茎通过谷物和牧草种子、农机具、洪水等方式传播。20世纪初混杂在紫花苜蓿种子中从土耳其传入加拿大，大约在1910年在澳大利亚的维多利亚州归化，目前已成为澳大利亚新南威尔士州部分地区的重要杂草，在维多利亚州的旱作中变得日益严重。
management_info:
防治方法：
（1）预防措施：匍匐矢车菊的远距离传播通常通过作物种子，除检验检疫措施外，预防匍匐矢车菊进入农田应在种子播种前做严格的纯度检验。另外，定期监测对于杂草管理同样非常重要。
（2）栽培管理：中耕易分散根系片段而引起蔓延，不宜使用。匍匐矢车菊在不同的环境下均具有竞争优势，对它的控制需要有足够长的时间，提供的控制方法应包括种植竞争性植物，再结合长期可持续控制。可与匍匐矢车菊竞争的植物包括无芒雀麦、河边冰草、冰草、粗穗冰草、俄罗斯野生黑麦等。
（3）机械清除：清除地上部分植株，防止种子产生。重复割草有助于耗尽根部的储备，直至不能发芽。
（4）化学方法：长效除草剂二氯吡啶酸和毒莠定常推荐用于匍匐矢车菊控制，应选择在易感的秋季幼苗期和种子生产期使用。
（5）生物控制：乌克兰和乌兹别克斯坦使用一种亚粒属线虫Subanguina picridis，这种线虫可在茎、叶和根冠处形成虫瘿，从春季繁殖直到8月，再分散到土壤直到次年，这两个国家还进行了用矢车菊瘤瘿螨Aceria acroptiloni控制种子形成的研究。
（6）综合控制：综合管理包括检测、预防、物理方法、化学或生物控制，结合修剪、除草剂处理和种植多年生牧草等。
remark:
该物种的分类地位存在争议，《中国植物志》等大部分的植物分类学文献和网站认可的学名为：Acroptilon repens (L.) DC.，菊科顶羽菊属。美国农业部等一些知名网站根据Hidalgo et al. （2006）的研究成果，将其学名定为Rhaponticum repens (L.) Hidalgo，归入菊科漏芦属。部分文献和中国2007年5月25日公布的《中华人民共和国进境植物检疫性有害生物名录》将其称为匍匐矢车菊Centaurea repens L.，归入菊科矢车菊属。
据Flora of American中认为，顶羽菊属与矢车菊属的不同之处在于其瘦果与基盘附着处留下的脱落疤痕为近基部而不为侧面，且外部无不育小花存在，染色体基数为13，大于大部分的矢车菊种类。且菜蓟族（Cynareae）属间关系的分子生物学研究支持顶羽菊属和矢车菊属存在种间隔离。矢车菊属的瘦果为侧生着生面与花托相连，而顶羽菊属瘦果为基底着生面与花托连接，因此《中国植物志》的作者认为矢车菊属在进化程度上高于顶羽菊属。

host_range: Russian knapweed is allelopathic and interferes with grain crops such as lucerne, wheat, barley and oats (Heap and Mitchell, 1992). It spreads rapidly in good pastures, and is a serious noxious weed of dryland crops in southern Russia (Watson, 1980).
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pRussian knapweed can have an economic impact. Allelopathic and competitive interactions with crop plants can reduce yields. The weed is so bitter that contamination of grain by as little as 0.01% can reduce the quality of flour produced (Watson, 1980; Heap and Mitchell, 1992). The quality of forage is decreased if contaminated with Russian knapweed, and attempts to control Russian knapweed can be expensive (DiTomaso, 2000). Horses with prolonged consumption of Russian knapweed can develop 'chewing disease' or equine nigropallidal encephalomalacia (ENE). ENE is a permanent disease caused by lesions in the brain. Symptoms include the inability to eat or drink, aimless or awkward movement, and spontaneous activity. Symptoms may occur after ingestion of 60-200% of its body weight for at least 30 days (Lacey and Olson, 1991; Panter, 1991).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pRussian knapweed contains allelopathic chemicals which can suppress other plant species, forming monoculture knapweed stands. Infestations reduce yields of desired plants and decrease the production quality of rangelands. Fortunately, Russian knapweed is not toxic to animals such as sheep and dogs, and cattle have grazed infested pastures with no evidence of toxicity (Watson, 1980; Lacey and Olson, 1991; Panter, 1991; Olson, 1999).^p^p^Social impact^pRussian knapweed has little or no impact on human health (Zouhar, 2001). ^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pRussian knapweed is considered a serious habitat invader. Isolated patches grow rapidly, producing allelopathic chemicals that suppress competition. In Idaho, USA, it has threatened rare species such as Spalding's silene (Silene spaldingii). Smallhead goldenweed (Pyrrocoma liatriformis), sagebrush Mariposa lily (Calochortus macrocarpus var. maculosus) and Idaho hawksbeard (Crepis bakeri ssp. idahoensis) have also been impacted (Zouhar, 2001).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; crop production; environment; livestock production; native flora; rare / protected species
description: Russian knapweed was introduced to Canada as a contaminant of Turkestan lucerne seed in the early 1900s. It arrived in California, USA, about 1910 as a contaminant of Turkestan lucerne seed or possibly sugarbeet seed. Contaminated crop seeds are probably responsible for its worldwide spread (Groh, 1940; Watson, 1980; Maddox et al., 1985).

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pSeeds are mechanically dispersed through small distances. The primary means of long-range seed dispersal is probably via contaminated hay and other seed (primarily lucerne). Relatively little moves with farm machinery and transport vehicles (Roche and Roche, 1988; Zouhar, 2001).^p^pVector Transmission (Biotic)^p^pBirds and rodents eat seeds and may transport them (Roche et al., 1986).^p^pAgricultural Practices^p^pRussian knapweed can be spread by planting contaminated crop seeds (Roche and Roche, 1988; Zouhar, 2001).^p^pAccidental Introduction^p^pAccidental introductions have occurred in contaminated grain seed (Zouhar, 2001).^p^pIntentional Introduction^p^pAs A. repens is not an ornamental, it has not been intentionally introduced.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - True Seeds (inc. Grain): Seeds.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Conveyances (transport Vehicles): Farm Vehicles; Road Maintenance Machinery (Zouhar 2001)

management_info: Introduction^p^pOne of the most effective management methods is prevention. As Russian knapweed is often introduced in contaminated seeds, seedlots should be checked for purity before planting (Sheley et al., 1999a; Woo et al., 2002).^p^pMonitoring is also important for weed management. If possible, monitor three times a year: in the spring when plants have bolted, in the summer when flowering plants are easy to see, and in the autumn to find plants regrowing from roots. Disturbed areas such as roadsides are good targets (Woo et al., 1999; Zouhar, 2001).^p^pControl strategy for Russian knapweed and many perennials involves stressing the plant by mowing or defoliation, causing depletion of nutrients in the root system. Plants should not be allowed to produce seed, and root fragments should be not be spread to other locations following treatment (Zouhar, 2001).^p^pCombining one or more treatments in an integrated vegetation management programme will generally be more successful than relying on one control method. The key to success is often competitive plantings to revegetate an area where a control has been applied (Woo et al., 2002).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pRussian knapweed has a competitive advantage in a variety of environments, and will continue to persist unless it is suppressed long enough to allow the introduction and establishment of desirable species (Bottoms et al., 2001). Once competitive plantings are established, Russian knapweed is suppressed due to shading. The number of shoots produced increases with light intensity (Roche et al., 1986). ^p^pAny treatment that provides control of Russian knapweed must either release competitive species present in the understory or be combined with reseeding before long-term sustainable control can be achieved (Whitson, 1999; Whitson, 2001). Plants that compete well with Russian knapweed include smooth brome, streambank wheatgrass, thickspike wheatgrass, crested wheatgrass and Russian wild rye. Sod-forming perennials such as streambank or thickspike wheatgrasses compete better than bunch grasses (Benz et al., 1999; Beck, 2003).^p^pAnimal grazing is not very effective as a control for Russian knapweed. Animals will not graze on it when other vegetation is available because of its bitter taste (Olson and Lacey, 1994; TD Whitson, Extension weed specialist, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY 82071, USA, personal communication, 1997). The weed is also poisonous to horses, producing a neurological condition called equine nigropallidal encephalomalacia. Symptoms include the inability to eat or drink and aimless or awkward movement. Russian knapweed is not toxic to sheep and dogs, and cattle have grazed infested pastures with no evidence of toxicity (Lacey and Olson, 1991; Panter, 1991).^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pRussian knapweed often invades riparian areas, where its ability to recover from treatment is enhanced by moist soils. Russian knapweed is a perennial with an extensive root system that can resprout from root fragments. Therefore, many physical or mechanical methods are not highly effective. As Russian knapweed can reproduce from cut rhizomes, cultivation and handpulling is not effective and often contributes to its spread (Roche and Roche, 1991).^p^pHand pulling is generally ineffective against mature Russian knapweed because of its deep roots, and its ability to resprout from root fragments. Hand pulling or cutting the plants to kill the tops will starve the roots if done repeatedly, but this might not be a practical solution. Hand pulling might be successful for the early rosette stage (TD Whitson, Extension weed specialist, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY 82071, USA, personal communication, 1997).^p^pCutting, mowing or disking Russian knapweed infestations several times annually will control the existing topgrowth and prevent seed production. Cutting or mowing three times a year depletes nutrients in the roots, but unless mowing is continued, plants will recover. M

management_info: Lilies grow in the field in the Netherlands from April to October. During this time flying aphids will spread non-persistently transmitted viruses, such as lily mottle potyvirus. This affects the incidence, which is now fairly low. Nevertheless, a loss of quality in the plants to be used as cut flowers and a reduction in bulb yields induce the need for efficient disease control. In the field diseased plants are rogued if symptoms characteristic to cultivars appear conspicuously in certain periods of the field season. The selection of planting material and material from which stocks will be bulked by scale-propagation profits greatly from the serological detection by ELISA of virus infection in the cultivars during storage. The Netherlands Flowerbulb Inspection Service strictly supervises all the activities to ensure the virus-health status of the crops. ^p^pThe variable but fairly rapid spread of airborne viruses prompted experiments to curtail spread. Mineral oil and synthetic pyrethroid insecticides are routinely sprayed on a large scale. The reduction of virus spread depends on the brand of oil used, concentration of the oil in the emulsion, frequency of spraying, weather conditions and the cultivation methods (Asjes, 1984). The addition of synthetic pyrethroid (Asjes, 1981) to the oil reduced the quantity of oil used by half without reducing effectiveness. Weekly sprays start in May and are also applied in June and July. In August and September, fortnightly sprays are applied as the seasonal incidence of flying aphids is at a much lower level and no new leaves will be formed in the lily crops while the level of susceptibility to virus infection decreases (Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 1994). The influx of virus-tested material propagated by tissue culture procedures has become routine (Asjes, 1976; Aartrijk and Linde, 1986). Bulking up is done under aphid-proof conditions in gauze houses (Asjes, 1997), as in Israel (Cohen et al., 1996). ^p^pAmong other factors, the effectiveness of rapid propagation by tissue culture procedures, detection of viruses by ELISA, the need to produce acceptable virus-tested lilies by preference, and the routine spraying of mineral oil plus pyrethroid insecticide to prevent the spread of the prevalent lily mottle potyvirus and lily symptomless carlavirus enabled growers to expand lily culture in the Netherlands from tens of hectares in the 1960s to ca 3500 in the second half of the 1990s (Asjes et al., 1996; Asjes, 1997).

Mineral oil and synthetic pyrethroid insecticides are routinely sprayed on a large scale. The reduction of virus spread depends on the brand of oil used, concentration of the oil in the emulsion, frequency of spraying, weather conditions and the cultivation methods (Asjes, 1984). The addition of synthetic pyrethroid (Asjes, 1981) to the oil reduced the quantity of oil used by half without reducing effectiveness. Weekly sprays start in May and are also applied in June and July. In August and September, fortnightly sprays are applied as the seasonal incidence of flying aphids is at a much lower level and no new leaves will be formed in the lily crops while the level of susceptibility to virus infection decreases (Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 1994).   被用作为插瓶花的质量的损失和鳞茎产量的降低促使有效病害控制的需求。在田间感病的植株被去劣如果栽培种症状特性显著地出现于田间季节的若干周期。种植材料和来自于树干会通过大范围繁殖而被膨胀的材料的选择大大地从在储存期间栽培种中通过病毒侵染的ELISA血清学的探测中得益。荷兰花鳞茎检查部门（The Netherlands Flowerbulb Inspection Service）严格监督所有的行为以确保作物病毒健康状态。 a loss of quality in the plants to be used as cut flowers and a reduction in bulb yields induce the need for efficient disease control. In the field diseased plants are rogued if symptoms characteristic to cultivars appear conspicuously in certain periods of the field season. The selection of planting material and material from which stocks will be bulked by scale-propagation profits greatly from the serological detection by ELISA of virus infection in the cultivars during storage. The Netherlands Flowerbulb Inspection Service strictly supervises all the activities to ensure the virus-health status of the crops.

potential_eco_desc: The widespread distribution of P. peruviana in South Africa indicates the risk to nearby field crops and the potential impact on crop yields. Therefore, it is suggested that weeds are more stringently managed to reduce the rate of vector transmitted viruses to economically important crops such as pepper, tomato, and tobacco.
description: In February 2015, a survey was conducted in KwaZulu Natal (KZN), South Africa, to identify the diversity of weed species in major agricultural regions of the province. A tomato farm was found moderately infested with Physalis peruviana L., a solanaceous weed otherwise known as Inca/Cape berry, among several other weed species. Mottling, mosaic, and chlorosis symptoms were observed on the leaves of P. peruviana harboring an abundance of aphids. Interestingly, tomato crops showed similar symptoms, including vein clearing typically associated with potyvirus infections. Owing to the prevalence of Potato virus Y (PVY) in KZN, symptomatic leaf tissue collected from P. peruviana and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) plants was identified. Based on DAS-ELISA and RT-PCR, the results indicate the possibility of a mixed infection with PVYO and PVYC strains may be present in the samples. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PVY on P. peruviana from South Africa.  Symptomatic Physalis peruviana plants harbored an abundance of aphids.
reference_name: First Report of Potato virus Y (PVY) on Physalis peruviana in South Africa

description: In Ecuador, tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) disorders caused by potyviruses have been reported in the past. In 2013, leaves from tamarillo plants showing severe virus-like symptoms (mosaic, mottling, and leaf deformation) were collected from orchards in Pichincha and Tungurahua. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) was extracted from three independent batches and used to generate cDNA libraries to screen for RNA viruses by shotgun cloning. Sequencing revealed the presence of the potyviruses Potato virus Y (PVY), Potato virus V (PVV), and Peru tomato mosaic virus (PTV), and the polerovirus Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV). To determine the occurrence of the viruses, leaf samples tested by RT-PCR. Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription was done. For symptomatic plants, PVY and PLRV were the most common with 64% and 30%, respectively. PVV and PTV were found in 8% and 10%, respectively, with only 4% of the plants coinfected by both viruses. Plants coinfected by PVY and PLRV were the most common with 22%, followed by plants coinfected by PVY and PTV (10%). PVY has long been considered the most common virus in tamarillo in Ecuador. This communication reports for the first time in tamarillo the presence of PVV and PTV, two potyviruses once considered strains of PVY. Further studies are needed to determine the significance of PVV and PTV in single and mixed infections in tamarillo.
reference_name: First Report of Potato virus V and Peru tomato mosaic virus on Tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) Orchards of Ecuador

management_info: Vector Control^p^pThe use of insecticides is largely ineffective in the control of aphid-borne spread of PVY (de Bokx and Huttinga, 1981; Salazar, 1996). The use of reflective surfaces and sticky insect traps, however, can reduce virus spread by the aphid vectors (Loebenstein and Raccah, 1980). The use of mineral oils may also be partially effective.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pInfection by PVY can be reduced by avoidance of infection by growing crops at higher altitude where vectors are absent or occur in very low populations, not growing crops in the proximity of established related crops and, to prevent late spread, destroying haulms of seed potato crops before maturity.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe genetics and breeding of potatoes for resistance to PVY has been reviewed by Brown and Corsini (2001). Genes for PVY resistance have been identified in close relatives of potato, pepper, tobacco and tomato, and have been used to develop resistance using classical breeding methods (Provvidenti and Hampton, 1992).  More recently, potato plants genetically modified to express viral sequences have been shown to have a high degree of resistance, although as yet these have not found widespread usage (e.g., Lawson et al., 1990; Kaniewski et al., 1990; Felis and Zimnoch-Guzowska, 2000; Maki-Valkama et al., 2001). Berger and German (2001) have recently reviewed the production and use of genetically modified potatoes. ^p^p^Certification Schemes^p^pPVY is best controlled by the production, propagation and distribution of elite virus-free planting stocks, nucleus stocks of which are maintained under stringent conditions to prevent infection. The production of such stocks (Faccioli, 2001), seed-potato certification (Franc, 2001) and the operation of some common certification schemes (Gutbrod and Mosley, 2001) have been recently well-reviewed.

description: PVY通过超过50个蚜虫品种以非持久方式传播(Kennedy et al., 1962; Sigvald, 1984; Salazar, 1996; Ragsdale et al., 2001; Robert and Bourdin, 2001)。更重要的媒介可能是那些移植的马铃薯的如马铃薯长管蚜（Macrosiphum euphorbiae）、蚕豆蚜（Aphis fabae）、桃蚜（Myzus persicae）和马铃薯囊管蚜（Rhopalosiphoninus latysiphon），虽然其他的如紫堇瘤蚜（M. (Nectarosiphon) certus）、忽布蚜（Phorodon humuli ）和Rhopalosiphon insertum也是重要的自然媒介(Kennedy et al., 1962)。蚜虫品种在它们传播病毒的效率上也有所不同，虽然不同的品种的相对的重要性的估计有所不同。大多数的研究显示桃蚜（Myzus persicae）是PVY的一个非常有效的媒介，虽然其他的如紫堇瘤蚜（Myzus certus）、鼠李马铃薯蚜（Aphis nasturtii）、苹果缢管蚜（Rhopalosiphum insertum）、忽布蚜（P. humuli ）和 豌豆蚜（Acyrthosiphon pisum）也被报道为有效的传播者。 PVY is transmitted in a non-persistent manner by more than 50 aphid species (Kennedy et al., 1962; Sigvald, 1984; Salazar, 1996; Ragsdale et al., 2001; Robert and Bourdin, 2001). The more important vectors are probably those that colonise potatoes such as Macrosiphum euphorbiae, Aphis fabae, Myzus persicae, and Rhopalosiphoninus latysiphon, although others such as M. (Nectarosiphon) certus, Phorodon humuli and Rhopalosiphon insertum are also important natural vectors (Kennedy et al., 1962). Aphid species are also known to vary in their efficiency of transmission of the virus, although estimates of the relative importance of different species vary. Most studies have shown M. persicae to be a very efficient vector of PVY and although others such as Myzus certus, Aphis nasturtii, Rhopalosiphum insertum, P. humuli and Acyrthosiphon pisum have also been reported to be efficient tranmitters.
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: 当与其他的马铃薯病毒如马铃薯 A、马铃薯X 和/或马铃薯S 病毒复合发生时，它特别具毁灭性，有时会毁灭全部的作物。在烟草上，能发生39-75%的产量损失(Latorre et al., 1984)，虽然PVYN分离种能由于株系、品种和侵染时间的不同而引起全部的产量损失。 When in complexes with other potato viruses such as potato A, potato X and/or potato S viruses, it can be particularly damaging, sometimes destroying the entire crop. In tobacco, yield losses of 39-75% can occur (Latorre et al., 1984), although PVYN isolates can cause complete crop loss depending on strain, cultivar and time of infection. 虽然PVY的多数分离种只在辣椒、烟草和番茄上引起轻微的斑驳，但一些分离种能在马铃薯上引起10－100％的产量损失(de Bokx and Huttinga, 1981; Salazar, 1996)。PVY在马铃薯上仍然是重要的因为它很容易传播并能大幅度降低产量。 Although most isolates of PVY cause only mild mottling in pepper, tobacco and tomato, some can cause yield losses of 10-100% in potato (de Bokx and Huttinga, 1981; Salazar, 1996). PVY is still of major importance in potatoes because it spreads so easily and can greatly decrease yield.

management_info: 杀虫剂的使用对PVY蚜虫传的传播的防治上是非常的无效的(de Bokx and Huttinga, 1981; Salazar, 1996)。然而，反射表面和粘性昆虫的陷阱的使用，能减少病毒通过蚜虫媒介的传播(Loebenstein and Raccah, 1980)。矿物油的使用也可部分地有效。 The use of insecticides is largely ineffective in the control of aphid-borne spread of PVY (de Bokx and Huttinga, 1981; Salazar, 1996). The use of reflective surfaces and sticky insect traps, however, can reduce virus spread by the aphid vectors (Loebenstein and Raccah, 1980). The use of mineral oils may also be partially effective. 马铃薯对PVY的抗性的遗传性的和育种已被Brown and Corsini (2001)研究。PVY的抗性基因在马铃薯、辣椒、烟草和马铃薯的亲密亲缘植物中被鉴定出，它们被利用传统的育种方法来用作抗性的培育(Provvidenti and Hampton, 1992)。 The genetics and breeding of potatoes for resistance to PVY has been reviewed by Brown and Corsini (2001). Genes for PVY resistance have been identified in close relatives of potato, pepper, tobacco and tomato, and have been used to develop resistance using classical breeding methods (Provvidenti and Hampton, 1992). PVY的侵染能通过在媒介是不存在的或以非常低的种群在发生的较高海拔的地方种植作物避免侵染、不在已建立的有关系作物的附近种植作物、以及在成熟之前毁坏种子马铃薯作物的茎来预防晚期传播来减少。 Infection by PVY can be reduced by avoidance of infection by growing crops at higher altitude where vectors are absent or occur in very low populations, not growing crops in the proximity of established related crops and, to prevent late spread, destroying haulms of seed potato crops before maturity.

management_info: Chemical control against dense nymphal populations might be justified on valuable trees, but control of sooty mould by means of fungicides is usually more useful. Chemical control of adults is difficult owing to their mobility and long life (Duso, 1984). For chemical control, timing is of the utmost importance, and at the very first signs of infestation, malathion, acephate, fenitrothion or pyrethroids should be applied at the edges of the fields (Ciampolini et al., 1987). Insecticide applications should be kept to a minimum; one application should be made on the crop and wild plants at the end of July/beginning of August to eliminate immature nymphs and newly-emerged adults, and a second application should be made on wild plants in the first half of August to prevent the adults from reinvading the crop. ^p^pOn fruit crops which already receive calendar treatments of insecticides, a product effective against M. pruinosa could be inserted into the control programme at these times. (Ciampolini et al., 1995). The most effective insecticides were fenitrothion, methidathion and quinalphos. Deltamethrin gave good control while pyridaphenthion gave mediocre control. Dimethoate gave better control on the leaves than on the fruit. Chlorpyrifos-methyl needed to be sprayed directly onto the adults to achieve maximum efficacy. Azinphos-methyl was the most persistent insecticide (about 10 days), followed by acephate, lambda-cyhalothrin, dimethoate, pyridaphenthion, methomyl and deltamethrin (5-8 days), and then microencapsulated parathion-methyl, methidathion, quinalphos, fenitrothion and chlorpyrifos-methyl (0-2 days). Chlorpyrifos-methyl, deltamethrin and quinalphos had a repellent activity, accounting for their low levels of persistence. (Stefanelli et al., 1994). Etofenprox had a sufficient and prolonged efficacy, contrasting with the high and brief activity of malathion. Applications of imidacloprid, a well-known systemic insecticide, in granular form to the foot of the plant or in liquid form to the trunk abolished negative effects on the urban population normally caused by spray treatments. Neem oil was not active against the adults, but it is suggested that it could be active against immature stages (Pasini et al., 1997). ^p^pSoap solutions cause almost all of the young stages of the pest to fall to the ground. In the absence of insecticide treatments, the colonies reform 8-10 days later. The treatment is also highly effective in washing away from the plants wax secretions and honeydew produced by the flatid. The treatment should be made as late as possible but before the appearance of adults (Greatti and Girolami, 1994).

host_range: CDV was initially isolated from ornamental Brugmansia spp. from Colombia. Since then, this virus has been detected in different solanaceous species in Europe. In Italy, CDV was detected for the first time in Brugmansia spp. from private gardens and one nursery in the Apulia region. This is the first report of CDV in a natural Mediterranean environment, and the first report of a potyvirus infection in mandrake.
description: In September 2014, flower and leaf mottle symptoms were observed on autumn mandrake(Mandragora autumnalis ) plants, growing in a natural reserve of the northwest Sicilian coast. Based on bioassay and sequence analysis the causal agent was identified as Colombian datura virus (CDV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of CDV in a natural Mediterranean environment, and the first report of a potyvirus infection in mandrake.  Colombian datura virus  is a member of the family Potyviridae transmitted by aphids in a nonpersistent manner, by mechanical inoculation and grafting.
reference_name: First Report of Colombian datura virus in Mandragora autumnalis in Sicily, Italy

host_range: Since its discovery in Angel’s trumpet plants (Brugmansia spp., family: Solanaceae) imported from Colombia to the United States and rediscovery in Europe, Colombian datura virus (CDV) disseminated all over the world to where infected Brugmansia species and hybrids have been introduced. In addition, CDV became a dangerous pathogen of important crops infecting tomato, tobacco, petunia, pepino, and cape gooseberry as well as Spiranthes cernua, Juanulloa aurantiaca, and Datura metel.
description: In May 2012, roadside grown Chinese lanterns(Physalis alkekengi) were observed in Nyíregyháza (Northeast Hungary) showing chlorotic mottle symptoms on leaves. Leaf sap inoculation to test plants proved the presence of a mechanically transmitted plant virus. Biological and molecular data proved that the virus isolated from Chinese lantern should be a strain of Colombian datura virus (CDV). This is the first record on the appearance of CDV in P. alkekengi. Besides Brugmansia spp., this plant may serve as a reservoir host and can be a primary source of CDV in Hungary.
reference_name: First Report on Natural Infection of Colombian datura virus (CDV) in Chinese Lantern (Physalis alkekengi)

host_range: 毛曼陀罗Datura inoxia
description: Colombian datura virus (CDV) has a worldwide distribution and broad host range which was first identified in Brugmansia plants (Solanaceae) from Colombia. A survey was conducted from January to May 2014 in Rajasthan India, to investigate the epidemiology of potyvirus. Datura showed characteristic symptoms of leaf reduction and flower distortion. The samples were collected and identified, based on serological detection and molecular detection showed that the causal agent was CDV. This is the first report of the natural infection of CDV causing severe mosaic symptoms on Datura inoxia in India. The distribution and economic impact of this virus is still unknown and further studies on the characterisation as well as determination of host range of CDV in India is required.

host_range: 番茄Solanum lycopersicum
description: In 2009, some commercially grown tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) plants in Chiba Prefecture, Japan, exhibited mosaic symptoms. Ten plants from a total of about 72,000 cultivated plants in the greenhouses showed such symptoms. The test demonstrated that the causal agent was Colombian datura virus（CDV） The first case of CDV on tomato was reported in Netherlands, indicating that CDV was transmitted by aphids from CDV-infected Brugmansia plants cultivated in the same greenhouse. We carefully investigated whether Brugmansia plants naturally grew around the greenhouses, but we could not find them inside or in proximity to the greenhouses. Therefore, sources of CDV inoculum in Japan are still unclear. This is the first report of a mosaic disease caused by CDV on commercially cultivated S. lycopersicum in Japan.  The first case of CDV on tomato was reported in Netherlands, indicating that CDV was transmitted by aphids from CDV-infected Brugmansia plants cultivated in the same greenhouse.
reference_name: First Report of Mosaic Disease Caused by Colombian datura virus on Solanum lycopersicum Plants Commercially Cultivated in Japan

description: In July 2013, during a survey to determine the presence of different viruses infecting weed plants in South Korea, three white clover (Trifolium repens) leaf samples showing yellow mosaic symptoms were collected from Taean County, South Chungcheong Do Province, South Korea. Based on molecular detection and the pathogenicity assay showed that the causal agent was Clover yellow vein virus (ClYVV). Up to now, in South Korea, ClYVV has been detected in gladiolus (Gladiolus gandavensis) and soybean (Glycine max). The presence of ClYVV could become an important threat to crop production in South Korea. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a ClYVV infection of the white clover plant in South Korea.  Clover yellow vein virus can be easily transmitted by insect, aphid, or mechanical inoculation and has a host range including tobacco, soybean, etc.

description: In Korea, eight viruses have been reported to infect soybean, including Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV), Cowpea mosaic virus (CPMV), Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), Soybean dwarf virus(SbDV), Soybean mosaic virus (SMV), Soybean yellow common mosaic virus (SYCMV), Soybean yellow mottle virus (SYMMV), and Peanut stunt virus (PSV). potential_eco_desc: Most of the concern about the impact of ClYVV has focussed on clovers, particularly white clover (Trifolium repens), which are mostly grown as perennials, especially in pastures. By 1975, some 13 viruses had been detected in white clover (Barnett and Gibson, 1975). Fields are often simultaneously infested by more than one virus, and mixed infection of single plants is prevalent. It is, therefore, hard to quantify the effect of ClYVV alone. ^p^pIn greenhouse experiments, five Ladino clover clones inoculated with Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV) and ClYVV (then identified as BYMV) showed a 23-55% loss (Kreitlow et al., 1957). Other loss assessments involved comparing clones of clover infected with an accumulation of viruses, including ClYVV, from long-term natural exposure with virus-free plants from these clones obtained by meristem tip culture (Barnett et al., 1975). In six clones of 'Tillman' white clover the average seed yield was reduced by the viruses to 25% of the controls as a consequence of a reduction in the number of heads per plant, number of seeds per head and per floret, and reduced seed weight (Barnett and Gibson, 1977). In another experiment, six clones of 'Tillman' white clover obtained from virus-free seedlings were transplanted to the field and tested for infection. During the first year, Peanut stunt virus (PSV) was more prevalent than ClYVV, early during the next year their incidence was similar, and later that year the incidence of ClYVV was highest and some AMV was also detected. At that time 87% of the plants were virus-infected and the reductions in yield (foliage dry weight), mainly due to ClYVV, ranged from 29.5 to 57.1% (Campbell and Moyer, 1984). In filtered-air enclosures in the field, ClYVV was found to reduce the yield of inoculated Ladino white clover by 9-26%; this was less than PSV (22-40%) and AMV which was intermediate (Gibson et al., 1982). In similar experiments, plants of arrowleaf clover (T. vesiculosum) singly inoculated with AMV, BYMV, ClYVV and PSV, reacted similarly to BYMV and ClYVV. Yield loss was greater for ClYVV than BYMV, reducing the per plant mean weight of oven dry leaves at early inoculation from 13.0 to 1.6 g (Gibson et al., 1979). Under such conditions, ClYVV reduced the total dry weight of white clover leaves from 1.1 to 0.9 g which was less than the damage by AMV and PSV. The length of stolons, the number of rooting nodes on stolons and root nodulation were also reduced by ClYVV (Gibson et al., 1981). ^p^pWhen two 'Ladino' white clover clones were examined in a transplanted clover-tall fescue system under field conditions for response to ClYVV, PSV  and ClYVV + PSV infection, all infected plants had considerably lower dry weight yield than plants of initially virus-free clover. Double virus infection reduced dry weights more than infection by either virus alone. Virus infections also reduced the number of stolons per plant, length of stolons, nodes per centimetre of stolon, and rooting nodes per stolon. ClYVV was less severe than PSV (Ragland et al., 1986). ^p^pInfection by viruses, including ClYVV, reduces the persistence of clovers in the field, particularly in mixed stands such as pastures (Pratt, 1967). In a field evaluation of several accessions of six clover species, 18-100% of T. pratense plants and 6-25% of T. hybridum remained 1 year after planting, indicating high rates of mortality due to Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV), ClYVV, White clover mosaic  virus (WCMV) and Red clover vein mosaic virus (RCVMV) (Alconero et al., 1986). ClYVV is claimed to be involved in the decline of subterranean clover in Australian pasture (Helms et al., 1993). A 4-year pasture study in Mississippi, USA, involving infection by a number of viruses, including ClYVV but predominantly PSV, showed a significant decline of the white clover population so that the clover had virtually disappeared from the pasture by the following autumn (McLaughlin et al., 1992). Aphis chloris has been suggested for the biocontrol of St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) in Australia and, although failing to transmit three persistent viruses, it was found to transmit ClYVV (Briese, 1989).^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pTests for seed transmission were negative (Hollings and Nariani, 1965; Barnett and Gibson, 1977; Okuda et al., 1992) but the numbers of seeds tested were too low to draw definite conclusions. Due to the high rates of seed transmission of related potyviruses (such as Bean common mosaic virus, Lettuce mosaic virus, Pea seed-borne mosaic virus and Bean yellow mosaic virus in some of its hosts), the possibility of seed transmission of ClYVV cannot be excluded.^p^pMovement in Plant Material^p^pClYVV may be translocated in live vegetative material for planting such as rooted stolons or cuttings. Because the virus has been reported to occur in Gladiolus, it could be transferred over long distances in corms; however, there is no information on the extent of natural infection in Gladiolus. management_info: Virus Elimination^p^pIt is possible to obtain virus-free white clover plants and descendent clones for experiments using cold or heat treatment (10 or 40°C, respectively), followed by propagation of stem tip cuttings (Baxter and McGlohon, 1959). Up to 83% of plants were freed from ClYVV by using cold treatment followed by culture of excised meristem tips (meristematic dome plus one or two leaf primordia) on a modified Murashige and Skoog medium (Barnett et al., 1975).^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pFor controlling disease in crops, cultural methods to prevent infection may be hard to implement. Old stands of clover, notably white clover, should be avoided when sowing new crops. Resowing clovers in old pastures is likely to lead to rapid reinfection. Likewise, it is recommended not to grow annual legumes such as faba bean, lupins, Phaseolus vulgaris and pea in the vicinity of old stands of white clover. Data on the effects of interplanting white clover with grass (Festuca arundinacea) to reduce the incidence of ClYVV and Peanut stunt virus (PSV) are conflicting (McLaughlin et al., 1992; Taylor et al., 1995). The beneficial effect of the grass may be limited to conditions where the grass is taller than the clover, thus tempting viruliferous alate aphids to land and probe on grass plants and rid their mouthparts of nonpersistently transmitted virus before moving on to clover.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pControl emphasis is on the use of resistant cultivars and on selection and breeding for genetic resistance. Most data on virus resistance in clovers originate from observations of field-grown collections with wide spacing that are subject to natural infection. They therefore concern multiple resistance. More targeted screening for resistance is by inoculation in the greenhouse. When submitting cultivars of Phaseolus vulgaris to ClYVV infection by mechanical, hypodermic and aphid inoculation, the percentages of infection were found to differ considerably. Because ClYVV, as well as many other clover viruses, is vectored by aphids in the field, screening plants for resistance by mechanical inoculation, may not, therefore, be a realistic means for identifying resistance or for screening breeding populations or lines (Dwadash-Shreni and Stavely, 1984). Evaluation of resistance is mainly by symptom severity, although this may not be a reliable parameter of resistance to damage (Bos and Parlevliet, 1995). Resistance to infection (true virus resistance) should be distinguished from mere tolerance, and be measured quantitatively by checking the presence of the virus and its concentration in infected plants by bioassay and/or serologically. Symptom appearance may also be delayed in more resistant genotypes (Alconero, 1983b). Considerable attention has been paid to resistance in clovers, but resistance in beans and peas has also been studied.^p^pWhite clover: resistance to ClYVV was first detected by Barnett and Gibson (1975) and later studies identified resistance to various viruses, including ClYVV, in several cultivars (Harville and Derrick, 1978; Campbell and Moyer, 1983; Ragland et al., 1986). Two clones of 'Tillman' white clover with differential resistance to ClYVV and PSV were used to study the effect of ClYVV on yield (Ragland and Campbell, 1983) and on susceptibility to Codinaea fertilis (Campbell and Moyer, 1983). In Mississippi, USA, germplasm derived from polycross progenies of 22 white clover clones with drought resistance, and registered as 'Brown Loam Synthetic No. 2', exceeded 'Regal' and 'Tillman' for forage yield and persistence for 4 years of testing, and showed significantly less infection by ClYVV and PSV (Knight et al., 1988). Germplasm with resistance to viruses prevalent in southeastern USA has later been registered as 'Southern Regional Virus Resistant' (SRVR) (Gibson et al., 1989). At Lexington, Kentucky, and in Mississippi it was found to have a significantly lower incidence of ClYVV and PSV

management_info: It is possible to obtain virus-free white clover plants and descendent clones for experiments using cold or heat treatment (10 or 40℃, respectively), followed by propagation of stem tip cuttings (Baxter and McGlohon, 1959). Up to 83% of plants were freed from ClYVV by using cold treatment followed by culture of excised meristem tips (meristematic dome plus one or two leaf primordia) on a modified Murashige and Skoog medium (Barnett et al., 1975). 就用于冷或热处理（10或40℃，各自的温度），随着茎尖端插条的繁殖(Baxter and McGlohon, 1959)的试验而言，获得抗病毒的白三叶草植株和无性系后代是可能的。高达83%的植株通过运用接着在改变的Murashige和Skoog培养基上切除的分生组织尖端（分生组织的原型顶物正一或二叶子原基）的培养物的冷处理从CIYVV中被摆脱(Barnett et al., 1975)。   防治的重要性是在抗病品种的使用和基因抗性的选择与繁殖上。大多数关于三叶草中病毒抗性的数据起源于遭受自然侵染的广阔空间的田间种植的综合种的观察资料。因此它们影响多类型的抗性。更多的对抗性的瞄准的筛选是通过在温室里接种。当认为菜豆的栽培种对CIYVV侵染是通过机械的，皮下注射的和蚜虫接种的时候，侵染的比例被发现是相当不同的。因为CIYVV，像很多其它的三叶草病毒一样，是以蚜虫为媒介的在田间里，因此，通过机械接种筛选抗性植株，可能不是实事求是的手段对确定抗性和筛选繁殖种群或系而言(Dwadash-Shreni and Stavely, 1984)。抗性的评价主要通过症状的严重性，尽管这可能不是抗性对损害的可靠参数(Bos and Parlevliet, 1995)。对侵染的抗性（真实的病毒抗性）应该被从仅仅的耐性中区别出来，且通过检查病毒的存在性和通过生物测定和/或血清学地它的在感染植株的集中定量地测量。症状出现可能被延缓在更具抗性的基因型中(Alconero, 1983b)。相当多的注意已经被注意到在三叶草中的抗性，但是在菜豆和豌豆中的抗性也已经被研究。 Control emphasis is on the use of resistant cultivars and on selection and breeding for genetic resistance. Most data on virus resistance in clovers originate from observations of field-grown collections with wide spacing that are subject to natural infection. They therefore concern multiple resistance. More targeted screening for resistance is by inoculation in the greenhouse. When submitting cultivars of Phaseolus vulgaris to ClYVV infection by mechanical, hypodermic and aphid inoculation, the percentages of infection were found to differ considerably. Because ClYVV, as well as many other clover viruses, is vectored by aphids in the field, screening plants for resistance by mechanical inoculation, may not, therefore, be a realistic means for identifying resistance or for screening breeding populations or lines (Dwadash-Shreni and Stavely, 1984). Evaluation of resistance is mainly by symptom severity, although this may not be a reliable parameter of resistance to damage (Bos and Parlevliet, 1995). Resistance to infection (true virus resistance) should be distinguished from mere tolerance, and be measured quantitatively by checking the presence of the virus and its concentration in infected plants by bioassay and/or serologically. Symptom appearance may also be delayed in more resistant genotypes (Alconero, 1983b). Considerable attention has been paid to resistance in clovers, but resistance in beans and peas has also been studied. 就在作物里防治病害而言，防止侵染的栽培的方法可能很难生效。三叶草的旧株，显而易见地白三叶草，应该被避开当播种新的作物时。在旧牧场里重新播种的三叶草可能导致快速的再侵染。同样地，不赞许在白三叶草的旧株的附近种植像蚕豆，羽扇豆，菜豆和豌豆等一年生豆科植物。关于白三叶草与牧草(Festuca arundinacea)的间作对减少CIYVV和花生矮缩病毒（PSV）的发病率的影响上的资料是有争议的(McLaughlin et al., 1992; Taylor et al., 1995)。牧草的有益的影响可能是对环境限制那里牧草比三叶草高，这样诱使携带病毒的有翅蚜虫降落和触摸于牧草上且在进展到三叶草之前摆脱它们的非持续传播的病毒的口器。 For controlling disease in crops, cultural methods to prevent infection may be hard to implement. Old stands of clover, notably white clover, should be avoided when sowing new crops. Resowing clovers in old pastures is likely to lead to rapid reinfection. Likewise, it is recommended not to grow annual legumes such as faba bean, lupins, Phaseolus vulgaris and pea in the vicinity of old stands of white clover. Data on the effects of interplanting white clover with grass (Festuca arundinacea) to reduce the incidence of ClYVV and Peanut stunt virus (PSV) are conflicting (McLaughlin et al., 1992; Taylor et al., 1995). The beneficial effect of the grass may be limited to conditions where the grass is taller than the clover, thus tempting viruliferous alate aphids to land and probe on grass plants and rid their mouthparts of nonpersistently transmitted virus before moving on to clover.

host_range: Tradescantia mild mosaic virus (TraMMV) was named and characterized in 2006 in Italy. A potyvirus with the name Tradescantia-Zebrina virus (TZV) was reported from the USA some years earlier in Tradescantia albiflora with leaf distortion and stunting, TZV and TraMMV could be the same virus. In July 2014, streaking and malformation of leaves were observed on several plants of Tradescantia spathacea in a public winter garden in Auckland, New Zealand. The samples were collected and identified, the causal agent was identified as Tradescantia mild mosaic virus (TraMMV). From July to November 2014, a further 12 tradescantia plants (of which 8 plants were symptomatic) representing the following species, T. fluminensis, T.sillamontana, T. spathacea, and T. zebrine were collected from different locations in the Auckland region. All symptomatic plants tested positive for TraMMV using the method previously described. Chenopodium amaranticolor and C. quinoa have been reported previously as experimental hosts of TraMMV (Ciuffo et al. 2006), and this study revealed that N. clevelandii and N. sylvestris can also be infected with TraMMV by mechanical inoculation.
description:
In July 2014, streaking and malformation of leaves were observed on several plants of Tradescantia spathacea in a public winter garden in Auckland, New Zealand. The samples were collected and identified, the causal agent was identified as Tradescantia mild mosaic virus (TraMMV) by molecular diagnostics. From July to November 2014, a further 12 tradescantia plants representing the following species, T. fluminensis, T.sillamontana, T. 
spathacea, and T. zebrine were collected from different locations in the Auckland region. All symptomatic plants tested positive for TraMMV. To our knowledge, this is the first report of TraMMV in New Zealand.  As a potyvirus, TraMMV may be transmitted by aphid, and if TraMMV and TZV are the same virus, it can be vectored by at least two species, Myzus persicae and Rhopalosiphon padi .
reference_name: First Report of Tradescantia mild mosaic virus in Tradescantia spp. in New Zealand
