potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pPeMoV was first found infecting groundnuts and soyabean in Georgia, USA (Kuhn, 1965), but it has since been reported to occur in groundnut (and, in some countries, in other leguminous species) in Africa (Burkina Faso, Egypt, Kenya, Niger, Sudan, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia), Asia (India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, Malaysia, Philippines and Taiwan), Australasia (Australia) and South America (Argentina and Colombia), North America (Canada and the USA) and the Caribbean (Cuba). Its widespread geographical distribution is probably due to its seed transmission in groundnut, which previously allowed its inadvertent international dissemination in contaminated seed stocks. Although mainly a pathogen of groundnut, PeMoV also occurs naturally in soyabean (Glycine max), bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), pea (Pisum sativum), cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), blue and white lupins (Lupinus spp.), bambara groundnut (Voandzeia subterranea), some forage crops (Alysicarpus vaginalis, Cyamopsis tetragonoloba, Stylosanthes spp., Trifolium spp.) and several weed species (Cassia spp., Crotalaria spp. and Desmodium canum); PeMoV has also been reported to occur in sesame (Sesamum sp.) in Indonesia. The virus is seed-transmitted at levels up to 8.5% in groundnut cultivars, but to less than 1% in bean, bambara groundnut, cowpea and lupin; it is not seed-transmitted in soyabean.^p^p^Groundnut^p^pIn the USA, yield losses attributable to commonly-occurring isolates of PeMoV range from 17-31% in field-grown crops and up to 68% in glasshouse experiments (Kuhn, 1965; Paguio, 1973; Paguio and Kuhn, 1973a; Kuhn and Demski, 1975; Kuhn et al., 1978); however, severe isolates can reduce yields by 68-72% (Sun and Hebert, 1972; Kuhn et al., 1978). Significant yield losses have also been reported from other countries (Ting et al., 1972; Ahmed, 1984; Inouye et al., 1988).^p^pIn Georgia, USA in 1971 the predominant mild strain of PeMoV in cv Starr caused a 26% loss in pod weight per plant (a 15 g loss from 58.3 to 43.3 g/plant), and in 1972 a 21% yield loss (a 19.8 g loss of pod weight from 92.9 to 73.1 g/plant) (Paguio and Kuhn, 1974b); the average yield loss in 1973 was 20% in Georgia. A careful comparison of pods from healthy and infected plants (1,000 g random sample of each) showed that the yield loss was mainly attributable to a reduction in the number and size of seeds from infected plants; thus, seed numbers were reduced by 15% (from 117 to 100 per plant) and, on average, seed weight was reduced by 8.6% (from 0.35 to 0.32 g) (Paguio and Kuhn, 1974b). Seed from infected plants may be malformed and discoloured (Kuhn, 1965; Estrada and Palomar, 1981; Varma, 1988).^p^pIn pot experiments in Malaysia, healthy plants of genotype V.13 yielded 11.5 pods/plant whereas infected plants yielded only 7 pods/plant, a loss of 43.5%; in these tests, the dry weight of pods was reduced from 12.6 to 6.5 g (48% loss) and dry weight of seeds from 8.8 to 4.6 g/plant (50% loss) (Geh and Ting, 1973). A similar yield loss of a totally infected crop was recorded previously in Selangor (Ting et al., 1972). In some South East Asian countries severe infections can reduce yields by 30-40% (Inouye et al., 1988) and, in the Indian Sub-Continent where groundnut is the main source of cooking oil, the virus is a potential but unquantified threat to groundnut production (Varma, 1988).^p^pVirus-induced crop losses are dependent upon the incidence of infection. description: Incidence^p^pPeMoV is seedborne in groundnut varieties at rates ranging from 0-30% (Anon., 1972;Paguio and Kuhn, 1973c, 1974c; Bock and Kuhn, 1975; Kuhn and Demski, 1975; Bharathan et al., 1984; Abdelsalam et al., 1987). Adams and Kuhn (1977) isolated PeMoV from embryos but not from cotyledons or seed coats. Conversely, Bharathan et al. (1984), using ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), detected the virus in groundnut embryos, cotyledons and seed coats. PeMoV is also seedborne at low rates in other hosts: less than 1% in Lupinus spp. (Demski et al., 1983a), Vigna unguiculata (Demski et al., 1983b) and Voandzeia subterranea (Li et al., 1991). management_info: Introduction^p^pAlthough some work has been done on regeneration of virus-free plants from tissue culture (Chen et al., 1990; Chen and Sherwood, 1991), the majority of research on controlling PeMoV centres around breeding for resistance and development of specific cultural practices.^p^pHowever, inasmuch as PeMoV is present in all commercial groundnut-growing regions around the world, and yield reductions are considered insignificant by many growers, control methods are not widely used for this virus (Demski and Kuhn, 1977; Zettler et al., 1993).^p^p^Breeding for Resistance^p^pIn Australia, two lines of Phaseolus vulgaris cv. Red Kidney have been identified as being resistant to PeMoV (Anon, 1976). Four other genotypes of P. vulgaris are also reported to be resistant to at least eight PeMoV isolates (Bijaisoradat et al., 1988; Redden, 1993). Provvidenti and Chirco (1987) identified 78 of 111 selections of P. vulgaris cv. Royalty Purple Pod which demonstrated resistance to PeMoV. This resistance was attributed to a single incompletely dominant gene. ^p^pOf 24 Vigna unguiculata cultivars screened, Demski et al. (1983) identified 10 which were resistant to PeMoV. Likewise, Bijaisoradat et al. (1988) identified four V. unguiculata genotypes resistant to eight PeMoV isolates. ^p^pAccessions of both Arachis hypogaea and Arachis diogi have been screened for resistance to PeMoV ICRISAT, 1981, 1982; Melouk et al., 1984a; Gibbons, 1987). Resistance to PeMoV was identified in five and two accessions of Arachis hypogaea and Arachis diogi, respectively (Melouk et al., 1984b), and 12 accessions of Arachis spp. (Rao et al., 1993). ^p^pSeveral cultivars of PeMoV-resistant Glycine max have been identified and/or registered (Demski and Kuhn, 1975; Shipe, 1978;Buss et al., 1979, 1983, 1985, 1987; Bays et al., 1986). This resistance is controlled by two dominant genes (Boerma and Kuhn, 1976; Demski and Kuhn, 1977; Shipe, 1978; Shipe and Buss, 1978; Shipe et al., 1979a,b; Roane et al., 1980;Roane et al., 1983a,b;Buss et al., 1985, 1988; Roane et al., 1985).^p^p^Cultural Practices^p^pBecause PeMoV is seedborne and infected groundnuts are the primary source of the virus, standard cultural practices of eliminating volunteer groundnuts from fields planted in legume crops each season, and roguing early each season, help to delay secondary spread by aphids (Demski, 1975; Demski and Kuhn, 1977). No effective or economically feasible aphid control measures are currently available. Establishing a 'mother block' system and isolating virus-free germplasm in aphid-proof greenhouses or by long distances [away from potential sources of virus] has also proven effective (Demski and Kuhn, 1977; Zettler et al., 1990; Zettler et al., 1993).

host_range: In nature, LYSV (common strain) is almost limited to leek. Onions and shallots are highly resistant, but not immune to the virus (Bos et al., 1978a), and the virus has been isolated from plants of these species near severely infected leek (Graichen, 1978a
potential_eco_desc: In leek crops, the incidence of yellow stripe may attain high levels. Near Aachen (Germany) 100% of the plants were often infected (Kupke, 1957). The same was found in autumn and winter crops in Belgium (Verhoyen and Horvat, 1973) and the Netherlands (Bos et al., 1978a) in the 1970s. Verhoyen (1973) reported an increase in incidence in Belgium from 40% in 1971 to 64% in 1972. In New Zealand, nearly 100% of the plants were infected on one holding (Mohamed and Young, 1980). Yield reduction in leek may be considerable (29-54% in Germany, Graichen, 1978b, and up to 50% in two cultivars in Belgium (Matthieu and Verhoyen, 1981), and the shelf life was reduced (Bos et al., 1978a). Diseased plants produced less seed and germination was 5-15% lower (Graichen, 1978b).^p^pMost publications on garlic mosaic report 100% virus infection of garlic. Together with carlaviruses and mite-borne viruses, the aphid-borne garlic strains of onion yellow dwarf potyvirus (OYDV) and LYSV are now known to play a prominent role in the ensuing damage. When testing numerous samples of garlic, wild garlic and great-headed garlic of world-wide origin, Van Dijk (1993a) found 45% of them to contain LYSV-G and 73% to contain OYDV-G. The two viruses often occur together. Garlic crops often show poor growth and development, to which growers may have become accustomed and which they often accept as normal because of total infestation of the crop. ^p^pConsiderable yield losses have only become apparent when relatively virus-free clones became available through visual selection for plant health and meristem-tip culture. Yield losses, for example, of 27-35% have been reported in France when a visually selected virus-free clone of cv. Blanc de la Drome was compared with virus-infected clones (Quiot et al., 1972). A yield reduction of 50% was observed with inoculated plants of a selected virus-free clone (Thermidor) of the same cultivar, and of 25% in 'Germidour' obtained virus-free from 'Violet de Cadours' by meristem-tip culture (Messiaen et al., 1981). In Great Britain, the yield of bulbs of most of the garlic cultivars obtained through meristem-tip culture was substantially higher than that from comparable infected stock. Leaf length was significantly greater and the proportion of bigger cloves was higher (Walkey and Antill, 1989). However, the exact effect of LYSV and OYDV and the other Allium viruses, alone and in combination, will remain unknown until totally virus-free propagules of garlic and pure cultures of the respective viruses become available for controlled inoculation and yield assessment experiments.

management_info: Crops grown from seed (for example, leek) or from vegetative planting material obtained virus-free via meristem-tip culture (for example, garlic) should be grown in spatial and/or temporal isolation from infested crops of the same species. A few tens of meters from infected crops considerably reduces the incidence of infection, but success depends on aphid population densities which differ according to location, time of year and weather conditions, and non-persistently aphid-transmitted viruses may be carried over much longer distances. The removal of diseased plants may reduce secondary spread within the crop. Insect control with insecticides is ineffective against non-persistently aphid-transmitted viruses, and spraying with oil is too expensive and not permitted for crops grown for human consumption. A leek-free period over an entire leek-producing area would break the ecological infection cycle, but may be hard to enforce.^p^pAlthough there is no immunity in leek to LYSV, cultivars may differ considerably in vulnerability (Paludan, 1980; Van Rijbroek and Riepma, 1983; Graichen et al., 1988). Dark-blue leek cultivars suffer less, perhaps because the wax layer is thicker on their leaves which protects them from attack by aphids (Benoit and Ceustermans, 1990.). Kurrat (Allium ampeloprasum aegypticum), which is cross-fertile with leek, has been advocated as a source of resistance to LYSV in leek (Van der Meer, 1980).^p^pFor reasons unknown so far, crops of garlic with a very high virus incidence were found to contain reasonably healthy plants (Messiaen and Marrou, 1965), and through visual selection relatively virus-free clones could be obtained (Quiot et al., 1972). Since the early 1970s meristem-tip culture has been used with varying degrees of success to obtain virus-free explants of garlic. The percentage of virus-free plants regenerated from these was increased from 25 to 85% if the parent plants were given a heat treatment before the tips were excised for in vitro culture (Walkey et al., 1987). Intensive and repeated testing is needed to guarantee absence of viruses, but for a long time, methods and tools (antisera) for such testing were inadequate. Such methods have recently shown that for garlic the elimination efficiency may be 100% for LYSV-G but decreasingly less for OYDV-G, GCLV and OMbLV-G, respectively (Verbeek et al., 1995). As for seed potatoes, fruit trees and vegetatively propagated ornamentals, certification schemes are required for maintaining a nuclear stock of virus-free or virus-tested stock plants under virus-free conditions. This involves indexing at regular intervals to ensure continued freedom from infection, and larger-scale multiplication to commercial plant propagation material in the open but under strict hygiene through isolation from other Allium crops particularly garlic, intensive roguing of infected or suspected plants, and by inspection, testing and final official certification for quality including the relative absence of harmful viruses.

management_info: When detected, it is important to gather all infected host fruits and destroy them. Protein baited traps should be used to monitor population size and spread continuously. Insecticide protection is possible by using a cover spray (the bait sprays used against fruit flies in tree fruits are not generally used for cucurbit crops). Shaheen et al. (1973) found that sprays of pirimiphos-methyl or trichlorphon were effective against D. ciliatus on autumn plantings of Cucumis melo (snake cucumber and sweetmelon). Saddik and Rizkallah (1970) found that fenthion, parathion and  trichlorphon all increased yield. Kazi (1976) found that adult D. ciliatus moved to non-host 'rest plants' between 1700h and 0800h, and suggested that the flies might be better controlled there than on the larval host. ^p^pPhysical protection provides a more environmentally acceptable approach. In Senegal, where D. ciliatus and D. vertebrates cause heavy losses to cantaloupe melon production, it was found that growing under the protection of tunnels increased yield (Froissart et al., 1995; Vaissiere and Froissart, 1996).^p^pPhytosanitary measures^p^pConsignments of fruits from countries where these pests occur should be inspected for symptoms of infestation and suspect fruit should be cut open in order to look for larvae. EPPO recommends (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) that such fruits should come from an area where D. ciliatus does not occur and where routine intensive control measures are applied. Fruits may also be treated in transit by cold treatment (13 or 14 days at 0.0 or 0.6°C, respectively) or, for certain types of fruits, by vapour heat (keeping at 43-44°C for 6-9 h, according to commodity) (FAO, 1983), or hot water treatment. Ethylene dibromide was previously widely used as a fumigant but is now generally withdrawn because of its carcinogenicity; methyl bromide is less satisfactory, damaging many fruits and reducing their shelf life, although treatment schedules are available for specific cases (FAO, 1983; Armstrong and Couey, 1989). Treatment methods against fruit flies are currently under review within EPPO and as part of a common programme of the regional plant protection organizations. ^p^pPlants of host species transported with roots from countries where these pests occur should be free from soil, or the soil should be treated against puparia. The plants should not carry fruits. Importation of such plants may indeed be prohibited.

De Santis and de Crouzel (1994) describe biological control in Argentina with an unidentified Aphytis sp. (similar to A. lingnanensis) from Mexico. ^p^pAphytis lepidosaphes (Aphelinidae), an ectoparasitoid originating from California, USA, was released in the Nelspruit, Richmond, Pietermaritzburg, Eshowe and Eastern Cape areas of South Africa during 1967-1970, achieving excellent control of Lepidosathes beckii, although L. gloverii was also attacked by this parasitoid from the second to the pre-productive female stages and the male in the pupal stages (Villiers, 1998).^p^pAn experiment in which Chilocorus nigrita was released into orchards showed that the long mussel scale can be controlled using this technique in South Africa (Bruwer, 1998). In recent years, C. nigrita has become established in citrus orchards in South Africa where parathion spraying has been stopped, and it is now regarded as an effective predator of most armoured scale insects (Samways, 1984).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pL. gloverii is mostly kept under good biological control, provided that ants are controlled and that chemicals used for the control of other pests, especially citrus thrips, do not upset the delicate balance. For this reason, chemical control of L. gloverii is seldom practised. However, if necessary, oil-based control programmes are recommended.

potential_eco_desc: P. nigra is a minor pest of many agriculturally important plants. In the past, it has caused major concern on: coffee in Africa, India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, Central and South America; rubber trees in Sri Lanka, India, Malaysia, Indonesia and South America; croton-oil plants in Sri Lanka, India, Malaysia, Hawaii and South America; cotton in Africa, Sri Lanka, India, China, Taiwan, Japan, South Pacific islands, Hawaii and South America; sandal trees in India; cherimoya in Sri Lanka, Australia and the West Indies; guava in Taiwan, Australia, USA (Hawaii, California) and West Indies; mango in South Africa, Hawaii, California and Florida; and papaya in Australia (Queensland), USA (Florida) and West Indies. However, prolonged major outbreaks and serious damage have been avoided as a result of natural enemy activity (Smith, 1944). Waterhouse and Norris (1987) regarded P. nigra as a major crop pest in the Pacific region.

remark: P. nigra is widely distributed in the tropics and is becoming established under glass in temperate regions. Its geographical range in temperate areas may increase as a result of global warming. The scale could potentially cause problems on citrus.^p^pP. nigra (as Saissetia nigra) is listed as a Series II/AI quarantine pest by the European Community. It is not likely to become a serious outdoor pest within the EPPO (European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization) region because of the limited distribution and minor importance of its hosts, and because of climatic constraints. In areas where it could establish outdoors, Saissetia oleae is usually present and is likely to provide a reservoir of appropriate natural enemies for its control. P. nigra could become a glasshouse pest in temperate regions.

management_info: Regulatory Control^p^pPlanting material of host-plant species of P. nigra should be inspected in the growing season prior to shipment and be found free of infestation. A phytosanitary certificate should guarantee absence of the pest from consignments of either planting material or produce.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe long oviposition period, intermittent feeding habits and waxy dorsal surface of P. nigra make it difficult to control with pesticides. Malathion has been used to control P. nigra on pomegranates in India (Jadav and Ajri, 1985), but use of insecticide is likely to kill any parasitoids and make biological control impossible. In addition, ornamental plants may be adversely affected by insecticides (Copland and Ibrahim, 1985).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pWhile the long oviposition period of P. nigra makes it difficult to control chemically, this feature makes it particularly suitable for biological control. In many of the countries where it was originally an introduced pest it is now successfully controlled by natural enemies originally introduced to control Saissetia oleae (Bartlett, 1978). However, ants attracted to the scales by honeydew may deter natural enemies from attacking them.^p^pThe biological control of P. nigra in California is discussed by Flanders (1959) and in glasshouses by Copland and Ibrahim (1985).

(1987).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pStudies in India showed that bagging of pomegranate fruits was effective as a physical measure for controlling the lycaenid Virachola isocrates [Deudorix isocrates], but could not be recommended as it resulted in increased infestation of the fruits by N. viridis (Shevale, 1994).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pIn Egypt, life table studies indicate that N. viridis should be controlled on lemon trees by means of insecticide application(s) during the first half of July, instead of the traditional control operations in spring, summer and autumn (Sharaf, 1996). Chemical control methods are also described by Sharaf and Meyerdirk (1987).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pStudies by Meyerdirk et al. (1988) showed that Anagyrus agraensis, which was released into the Jordan River Valley from Guam, greatly reduced infestations of N. viridis in areas where A. agraensis was abundant. Bartlett (1978) also discusses biological control of N. viridis. ^p^pNechols and Seibert (1985) found that survivorship of N. viridis in northern Guam was significantly higher on Leucaena leucocephala tended by the ant Technomyrmex albipes than when T. albipes was excluded. The presence of T. albipes decreased the percentage of N. viridis parasitized by the encyrtid Anagyrus agraensis and the mortality attributable to host killing by A. agraensis and predation by other arthropods.^p^pIn South Africa, this mealybug is considered to be well controlled by natural enemies. Outbreaks generally result from chemical disruption of such natural enemies (Hattingh et al. 1998).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pR. invadens does not seem to be of great economic importance in India. In fact, the species had not been recognized and was mistaken for R. spinosus, before it was accidentally introduced into Africa (Williams, 1986). Wherever this mealybug appeared in Africa it became a pest of prime importance on mango with yield losses estimated at 89% in Benin (Bokonon-Ganta et al., 2002), sometimes on citrus, and on many horticultural crops and shade trees (Agounke et al., 1988; Ivbijaro et al., 1992). Serious infestations resulted in almost complete loss of production whereas lighter attack led to significant reductions in ash content, crude fibre and sugar levels of ripe and unripe fruit (Tobih et al., 2002) and protein, fat and carbohydrate levels (Pitan et al., 2002).^p^pIn severely affected areas, mango production was reduced by 89-100%  and citrus production was also greatly reduced (Vogele et al., 1991; Agounke et al., 1988;Bokonon-Ganta et al., 1995, 2002).^p^p^Environmental impact^pLarge numbers of mealybugs would have been prey for indigenous predators and parasitoids and possibly some lizards and birds. Defoliation of large trees would have had some local impact in terms of increased UV irradiation and probably water erosion of soil immediately under these trees. These components were not studied in depth.^p^p^Social impact^pMarked effects on social activity include disruption of village life, often conducted under significant mango trees, animist beliefs as spiritually important trees were attacked, superstitious fears as one generalist predator has a pupal stage which is regarded as bringing bad luck, and the loss of medicinally valuable resources from plants (Vogele et al., 1991). Livelihoods were affected as roadside sales of fruits were reduced, childhood malnutrition was thought to have increased from reduced provision of fruits with high vitamin A and C content and increased fly numbers were believed to have been promoted by excess honeydew, causing nuisance to villagers and tourists (Vogele et al., 1991). Anecdotal information refers to householders destroying trees as a control measure and hotel and religious gardens being spoiled by infestations.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pNo problems have been reported. In theory the mealybug could cause problems for uncommon mango varieties, but biological control removed that possibility.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>environment; crop production; human health; animal / plant products; trade / international relations; tourism

management_info: Biological control by Gyranusoidea tebygi and Anagyrus mangicola has led to satisfactory control of the mango mealybug in Africa. No other interventions were needed, although it must be stressed that, particularly in urban environments, more than 1 year is needed before low host equilibria are established.^p^pThe establishment and spread of G. tebygi in Togo (six releases, Agricola et al., 1989) in Congo (where it appeared without deliberate releases, Matokot et al., 1992), and of the two parasitoids in much of West Africa (a total of 42 releases of G. tebygi and 22 releases of A. mangicola, Neuenschwander, 1989; Neuenschwander et al., 1994) are well documented. The impact, mostly of G. tebygi, was demonstrated by population dynamics studies (Agricola et al., 1989 in Togo; Matokot et al., 1992 in Congo; Boavida and Neuenschwander, 1995a in Benin, Pitan et al., 2000 in Nigeria) and by a parasitoid exclusion experiment by means of sleeves (Boavida et al., 1995b). Similarly, quantitative survey results covering all infested zones in Benin indicated a reduction of R. invadens following the introduction of G. tebygi, a corresponding reduction in sooty mould cover, and an increase in the number of new leaves (Bokonon-Ganta and Neuenschwander, 1995). R. invadens populations invariably crashed during the year following the first introduction or observation of G. tebygi. As the mealybug population was reduced, the number of host plants attacked was also diminished (Boussienguet and Mouloungou, 1993). A first attempt at economic impact analysis was made by Vogele et al. (1991). Subsequently, Bokonon-Ganta et al. (2002) estimated the benefit-cost ratio of the biocontrol project as 145:1 for Benin alone.^p^pIn addition to these field studies, both parasitoids were also studied in detail in the laboratory in order to understand their interactions with the host and with each other (Willink and Moore, 1988;Moore and Cross, 1992, 1993; Cross and Moore, 1992;Bokonon-Ganta et al., 1995, 1996; Boavida et al., 1995a). Though there is some niche overlap, the two parasitoids can coexist on the same host population. Initial fears, derived from an early simulation model (Godfray and Waage, 1991), that the addition of A. mangicola to the system could be harmful, were thereby allayed by these studies.

description:
香蕉枯萎病，又称巴拿马病、黄叶病。巴拿马病是香蕉枯萎病最早广泛使用的名称．这让很多人误以为该病最初发生于巴拿马。1906年苏里南暴发香蕉枯萎病，蕉同大片毁灭。而此前巴拿马已经发生过该病，苏里南人认为该病由巴拿马传入，因此，将其称为巴拿马病。而事实上，即便在1906年以前，发生香蕉枯萎病的也不仅限于巴拿马，中美洲一带的古巴、洪都拉斯等热带地区均有发生[3]。
    1874年2月，澳大利亚的．Joseph Bancroft在昆士兰州的布里斯班郊区的一个农场里发现呈现枯萎症状的香蕉，并对感病香蕉的叶片、维管束等部位的受害症状进行了较为详细的描述，并且发现该病当时仅为害Silk香蕉(AAB)却没有侵染旁边的Cavendish香蕉。这被认为是关于香蕉枯萎病的最早文字记录[4]。1904年，Higgins记录了美国夏威夷火奴鲁鲁附近发生的3种香蕉病害，其中就包括由镰刀菌(Fusarium sp．)引起的枯萎病。该文献对枯萎病的症状进行了简单描述，并明确了枯萎病的病原为镰刀菌[5]。1910年，Smith对古巴的香蕉病样进行了分离和病原菌的鉴定．将病原菌命名为古巴镰刀菌(Fusarium cubense E．F．Smith)，首次确定了病原菌的种名[6]。同年，苏里南的Essed发表了自己的鉴定结果，虽然在他的论文描述及插图中均涉及有大量镰刀形的孢子，但他将病原菌鉴定为黑粉菌(Ustilagineae)，并且在随后发表的两篇文章中并没有对此进行纠[7]。也正因如此，在这之后研究者们的论文中极少有人提及Essed的这3篇论文。至1913年，Ashby完整而详细地描述了发生在牙买加的香蕉枯萎病的症状和病原，再次确认病原菌为古巴镰刀菌。

description: 1890年在巴拿马和哥斯达黎加首次发现，1910年巴拿马因该病造成很大损失，1935~1939年南美香蕉枯萎病发生严重。现分布遍及亚洲、非洲、澳大利亚、南太平洋岛国及热带美洲的香蕉产区。  蕉苗、流水、土壤、农具、线虫等均可带病传播，有明显的发病中心。带病菌的吸芽、土壤及二级苗是远距离传播的主要方式。
management_info: ①加强检疫，特别是4号生理小种的传播。②选种抗病、耐病品种，推广种植无病组培苗。③重视栽培管理。高畦栽培，注意排水；多施用木薯渣、草菇渣、蔗渣、石灰等物质改善土壤环境；增施农家肥和合理地增施氮、磷、钾、钙、镁肥，施肥适当远离蕉头，防止伤根、断根；定期检查蕉园，发现零星病株应及时清除销毁，并撒施石灰或尿素处理土壤。重病区可考虑全园销毁，改种水稻、花生、甘蔗等经济作物，短期内有效控制香蕉枯萎病的蔓延。④化学防治。25%的咪鲜胺EC(浓度1mg/L)、45%恶霉灵?溴菌腈混剂(300~225mg/L)对初罹病香蕉苗防治效果较好，建议在病田重新栽种香蕉之前或夏初蕉苗旺长期用药为宜。发病初期还可用多菌灵、绿亨一号、甲基托布津、抗枯灵、恶霉灵、咪鲜胺、必速灭等农药对水淋施蕉身、蕉头及土壤，可在一定程度上防止病害的蔓延。发现病株可用10%草甘膦(或41%农达水剂)10ml加3g 50%多菌灵注射生长点，或于蕉茎基部和地上1m处注射以加速病株死亡，然后清除茎叶烧毁和挖去蕉头，2m范围内植穴用32.7%威百亩300倍液淋土，穴外用石灰水淋施杀菌消毒。同时施米乐尔防地下害虫。⑤生物防治。筛选高效的生物菌株。⑥隔离病区，发病30%以上的蕉园，毁灭病株。应改种水稻或水生作物，水淹两年后再种蕉。山地蕉园可与甘蔗、花生轮作。⑦病土与工具处理：病株除去后，病穴施石灰及多菌灵杀灭病菌，并以土覆盖。病穴周围两米范围的蕉株用50%多菌灵500倍液淋根；病区内实行独立排灌，严禁带菌水流入无病蕉园；病区耕作用过的工具必须浸入50%福尔马林药液消毒后，才能用于无病蕉园耕作。

description: 1960年前只在广西壮族自治区的南宁、扈宁、博白等地发生，主要为害西贡蕉。1975年以来在广东省中山、新会、广州和海南省亦有发生，主要为害粉蕉类甘蕉。
remark:
1.严格检疫 严格限制从国内外输入蕉类植物。经许可输入的蕉苗必须从无病地点选取，确无可疑症状，在隔离区种植观察2年，还应取样检查观察根茎内部，并进行组织分离培养，以确证输入的蕉种没有带病、带菌，才可逐步推广种植。
2.选用抗病品种 目前在广东、广西和海南只发现粉蕉和西贡蕉发病；香蕉、大蕉及其他蕉类还未发现感病。因此在病区可以种植香蕉和大蕉，暂停种植粉蕉和西贡蕉。
3.培养无病种苗 可以利用组织培养技术，繁殖无病种苗。
4.隔离病区，毁灭病株，处理病土 蕉园或蕉区发现病株后要实行隔离封锁措施。禁止蕉苗、土壤、农具移出至附近蕉园或蕉区，并以病株为中心向四周约10m或两个株距的边缘为界，把界内病株和健株连同土壤掘起就地晒干焚毁。可用草甘膦溶液注射于蕉茎及吸芽内，毒死病株并烧毁。界内土壤可撒施大量石灰，亦可每平米喷洒2%福尔马林液或多菌灵杀菌剂10L。病地进行甘蔗轮作1~2年。

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pFusarium wilt was responsible for the decimation of the export trades in Central and South America and the Caribbean that were based on the cultivar 'Gros Michel' (AAA genome) which is susceptible to race 1 of the fungus. It has been estimated that about 40,000 ha became unproductive over a period of 50 years (Stover, 1972). The industry was saved by changing to cultivars in the Cavendish subgroup (AAA genome), which were resistant to race 1. However, Cavendish cultivars in plantations in subtropical Australia, the Canary Islands, South Africa and Taiwan were subsequently affected by F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense 'subtropical race 4'. More recently, Cavendish cultivars planted on a large scale in South-East Asia are succumbing to F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense 'tropical race 4' (Ploetz and Pegg, 2000). At least one major plantation has been forced to abandon production.^p^pCultivars that are favoured by smallholders are also affected by Fusarium wilt. 'Silk' (AAB genome) is a very popular dessert banana in Brazil, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere, but it is extremely susceptible to the disease and is almost impossible to grow in some areas. Cultivars in the Pome (AAB genome) and Bluggoe (ABB genome) subgroups, and 'Pisang Awak' (ABB genome) are also attacked and losses are significant. Fusarium wilt is a major factor limiting the production of many cultivars.^p^pBecause conventional banana planting material can carry F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense and other pathogens, the local and international movement of banana suckers and corm pieces is viewed as undesirable. This has led to the development of alternative strategies, such as micropropagation techniques for producing clean planting material.^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe seriousness of Fusarium wilt in commercial plantations of 'Gros Michel' (AAA genome) in the Latin American/Caribbean region led to the abandonment of cultivation on vast tracts of land. To compensate, new land in the coastal tropics had to be cleared for cultivation. This cycle continued as the disease gradually spread throughout new plantings. Large areas of natural vegetation were eventually destroyed so that production could be maintained. However, the introduction of Cavendish cultivars, which are resistant to races of the pathogen present in the Latin America/Caribbean region, into commercial production in the 1960s meant that cultivation could be maintained almost indefinitely on the same land.^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pThe presence of Fusarium wilt in cultivated land has led to some small growers abandoning the cultivation of some susceptible cultivars. 'Silk' (AAB genome), which is a popular cultivar in many countries, is extremely susceptible to the disease. Because of high losses of plants, cultivation of 'Silk' has been reduced. It is possible that some plants that are difficult to grow because of Fusarium wilt may disappear from cultivation. However, a scarcity of supply can lead to higher prices for favoured fruit, which may compensate growers for losses due to disease and allow some vulnerable cultivars to survive in cultivation.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; crop production; trade / international relations
description: Evidence suggests that F. oxysporum f, sp. cubense co-evolved with banana in Southeast Asia (Pegg et al., 1993; Bentley et al., 1995). Therefore, the pathogen could have been carried to new areas in Asia in prehistoric times with the first waves of transported rhizome planting material. Such spread would have been inevitable because symptoms on planting material, even if apparent, may not have been associated by early farmers with the later decline and death of plants (Jones, 2002). It is likely that the disease was afflicting susceptible banana cultivars in many locations around the world by the time it was first described on the highly susceptible cultivar 'Silk' (AAB genome) in Australia in the 19th century (Bancroft, 1876). Therefore, details of the initial spread of the disease, which seems to have occurred before plant pathology became an exact science, are not known.^p^pIt was only after the commercial production of the cultivar 'Gros Michel' (AAA genome) started in the Latin American/Caribbean region late in the 19th century that the disease became important. Here it acquired the name Panama disease after the country where it first caused extensive damage. Although the pathogen was almost certainly disseminated with planting material of 'Gros Michel', it is highly likely that it alreadyexisted in many locations in small plantings of cultivars like 'Silk', which were introduced to the Americas in colonial times. Luckily for the industry, a commercially acceptable cultivar resistant to populations of F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense present in the Americas was found in the form of the 'Valery', which is a cultivar in the Cavendish subgroup (AAA genome) (Jones, 2002). 'Valery replaced 'Gros Michel' in the 1960s to be the main cultivar of the trades. Since 'Valery', other Cavendish cultivars, such as 'Robusta', 'Williamns' and 'Grand Nain', have also gained prominence.^p^pPerhaps the greatest threat to export banana production comes from Cavendish cultivar-attacking populations of the Fusarium wilt pathogen designated F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense 'tropical race 4'. Luckily, populations of this particular form of the pathogen have not spread outside the South-East Asian/Australasian region. If this pathogen were to establish and spread in the Latin American/Caribbean region then Cavendish cultivation would become uneconomical just as the production of 'Gros Michel' became uneconomical in the 1950s. However, this scenario of total destruction of export crops should not eventuate today. An outbreak of Fusarium wilt on a commercial plantation of Cavendish in the Latin American/Caribbean region would almost certainly be quarantined. In addition, the industry would by necessity replant exclusively with plants derived from tissue-cultured to avoid dissemination of the pathogen with traditional planting material. The practice of annual cropping, which is gaining popularity in Taiwan and the Philippines, would also be expected to reduce the effects of the disease (Jones, 2002).

remark: The pathogen is commonly spread locally, nationally and internationally in infected rhizomes or suckers and attached soil. Infected plant material may not exhibit symptoms. The fungus can also be spread in soil attached to farm machinery, implements and vehicles.^p^pAlthough Fusarium wilt is found in most banana-growing regions, it has not been confirmed as present in many South Pacific countries. Banana material should only be introduced to this region as tissue cultures which would be free of the disease.^p^pAt least one pathotype of F. oxysporum f.sp. cubense, which is capable of attacking Cavendish cultivars (AAA genome) in the tropics, exists in South-East Asia, but is not found in the Latin American/Caribbean region where most Cavendish bananas for export are produced. Plantains (AAB genome), which are an important food resource in Africa and the Americas, have succumbed to a 'subtropical race 4' isolate in Australia. Care must be taken to ensure that strains that are now of limited distribution, but which have the capability of causing severe damage in other parts of the world, are not inadvertently moved to other countries. Movement of Musa germplasm by tissue culture is seen as essential to prevent dissemination of the more potent pathotypes (Jones and Diekmann, 2000).
author: CPC2006

management_info: There is no satisfactory method to control Fusarium wilt. Chemical control, flood fallowing, crop rotation and the use of organic amendments have not been effective in managing the disease (Ploetz and Pegg, 1999).^p^pSeveral factors influence the development of Fusarium wilt. The banana cultivar is of primary importance; drainage, environmental conditions and soil type also influence host-pathogen interactions. Suppressive soils, in which microbial populations suppress the pathogen population, were first described in the 1930s in Central America. Such soils have also been recorded in the Canary Islands, Australia and South Africa.^p^pThe only effective means of control is by host resistance. Natural sources of resistance exist in wild species and cultivars and in synthetic diploids developed by breeding programmes. Major, conventional breeding programmes are located in Honduras - Fundacion Hondureno de Investigacion Agricola (FHIA), Brazil - Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuaria (EMBRAPA), Nigeria - International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Guadeloupe - Centre de Cooperation Internationale en Recherche Agronomique pour le Developpement (CIRAD) and Cameroon - Centre Regional Bananiers et Plantains (CRBP). These programmes have concentrated on using resistance in 'Pisang Jari Buaya' (AA genome), 'Pisang Lilin' (AA genome) and Musa acuminata subsp. burmannicoides (accession Calcutta 4). Although it has not been possible to breed a 'Cavendish' replacement for Cavendish cultivars by conventional techniques because of fertility constraints, useful hybrids can be bred to replace AAB dessert and ABB cooking banana types. Biotechnology, mutation breeding and somaclonal variation techniques are also being used to produce resistant genotypes. The Taiwan Banana Research Institute (TBRI) have developed clones of Pei-Chiao (AAA, Cavendish subgroup) by somaclonal variation which are much more resistant to Fusarium wilt than the parent plants. These are now being adopted by the local banana industry (Jones, 1999).^p^pQuarantine and exclusion procedures are effective in controlling the disease by restricting the movement of corms, suckers and soil that could be carrying F. oxysporum f.sp. cubense from infested to clean areas.^p^pThe use of micropropagated planting material should be encouraged (Jones and Diekmann, 1999), as this, if managed correctly, should be free from contamination by the pathogen. Plants derived from tissue culture and planted in soil where bananas have not been previously grown should remain free of Fusarium wilt for a considerable period.

potential_eco_desc: Although the virus has a wide geographical distribution in Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America, its effect on the growth and yield of infected plants has been little studied. ^p^pIt is reported to be of minor importance in cowpea crops in Papua New Guinea (Philemon, 1987), in mung beans and French beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) in Tanzania (Mink and Keswani, 1987), and in French beans and soyabeans in Brazil (Costa et al., 1983). By contrast, the virus can cause yield losses of 64-80% in groundnuts in Kenya Bock et al., 1976, 1977). It also causes conspicuous leaf chlorosis and stunting, but unstated yield losses, of infected groundnuts, soyabeans, bambara groundnuts (Vigna subterranea) and winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus) elsewhere, including the Cote d'Ivoire, India and Indonesia (Fauquet et al., 1979; Fortuner et al., 1979; Dubern and Dollet, 1981; Thouvenel et al., 1982; Fauquet and Thouvenel, 1987; Saleh et al., 1989; Reddy, 1991).

description: Incidence^p^pUsing ELISA detection methods, CPMMV could not be detected in seeds from 60 cowpea pre-introductions from Botswana, India and Kenya (Gillaspie et al., 1995), in 4144 seeds harvested from seven CPMMV-infected soyabean genotypes or in 214 seeds collected from CPMMV-infected groundnut plants (cv. Gajah) (Horn et al., 1991).^p^p^Seed Transmission^p^pReports of the seed transmissibility of CPMMV are contradictory. The original Ghanaian isolate, obtained from a seed-infected cowpea seedling, was subsequently shown to be seed-transmitted in cowpeas, soyabeans and French beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) (Brunt and Kenten, 1973). The virus was later reported to be seedborne to a level of 1-3% in cowpeas in India (Nain et al., 1994), to 0.9% in soyabeans in Thailand (Iwaki et al., 1982), to 0.05-1.66% in 25 soyabean cultivars in India (V Muniyappa, University of Agricultural Science, Hebbal, Bangalore, India, personal communication, 1990), to unreported levels in soyabeans in the Cote d'Ivoire (Fauquet and Thouvenel, 1987), to unstated levels in cowpeas in India (Mali et al., 1989), Burkina Faso and Swaziland (Hampton et al., 1992) and to 6-21% in bambara groundnuts (Vigna subterranea) in the Cote d'Ivoire (Fauquet and Thouvenel, 1987). A severe strain, although not a mild strain, of CPMMV was seedborne in groundnuts in India (Sivaprasad et al., 1990). Moreover, infection in mung beans and French beans in Tanzania is thought to have originated from nearby seedborne infection in imported mung bean germplasm from India (Mink and Keswani, 1987). In a study in Egypt, El-Hammady et al. (2004) claimed transmission rates from seeds to plants of 3.1% through seeds of the soyabean cultivar Clark and 6.3% through seeds of the cultivar Crawford.^p^pHowever, seed transmission of the virus has not been detected by stringent tests in the following cases: French beans and soyabeans in Brazil (Costa et al., 1983), groundnuts and soyabeans in India (Anon., 1982; Iizuka et al., 1984), cowpeas and soyabeans in Nigeria Rossel and Thottappilly, 1985, 1993; Anno-Nyako, 1987), soyabeans and groundnuts in Indonesia (Horn et al., 1991).^p^pSeed transmissibility of the virus is thus probably dependent on the interaction between virus strain, plant genotype, duration of infection and, possibly, environmental conditions.^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pELISA detection methods exist for CPMMV, but have not so far detected the pathogen in seeds (Horn et al., 1991; Gillaspie et al., 1995).

description:
烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci）首次被Iwaki et al. (1982)报道是CPMMV的自然传播媒介。通过这粉虱品种传播该病毒的实验室传播能力之后在以色列 (Cohen and Antignus, 1982)、巴西(Costa et al., 1983)、印度(Muniyappa and Reddy, 1983; Iizuka et al., 1984; Muniyappa and Veeresh, 1984; Mali et al., 1987; Bhargande et al., 1987)、尼日利亚(Rossel and Thottappilly, 1985; Anno-Nyako, 1986; Thottappilly and Rossel, 1992)、和印尼 (Saleh et al., 1989) 被证实。
该病毒开始被认为是以半持久的方式传播的(Iwaki et al., 1982; Anno-Nyako, 1986)。然而，现在有强有力的证据证明它是以非持久的方式传播的(Costa et al., 1983; Muniyappa and Reddy, 1983)。 Bemisia tabaci was first reported to be the natural vector of CPMMV by Iwaki et al. (1982). Laboratory transmissibility of the virus by this whitefly species has since been confirmed in Israel (Cohen and Antignus, 1982), Brazil (Costa et al., 1983), India (Muniyappa and Reddy, 1983; Iizuka et al., 1984; Muniyappa and Veeresh, 1984; Mali et al., 1987; Bhargande et al., 1987), Nigeria (Rossel and Thottappilly, 1985; Anno-Nyako, 1986; Thottappilly and Rossel, 1992), and Indonesia (Saleh et al., 1989).
The virus was originally considered to be transmitted in the semi-persistent manner (Iwaki et al., 1982; Anno-Nyako, 1986). However, there is now cogent evidence that it is transmitted in the non-persistent manner (Costa et al., 1983; Muniyappa and Reddy, 1983).

Gajah) (Horn et al., 1991). 虽然该病毒在非洲、亚洲、大洋洲和南美洲有广泛的地理分布范围，但是它对感染植物的生长和产量的影响很少被研究。
它被报道在巴布亚新几内亚的豇豆作物上(Philemon, 1987)、在坦桑尼亚的绿豆和法国菜豆(Phaseolus vulgaris)上(Mink and Keswani, 1987)、以及在巴西的法国菜豆和大豆上(Costa et al., 1983)只有不大的影响。相比较下，该病毒在肯尼亚的花生上引起64-80％的产量损失。它也能引起其他地方包括科特迪瓦、印度和印尼的感染花生、大豆、赤小豆(Vigna subterranea) 和四棱豆(Psophocarpus tetragonolobus)的显著的叶片褪绿和矮缩(Fauquet et al., 1979; Fortuner et al., 1979; Dubern and Dollet, 1981; Thouvenel et al., 1982; Fauquet and Thouvenel, 1987; Saleh et al., 1989; Reddy, 1991) 。 Although the virus has a wide geographical distribution in Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America, its effect on the growth and yield of infected plants has been little studied. 
It is reported to be of minor importance in cowpea crops in Papua New Guinea (Philemon, 1987), in mung beans and French beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) in Tanzania (Mink and Keswani, 1987), and in French beans and soyabeans in Brazil (Costa et al., 1983). By contrast, the virus can cause yield losses of 64-80% in groundnuts in Kenya (Bock et al., 1976, 1977). It also causes conspicuous leaf chlorosis and stunting, but unstated yield losses, of infected groundnuts, soyabeans, bambara groundnuts (Vigna subterranea) and winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus) elsewhere, including the Cote d’Ivoire, India and Indonesia  (Fauquet et al., 1979; Fortuner et al., 1979; Dubern and Dollet, 1981; Thouvenel et al., 1982; Fauquet and Thouvenel, 1987; Saleh et al., 1989; Reddy, 1991).

description: Mazus reptans N.E. Br (creeping mazus; Phrymaceae) is a perennial flowering groundcover plant. A plant of M. reptans‘Alba’ with mild mosaic symptoms was obtained from a Maryland nursery in 2010. Ligustrum necrotic ringspot virus (LNRV), Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) subgroup I and Alternanthera mosaic virus (AltMV) were detected from Mazus reptans ‘Alba’ plants by molecular diagnostics. management_info:
在荷兰，矿物油喷射已被用来维持高水平的病害控制(Asjes, 1984)。病毒传播的降低取决于矿物油的品质，乳剂中卡矿物油的浓度，油制剂品质，喷射的频率，天气条件和耕作方法。合成的拟除虫菊酯的运用被引人于20世纪80年代早期(Asjes, 1981)。在荷兰，目前被推荐的防止百合中LSV传播和其它口针传播的病毒的方法由矿物油加拟除虫菊酯杀虫剂的每周的喷射在五月，六月和七月，和在八月和九月每两周的喷射(Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 1994; Asjes et al., 1996)。 In the Netherlands, mineral oil sprays have been used to maintain a high level of disease control (Asjes, 1984). Reduction in virus spread depended on the brand of oil, concentration of oil in the emulsion, the formulation of the oil brand, frequency of spraying, weather conditions and the cultivation methods. The application of synthetic pyrethroid insecticides was introduced in the early 1980s (Asjes, 1981). The present recommended measures to prevent the spread of LSV and other stylet-borne viruses in lilies in the Netherlands consists of weekly sprays of mineral oil plus pyrethroid insecticide in May, June and July, and fortnightly sprays in August and September (Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 1994; Asjes et al., 1996).   确保高质量材料的生产，使百合解放于LSV和其它的病毒和维持病毒侵染的最低水平当大批的散装的和繁殖测试病毒的大量的栽培种，需要一系列的措施。
这些措施包含：
1.	来源于组织培养的中心树干的准备；
2.	通过快速的组织繁殖的测试病毒的树干的增加；
3.	在温室和/纱网房中在蚜虫不能透入的条件下基础树干的栽培；
4.	在离严重受病毒侵染的大量的百合较远下非常合格的树干的栽培；和
5.	防止病毒传播的矿物油和杀虫剂的田间常规喷射(Asjes, 1990; Cohen et al., 1996)。 A series of steps are needed to ensure the production of high quality material, to free lilies from LSV and other viruses and maintain the lowest level of virus infection while bulking up and propagating virus-tested lots of many cultivars. 
These steps comprise: 
1. preparation of nuclear stocks originating from tissue culture; 
2. increase of virus-tested stocks by rapid tissue propagation; 
3. culture of foundation stocks under aphid-proof conditions in a greenhouse and/or gauze house; 
4. culture of highly qualified stocks at a distance from severely virus-infected lots of lilies; and 
5. routine spraying of fields with mineral oil and insecticide to prevent virus(es) spread (Asjes, 1990; Cohen et al., 1996).

description: At the beginning of 2015, symptoms of yellowing and reduced growth were observed on autochthonous garlic cultivars in commercial fields in Zadar County (northern Dalmatia) and in an experimental field in Zagreb (planting material originating from eastern part of Croatia). The symptomatic samples were collected and analyzed. Plants were initially tested with ELISA for the presence of Onion yellow dwarf virus (OYDV), Leek yellow stripe virus (LYSV), and Garlic common latent virus (GCLV) using commercial kits, then we performed the molecular diagnostics, the results showed that OYDV, LYSV, and GCLV were present in garlic. Among these three viruses only OYDV has been previously known to occur in Croatia, that report concerned onion infections. To our knowledge, this is the first report of OYDV, LYSV, and GCLV on garlic in Croatia.  OYDV, LYSV, and GCLV are all transmitted by aphids in a nonpersistant manner.
reference_name: First Report of Onion yellow dwarf virus, Leek yellow stripe virus, and Garlic common latent virus on Garlic in Croatia
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 大蒜Allium sativum
description: In June 2011, garlic plants showing virus-like symptoms including mild mosaic and yellow streaks on leaves followed by growth reduction were observed in one bulb crop in the Ljutovo locality (North Ba?ka District) in Serbia. Affected plants occurred throughout the field and disease incidence was estimated at 30%. The symptomatic plants were collected and tested using commercial double-antibody sandwich (DAS)-ELISA diagnostic kits for the presence of several Allium viruses. GarCLV was detected serologically in garlic samples. For further confirmation of the virus identity by molecular detection, GarCLV was determined to be the causal agent. To our knowledge, this is the first report of GarCLV on garlic in Serbia. Although the distribution and economic impact of GarCLV on garlic crops in Serbia still needs to be investigated, the presence of this pathogen is of great importance regarding its demonstrated ability to compromise garlic production.
reference_name: First Report of Garlic common latent virus Infecting Garlic in Serbia

host_range: 蒜Allium sativum （cv. Blanko, Harna?, Jarus, and Mega）

host_range: P. aquilinum affect grasslands, forestry plantations, and some cultivated areas.
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pWhen mature and tough, fronds of P. aquilinum are poisonous to horses and cattle. The rhizomes are five times more toxic than the leaves, but are seldom eaten. Sheep have been poisoned experimentally, but natural poisoning is not common. The poison is cumulative over about 1 month for horses and 1-4 months for cattle before symptoms appear. Horses are usually poisoned by eating large amounts of contaminated hay, containing over 20% P. aquilinum, whereas cattle are poisoned by consuming an amount of green or dried leaves approximately equal to the animal's weight. In the UK, it is a weed of grasslands and forestry and is increasing in the uplands and is difficult to eradicate (Grime et al., 1988). It affects farmers in many parts of the world, with lost opportunity costs associated with the invasion of productive grazing land, veterinary costs associated with poisoning and tumours, ticks and associated disease problems and direct bracken control costs. In forestry plantations, control is often required during the establishment phase (Pakeman et al., 2003).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pIn terms of conservation, P. aquilinum often has little biodiversity interest and in Britain it has generally replaced habitats of greater importance (Pakeman et al., 2003).^p^p^Social impact^pThe plant is toxic to livestock and humans (Grime et al., 1988; Crane, 1990). The impact on human health is difficult to quantify, but Pakeman et al. (2003) consider that it could be locally important. There is unproven speculation that drinking water taken from catchments that are predominantly covered with P. aquilinum may contain carcinogens or other toxins that are harmful to human health.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pIn Europe there is some evidence that a decrease in species richness over time may be due to competitive exclusion by P. aquilinum (Lameire et al., 2000).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; crop production; livestock production; forestry production; rare / protected species
description: Little is known about the potential dispersal of the species but it is unlikely to have been intentionally moved by humans and if it has it would have been restricted to a few regions of the world. It is likely that some movement of the plant (rhizome) has happened via movement of soil. The only report of the species being exotic is from Jamaica and the Bahamas, and it would appear that it is only invasive in the former location (Kairo et al., 2003).
author: CPC2006

description: Spores are principally wind-dispersed. There is no known natural dispersal of spores. Soil containing live rhizomes either attached to agricultural machinery or disposed of in landfill sites are possible means of introduction to new areas though no instances have been documented. Intentional introduction is a most unlikely pathway in view of the limited uses and no positive traits of this species.
author: CPC2006

remark: P. aquilinum is cosmopolitan in its distribution and there appears to be only a limited risk of further introduction.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pThe plant is susceptible to damage by the trampling of fronds by large mammals, but this does little to control the plant. Frequent liming (to increase soil pH) and fertilizer applications used in upland grassland improvement also have the additional benefit of reducing infestations of P. aquilinum, as it is a plant of infertile acid soils. Reseeding with preferable forage grasses or herbaceous species also appears to reduce the cover of P. aquilinum, such as has been achieved with Festuca rubra and Vicia cassubica in Bulgaria (Petrov and Marrs, 2000).^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pDuc et al. (2000) have considered the mechanical control of P. aquilinum in the UK by cutting it once or twice a year, which reduced the total dry mass per unit area by approximately 60% after 5 years. Any mechanical treatment must be conducted over a number of years if it is to have any noticeable effect (Marrs et al., 2000). Also timing of the cuts is very important, for example the optimal time is in the autumn, before P. aquilinum has transferred its nutrient reserves from the above-ground parts back down to the rhizomes for the dormant winter period. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pControl by herbicide is generally difficult. Asulam has been the main chemical used in control programmes in the UK since the early 1970s, primarily because it is licensed for aerial spraying. Of other chemicals that have been tried, only glyphosate has been used in some situations where P. aquilinum is one of a number of weeds to be controlled. In recent years, aerial spraying using helicopters has been carried out on around 5000-8000 ha per year. However, only about 25% of sites sprayed with asulam show long-term suppression of bracken whilst the remaining sites normally revert back to complete P. aquilinum cover within 5-10 years. Therefore appropriate follow-up treatment is essential, such as knapsack or vehicle-based spot spraying of missed areas or regenerating fronds (Pakeman et al., 2003). In Bulgaria, glyphosate applied to a permanent meadow infested with P. aquilinum reduced the infestation but it rapidly recovered where no follow-up operations were carried out, and was more successful when carried out in combination with a follow-up weed wiping application of glyphosate (Petrov and Marrs, 2000). Metsulfuronmethyl and glyphosate-trimesium are recommended for use on P. esculentum in Tasmania (Anon., 2003).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pIn the UK, where P. aquilinum is a major weed of pasture in particular, studies on biological control were initiated in the 1970s. Lawson (1976) identified 40 arthropod species feeding on P. aquilinum, but noted their inability to prevent spread of infestations owing to the impact of native natural enemies of the arthropods. Lawton (1988) summarized the situation in the UK and discussed the requirements for successful biological control agents, emphasising the need for agents of the same subspecies of the weed, comparable climates, and for agents which would be free from attack ny native natural enemies. South Africa appeared to provide the best likelihood of finding such agents, and Lawson (1988) listed arthropods associated with P. aquilinum there, from hitherto unpublished observations. Two defoliating moths, Panotina angularis and Conservula cinisigna and an unidentified eriophyid mite were considered promising. The moths were imported into quarantine in the UK, screened and found to be host specific (Fowler et al., 1989). However, the programme was abandoned because of the costs of field testing and doubts over the wisdom of using biological control to manage a native weed (Cruttwell McFadyen, 1998). Comparative studies on the arthropod fauna of P. aquilinum on other continents; New Mexico, USA (Lawton, 1982) and Brazil (Martins et al., 1995) have also been made.^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pDuc et al. host_range: P. aculeata is generally a weed of rangelands, only rarely is it considered a problem weed in cultivated land.
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pEffects upon livestock grazing are considerable in Australia, though no specific economic data has been forthcoming. Not only does competition affect the production of forage grasses, but access to water sources is restricted by the presence of extensive stands, and the thorns may have negative effects on livestock through damage to hooves and infected sores.^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pInvasion of watercourse may have a negative impact upon the hydrology of a region.^p^p^p^Social impact^pThorns are considered an occasional hazard. ^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pReports are not available on invasion of protected areas, though considering the spread of this species, this must have surely occurred. There are no known instances of P. aculeata threatening another species survival, but rather the reverse, that the dense thickets formed may provide a welcome refuge for birds and small mammals from predators or hunters.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>environment; livestock production; animal / plant products
description: It may be assumed that P. aculeata can now be found in most tropical, sub-tropical and Mediterranean countries. The documentation of introductions and the establishment of naturalized populations of P. aculeata outside of the New World is incomplete. Introduction to Australia was in the mid to late 1800s (Woods, 1992). Extensive weedy populations are now established across the Northern Territories and Western Australia, and there are infestations in Queensland and northern New South Wales (Miller and Pickering, 1980; Wilson and Miller, 1987; Woods 1992). Promotion in Australia as an evergreen hedge (von Mueller, 1888) does not indicate the earliest intercontinental movement of the species. Specimens collected from former Persia and present day Senegal, India, Pakistan and the Mascarenes prior to 1850 are deposited in the Kew herbarium.^p^pThe use of P. aculeata throughout arid regions of the British Empire, and later the Commonwealth, as an ornamental, for soil fixation and as a hedging plant was documented by Troup and Joshi (1983) and by Streets (1962). P. aculeata has a widespread distribution in Africa, and is becoming naturalized in many areas. Dale (1953) recommended P. aculeata for forestry usage in Uganda, and Brenan (1967) noted cultivation of P. aculeata in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. Neither were aware of naturalization in East Africa, though more recently an extensive naturalized population has been discovered in the vicinity of Nakuru, Kenya. P. aculeata is cultivated for ornament, shade, wind-breaks and hedging and is sometimes naturalized in Somalia (Madany, 1991; Thulin, 1993). Palgrave (1977) noted cultivation of P. aculeata as an ornamental in South Africa, and naturalized populations also in Mozambique along the Limpopo River, between Nelspruit in the Transvaal and Maputo in Mozambique and in the vicinity of Bulawayo, Zimbabwe.^p^pP. aculeata is planted throughout West Africa (Hutchison and Dalziel, 1928) and is commonly planted in dry zone Nigerian towns and villages (Keay et al., 1964). It has been introduced to the Cape Verde Islands as a forestry species: specimens deposited at Kew were collected from Cape Verde as early as 1895; specimen notes from 1919 indicate the use of P. aculeata as a hedging plant. P. aculeata was not included in the first edition of the Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai (Post, 1896); in the second edition Post and Dinsmore (1932) noted widespread cultivation. Lock and Simpson (1991) indicate cultivation in Iran, Iraq, Oman and South Yemen. Le Houerou (1984) considered P. aculeata well adapted to the climate of the Mediterranean zone, indeed, naturalized individuals have been reported from Sicily (Orlando and Grisafi, 1977) and the species appears to be established as a weed in the environs of Athens. ^p^pThe distribution of P. aculeata in Asia, other than in India, is less extensive, and may represent more recent introductions. Lock and Heald (1994) note that P. aculeata is sometimes cultivated in Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.
author: CPC2006

description: Birds are known to spread seed, and although the pods are not particularly palatable, wild mammals and livestock must surely play a part. Oceanic dispersal may be possible, though this is not certain. Effective water dispersal of pods facilitates invasion of seasonally flooded land and of water courses.^p^pThe main reason for international spread was intentional introduction as a fodder tree, for hedging, or as an ornamental. However, awareness of its status as a weed now means further introductions are less likely. The attractive characteristics of P. aculeata (performance under difficult or harsh environmental conditions; coppicing ability, pollarding response and resistance to browsing; plentiful production of seed) are those which are also problematic weedy characteristics (Hughes, 1994).
author: CPC2006

remark: Since spontaneous populations are found wherever the species is introduced, the potential utility at any site must be weighed against the risk of infestation before P. aculeata is chosen for planting. In Australia, P. aculeata has been declared a P2 or a P3 weed under the Rural Lands Protection Act 1985 (DNR, 1998); P2 being that the plant must be destroyed, individual landholders are required to destroy all plants on the land concerned; and P3 being that the number and density of infestations must be significantly and progressively reduced, with individual landholders required to destroy all plants or take other action as approved by the local government in accordance with the act.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pWith a sufficient fuel load, fire can kill smaller seedlings, however adult plants will usually survive (DNR, 1998). Singh (1989) noted that waterlogging and browsing animals could negatively affect seedling survival. In Australia, improving pasture conditions is suggested to manage P. aculeata through competition (DNR, 1998).^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pSmall seedlings and juveniles can be hand pulled, taking care not to injure oneself on the thorns (Starr et al., 2003). Mechanical removal by bulldozing, pulling with a tractor or grubbing gives effective control, especially where subsequent seedling growth can be controlled (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992). In Australia (DNR, 1998), blade ploughing or ripping is found to be effective, though it can only be done in level areas away from watercourses. In addition, follow up work is crucial for total control as disturbance often leads to subsequent seed germination.^p^p^Chemical Control ^p^pGood control of mature trees is possible with herbicides, with basal bark or cut stump treatments usually giving better results than an overall spray (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992). Picloram + 2,4-D or triclopyr in diesel oil applied to the basal 75 cm of trunk, completely circling it and thoroughly drenching the bark was effective, as were cut stump treatments, swabbing the whole of the butt with picloram, 2,4-D or triclopyr as basal bark sprays immediately after cutting (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992). Alternatively, hexazinone can be applied to the soil surface close to the base of the stems and when washed into the soil by subsequent rains slowly kills the shrubs. The severed aerial growth should be burned when dry.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pIn Australia, three biological organisms have been introduced to try to reduce the invasion of Jerusalem thorn, two seed beetles (Penthobruchus germaini and Mimosestes ulkei) which attack the mature seeds, and one leaf bug (Rhinacloa callicrates) which feeds on the leaves and shoots (DNR, 1998). Although all three insects have established at release sites, Penthobruchus germaini is currently the most effective at establishing and attacking seeds of P. aculeata. The following information on biological control agents introduced to Australia for control of P. aculeata is from DNR (1998).^p^pPenthobruchus germaini is a small brown beetle from Argentina. It was first released in Australia in 1995 and has established more readily than Mimosestes ulkei. It has established and spread rapidly at all release sites in Australia. Up to 95% seed predation has been documented in some of the release sites. This species is documented as a very important tool in the management of P. aculeata in Australia. Female beetles lay up to 350 eggs of the surface of seed pods. Larvae tunnel into seeds soon after hatching. Each larvae spends its developmental period in the same seed which it enters after hatching. There it will eat all of the living contents of the seed preventing germination of that seed before exiting from the end of the seed and seed pod. Life cycle ranges from 5-12 weeks. This species is not reported from Hawaii (Nishida, 1994).^p^pMimosestes ulkei is a small 2-toned grey beetle from the USA, first released in Australia in 1993. It has established at several release sites in Australia, though not nearly as readily as Penthobruchus germaini. The life cycle and means of attack of this seed beetle is similar to that of P. germaini. Female beetles lay clusters of eggs in cracks and holes in seed pods. The larvae tunnels into seeds after hatching where it spends the rest of its developmental stage eating the living contents, preventing germination of that seed. Larvae pupate then exit through the side of the seed then out of the pod. Life cycle ranges from 5-12 weeks. ^p^pRhinacloa callicrates was introduced into Queensland, Australia; under evaluation (Julien, 1992). host_range: M. quinquenervia is generally an environmental weed though it is known to invade grasslands, cultivated land and natural forests.
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe integrated management control efforts of M. quinquenervia in Florida cost $25 million up to 1999, but it is estimated that failing to control the species would cost $161 million annually in lost revenues, etc. (Laroche, 1999).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pM. quinquenervia has become a threat to the stability of Florida's Everglades ecosystem (Flores, 2002). In areas where M. quinquenervia has spread it has displaced native plants and animals, altered the hydrology of wetlands and created fire hazards (Anon., 2002).^p^p^p^Social impact^pThe spread of M. quinquenervia in south Florida, USA could restrict the use of some of the parks and recreational areas (Mazzotti et al., 1998). In southern Florida, the pollen is suspected to cause serious allergic reactions and acute respiratory problems (Geary, 1988). ^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pUnmanaged weedy stands may have tree densities of 7000-20,000 stems/ha, thus crowding out native vegetation and wildlife habitats (Geiger, 1991; Loope et al., 1994). M quinquenervia forms dense forest stands displacing native species, for example in the Everglades were it has affected the graminoid marshes (Mazzotti et al., 1998). Austin (1978) reported that species diversity decreases by 60-80% in wet prairies and marshes where M. quinquenervia invades. In its native range, it has a positive benefit on biodiversity. Remnant M. quinquenervia forests near Brisbane, Australia are important habitats for the conservation of bird species (Grover and Slater, 1994).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; environment; human health; native fauna; native flora; tourism
description: The species has been planted in the tropical lowlands of India, Mexico, northern Nigeria, Philippines, Puerto Rico, southern Africa, West Indies, and in southern California, Florida, Hawaii and in the extreme south of Texas, USA (Streets, 1962; Ruskins, 1983; Turnbull, 1986; von Carlowitz, 1991; Geary, 1988). It is recorded that two million trees have been planted on State Forest Reserve alone in Hawaii. It was first cultivated in Hawaii in 1920 with seeds from Florida. The species is now naturalized in undisturbed mesic forest (altitude 30-890 m) (Binggeli, 1997). M. quinquenervia was first introduced to the Atlantic Coast in southern Florida in 1906, around Miami as an agricultural windbreak, soil stabiliser and as an ornamental. In 1936, seeds were scattered from an aeroplane to forest the Everglades (Westbrooks, 1998). The species escaped cultivation on seasonally wet sites and has since assumed weed status (Ruskins, 1983). According to Cost and Craver (1982) it then covered 186,000 ha or about 6% of the land in southern Florida. Since 2000, its range has increased and it now covers over 200,000 hectares (Anon, 2003). In the Bahamas, M. quinquenervia occurs in swamp forests, and around ponds and scrublands on the edges of pinelands and is an aggressive invasive in the wetlands. M. quinquenervia has recently been introduced to the Mekong Delta of Vietnam for species and provenance trials on seasonally inundated and potentially acid-sulphate sites, which are very difficult for tree establishment (Hoang Chuong et al., 1996). However, the performance of the species in these trials was unexpectedly poor, thought to be due to the use of provenances which were poorly adapted to the harsh conditions.
author: CPC2006

description: M. quinquenervia seeds are dispersed by wind and water (ISSG, 2003). Long-distance movement has been through international introductions throughout the tropics as an ornamental.
author: CPC2006

remark: This species has become invasive in Florida, USA, Puerto Rico and the Bahamas. Due to the severe consequences of its invasive behaviour, which carry economic, environmental, social and biodiversity impacts, exotic plantings in other locations should be monitored for early signs of invasiveness and introductions should be subject to thorough risk assessments which take into account local environmental conditions.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pIf used at appropriate times, fire and water level manipulation have been suggested to control the establishment of M. quinquenervia. Fire can be used at times when conditions are unfavourable for the seeds that are released, for example immediately after the onset of the summer rains so that the seedlings are exposed to extended flooding which many do not survive (Laroche, 1999). Weber (2003) also notes that in fire-tolerant communities, fires can be used during the dry season to control the seedlings.^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pHand pulling is an effective control for small seedlings (ISSG, 2003), whereas mechanical cutting is used for large trees, followed by application of herbicide to the stumps. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pCut stumps are treated with imazpyr and trees can also be girdled and treated with herbicide (Weber, 2003). Herbicides are used to prevent resprouting, but studies suggest that the use of herbicides can cause the tree to release a large amount of stored seeds ( Swearingen, 1997).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pSurveys in Australia for potential biological control agents of M. quinquenervia for possible release in Florida, USA have revealed several promising insect species (Center, 1992; Balciunas and Burrows, 1993;Balciunas et al., 1993a, b; Purcell and Balciunas, 1994) and two biological control agents have subsequently been released. The melaleuca leaf weevil, Oxyops vitiosa was first released in 1997 and has now become well established in Florida. The larvae of these beetles cause stunted growth and a reduction in foliage production. In 2002, around 100,000 sap-sucking psyllids, Boreioglycaspis melaleucae, were released in south Florida (Flores, 2002; Anon, 2003) and studies are underway to determine its establishment and impact. Several other studies have been carried out in Australia on potential control agents, including the tube-dwelling moth, Poliopaschia lithochlora, the gall-forming cecidomyiid midge, Lophodiplosis indentata and Lophyrotoma zonalis. Field studies have also begun on a stem-boring cermabycid beetle, a bud feeding haplonyx weevil, and the bud-feeding holocola moth. The leaf-blotching mirid, Eucerocoris suspectus, was eliminated as a control agent as it was found to damage guava (Anon, 2003). Fungi are also under investigation as potential biological control agents Rayachhetry et al., 1996a, b. The gall fly, Fergusonina turneri, and its obligate nematode Fergusobia quinquenervae, have been recommended for release in Florida, USA in March 2004 (Anon., 2004).^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pControl methods are complicated by the fact that if there is any death to any aerial parts of the tree there is a subsequent release of seeds and resprouting from the roots. Cronk and Fuller (1995) suggest controlling M. quinquenervia at the critical stages in its life cycle, for example by treating trees in seed with herbicide after a frost to reduce resprouting. In 1990, the Exotic Pest Plant Council and South Florida Water Management District jointly organized a task force to develop a comprehensive plan to manage M. quinquenervia in the Everglades region (Laroche, 1999), involving cultural, mechanical, chemical and biological control. The strategy of removing the mature seed-bearing tree then eliminating the trees towards the source of the infestation has been successful in reducing the acreage so far.
author: CPC2006

host_range: Allium sativum.
potential_eco_desc: Study shows the coinfection of the most important viruses from the genera Potyvirus and Carlavirus in Ecuadorian garlic.
description: The garlic leaves were sampled from symptomatic plants showing mild to severe chlorotic streaking and leaf curling in the fields of an experimental farm in Tumbaco (Pichincha Province), these samples corresponded to clove seeds collected during April 2011 from commercial cultivars; some from Pungalá (Chimborazo Province), Cebadas (Chimborazo Province), Pelileo (Tungurahua Province), and local markets in Quito (Pichincha Province). Based on molecular diagnostics showed the presence of Leek yellow stripe virus (LYSV), Shallot latent virus (SLV) and Onion yellow dwarf virus (OYDV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of LYSV, OYDV, and SLV in garlic from Ecuador.  Garlic (Allium sativum L.) is affected by several potyviruses and carlaviruses that induce chlorotic leaf striping, growth reduction, and lead to yield losses. The disease is spread by seed bulbils or cloves due to the vegetative propagation of the crop; this causes accumulation of viruses over generations.
reference_name: First Report of Leek yellow stripe virus, Shallot latent virus, and Onion yellow dwarf virus in Garlic From Ecuador
