potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pXylosandrus species are known pests of various forest and agricultural plants, and have the potential to transmit pathogenic fungi to their host plants. X. crassiusculus has been recorded killing saplings of forest trees shortly after transplanting. Browne (1968) notes 'devastating' attacks on newly formed plantations of Aucoumea klaineana and Khaya ivoriensis in Ghana. It has also been found in apparently healthy Cinchona trees in Java, Indonesia (Kalshoven, 1959). No known stress factors could be associated with primary attacks on peach orchards in South Carolina, USA (Kovach and Gorsuch, 1985). Atkinson et al. (2000) note large numbers of attacks in Florida, USA on Shumard oak saplings which showed no other symptoms of stress, disease or attack by other insects, and consider that the beetles caused the death of the trees. Atkinson et al. (2000) also noted isolated attacks on large Drake elm saplings. The attacks did not kill the tree directly, but large cankers developed at the site of the attacks, and these sometimes resulted in the death of the trees by girdling. The species can breed successfully in newly sawn timber (Browne, 1961).^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversitySamuelson (1981) notes that in Hawaii, X. crassiusculus has spread into native forest environments, where its hosts include the important endemic trees, Acacia koa and Metrosideros collina. Maeto et al. (1999) noted a large influx of the species from oil palm plantations, where it breeds in fallen palm leaf stalks, into lowland rain forest in Peninsular Malaysia.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>crop production; forestry production; rare / protected species; native flora; animal / plant collections
description: X. crassiusculus was probably introduced to the Afrotropical region from the Oriental region hundreds of years ago by early traders. It has become one of the commonest ambrosia beetles in the rain forest (Schedl, 1963) in both East and West Africa. In North America, it was first discovered near Charleston, South Carolina in 1974 (Anderson, 1974). From there it spread to North Carolina (Hunt, 1979), Louisiana and Florida (Chapin and Oliver, 1986; Deyrup and Atkinson, 1987), and to Mississippi and Texas (Atkinson et al., 1991). Most recently, it has been reported from Tennessee (Oliver and Mannion, 2001). The species is now well-established in south-eastern USA, and may be expected to spread further where climatic conditions are suitable. X.crassiusculus was intercepted in Canada in 1997, but has not established there (Krcmar-Nozic et al., 2000). It seems likely that climatic conditions are too harsh there for the species. In the Hawaiian islands, the species was first found on Hawaii in 1950, and became established on most of the windward islands during the 1950s (Samuelson, 1981). There is no information on when it was introduced to other Pacific Islands. In all cases, the introduction has been accidental.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural Dispersal^p^pAdult females fly readily, and flight is one of the main means of movement and dispersal to previously uninfected areas. Of more importance for long distance movement, however, is the transport of infested seedlings, saplings or cut branches. X. crassiusculus usually attacks stems of small diameter (not more than 5 cm diameter), but is sometimes found in larger timber, especially if fresh. Hence it may also be transported in crates or other packing material.^p^pVector Transmission^p^pThe female has a mycangium, a pouch used to carry spores of the ambrosia fungus on which both adult and larvae feed, opening between the pronotum and mesonotum, and extending below the pronotum (Beaver, 1989). The ambrosia fungus of X. crassiusculus is a species of Ambrosiella (Kinuura, 1995; Dute et al., 2002). Ambrosiella spp. are not pathogenic, although they do cause staining of the wood around the gallery systems. 'Contamination ' of the mycangia by the spores of pathogenic fungi is possible. Spores of pathogenic fungi can also be transported on the cuticle of the beetle, although their chance of survival there is much less than in the mycangial pouch. There is some evidence for the transmission of wilt fungi by X. crassiusculus (Davis and Dute, 1997). The species has been reported to vector the sap-stain fungus, Botryodiplodia theobromae, into shade trees (Grevillea robusta) in coffee plantations in India (Sreedharan et al., 1991).Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Adults; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Wood: Eggs, Larvae, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. Pods)^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx^p - Leaves^p - Roots^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain).

remark: Two other species of Xylosandrus, Xylosandrus compactus and Xylosandrus morigerus, with similar habits to X. crassiusculus, have become important pests of tree crops, ornamental and native trees in tropical and subtropical areas where they have been introduced. The risk of introduction for X. crassiusculus must be considered high, most probably in the twigs and small branches of imported plants, although, because it can also breed in fresh timber, other pathways are also possible. Once established, such species are difficult to eradicate, and are likely to spread with the movement of infested plants, as well as by normal dispersal of the adults. X. crassiusculus is listed as a quarantine pest in New Zealand, but apparently not elsewhere. This should be remedied.
author: CPC2006

management_info: When Xylosandrus species are detected in plant material, it is necessary to immediately destroy all of the infested material. When they are detected in traps, plant material in the vicinity of the trap should be inspected, with special attention directed towards imported woody products such as crating, dunnage and lumber milling scraps. If an active infestation is detected, chemical control using insecticides  is not generally effective since the adult beetles bore deep into the host material. The following insecticides were found to be effective against a species of Euwallacea, destructive to tea: fenvalerate, deltamethrin, quinalphos, cypermethrin and dichlorvos (Muraleedharan, 1995); these insecticides may also be effective against other ambrosia beetles. Bambara and Casey (2003) suggest the use of permethrin, but multiple treatments may be required during a season. They note that lindane and dursban are ineffective. They also suggest the use of some attacked trees as trap trees, which need to be removed and burned before the life cycle of the beetle (about 55 days in North Carolina, USA) is completed. The concealed habitats in which these species feed and reproduce, the difficulties and high costs of insecticide application, and environmental concerns, all limit the effectiveness of chemical control. The use of radiation to kill, sterilize or inhibit the emergence of beetles in cut timber (Yoshida et al., 1975), is unlikely to be practical.

remark: Cherry necrotic rusty mottle is listed as an A2 pest by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1978), but is not officially designated as a quarantine pest by any other regional plant protection organization. management_info: Measures to control the disease require the use of virus-free propagation stock, perhaps from a certification programme. Heat therapy (thermotherapy) has been successfully used to eliminate the virus from budwood material (Nyland, 1959). The virus was inactivated when buds of cv. Lambert cherry were soaked in water at 50°C for 10 or 13 minutes, or at 52°C for 5 minutes. Symptomless cultivars should be indexed before budwood is taken for propagation. It is suggested that all budwood used for propagation could be routinely subjected to heat therapy. This would be less time consuming and of much lower cost than indexing. Resistant cultivars should be planted instead of susceptible cultivars, where possible. Although no vectors of the disease have been identified, diseased trees should be removed as soon as they are discovered.

description: CNRMV通过嫁接和芽接传播，接种期范围从10个月到3年。有时候在第一个生长季节当中，一棵树只有些部分显示症状，但该病毒在第二个季节中散步于整棵树木当中。在八月接种的树木在接下来的春天产生症状，但在萌芽时期接种的树木通常在10天之内产生症状(Wadley, 1959; Wadley and Nyland, 1976)。机械传播还未被证实，虽然一份由Ramaswamy (1973)做出的报道显示，CNRMV通过使用结冰的液氮摩成粉末的组织的摩擦接种从Merton Bounty樱桃传播到黄瓜中去。 CNRMV is spread by grafting and budding, with incubation periods ranging from 10 months to 3 years. Mechanical transmission has not been confirmed although a report by Ramaswamy (1973) suggests that CNRMV was transmitted by rub-inoculation from Merton Bounty cherry to cucumber using liquid nitrogen frozen powdered tissue.

该病毒在一些商业的酸樱桃品种上引起重大的损失（例如蒙特默伦西樱桃)。受感染的果实是苦的和口味不好的，这导致作物的销售能力大大的降低。在观赏性的开花樱桃上，该病毒引起叶片的偏上生长、树皮爆裂和有时候顶枯(N閙eth, 1986; Smith et al., 1988)。
在潜伏侵染的水果品种上，如甜樱桃、桃或杏，生长和产量上的影响还没被确定(N閙eth, 1986)，但一般来说，该病毒只对树木的生长或产量有小量的影响或没有影响(Parker et al., 1976)。 The virus can cause significant losses in some commercial sour cherry cultivars (e.g., Montmorency). Infected fruits are bitter and off-flavour, leading to significant reductions in the marketability of the crop. In oriental flowering cherry, the virus causes epinasty of the foliage, bark splitting and sometimes dieback (N閙eth, 1986; Smith et al., 1988).
In latently infected fruit species such as sweet cherry, peach or apricot, the effect on growth and crop yield have not been established (N閙eth, 1986), but in general, there appears to be little or no impact on tree growth or yields (Parker et al., 1976).

description: In a survey of peach trees for viruses and viroids during May 2013, leaf samples from five different peach cultivars were collected in South Korea and were subjected to total RNA extraction using the method combining Fruit-mate for RNA Purification (Takara, Shiga, Japan) and the RNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Several contigs were identified from two peach cultivars, Baekcheonhwangdo (BC) and Janghowonhwangdo (JH), with yellow-colored fruits. A BLAST search and alignment of contigs on the APV reference genomes revealed that the BC cultivar was infected by only APV2 while the JH cultivar was infected by both APV1 and APV2. The results were confirmed by RT-PCR. The two cultivars showed very mild disease symptoms, including leaf spots and chlorosis, in some young leaves during 2014–15 and produced high-quality peach fruits. To our knowledge, this is the first report of APV1 and APV2 infecting peach trees in Korea.
reference_name: First Report of Asian prunus viruses in Peach Trees in Korea

However, as ASPV often occurs in mixed infections with other latent viruses it has been difficult to assess the change of the growth characteristics of the infected pome fruit cultivars and rootstocks Campbell, 1963, 1966, 1967; Posnette et al., 1963; Welsh and May, 1967; Campbell and Bould, 1970; Schmidt, 1972; Cropley and Posnette, 1973; Westwood and Cameron, 1974; Thomsen, 1975; Waterworth, 1976; Campbell and Sparks, 1977; Penrose et al., 1988). ^p^pIn addition to the rootstock decline of Virginia Crab after grafting with infected material, the cultivar Charden showed incompatibility on Malling rootstocks due to ASPV infection (Lemoine, 1977). description: To detect and identify viruses and viroids infecting Japanese apricot in Korea, leaf samples from two cultivars, Takada and Wallyoung (WY), grown in an orchard in September 2015, were harvested. host_range: In Tunisia, GRSPaV is common in table grape cultivars, this is the first report of GRSPaV in wild grapevines.
description: In Tunisia, GRSPaV is common in table grape cultivars, but no data are currently available on the presence of viruses in Tunisian wild grapevines(Vitis vinifera spp. sylvestris). To address this knowledge gap, a survey was carried out in the mountain forests of northern Tunisia. Samples of wild grapevines were labeled during the vegetative season, and dormant canes from 84 accessions (male and female plants) were collected during winter. RT-PCR test results showed that 51% (43/84) of the samples were infected by GRSPaV. To our knowledge, this is the first report of GRSPaV in wild grapevines in Tunisia.  Grapevine rupestris stem pitting-associated virus has been detected in the pollen of infected grapevines, but its spread through pollen is not confirmed, although it is transmitted by seed from infected mother plants to their progeny. Tunisian wild grapevines can play a role in the dissemination of viruses to the cultivated grapevines.
reference_name: First Report of Grapevine rupestris stem pitting-associated virus in Wild Grapevines (Vitis vinifera spp. sylvestris) in Tunisia

To our knowledge, this is the first report of GRSPaV infecting grapevine in Korea.

host_range: This is the first molecular evidence for the occurrence of BanMMV in banana in India.
description: During 2013 to 2015, we collected 347 banana leaf samples showing mild chlorotic streak symptoms from Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Goa, and the research fields of ICAR-National Research Centre for Banana, Tiruchirapalli, India, and disease incidence was estimated to be 0 to 33%. Based on molecular diagnostics showed the presence of Banana mild mosaic virus (BanMMV). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first molecular evidence for the occurrence of BanMMV in banana in India and the genetic variability appears to be high between the Indian isolates and others. This report is the primary step to initiate research on the impact of the virus in banana production and germplasm exchange.

potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pPVX has a wide natural host range, occurring in at least 62 plant species of 27 families (Edwardson and Christie, 1997). The virus is especially important worldwide in potato (Bode, 1968; Beemster and de Bokx, 1987) and in many countries in a few major solanaceous crops including peppers (Paulus et al., 1960; Steepy et al., 1967; Fribourg and Fernandez-Northcote, 1972; Makkouk and Gumpf, 1974), tobacco (Hansen, 1946; Bode, 1953; Bode and Klinkowski, 1968), and tomato (Vanterpool, 1926; Ainsworth, 1934). Although many of its natural hosts are weeds, PVX also occurs naturally in other crop species including winter cherry (Nicandra physalodes) and turnip (Brassica rapa) in India (Sangar et al., 1980; Samad et al., 1991), artichoke (Cynara scolymus) and grapevine (Vitis vinifera) in Italy (Chabbouh et al., 1990; Giunchedi, 1973), and red clover (Trifolium pratense) in Belarus (Ambrosov and Bltoskaya, 1978)^p^p^Potato^p^pEarlier reports of the effects of PVX on the growth and yield of infected potatoes are inconsistent, probably due to infection by virus strains of different virulence, the use of cultivars differing in tolerance and/or resistance, the occurrence of unsuspected virus mixtures, different environmental conditions (especially soil fertility and fertilizer treatments), date of harvest and the earlier lack of comparable virus-free plants necessary for critical comparative tests.^p^pAs most strains of PVX induce only inconspicuous or symptomless infections in many potato cultivars, mild strains were earlier thought to be of little economic importance (Bald, 1944; Clinch and McKay, 1947). For example, no statistically significant yield reductions were recorded in cvs Up-to-Date, Arran Banner, Majestic or President in Eire (Clinch and McKay, 1947: McKay and Loughnane, 1953), cvs Kennebec and Katahdin in Maine, USA (Murphy et al., 1966), and in cv. Sebago in Ontario (Rowberry and Johnston, 1975) and cv Netted Gem (syn. Russet Burbank) in British Columbia, Canada (Wright, 1970). By contrast, commonly-occurring isolates of the virus have been reported to reduce tuber yields of many potato cultivars by 2-23% (Emilsson and Gustafsson, 1956; Sung, 1967; Bode, 1968; Mellor and Stace-Smith, 1977; Beemster and de Bokx, 1987). Thus, tuber yield losses of 2-7% have been recorded in cvs Alpha and Up-to-Date, of 7-9% in cv Bintje in Denmark (Hansen, 1963), and of 5-20% in several cultivars in Australia (Norris, 1953). Yield reductions of 12% have been recorded in cv Up-to-Date in Australia (Bald, 1943) and cv Russet Burbank (from 40.6 to 35.7 t/ha) in British Columbia, Canada (Wright, 1977) and, in the USA, of 7.3% in cv Mohawk, 11.2% in cv Kennebec, 13.7% in cv Chippewa, 14.9% in cv Katahdin, 16% in cv Sebago, and 18.3% in cv Teton in Maine (Bonde and Merriman, 1951), 17.5% in cv Sebago (Lim et al., 1966), 21.9% in cv Red Pontiac (Hoyman, 1964), and 9-32 % depending on year (Davies and Allen, 1984) or 23% (from 353 to 272 cwt/acre) in cv Russet Burbank in Idaho (Ohms et al., 1977). It has been estimated that from 1931-1951 PVX caused an annual yield loss in the USA of 13% (110,000 bushels), a reduction two times greater than the combined effects of late blight and Rhizoctonia (Chester, 1955).^p^pMore virulent strains can reduce yields of intolerant cultivars by up to 50% (Broadbent et al., 1962; Romanova and Reifman, 1978; Beemster and de Bokx, 1987). In England, PVX caused an average annual yield loss of three cultivars over three years of 30% (from 2.25 to 0.72 lb/plant). management_info: Resistant Cultivars^p^pThe most effective method of protecting potato crops is the use of potato cultivars containing major genes for resistance; such cultivars have been grown for many years and resistance has been durable. The cultivar Prestile is reported to be immune to PVX (Reeves et al., 1994). ^p^pSome strain-specific genes, including those designated Nx and Nb, result in hypersensitivity when plants are exposed to infection (Cockerham, 1955). Two other genes, Rxadg and Rxacl, confer extreme resistance to all four groups of strains (Cockerham, 1970). The Nb and Rx2 genes are now known to be located on chromosome 5 (Jong et al., 1997). One strain (designated PVX/HB) is able to overcome all known genes for resistance, but is mostly restricted to South America (Moreira et al., 1980). Resistance to PVX-HB has been found in Solanum sucrense (Querci et al., 1995).^p^pWithin the last decade, virus resistant plants have been produced by genetic engineering techniques and an understanding of resistant mechanisms obtained (Angell and Baulcombe, 1997; English et al., 1997); although not yet used commercially, the resistance of such plants has proved durable and so has great future potential (Jongedijk et al., 1992). After infection, transgenic potato (cultivars Bintje and Escort) and tobacco plants expressing the virus coat protein gene develop symptoms much more slowly and significantly suppress virus replication (Hemenway et al., 1988; Hoekema et al., 1989). Such plants are resistant to both virus particles and viral RNA. Similarly, transgenic plants containing the viral replicase gene are also resistant to PVX (Braun and Hemenway, 1992; Davenport and Baulcombe, 1997).^p^pPVX-resistant potato and tomato cultivars have also been produced by conventional breeding techniques (Rashid et al., 1989), and sources of genetic resistance for peppers identified (Edwardson and Christie, 1997).^p^p^Cultural Practices^p^pThe most appropriate and effective method of control in potato crops is to use virus-free planting stock of virus-resistant and/or tolerant cultivars and, during cropping, to inspect crops and remove any plants shown to be or suspected of being infected. Well established methods (meristem tip culture combined with thermotherapy and/or chemotherapy) are available for the production of virus-free plants of cultivars that have become totally infected. Schemes for the use of such elite stocks, described fully by van der Zaag (1987) and Salazar (1996), are now in operation in many countries.

potential_eco_desc: Cassava common mosaic disease (CCMD) can cause root yield losses of approximately 30% in cassava.
description: Given the presence of Cassava common mosaic disease (CCMD) caused by Cassava common mosaic virus (CsCMV) in neighboring countries, a field survey for virus diseases in cassava was organized during June 2016 in the province of Huaral, in the central coast of Peru, where typical leaf mosaic and leaf deformation symptoms associated to CCMD were observed in local cassava varieties. The youngest leaves of cassava plants showing virus-like symptoms were collected, based on (DAS)-ELISA tests, inoculation identification, RT-PCR tests and sequences analysis confirmed that CsCMV was the causal agent of CCMD. This is the first report of CCMD and CsCMV infecting cassava in Peru.  CsCMV, a mechanically transmitted potexvirus that can be disseminated via infected stem cuttings used for cassava propagation.

author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: CsCMV has been previously reported in cassava (Manihot esculenta) in Venezuela. This is the first report of CsCMV in chaya in Venezuela.
description: During 2013-2014, chaya plants maintained in a group of nurseries located at San Diego de Los Altos (Miranda State, Venezuela) showing extensive mosaic and leaf deformation were noticed. Incidence of symptoms was approximately 30%.  The samples were collected and identified. Based on the analyses by TEM, RT-PCR, nucleotide, and amino acid sequence identities, we identify the virus as a Venezuelan chaya isolate of Cassava common mosaic virus (CsCMV). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of CsCMV in chaya in Venezuela.  The use of CsCMV-infected cuttings for the vegetative propagation of chaya could pose a significant threat to this crop industry in the country.
reference_name: New Record of Cassava common mosaic virus Infecting Chaya (Cnidoscolus chayamansaMcVaug) in Venezuela
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 木薯Manihot esculenta
description: Recent field surveys in Argentina have identified the presence of severe leaf mosaic symptoms in local cassava varieties while historical virus indexing records of cassava plantlets maintained in vitro at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) indicate the presence of Cassava common mosaic virus (CsCMV; genus Potexvirus) in Argentinian accessions collected in 1993. To confirm the current presence of CsCMV in Argentina, a total of 19 samples were collected in 2012 and 2014 from the fields in Corrientes (Corrientes), El Colorado (Formosa), and Puerto Rico (Misiones), and assayed for CsCMV and other viruses reported in the Americas. These plants showed virus-like symptoms including leaf mosaic and leaf deformation. Based Plate trapped antigen (PTA)-ELISA tests detected CsCMV in 16 out of the 19 samples. RT-PCR confirmed the presence of CsCMV in the originally collected cassava samples and detected a mixed infection with Cassava frogskin-associated virus (CsFSaV; tentative genus Oryzavirus) in one plant.
reference_name: First Report of Cassava common mosaic virusand Cassava frogskin-associated virus Infecting Cassava in Argentina
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: PAMV has been previously recorded affecting potato in the UK, but it is considered to be uncommon. This finding in Solanum jasminoides is believed to be the first record of a naturally occurring infection of PAMV outside of potato.
description: In March 2016, samples of Solanum jasminoides plants were submitted from a nursery in southeast England. The samples exhibiting slight leaf mottling were sent to the laboratory as part of plant health monitoring for latent viral diseases. Based on biological testing and sequences analysis showed Potato aucuba mosaic virus (PAMV) was presence in the samples. This is the first report of Potato aucuba mosaic virus in Solanum jasminoides in the United Kingdom.
reference_name: First report of Potato aucuba mosaic virus in Solanum jasminoides in the United Kingdom

potential_eco_desc: Strawberry mild yellow edge disease is one of the major diseases of strawberries in most parts of the world. However, because of the interaction of cultivars, viruses and virus strains, crop management and environment, it is difficult to assess the importance of the disease in terms of economic loss. Alone, it is not particularly damaging to most cultivars, but it seldom occurs alone. The complex of the disease with other pathogens, for example, strawberry mottle agent, Strawberry crinkle virus, Strawberry veinbanding virus (EPPO/CABI, 1996), or strawberry pallidosis agent, can cause severe loss of plant vigour, yield and fruit quality (Converse et al., 1987).
author: CPC2006

description: Under natural conditions, the virus(es) on strawberries are dispersed by the strawberry aphid Chaetosiphon fragaefolii. Movement also occurs with runners, or with propagated material from tissue culture. Seed transmission is not known.
author: CPC2006

remark: Neither of the virus(es) associated with strawberry mild yellow edge disease is considered to be a quarantine pest by any regional plant protection organization. Quarantine status cannot be justified in view of the extremely wide distribution of the disease. Normal virus-free certification, along the lines of the EPPO certification scheme, provides an appropriate means of control for strawberry material traded both nationally and internationally.^p^pPhytosanitary Measures^p^pTreated plant material should meet the conditions that EPPO recommends in its certification scheme for pathogen-free strawberries. Diseased plant material should be eradicated.

potential_eco_desc: 草莓轻型黄边病害是草莓主要病害的一种在世界的大部分中。然而，由于栽培种的相互作用，病毒和病毒株系，作物管理和环境，在经济损失条件中评价病害的重要性是很难的。独自地，对大多数栽培种造成不是很显著的损害，但它很少独自发生。该病害与其它病原体的联合，如草莓斑驳病原，草莓皱缩病毒，草莓镶脉病毒(EPPO/CABI, 1996)，或草莓pallidosis病原，能造成植株活力、产量和果实质量的严重损失(Converse et al., 1987)。 Strawberry mild yellow edge disease is one of the major diseases of strawberries in most parts of the world. However, because of the interaction of cultivars, viruses and virus strains, crop management and environment, it is difficult to assess the importance of the disease in terms of economic loss. Alone, it is not particularly damaging to most cultivars, but it seldom occurs alone. The complex of the disease with other pathogens, for example, strawberry mottle agent, Strawberry crinkle virus, Strawberry veinbanding virus (EPPO/CABI, 1996), or strawberry pallidosis agent, can cause severe loss of plant vigour, yield and fruit quality (Converse et al., 1987).
author: zhangjianjun

description:
直到1990年，在马铃薯X病毒被鉴定与草莓轻型黄边有关的时候该病害被认为是由一种黄症病毒引起的。这个学问被建立在它的病因草莓蚜虫草莓钉蚜（Chaetosiphon fragaefolii）的持续传播和它的症候学的基础上。作为病原的黄症病毒的根据被提供于球形微粒，局限于韧皮部细胞的，被发现于薄的部分(Yoshikawa et al., 1984)及也于部分纯化的病毒制剂(Martin and Converse, 1985)中的时候。球状病毒微粒的部分纯化制剂与甜菜西方黄化病毒的血清学关系由Spiegel et al. (1986)报道。
然而，被认为是黄征病毒起源的感染的草莓组织的dsRNA证明是马铃薯X病毒复制的核酸(Jelkmann et al., 1990)。该病毒后来被详细地描述且它的全部核苷序列已被获得（Jelkmann et al., 1990, 1992)。一种在活的有机体内有侵染性的全长的cDNA无性系的生产和使用已证实这个病毒这个病害的病原(Lamprecht and Jelkmann, 1997)。
虽然关于马铃薯X病毒蚜虫传播是不明确的，但SMYEV田间隔离种群能被草莓钉蚜（C. fragaefolii）以持续的方式传播。这不寻常特征的机制是不明确的。蚜虫媒介传播不总是成功的由于效率低的蚜虫的生物型或株系，或一些较不易传播的病毒株系的使用。草莓钉蚜的蛹、无翅的和有翅的都同样地传播该病毒。100%的传播随着2天的取食期的获得和8天的取食期的传播发生(Krczal, 1979)。蚜虫传播不从已被用具侵染性的的cDNA无性系接种的草莓获得，这样显示协助者病毒可能使田间隔离种群的媒介传播成为可能。 Until 1990, when a potexvirus was identified in association with strawberry mild yellow edge the disease was believed to be caused by a luteovirus. This knowledge was based on the persistent transmission of its agent(s) by the strawberry aphid Chaetosiphon fragaefolii and its symptomatology. Evidence for a luteovirus as the causal agent was given when spherical particles, limited to phloem cells, were found in thin sections (Yoshikawa et al., 1984) and also in partially purified virus preparations (Martin and Converse, 1985). A serological relationship of partially purified preparations of spherical virus particles with Beet western yellows virus was reported by Spiegel et al. (1986).
However, dsRNA from infected strawberry tissue that was thought to be of luteovirus origin proved to be replicative nucleic acid of the potexvirus (Jelkmann et al., 1990). This virus has since been described in detail and its full nucleotide sequence has been obtained （Jelkmann et al., 1990, 1992). Production and use of an in vivo infectious full-length cDNA clone has confirmed that this virus is the causal agent of the disease (Lamprecht and Jelkmann, 1997). 
Although aphid transmission is not known for potexviruses, SMYEV field isolates can be transmitted in a persistent manner by C. fragaefolii. The mechanism for this unusual characteristic is unclear. Aphid vector transmission is not always successful due to the use of inefficient biotypes or strains of aphids, or some less easily transmitted virus strains. Nymphs, apterae and alatae of C. fragaefolii all transmit the virus(es) equally well. Transmission of 100% occurred with an acquisition feeding period of 2 days and a transmission feeding period of 8 days (Krczal, 1979). Aphid transmission was not obtained from strawberries that had been inoculated with the infectious cDNA clone, thus suggesting that a helper virus may enable vector transmission of field isolates.
author: zhangjianjun

management_info: 抗病毒材料可以通过热疗法和分裂组织顶端培养的结合而获得。SMYEV的热疗法是相当成功地（多于90％的抗病毒植株被获得）当0.4和0.5 mm之间的分裂组织被移除和在植株已受38℃的影响至少6周后重生的时候。 Virus-free material can be obtained by a combination of thermotherapy and meristem tip culture. Thermotherapy for SMYEV is quite successful (greater than 90% virus-free plants obtained) when meristems between 0.4 and 0.5 mm are removed and regenerated after plants have been subjected to 38℃ for at least 6 weeks.

host_range: PepMV infected a relatively broad host range of plants in the Solanaceae, particularly tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and causes significant losses.
description: In 2014 five tomato fruits grown near the towns of El Jadida and Skhirat were sampled from markets in Rabat, three of which displayed symptoms typical of PepMV infection and two had non-typical symptoms. Extracts from all five tomatoes tested positive for PepMV infection following DAS-ELISA using monoclonal antibodies raised against a PepMV isolate. The presence of PepMV in samples from both surveys was confirmed by RT-PCR amplification. To our knowledge this is the first report of PepMV incidence in Moroccan tomatoes.  PepMV has become an endemic disease in many countries and is possibly seed transmitted, efforts should focus on phytosanitary control for both import and export of both tomato fruit and seeds.

potential_eco_desc: Infection of tomato crops with PepMV does not necessarily result in significant economic damage since fruit symptoms may be absent. However, experimental data (unpublished) suggest that yield may be affected and fruit setting may be delayed.
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pPepMV was detected by serology in tomato seeds (Salomone and Roggero, 2002).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pSeed^p^pPepMV was detected by serology in tomato seeds but it was not seed transmissible to 50 seedlings (Salomone and Roggero, 2002).^p^pOther sources^p^pPepMV is a very contagious pathogen, easily spread mechanically via contaminated tools, shoes, clothing, hands and plant-to-plant contact (Pospieszny and Borodynko, 2002).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pSeeds lots can be tested for the presence of the virus either by ELISA (Salomone and Roggero, 2002) or by PCR using Potex group-specific or PepMV primers sets.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural dispersal (non-biotic)^p^pLeaves and fruits of infected plants can contain high concentrations of virus. Spread of the virus is by mechanical contact. Roots of infected tomato plants also show significant concentrations of virus. Upon damage or death of these roots, virus particles are likely to be released in the soil or drainage water.^p^pVector transmission^p^pIn glasshouse experiments, the virus was shown to be transmitted by contact through bumblebees (Bombus terrestris). It is not transmitted by aphids.^p^pSeedborne spread^p^pThe virus can be present on the outside of seeds collected from infected fruits. Seed lots should therefore be disinfected. There are no indications that the virus is transmitted inside the seed.^p^pAgricultural practices^p^pThe virus is easily mechanically transmissible and symptoms can be weak under certain conditions. When not recognized in time the virus is likely to spread rapidly through tomato crops by normal cultural practices through hands, tools, clothing and machinery. The use of skimmed milk to disinfect hands and tools is recommended. Experimental evidence (unpublished) suggests that PepMV is less stable then PVX. Standard disinfection and hygiene protocols that apply for PVX are also expected to be sufficient for PepMV.^p^pMovement in trade^p^pFruits may contain high virus concentrations. Crates and packaging materials are likely to get contaminated following fruit damage. Reusable crate material should be thoroughly cleaned and disinfected.^p^pPlanting material originating from nurseries should be tested before transfer to production facilities.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Fruits (inc. Pods): borne internally; invisible.^p - Leaves: borne internally; invisible.^p - Roots: borne internally; invisible.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; invisible.^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain): borne externally; invisible.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Containers And Packing^p - Soil, Gravel, Water, Etc.: Drainage Water. (Stijger et al. 2000)
author: CPC2006

remark: PepMV is easily mechanically transmissible. Since symptoms are not always readily recognized, there is a danger that the virus can spread rapidly and unnoticed. Host plant studies show that other Solanaceous crop plants like aubergine and potato can be infected.

management_info: The virus should be controlled by the use of virus-free seed and planting material and strict hygienic measures.

potential_eco_desc: PapMV infection initiated at the seedling stage on pawpaw (Carica papaya) results in a slightly stunted plant with leaf mottle, still able to produce fruit with no significant reduction on size or yield. Other species of the Caricaceae family are also subject to infection by PapMV which, in some, is lethal.^p^pMixed infections of viruses in pawpaw induce disease symptoms that can be more serious than those associated with a single infection. Severe leaf mottle and malformation, shortened petioles and rapid decline may occur. PapMV alone causes symptoms of minor concern, as do milder strains of Papaya ringspot virus, but a combination of the two viruses can result in lethal decline (Conover, 1964; Cook and Zettler, 1970).
author: CPC2006

description: PapMV is a very stable virus and is easily transmitted.  Humans provide the main means for spread, primarily through contamination by infective plant sap on hands, cutting tools, pots and benches. Living plant debris remaining in soil may also serve as a source of infection for newly transplanted seedlings.^p^pSeveral hosts of potexviruses serologically-related to PapMV are propagated by rooted cuttings, sprouted tubers, divisions, suckers, or grafted rootstocks. They are grown for either edible fruit or as ornamentals. Such hosts include Boussingaultia spp., Carica x pentagona, Olea europaea, Salvia buchananii and Ullucus tuberosus (Bailey and Bailey, 1976).^p^pThere are no known insect vectors of PapMV and no reports of its seed transmission (Purcifull and Hiebert, 1971).Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: borne internally; invisible.^p - Fruits (inc. Pods): borne internally; invisible.^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx: borne internally; invisible.^p - Leaves: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: borne internally; invisible.^p - Roots: borne internally; invisible.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; invisible.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain)^p - Wood.
author: CPC2006

remark: PapMV has not been given quarantine status. The disease associated with infection is mild, with no significant crop losses being reported. However, PapMV can exacerbate the effect of other viruses in mixed infections.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control measures include: planting virus-free seedlings; transplanting virus-free seedlings into new field soil or rotating with non-host crops; inactivating the virus on contaminated tools and pots by first removing excess dirt and plant debris, and then, either heating for 1 hour in an oven at 150°C, or soaking for a few minutes in 0.525% sodium hypochlorite solution (rinse with water to remove excess sodium hypochlorite). ^p^pWhen working with plants it is very important to keep hands clean and wear plastic gloves that can be dipped in 0.525% sodium hypochlorite which is then rinsed in water. Symptomatic plants should be rogued and burnt if possible.
author: CPC2006

description: In 2013 and 2015, three white clover leaf samples were collected near two crop fields (soybean [Glycine max] and peach [Prunus persica]) in two regions (one in Suwon, two in Cheongdo) in Gyeonggi-do and Gyeongsangbuk-do provinces. Three samples exhibited yellowing mosaic and mottle. Based on molecular diagnostics  and inoculation identification confirming White clover mosaic virus(WClMV) was presence in the samples. This is the first report of WClMV infection of white clover in Korea.
remark: White clover mosaic virus has been designated as a quarantine virus in Korea. In view of to widespread distribution suggest that WClMV should be removed from quarantine virus list in Korea.

host_range: This is the first report of infection of garlic mustard with TuMV and WClMV.
description: In spring 2015, 12 weedy garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata) plants with mosaic symptoms were found in a garden in State College, PA. The same symptoms are seen on many weedy garlic mustards in the area each spring, as they were in previous years at this location. Incidence was ～10% in the garden, with 2 of ～20 groups of 4 to 6 plants infected. The samples were collected and identified, results revealed that White clover mosaic virus (WClMV) and Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) mixed infection on garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata). To our knowledge, WClMV and TuMV have not been previously reported in garlic mustard plants in Pennsylvania. Other potyviruses including TuMV have been reported in garlic mustard and Brassicaceae while WClMV to our knowledge was never reported in Brassicaceae or in garlic mustard before. This is the first report of infection of garlic mustard with TuMV and WClMV, which have the potential to reduce the fitness of this plant species that is considered invasive in North America.  The mode of transmission of WClMV is not known and reports of its transmission by contact or by dodder (Cuscuta spp.) (probably under experimental conditions) have been controversial; therefore, it is hard to speculate if this virus can move from crops to natural environment and vice versa.
reference_name: First Report of White clover mosaic virus and Turnip mosaic virus Mixed Infection on Garlic Mustard in Pennsylvania

host_range: PlAMV can infect natural hosts including Plantago asiatica (Russian Far East, Korea), Nandina domestica (USA), Rehmannia glutinosa (Korea) and Lilium and Primula spp. (Japan), as well as a number of wild plant hosts.
potential_eco_desc: PlAMV is not regulated in the UK however necrotic streaking on the leaves makes infected lilies unsaleable. Losses of up to 80% have been reported in commercial cut-flower lily production in The Netherlands.
description: In April 2018, a sample of Oriental hybrid lily (Lilium spp.) with distinctive symptoms was submitted to Fera Science Ltd. for diagnosis from a nursery in southern England by the Plant Health and Seed Inspectorate (PHSI). From the rusty-coloured, necrotic streaking on the leaves it was initially suspected that Plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV, genus Potexvirus) was the causal agent. The result was confirmed using sequences analysis. PlAMV has been reported in several countries in Europe, the Americas, Korea, China and Japan. The infected plants identified in 2018 were grown in the UK from bulbs originating in The Netherlands, where PlAMV has previously been reported. A lily sample was diagnosed by Fera as being infected with PlAMV in 2012. These bulbs were grown in Spain and intercepted in the UK by PHSI, and the virus was not thought to have established. The lily samples in 2012 and 2018 were both from plants or propagation material originating in another country however the 2018 outbreak is the first report of PlAMV being detected from lilies actually grown on-site in the UK.  This potexvirus can be transmitted both in contaminated soil and during the bulb washing processes via contaminated water.
reference_name: Plantago asiatica mosaic virus detected in Lilium in the UK
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: PlAMV was isolated from Plantago asiatica in the Russian Far East. It has been detected in lilies in Japan, Netherlands, Hungary and southern Italy. This is the first report of PlAMV in lily hybrids in China.
description: In the winter of 2015, severe leaf necrotic streaking was observed on plants of an Asiatic hybrid lily (Asiatic ‘Tiny Padhye’) in the greenhouse of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Beijing, China). Total RNA was extracted from symptomatic plant, the presence of Plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV) was confirmed by RT-PCR. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PlAMV in lily hybrids in China.
reference_name: First Report of Plantago asiatica mosaic virus in Lily Hybrids in China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of PlAMV on Lilium plants worldwide, and the first report of the disease called necrotic streaking of lily caused by PlAMV in Chile affecting Asiatic cultivars.
description: Plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV) was first detected in Chile by the Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero de Chile (SAG) associated with symptomless Lilium plants in 2013. In Quillota, Chile, a survey was done during spring of 2015 on greenhouse Asiatic hybrid lilies being grown for cut flowers. Symptomatic plants of cvs. Amsterdam, Indian Summerset, Litouwen, and Serengeti were found. The samples were collected from symptomatic plants. PlAMV was identified using molecular methods, and pathogenicity test was performed. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PlAMV on Lilium plants worldwide, and the first report of the disease called necrotic streaking of lily caused by PlAMV in Chile affecting Asiatic cultivars.
reference_name: First Report of Necrotic Streaking of Asiatic Lilies Caused by Plantago asiatica mosaic virus in Chile
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: Lilium spp.
description: In the winter of 2013 and 2014, severe necrotic streaking in midstem leaves were observed on plants of lily hybrids (Lilium sp., family Liliaceae) in several greenhouses of the Campania region (southern Italy). Based on ELISA and molecular characteristics the pathogen was identified as Plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV). This is the first report of PlAMV in Lilium spp. in Italy.

potential_eco_desc: In the case of Lilium sp. ‘Rialto’ variety, the virus incidence was more than 50%, and 30% infection was determined on ‘Conca d’Or’ variety by visual inspection of 10,000 plants.
description: During the winter of 2013, a 2-ha greenhouse complex at the largest lily flower producer in Dabas City, Hungary, was surveyed. Extensive areas of necrosis were observed along the veins of Lilium sp. leaves. The samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was Plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV). management_info: Introduction^p^pControl of CymMV is primarily preventive. A strict sanitation programme is necessary to prevent wound transmission of the virus from infected plants to healthy plants. Cutting tools should be sterilized between each use. Pots and benches previously containing diseased plants should be disinfected.^p^pHeat is the safest and most effective method of sterilizing tools. Re-usable razor blades or knives can be heated in an oven at 150°C for 1 hour. Knife blades can be dipped into alcohol and flamed for several seconds (Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Anamthawat and Vajrabhaya, 1979).^p^pFreshly prepared 1-2% sodium hydroxide can inactivate CymMV effectively. Skimmed milk is also effective (Hu et al., 1994).^p^pInfected plants should be burned and not placed in a compost heap.^p^pDiseased plants should be removed from greenhouses containing healthy plants (Wisler et al., 1987b). Care must be taken to ensure that run-off water from infected plants does not contact healthy plants.^p^pVirazole (Ribovirin) has broad spectrum antiviral activity and can suppress the multiplication of plant viruses and can inhibit the replication of CymMV (Albouy et al., 1988; Loi et al., 1991); it is a useful additive to culture media used for the meristem tip culture in attempts to obtain virus-free plants (Kuehnle, 1996; Porter and Kuehnle, 1997; Yap et al., 1999).^p^pThin section cultures of infected plantlets and protocorm-like bodies with or without Ribavirin treatment will generate CymMV-free orchids (Lim et al., 1993a).^p^pMeristems of CymMV-infected protocorms treated with antiserum can also produce virus-free plants (Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Ishii, 1974; Inouye, 1983).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pVirus-free plants can be selected using naturally resistant plants (Kobayashi and Kamemoto, 1989).

potential_eco_desc: 危害兰花，失去商品价值。

CymMV是在栽培兰花中发现的最具优势的两个病毒中的一个。在栽培兰花中的CymMV被推测可随栽培时间长度的增加而增加。它能通过在剪切工具、设备和栽入花盆媒介上的感染汁液而机械地传播，该病毒也具有热稳定性，并能栽感染果园中系统地存活。受CymMV侵染的兰花表现较少活力、大小较小的花和较短的花序。商业兰花产品的品质和数量都会由于CymMV侵染而严重的降低，于是它的经济重要性是重大的。 CymMV is one of the two viruses most prevalently found in cultivated orchids. It is speculated that CymMV in cultivated orchids may increase with increasing length of cultivation period. Being mechanically transmitted via infected sap on cutting tools, equipment and potting media, the virus is also heat stable and is able to survive in infected orchids systemically. CymMV infected orchids may show less vigour, smaller size flowers and shorter inflorescences. Both the quality and quantity of commercial orchid production can be greatly reduced due to CymMV infection and hence the economic impact is significant (Tan et al., 1999).
author: zhangjianjun

management_info:
无病毒植物能从自然抗性植物中筛选出(Kobayashi and Kamemoto, 1989)。 Virus-free plants can be selected using naturally resistant plants (Kobayashi and Kamemoto, 1989). CymMV的防治主要是预防性的。需要一个严格的卫生程序来防止病毒从感染植物到健康植物的伤口传播。剪切工具栽每次使用间应进行消毒。先前含有生病植株的花盆和苗床应该消毒。
加热是最安全和最有效的消毒工具的方法。可重复使用的剃刀刀片或小刀可通过在一个烤箱内在150℃下加热一个小时来消毒。小刀刀片可浸到酒精中并投到火焰中几秒来消毒(Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Anamthawat and Vajrabhaya, 1979)。
新鲜制备的1-2%的氢氧化钠能有效抑制CymMV。脱脂牛奶也是有效的(Hu et al., 1994)。
受感染的植物应烧毁，并不能堆放在混合肥料堆中。
生病植物应从含有健康植物的温室中移除(Wisler et al., 1987b)。必需谨慎确保从感染植物流走的水不接触健康植物。
病毒唑(Ribovirin)广谱的抗病毒活性，它能抑制植物病毒的复制，和抑制CvmMV的复制(Albouy et al., 1988; Loi et al., 1991) ；它是一个添加到用作获得无病毒植株的分生组织顶端培养的栽培媒介中有用的添加剂 (Kuehnle, 1996; Porter and Kuehnle, 1997; Yap et al., 1999) 。
含有病毒唑处理或不含病毒唑处理的感染苗和类似原始球茎体的薄片栽培能产生无CymMV的兰花(Lim et al., 1993a)。
用抗血清处理过的受CymMV侵染的的原始球茎的分生组织也能产生无病毒的植株(Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Ishii, 1974; Inouye, 1983)。 Control of CymMV is primarily preventive. A strict sanitation programme is necessary to prevent wound transmission of the virus from infected plants to healthy plants. Cutting tools should be sterilized between each use. Pots and benches previously containing diseased plants should be disinfected.
Heat is the safest and most effective method of sterilizing tools. Re-usable razor blades or knives can be heated in an oven at 150℃ for 1 hour. Knife blades can be dipped into alcohol and flamed for several seconds (Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Anamthawat and Vajrabhaya, 1979).
Freshly prepared 1-2% sodium hydroxide can inactivate CymMV effectively. Skimmed milk is also effective (Hu et al., 1994).
Infected plants should be burned and not placed in a compost heap.
Diseased plants should be removed from greenhouses containing healthy plants (Wisler et al., 1987b). Care must be taken to ensure that run-off water from infected plants does not contact healthy plants.
Virazole (Ribovirin) has broad spectrum antiviral activity and can suppress the multiplication of plant viruses and can inhibit the replication of CymMV (Albouy et al., 1988; Loi et al., 1991); it is a useful additive to culture media used for the meristem tip culture in attempts to obtain virus-free plants (Kuehnle, 1996; Porter and Kuehnle, 1997; Yap et al., 1999).
Thin section cultures of infected plantlets and protocorm-like bodies with or without Ribavirin treatment will generate CymMV-free orchids (Lim et al., 1993a).
Meristems of CymMV-infected protocorms treated with antiserum can also produce virus-free plants (Lawson and Hearon, 1973; Ishii, 1974; Inouye, 1983).
author: zhangjianjun

host_range: Allium ascalonicum.
description: During a survey on viruses infecting garlic in the Latium region (central Italy), shallot plants showing virus-like symptoms were noted in one of the farms surveyed. Samples of three local cultivars ('Bianco', 'Violetto romagnolo' and 'Allungato violetto della Romagna') were screened for the most common viruses affecting Allium species. Using DAS-ELISA, Onion yellow dwarf virus (OYDV) was found in all samples. The presence of allexiviruses was assessed by a modified one-step RT-PCR amplification procedure using degenerate oligonucleotide primers. All nucleotide sequences were assembled and BLAST searches identified the presence of Shallot virus X (ShVX). Allexiviruses cause asymptomatic infection on Allium spp. (Katis et al., 2012). The severe symptoms observed on shallot plants in this investigation were due to mixed infections with ShVX and OYDV, the latter being widely found in nearby onion and garlic crops. In Italy, allexiviruses have been reported in garlic (Dovas & Vovlas, 2003; Lanzoni et al., 2006) but this is the first report of ShVX on shallot in Italy and a wider distribution of allexiviruses is feared by farmers in the country.

management_info: Research indicates that eradication of the seed wasp is not possible. Insecticide application is not a means of permanent control. The wasp will always be present where alfalfa is grown and the key to management is to live with the presence of the pest but make changes to the management in order to reduce its impact on seed yield (De Barro, 2001b).^p^p^ Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pCultural practices are important in managing this pest. In the spring, the cultivation of the soil using a disc cultivator and irrigation kills infested seeds on the soil surface. Clipping-back established stands helps to delay bloom, provides a shorter pollination window and reduces the time that the green pods are available for egg laying. The elimination of volunteer alfalfa along roadsides and ditch banks is also important in minimizing seed chalcid populations (Peterson, 2003).^p^pSeed wasps develop populations where alfalfa is flowering and setting seed. Sanitation practices such as mowing, grazing and herbicide spraying significantly reduce the presence of the wasps in the seed crops by reducing the availability of the alfalfa outside the seed crop for population development. Australian alfalfa seed producers can individually and in co-operation with the adjacent landowners/seed producers, implement simple sanitation practices on a wide scale level to reduce seed wasp populations and damages to the seed crops.^p^pResearch has shown that by reducing the presence of flowering alfalfa around sheds, gardens, stock yards, fence lines, irrigation channels, check banks, stock raceways, along roadsides and in grazing pastures, the presence of the seed wasp in seed crops is reduced. The best results are obtained by maintaining those sanitation efforts from the time that the alfalfa first flowers through to when the seed crops have finished flowering. In practice this may require a combination of grazing, spraying and mowing two or three times in a single season.^p^pMany Australian seed producers stop the seed production of alfalfa in December so that the crops flower in January and February when the warm/hot weather is optimal for pollination. However, this management strategy permits maximum wasp damage. The producers need to assess their management concepts. By closing a crop 2-4 weeks earlier than usual (e.g. in November), harvesting at 100% ripeness is permitted as opposed to 80-90% ripeness, later in the season and prior to the autumn rainfall. Seed wasp damage is reduced by earlier crop closure due to lower wasp populations being present at the time of flowering and seed set. The net return from a seed crop that is closed in the traditional December period is often the same or less than the net return from a similar standard seed crop that is closed earlier. In December, the crop is not permitted to reach complete ripeness prior to desiccation, whereas the crop that is closed earlier reaches full ripeness and has less seed wasp damage.^p^pIn combination with alterations in crop closure timing, both sanitation and closing date operate synergistically to diminish seed wasp populations. With a sanitation and closing date management programme in operation, the population of seed wasp in the area will decline over a period of seasons. Seed producers need to assess the economics of management decisions that influence the susceptibility of seed crops to seed wasp damage in conjunction with net returns (De Barro, 2001b).^p^pThose methods can be applied anywhere according to the seasons and development of alfalfa.^p^pVarious border stands alongside alfalfa were investigated in southern Hungary in 1992-1994. description: In September 2013, yellowing symptoms were observed in a tomato greenhouse crop in Messini (Kalamata), which were similar to those caused by whitefly-transmitted viruses (family Closteroviridae), such as Tomato infectious chlorosis virus (TICV) and Tomato chlorosis virus (ToCV). Infected plants hosted high densities of the whitefly Trialeurodes vaporariorum. In order to achieve whitefly control, the predator Macrolophus caliginosus was used, while a large number of false yellowhead (Dittrichia viscosa, family Asteraceae) plants, which were the only weed species, were installed as banker plants in the greenhouse. Total RNA extraction from leaf samples of symptomatic tomato plants and asymptomatic false yellowhead plants, based on nested RT-PCR, both plants revealed TICV. In addition, TICV was successfully transmitted from false yellowhead to tomato plants through whitefly adults of T. vaporariorum by transmission experiments. This is the first report of a banker plant acting as a reservoir of TICV in nature. False yellowhead is a widespread weed species in the Mediterranean region, used as a banker plant for the attraction of beneficial insects; given that TICV is widespread in tomato crops in Greece, the use of D. viscosa as a banker plant should be avoided in areas where the virus prevails. Based on nested RT-PCR, TICV was present in false yellowhead which was the only weed species in tomato fields. Transmission experiments show that TICV in fake canaries can be transmitted to tomato plants through whitefly.

potential_eco_desc: Since the late 1970s, cucumbers and melons grown in 16,000 ha of polyethylene-covered glasshouses in south-east Spain have been seriously affected by yellowing diseases transmitted by whiteflies. The first epidemics were caused by Beet pseudoyellows virus (BPYV) transmitted by Trialeurodes vaporariorum. Since the early 1990s, in addition to BPYV, CYSDV has been associated with these diseases. Surveys undertaken in 1994/1997 have shown that CYSDV has displaced BPYV as the major virus pathogen. No figures are available on losses caused by CYSDV. In Lebanon, the incidence of CYSDV has been high in summer and early autumn cucurbit crops grown in polyethylene tunnels along the coast. Yield reductions of 40-60% have been reported by farmers. remark: Cucurbits are important crops in the EPPO region, both in the field and under glass, and CYSDV causes a serious disease notably on cucumbers and melons in Spain, Portugal, Turkey and the Middle East. Within Europe, cucumber and gherkin production is significant. In 2000, 1.66 million t were harvested in the EU. The Netherlands and Spain were the biggest producers, harvesting 465,000 and 420,000 t, respectively, according to FAO. Economic losses from CYSDV that could be expected in glasshouse-grown cucurbits, especially cucumber, in northern Europe are difficult to predict, but are likely to be substantial. Spread of the pest is likely to be much facilitated by the presence of its vector Bemisia tabaci in glasshouses in many countries of the EPPO region. Control of CYSDV is difficult due to the ability of the vector B. tabaci rapidly to become resistant to insecticides. A breakdown of efficacy of insecticides could result in serious problems. There is a strong probability that CYSDV will become a serious problem in other Mediterranean countries and in northern Europe, if introduced.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pThe control of CYSDV is dependent on the control of its vector Bemisia tabaci, and elimination of sources of infection. In particular, cucurbit seedlings for planting should come from disease-free stocks. Roguing infected cucurbit plants and removing overwintering crops early in the spring prior to the emergence of adult whiteflies may prove useful. To be effective, this sort of control measure should be applied over a whole area and preferably where there is no continuous production in glasshouses, which are often the sites of whitefly activity and active virus spread throughout the year. Weeds in and surrounding glasshouses should also be destroyed as they could act as hosts for Bemisia tabaci. In Israel, covering the soil with a mulch of sawdust, fresh wheat straw or yellow polyethylene sheets has markedly reduced populations of B. tabaci. Whiteflies are attracted to the yellow colour and are killed by the heat. The fading of the mulch colour and changes in the ratio of canopy to mulch area is believed to cause a reduction in control. Interplanting with a species that is a good host for the vector, but not the virus may reduce virus incidence. In Lebanon, insect-proof nets and sticky yellow traps are used for control (Abou-Jawdah et al., 2000). Growing plants under physical barriers, such as low mesh tunnels and shade-cloth, may also have a positive effect. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control of populations of B. tabaci to levels that result in a significant drop in disease incidence has proved difficult. In general, chemical control of the vectors of Closteroviridae has not been effective in preventing the spread of the diseases they cause (Berdiales et al., 1999). Some of the difficulties are the wide host range of the vector, the presence of the whitefly on the undersides of leaves, the extreme motility of adults and the ability of B. tabaci to develop resistance to most classes of existing insecticides. Many conventional insecticides such as organophosphorus compounds, carbamates and pyrethroids have effectively reduced whitefly populations, but provided only partial virus control even when sprayed as frequently as 2-3 times a week (Nakhla and Maxwell, 1998). Imidacloprid, a systemic insecticide that can be applied to soil and foliage, is used to control whiteflies, but resistance has been reported (Elbert and Nauen, 2000). Insects resistant to aldicarb and buprofezin were also detected (Anon., 1996). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pThe parasite Encarsia formosa and the fungus Verticillium lecanii can be used as biological agents against B. tabaci, but are unlikely to affect virus transmission. ^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pCYSDV was added to the EPPO A2 action list in 2004, and endangered EPPO member countries are thus recommended to regulate it as a quarantine pest. There are, as yet, no specific measures against CYSDV in Europe, and in particular there are no restrictions on the movement of cucurbit seedlings from areas where the disease occurs. There is a potential danger that infected seedlings could move from countries where CYSDV occurs to other parts of the region, thus spreading the virus. Possible measures would be the same as those proposed for Cucumber vein yellowing virus (CVYV; OEPP/EPPO, 2005a).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pNo resistant cultivars of susceptible hosts are currently available commercially. Preliminary attempts have been made to obtain select resistant melon genotypes (Sese et al., 1999; Marco et al., 2003).

However, in combination with Sweet potato feathery mottle (SPFMV) the viruses interact synergistically to cause Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD), a severe disease causing substantial or almost complete yield loss in Africa, Asia and  Central America (Hahn, 1979; Milgram et al., 1996; Gibson et al., 1998; Byamukama et al., 2002; Gutierrez et al., 2003; Njeru et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2005). The severity caused by the virus complex is due to SPCSV inducing an increase, estimated to be upto 600-fold greater (Kreuze, 2002), in the replication and concentration of SPFMV Karyeija et al., 2000a, 2001). In Argentina, the chlorotic dwarf disease (caused by SPCSV in complex with SPFMV and Sweet potato mild speckling viruses) can result in yield losses of up to 80% Feo et al., 1995, 2000).
author: CPC2006

description: There is no evidence that SPCSV is seedborne.
author: CPC2006
