host_range: The domesticated tomato (Lycopersicon esculentum) is the primary host of TYLCV. Most of the wild tomato species such as Lycopersicon chilense, L. hirsutum, L. peruvianum and L. pimpinellifolium include accessions that are symptomless carriers (Zakay et al
potential_eco_desc: TYLCV was first described from Israel and until the late 1980s was known as a problem in the eastern Mediterranean. Since then, the geographic distribution of TYLCV has increased to include countries in the Western Mediterranean, the Caribbean, Mexico, the USA and Japan. The TYLCV isolates in the New World are more than 95% homologous to TYLCV, indicating a recent import. Similarly TYLCSV, which was found in Italy and in Spain, has recently spread to Morocco. TYLCV causes heavy economic losses wherever it occurs, although initially after introduction losses may be relatively low, as is currently the situation in Mexico (Yucatan) and the USA (Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina) (Ascencio-Ibanez et al., 1999; Momol et al., 1999; Polston et al., 1999a; Pappu et al., 2000).^p^pAlthough TYLCV has a broad host range, it is primarily known as one of the most damaging viruses to infect tomatoes. The virus affects yields by greatly reducing the number of fruit produced. Fruit developing at the time of infection remain on the plant, but very few fruit will set once infection has occurred.^p^pExperimental studies from many locations document the dramatic effect that TYLCV has on the yield of tomato. Inoculation of tomato plants 3 weeks after transplanting in the field in Lebanon showed a 63% reduction in yield compared with non-infected plants (Makkouk et al., 1979). Studies in the glasshouse in Jordan revealed that inoculation with TYLCV 10 weeks after sowing reduced yields by 63%, whereas inoculations at 15 weeks did not reduce yields significantly (Al-Musa, 1982). In cultivar evaluation trials in Cyprus, yields of more than half the cultivars tested were reduced by 50 to 80% (Ioannou, 1985). Field trials in Israel using tomato transplants of susceptible cultivars inoculated at the first true leaf stage, demonstrated a 99% reduction in the yield of inoculated plants compared with non-inoculated plants (Pilowsky et al., 1993). In field studies in Turkey, two susceptible tomato cultivars showed yield reductions of 60 and 70%, respectively. In a study in commercial tomato fields in Florida, TYLCV significantly reduced the number of fruit, but not the fruit size, compared with non-infected plants (Polston et al., 1999b). The younger the plants were at the time of infection, the more severe the reduction in fruit number.^p^pDocumentation of losses to commercial production, although dramatic, is rare. Severe reductions in tomato yields in 1995 were reported from Portugal (Louro et al., 1996). A survey conducted in Reunion Island from 1997 to 1998 indicated that of 123 commercial sites examined, 52 had at least one TYLCV infected plant; of these, 11 exhibited a 40 to 60% yield reduction, and 14 a 60 to 100% yield reduction (Peterschmit et al., 1999). In the Dominican Republic, annual yield losses for the Azua valley in the southern part of the country ranged between 20 and 95% from 1988 to 1995. In the northern part of the Dominican Republic, annual losses for that region peaked in 1993 at 80% (Alvarez and Abud-Atun, 1995). Losses of 30% were reported from Cuba for the 1990-1991 season (Calixto et al., 1995). Another report states a 100% loss of tomato crops from the La Habana area of Cuba (Ramos et al., 1996). In the USA, incidences of TYLCV-infected tomatoes have remained low due in part to aggressive intervention by tomato growers. Most growers suffered only minor losses in 1997-2000 production seasons, although a few growers (less than 10%) had greater than 50% crop loss in 1998. ^p^pIn addition to tomato, TYLCV was reported to cause severe losses in bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) in commercial production in Israel (Navot et al., 1992) and in southern Spain (Navas-Castillo et al., 1999), and the virus was reported to be a limiting factor in the production of lisianthus (Eustoma grandiflora) in Israel (Cohen et al., 1995).

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pGrowing tomato in open fields is much more constraining than growing under cover. In all regions where TYLCV is endemic, seedlings need to be grown and kept in a glasshouse or a screenhouse in order to prevent early infection by whitefly feeding. In Thailand, farmers grow tomato plants in isolated paddy fields after rice harvesting. In Egypt the spread of TYLCV in open fields was successfully controlled by roguing infected plants and removing all overwintered tomato crops before the emergence of whitefly populations (Mazyad et al., 1986). Similar measures were undertaken in Cyprus over 3 consecutive years resulting in a decrease in the incidence of the disease from 50 to 5% (Ioannou, 1987). Early planting when the incidence of B. tabaci is low, effectively reduced TYLCV infection in Egypt, Israel and Cyprus. Interplanting with rows of TYLCV non-host trap plants such as squash and cucumber have been used to divert whiteflies from tomato in the Jordan Valley, delaying TYLCV infection by 2 months (Al-Musa, 1982). Sticky yellow plastic polyethylene sheets have been used, with limited success, to decrease the pressure of the whitefly population (Cohen et al., 1974). When economically feasible, growing tomatoes in greenhouses covered with insect-proof 50-mesh screens and double-doors constitutes the optimal solution for crop protection against the TYLCV whitefly vector (Cohen and Berlinger, 1986; Ioannou, 1987). UV-absorbing plastic sheets or UV-absorbing 50-mesh screens, used as tunnels or as screenhouse covers, greatly reduced the infestation of tomato plants by B. tabaci and the incidence of TYLCV (Antignus et al., 1998). Whitefly natural enemies (Gerling, 1990) have not been used on a large scale in open fields. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pApplying systemic insecticides as soil drenches or regular spraying during the seedling stage can reduce the population of the B. tabaci vector and the incidence of TYLCV. Many insecticides such as organophosphates, carbamates and pyrethroids effectively reduce the whitefly population, whether sprayed one insecticide at a time, alternately, or together with oil and emulsifiers (Makkouk and Laterrot, 1983). However, these insecticides provided only partial TYLCV control, even when sprayed daily (Cohen and Antignus, 1994). Continued extensive use of insecticides is not only detrimental to the environment but it promotes the development of resistant whitefly populations (Cahill et al., 1995). More potent insecticides with novel modes of action such as imidacloprid were introduced in the 1990s (Elbert et al., 1990). Over the past few years imidacloprid has assumed major importance for control of B. tabaci in the field and in greenhouses. To be efficient, the insecticide has to induce the death of all whiteflies within 35-40 min before it succeeds in infecting the plant, thereby preventing inoculation of TYLCV, which is not always the case in the field (Rubinstein et al., 1999). As for other commonly used insecticides, whitefly populations resistant to imidacloprid have been emerging in many places (Williams et al., 1997). More friendly non-toxic insecticides for the control of B. tabaci are being developed and tests in greenhouses and in the open field are under way (EWSN, 2001).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pBreeding programmes aimed at producing tomato cultivars resistant to TYLCV started in the late 1960s and have expanded since. These programmes are based on the introgression into the domesticated tomato Lycopersicon esculentum of resistance or tolerance found in some accessions of wild tomato species such as L. peruvianum, L. chilense, L. pimpinellifolium and L. cheesmaniae. Depending on the plant source, resistance was reported to be controlled by one to five genes, either recessive or dominant (Zakay et al., 1991; Pico et al., 1996; Nakhla and Maxwell, 1998). description: During summer season surveys in Barasat, West Bengal, India in 2013 and 2014, both Litsea apetala and L. sebifera (Lauraceae) exhibited typical symptoms of geminivirus infection, including leaf curling, deformation, leaf yellowing, vein clearing, mosaic and stunted growth. To the best of our knowledge this is the first report of L. apetala and L. sebifera as natural and alternative hosts of BYVMV in India. This result supports the notion that geminiviruses are important emerging and devastating viruses causing threats to crops.

description: Surveys of kalmegh fields carried out in September and October 2010 in Lucknow, India, revealed symptomatic plants that initially showed yellow veins on younger leaves and later upward leaf curling, vein clearing, chlorosis, reduced leaf size, poor inflorescence, and stunted growth leading to drastic reduction in herb yield. The disease incidence was estimated at 25 to 40%. The test demonstrated that the causal agent was Eclipta yellow vein virus (EYVV). EYVV (family Geminiviridae; genus Begomovirus) was reported for the first time from Pakistan in 2006 on Eclipta prostrata (GQ478343.1). To our knowledge, this is the first report of a new isolate of EYVV infecting A. paniculata in India.  Healthy whiteflies were used for acquisition feeding on the naturally infected twig of A. paniculata and then transferred to healthy seedlings for an overnight inoculation feeding. After inoculation feeding, whiteflies were killed by insecticide. Four out of six plants were positive after whitefly transmission.
reference_name: A New Isolate of Eclipta yellow vein virus Along with a Betasatellite Associated with Yellow Vein Leaf Curl Disease of Andrographis paniculata in India
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

potential_eco_desc: SLCV causes severe losses of all squash and pumpkin cultivars, and minor losses in cucumbers and melons in Arizona, California (Dodds et al., 1985; Brown and Nelson, 1986) and Texas, USA (Isakeit et al., 1994) and in Coahuilla and Sonora, Mexico (JK Brown, unpublished data; Ramirez-Arredondo et al., 1995). Although recorded to infect Phaseolus vulgaris, there is no indication that it has any importance on that host naturally Brown and Nelson, 1986, 1989). The leaf curl disease was first observed in 1977/78 (Flock and Mayhew, 1981) and on cultivated buffalo gourd in Arizona in 1976/77 (Rosemeyer et al., 1986) and is caused by one (or more) of a group of viruses which were transmitted by the A type of B. tabaci (native to the deserts of the south-western USA and Sonora, Mexico) and has become even more important since the introduction and spread of biotype B of B. tabaci in about 1987/88 (Costa and Brown, 1991).

remark: SLCV has recently been added to the EPPO A1 list, but has not been classified as a quarantine pest by any other regional plant protection organisation. This is no doubt partly due to the fact that its appearance as a significant pest is very recent. If introduced outside of its native habitat, it presents a severe threat to the cultivation of cucurbits (especially courgettes, melons and watermelons) in the open in southern Europe or under glass in northern Europe, wherever B. tabaci and especially the B biotype, occurs. ^p^pHost plants of B. tabaci from areas where SLCV occurs should come from a production nursery free from SLCV and B. tabaci (or treated against B. tabaci) during the last growing season. This applies especially to the ornamental Euphorbia pulcherrima or other ornamental species that are well known to carry B. tabaci inconspicuously.
author: CPC2006

management_info: SLCV is spread naturally only by its vector Bemisia tabaci which spreads it between fields (and presumably glasshouses) in infested areas. In international trade, it is unlikely to be carried by plants of its main cultivated hosts, since these are short-lived vegetable crops not normally transported except as seedlings. Young seedlings for transplanting might constitute a pathway, but would still be unlikely to be moved in intercontinental trade. The vegetables as such would not be likely to carry B. tabaci. So the main risk of movement is in B. tabaci on other host plants (for example, ornamentals), given the fact that the vector moves readily from one host to another and that the virus can persist in the vector for several weeks (to life) after virus acquisition (Cohen et al., 1983; Rosell et al., 1999).^p^pIn the field, disease control is mainly aimed at eliminating or excluding the whitefly vector, B. tabaci. Endosulfan and other insecticides have been used in an attempt to reduce whitefly density. Protecting rows of seedlings with spun-bonded polyester as a floating cover has also been effective (Natwick and Durazo, 1985). Some cultivars of Cucurbita pepo have shown resistance to SLCV McCreight, 1984, 1991).
author: CPC2006

management_info: 在田间，控制病害主要目的在于排除或除去粉虱，烟粉虱这些病毒携带者。硫丹及其他杀虫剂已被尝试用于降低粉虱的密度。用仿聚酯以一个漂浮保护盖的形式保护秧苗的行数是有效的(Natwick and Durazo, 1985)。一些北瓜的培育品种已经被证实对SLCV有抵抗力(McCreight, 1984, 1991). In the field, disease control is mainly aimed at eliminating or excluding the whitefly vector, B. tabaci. Endosulfan and other insecticides have been used in an attempt to reduce whitefly density. Protecting rows of seedlings with spun-bonded polyester as a floating cover has also been effective (Natwick and Durazo, 1985). Some cultivars of Cucurbita pepo have shown resistance to SLCV (McCreight, 1984, 1991).   只有通过它的携带者――烟粉虱在感染区域的原野（温室）传播病毒，才使SLCV容易地扩散起来。在国际交易上，因这些是短期生长的蔬菜作物，若它们不是秧苗的话，是不能正常地进行交易的。这就不可能通过它们主要培养作物上的寄主携带病毒。移植幼嫩的秧苗应该开一条路径，但这些秧苗仍不可能在洲际贸易间流动。像这样的蔬菜不可能携带烟粉虱。所以，主要的交易风险是在于在其他寄主植物上的（例如，观赏植物）烟粉虱。事实上，这些携带病菌的动物很容易地从一种寄主植物迁移到另一种寄主植物上，通过这种方式使病毒能够在其获得寄主植物之前，可持续地在其携带者上逗留几个星期（生活）。(Cohen et al., 1983; Rosell et al., 1999)。 SLCV is spread naturally only by its vector Bemisia tabaci which spreads it between fields (and presumably glasshouses) in infested areas. In international trade, it is unlikely to be carried by plants of its main cultivated hosts, since these are short-lived vegetable crops not normally transported except as seedlings. Young seedlings for transplanting might constitute a pathway, but would still be unlikely to be moved in intercontinental trade. The vegetables as such would not be likely to carry B. tabaci. So the main risk of movement is in B. tabaci on other host plants (for example, ornamentals), given the fact that the vector moves readily from one host to another and that the virus can persist in the vector for several weeks (to life) after virus acquisition (Cohen et al., 1983; Rosell et al., 1999).
author: zhangjianjun

host_range: Corchorus olitorius.
potential_eco_desc: 在中国尚无危害.
description: In September 2015, a virus-like disease was found in a small garden of jute in the campus of Fujian Agricultural University, Fuzhou, Fujian Province, China. The samples were collected and DNA was extracted, the virus was identified as Corchorus yellow vein Vietnam virus (CoYVV) by PCR. CoYVV has not been found anywhere outside of Vietnam. Our results show that CoYVV may have a wider distribution than expected or that this virus is spreading.  In the small jute garden, the abundance of whiteflies that feed on the jute plants suggested a begomovirus etiology.
reference_name: First Report of the Occurrence of Corchorus yellow vein Vietnam virus on Jute in China

host_range: 苎麻Boehmeria nivea.
potential_eco_desc: The incidence of the disease varied from 2 to 10% in experimental fields of the CRIJAF research farm, Barrackpore, India.
description: In May 2013, ramie(Boehmeria nivea) plants exhibiting yellow mosaic symptoms were noted in experimental fields of the CRIJAF research farm, Barrackpore, India. The incidence of the disease varied from 2 to 10%. The samples were collected from the field and DNA was extracted. Based on molecular diagnostics showed the causal agent was Corchorus golden mosaic virus (CoGMV). To our knowledge, this is the first report that CoGMV infects ramie plants. The incidence of CoGMV in ramie is relatively low, but in the future it may negatively affect the yield.
reference_name: First Report of Corchorus golden mosaic virus(CoGMV) Infecting Ramie (Boehmeria nivea) in India
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 假连翘Duranta erecta, Bougainvillea peruviana, Clerodendron inerme.
description: During a survey in August 2013, yellow mosaic disease was observed on Duranta erecta growing in several public gardens/parks at Lucknow, India (Latitude: 26° 55' N; Longitude: 80° 59' E) with disease incidence 80-90%. The symptoms reminiscent of a begomovirus infection reported previously on D. erecta in Pakistan (Iram et al., 2004) and hence a similar infection was suspected. The leaf samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was Clerodendron yellow mosaic virus (ClYMV) by molecular diagnostics. Begomoviruses are associated with leaf curl disease in D. erecta (Iram et al., 2004); Catharanthus yellow mosaic virus in D. repens (Mustujab et al., 2015) and Tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus in D. repens (Tahir et al., 2006) from Pakistan. ClYMV has been reported on Bougainvillea peruviana (Nehra et al., 2014) and Clerodendron inerme (Sivalingam et al., 2011) in India, but to the best of our knowledge this is the first report of natural occurrence of ClYMV on D. erecta in India.
reference_name: First report of Clerondendron yellow mosaic virus on golden dewdrop (Duranta erecta) in India
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: WmCSV typically infects cucurbits, and it has reported of infecting tomato in Jordan (Ahmad et al. 2013), this is the first record of a Datura species as a natural host of WmCSV.
description: In October 2016, yellowing and leaf deformation symptoms were observed in Datura innoxia plants in Kharthoum, Sudan. Leaf samples from symptomatic plants were collected and total nucleic acids were extracted, based on molecular diagnostics confirming the presence of Watermelon chlorotic stunt virus (WmCSV) in all analyzed samples. To our knowledge, this is the first record of a Datura species as a natural host of WmCSV.  Datura innoxia could play as a role of WmCSV reservoir host between cropping seasons.
reference_name: First Report of Datura innoxia as a Natural Host of Watermelon chlorotic stunt virus in Sudan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 西瓜Citrullus lanatus
description: During the spring of 2014, watermelon leaves exhibited yellowing and severe chlorotic mottling symptoms. The foliar symptoms were reminiscent of Watermelon chlorotic stunt virus(WmCSV), a bipartite begomovirus previously reported in several neighboring countries. The samples were collected and WmCSV was confirmed. To our knowledge, this is the first report of WmCSV in Saudi Arabia. WmCSV poses a serious threat to the production of this highly valued crop in Saudi Arabia and considerably reduces crop yield.
reference_name: First Report of Watermelon chlorotic stunt virus Infecting Watermelon in Saudi Arabia
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: Both Momordica charantia and Sechium edule together with cucumber, pumpkin, and squash belong to the Cucurbitaceae whose members are commonly infected by begomoviruses worldwide. While S. edule is a widely consumed vegetable crop having high nutritional value, M. charantia is a noncultivated species. The occurrence of ChaYMV in both M. charantia and S. edule suggests that M. charantia is an alternative host of this virus, which is likely transmitted between these species, implicating a role of M. charantia in the epidemiology of ChaYMV for the first time.
description: Yellow mosaic symptoms, frequently associated with family Geminiviridae, genus Begomovirus, were observed in 60 to 80% of bitter melon (Momordica charantia) plants in surveys conducted in three countries in West Africa. In August 2014, leaf samples were collected from three symptomatic and one nonsymptomatic M. charantia plants exhibiting yellow mosaic symptoms in Togo, Benin, and Nigeria (6°10.397′ N; 1°07.316′ E), (6°10.938′ N; 1°09.715′ E), and (7°29′57.5′ N; 3°54′11.3′ E), respectively. Based on molecular diagnostics showed that Chayote yellow mosaic virus (ChaYMV) was present in bitter melon plants. The occurrence of ChaYMV in both M. charantia and Sechium edule suggests that M. charantia is an alternative host of this virus, which is likely transmitted between these species, implicating a role of M. charantia in the epidemiology of ChaYMV for the first time. The identification of ChaYMV in Benin, Nigeria, and Togo strongly indicates that it has a wider-than-reported geographical distribution, and has the potential to become more problematic. reference_name: First Report of Chayote yellow mosaic virus Infecting Bitter Melon (Momordica charantia) Exhibiting Yellow Mosaic Symptoms in Benin, Nigeria, and Togo

host_range: The only known natural hosts of CLCrV are cotton, bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and Malva parviflora (Brown and Nelson, 1987; Brown et al., 1986). The experimental host range of the virus is rather narrow and, with a few exceptions, generally confined to Malv
potential_eco_desc: Up to 100% infection by CLCrV now occurs by the end of most cotton growing seasons in the lowland areas of the south-western US and north-western deserts of Sonora. When infection occurs during rapid foliar growth stages, losses ranging from 16-85% have been reported (Brown, 1992). Losses are attributed to reduced boll set, fewer open bolls, and lower seed indices (Brown et al., 1987; Butler et al., 1986; Schaik et al., 1962). CLCrV is not seedborne (Brown and Nelson, 1987).
author: CPC2006

remark: Risk could be incurred if viruliferous whiteflies were introduced to cotton-growing areas in which the virus is not established. Examples in the USA are the south-eastern cotton production regions and the Rio Grande Valley of Texas.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Resistant varieties will ultimately be the most effective in reducing losses and will be most cost effective. Several promising lines exhibiting disease tolerance have been identified in preliminary studies Wilson et al., 1990, 1991). Control of the disease by reducing vector pressures has become less promising in light of the great potential for development of insecticide resistance in whitefly populations. Eliminating the practice of ratooning cotton to achieve perennial production reduces residual inoculum for early spring infection in Arizona. Although alternative weed hosts of the virus are not known, reducing or eliminating weeds near fields that may provide reservoirs for the whitefly vector is highly recommended.

host_range: CGMMV is easily transmitted mechanically in cucurbits (watermelon, cucumber, melons, zucchini, pumpkin, squash, bitter gourd, and bottle gourd).
potential_eco_desc: CGMMV causes severe yield and quality losses of cucurbit crops worldwide. The rapid spread of CGMMV in cucumbers in Canada has led to a serious decline ranging from 10 to 15%.
description: In 2016, in the western part of Poland (the Wielkopolska region), virus-like disease symptoms were observed in greenhouse grown cucumbers (Cucumis sativus). During the spring and summer period, samples of cucumber plants were collected and tested at the Plant Disease Clinic of the Institute of Plant Protection - National Research Institute in Poznań. Based on transmission electron microscopy, (DAS)-ELISA, RT-PCR and sequences analysis, the pathogen was identified as Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of CGMMV infecting greenhouse cucumber in Poland.  CGMMV is easily transmitted mechanically in cucurbits. It can be spread via cucumber pollen and by infected seeds. The seed transmission rates ranged from 16.7 to 100%. The virus can be introduced into a crop in many ways, but contaminated seeds and soil are the most common ones.
reference_name: The Occurrence of Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus Infecting Greenhouse Cucumber in Poland
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 短毛独活Heracleum moellendorffii
description: In April 2014, leaf mosaic, mottling, and deformed plant symptoms were observed on the diseased plants in the Eosuri-growing areas of Andong-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do Province. The leaf samples collected from the affected plants, based on virus-specific Immunostrip kits and RT-PCR tests confirmed that the pathogen was Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report on the sequence of CGMMV derived from H. moellendorffii Hance in Korea.  Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus can be especially problematic, owing to the ease with which it is transmitted. It also shows a higher viability in the soil, in plant debris, or in a greenhouse.
reference_name: First Report of Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus Infecting Heracleum moellendorffii in Korea

host_range: The occurrence of CGMMV was reported in bottle gourd and musk melon earlier in India.
potential_eco_desc: A loss of 10 to 15% was reported due to CGMMV infection in cucumber grown in greenhouses in Canada and in China.
description: During a field survey conducted to document the viruses infecting cucurbitaceous crops in Tamil Nadu State during 2014, a snake gourd field near Coimbatore was identified with symptoms of virus diseases: mosaic, mottling with reduction of leaf size, and phylloid flowers. Nicotiana glutinosa plants inoculated with crude sap extracts from symptomatic leaves of snake gourd showed systemic mosaic mottling symptoms, indicating the presence of a mechanically transmissible virus. Symptomatic leaf samples from snake gourd and N. glutinosa were collected and identified, based on serological detection and molecular characteristics, the results confirmed the presence of Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV). The occurrence of CGMMV was reported in bottle gourd and musk melon earlier in India. To our knowledge, this is the first documented serological and molecular evidence for the occurrence of CGMMV in snake gourd in India.  CGMMV is a highly transmissible virus of the family Virgaviridae and the genus Tobamovirus.
reference_name: First Report of Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus in Snake Gourd (Trichosanthes cucumerina) in India

description: In July 2013, a melon (Cucumis melo var. Saski) field in Yolo County, California, was inspected as part of a phytosanitary inspection for seed production. The leaves of the plants showed mosaic, green mottle, and blotches. The samples were collected and identified, the analyses confirm the virus was Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus（CGMMV）. The melon field affected by CGMMV was immediately adjacent to fields of cucumber (Cucumis sativus var. Marketmore 76) and watermelon (Citrullus lanatus var. Sugar Baby) crops, both for seed production with no barrier between the crops. To our knowledge, this is the first report of CGMMV in the United States.

host_range: In addition to maize (Zea mays), including field maize, sweetcorn, popcorn and maize inbred lines (seed crop), MDMV has been isolated from the following naturally-infected plant species:^p^pSorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is the other very important host of MDM
potential_eco_desc: MDMV causes economic losses in maize, including field maize, sweetcorn and maize inbred lines (seed crop), as well as sorghum, including silage sorghum, grain sorghum and broom maize. Infection on maize plants affects growth stages of development, leaf area, fertility and mature weights, number of seeds and rows, yield (seed yield, total yield), 1000 grain weight, seed quality (viability), and susceptibility of infected plants to other pathogens/diseases.^p^pThe extent of pathological changes induced by MDMV mainly depends on cultivar susceptibility, time of infection, water conditions, nutrients etc.^p^pEarly infection with MDMV delays all stages of maize development, for ca 2 weeks or more (Dimitrijevic, 1969; Scott and Nelson, 1972; Mikel et al., 1981).^p^pThe height of maize plants infected with MDMV is reduced by up to 23% (Tosic and Misovic, 1967; Popov, 1972; Sum et al., 1979; Olsen et al., 1990). In extreme cases, especially with maize inbred lines, the diseased plants are 25-50% of the height of healthy plants (Jansen and Ellet, 1963; Tosic et al., 1990a).^p^pLeaf area reduction in maize plants infected with MDMV is up to 11%, but after early infection and early water stress, the leaf area could be reduced by 33% or more (Olsen et al., 1990). Leaf area reduction, along with a decrease in plant height, have a large influence on crop productivity.^p^pSterility, which is more frequent with infected maize plants, contributes to the economic impact of MDMV. Reduced growth and development, and changes in some plant development stages (Dimitrijevic, 1969; Scott and Nelson, 1972; Mikel et al., 1981) can lead to sterility in up to 25% of infected plants (Tosic and Misovic, 1967), but in the case of maize inbred lines the sterility can be even higher (Tosic et al., 1990a).^p^pThe number of ears per plant, especially of marketable ears of sweetcorn crops, is markedly reduced by MDMV infection (Gregory and Ayers, 1982; Mikel et al., 1982). Fresh weight of ears can be reduced by 30% or more by MDMV infection. (Anzola et al., 1980; Mikel et al., 1981; Antignus, 1987). Ear length reduction due to MDMV infection ranges by up to 25.6% (Tosic and Misovic, 1967; Mikel et al., 1981; Peti, 1983). The diameter of ears of maize plants infected with MDMV is also affected (Mikel et al., 1981). Ear yield can be drastically reduced by MDMV, especially after an early infection. The reduction in ear weight caused by MDMV infection can be nearly 50% (Tosic and Misovic, 1967; Antignus, 1987; Fuchs et al., 1990b; Olsen et al., 1990). Ears of maize plants infected with MDMV are poorly filled and the number of kernels and rows of kernels are reduced (Tosic and Misovic, 1967; Olsen et al., 1990; Kovacs et al., 1994).^p^pKernels of maize plants infected by MDMV are usually smaller, especially at the basal portion of the ear (Mikel et al., 1981). Consequently, the 1000 grain weight can be reduced by up to 26% (Peti, 1983; Kovacs et al., 1994).^p^pThe total yield of maize can be very much affected by MDMV infection. Yield reduction per fertile field maize plant infected with MDMV can be up to 42% (Tosic and Misovic, 1967). However, with maize inbred lines or with sweetcorn, especially after later sowing, the yield can be reduced by 75% or more (Forster et al., 1980).^p^pGerminability of seeds formed on maize plants infected with MDMV may be reduced by nearly 20%, while the length and width of primary roots are smaller by 7.4 and 20.0%, respectively (Stakic and Savic, 1984).^p^pSorghum is the second main crop which can be affected by MDMV. Symptoms on sorghum plants infected with MDMV can be more severe than those caused by the same virus on maize plants. The symptoms on sorghum depends on cultivar susceptibility, time of infection, and environmental conditions (mainly temperature). Besides mosaic and growth reduction, infected sorghum plants show red stripes and necrosis. Red stripe is a common symptom, characteristic of sorghum plants infected by MDMV

description: Incidence^p^pMDMV has been detected at levels of about 0.5% in maize seeds (Shepherd and Holdeman, 1965; Williams et al., 1968; Boothroyd, 1977; Hill et al., 1974; Mikel et al., 1984b). There is some indication that newer strains might be transmitted at higher rates than older ones (Knoke and Louie, 1981). In sweetcorn plants leaf-inoculated by a mixture of strains A and B, MDMV was detected in the pericarp, but rarely in the endosperm and embryo of seeds at 21 days after pollination. In mature seeds, MDMV was occasionally detected in the pericarp and endosperm, but not in the embryo (Mikel et al., 1984b). With respect to the process of infection of seeds, Nemchinov et al. (1990) showed that MDMV is present in all floral meristems of male and female reproductive structures of all stages of organogenesis of ears and cobs of infected maize. The virus was also found in suspensions from mature pollen grains as well as in all parts of the mature seed. Mikel et al. (1982) proved that MDMV is present in the silks, but did not find the virus in pollen grains. They also showed that pollen from infected maize plants develops shorter germ tubes in vitro as well as in vivo. Mikel et al. (1984b) showed that MDMV is also present in glumes, anthers and unfertilized or fertilized kernels.^p^pMiao HongQin et al. (1998) studied the effects of time of plant infection by MDMV on seedborne infection as follows: in an insect-proof greenhouse, three maize inbred lines (Huangye 4-3, 7922 and 81515) were inoculated with MDMV at the 3 to 5, 6 to 8, 9 to 11 and 13 to 15-leaf stages. Bioassays showed that the rate of seedborne MDMV was 0% in Huangye 4-3 (a resistant line), 1.65% in 7922 (a susceptible line) and 0% in 81515 (a resistant line). The rates of MDMV infection at the four growth stages (from seedling to booting) in line 7922 were 100, 100, 63.6 and 10.1%, disease indexes were 95.6, 82.4, 63.6 and 11.1 and the rates of seedborne MDMV were 2.3, 1.5, 3.3 and 0.78%, respectively. Evaluation of the three inbred lines suggested that resistance levels were related to infected plant growth periods. The younger the plants, the lower the resistance they showed to MDMV infection.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pOne report indicated that germination of seed from MDMV-infected plants was not suppressed, but shoot and root growth was reduced (Panayotou, 1981). Another study showed that both germination and root development were reduced (Stakic and Savic, 1984). More recently, Achon and Sin (1998) artificially infected two inbred lines, Mo17 (susceptible) and B73 (tolerant) and their hybrids with MDMV. Virus infection reduced the number of seeds produced on infected plants. The reductions were 30-33% on Mo17, 20.9% on Mo17XB73, 7.5-7.7% on B73 and 4.4-8.3% on B73XMo17. ^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pTransmission of MDMV from infected maize seeds to seedlings has been demonstrated in sterilized soil (Shepherd and Holdeman, 1965; Williams et al., 1968; Hill et al., 1974; Mikel et al., 1984b). The virus could not be transmitted through seeds of infected sorghum (Madhulika Mishra et al., 1998).^p^pWeed hosts, in particular Johnsongrass (Knoke et al., 1983), and aphids (Knoke and Louie, 1981; Knoke et al., 1983; Rest et al., 1985; Scott, 1985) are considered to be major inoculum sources. Aphids transmit the pathogen nonpersistently.^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pNo known seed treatment will eliminate MDMV infection. Imidacloprid seed treatment has been investigated, but control under field conditions by reduction of aphid transmission of MDMV was not demonstrated (Epperlein et al., 1995).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pGrow-out: seeds are grown in sterile soil and examined for symptom development (Shepherd and Holdeman, 1965; Williams et al., 1968; Hill et al., 1974; Mikel et al., 1984).^p^pSerological: ELISA successfully detected the pathogen in seed parts (Mikel et al., 1984). management_info: Introduction^p^pThe economic importance, due to damage caused in maize and sorghum production, make control of MDMV mandatory. Since it has a wide host range of ca 250 different plant species and more than 20 aphid vectors, control of MDMV is not easy. Therefore, many measures which can contribute to disease control have to be applied. Integrated MDMV control management should comprise three basic measures: destruction of Johnsongrass plus other wild hosts (the source of MDMV under field conditions); control of aphid vectors; and breeding of resistant maize and sorghum genotypes (Milinko et al., 1979; Gorbunova et al., 1980).^p^pJohnsongrass is usually infected by up to 100% with MDMV (Pop, 1962; Shepherd et al., 1964; Sutic and Tosic, 1966; Reeves et al., 1978). Such a high incidence of infection is due to inoculum accumulation in the perennial Johnsongrass. Therefore, Johnsongrass serves as a permanent source (one of the best) of MDMV under field conditions (Tosic and Simova, 1967; Onazi and Wilde, 1974).^p^pAlthough nearby sources of MDMV inoculum are the most important (Damsteegt, 1976; Madden et al., 1986), sudden epidemics of MDMV in areas without Johnsongrass was hypothesised by long distance aphid vector movement (Zeyen et al., 1987). Therefore, Johnsongrass should be destroyed wherever possible.^p^pJohnsongrass should be controlled as early as possible after emergence (Vangessel and Coble, 1993). When Johnsongrass is controlled late in the season a higher incidence of MDMV occurs, especially on maize hybrids susceptible to MDMV (Eberwine and Hagood, 1995).^p^pMDMV control by systemic insecticides against aphid vectors is also a big challenge. MDMV is transmitted nonpersistently group of viruses. Thus, viruliferous aphids can inoculate healthy plants before being affected by insecticide. Carbofuran treatment did not affect MDMV incidence but did greatly reduce aphid populations (Rains and Christensen, 1983). It is suggested that the application of insecticides to source plants of the virus would lead to better results.^p^pOil application weekly or twice-a-week gave better, but not consistent, results (Ferro et al., 1980; Szatmari-Goodman and Nault, 1983).^p^p^Host Plant Resistance^p^pThe crucial measures for controlling MDMV is breeding resistance genotypes in maize and sorghum. For this, it is necessary to determine a source of resistance and then to transfer and incorporate the resistance into maize and sorghum genotypes growing in production. Mikel et al. (1984) transferred genetic resistance from Pa405 field maize inbred into sweetcorn.^p^pThe resistance against MDMV in maize or in sorghum can be recognised by: (1) the absence of infection or mild symptom expression (Kuhn and Smith, 1977; Fuchs and Bedri, 1993); (2) a lower percentage of plants developing symptoms (Kuch and Smith, 1977; Fuchs and Bedri, 1993); (3) a long incubation period (Kuhn and Smith, 1977; Fuchs and Bedri, 1993); (4) suppressed virus translocation-movement within the infected plant (Jones and Tolin, 1972; Ford and Hill, 1976; Kuhn and Smith, 1977; Law et al., 1987; Fuchs and Bedri, 1993); (5) virus presence restricted to certain leaf areas showing symptoms (stripes, bands etc.) (Jones and Tolin, 1972); and (6) a low virus titre (Fuchs and Bedri, 1993).^p^pResistance to MDMV should be tested both under greenhouse and field conditions. In some cases, similar results were obtained (Kuhn and Smith, 1977; Kovacs et al., 1993) but different results were obtained in others (Kuhn and Jellum, 1970; Louie et al., 1990; Kovacs et al., 1993; Kovacs et al., 1994). The results concerning resistance to MDMV, and obtained under greenhouse conditions, can be used to predict possible resistance under field conditions (Zuber et al., 1973). Selection of parental lines should be based on the results obtained under both greenhouse and field experiments (Naidu and Josephson, 1976).^p^pMany maize genotypes were shown to possess the resistance gene. description: During the summer of 2013, leaf samples (n=76) with virus-like symptoms were collected from Phaseolus vulgaris plants in fields around the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute and in private gardens in regions near Plovdiv, Bulgaria. Disease incidence varied from 10 to 50%. Symptoms consisted of green or yellow mosaic, blisters, and leaf distortion. In some locations the prevalent disease was associated with severe stunting. Based on DAS/TAS-ELISA, Electron microscopy and RT-PCR tests, results revealed the presence of PSV in three samples. To our knowledge this is the first report of PSV in Bulgaria and the second report of the occurrence of the Western strain of PSV in Europe (Diaz-Ruiz et al., 1979).  As a nonpersistently transmitted aphid-borne cucumovirus, PSV might spread to other legumes including forage crops in Bulgaria.

potential_eco_desc: In the 1960s, PSV was a problem in Virginia, North Carolina and Georgia, but it is not of economic importance for groundnut production in the USA. However, PSV sporadically causes a high incidence of peanut stunt disease in Hebei, Henan and Liaoning provinces in China (Xu et al., 1992).In greenhouse studies, PSV has been implicated as a weakening factor in white clover plants, because it renders them more susceptible to injury and death from environmental stress and diseases (Gibson et al., 1981). Alternatively, plants may die as a direct result of PSV infection. Both these situations contribute to the lack of persistence of white clover in pastures in the USA (Gibson et al., 1982). Nodulation ratings were lower (fewer nodules, smaller nodules, abnormal colour or shape) in white clover plants infected with PSV (Gibson et al., 1981). The greatest yield losses occurred at higher temperatures.PSV seems of little economic importance in lupins.

description:
PSV通过属于蚜科的昆虫媒介自然传播，例如豆蚜，绣线菊蚜和桃蚜，而不是棉蚜。它是以非持续性方式传播(Herbert, 1967; Tolin et al., 1970)。PSV也能通过机械接种传播。PSV被传播于落花生种子和大豆(Iizuka and Yunoki, 1974)的比例很小（落花生的约为0.1%）(Kuhn, 1969; Troutman et al., 1967)。在美国，对落花生、烟草和大豆的侵染，白三叶草是一种重要的病毒越冬病原 (Choopanya, 1968; Herbert, 1967)。黑飞蝗花叶树（刺槐）在中国被发现是PSV的主要病原(Zhang et al., 1990)。
来自早期受侵染的植株的种子呈现畸形，通常有裂开的子实体包被壁，且缺乏变异性。因为源于这些种子的幼苗显露迟和生长发育不足，种子传播不被认为是重要因素在病害传播中。当多年生植物寄主存在时，种子传播被认为是不重要的。在寄主里除了落花生和大豆外，PSV的种子传播尚未被报道。 PSV is transmitted in nature by insect vectors belonging to the Aphididae, such as Aphis craccivora, A. spiraecola and Myzus persicae, but not by A. gossypii. It is transmitted in the non-persistent manner (Herbert, 1967; Tolin et al., 1970). PSV can also be transmitted by mechanical inoculation. PSV is transmitted in a small percentage of groundnut seeds (about 0.1%) (Kuhn, 1969; Troutman et al., 1967) and soyabeans (Iizuka and Yunoki, 1974). White clover is an important overwintering source of the virus for infection of groundnuts, tobacco and beans in the USA (Choopanya, 1968; Herbert, 1967). The black locust mosaic tree (Robinia pseudoacacia) was found to be a primary source of PSV in China (Zhang et al., 1990).
Seeds from plants that were infected early appear misshapen, frequently with a split pericarp wall, and have poor viability. As seedlings from such seeds emerge late and grow poorly, seed transmission is not considered an important factor in the spread of disease. Seed transmission is also not considered of importance when perennial hosts are present. Seed transmission of PSV in hosts other than groundnuts and soyabeans has not been reported.
author: zhangjianjun

management_info: 因为PSV不是一种经济重要性病害在落花生中，所以没有控制措施是可用的。然而，使用栽培实践像消除侵染性的病原和运用高质量种子预防病害传播，它是可取的。在饲料豆科植物的实例中，例如在多年生植物草原里的三叶草，抗病品种或忍耐性品种的使用是被赞许的。 Because PSV is not an economically important disease in groundnuts, no control methods are available. However, it is advisable to use cultural practices such as eliminating the source of infection and using good quality seed to prevent the disease spreading. In the case of forage legumes, such as clover in perennial pastures, the use of resistant or tolerant varieties is recommended.

host_range:
The main woody hosts are the species of Prunus grown for fruit production, including apricot (P. armeniaca), peach (P. persica) and plum (P. domestica and P. salicina). Almond trees (P. dulcis) can be infected by PPV but show few symptoms (Dallot et al., 1997, Damsteegt et al., 2007). Natural infection of P. cerasus and P. avium, attributed to the cherry adapted PPV-C strain has been sporadically observed in Europe (Kalashyan et al. 1994; Crescenzi et al., 1997). The recent identification of two other cherry-adapted strains (PPV-CR and CV, Glasa et al., 2013; Chirkov et al., 2018) also shows the epidemiological potential of these PPV strains in the cherry hosts.

Many Prunus species used as rootstock or as ornamentals are natural hosts of PPV, together with a range of wild Prunus species, including their interspecific hybrids (James & Thompson, 2006; Damsteegt et al., 2007). PPV infects most wild or ornamental species of Prunus, such as P. besseyi, P. cerasifera, P. insititia, P. spinosa, P. tomentosa, serving as a potential reservoir and source of virus inoculum. Numerous annual cultivated plants or weeds have been shown to be experimental hosts of PPV (Virscek Marn et al., 2004; Llacer, 2006). However, as reports of natural infection of such herbaceous hosts have never been confirmed using two independent diagnostic techniques, and sequence information on the isolate(s) involved has never been provided, their host status is unconfirmed. In any case, natural transmission between such herbaceous plants and Prunus has never been demonstrated in nature, so that the epidemiological contribution of herbaceous hosts, if any, remains questionable.
Host list: Prunus americana, Prunus armeniaca, Prunus avium, Prunus besseyi, Prunus brigantina, Prunus cerasifera, Prunus cerasus, Prunus curdica, Prunus domestica subsp. insititia, Prunus domestica subsp. italica, Prunus domestica, Prunus dulcis, Prunus glandulosa, Prunus holosericea, Prunus incisa, Prunus japonica, Prunus laurocerasus, Prunus mahaleb, Prunus mandshurica, Prunus maritima, Prunus mume, Prunus nigra, Prunus persica, Prunus pumila, Prunus salicina, Prunus serotina, Prunus serrulata, Prunus sibirica, Prunus simonii, Prunus spinosa, Prunus tomentosa, Prunus triloba, Prunus virginiana, Prunus x blireana, Prunus x cistena, Prunus, Spiraea sp., Tilia.
potential_eco_desc: The importance of sharka disease on the European stone-fruit production has been reviewed by Cambra et al. (2006b). The disease incidence is particularly high in the fruit-producing areas of central and eastern Europe. Virus infection can lead to considerable yield losses, reaching 100%. European plums may show premature fruit drop, while Japanese plums and peaches show ring-spotting on fruit, and apricots show serious fruit deformation.
management_info: There is no anti-virus treatment available to control sharka disease in orchards. There are, however, considerable differences in susceptibility between the cultivars available for use in countries where infection is widespread (Kegler et al., 1998, Martínez-Gómez et al., 2000). However, the frequent plantation of tolerant Prunus cultivars (their fruits remaining generally symptomless in case of infection) has probably contributed to the further spread of PPV in these countries (Glasa et al., 2004). Biological control by inoculation of trees with hypo-aggressive strains has not proved as successful in the field as under controlled conditions (Kerlan et al., 1980) and is not considered a realistic preventative option. Other effective control methods are the production and use of healthy plants for planting within a certification system, and the eradication of diseased trees or orchards to reduce inoculum pressure (Rimbaud et al., 2015a). As for other potyviruses, the control of aphid vectors by regular treatment with aphicides or mineral oils shows only limited effectiveness, with the possible exception of nurseries where some protection has been recorded (Vidal et al., 2013). Such methods are used to contain PPV in several countries (e.g. France, Italy). EPPO recommends a certification scheme for fruit trees, which takes into account PPV (EPPO, 1991/1992). Resistance to PPV shows some promise, whether by traditional breeding or by transgenic methods. The hypersensitive response in plums, resulting in localized cell death, has been found to be an effective resistance mechanism against PPV (Hartmann, 1998). Apricot varieties resistant to the PPV-D strain are now extensively planted in some areas of Spain. While progress has been obtained in plum and apricot, the development of resistant peach varieties has remained a challenge due to the paucity of resistance sources. Biotechnology has also contributed with the development of the transgenic plum cultivar Honeysweet which shows a high, broad spectrum resistance (Scorza et al., 2016).

potential_eco_desc: PPV is a causal agent of plum pox (sharka), the most serious viral disease for the stone fruit crops (Prunus spp.).
description: In June 2016, some Japanese apricots and apricot (P. armeniaca) trees were found with typical Plum pox virus (PPV) symptoms such as ringspot and mottle on leaves, along with some peach (P. persica) trees with mild mottle on leaves, in Yokohama, Japan. These trees were distributed in a small area in Yokohama city. Most of them were grown in home gardens, and some were on roadsides, parks, and orchards. The ages of these trees varied, ranging from those estimated to be about 5 years old to 20 years or more. The leaves sampled from these trees were tested by immunochromatography, RT-LAMP and double antibody sandwich indirect ELISA with PPV-M specific monoclonal antibody line AL(Agritest, Italy), all of samples showed positive results. This is the first detection of PPV-M in Japan.
reference_name: First Report of Plum pox virus Strain M in Japan

host_range: Prunus domestica（cv. Quetsche d'Alsace 3066）
description: During surveys in the Alsace region of France in spring 2013, a plum orchard with trees (Prunus domestica cv. Quetsche d'Alsace 3066) showing dubious leaf symptoms possibly reminiscent of PPV infection was identified. Testing of material from this plant by ELISA gave clear positive reactions, putting the overall infection rate of the orchard at 6.25%, while a second nearby orchard was found infected at a rate of 0.8%. The presence of PPV was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification using either the P1-P2 polyvalent primer pair or the P3M-P4b primer pair, which allows the specific amplification of isolates of the Rec and M strains. Sequencing of the 467-nt-long P3M-P4b PCR product (Genbank Accession No. KM035763), which spans the end of the NIb gene and the N-terminal hypervariable end of the coat protein gene, provided clear identification of the PPV isolate as belonging to the Rec strain, since it contained all the PPV-Rec specific mutations in the amplified region and showed 98.7 to 97.7% identity with a range of PPV Rec isolates mostly originating from the Balkans. Identification as a PPV-Rec isolate was also confirmed using a strain-specific reverse-transcription–PCR assay. This is, to our knowledge, the first report of the presence of PPV-Rec in France.
reference_name: First Report of the Presence of Plum pox virus Rec Strain in France

description: In 2012, two new foci of sharka in a coastal area of Catania in Sicily were first reported by the national plant protection service to the European Commission (DG-SANCO). In spring 2013, plants of different varieties of apricot (Prunus armeniaca) and peach (P. persica) showing typical symptoms of flower color break, yellowing and leaf deformation, chlorotic spots or rings, and malformation on fruits were tested positive to Plum pox virus (PPV) by DAS-ELISA using polyclonal antibodies. Further tests confirmed that Sicilian isolates belong to the PPV-M strain showing 99% similarity with those already present in GenBank.  Plum pox virus transmitted by aphids in a non-persistent manner and by grafting.

potential_eco_desc: 在希腊、瑞士、英国等国家和地区已经造成严重经济损失。并在其他一些国家如：澳大利亚、德国、匈牙利、波兰、罗马尼亚、土耳其、前苏联、南斯拉夫等国家和地区引起灾难性的损失。在保加利亚，感病品种中有80%-100%提前落果，1968年损失约鲜重30,000吨，在某些年份，损失高达60,000吨。在波兰，李痘病毒使普通洋李品种因为提早落果和果实变小而减产50%以上。在前捷克斯洛伐克，平均产量下降83.4%。
description:
机械接种传毒；嫁接传毒；植株间接触不传毒。
介体传毒:主要传毒介体有Brachycaudusc cardui(蓟短尾蚜)、Brachycaudusc helichrysi(桃短尾蚜)、Phorodon humuli(忽布疣额蚜)、Myzus persicae(桃蚜)；还有：Aphis craccivora、Aphis spiraecola 、Myzus varians、Myzus humuli等以非持久方式传播病毒。
种子和花粉可以传毒，但因寄主而异。杏(Prunus armeniaca)和桃(Prunus persica)种传。杏树、桃树、李树种子传毒率为13.9%，花粉传毒率是20%-80%。但李树有的品种病毒不能通过种子传播。
remark:
将李痘病毒列为检疫对象的国家和地区有：前南斯拉夫、挪威、罗马尼亚、荷兰、瑞典、西班牙、丹麦、马耳他、埃及、前苏联、土耳其、加拿大、欧洲地中海、希腊、英国、大不列颠。俄罗斯把李痘病毒(PPV)作为当代检疫难题之一来看待。
1997年我国将李痘病毒列入进境检疫三类有害生物名录。2007年我国将该病毒作为检疫性有害生物，对其依法实施检疫。

host_range:
The main woody hosts are the fruit-producing species of Prunus, including apricots ( Prunus armeniaca ), peaches ( Prunus persica ) and plums ( Prunusdomestica, Prunussalicina and Prunuscerasifera ). Almonds ( Prunusdulcis ) can be infected with PPV, but show few, if any, natural symptoms ( Festic, 1978 ; Llácer and Cambra, 2006). Almond trees in Chile were naturally infected with PPV ( Herrera et al., 1998 ), but similar surveys in France failed to demonstrate natural infection by PPV in almond. Isolates of the D and M serotypes were transmitted experimentally to different cherry species, but infection remained localized and the virus was not shown to be translocated ( Dosba et al., 1987 ). However, a Pennsylvanian isolate of PPV was transmitted to several ornamental flowering cherries and sweet cherry ( Prunus avium ) by aphids and grafting, with symptom development and subsequent back-transfer to peach ( Damsteegt et al., 2007 ).^p^Natural infections of Prunus cerasus (sour cherry) and P. avium with PPV-C in four European countries have been reported ( Crescenzi et al., 1994, 1995, 1997; Nemchinov and Hadidi, 1996 ; Nemchinov et al., 1996, 1998a, c). PPV-C has been transmitted by grafting or vectors to other stone fruit species ( Kalashyan et al., 1994 ; Nemchinov et al., 1996, 1998c; Crescenzi et al., 1997 ).

Most wild or ornamental species of Prunus can be experimentally infected by PPV-D through aphid feeding and grafting ( Damsteegt et al., 2007 ).^p^p^Natural secondary hosts^p^Prunus spinosa (blackthorn) was long considered to be a natural host of PPV. Results obtained in the former Yugoslavia did not confirm this (Rankovic and Dulic-Markovic, 1992); however, it has been shown to be a systemic host in France ( Labonne et al., 2004 ) and the Czech Republic (Polak, 2004). In addition, Polak (2001) reported natural infection in Ligustrum vulgare (European privet) and Euonymus europaea (European spindletree). Other reported natural hosts are P. avium, Prunus besseyi (bessey cherry), P. cerasifera (myrobalan plum), Prunus tomentosa (Nanking cherry tree), Prunus glandulosa (flowering almond), Prunus japonica (Japanese bush cherry tree), Prunus serotina (black cherry) and Prunus x blireiana (prunier double) (James and Thompson, 2006).^p^Susceptible Prunus spp. are widely grown for fruit production (varieties and rootstocks) worldwide and throughout all European parts of the EPPO region. Wild woody and herbaceous hosts are widespread and are potential reservoirs of the pathogen, although a direct contribution of these hosts to the epidemiology of PPV has never been clearly demonstrated. Numerous cultivated or weedy annual plants have been shown to be experimental and natural hosts of PPV (Nemeth, 1986; Milusheva and Rankova, 2002 ; Viršcek et al., 2004 ; Llácer, 2006 ).
potential_eco_desc:
Impact: Economic^p^P^PPV is an EPPO A2 quarantine pest (OEPP/ EPPO, 1983, 1990, 2004). It is also considered to be a quarantine pest by IAPSC and NAPPO ( Foster and Hadidi, 1998 ; Thompson, 1998 ). In the EPPO region, it presents a major risk to apricots ( Prunus armeniaca ), plums and peaches ( Prunus persica ) in many countries where it is still absent or very localized ( Diekmann and Putter, 1996 ). In addition, its presence in a country creates difficulties for the export of certified planting material. An EPPO quarantine procedure for PPV has been prepared (OEPP/EPPO, 1992).
Németh (1994), Kegler and Hartmann (1998) and Nemchinov et al. (1998a) have reviewed the importance of plum pox on European stone-fruit production. Sharka disease is particularly serious in the fruit-producing areas of central and eastern Europe. During the past decade, it has progressively spread to some Mediterranean countries such as Egypt ( Wetzel et al., 1991a ; Mazyad et al., 1992 ), Spain (Llácer et al., 1985) and Portugal ( Louro and Monte Corvo, 1986 ). It has also been reported from Chile ( Herrera et al., 1998 ). Virus infection can lead to considerable yield losses, reaching 83-100% in highly susceptible varieties ( Kegler and Hartmann, 1998 ; Nemchinov et al., 1998a ; Waterworth and Hadidi, 1998 ). European plums ( Prunus domestica ) may show premature fruit drop, while Japanese plums ( Prunus salicina ) and peaches show ring spotting on fruit, and apricots show serious fruit deformation. The disease impact is, however, modulated to a large extent by the variability in susceptibility/tolerance shown by individual cultivars of its Prunus host species. Sweet cherry ( Prunus avium ) fruits undergo premature fruit dropping and leaves develop chlorotic and necrotic ring spots or notches ( Nemchinov et al., 1998a ). An evaluation of the global cost associated with plum pox management worldwide, excluding indirect trade costs, has been estimated at 10,000 million euros (Cambra et al., 2006).^p^p^Impact: Environmental^p^Because of a loss of value of the trees, orchards are removed much earlier than normal. Often areas are taken out of production of either certain varieties or fruit species that may change the agricultural pattern for a given area.^p^p^Impact: Social^p^The greatest impact caused by PPV is economic. It does not actually kill trees by itself, but renders the fruit unpalatable. The fruit do not pose a health problem for humans or animals.

management_info: There is no anti-virus treatment available to control sharka disease in orchards. However, there are considerable differences in susceptibility between the cultivars available for use in countries where infection is widespread (Hamdorf, 1986; Kegler et al., 1989; Mainou and Syrgianidis, 1992). Biological control by inoculation of trees with hypo-aggressive strains has not been as successful in the field as under controlled conditions (Kerlan et al., 1980).^p^pOther effective control methods are to produce healthy plants for planting within a certification system, to control aphid vectors by regular treatment with aphicides, and to destroy diseased trees in orchards. Such methods are being used to contain PPV in several countries (for example, France and Italy) (Barba, 1998; Kegler and Hartmann, 1998). ^p^pEPPO recommends a certification scheme for fruit trees, which takes account of PPV (OEPP/EPPO, 1991/1992). Resistance to PPV has been reviewed by Dosba et al. (1994) and Kegler and Hartmann (1998) and this approach shows some promise, whether by traditional breeding or selection by transgenic methods (Camara Machado et al., 1992b; Escalettes et al., 1994; Ravelonandro et al., 1998; Scorza et al., 1998). New PPV-resistant plum, apricot, peach, and nectarine cultivars were bred or selected with different types or mechanisms of PPV-resistance (Hartmann, 1998; Kegler and Hartmann, 1998; Lahmatova et al., 1998; Paprtsein et al., 1998; Polak, 1998; Rankovi and Paunovi , 1989; Toma et al., 1998).^p^pEPPO recommends that all imported host material (except seeds) should come from a field subject to growing-season inspection. If the virus is present in the exporting country, this inspection should also concern the immediate vicinity of the field, and the material should derive from tested mother plants (OEPP/EPPO, 1990).

potential_eco_desc: 栎枯萎病是栎树上的毁灭性病害，对各种树龄的树均能造成危害。该病发展迅速，可使病树在表现症状后几周内死亡，一旦形成发病中心，即以每年11～16m的速度在局部地区扩展，极难根治。
description: 通过树根之间的接触、媒介昆虫传播，原木、木材及苗木的运输行远距离传播。
management_info:
1. 必须严格禁止有病栎树(包括苗木、木材及原木)的进口。许多国家规定，进口栎树木材和原木，必须来自发病地区80km以外的无病栎树。
2. 彻底消毁病树、切断病健树根部接触和消灭传病介体是3个主要的防治途径。具体做法是，先彻底消毁病株，随后将其周围15m内的健株清除掉(也可用1:3威百亩浇入环树挖成的洞内，使之迅速枯死)。为消灭传病介体，除喷施杀虫剂外，还可在树干中注入卡可酸(cacodylio acid)，浓度为14.4%，药量为dbh(树干胸高直径)×80ml/cm以下。
3. 在发病初期或作为预防措施，注射丙环唑(propiconazole)可有较好的效果。
4. 为防止介体昆虫传病，应尽量减少各种伤口的形成，在冬季中期至初夏，可将伤口包扎起来或是涂上一层涂抹剂。
5. 对于原木中所带病菌，可用240g/m3的溴甲烷在3℃或3℃以上熏蒸3天的方法来消除。

remark: Atropellis spp. are regulated by the European Union (EU, 2000) and by various EPPO countries (Russia, Turkey) as A1 quarantine pests. They present a hazard to exotic Pinus spp. such as P. contorta and P. strobus, which are hosts in North America and have been planted in other continents. The European species P. nigra and P. sylvestris have been observed to be susceptible when planted in North America, and so are certainly at risk in their native range.^p^pPhytosanitary measures: EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) recommends that importing countries should prohibit import of plants for planting, and isolated bark, of Pinus from North America. If isolated bark of Pinus is imported from North America, the consignment should have been heat-treated. If wood of Pinus is imported from North America, the consignment should have been debarked or kiln-dried.^p^pThere is no evidence that Atropellis spp. have ever been carried by wood packing. However, wood is liable to carry these pests in international trade.

host_range: Solanum tuberosum cv. Russet Burbank.
description: Ten tubers of potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) cv. Russet Burbank grown in southern Alberta that exhibited internal brown spots and arcs typical of infection by Potato mop-top virus (PMTV) or Tobacco rattle virus (TRV) were collected in June 2016 from commercial potato storage. The samples were tested by RT-PCR and DAS-ELISA showed PMTV is present in southern Alberta. This is the first report of PMTV infecting potatoes in Alberta.  PMTV is transmitted by the soilborne powdery scab pathogen, Spongospora subterranean, which is widespread and occurs in most major potato growing areas.
reference_name: First Report of Potato mop-top virus Infecting Potatoes in Alberta

description: During the summer season of 2012, native potato (Solanum tuberosum L. ssp. tuberosum) leaves showing virus-like symptoms were collected on several points within the Chiloé Archipelago (Chiloé Province, southern Chile), one of the centers of origin and diversity of cultivated potatoes. // Subsequently, three farms growing native potatoes (local varieties Michu?e negra, Michu?e roja, and Clavela lisa) with symptoms associated with Potato mop-top virus (PMTV) infections were identified in Puqueldón (Lemuy Island, Chiloé Province) during the summers of 2013 and 2014. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PMTV in Chile. However, the powdery scab pathogen, S. subterranea f. sp. subterranea, is widespread in the potato-production areas near Chiloé Province. These results provide important and cautionary information to be considered by programs managing seed tuber production and plant quarantine for potato pathogens in Chile.  PMTV is transmitted by spores of Spongospora subterranea f. sp. subterranea, the causal agent of powdery scab of potato. S. subterranea f. sp. subterranean is widespread in the potato-production areas near Chiloé Province.
reference_name: First Report of Potato mop-top virus in Chile

description: Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) tubers cv. FL2048 and cv. Atlantic were sent to the laboratory from fields in Saguache County in Colorado and in San Juan County in New Mexico, respectively, during the spring of 2013. The tubers from both locations had multiple, internal, concentric, necrotic arcs and circles. The test demonstrated that the causal agent was Potato mop-top virus  (PMTV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of PMTV in potato in states of Colorado and New Mexico.  Potato mop-top virus  (PMTV) is an important pathogen of potato vectored by the plasmodiophorid Spongospora subterranea f. sp. subterranea (Sss), which causes powdery scab of potato. Sss and PMTV are usually associated with cool and humid environments.
reference_name: First Report of Potato mop top virus Causing Potato Tuber Necrosis in Colorado and New Mexico

host_range: Potato mop-top virus was first characterised by Calvert and Harrison (1966) and potato is probably the only important host plant at least in Scotland (Jones and Harrison, 1972).Artificial HostsHarrison and Jones (1970) reported the most comprehensive analysis of the experimental host range of Potato mop-top virus. Nineteen of twenty species of Solanaceae, seven of eight species of Chenopodiaceae, and Tetragonia expansa can be infected by the virus following manual inoculation of sap. Systemic infection was found only in the following solanaceous species: Datura stramonium, Lycopersicon esculentum cv. Kondine Red, Nicotiana benthamiana, N. debneyi, N. clevelandii, N. glutinosa, N. megalosiphon, N. rustica, N. tabacum cvs Xanthi-nc and White Burley, and Physalis floridana.
potential_eco_desc: Potato mop-top virus infection of potato has been reported to cause a decrease in crop yield but the most serious effect in Europe is on crop quality particularly in varieties that are widely used for processing (Sandgren, 1995).
author: CPC2006

description: Vector Transmission^p^pPotato mop-top virus is spread by the plasmodiophoromycete fungus Spongospora subterranea (Jones and Harrison, 1969; Arif et al., 1995) and survives for long periods in resting spores (Jones and Harrison, 1972). Factors affecting the germination of resting spores of S. subterranea are unclear but once germinated the resulting zoospores remain motile for 48 hours at 15°C, and although they can probably only swim a few centimetres they are probably carried much further by the movement of water through soil (Harrison et al., 1997). Vector transmission of the virus therefore probably occurs only over short distances within a field.^p^p^Seedborne Spread^p^pThere is no evidence for transmission of Potato mop-top virus in true seed of potato.^p^p^Agricultural Practices^p^pOne method of preventing virus infection is to avoid growing potato crops in fields that have been identified as containing viruliferous S. subterranea. The persistence of the virus in resting spores of S. subterranea could mean that it would be impossible to grow potato in such fields for many years.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants: borne internally; invisible.^p - Leaves: borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Roots: borne internally; invisible.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; visible to naked eye.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Soil, Gravel, Water, Etc.: Soil From Field Where Virus Is Endemic (Sandgren 1995)

management_info: Not all the tubers produced by an infected plant will themselves be infected. It is thus possible that rigorous roguing of symptom-bearing plants combined with growth on virus-free soil can lead to rapid elimination of the virus from stocks of certain cultivars (Cooper et al., 1976). Control of the vector, Spongospora subterranea in soil or on infected tubers is possible by treatment with a variety of chemicals but is likely only to be effective at low inoculum levels and the chemicals involved are not environmentally acceptable (Harrison et al., 1997). There are no sources of resistance or tolerance to Potato mop-top virus that have been deliberately used in breeding programmes to produce resistant cultivars (Barker et al., 1998b). An extremely effective source of resistance has been produced by transformation of N. benthamiana with the coat protein gene of the virus (Reavy et al., 1995). This resistance seems to operate by a novel mechanism (Barker et al., 1998b) and is also effective in potato (Barker et al., 1998a). The coat protein genes of different isolates of Potato mop-top virus are highly conserved (Mayo et al., 1996; Reavy et al., 1997) and the resistance conferred by the coat protein gene of a Scottish isolate is also effective against Scandinavian isolates (Reavy et al., 1997). This transgenic resistance is not yet commercially available.

host_range: This is the first report of Potato virus V on tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) orchards of Ecuador.
description: In Ecuador, tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) disorders caused by potyviruses have been reported in the past. In 2013, leaves from tamarillo plants showing severe virus-like symptoms (mosaic, mottling, and leaf deformation) were collected from orchards in Pichincha and Tungurahua. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) was extracted from three independent batches and used to generate cDNA libraries to screen for RNA viruses by shotgun cloning. Sequencing revealed the presence of the potyviruses Potato virus Y (PVY), Potato virus V (PVV), and Peru tomato mosaic virus (PTV), and the polerovirus Potato leaf roll virus (PLRV). To determine the occurrence of the viruses, leaf samples tested by RT-PCR. Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription was done. For symptomatic plants, PVY and PLRV were the most common with 64% and 30%, respectively. PVV and PTV were found in 8% and 10%, respectively, with only 4% of the plants coinfected by both viruses. Plants coinfected by PVY and PLRV were the most common with 22%, followed by plants coinfected by PVY and PTV (10%). PVY has long been considered the most common virus in tamarillo in Ecuador. This communication reports for the first time in tamarillo the presence of PVV and PTV, two potyviruses once considered strains of PVY. Further studies are needed to determine the significance of PVV and PTV in single and mixed infections in tamarillo.
reference_name: First Report of Potato virus V and Peru tomato mosaic virus on Tamarillo (Solanum betaceum) Orchards of Ecuador

host_range: PYDV principally occurs in wild Solanaceae and has been transmitted experimentally to species in the families Apocynaceae, Asteraceae, Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Lamiaceae, Polygonaceae and Scrophulariaceae (Black, 1970; OEPP/EPPO, 1980). Yellow dwarf disease caused by PYDV has become more difficult to find in potato (Solanum tuberosum) recently. However, the virus was identified sporadically in periwinkle plants (Catharanthus roseus) in California, USA (Falk et al., 1981), and from diseased ornamental tobacco (Nicotiana alata), marigold (Tagetes erecta), zinnia (Zinnia elegans), and four-o‘ clock (Mirabilis jalapa) in Minnesota, USA, from 1986-88 (Lockhart, 1989). PYDV is the only leafhopper-borne virus that is mechanically transmissible and induces local lesions in inoculated leaves.
potential_eco_desc: PYDV is not primarily a pathogen of potato and occurs only sporadically in the crop. It had not been detected in the mid-west of the USA for 40 years, until a recent outbreak occurred on ornamental plants (not on potato) (Lockhart, 1989). The virus is more of academic significance rather than economic importance.
reference_name: Potato yellow dwarf virus (yellow dwarf of potato)
author: CPC2006

description: Vector Transmission^p^pPYDV is spread locally by its insect vectors. The virus can overwinter in adult vectors even in the absence of food plants. Transmission is in a persistent manner. The virus is retained when the vector moults. Two vector-specific serotypes of PYDV are known (Black, 1941). SYDV is transmitted by Aceratogallia sanguinolenta but not by Agallia constricta, and CYDV has an inverse vector relationship (Black, 1970). Other leafhoppers including Agallia quadripunctata transmit both SYDV and CYDV but with different efficiencies.^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pPYDV is carried by potato tubers, but not by true seed. In principle, PYDV could be carried by potato tubers in international trade.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark^p - Fruits (inc. remark: PYDV is included among the non-European potato viruses of the EPPO A1 quarantine list (OEPP/EPPO, 1984). It does not, however, originate in the high-risk centre of diversity of potato in South America, but in North America where it appears to infect potatoes only incidentally and very sporadically and is not regarded as a significant problem for potato production. The virus appears to survive more as a laboratory curiosity than as a real problem in the field. It can therefore be regarded as of very minor importance for the EPPO region. There is, however, a perceived risk of the introduction of PYDV into seed-potato production schemes, causing some difficulties with respect to the phytosanitary certification of exports.^p^pPYDV can be relatively easily excluded by prohibition of commercial trade in potato tubers. The risk of introduction with breeding material is minor, since it is not carried by true seed, and besides would probably cause obvious symptoms on material held in quarantine.
reference_name: Potato yellow dwarf virus (yellow dwarf of potato)
author: CPC2006

management_info: No particular measures are needed in practice to control PYDV. However, as with all potato viruses, high-quality seed potatoes must be derived from virus-free nuclear stock, including freedom from PYDV.Seed potatoes from countries where PYDV occurs should fully meet the requirements of an official virus certification scheme covering PYDV. Ware potatoes for processing and consumption should be treated to suppress the possibility of germination.
reference_name: Potato yellow dwarf virus (yellow dwarf of potato)

remark: PNRSV does not have a quarantine status. In certain countries PNRSV was spread among orchards by transferring bee-hives from contaminated areas. More generally, infected budwood, rootstock seeds and seedlings, and grafted nursery material are responsible for virus dissemination within and among the countries where it occurs.
reference_name: Prunus necrotic ringspot virus (almond bud failure)
author: CPC2006

management_info: Traditional Prunus rootstocks are tolerant to PNRSV (Digiaro et al., 1992; Lang et al., 1997). Cultivated Prunus species are usually not tolerant and a search for resistance genes for breeding purposes was not successful (Heuss et al., 1998). Orchard management practices such as removal of diseased plants, avoiding use of commercial bee-hives previously employed in other orchards, and use of virus-free wood for topworking, can prevent or contain tree to tree virus spread (Mink, 1995). Stone fruit trees grown for the production of virus-tested seeds and scionwood must be planted in areas isolated from possible sources of infection (Fridlund, 1976). Use of certified virus-tested or sanitized material is recommended for establishing orchards (Mink, 1995; Martelli and Savino, 1997). PNRSV-free stocks can be obtained by thermotherapy with hot air (Quacquarelli and Martelli, 1972; Navarro et al., 1997), hot water (Pandey et al., 1972), shoot tip grafting in vitro (Juarez et al., 1989; Navarro et al., 1997), and meristem tip culture alone (Deogratias et al., 1989; Knapp et al., 1995) or in combination with thermotherapy (Spiegel et al., 1995; Gella and Errea, 1998).
reference_name: Prunus necrotic ringspot virus (almond bud failure)

potential_eco_desc: 几乎所有的李属植物都能受其侵害，造成坏死，皱缩、花叶、环斑等。特别是造成苗圃严重病状。

PNRSV能通过减少花芽的数量以及生产的质量和数量来严重侵染桃的生产，超过95％的作物损失(Schmitt et al., 1981; Lazarova-Topchiiska, 1984; Wood et al., 1997)。减少超过60％的生长和产量在酸和甜樱桃上观测得到(Kajati and Szonyegi, 1966; Hilsendengen, 1999)，平均25％的损失从受杏仁花叶侵染得杏仁中被记录，这是一个含有PNRSV的复合的病害(Martelli and Savino, 1997)。 PNRSV can severely affect peach production by reducing the number of flower buds and the quality and quantity of the yield with losses of up to 95% of the crop (Schmitt et al., 1981; Lazarova-Topchiiska, 1984; Wood et al., 1997). Growth and yield reduction up to 60% was observed in sour and sweet cherries (Kajati and Szonyegi, 1966; Hilsendengen, 1999), and average losses of 25% were recorded from almond affected by almond mosaic, a complex disease in which PNRSV is involved (Martelli and Savino, 1997).
author: zhangjianjun

description:
PNRSV是嫁接传播和持续存在于所有寄主品种德繁殖材料（芽木、根砧木和嫁接苗圃植物）中。该病毒在一些李属品种(Garret et al., 1985; Mink, 1995)和在栽秧泡（Rubus ellipticus） (Anupama et al., 1998)中也是花粉传播的，在外部被携带，内部在花粉粒中(Cole et al., 1982; Hamilton et al., 1984; Digiaro and Savino, 1992; Aparicio et al., 1999b)。虽然发育能力有所减少(Marenaud and Saunier, 1974)，但感染的花粉被看作是病毒自然传播的主要原因，它是以授粉昆虫为媒介，特别是蜜蜂(George and Davidson, 1963; Davidson, 1976)。
在温室实验中，PNRSV能通过烟蓟马（Thrips tabaci ）和其他蓟马（包括西花蓟马（Frankliniella occidentalis））携带来自感染来源的花粉而传播到黄瓜中去，但不能传播给桃幼苗。这发现(Greber et al., 1991, 1992)是否有任何病毒流行的实际蕴涵目前还未确定(Milne and Walter, 1997)。
该病毒在田间的传播可能是非常快速的。在美国纽约州，在四年中一个樱桃果园中的从2％增加到78％的侵染被记录(Klos and Parker 1960)。在加州的一个桃果园中，侵染的发生率在13年中从27％增加到92％(Uyemoto et al., 1992)。在澳大利亚，啤酒花的侵染在6年中从2％增加到60％(Pethybridge et al., 1998)，以及在新西兰在两年中17％的啤酒花侵染(Hay et al., 1992)。 PNRSV is graft-transmissible and persists in propagative material (budwood, rootstocks and grafted nursery plants) of all host species. The virus is also pollen-borne in several Prunus species (Garret et al., 1985; Mink, 1995) and in Rubus ellipticus (Anupama et al., 1998), being carried externally and internally on pollen grains (Cole et al., 1982; Hamilton et al., 1984; Digiaro and Savino, 1992; Aparicio et al., 1999b). Notwithstanding a reduced viability (Marenaud and Saunier, 1974), infected pollen is regarded as the major agent of virus spread which, in nature, is mediated by pollinating insects, especially honeybees (George and Davidson, 1963; Davidson, 1976). 
In glasshouse experiments, PNRSV was transmitted to cucumber but not to peach seedlings by Thrips tabaci and other thrips, including Frankliniella occidentalis, carrying pollen from infected sources (Greber et al., 1991, 1992). Whether this finding has any practical implication on virus epidemiology has not been determined (Milne and Walter, 1997). 
Virus spread in the field can be very fast. An increase from 2 to 78% infection was registered in four years in a cherry orchard in New York State, USA (Klos and Parker 1960). In a Californian peach orchard, infection incidence increased by 82% in 13 years (Schmitt et al., 1981), and in another it increased from 27 to 92% in 4 years (Uyemoto et al., 1992). Infection in hop increased from 2 to 60% in 6 years in Australia (Pethybridge et al., 1998) and by 17% in 2 years in New Zealand (Hay et al., 1992).

description:

The virus is also pollen-borne in several Prunus species (Garret et al., 1985; Mink, 1995) and in Rubus ellipticus (Anupama et al., 1998), being carried externally and internally on pollen grains (Cole et al., 1982; Hamilton et al., 1984; Digiaro and Savino, 1992; Aparicio et al., 1999b). Notwithstanding a reduced viability (Marenaud and Saunier, 1974), infected pollen is regarded as the major agent of virus spread which, in nature, is mediated by pollinating insects, especially honeybees (George and Davidson, 1963; Davidson, 1976). 
In glasshouse experiments, PNRSV was transmitted to cucumber but not to peach seedlings by Thrips tabaci and other thrips, including Frankliniella occidentalis, carrying pollen from infected sources (Greber et al., 1991, 1992). Whether this finding has any practical implication on virus epidemiology has not been determined (Milne and Walter, 1997).
