(1980)发现是有效的。温热疗法和萌芽叶腋培养上也被报道出在估计PSTVd是有效的(Stace-Smith and Mellor, 1970)。 Elimination of PSTVd by low temperature treatments (5-8℃) of infected plants and subsequent meristem culture was found to be effective by Lizarraga et al. (1980). Thermotherapy and axillary bud culture was also reported to be effective in eliminating PSTVd (Stace-Smith and Mellor, 1970). 没有对于PSTVd有效的化学防治被报道出来。 No effective chemical control for PSTVd has been reported. 没有已知的对于PSTVd有自发抗性发生在马铃薯的栽培作物上。Solanum acaule OCH 11603对于通过自然传入的PSTVd有抗性，但随着含有PSTVd农杆菌感染的cDNAs而易染病(Salazar et al., 1988b)。因此，它存在“田间抗性”，但不含有真正免疫性。一些抗病的根源已在马铃薯上被报道出来(Harris et al., 1979; Pfannenstiel and Slack, 1980)，但类病毒依然出现在复制上虽然没有症状出现。这些植物因此而忍耐，对于PSTVd的侵染无抗性。Singh (1985)也报道了通过汁液嫁接接芽的Solanum berthaultii复制品对于PSTVd有抗性，但不预防接种。
最近尝试建造马铃薯植株对于PSTVd的抗性已显示出一些成功。Yang et al. (1997)表达了在遗传工程马铃薯植株上对于PSTVd的核酶，在34条测试中的23个有效的抗性基因。Sano et al. (1997)表达了在马铃薯上的一个特定双链RNA核糖核酸酶并且这些植株确实了一些对于感染PSTVd的抗性，类似在一些植株上所显示的缺少的侵染，及在类病毒浓度和症状上的减少。实用和被采用的防治PSTVd技术需要较深入的测试
类病毒能通过交互保护互相对抗，至少在一些结合体上(Niblett et al., 1978)。Singh et al. (1993a)发现了在通过嫁接2个侵染马铃薯栽培种类上的再侵染的植株而获得的PSTVd强烈种类是没有干预的。然而，他们建议这在通过机械接芽的初侵染阶段能发生的。 No known naturally occurring resistance to PSTVd occurs in cultivars of potato. Solanum acaule OCH 11603 is resistant to mechanical inoculation by PSTVd, but was susceptible following agroinfection with PSTVd-containing cDNAs (Salazar et al., 1988b). It therefore exhibits “field resistance”, but not true immunity. Some sources of resistance have been reported in potatoes (Harris et al., 1979; Pfannenstiel and Slack, 1980), but the viroid still appears to replicate even though no symptoms are evident. These plants are therefore tolerant, not resistant, to PSTVd infection. Singh (1985) also reported that clones of Solanum berthaultii are resistant to PSTVd by sap graft inoculation, but not inoculation.
Recent attempts to engineer potato plants resistant to PSTVd have shown some success. Yang et al. (1997) expressed a ribozyme to PSTVd in transgenic potato plants, with effective resistance in 23 of 34 lines tested. Sano et al. (1997) expressed a double-stranded RNA specific ribonuclease in potato and these plants conferred some resistance to PSTVd infection as shown by the lack of infection in some plants, and a reduction in viroid concentration and symptoms. The utility and adoption of this technology for control of PSTVd awaits further testing.
Viroids are able to cross-protect against one another, at least in some combinations (Niblett et al., 1978). Singh et al. (1993a) observed no interference between mild and severe strains of PSTVd in secondarily infected plants obtained by grafting two infected potato cultivars together. However, they suggest that it may occur in the initial infection step made by mechanical inoculation. PSTVd最有效的防治方法是防止受感染的材料引入到田间，i.e.确定为没类病毒的耕作材料及其他材料的使用和保持清洁的栽培耕作(Singh and Crowley, 1985a; Harris and James, 1987; Salazar, 1989)。其他防治方法包括通过来自尖端培养的分生组织蓄积栽培作物PSTVd的估计及抗性栽培作物的发展(see also Maramorosch, 1985)。
PSTVd能通过处理工具在2%的氢氧化钠溶液中被破坏(Maramorosch, 1985)但这对于大的栽培作物配置处理是不适用的。 The most effective means of control of PSTVd is prevention of introduction of infected materials into the field, i.e. the use of materials certified as viroid-free as planting material and the maintenance of sanitary cultural practices (Singh and Crowley, 1985a; Harris and James, 1987; Salazar, 1989). Other methods of control include elimination of PSTVd from stock cultivars by meristem tip culture and the develop of resistant cultivars (see also Maramorosch, 1985).
PSTVd can be destroyed by treatment of tools in a 2% sodium hydroxide solution (Maramorosch, 1985) but this is not practical for the treatment of large cultivation equipment.
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc:
PSTVd已在几种采集的种质马铃薯(TPS)和繁殖方式(Cammack and Harris, 1973; Salazar et al., 1983; Grasmick and Slack, 1986, 1987)上有用的马铃薯种子找到。它也同时地从这些采集物上消除(Scottish Plant Breeding Station, 1976; Schwinghammer et al., 1983)。PSTVd已报道来自中国近亲交配的TPS高达 70%的水平，及在储藏了21年的TPS上找到(Singh et al., 1991)。
来自可用的马铃薯和花粉的全部核酸上，使用RT-PCR来诊查类病毒 (Shamloul et al., 1997)。Singh et al. (1992)给来自由于在花序基部染病叶片，顶端叶片和块茎上的感染PSTVd的植株上带有花粉的健康Katahdin植株授粉。果实的电脉分析指示出PSTVd在萼片上，果皮和果肉上偶尔发生的侵染。来自每个果实上可用的马铃薯种子有35-66%受到PSTVd的浸染。随着个体植株而变化的种子侵染百分比和花序位置或在相同花序所产生的果实数量是不受影响的。 PSTVd has been found in true potato seed (TPS) of several potato germplasm collections and breeding lines (Cammack and Harris, 1973; Salazar et al., 1983; Grasmick and Slack, 1986, 1987). It has also been eliminated from these collections (Scottish Plant Breeding Station, 1976; Schwinghammer et al., 1983). PSTVd has been reported at levels of up to 70% in seedlots of TPS from inbred lines in China, and was found in TPS stored for 21 years (Singh et al., 1991).
The viroid was also detected using RT-PCR from total nucleic acid in true potato seed and pollen. (Shamloul et al., 1997). Singh et al. (1992) pollinated the flowers of healthy Katahdin plants with pollen from PSTVd-infected plants resulting in infection of leaves at the base of inflorescences, apical leaves and tubers. Electrophoretic analysis of fruits indicated sporadic PSTVd infection of sepals, fruit skin and fruit pulp. True potato seed from each fruit was 35-66% infected with PSTVd. Percentage of seed infection varied with individual plants and was not affected by the location of an inflorescence or by the number of fruits produced on the same inflorescence. 几种报道提供了受到PSTVd感染的马铃薯田间损失量。Le Clerg et al. (1944) 确定了田间市场块茎不同数量的PSTVd的影响。31个在美国几个州的5个不同种类的试验，侵染4%的水平引起了2.6%的市场块茎的损失，这包括了田间影响和作物的市场品质。超过24%的块茎产量减少已在受到PSTVd 温和种类侵染的Saco栽培作物上发生(Singh et al., 1971)。然而，严重种类减少了产量达到64%。估计增加到4.6%在Russet Burbank栽培种类上的发生率已被发现。以几个要素为基础，Singh et al. (1971)估计一个全部马铃薯作物1%的损失。Pfannenstiel 和Slack (1980)更多的近期学说显示了马铃薯栽培作物块茎重量的减少和它们受到PSTVd侵染的时间长度。块茎侵染了一到三年后的每株植株块茎的重量有显著的减少。 Several reports attribute losses in potato yield to infection by PSTVd. Le Clerg et al. (1944) determined the effect of different amounts of PSTVd on yield of marketable tubers. In 31 trials with five varieties in several states of the USA, a 4% level of infection resulted in a loss of marketable tubers of 2.6%, which includes effects on the yield and market quality of the crop. Up to 24% reductions in tuber yield have been reported in cultivar Saco infected with mild strains of PSTVd (Singh et al., 1971). However, the severe strain reduced the yield by up to 64%. Estimates of up to 4.6% incidence in cultivar Russet Burbank were observed. Based upon a number of factors, Singh et al. (1971) estimate an overall loss of 1% of the potato crop. More recent studies by Pfannenstiel and Slack (1980) showed that reduction of tuber weight depended on the potato cultivar and the length of time they were infected with PSTVd. There was a significant decrease in tuber weight per plant from the first to the third year that the tubers were infected.
author: zhangjianjun

description:
PSTVd逐渐通过植物种子和番茄及马铃薯的花粉传播(Benson and Singh, 1964; Hunter et al., 1969; Singh, 1970)。
PSTVd容易由机械传播。Bonde 和 Merriam (1951)发现传播能够发生在受到使用了染病汁液所污染的修剪工具的块茎繁殖上，受到污染的幼嫩块茎嫩芽引起了最高传染百分率。Merriam 和 Bonde (1954)发现当拖拉机轮胎受到染病汁液污染后而引起十分激烈的染病的马铃薯植株里，80-100% PSTVd在田间传播到健康马铃薯植株上。Manzer和 Merriam (1961)发现几乎100%受到栽培和堆土工具的传播，在那里大株的植物是存在的，及当植株较小是和当栽培物在早季里种植是非常小的传播才发生。
de Bokx和 Pirone (1981) 证明了由大戟长管蚜，而不是由烟蚜或马铃薯长须蚜所引起的低机率。然而，烟蚜在植株间传播PSTVd加倍地受到PSTVd和马铃薯卷叶病毒(PLRV) (Salazar et al., 1995)的影响。它已随后地显示出在极小量PLRV 发生的PSTVd异源性衣壳化，及能够解释出可观察到的昆虫传播。这对于在马铃薯田间PSTVd的流行和传播有重要含义(Querci et al., 1997)。 PSTVd is readily transmitted through botanical seed and pollen of tomato and potato (Benson and Singh, 1964; Hunter et al., 1969; Singh, 1970).
PSTVd is easily mechanically transmitted. Bonde and Merriam (1951) found that transmission could occur when infectious sap contaminated cutting knives used for tuber propagation, with contamination of young tuber sprouts with infectious sap resulting in the highest percentage of infection. Merriam and Bonde (1954) found 80-100% field transmission of PSTVd to healthy potato plants when tractor wheels became contaminated with infectious sap due to bruising of diseased potato plants. Manzer and Merriam (1961) found nearly 100% transmission with cultivating and hilling equipment, where large plants were present, and very little transmission when plants were smaller and when cultivation was performed earlier in the season.
de Bokx and Pirone (1981) demonstrated a low rate of transmission by the aphid Macrosiphum euphorbiae but not by Myzus persicae or Aulacorthum solani. However, Myzus persicae transmitted PSTVd in plants doubly infected with PSTVd and potato leafroll luteovirus (PLRV) (Salazar et al., 1995). It has subsequently been shown that heterologous encapsidation of PSTVd in particles of PLRV occurs, and may explain the observed insect transmission. This has important implications for epidemiology and spread of PSTVd in potato fields (Querci et al., 1997).

description: In 2015, we found lotus plants with late germination, early dormancy, decline growth, thin stems, and deep colored, spotted, and striped leaves in Jiangsu province of China. These symptoms seriously affected the quantity and quality of lotus. To identify pathogens associated with lotus samples of cultivar Meirenhong that exhibited yellowing and mosaic symptoms during June to September 2015. Based on RT-PCR and ELISA tests confirming the presence of Apple stem grooving virus (ASGV) and indicating the ASGV infection is common in lotus. To our knowledge, this is the first report of ASGV in lotus in China.

description: In order to validate whether viruses presenting on apple trees in Ethiopia, the samples were collected from different cultivars growing in the southwest part of the country in October 2015. Based on RT-PCR and ELISA tests confirmed Apple stem grooving virus (ASGV), Apple stem pitting virus (ASPV), Apple chlorotic leaf spot virus (ACLSV) in apple trees. To our knowledge, this is the first report of mixed infections of ASGV, ASPV, and ACLSV in apple trees growing in Ethiopia.

host_range: ASGV infect Rosa chinensis and R. multiflora in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China.
description: Apple stem grooving virus (ASGV) was recently found infecting wild rose (Rosa multiflora). In order to grasp whether other roses were infected by the ASGV, eight asymptomatic and seven symptomatic (showing rosette leaf) samples of R. rugosa(6 samples), R. chinensis grown on their roots (4), and R. multiflora (5) were collected from Wuhan, Hubei Province, China.  Total RNA was extracted and subjected to RT-PCR. The results indicated that three R. chinensis(asymptomatic) and two R. multiflora (one asymptomatic and one rosette leaf) samples were positive for ASGV. These samples positive by RT-PCR were tested by double antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay with ASGV polyclonal antibody and confirmed positive. To our knowledge, this is the first report of ASGV infecting R. chinensis, extending the known host range of ASGV and identifying a potential viral threat to rose production.
reference_name: First Report of Apple stem grooving virus Infecting Rosa chinensis in China

人工接种可侵染的植物：在人工接种条件下，该病毒可以侵染9科20种植物，多数为无症状侵染。主要有：苹果(Malus pumila Mill.)，榅桲(Cydonia oblonga Mill.)，梨属(Pyrus)植物包括西洋梨(P.communis L.)、白梨(P.bretschneideri Rehd.)、沙梨(P.pyrifolia (Burm.) Nakai.)、秋子梨(P.ussuriensis Maxim.)等，大果海棠(M. platycarpa)，昆诺藜(Chenopodium quinoa ) ，心叶烟(Nicotiana glutinosa )，菜豆(Phaseolus vulgaris ) 。
potential_eco_desc: 在果园中ASGV与苹果褪绿叶斑病毒(ACLSV)、苹果茎痘病毒（ApSPV）同时混合侵染，加重对苹果树生长和结果的影响。在日本，ApSPV单独侵染，病树生长量减少10%-15%，产量降低5%-10%；当它与苹果褪绿叶斑病毒混合侵染时，病树生长量减少20%-30%，产量下降10%-15%。
description:
第一次是美国在苹果品种弗吉尼亚小苹果(Malus pumila  cv. Virginia crab)上发现并报道了ASGV（1965,1967,1969）。  苹果茎沟病毒可通过病、健树根系接触传播。病毒经嫁接传染，随带毒无性繁殖材料传播。用染病树花瓣、嫩叶、芽和嫩枝皮层组织和幼果作毒源，可机械传染该病毒到草本植物。
ASGV主要通过嫁接传染。用芽接、汁液、机械传染，接种组织主要有嫩叶、花瓣和芽片。提取缓冲液中加入3%尼古丁，可显著提高转接成功率。通过靠接和劈接的方法，可将ASGV由昆诺阿藜回接到苹果实生苗上。
ASGV自然扩散的现象很少见，但在果园中，病毒可通过病、健树根系接触传播。
remark:
我国苹果砧木多不耐苹果茎沟病毒(ASGV)的侵染。在这些砧木上嫁接带病毒的接穗，常常导致苗木发病。
2004年我国经评估审定，将ASGV列入《进境植物检疫危险性病虫杂草名录》，对其依法实施检疫。

management_info: Measures to control the disease require the use of virus-free propagation stock, perhaps from a certification programme. There is evidence that thermotherapy may be used for the elimination of ASGV (Howell et al., 1998; Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999).  The virus was eliminated from Nicotiana occidentalis and apple by in vitro chemotherapy, using a combination of the antiviral chemicals quercetin and ribavirin (10 μg/ml each, for 9-12 weeks) with confirmation of virus absence using RT-PCR and immunocapture RT-PCR (James et al., 1997). ^p^pThere have also been reports of virus elimination after treatment with ribavirin (Virazole) (Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999). Xue et al. (1996) were able to eliminate ASGV from pear rootstocks and cultivars using shoot tip culture, but found that the combination of thermotherapy and shoot tip culture, or in vitro thermotherapy and shoot tip culture were more effective. ^p^pSymptomless cultivars should be indexed before budwood is taken for propagation. It is suggested that all budwood used for propagation could be routinely subjected to heat therapy. This would be quicker and cheaper than indexing. Resistant cultivars could be planted where possible instead of susceptible cultivars. Although no vectors of the disease have been identified, diseased trees should be removed as soon as they are discovered.

description:
该病毒是通过嫁接和芽接在木本寄主之间传播的，潜伏期为14－15个月(N閙eth, 1986; PWelsh and Van der Meer, 1989)。有可靠的证据说明弗吉尼亚小苹果(Virginia Crab)是十分敏感的，而温柏树显示着若干免疫性，结果在这些植物中存在着低水平的ASGV(Welsh and Van der Meer, 1989)。于是推荐，接种芽应在鉴别寄主的发芽之前几个月被应用到树的更敏感部分去允许病毒浓度的增加。
ASGV能通过实验性地通过机械传播从木本寄主传播到草本寄主中去(Lister, 1970; Van der Meer, 1976; James et al., 1997)。该病毒能通过贴接从草本寄主传播到木本寄主中去(de Sequeira, 1967; Fridlund, 1980)，通过裂接从感染地茴藜传播到苹果幼苗中去(Van der Meer, 1976)。
有关于ASGV自然传播的稀少的陈述，并且这被归类到在健康树木和感染树木之间的根部嫁接中去(Welsh and Van der Meer, 1989)。茴藜（C. quinoa）和扁果海棠的种子传播已被报道(Van der Meer, 1976)。 The virus is transmitted among woody hosts by grafting and budding with an incubation period of 14-15 months (N閙eth, 1986; PWelsh and Van der Meer, 1989). Available evidence suggests that Virginia Crab is hypersensitive and quince displays some immunity, resulting in the presence of low levels of ASGV in these plants (Welsh and Van der Meer, 1989). It is therefore recommended, that inoculum buds be applied to more susceptible components of the tree a few months before the buds of the indicator, to allow the virus titre to increase. 
ASGV has been transmitted experimentally from woody hosts to herbaceous hosts by mechanical transmission (Lister, 1970; Van der Meer, 1976; James et al., 1997). The virus has been transmitted from herbaceous to woody hosts by approach-grafting (de Sequeira, 1967; Fridlund, 1980) and by cleft-grafting infected Chenopodium quinoa to apple seedlings (Van der Meer, 1976).
There have been rare claims of natural spread of ASGV and this has been attributed to root grafting between healthy and infected trees (Welsh and Van der Meer, 1989). Seed transmission in C. quinoa and Malus platycarpa has been reported (Van der Meer, 1976).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc: 该病毒在幼芽和根茎的敏感结合的嫁接处引起坏死，而且是日本苹果整顶嫁接病害的其中一个病原物(Yanase et al., 1990)。 The virus causes necrosis at the graft union of sensitive combinations of scion and rootstock and is one of the causal agents of apple topworking disease in Japan (Yanase et al., 1990).

management_info: 防治该病害的方法要求使用无病毒繁殖茎，这或许经鉴定程序得来。有证据表明温热疗法可用作去除ASGV(Howell et al., 1998; Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999)。Nicotiana occidentalis和苹果上的病毒可通过试管化学疗法去除，利用抗过滤性病原体的化学槲索和病毒唑(10 礸/ml each, for 9-12 weeks)，利用RT-PCR和免疫捕获RT-PCR法确定病毒的不存在(ÀJames et al., 1997)。 Measures to control the disease require the use of virus-free propagation stock, perhaps from a certification programme. There is evidence that thermotherapy may be used for the elimination of ASGV (Howell et al., 1998; Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999). The virus was eliminated from Nicotiana occidentalis and apple by in vitro chemotherapy, using a combination of the antiviral chemicals quercetin and ribavirin (10 礸/ml each, for 9-12 weeks) with confirmation of virus absence using RT-PCR and immunocapture RT-PCR (ÀJames et al., 1997). 病毒在用病毒唑(Virazole)处理后能清除，也已经被报道(Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999)。Xue et al. (1996)利用插条顶断栽培法去除梨根茎上的ASGV，但发现联合温热疗法和插条顶端栽培法，或试管温热疗法和插条顶端栽培法是更有效的。 There have also been reports of virus elimination after treatment with ribavirin (Virazole) (Cieslinska and Zawadzka, 1999). Xue et al. (1996) were able to eliminate ASGV from pear rootstocks and cultivars using shoot tip culture, but found that the combination of thermotherapy and shoot tip culture, or in vitro thermotherapy and shoot tip culture were more effective.   无症状品种应该在芽木用作繁殖之前检索。所有用作繁殖的芽木常规性地受制于加热治疗。这会比检索更快捷和更便宜。抗性品种应该种植在可能代替敏感品种的地方。虽然没有该病害的传播媒介，生病树木应该在发现之后尽快移植到远离的地方。 Symptomless cultivars should be indexed before budwood is taken for propagation. It is suggested that all budwood used for propagation could be routinely subjected to heat therapy. This would be quicker and cheaper than indexing. Resistant cultivars could be planted where possible instead of susceptible cultivars. Although no vectors of the disease have been identified, diseased trees should be removed as soon as they are discovered.
author: zhangjianjun

host_range: 番木瓜Carica papaya，胜红蓟Ageratum conyzoides、田麻Corchoropsis tomentosa和番茄Lycopersicon esculentum是番木瓜曲叶病毒病的中间寄主。
potential_eco_desc: 一般5月初开始发病，以后随着气温升高，烟粉虱大量暴发，曲叶病便迅速蔓延开来，根据调查，心圩乡、沙井乡、江西乡和石埠等重病区6月份发病率为47.23%-70.65%，但到了8月和11月份，发病率增加到88.52%-100%。在广西南宁，番木瓜曲叶病毒病已成为番木瓜生产的头号病害，其造成的损失是毁灭性的，比番木瓜环斑病毒病还要严重得多。
description: 经2002-2004年调查，广西南宁市郊重病果园发病率高达47.23%～100%。  番木瓜曲叶病毒病可以通过烟粉虱Bemisia tabaci传染。
management_info: 在防治上建议抓好如下几个方面：(1)隔离种植，远离病区；(2)清除果园周围的番茄和胜红蓟等中间寄主；(3)及时防治传毒媒介：用吡虫啉或啶虫咪等杀虫剂喷杀烟粉虱；(4)有条件的应用防虫网大栅保护种植。
reference_name: 中国番木瓜曲叶病毒在南宁的发生及其烟粉虱传播和中间寄主初步研究
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of the PaLCuGdV infection in lisianthus in Taiwan.
potential_eco_desc: The disease incidences were about 20 to 30% in lisianthus in FangYuen and BeiGung areas in south-central Taiwan.
description: Lisianthus(Eustoma grandiflorum) plants showing leaf curl and enation on cup-shaped upper leaves and flower petals were observed in FangYuen and BeiGung areas in south-central Taiwan during September 2015. Symptomatic lisianthus plants were collected in both areas. Based on sequences analysis and infectivity tests showed the causal agent was Papaya leaf curl Guangdong virus (PaLCuGdV). To our best knowledge, this is the first report of the PaLCuGdV infection in lisianthus in Taiwan.  The presence of whiteflies on the infected plants.
reference_name: First Report of Papaya leaf curl Guangdong virus Infecting Lisianthus in Taiwan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

potential_eco_desc: Disease incidence in the fields was in the range of 70 to 80%.
description: In November 2015, Citrullus lanatus plants exhibiting leaf curl as well yellowing and crumpling of leaves were observed at the Agricultural Experimental Station at Sultan Qaboos University Oman. Due to the presence of large numbers of whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci, the vector of begomoviruses) on the plants, a begomovirus (genus Begomovirus, familyGeminiviridae) was suspected to be the causal agent. The samples were collected, based on electron microscopy and molecular diagnostics showed the causal agent was virus, and they are Chilli leaf curl virus(ChiLCV) and Tomato leaf curl betasatellite(ToLCB). To our knowledge, this is the first report of a monopartite begomovirus associated with betasatellite infecting C. lanatus in Oman. ChiLCV has been reported to infect several important horticulture crops in South Asia and Oman.  The presence of large numbers of whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci, the vector of begomoviruses) on the Citrullus lanatus plants infected by viruses.
reference_name: First Report of Chilli leaf curl virus and Tomato leaf curl betasatellite Infecting Watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) in Oman
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: ChiLCV associated with different betasatellites has been reported to infect important vegetables including chili, tomato, and potato in India and Pakistan.
description: Weeds act as reservoirs of begomoviruses and ‘‘mixing vessels’’ leading to emergence of new viruses that may infect crops once a susceptible host plant is introduced into an agro-ecological system. Owing to the importance of weed hosts in the emergence of begomoviruses, we evaluated “nettle weed” (Urtica dioica L.) showing leaf curl and vein-yellowing symptoms, suspected of begomovirus infection in Lahore, Pakistan, during 2013. Total DNA was extracted from Urtica dioica plants, experimental results showed the presence of  Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV) and associated alpha- and beta-satellite DNAs. This is the first isolate of ChiLCV infecting nettle weed.
reference_name: First Report of Chilli leaf curl virus and Associated Alpha- and Beta-satellite DNAs Infecting Nettle Weed (Urtica dioica) in Pakistan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

potential_eco_desc: 曲叶病是印度喀拉拉邦蒂鲁文南特布勒姆地区（分布）辣椒上的一种严重病害，2008年该病在这一地区的发病率为100%。 Leaf curl disease of chilli has become a serious problem in the Vellanad district of Kerala, one of the major chilli growing areas of India. Disease incidence up to 100% was recorded during December 2008 in this region.
reference_name: A new monopartite begomovirus species, Chilli leaf curl Vellanad virus, and associated betasatellites infecting chilli in the Vellanad region of Kerala, India

description: Since May 2010, typical symptoms such as yellow vein, leaf yellowing, mosaic, crinkling, and cupping were observed, which led to significant yield loss in spearmint (M. spicata var. Neera) at CIMAP experimental fields and farmers' fields of Badaun, Rampur, and Moradabad regions of Uttar Pradesh province, India.

host_range: ChiLCINV has been isolated from Capsicum sp., Mirabilis arvensis and spicata in India and Duranta repens in Pakistan. This is the first report of ChiLCINV infecting M. jalapa.
potential_eco_desc: The disease incidence was about 45%.
description: Possible disease symptoms were observed on a number of Mirabilis jalapa plants growing in the gardens of CSIR-NBRI, Lucknow (26°55′ N; 80°59′ E), India. The disease incidence was about 45% with plants exhibiting upward leaf curling and stunting in comparison with apparently healthy plants. Based on the symptoms a begomovirus infection was suspected. Total DNA was isolated from the leaves of jalapa plants. Based on sequences analysis confirming that the pathogen was Chilli leaf curl India virus (ChiLCINV). This is the first report of ChiLCINV infecting M. jalapa in India.
reference_name: First report of Chilli leaf curl India virus infecting Mirabilis jalapa in India

host_range: H. mantegazzianum is not normally a weed of crops but there are reports of its encroachment into crop fields, for example, in potatoes in Sweden (Lundstrom, 1984).
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pH. mantegazzianum is an alternative host of the carrot fly, Psila rosea, and of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Tiley et al., 1996). Lundstrom (1984) suggests that the presence of the weed may increase the risk of crops being affected by S. sclerotiorum but there are no records of direct impact on crops. There must, however, be a highly significant cost involved in measures taken to control the weed in amenity and other areas.^p^p^Environmental impact^pH. mantegazzianum competes with natural vegetation, reducing grass and other low-growing plants. This can lead to soil erosion as well as a loss in biodiversity. Substantial programmes have been instituted in a number of European countries in order to control the weed, partly because of the human health hazards involved, but equally to reduce the environmental damage caused, especially to riverside habitats. Such programmes are described by Lundstrom (1984) in Sweden, Williamson and Forbes (1982) and Tiley and Philp (1992) in Scotland, and Caffrey and Madsen (2001) in Ireland.^p^p^Social impact^pThe bristly hairs on H. mantegazzianum contain furanocoumarins and any contact of skin with the plant can result in painful watery blisters. This occurs within 2-3 days on exposure to sunlight. It may occasionally cause a recurrent dermatitis which can become a serious handicap (Williamson and Forbes, 1982). The health hazards of this species are one of the main reasons for concern over its spread. In tests on bacteria, Clarke (1975) showed that the sap of H. mantegazzianum could be mutagenic.^p^pDense infestations can seriously interfere with access to amenity areas, river banks etc. Along roadsides, large stands can reduce visibility and result in a safety hazard.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pIn amenity areas, established colonies compete strongly with, and rapidly replace most other plants except trees (Williamson and Forbes, 1982). Along river banks, it can almost totally replace the natural vegetation and threaten biodiversity.  In Sweden it can build up to a 'giant hogweed landscape' (Lundstrom, 1984). It has not been documented as a problem in national parks but has the capacity to be so.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; environment; human health; native fauna; tourism
description: H. mantegazzianum has been repeatedly introduced to other countries as a garden ornamental. The original dates are rarely known, though the first records of naturalization (e.g. 1828 in UK) give some indication. Pysek and Prach (1993) and Pysek (1994), discussing the weed's spread in the Czech Republic, indicate that from 1862 up to about 1943, spread appeared to be exclusively due to cultivation as a garden ornamental but after that there was natural spread along the main rivers. Most recently it has spread further, regardless of altitude.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pPropagation is completely by seeds, which are produced in very large numbers. Short-distance dispersal (2-10 m) is by wind, while longer-distance dispersal is achieved by water, the seeds being able to float for at least 3 days.^p^pVector Transmission (Biotic)^p^pMovement occurs by man, collecting the seed-heads for ornament and then disposing on rubbish heaps; also as a result of movement of soil in the course of building works, and by attachment to vehicles or in the slip-stream of road and rail vehicles.^p^pAgricultural Practices^p^pNo relevant instances have been documented.^p^pAccidental Introduction Fowler (1998) notes that H. mantegazzianum is one of the three commonest proscribed species to be intercepted at entry points to USA, comprising 14% of all such interceptions. One pathway is the accidental contamination of cumin seed (Westbrooks, 1991).^p^pIntentional Introduction^p^pDeliberate introduction of H. mantegazzianum is quite likely, as it is used as a spice and also as an ornamental. Such introduction is encouraged by the availability of seed from commercial nurseries via mail-order catalogues and from websites in, for example, Canada, The Netherlands and the UK.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Fruits (inc. Pods): Seeds.^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants: Seeds.^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx: Seeds.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark^p - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Leaves^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants^p - Roots^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain)^p - Wood.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Mail: Internet (Websites in UK Canada Netherlands (via Google))^p - Soil, Gravel, Water, Etc.: Rivers (Pysek 1994)^p - Travellers And Baggage: Food/contaminant (e.g. Cumin Seed) (Westbrooks 1991; Fowler 1998)
author: CPC2006

remark: Further spread is highly probable, owing to the risks of both accidental movement as a seed contaminant of crop seed and other agricultural produce, and deliberate introduction as a foodstuff (see Pathway table) or as an ornamental. This is encouraged by availability from commercial nurseries via mail-order catalogues and websites, for example, in Canada, The Netherlands and the UK. ^p^pH. mantegazzianum is already prohibited as a noxious weed in the USA (USDA, 2002). In the UK, it is included in legislation requiring land owners to take steps to control it and prevent further spread (Willoughby, 1996).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control ^p^pH. mantegazzianum is not effectively controlled by light grazing, but intensive grazing, especially by sheep has provided good control and the rooting of pigs can also be highly effective (Tiley et al., 1996). Anderson and Calov (1996) reported on a 5-year study in Denmark in which the population of the weed was much reduced after 2 years of sheep grazing and completely eliminated after 5 years, when no viable seeds were found to remain in the soil. The weed may be slightly less palatable to cattle, but grazing by cattle as well as pigs is recommended in Ireland (Lucey, 1994.) ^p^p^Mechanical Control ^p^pHand-pulling (with gloves) can be effective on young seedlings but is impractical on larger plants. Mechanical cutting is frequently used to clear river banks, etc., but provides no long-term control, as there is rapid re-growth from below ground, and it may encourage the perennation of flowering shoots which would otherwise die after flowering. Cutting in May and June was somewhat more effective in reducing seed production and/or re-growth than cutting in March. Digging or ploughing to destroy the crown (below 10 cm soil depth) can completely kill the plant.^p^p^Chemical Control ^p^pIn the UK, herbicides recommended for control of H. mantegazzianum include glyphosate, triclopyr and imazapyr but all must be applied early in the season (March to May) for best effect. Imazapyr has a residual effect in the soil that will prevent further germination but may also have a later effect on non-target species. Glyphosate is the most widely used compound, usually applied in April or May, but owing to risks of toxicity to fish and algae, a buffer zone of 2 m should be left unsprayed adjacent to any river or other water body (Marcher, 2001).^p^p^Biological Control ^p^pApart from the use of grazing animals, no other biological control method has yet been developed, though the possibilities have been discussed (Fowler et al., 1991; Fowler and Holden, 1994; Burki and Nentwig, 1998).^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pDue to the likely spread of seed down a river, it is important to ensure that upstream infestations are dealt with before attempting eradication further down (Williamson and Forbes, 1982). Tiley and Philp (1992) describe an integrated 2-year programme of spraying with glyphosate in April/May, combined with cutting below ground when or where spraying is not feasible, and dealing with large plants threatening to flower before dealing with vegetative plants.
author: CPC2006

description: During May to June 2017, a survey of leguminous plants was conducted in the Ecuadorian localities of Santa Elena (Santa Elena province), Milagro (Guayas province), and Pallatanga (Chimborazo province). Some plants showing leaf deformation and/or mosaic symptoms were sampled, including common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) , soybean (Glycine max), and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan). Most common bean plants were infested with whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) that were also collected. Total DNA was extracted from leaf samples. Based on molecular diagnostics, the isolate characterized belongs to a new strain of Pepper leafroll virus (PepLRV). This is the first report of PepLRV in Ecuador and of soybean as a host for the virus, which had been identified only in Peru to date. Also, this is the first molecular evidence of the presence of B. tabaci MEAM1 in the country.  Direct sequencing of PCR products showed that seven sequences were identical to numerous sequences of Bemisia tabaci Middle East-Asia Minor 1 (MEAM1, formerly B biotype), known to be an efficient vector of begomoviruses.
reference_name: A Novel Strain of Pepper Leafroll Virus Infecting Common Bean and Soybean in Ecuador
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 辣椒Capsicum annuum
potential_eco_desc: The symptomatic plants were scattered with an incidence of about 20%.
description: In June 2013, symptoms of yellow mosaics, intervenal chlorosis, wrinkling, and stunting were observed in sweet pepper(Capsicum annuum) plants in a commercial greenhouse from Guasave Valley in northern Sinaloa. Pepper plants with the same symptoms also were observed in 2014 and 2015. During 2013 to 2015, 24 leaf samples of symptomatic sweet pepper plants were collected and processed to identify the causal agent. PCR analyses with specific primers confirmed the presence of Pepper huasteco yellow vein virus (PHYVV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of natural infection of a new PHYVV isolate affecting sweet pepper in Sinaloa, Mexico.  Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci Genn.) were present in the greenhouse with the symptomatic plants.
reference_name: Pepper huasteco yellow vein virus Associated to Sweet Pepper Disease in Sinaloa, Mexico
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: In January 2012 and August 2013, severe yellowing, leaf curling and deformation symptoms, resembling those of PYVD were observed on pepper (Capsicum spp.) across C?te d'Ivoire. The leaf samples from pepper plants with symptoms were collected, based on PCR and sequences analysis confirmed PepYVMLV exists. To our knowledge, this is the first report of PepYVMLV associated with PYVD in C?te d’Ivoire. Our results confirm the geographical distribution of PepYVMLV in West Africa and the close genetic relationship of this  viral population.
reference_name: First report of Pepper yellow vein Mali virus associated with pepper yellow vein disease in Cote d’Ivoire

host_range: In Florida three weed hosts tested positive for BGMV: Euphorbia (Chamaesyce) sp., Ludwigia palustris and Phyllanthus sp. However, only Euphorbia sp. has been shown to be an alternative host of BGMV. BGMV was transmitted by whiteflies from bush bean plants
potential_eco_desc: BGMV and Bean golden yellow mosaic virus (BGYMV) are devastating diseases of Phaseolus vulgaris in tropical America. Early or late infection by BGMV under field conditions in Brazil reduced the number of pods per plant, seeds per pod, yield, seed weight and seed germination. The reduction was greater with early infection (73%) than with late infection (43%) (Almeida et al., 1984). In trials with beh bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) cv. Carioca 6C2, infection with BGMV [BGYMV] reduced the yield of consumable beans by 64%, seed yield by 71%, weight of 100 seeds by 36.8%, seed germination by 4.8% and emergence by 5.3% (Menten et al., 1980).^p^pBGMV [BGYMV] was found in bean plants in all provinces in Cuba, with incidence reaching 100% in some areas. No pods were formed on infected plants (Blanco-Sanchez and Bencomo, 1981). Losses in bean crops caused by BGMV, transmitted by Bemisia tabaci, can reach 100% in Sao Paulo, Brazil (Menten and Roston, 1980). Early spring losses in bean crops due to BGMV [BGYMV], transmitted by B. argentifolii, can reach 100% in southern Florida, USA (McMillan, 1994). Bean production declined steadily between 1992 and 1994 with the incidence of BGMV in bush beans ranging from as high as 100% to as low as 5% and in pole beans BGMV [BGYMV] infection may be as high as 100% to as low as 1% (McMillan et al., 1994).
author: CPC2006

description: BGMV is not reported to be seedborne.^p^p^Incidence^p^pSeeds of Phaseolus vulgaris cultivars Carioca and Jalo and soyabean cultivars Davis, Doko, Eureka, Cariri, BR-15 and Cristalina were bombarded with two cloned components (A and B) of BGMV, isolated in Brazil. P. vulgaris cultivars Carioca and Jalo, and soyabean cultivars Davis and Cariri developed typical golden mosaic symptoms. The presence of the virus was confirmed by squash blot hybridization (Aragao et al., 1995).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pCultivated tepary bean (Phaseolus acutifolius var. latifolius) has the potential for production during the hot, dry seasons in the tropics. However, BGMV and Bean golden yellow mosaic virus (BGYMV seriously limit production of Phaseolus spp. in such environments. Twelve tepary bean lines were evaluated for reaction to BGMV [BGYMV] in four field nurseries near Isabela, Puerto Rico. Measurement of seed yield (kg/ha) and 100-seed weight principally determined disease reaction. All tepary beans possessed some tolerance to BGYMV, as they produced comparatively moderate seed yield despite expression of severe foliar yellow mosaic symptoms. On average, tepary bean yielded 133% of the BGYMV-resistant Phaseolus vulgaris cv. Dorado control. Four teparies, Neb-T-6-s, GN-610-s, Neb-T-8a-s and PI 321637-s, expressed superior tolerance to BGYMV as they yielded above the trial mean in at least three of the four trials. Harvested seed quality was uniformly poor in all lines, with 100-seed weight averaging 18% less than in the non-BGMV trials. The combination of the observed tolerance with escape mechanisms and cultural disease control practices may enable production of tepary bean in regions and seasons that experience moderate to severe BGYMV epidemics (Miklas and Santiago, 1996).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe following information refers to the control of BGMV and/or the recently distinguished Bean golden yellow mosaic (BGMYV). ^p^p^Antiviral Chemicals^p^pSystemic symptoms in Phaseolus lunatus were delayed by up to 15 days after whitefly inoculation by using polyacrylic acid, aciclovir, aspirin, distamycin A, EHNA, foscarnet and a pyrazino-pyrazine derivative. Although promising at first, the effect decreased 30 days after inoculation, and disappeared completely in almost all cases (Caner et al., 1985).^p^p^Natural Inhibitors^p^pLeaf extracts of Alternanthera brasiliana, A. ficoidea, Bougainvillea spectabilis, Chenopodium amaranticolor, C. ambrosioides, Iresine herbstii, Mirabilis jalapa and Phytolacca thirsiflora were applied to Phaseolus vugaris plants prior to whitefly inoculation with BGMV. Three successive sprays with the only two effective extracts, from I. herbstii or P. thirsiflora, inhibited symptoms in 58 and 50% of the plants (Alexandre et al., 1987).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pSince 1993, BGMV has caused millions of dollars in losses to commercial growers of snap bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) in southern Florida, USA (McMillan et al., 1994). Late generation pole bean BGMV-resistant lines were planted in southern Florida (McMillan et al., 1998). The early generation bean lines were planted each year from 1995 to 1998 in different growers fields with the susceptible 'McCaslan 42' randomly included. All of the late generation advanced BGMV-resistant pole bean lines were asymptomatic. All susceptible pole bean cultivar 'McCaslan 42' plants were symptomatic for BGMV on the basis of PCR results. All of the lines were resistant but not immune to BGMV (McMillan et al., 1998).^p^pBrazilian bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) lines MD 806, MD 807, MD 820, MD 829, MD 808 and MD 821 were found to have high levels of resistance to BGMV when selected under field conditions in Brazil. The lines were selected on a scale of 1 to 9, 1 = syptomless and 9 = severe. The mean severity of the MD lines ranged from 1.7 to 3.9 for mosaic symptom (foliar yellowing) and 1.7 to 2.2 from malformation (Bianchini, 1999).^p^pTwenty two advanced Argentinean black bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) lines were evaluated in 1996 and 1997 for resistance to BGMV. Data on disease resistance were evaluated on a scale of 1-9 with six yield components noted. The most resistant line was T95-28 (Vizgarra and Acenolaza, 1997).^p^pThe inheritance of resistance to BGMV in Phaseolus vulgaris was investigated in crosses between susceptible cultivar XAN176 and resistant breeding lines 9236-6 (T446/A429) and 9245-94 (DOR303/T968). Disease response data were taken on plants from four generations derived from each cross (parents, F1, F2 and backcrosses (BCs) of F1 to both parents) at 25 days after plants were inoculated with BGMV using Bemisia argentifolii. The segregation ratios obtained from F2 and BC generations were consistent with the hypothesis that resistance in 9236-6, which prevents a chlorotic response, is conferred by a single recessive gene. The disease response in 9245-94 was controlled by two genes: a dominant gene controlling a dwarfing reaction; and a recessive resistance gene preventing a chlorotic response to BGMV infection. An allelism test demonstrated that the gene controlling resistance in 9236-6 was nonallelic, with the recessive gene controlling resistance in 9236-94. The gene symbol bgm was proposed for the recessive resistance gene (originally from A429) in 9236-6. The gene symbol bgm 2 was proposed for the recessive resistance gene (originally from DOR303) in 9245-94 (Velez et al., 1998).^p^pResistance to BGMV in the French bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) germplasm collection of the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research at Bangalore was investigated. description: 银叶粉虱（Bemisia argentifolii）和烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci）传播BGMV。银叶粉虱（Bemisia argentifolii）和烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci）的成虫可从感染植物上仅仅6分钟就获得病毒，但有效的传播需要更长的获毒时间。粉虱能传播病毒的时间范围从几天到几个星期，而且很可能直到最后一次蜕皮。一个单独的昆虫的传播效率通常是断断续续的和不稳定的。雄性和雌性粉虱有着相同的传播效率。没有证据发现，BGMV能通过卵巢传播(Haber et al., 1981) The whiteflies B. tabaci and B. argentifolii transmit BGMV. Adult B. tabaci and B. argentifolii may acquire the virus from infected plants in as little as 6 minutes, but efficient transmission requires longer feeding periods. Whiteflies can transmit the virus for periods ranging from a few days to several weeks and probably through the last moult. Transmission efficiency of an individual insect is often intermittent and erratic. Male and female whiteflies transmit with equal efficiency. No evidence has been found that BGMV can be transmitted through the ovaries (Haber et al., 1981).

management_info: 在Phaseolus lunatus上的系统性症状在利用聚丙烯酸、阿昔洛韦、乙酰水杨酸、远端霉素A、EHNA、膦甲酸和a pyrazino-pyrazine derivative接种粉虱后会被延迟超过15天。虽然开始时预期，但效果在接种30天后有所减少，而且在几乎所有情况下全部消失(Caner et al., 1985)。 Systemic symptoms in Phaseolus lunatus were delayed by up to 15 days after whitefly inoculation by using polyacrylic acid, aciclovir, aspirin, distamycin A, EHNA, foscarnet and a pyrazino-pyrazine derivative. Although promising at first, the effect decreased 30 days after inoculation, and disappeared completely in almost all cases (Caner et al., 1985). Mycotrol，一种被用在午后防止UV光的损害的白僵菌（Beauveria bassiana）的基础杀虫剂，能有效防治在菜豆(Phaseolus vulgaris)上银叶粉虱（Bemisia argentifolii）的成虫、卵和蛹 (McMillan and Seal, University of Florida, USA, 1998, unpublished data)。 Mycotrol, a Beauveria bassiana-based insecticide, applied late in the afternoon to avoid UV light damage, was effective in controlling Bemisia argentifolii adults, eggs and nymphs on beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) (McMillan and Seal, University of Florida, USA, 1998, unpublished data).

potential_eco_desc: BGMV在古巴所有种植菜豆植物的省份里发现，在一些地区发病率还达到100％。没有豆荚在感染植株上形成(Blanco-Sanchez and Bencomo, 1981)。由烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci）传播的BGMV导致的菜豆作物的损失在巴西圣保罗达到100％(Menten and Roston, 1980)。由烟粉虱（Bemisia tabaci）传播的BGMV引起的菜豆作物的早春损失在美国南佛罗里达州能达到100％(McMillan, 1994)。菜豆生产在1992至1994年间稳定地减少，BGMV在矮菜豆上的发病率能高达100％低至5％，在敏豆上BGMV感染能高达100％低至1％(McMillan et al., 1994)。 BGMV was found in bean plants in all provinces in Cuba, with incidence reaching 100% in some areas. No pods were formed on infected plants (Blanco-Sanchez and Bencomo, 1981). Losses in bean crops caused by BGMV, transmitted by Bemisia tabaci, can reach 100% in Sao Paulo, Brazil (Menten and Roston, 1980). Early spring losses in bean crops due to BGMV, transmitted by B. argentifolii, can reach 100% in southern Florida, USA (McMillan, 1994). Bean production declined steadily between 1992 and 1994 with the incidence of BGMV in bush beans ranging from as high as 100% to as low as 5% and in pole beans BGMV infection may be as high as 100% to as low as 1% (McMillan et al., 1994). BGMV在热带的美洲是菜豆（Phaseolus vulgaris）毁灭性的病害。在巴西，在田间条件下BGMV早期或后期侵染减少了每棵植物豆荚的数量、每颗豆荚种子的数量、产量、种子重量和种子的萌发。早期侵染的减少量(73%)比后期侵染的要多(43%) (Almeida et al., 1984)。在利用beh bean (菜豆)品种Carioca 6C2的实验中，BGMV侵染减少可供消费的菜豆产量达64％，种子产量减少了71%，100颗种子的重量减少36.8%，种子萌发减少4.8%以及出苗减少5.3% (Menten et al., 1980)。 BGMV is a devastating disease of Phaseolus vulgaris in tropical America. Early or late infection by BGMV under field conditions in Brazil reduced the number of pods per plant, seeds per pod, yield, seed weight and seed germination. The reduction was greater with early infection (73%) than with late infection (43%) (Almeida et al., 1984). In trials with beh bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) cv. Carioca 6C2, infection with BGMV reduced the yield of consumable beans by 64%, seed yield by 71%, weight of 100 seeds by 36.8%, seed germination by 4.8% and emergence by 5.3% (Menten et al., 1980).

host_range: 木薯Manihot esculenta.
description: To determine the suspected begomoviruses associated with Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) symptoms, leaf samples were collected from five symptomatic cassava plants in Cameroon, and from three symptomatic plants in Togo in August 2014. Total DNA was isolated, the African cassava mosaic virus (ACMV) DNA-A and B components as expected, the DNA-A and B components of Soybean chlorotic blotch virus (SbCBV) (Olufemi et al., 2010) and West African Asystasia virus 1 (WAAV1) (Wyant et al., 2015) were also identified. For SbCBV, sequence identities ranged from 97-99% and 95-96% for the DNA-A and B components, respectively, whereas for WAAV1, sequence identities ranged from 92-95% and 93-96% for the DNA-A and B components, respectively. To confirm the presence of SbCBV and WAAV1 in the cassava samples, PCR was carried out using specific primers designed to the CP and BV1 gene, located on the DNA-A and B components of SbCBV and WAAV1, respectively. The DNA sequence for each cloned amplicon was determined by Sanger sequencing. Amongst the five samples collected from Cameroon, three were infected only with ACMV, one was infected with ACMV and WAAV1, and one was infected with ACMV, SbCBV and WAAV1. The three Togolese samples were all infected with ACMV and one was also infected with SbCMV. BLASTn analysis of the CP and BV1 genes indicated that they shared 99-100% sequence identity with the NGS- determined sequences. To our knowledge, this is the first report that cassava may be infected by SbCBV or WAAV1 in Africa. The isolates shared a close phylogenetic relatedness with previously described SbCBV and WAAV1 isolates, respectively.
reference_name: First report of Soybean chlorotic blotch virus and West African Asystasia virus 1 infecting cassava and a wild cassava relative in Cameroon and Togo

host_range: Eclipta prostrate has been reported as a host for multiple begomoviruses like AlYVV. This is the first report of AlYVV on E. prostrata in Pakistan.
potential_eco_desc: Eclipta prostrata has been reported as a host for multiple begomoviruses like AlYVV, and could therefore serve as an alternative virus reservoir, with an important role in the epidemiology of the disease.
description: In July 2015, during a field survey of the Tando Mohammad Khan area in Sindh province and the Faisalabad area in Punjab province, Pakistan, symptoms of vein yellowing and swelling were observed on leaves of Eclipta prostrata. It is a common weed in Pakistan and was recently reported as a host for AlYVV in China. Symptomatic plants and one asymptomatic plant were collected and total DNA was extracted, based on molecular diagnostics showed AlYVV was presence in E. prostrate.  Alternanthera yellow vein virus is transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
reference_name: First Report of Alternanthera yellow vein virus From Eclipta prostrata in Pakistan
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

description: In April 2018, diseased corn leaf samples were collected in commercial fields in the western region of the state of Paraná, Brazil. Based on molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests, the pathogen was identified as Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum. This is the first report of the occurrence of bacterial leaf streak of corn caused by X. vasicola pv. vasculorum in Brazil. The disease was present in commercial fields in at least eight municipalities of corn-producing regions of the state of Paraná, Brazil. In addition, bacterial leaf streak of corn was detected under natural conditions on Zea mays plants of at least 30 different commercial hybrids.
reference_name: First Report of the Occurrence of Bacterial Leaf Streak of Corn Caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum in Brazil
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

potential_eco_desc: Disease severity was low (less than 5%).
description: Following reports of a new bacterial disease of corn (Zea mays) caused by Xanthomonas vasicola in the nearby states of Colorado, Kansas, and Nebraska, irrigated corn fields in Caddo, Garvin, Kingfisher, and Texas Counties of Oklahoma were surveyed for symptoms of bacterial leaf streak in August 2016. Symptoms consisting of elongated necrotic lesions mostly confined within leaf veins, with irregular yellow to orange colored margins, were observed in several fields in Texas County, although disease severity was low (less than 5%). Samples were collected and colonies, fungi were isolated, the pathogen was identified as Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum   by colony characteristics and the PCR primers. This is the first report of bacterial leaf streak of corn caused by X. vasicola pv. vasculorum in Oklahoma and expands the current reported geographic range of this new disease in the United States.
reference_name: First Report of Bacterial Leaf Streak of Corn Caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. vasculorum in Oklahoma

host_range: Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa（cv. Roquette）
potential_eco_desc: Approximately 80 to 100% of each planting was affected, with greater rates of infection occurring after periods of high humidity.
description: In 2011, bacterial blight of arugula (Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa; cv. Roquette) was observed in organically grown plants under overhead irrigation in a field near Delano, MN. Based on biological detection, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity assay showed that the causal agent was Pseudomonas cannabina pv. alisalensis. To our knowledge, this is the first report of bacterial blight of crucifers caused by P. cannabina pv. alisalensis in Minnesota.
reference_name: First Report of Bacterial Blight of Crucifers Caused by Pseudomonas cannabina pv. alisalensis in Minnesota on Arugula (Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa)
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 芥菜Brassica juncea，芜青Brassica rapa
description: In 2010, a brassica leafy greens grower in Sunflower County, MS, observed scattered outbreaks of a leaf blight on mustard greens (Brassica juncea) in a 180-ha field. A severe outbreak of leaf blight occurred on mustard greens and turnip greens (B. rapa) in the same field in 2011 with more than 80 ha affected. The affected field, established in 2010, had no prior history of being cropped to brassica leafy greens. Whole plants of the mustard greens cv. Florida Broadleaf were collected in 2011 from the symptomatic field. The test demonstrated that the isolated bacteria was Pseudomonas cannabina pv. alisalensis (Pca). This is the first report of bacterial leaf blight on Brassica juncea caused by Pca in Mississippi. Over the past 10 years, Pca has been found in numerous states in the United States, as well as in Europe, Australia, and Japan.
reference_name: First Report of Bacterial Leaf Blight on Mustard Greens (Brassica juncea) Caused by Pseudomonas cannabina pv. alisalensis in Mississippi

description: Due to the importance of weed hosts in the epidemiology and evolution of begomoviruses, we evaluated a widespread weed, Malvastrum coromandelianum, exhibiting leaf curl symptoms reminiscent of those caused by begomoviruses (Geminiviridae) in Lahore, Pakistan, during 2012.

host_range: 灌木金盏花Calendula officinalis.
description: In January 2014, yellow vein net disease was observed on a number of C. officinalis plants growing in a garden at Lucknow, India. Total DNA isolated from the samples and be tested by PCR amplification with begomovirus degenerate and betasatellite specific primers, the results suggest the association of a begomovirus and a betasatellite with the yellow net disease of C. officinalis. For molecular identification of the begomovirus, the result showed that pathogens were Ageratum enation virus (AEV) and Ageratum leaf curl betasatellite (ALCuB). This is the first report of AEV and ALCuB infecting C. officinalis in India.
reference_name: First report of Ageratum enation virus and Ageratum leaf curl betasatellite infecting Calendula officinalis in India
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 千穗苋Amaranthus hypochondriacus
description: During a survey in February 2011, severe symptoms of upward leaf curling, vein enation on lower side of the leaves, and shortening of internodes were observed on 20 out of 117 Amaranthus hypochondriacus plants (17% disease incidence) examined at breeding plots of CSIR-NBRI, Lucknow. These symptoms are typical of begomovirus infection. The test demonstrated that the pathogen  was Begomovirus ageratum enation virus（Betasatellite and Alphasatellite）. This is the first report of Ageratum enation virus, Betasatellite and Alphasatellite causing leaf curl and enation disease of Amaranthus hypochondriacus in India.
reference_name: First Report of Ageratum enation virus, Betasatellite and Alphasatellite Causing Leaf Curl and Enation Disease of Amaranthus hypochondriacus in India

host_range: 海雀稗Paspalum vaginatum cv. Sea Isle Supreme
description: In Barbados, on a newly constructed golf course, seashore paspalum ‘Sea Isle Supreme’ sprigs were imported from Georgia (United States) and were planted over 2006 and 2007 on greens, tees, fairways, and rough. Golf greens were constructed following the United States Golf Association Green Section (Far Hills, NJ) putting green guidelines. Two years after the grow-in, the putting greens began to exhibit irregular chlorotic patches, followed by gradual thinning and decline of turfgrass stand density in those areas. In May 2013, the samples were collected and identified, three genera of plant parasitic nematodes were found in all the samples from the symptomatic areas: Helicotylenchus, Mesocriconema, and Pratylenchus. Nematode populations of these genera averaged 30, 60, and 200 nematodes per 100 cm3, respectively. To our knowledge, this is the first report of plant parasitic nematodes associated with seashore paspalum maintained as putting greens in Barbados.
reference_name: First Report of Plant-Parasitic Nematodes on Seashore Paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum) in Barbados

description: In July 2016, virus-like symptoms, including mosaic and yellow ring spots on leaves, were observed in Humulus japonicus in Eum-Sung, Korea. Based on transmission electron microscopy (TEM), (DAS)-ELISA kits, RT-PCR confirming that the causal agent was Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV). This report suggests that H. japonicas plays a role in TSWV reservoir because the plant species is considered a weed in Korea. To our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV in H. japonicus in Korea.  Humulus japonicas plays a role in TSWV reservoir in Korea.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus in Humulus japonicus in Korea

host_range: TSWV causes serious diseases in many economically important plants, including dicots and monocots. TSWV’s natural occurrence in pepper, tomato, and wild plant species has been previously reported from Korea. This is the first report of TSWV in soybeans in Korea.
potential_eco_desc: The tests results showed that only soybean plants in limited regions of Korea were infected by TSWV.
description: In June 2016, soybean leaf samples displaying viral disease symptoms, such as chlorosis, mosaic, mottling, stunting, and yellowing, were collected from soybean-growing provinces in Korea and categorized by collection region. Based on molecular diagnostics confirming that it was presented with tomato spotted wilt virus(TSWV) in the samples. The soybean samples from Gyeonggi Province were coinfected by different viruses, such as Soybean mosaic virus, Peanut mottle virus, Soybean yellow mottle virus, Soybean yellow common mosaic virus, and Peanut stunt virus, which was confirmed by RT-PCR. TSWV’s natural occurrence in pepper, tomato, and wild plant species has been previously reported from Korea. It should be noted that this is the first report of TSWV in soybeans in Korea.  Soybean plants in Korea are usually grown together with peppers and tomatoes, which are also hosts for TSWV. Therefore, TSWV infections in soybeans may be strongly associated with TSWV in other plants.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus Infecting Soybean in Korea
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of a resistance-breaking(RB) strain of TSWV infecting tomatoes with the Sw-5 tospovirus-resistance gene in California.
potential_eco_desc: Disease incidences of 30 to 50% were observed in some fields, and later reached 50 to 80%.
description: In April 2016, severe tospovirus-like disease symptoms (i.e., stunting; leaf, stem, and petiole necrosis; and concentric rings on fruits) occurred in fields of fresh market tomato cultivars with the Sw-5 gene, which confers resistance to TSWV in Fresno County. Leaves with symptoms were collected from four fresh market fields in Cantua Creek and one in Firebaugh, as well as from nearby processing tomato fields. These plants were all positive for infection by TSWV when tested with AgDia immunostrips and RT-PCR. The tests results indicate that a TSWV RB strain has emerged in California, which can infect and cause typical symptoms in commercial fresh market and processing tomato cultivars with the Sw-5 gene. In field surveys, the TSWV RB strain was detected in Fresno. This strain likely arose following a mutation, as Sw-5 cultivars have been widely grown in California over the past 5 years (e.g., ～50% of processing cultivars grown in 2016).
reference_name: First Report of a Resistance-Breaking Strain of Tomato spotted wilt virus Infecting Tomatoes With the Sw-5 Tospovirus-Resistance Gene in California
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: In July 2014, two symptomatic Bidens pilosa plants were observed around farmers’ tobacco fields in Luxi County, Yunnan Province. The presence of TSWV was confirmed using DAS-ELISA and PCR, this is the first report of TSWV associated with a disease in B. pilosa in Yunnan Province, China.
potential_eco_desc: Bidens pilosa is an invasive annual weed in Yunnan Province, present in fields from March to January, with the potential to serve as a reservoir for both TSWV and one of its thrips vectors. The potential role of B. pilosa in TSWV epidemiology in China remains to be determined and further studies will be necessary to determine the movement of TSWV between crops and B. pilosa.
description: In July 2014, a survey for tospoviruses (family Bunyaviridae) was carried out on family-owned flue-cured tobacco farms that had about 5% flue-cured tobacco plants showing typical tospovirus symptoms of chlorotic ringspots and necrosis on both young and older leaves. Two symptomatic Bidens pilosa plants were observed around farmers’ tobacco fields in Luxi County, Yunnan Province, southwest China. Symptomatic leaves of B.  pilosa  plants were tested by direct double-antibody sandwich (DAS)-ELISA and PCR showed the presence of Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV).  TSWV has been reported previously to infect B. pilosa in Hawaii. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV associated with a disease in B. pilosa in Yunnan Province.  Bidens pilosa has been reported to support the TSWV thrips vector Frankliniella cephalica in Japan.
reference_name: Bidens pilosa is a Natural Host of Tomato spotted wilt virus
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: To our knowledge, this is the first record of a mixed infection of pepper by TSWV and PVY in Zimbabwe.
description: During tospovirus surveys conducted in January 2015, pepper plants with typical viral symptoms, including plant stunting, leaf chlorosis, mottling, and curling were observed at a farm in Goromonzi District of Zimbabwe. Visual observations estimated the symptoms incidence at 15%. Symptomatic and nonsymptomatic leaves were collected and identified. The presence of Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) and Potato virus Y (PVY) was confirmed by serological and molecular methods. To our knowledge, this is the first record of a mixed infection of pepper by TSWV and PVY in Zimbabwe.  There was a high incidence of Frankliniella occidentalis and Myzus persicae at the farm of pepper plants in Goromonzi District of Zimbabwe.
reference_name: First Report of a Mixed Infection of Potato virus Y and Tomato spotted wilt virus on Pepper (Capsicum annuum) in Zimbabwe
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: TSWV was first detected in North Carolina in 1988 in tobacco and tomato fields.
description: In February 2015, virus-like symptoms were observed on stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) plants in a research greenhouse in Raleigh, NC. Symptomless plants were dug from the field in the fall of 2014 and moved to the greenhouse to make crosses. Leaf tissue from symptomatic plants was collected for Immunostrip testing (Agdia Inc., Elkhart, IN). All symptomatic tissue tested positive for Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV). Diagnosis was further confirmed through sequence analysis of a nucleocapsid (N) protein gene fragment amplified by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). This is the first known report of TSWV infection in stevia in the United States.  Adult thrips, identified as Frankliniella occidentalis, were present throughout the greenhouse and on plant material.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus in Stevia rebaudiana in North Carolina
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of Tomato spotted wilt virus infecting butternut squash (Cucurbita moschata) in Zimbabwe.
description: During the 2014–15 summer season, butternut squash plants growing at a Harare farm displayed symptoms of viral etiology, characterized by leaf mottling, crinkling, and mosaics. Disease incidence was estimated at 30%. The test demonstrated that the pathogen was Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV). To our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV infecting butternut squash in Zimbabwe. Given the importance of butternut squash in Zimbabwe, the occurrence of TSWV may negatively affect crop yield, farmers’ income and household food security.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus Infecting Butternut Squash (Cucurbita moschata) in Zimbabwe
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: To our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV on any woody species other than Hydrangea macrophylla in the United States, and represents an expansion of the host range of this commercially important virus.
description: In July 2014, a sample of Pittosporum tobira (cultivar unknown) from a landscape in Isle of Wight County, Virginia, with symptoms of foliar chlorotic ring spots and line patterns, was submitted to the Virginia Tech Plant Disease Clinic for diagnosis. The sample tested positive for Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) with immunostrips and molecular diagnostics. We designate this causal agent as TSWV-Pt-VA. To our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV in the United States.  The symptomatic Virginia P. tobira plant had been in the landscape for at least 16 years before developing symptoms; therefore, it is unlikely that the virus was present in the plant when purchased. Based on a BLAST search, the N gene sequence of TSWV-Pt-VA has 99% identity to numerous peanut TSWV isolates from an adjacent county in Virginia, suggesting thrips transmission from a regional peanut or weed host.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus on Pittosporum tobira in the United States
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 豇豆Vigna unguiculata.
description: In July 2014, cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) leaves showing mottling, shrinking, chlorosis, necrotic concentric rings, and yellow vein were observed in fields in Dali and Dehong autonomous prefectures, Yunnan Province, China. The disease incidence based on symptom observation was 1 to 3%. Leaf samples were collected from diseased plants and tested by dot-enzyme linked immunosorbent assay, RT-PCR and sequential sequencing, the Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) infection of cowpea plants was confirmed. Cowpea plants with similar symptoms were also observed in Yuxi City of Yunnan and one of the plants was confirmed infecting with TSWV by dot-ELISA and RT-PCR. Our results showed that TSWV was a common causal agent of the cowpea viral diseases in Yunnan. TSWV is one of the most economically important plant viruses, and causes serious losses in numerous crops. To our knowledge, this is the first report of TSWV infecting cowpea in China.
reference_name: First Report of Tomato spotted wilt virus Infecting Cowpea in China
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 辣椒. sweet pepper harboring the Tsw gene.
description: In November 2013, the sweet pepper harboring the Tsw resistance gene showing typical Tospovirus symptoms were observed in La Plata. Symptoms appeared 20 days after transplanting in early spring, and by midsummer 100% of the plants were affected in many greenhouses, causing important economic losses in this season. Based on biological, serological, and molecular features confirmed that the pathogen was Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) and TSWV shared common characteristics with the resistant-breaking isolates infecting sweet pepper cultivars carrying the Tsw gene .

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pNo quantitative information is available on the impact of P. weirii in Asia (Aoshima, 1953; Dai and Qin, 1998). The cedar form in North America causes an important butt rot of old western red cedar (Thuja plicata), but losses are not quantified, and the disease is apparently less important in young cedar stands. The Douglas-fir form is considered the most damaging pathogen of young Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) in North America. An estimated 8% of the land area of Douglas-fir forests in the Pacific Northwest is colonized by the pathogen, with losses of 40-70% within these areas. In individual stands, 20% of the area may be out of production due to root rot. In other stands there may be little or no laminated root rot. Differences are apparently not the result of genetic differences in aggressiveness of the fungus, but relate to stand history and continuous occupancy by susceptible conifers (Hansen, 1986; Kastner et al., 1994). Annual losses in Canada and the USA are estimated at 4.4 million m3. This represents the combined effects of mortality and growth loss (Childs and Shea, 1967; Childs, 1970; Gedney, 1981; Filip and Goheen, 1984; Thies and Sturrock, 1995). Tree failure from laminated root rot also threatens loss to life and property in established recreation areas (Filip and Goheen, 1982).^p^p^Environmental impact^pLaminated root rot is an indigenous pathogen in all areas where it is known. In many places it is a significant factor in shaping the western forest, often killing trees in concert with bark beetles (Partridge and Miller, 1972; Hertert et al., 1975; Lane and Goheen, 1979; Goheen and Hansen, 1993). It is usually the most important agent of disturbance in the long intervals between stand-replacing wildfire. The slowly expanding gaps break up the normal continuous canopy of Douglas fir, mountain hemlock or true firs, allowing increased light on the forest floor, and a resulting change in vegetation and nutrient cycling. In many situations plant and animal diversity is increased, although the specific effect on diversity and succession depends on which species are present and able to take advantage of the gaps (McCauley and Cook, 1980; Dickman and Cook, 1989; Cromack et al., 1991;Holah et al., 1993, 1997; Ingersoll et al., 1996; Hansen and Goheen, 2000). Where western hemlock succeeds Douglas fir, the result may be a local decrease in diversity because of the very dense hemlock canopy.
author: CPC2006

description: P. weirii produces viable basidiospores from its resupinate conks that are capable of initiating decay in experimental conditions, but new infections from basidiospores have never been demonstrated in the field Nelson, 1971, 1976). Rather, all field infections that have been critically examined arose from vegetative contact with a previous infection. Where genetic analysis has been done, P. weirii from young trees is of the same somatic incompatibility type, mating type and DNA fingerprint as mycelium recovered from old infected roots from the previous stand on the same site. Although it is presumed that spore infections must occur at least rarely, the epidemiology of this pathogen is best explained by its slow, vegetative, root-to-root spread and long saprobic survival.^p^pNatural Dispersal (non-biotic)^p^pIn rare instances, earth-moving equipment may carry infected roots and deposit them in contact with healthy roots, initiating a new infection centre.^p^pVector Transmission^p^pNone known.^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pNone Known.^p^pSilvicultural Practices^p^pAlthough forest management activities may increase or decrease disease expression, they do not spread the pathogen.^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pNot known.

management_info: In most situations, no direct control of laminated root rot is practised. Awareness of the pathogen and timely salvage of killed trees during thinning operations will recoup much of the current loss. Careful marking of trees to be removed in thinning can break up the opportunity for root-to-root spread within a stand (Sturrock and Fraser, 1994). Where disease is severe, an early harvest may be justified. The best opportunities for reducing future losses occur at harvest and regeneration. Replanting with immune hardwoods such as red alder (Alnus rubra) or root-rot tolerant conifers such as western red cedar (Thuja plicata), pines or western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla), will reduce future losses, although in most situations alternative species command a lower stumpage price than Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) (Thies and Sturrock, 1995).^p^pWhere the disease is especially severe, and where soil conditions and environmental constraints allow, the physical removal of infected stumps from the ground may be feasible (Bloomberg and Reynolds, 1988; Thies et al., 1994). 'Stumping', if carefully done, will dramatically reduce future losses due to laminated root rot. Trenching around established infections will halt further vegetative spread, but is usually impractical (Wallis and Buckland, 1955).^p^pAlthough other strategies to eliminate the pathogen from infested sites have been tried, most are impractical or ineffective. Fumigant chemicals will kill P. weirii in roots and stumps and even in living trees Thies and Nelson, 1982, 1996; Thies, 1984; Nelson, 1989; Morrell and Forsyth, 1994; Frasier et al., 1995); though registered for such use in the USA, they are never used. Biological control is subject to continuing experimentation, but so far no microorganisms have been found that can replace P. weirii effectively within colonized stumps and root systems. Li (1967) and Tarrant and Trappe (1971) theorized that increased soil nitrogen from fertilization or fixation by red alder would reduce the survival of P. weirii. However, subsequent research did not support the hypothesis (Hansen, 1975; Wallis and Reynolds, 1974; Nelson et al., 1994). The search for root-rot resistant trees continues, but there is no resistant material available at this time.^p^pSeveral models have been developed to predict future losses to laminated root rot under different stand and silvicultural conditions (Reynolds and Bloomberg, 1982; Frankel, 1998; Hansen and Goheen, 2000).

remark: There are only two risks to consider. Firstly, infection by spores is through freshly cut stumps. Therefore, preventing stumps being susceptible to infection by either poisoning the stump or removing it eliminates this risk. The second risk is from infected root fragments which may harbour viable fungus for up to 4 years in buried roots 3 inches in diameter. The accidental movement of such fragments in soil poses a risk of spreading the disease, and soil should not be removed from infested areas. Non-susceptible annual crops can assist in the breakdown of these fragments, and it is recommended that infested soil should not be re-planted with susceptible trees for a period of several years. This is often ignored in the redevelopment of old plantations due to economic pressures, but the earlier re-planting may be a false saving if this disease is still present, as it will destroy the new planting very quickly.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control measures depend on routine inspection and removal of diseased trees. Recommendations in the past have concentrated on digging exclusion trenches around the infected tree and digging along infected roots until the infection front is located. This, however, has proved to be of limited practical value on a large scale. Various fungicides have been found to have activity against the pathogen (Lim et al., 1990; Mappes and Hiepko, 1984), but routine field treatments with these fungicides are not economical. ^p^pThe establishment of a good ground cover to hasten the decay of root fragments is recommended when clearing land. This will enhance the breakdown of any infected root fragments which otherwise would provide an inoculum source for the following crop.^p^pSpore infection can be prevented by the chemical poisoning of stumps with compounds which are not toxic to this pathogen (Anon., 1976). Spores require a freshly cut surface, and cannot infect a dead surface.^p^pOther chemicals which have been found to be effective eradicants are soil fumigants (Ram and Venkataram, 1975), but are not used on a plantation scale due to prohibitive cost, and potential danger to users. Volatile ammonia generated from urea is fungicidal to P. noxius in infested wood (Chang and Chang, 1999).^p^pBiocontrol with species of Trichoderma is recognised as a method to prevent spore infection of freshly cut stumps (Anon., 1993). P. noxius is not a strong competitor and is unable to colonize a stump if another organism, such as a species of Trichoderma, is already present. But the method is technically more demanding than poisoning stumps, and is not currently widely used. The potential for biocontrol in the rhizosphere has been demonstrated, particularly with species of Trichoderma (Lim and Teh, 1990; Jacob et al., 1991; Kothandaraman et al., 1991).

potential_eco_desc: Peries and Liyanage (1985) ranked white root disease as the second most important disease of rubber. However, in a recent survey, R. lignosus was ranked the most important in the main rubber-growing countries (Allen and Cronin, 1994). The disease is most important within the first 5 years of a plantation. Although the annual incidence may be low, the accumulated losses from spread to adjacent trees may result in large vacant patches. Losses vary from country to country and from field to field, greatly influenced by moisture level. The incidence reported varies from 2% per year in Cameroon, Gabon and Ivory Coast, 8-10% in Sri Lanka (Peries and Liyanage, 1985) to 10-15% (Basuki et al., 1976) and 5-10% (Soepena, 1993) in Indonesia. Soepena (1993) reported that there were many cases of blocks of 3-year-old plantings with 30% incidence in Indonesia; the incidence was 40-60% in smallholdings. Consequently, such areas would have to be replanted early (before 20 years old) as by then less than 30% of the original stand would remain. In a survey of smallholdings in Malaysia, white root disease was a problem to 43% of the respondents (Sail et al., 1990), although the incidence was not stated.^p^pThe economics of white root disease has been discussed (Liyanage, 1977). Apart from yield loss due to tree death, the cost of treating root diseases contributes to the increased cost of production.
