management_info: Introduction^p^pControl of white root disease is highly necessary to prevent it from spreading to neighbouring trees. Disease control should commence as early as possible, normally about 1 year after planting, and be regularly continued thereafter. White root disease incidence should be eradicated, or be at its very minimum, by the time the rubber trees are opened for tapping at 5-6 years old.^p^p^Resistant Clones^p^pThere are no known species of Hevea or clones that are resistant to white root disease. A few studies indicated that certain clones are more resistant than others (Liyanage et al., 1977; Peries and Liyanage, 1985). However, resistance is not given any emphasis when clones are chosen for planting.^p^p^Cultural Practices^p^pCultural practices form a major component of control, especially that targeted to reduce the inoculum level. When a rubber area is to be replanted, the methods used to clear old trees from the land determine the residual level of inoculum. Full mechanical clearing - uprooting the trees, ploughing and raking the land to collect and dispose of the rubber roots - offers the least incidence of root disease in a replanting (Newsam, 1967). This procedure is expensive and cannot be adopted by smallholders, who may clear the land by felling the trees with chainsaws and applying aboricides to promote faster decay (Newsam, 1967; Lim and Abdul Aziz, 1981). Painting the cut surfaces of the stumps with creosote was once suggested, to prevent colonization of the stumps via basidiospores (John, 1965), but the practice was questioned by Fox (1977).^p^pPlanting of creeping legume covers assists in reducing incidence of white root disease by promoting faster decay of inoculum as well as creating suppressive environments to R. lignosus (Newsam, 1963;Fox, 1965b, 1977).^p^pWorkers should avoid injuring the roots of the plants in order to prevent infection by the spores. Infected trees along with the roots should be removed where possible. Alternatively, infected trees, especially in a mature rubber area, should be enclosed within a trenched area to prevent contact between roots of diseased and healthy trees (Rubber Research Institute of Malaysia, 1974b).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control is a common practice in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Collar protectant dressings (i.e. formulations of fungicide in bituminous compound) are painted onto exposed parts of lateral and tap roots as well as tree collars after surgically removing all infected tissues Fox, 1961b, 1965a, 1966; Riggenbach, 1958). Quintozene may be used as a fungicide (Fox, 1966).^p^pApplying the collar protectant dressing involves digging and is laborious. It is thus being replaced by another method of fungicide application, by drenching aqueous solutions of fungicides in a shallow furrow dug immediately around the base of the tree. In Malaysia, triadimefon and propiconazole were first used (Tan and Ismail, 1992). Since then, hexaconazole has been found effective. In Africa, tridemorph was first used in the drenching treatment (Canh, 1986). Later, cyproconazole and triadimenol were also found effective (Gohet et al., 1991).^p^pSoil drenching of fungicide as a method of controlling R. lignosus on rubber is more suitable for younger trees as it is less or even not effective on larger and more mature trees. It is also not effective on trees with advanced disease, i.e. trees with obvious foliage symptoms (Tan and Ismail, 1992).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pSoil sulphur amendment, a form of indirect biological control, is being practised in Malaysia and Indonesia. Because sulphur is non-fungicidal to R. lignosus in laboratory tests, the mechanism of control is attributed to the build-up of antagonists, especially species of Trichoderma and Penicillium, in sulphur-amended soils due to a reduction in pH (Satchuthanan Thavale and Halangoda, 1971; Basuki et al., 1976; Peries and Liyanage, 1983; Ismail Hashim and Azaldin, 1985). management_info: Cultural Control^p^pResistant cultivars are available for species of Medicago (Bretag and Kollmorgen, 1986; Barbetti, 1989). Brassica tissue can suppress P. irregulare and other pathogens in vitro (Kirkegaard et al., 1996). Composts can be used to suppress damping-off caused by P. irregulare (Ben and Nelson, 1999)^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pMetalaxyl was incorporated in soil to effectively control root rot (Cook and Zhang, 1985; Bretag and Kollmorgen, 1986), in spraying to control cavity spots in carrots (Shlevin et al., 1987), in soil or seed treatments to control damping-off in white clover and lucerne (Skipp and Watson, 1987), in soil fumigation to control infection of sweet onion (Sumner et al., 1997) and of ornamental plants (Jamart et al., 1988). Furalaxyl inhibted growth of P. irregulare and controlled cucumber root rot in hydroponic systems (Price and Fox, 1986). Seed treatment with metalaxyl and thiram controlled pre-emergence damping-off in cabbage and cauliflower (White et al., 1984).^p^pSoil fumigation with methyl bromide and chloropicrin reduced black root rot of strawberry and increased yield (Yuen et al., 1991; Scott et al., 1992), and also reduced rootlet colonization of lucerne by P. ultimum and P. irregulare and increased foliage yield (Hancock, 1993).^p^pPropamocarb hydrochloride significantly reduced loss of tomato plants by Pythium species (Rapp and Richter, 1982). Seed treatment with captan and captan plus Certop [a polymer] increased the emergence rate index, seed emergence, and seedling height, and reduced seed infection by P. irregulare and P. ultimum (Rivas et al., 1998). Soil drenching with pyroxychlor, fenaminosulf, benomyl, metalaxyl, propamocarb and etridiazole reduced the percentage of diseased poinsettia roots (Raabe et al., 1981).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBinucleate Rhizoctonia isolates completely controlled damping-off of Capsicum annuum caused by P. irregulare (Harris and Adkins, 1999). A strain of Bacillus sp. controlled three root diseases of wheat including Pythium root rot caused by P. ultimum and P. irregulare (Kim et al., 1997). Pseudomonas fluorescens produces the antibiotic 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol and suppresses many plant pathogens including P. irregulare (Levy et al., 1992). A combination of Bacillus species and metalaxyl at a low rate could be used to improve the establishment and growth of field pea in Pythium-infested soils (Hwang et al., 1996).

potential_eco_desc: In the north-west Pacific area of the USA frequencies of tubers with corky ringspot of 5-10% have been found, sometimes compromising the sale of entire field production (Williams et al., 1996).^p^pIn southern Italy (Campania region), lettuce yield losses have been attributed to TRV in complex with other viruses (Ragozzino et al., 1978); in central Italy (Umbria region), pepper fields with 30-40% infected plants and significant yield losses have been reported (Marte et al., 1979).^p^pPotato tuber spraing is a cause of concern for growers in Halland in south-west Sweden, giving rise to yield losses on light sandy soils where nematode vectors (Trichodorus spp.) are also common (Svensson, 1974). In Sweden average yield losses due to virus infections including TRV is estimated to be in the range of 10 to 30% (Lihnell et al., 1975).^p^pIn Belorussia potato viruses, including TRV, are widespread and losses are increased by mixed infections (Ambrosof and Sokolova, 1976).^p^pYearly losses in carrot from virus diseases including TRV exceeded 50% in eastern Germany (Wolf and Schmelzer, 1973).
author: CPC2006

description: Pathogen Transmission^p^pSeed transmissibility of a pathogen plays an important role in catastrophic epidemics in many crops. Evidence for TRV seed transmissibility has not been found on crops but only, and rather sparsely, on wild species. In Viola arvensis and occasionally in other weeds, 2-10% infected seeds were found (Cooper and Harrison, 1973). Seed dissemination has so far been irrelevant in TRV dispersal, but wild species including weeds have a role in the epidemiology of the nematode-borne TRV (Cooper and Harrison, 1973).^p^pThe use of potato tubers showing spraing symptoms of TRV was irrelevant for the establishment of field infection, because virus spread depended on the presence of weeds (Harrison et al., 1982, 1983).^p^pTRV also infects plants through parasitic weeds of the genus Cuscuta (Lucas, 1975).

remark: There are no reported quarantine restrictions for TRV.

management_info: Agronomic practices, resistant cultivars and other means of reducing inoculum potential should be used to prevent TRV infection.^p^p^Cultural Practices^p^pInoculum potential can be reduced by growing crop species which do not support nematode populations, but fallow in potato rotations has proved to be more effective than the production of a non-host nematode crop (Langels, 1994).^p^pCultivation of susceptible crops or cultivars should be avoided in fields containing TRV-infected nematodes. Marked decreases in TRV frequency have been observed on potato following barley, lupin, radish or lucerne, with barley the most effective nematode suppresser (Barchend and Heidel, 1985; Gripwall, 1986).^p^pEarly harvesting is recommended to reduce spraing symptoms in potatoes, especially in wet years which favour the development of spraing disease (Svensson, 1974).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pAlthough direct control of the virus is not feasible, indirect control by reducing soil nematode populations is possible but difficult because vectors live in deep soil layers (up to 1 m deep). Chemical treatments, including soil fumigation or spraying plants with systemic chemicals, reduce nematode populations effectively only in the upper 0-20 cm of the soil (Pelsmaeker, 1987). Fumigation with methyl bromide, vapam-metham, basamid, dichloropropene and telone (trichloropropene + chloropicrin) is recommended for seedbeds.^p^pChemicals kill nematodes or inhibit feeding activity (Koot and Molendijk, 1997). Telone has been reported to reduce nematode populations and corky ringspot of tubers caused by TRV (William et al., 1996). Granular fumigants such as aldicarb and fenamiphos, only slightly reduce infestation levels of Trichodorus nematodes in potato fields in loamy soils (Koot and Molendijk, 1997). Field fumigation is very expensive and not always advisable for economic and environmental reasons and, furthermore, the use of chemicals such as methyl bromide is restricted or banned in many countries.^p^pPlots of bait-plants can be used to gather information on distribution trends of nematode vectors of TRV (Ploeg et al., 1996).^p^pThe incidence of nematodes and the occurrence of TRV-infected plants are positively correlated, but the reduction of nematode populations has occasionally resulted in an increase of TRV infections (van Hoof, 1973).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBreeding for resistance to TRV is being explored using various approaches. Insertion of the virus coat protein (CP) gene or other non-structural protein genes in susceptible potato genotypes hinders infection by mechanically inoculated virus, but not that transmitted by Trichodorus or Paratrichodorus (Ploeg et al., 1993a). This suggests that either a far higher number of virus particles are injected by nematodes or that TRV mutation occurs during nematode transmission. CP-transgenic plants do not give protection against NM-types (non-producing CP).^p^pTransgenic tobacco plants expressing the CP gene of a TRV-strain were resistant to infection by the homologous virus and by the related pea early-browning tobravirus, but not to an unrelated TRV-strain or by homologous TRV-RNA alone (van Dun and Bol, 1988; Angenent et al., 1990).^p^p^Resistant Cultivars^p^pThere are no tobacco cultivars available that are resistant to TRV. Some potato cultivars have factors of resistance to TRV-induced spraing (Carlsson, 1986) while others are tolerant of the virus (Robinson and Dale, 1994). The cultivar British Queen is very susceptible to spraing, while cv. Bintje is quite resistant because of the hypersensitivity reaction (Engsbro, 1973); cultivars King Edward, Provita and Saturna show intermediate resistance (Svensson, 1974; Carlsson, 1986).^p^pNative Solanum species such as S. acaule, S. boliviense, S. chacoense, S. demissum, S. paucissectum and S. aliandiae (Kalfov and Melard, 1972) have resistance factors to TRV, but these have not yet been used in potato breeding. description: TRV不能在地面上由昆虫媒介或植物操作而传播。在苗床和作物田地里，TRV主要由两个属（毛刺线虫属(Trichodorus)和异毛刺线虫属(Paratrichodorus) ）的植物寄生性线虫传播的。一共14种线虫被发现能传播该病毒，其中T. primitivus, T. similis和P. pachydermus是最为广泛分布的媒介(Pelsmaeker and Coomans, 1986; Ploeg and Decraemer, 1997)。TRV也能通过菟丝子（Cuscuta）科的寄生野草来侵染植物(Lucas, 1975).。通过线虫的自然主动传播是非常慢的。通过携带土壤微粒的风传播和在水的表面传播更快(Polak, 1994)。虽然马铃薯植株的块茎传播是相当少的(Engsbro, 1976)，但是远距离传播由感染的苗木或感染的马铃薯块茎的运输促使。 TRV is not transmitted above ground by either insect vectors or plant manipulation. In seedbeds and crop fields TRV is mainly transmitted by species belonging to two genera of plant parasitic nematodes, Trichodorus and Paratrichodorus. A total of 14 species have been found to transmit the virus, T. primitivus, T. similis and P. pachydermus being the most widespread vectors (Pelsmaeker and Coomans, 1986; Ploeg and Decraemer, 1997). Natural active spread by nematodes is very slow. Dissemination is swifter by wind carrying soil particles and in surface waters (Polak, 1994). Dissemination over longer distances is fostered by transport of infected plantlets or infected potato tubers, although tuber transmission to potato plants is rather rare (Engsbro, 1976).TRV also infects plants through parasitic weeds of the genus Cuscuta (Lucas, 1975).

host_range: Natural infection with PEBV has been reported mainly in legume species, including pea (Pisum sativum), faba bean (Vicia faba major, var. equina and var. minor), French bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), lupin (Lupinus spp.), and alfalfa (lucerne) (Medicago sativa
potential_eco_desc: Poor growth, death of plants and weed infestation in PEBV-infected areas of pea crops causes yield reduction. The importance of PEBV in commercial pea crops in the Netherlands is such that a certification scheme was introduced in 1959 and is still continuing (see Control). Bos and van der Want (1962) recommended that susceptible crops should not be grown on land where PEBV is known to be present. Many farmers in England, UK, avoid growing peas on infested land, but sowing very early crops on light land is often essential in order to meet the requirements of commercial processors for continuity of harvesting. The severe symptoms of BBYBV in Italy (Russo et al., 1984) imply that yield losses may have occurred (Jellis et al., 1998).Fiederow (1983) found that mechanical inoculation with PEBV alone reduced the seed yield of faba beans by an average of 27%. Broad bean true mosaic comovirus (BBTMV) alone caused a 44% yield loss, but plants co-infected with PEBV and BBTMV suffered a 77% yield loss.
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pPEBV is seedborne in several hosts. Lockhart and Fischer (1976) found that a Moroccan isolate of PEBV could be recovered from 30% of pea seeds, but the seed coat did not contain any virus. In Poland, Kowalska (1979) also reported isolation of PEBV from pea seed. Cockbain et al. (1983) reported seed infection of up to 5% in two out of three varieties of faba bean following sap inoculation. Fiederow (1980, 1983) reported infection with PEBV of 10% and transmission of up to 8% in faba bean seed grown in the glasshouse, but only 0.3% of the seed from plants grown under field conditions was infected. Seed from sap-inoculated and systemically infected plants of Phaseolus vulgaris, tested by Bos and van der Want (1962), did not contain PEBV. An infection rate of 4% was recorded in seed from Nicotiana rustica inoculated with AlgR10, the first report of seed transmission of PEBV in a non-legume.^p^pEmbryos of peas were uniformly infected with PEBV from the earliest stages of embryo development, and the virus was detected in the egg cell and pollen grains, indicative of gametic transmission into the embryo (Wang and Maule, 1997).^p^pWang et al., (1997) introduced mutations into the PEBV genome to investigate the viral determinants of transmission of virus from mother plant to seed in peas. Deleting the part of the genome containing the three nonstructural genes in RNA2 or interrupting any of the three genes did not affect PEBV seed transmission. Removing the coding sequence of the 12K gene in RNA1 almost completely prevented viral seed transmission. Without the 12K gene the virus caused more severe symptoms on pea leaves and pods, and accumulated at higher levels in these tissues. However, it did not accumulate in anthers and carpels and was not detected in pollen grains or ovules. It is suggested that the 12K gene is involved in the infection of gametic cells and hence in seed transmission of PEBV in peas.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality ^p^pBos and van der Want (1962) found that PEBV-infected plants of the pea variety Rondo could produce a proportion of wrinkled and greenish-grey seed.^p^p^Pathogen TransmissionWang and Maule (1997) reported that pea seed embryos were uniformly infected with PEBV from the earliest stages of embryo development.^p^pAccording to Bos and van der Want (1962) the incidence of PEBV in a crop grown on soil not previously carrying the virus will depend on the amount of the initial seed infection and on its transmission to the progeny plants and possibly between them, if vector nematodes are present. The virus is not spread above ground by foliar contact or insect vectors, for example, and a low percentage of seed infection would be unlikely to result in serious crop damage. Bos and van der Want (1962) also noted that for a previously virus-free soil to become contaminated through infected seed, it had to be 'receptive'. A receptive soil would be a sandy or light-textured type where the vector species of nematodes are present, and conditions are favourable for them to be active for acquisition, retention, and transmission of the virus isolate. Infective nematodes are unlikely to spread virus over more than short distances by natural means.^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pSerological ^pDot-immuno-binding (Lange et al., 1989), ELISA (Van Vuurde and Maat, 1985) and Disperse-dye immuno assay (Van Vuurde and Maat, 1985) procedures have been described.

management_info: Introduction^p^pBos and van der Want (1962) noted that prevention is in most cases the only means of control of virus diseases, and that methods of prevention included the use of highly resistant or immune varieties and the avoidance of sources of infection. Harrison and Robinson (1986) also included decreasing the numbers or the activity of the nematode vectors of tobraviruses.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pConventional breeding of good pea varieties with comprehensive resistance is difficult because of the wide variation of PEBV isolates. Hubbeling and Kooistra (1963) attempted to identify pea varieties with resistance to PEBV by means of artificial infection in the glasshouse. Inoculum was prepared from diseased plants or seeds and rubbed onto the leaves of seedlings. Although some varieties appeared resistant in these tests they became infected when grown in PEBV-infested soil in field conditions. Wide variation was found in the degree of susceptibilty of a large number of varieties when they were sown early on an infested field, and more than 30 varieties were identified as highly tolerant, or as resistant if symptoms never occurred. These varieties also showed no seed transmission of virus. The results were similar in each of 4 years of testing. Harrison (1966) tested 31 of these varieties with the British serotype, by sap inoculation and by growing them in soil containing infective nematodes obtained from two different sites. Almost all were susceptible by sap inoculation, and all were susceptible to a virus isolate transmitted by nematodes from one site. However, 26 varieties were still resistant to nematode transmission of the other British isolate. These results show that resistance-breaking isolates occur even within the same serotype, and that the ability to infect pea cultivars varies independently of antigenic constitution (Harrison and Robinson, 1978). The results stress the importance of testing for resistance by means of natural transmission, utilising many different field sites, rather than by sap inoculation.^p^p^Regulatory Control^p^pIt is most important to ensure that crops are sown with virus-free seed, to reduce the incidence of PEBV in commercial seed and to reduce spread of the virus to previously uninfested sites. The General Netherlands Inspection Service for Seeds of Field Crops and for Seed Potatoes (NAK) initiated the field inspection of pea crops for certification in 1959 (Bos and van der Want, 1962) and this is still continuing. Currently there is zero tolerance for PEBV in plants within prebasic and basic seed crops, and for certified seed production a crop is rejected if there is more than one PEBV-infected plant in 100 square metres. Seed is also visually inspected and samples are tested by ELISA if the presence of PEBV is suspected. Not more than two infected seeds per kilogram are tolerated for prebasic and basic seed and not more than 12 infected seeds per 500 g for certified seed (Boulton, 1996).^p^pBreeders and others involved with national and international crop improvement should also try to ensure that only healthy seed is acquired and exchanged.^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pWeed control may also help to reduce sources of infection, and the persistence of virus in the vector population. Control must be effected throughout the growing season and for a number of years, because of the long retention of the virus by the vectors and the possible longevity of PEBV in dormant weed seed. Rigorous weed control actually increased the incidence of TRV in potato crops in the short term (Cooper and Harrison, 1973) probably because the vectors prefer to feed on weeds but in their absence were obliged to feed on potato.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical treatments which kill nematodes, or inhibit their activity, can be applied as soil fumigants or through granular or spray applications which become systemic in the host plants (Harrison and Robinson, 1986). Approximately 30% of the trees had blighted shoots and 10% had stem canker leading to death of entire tree. Symptomatic tissues were collected and fungi were isolated, the causal pathogen was identified as Neofusicoccum parvum based on morphological and molecular identifications and pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of N. parvum causing shoot blight and stem canker on pomegranate in Florida.

description: Since 2012, a severe wilt disease has been discovered on sandalwood in several commercial plantations in Dongguan, Guangdong Province. Under suitable conditions (with 30 to 35°C air temperature and 65 to 95% relative humidity), the disease incidence could increase rapidly to 60% in a plantation. Fungal isolates were isolated from the internal stem bases of diseased sandalwood trees. Based on morphology and molecular diagnostics, the pathogen was identified as Neofusicoccum parvum. This pathogen has been reported to cause dieback and canker in a wide range of fruit crops, including Juglans sinensis and Vitis heyneana. To our knowledge, this is the first report of N. parvum causing wilt and stem rot on S. album.

host_range: Vitis vinifera.
description: Decline of grapevine caused by Neofusicoccum parvum in France has, until now, only been observed in old vines of Vitis vinifera, typically at least more than 10 years old. In recent years, decline symptoms have been observed in young vines between 3 and 6 years old in the vineyards of C?tes-de-Provence. Between 2007 and 2008, 30% of plants in affected vineyards monitored showed decline symptoms resulting in serious economic loss. During the summers of 2007 and 2008 (July), 27 young plants (Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, and Sauvignon blanc) were inspected both externally and internally from eight Provence vineyards. To verify the identification based on morphology, sequencing of the internal transcribed spacer region (ITS), β-tubulin gene (BT2), and the translation elongation factor 1-α gene (EF1-α) were conducted on DNA from one Neofusicoccum parvum isolate. The resulting DNA sequences were 100% identical to N. parvum sequences present in GenBank. Grapevine decline in young vineyards (less than 8 years old) is a common symptom worldwide and several fungal species have been identified as causal agents. Here, we show that N. parvum is directly associated with young grapevine decline in France and should be considered in future investigations and when diagnosing the cause of decline in young vines.
reference_name: First Report of Young Grapevine Decline Caused by Neofusicoccum parvum in France

A literature review for fungal diseases of G. biloba in Iran revealed only Phyllosticta ginkgo causing a leaf spot, but no reports of N. parvum. However, N. parvum has been associated with grapevine decline in Iran. To the best of our knowledge, this is first record of this pathogen as causal agent of leaf spot on ginkgo in the world.

description: In July 2013 in coastal (Santa Barbara County) California, commercial plantings of southern highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) developed symptoms of a previously undiagnosed disease. The samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was Neofusicoccum parvum. Many Botryosphaeriaceae species, including N. parvum, are associated with canker and dieback symptoms on blueberry worldwide. To our knowledge, this is the first documentation of stem blight caused by N. parvum on blueberry in CA. Blueberry is a rapidly expanding industry in the state, with 960 ha planted in 2005 increasing to 2,830 ha in 2012. Drought stress predisposes plants to stem blight caused by Botryosphaeriacease species; therefore, expansion into arid areas of CA could increase the incidence and severity of N. parvum.

host_range: N. parvum是一种世界性的多寄主病原，已有导致几种有经济重要性的寄主病害，包括葡萄、猕猴桃，以及导致新西兰鳄梨果实和西班牙鳄梨小枝的蒂腐病的报道。
description: 2009年春季，发现鳄梨果实表面有光滑、黑色、圆形斑。2010年冬季，在墨西哥米却肯州Nuevo Parangaricutiro县(19°25′00″ and 102°07′43″)的果园有黑斑症状的鳄梨上分离出真菌病原，经鉴定，病原为Neofusicoccum parvum。这是墨西哥首次报道Neofusicoccum parvum导致鳄梨果实黑斑病。
management_info:
从未成熟鳄梨果实的病斑边缘取样，在PDA上培养得到几个真菌菌株。使用通用引物ITS5和ITS4，对rDNA的内转录间隔区(ITS) 扩增测序，在GenBank中BLAST 搜索结果表明与Neofusicoccum parvum的核酸序列相似性为100%。在酸化PDA 上，N. parvum菌株产生气生紧凑菌丝体，无性阶段为Botryosphaeria parva。菌丝体初为白色，后逐渐变为灰色至黑色。分生孢子单胞、透明、椭圆形至梭形，外部光滑，薄壁，无隔，随生长产生1-2个隔膜, 一般大小为14.5 (9.5～19) × 5.8 (4.0～7.2) μm。
用哈斯鳄梨果实进行致病性检测。果实表面接种，均以针刺破组织，浸于N. parvum的分生孢子团中或注入孢子悬浮液。接种果实置于25°C的潮湿室内2周。2天后在针刺伤口处出现黑斑，4天后在非伤口处出现黑斑，症状发展的延迟可能是由于病菌通过皮孔渗入，要花费更长的时间引发侵染。对照果实上无症状。在所有接种果实病斑上重新分离到病原，因此满足柯赫氏法则。
reference_name: First Report of Black Spots on Avocado Fruit Caused by Neofusicoccum parvum in Mexico

host_range: Lasiodiplodia theobromae causing bot gummosis was previously reported in Citrus affecting C. aurantium, C. aurantifolia, and C. sinensis in Mexico. To our knowledge, this is the first report of L. theobromae causing bot gummosis of C. limon in Chile and worldwide.
description: In June 2016, Citrus limon trees located in the Pica oasis, Tarapacá Region, were observed showing trunk canker, branch dieback, vascular streaks, and gummy orange-brown exudation. Samples from affected trees of one orchard were taken and were sent to the Plant Pathology Lab for analysis. Based on morphological and molecular identification, the pathogen was identified as Lasiodiplodia theobromae.  To our knowledge, this is the first report of L. theobromae causing bot gummosis of C. limon in Chile and worldwide. This new disease in Chile was detected in Pica oasis, and it is important that this pathogen does not disseminate to the central zone of Chile, where the main Citrus commercial orchards are located.

host_range: Lasiodiplodia theobromae is found worldwide and has an extremely broad host range, causing canker, dieback, root rot, and postharvest diseases on more than 500 hosts.
description: Between March and September 2013, three Polyscias fruticosa samples with extensive cankers were submitted to the California Department of Food and Agriculture Plant Pest Diagnostics Center in Sacramento, CA. Two samples were collected from a nursery in Los Angeles County and the other from one in San Diego County. Plants originated in Costa Rica. Dark brown to black stem cankers extended from the soil line to the lateral branches, and averaged 14.3 cm in length. Removal of the outer epidermis revealed very little healthy cambium tissue and the stems were nearly girdled. The pathogen was identified as Lasiodiplodia theobromae by morphological characteristics, ITS sequence analysis and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of L. theobromae on P. fruticosa.
reference_name: First Report of Lasiodiplodia theobromae Associated with Collar Rot and Dieback on Polyscias fruticosa in California

host_range: Lasiodiplodia theobromae has been reported to cause cankers in a wide range of hosts, such as fruit and vegetable crops, and it is also reported to attack maize in India and Cuba. To our knowledge, this is the first report of L. theobromae causing ear rot on maize in China.
potential_eco_desc: About 4% of maize ears with black gray mold was observed in seed fields at Ledong, Hainan Province, China (18°29′N, 108°54′E).
description: In February 2015, about 4% of maize ears with black gray mold was observed in seed fields at Ledong, Hainan Province, China (18°29′N, 108°54′E). The pathogen was identified as Lasiodiplodia theobromae by morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of L. theobromae causing ear rot on maize in China.  It is necessary to strengthen quarantine measures against spread of the pathogen from Hainan to the mainland through seed-breeding.
reference_name: First Report of Lasiodiplodia theobromae Causing Maize Ear Rot in Hainan Province in Southern China

description: 茶黑心根腐病1882年在巴基斯坦发现，1920年前后在斯里兰卡严重发生，同时印度尼西亚也有记载，我国有记载，但分布不详。
management_info:
1.做好田间卫生 冬季至少在腰果树开花前，清除所有残留的病果、病枝和落在地面的枯枝、落叶，集中烧毁，以减少田间菌源。
2.药剂防治 开花时期喷施有效的杀菌、杀虫混合剂。如用1.5g/L有效成分的敌菌丹与50%马拉硫磷2000倍液（或与乐果）混合的杀菌杀虫混合液喷雾，每株次喷5L，7天一次，连续喷2次，或用50%代森锌可湿性粉剂1000倍液与50%敌百虫或敌敌畏乳油1000倍混合剂，或代森锌与50%杀螟松乳油或50%马拉硫磷乳油2000倍混合液喷雾，能有效控制盲蝽等昆虫对腰果伤害，减轻回枯病的发生。

potential_eco_desc: B. theobromae affects a very wide range of crops (see Host Range), particularly at the postharvest stage. As such rots are caused by complexes of pathogens, the economic impact is hard to quantify. However, Wadud and Ahmed (1962) have reported that B. theobromae caused maize seedling mortality up to an average of 57%.^p^pThe fungus is most important as a cause of postharvest food decay. It also causes damage in cocoa in the form of dieback disease. In citrus it causes stem end rot of the fruit and is the most important postharvest disease. In rambutan, stem-end rot caused by B. theobromae has been reported from Sri Lanka (Sivakumar et al., 1997).^p^pB. theobromae has been identified as one of the major postharvest pathogens of mango (Mascarenhas et al., 1996), sweet potato (Ray and Punithalingam, 1996), cocoyams (Ugwuanyi and Obeta, 1996), durian (Sivapalan et al., 1998). For the first time, the occurrence B. theobromae in postharvest disease of quince has been reported in India by Sharma and Sumbali Geeta (1997).^p^pIn Nigeria, B. theobromae has been asociated with rot of black plum (Eseigbe and Bankole, 1996) and wilted groundnut plants (Osuinde and Daibo, 1999).
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pB. theobromae is reported to be seedborne in at least 24 plant genera (Richardson, 1990). These include seeds of the following economically important crops: groundnut (Wilson, 1945), cotton (Anon., 1951; Oliveira et al., 1996; Lima et al., 1998; Patricio et al., 1999), cocoa (Wellman, 1954), maize (del Rosario, 1954), rubber Srivastava, 1956, 1964), Musa spp. (Goos et al., 1961), jute (Wadud and Ahmad, 1962), artichokes (Michail et al., 1965), Macrotyloma uniflorum (Maholay and Sohi, 1977), Cajanus cajan (Ellis et al., 1978), Artocarpus integer (Manoharachary et al., 1978), sorghum (Rani et al., 1978), wheat (Giha, 1977) and soyabean (Ellis et al., 1979). Incidences of seed infection above 50% have been recorded in maize (Kumar and Shetty, 1983), 11% in cowpeas (Barros et al., 1990), 29% in pigeon peas (Hepperly and Rodriguez, 1984; Bankole et al., 1996) and up to 100% in squashes (Maholay and Sohi, 1982). The pathogen survived for 12 months in seeds of bottlegourds, 7 months in those of squashes (Maholay and Sohi, 1982), and 7 months in the seeds of cotton (Oliveira et al., 1996).^p^pHistological studies of seed infection detected the pathogen in the pericarp, embryo and endosperm of maize (Kumar and Shetty, 1983). B. theobromae was found only in the seed coat or micropylar plug in the seeds of Musa bulbisiana (Goos et al., 1961). Although infected seeds of Hevea brasiliensis hardly showed any external symptoms, the various stages of infection became apparent on splitting open the affected seeds (Srivastava, 1964); in the earliest stage there was a slight browning of the endosperm compared to that of the healthy seed and later both the embryo and endosperm turned black, the change in colour usually commencing from the hilum end of the seed. In advanced stages a blackish felt-like layer, about 1 mm thick and largely composed of fungal hyphae, was also noticed surrounding the endosperm underneath the testa. Severely diseased seeds showed various stages of disintegration of the embryo and the endosperm, indicating the internal seedborne nature of B. theobromae.^p^pIn a study of the process of seed infection in the field over a period of 3-10 weeks of seed development and maturation, B. theobromae was found in developing seeds of jute from 5-week-old pods (Khan and Fakir, 1992). The incidence of B. theobromae infection of slash pine (Pinus elliottii var. elliottii) seeds was greatest in cones collected earliest and left in contact with the ground before storage. The incidence of disease decreased with later collection dates. Fungus-damaged seeds were not present in cones dried immediately after collection, regardless of the collection date. Fungi were rarely established in seeds when cones were removed from trees; they apparently colonized seeds and caused disease during cone harvest and storage (Fraedrich et al., 1994). A 3 week delay in harvest drastically increased the incidence of B. theobromae in pigeon pea (Hepperly and Rodriguez, 1984). Seeds from field-grown pigeon pea plants sprayed with benomyl had significantly fewer internal seedborne fungi including Botryodiplodia and significantly greater in vitro germination and field emergence (Ellis et al., 1977).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pSeeds of maize infected by B. theobromae are shiny-black or have grey-black streaks. Pycnidia may form on them. Severely infected seeds are rotten and fail to germinate (del Rosario, 1954; Kumar and Shetty, 1983). Manoj-Kumar (1998) reported that black and spotted maize seeds with reduced germination, caused by B. theobromae infection, could be controlled using thiram, iprodione, mancozeb, zineb, metalaxyl and carbendazim. Wadud and Ahmad (1962) have reported jute seedling mortality of up to 57% for both pre- and post-emergence, due to seedborne infection by B. theobromae. potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe economic impact caused by the pine shoot beetles is threefold: firstly, growth losses may be caused by extensive shoot-feeding in the pine crowns; secondly, stem attacks cause tree mortality; and thirdly, deterioration of timber quality may occur due to beetle-vectored blue-staining of saw logs and pulpwood.^p^pIn T. piniperda, the third type of damage is the least problem, mainly because the forest industry has developed routines to avoid timber damage by timber insects including pine shoot beetles. Compared to T. minor, the blue-staining caused by T. piniperda occurs less frequently in timber and is often more superficial, but it still poses a major problem, as indicated by a series of Finnish studies, because T. piniperda is so common (Loyttyniemi and Uusvaara, 1977; Uusvaara and Loyttyniemi, 1978). Recently, sap staining of Korean pine logs due to T. piniperda attack was reported as a timber storage problem in Korea (Kim et al., 2002). No estimates of the economic losses due to blue-staining caused by T. piniperda are available, but the presence of any blue-staining in conifer saw logs reduces the value to a fraction (ca 20%) of the price of prime timber on the timber market, hence, saw mills have developed timber handling practices that minimise insect damage. Although some blue-staining is acceptable in pulpwood, there is a cost connected to the processing of blue-stained timber, as more chemicals are needed for bleaching (Loyttyniemi et al., 1978).^p^pIn contrast to the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) and a few other aggressive bark beetles, T. piniperda cannot overwhelm and kill healthy pine trees, probably because it lacks aggregation pheromones. Thus, tree mortality due to pine shoot beetle attacks occurs only when trees are weakened by some other cause such as defoliation, fire damage, drought stress, flooding, etc. There are several European examples of defoliator outbreaks rendering pine trees susceptible to pine shoot beetle attacks (Saalas, 1929; Butovitsch, 1946; Lekander, 1953; Crooke, 1959; Habermann and Geibler, 2001; Langstrom et al., 2001; Cedervind et al., 2003), but tree mortality varies from a few to more than 50% of trees. In the worst case, 2 years of severe to total defoliation led to ca 50% pine mortality over a 5-year period, half of which was attributed to T. piniperda, whereas stands sprayed with Dimilin suffered 1 year of defoliation, no mortality and modest growth losses (Langstrom et al., 2001). In another case, beetles caused substantial tree mortality after 1 year of defoliation (Crooke, 1959), whereas normally such defoliation would result in only a few and mainly suppressed trees dying from subsequent beetle attack (Lekander, 1953; Cedervind et al., 2003). Each defoliation case is unique and difficult to generalise; however, in most cases studied, trees with less than 10% of the normal foliage left are in great danger of fatal beetle attacks, whereas trees with more than 30% foliage are safer.^p^pPine trees may also become susceptible to Tomicus attack by fungal diseases. There is one report from Denmark (Jorgensen and Bejer-Petersen, 1951) and from Poland (Sierpinski, 1969), and several from Russia Bogdanova, 1988, 1998; Kolomiets and Bodganova, 1992) showing that the root rot fungus (Heterobasidion annosum) may predispose pine trees to fatal attacks by T. piniperda. Similarly, pine shoot beetle attacks have followed outbreaks of the fungal shoot disease (Gremmeniella abietina) in Fennoscandian pine forests (Kaitera and Jalkanen, 1994; Cedervind, 2003). Industrial pollution may also render pine trees susceptible to beetle attacks (Sierpinski, 1971; Krol, 1980; Duda, 1981; Oppermann, 1985; Heliovaara and Vaisanen, 1991; Kolomiets and Bogdanova, 1998). management_info: As both T. piniperda and T. minor are dependent on a continuous supply of suitable host material for their survival, silvicultural and logging practices may greatly affect the population density of these beetles both locally and regionally. The concept of forest hygiene, i.e. keeping the amounts of brood material available for bark beetles during their flight period as low as possible, has long been a key strategy in forest protection (Escherich, 1923; Speight and Wainhouse, 1989; Dajoz, 2000). This means that silvicultural operations should be carried out with a minimum of suitable host material left in the forests, that snow-breaks and wind-falls should be cleared up before beetle attack or at least before beetle emergence, and that the timber should be removed from the woods in due time. All this is easier said than done, and when beetle outbreaks occur, trap trees are the common method used to reduce the populations (e.g. Escherich, 1923; Hanson 1937, 1940).^p^pA major change took place in forestry operations after World War II when the timber, which had until then mainly been debarked in the forests prior to transportation (often by floating), was instead stored unbarked along road sides until it was taken to the industry by trucks. In contrast to earlier practice, forest operations were also conducted all-year-round. This created a entirely new situation with huge amounts of unbarked timber stored in the forests during beetle flight, especially in Fennoscandia, where annual cuttings were large and roads often unaccessible during the thawing period in spring. Little has been written about this phenomenon, leading to constantly elevated bark beetle populations Eidmann, 1985, 1992; Jaaskela et al., 1997; Day and Leather, 1997).^p^pIn Sweden, the huge storm-felling in 1969 when 20 million m3 blew down, resulted in bark beetle outbreaks of unprecedented magnitude (Nilsson, 1976) and a similar situation developed in Finland a few years later (Annila and Petaisto, 1978). These events eventually led to changes in the forestry legislation when forest protection became regulated by law (Eidmann 1985, 1992; Jaaskela et al., 1997). In principle, unbarked timber must not be stored during the flight and emergence of pine and spruce bark beetles, unless certain precautions are taken. In Sweden, up to 5 m3 of storm-felled trees per hectare can and should, according to the current debate about dead wood and biodiversity (Ehnstrom et al., 1995), be left without countermeasures being taken. Similar legislation exists in other European countries.^p^pThus, the main option to avoid bark beetle damage was, and still is, rapid transportation (i.e. before beetle flight in spring) of saw logs and pulpwood from the forest to the industry, where it is barked or submerged in water immediately, until processed. In Sweden, where timber storage and fallen Tomicus-attacked shoots were monitored nation-wide through the 1970s and 1980s, a substantial reduction in Tomicus populations was recorded with decreasing timber storage figures. Growth losses nowadays mainly occur around saw and paper mills with constant timber storage (e.g. Langstrom and Hellqvist, 1990; and many unpublished reports) for at least a decade.^p^pIf timely transportation is not feasible, the timber can be protected in different ways. The earlier barking at the felling site is now abandoned as being too expensive. Instead, the timber can be protected by spraying with insecticides, but this has to take place before beetle flight. There are many references mainly from the 1970s dealing with timber protection with insecticides; originally, DDT was used, followed by lindane and, in the 1980s, synthetic pyrethroids such as permethrin became the main option (Srot, 1968; Doom and Luitjes, 1970; Novak, 1972; Dowding, 1974; Dominik and Kinelski, 1979; Szmidt, 1983; Glowacha and Wajland, 1992). Economic impact^pWhen the winter snow and spring thaw make it impossible to load out logs that have already been felled in the forest, the spring flight of the striped ambrosia beetle is able to colonize a large proportion of the log inventory. Although the beetles most often complete their life cycle before the lumber milled from these logs reaches the market, their dark stained galleries cause considerable degradation of the normally high-value lumber milled from the outer regions of logs. Estimates of this degradation are as high as C$63 million in British Columbia (Canada) alone (McLean, 1985). Degrade values vary greatly according to log grade, ranging from nothing in small-diameter pulp grade logs to more than C$77.40/m3 for high grade Douglas-fir saw logs (Orbay et al., 1994). A year-long Ambrosia Beetle Task Force in coastal British Columbia in 1990/91 showed that one forest company lost $11 million dollars from lumber degrade on a 5 million m3 log inventory. Efficient log inventory management (http://www.forestry.ubc.ca/fetch21/fetch21/tinybeetles.html) is the best method for reducing these losses.^p^p^Environmental impact^pAmbrosia beetles are one of nature's recycling agents for coarse woody debris. They have no adverse environmental impacts.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural Dispersal^p^pAssessment of beetle dispersal by capturing beetles, dusting them with fluorescent powders and releasing them in a second growth forest under gentle wind conditions showed strong upwind responses to pheromone-baited traps 5 m and 25 m from the release point. Catches were randomly distributed at 100 m, and at 500 m most catches were in the downwind traps (Salom and McLean, 1989). In a laboratory wind tunnel, percentages of catches to an upwind trap or log were shown to decrease with an increase of wind speed to 0.9 m/sec. Sustained flight was not maintained over 60 cm/sec (2.16 km/h). Catches to both pheromone-baited traps and logs was highest at 0.0 m/sec indicating arrestment in response to a known attractant (positive chemokinesis?). In a forested valley setting, higher catches were recorded within the forest as compared to adjacent clearcut areas. Pheromone-baited traps are far more effective in the quieter wind conditions within a forest than in adjacent clearcut areas or log boom storage areas (Lam and McLean, 1992) where breezes exceed flight capability and beetles are displaced downwind. Marked beetles released at noon were recaptured in pheromone-baited traps 2 km downwind (up valley) (Salom and McLean, 1991). In an industrial setting, marked T. lineatum were released in several locations by Shore and McLean (1988). Greatest catches were on traps less than 200 m from the release points; however, several beetles were also collected on traps 500 m away across a log boom storage area.^p^pMovement in Trade/Transport^p^pWinter-felled logs that are in the woods during the spring attack flight have the highest risk of attack. T. lineatum stays in the logs for a relatively short time and the brood population has generally emerged from the log by the autumn. Nevertheless, infested logs loaded out in the early summer complete with an active brood will release beetles from July onwards. These beetles go into forested margins to overwinter. By the time the log is sorted by grade at a dry land sorting area and made into a log boom for shipment to a sawmill, most of the beetles will have emerged. Beetles that overwinter in the forested margins around the log booming ground come out of hibernation the following spring and infest the fresh logs in storage areas. In this way the cycle of industrial infestation is compounded into a second year and soon infestations are rampant throughout the whole transportation system and in the sawmills. In the world of commerce, log movements from jurisdictions where transportation cannot start until the roads have hardened after snowmelt in the spring, are at greatest risk of an attack flight and the movement of T. lineatum to new areas. Unlike other ambrosia beetles, T. lineatum has not been known to attack and survive in green lumber. remark: T. lineatum is of low phytosanitary risk. New broods of beetles leave the logs within 3 to 6 months. There are no records of the successful completion of life cycles in sawn lumber as has been noted for the sympatric ambrosia beetle Gnathotrichus sulcatus in British Columbia, Canada (McLean and Borden, 1975). Black-stained pinholes indicate that wood was once attacked but the impact of T. lineatum pinholes is mainly the lower value placed on such lumber.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pWindfalls and broken trees caused by winter snow and ice storms provide a continuous source of host trees for T. lineatum. In an extensively forested area it is difficult to remove these trees quickly so operators should expect ambrosia beetles to be in all conifer forests. Stumps and logs need to 'ripen' for about 3 months to accumulate stimulation levels of ethanol that will encourage attack. This brief window is particularly important in the northern hemisphere in spring periods when roads are impassable until the snow has melted.^p^pWhen a new road is cut into a forest, the time between the felling of the right of way and the construction of the road needs to be as short as possible. As soon as the roadbed has been constructed, self-loading trucks should be used to move the freshly cut logs to the sawmill to prevent ambrosia beetle attack on the logs. The residual stumps are attacked by T. lineatum, which means that a residual population is maintained in the forest.^p^pThe timing of the subsequent felling of the new setting, yarding of the logs to the roadside and their transportation to a sorting area should be completed before it snows in early winter. Logs trapped under snow have a very high probability of being heavily attacked before any loading out can be completed in the following spring. Large-diameter debris and stumps will be attacked by T. lineatum.^p^pLogs are scaled in dry land sorting areas. Transit time in these areas in British Columbia (Canada) is usually short, often only a matter of hours, before bundles of similar grades of logs are either loaded on to logging trucks for transportation to a sawmill or are made up into a log boom for water transportation. Logs attacked in the forest are able to release new brood beetles throughout the summer as soon as they mature. These beetles fly to forested margins around the dry land sorting areas, log booming areas and sawmills. They overwinter and emerge during the first warm days of spring, when temperatures exceed 16°C, to attack any new logs that happen to be in the area. These forested margins can be clear felled to increase the dispersal distance for overwintered beetles. Pheromone-baited traps set in the forested margin intercept these spring flying beetles. In addition, pheromone-baited bundles of low grade saw logs or pulp logs can be set out around the margins of dry land sorting areas to intercept beetles flying in from forested margins. These trap bundles need to be processed before mid-summer in order to kill beetle broods developing therein.^p^pA full sequence of log inventory controls including hot logging and rapid processing of logs plus the strategic use of mass trapping in areas where high value inventories are stored in dry land sorting areas and booming grounds has been detailed by Borden and McLean (1981) and McLean and Stokkink (1988).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pNo chemicals are currently registered in Canada as sprays for use against ambrosia beetles although much spraying has been done in the past. In the past, benzene hexachloride [gamma-HCH] and Methyl Trithion [S-[[(4-chlorophenyl)thio]methyl] O,O-dimethyl phosphorodithioate]have been sprayed on log inventories to prevent ambrosia beetle attack (Richmond, 1986).^p^p^IPM^p^pThere are IPM systems for minimising the impact of the striped ambrosia beetle. The best method for preventing attack by T. lineatum is to ensure that logs are removed from the forest before the beginning of the spring flight period. Large log inventories in dry land sorting areas can be protected by continuous water misting which deters beetles from landing on them (Richmond and Nijholt, 1972). The aggregation pheromone for T. lineatum has been identified, synthesized and is currently available for use as baits in traps such as the Lindgren multiple funnel traps (Lindgren, 1983). remark: APMoV is included among the non-European potato viruses of the EPPO A1 quarantine list (OEPP/EPPO, 1984a). The virus is considered of quarantine concern by NAPPO and COSAVE and, in general, all regional plant protection organizations outside South America recommend very strict measures for potato material from that continent. The principal perceived risk is the introduction of new viruses into seed potato-production schemes, increasing the cost and difficulty of operating these schemes, and opening up new possibilities for yield losses from single or mixed virus infections.^p^pPhytosanitary risk is particularly important because of the simple pathway that exists from useful germplasm material (local potato cultivars, wild tuber-forming Solanum spp.) in the potato's centre of diversity in South America through to nuclear stock material of new cultivars in seed potato-producing countries. Thus there is a great risk of introduction due to the increased international exchange of breeding material and germplasm, whether in the form of tubers, rooted cuttings or in vitro cultures.^p^pAPMoV could be regarded as of major importance for the EPPO region among the group of South American potato pathogens. It is distinguished by being a relatively widespread and damaging disease. It can, however, be excluded relatively easily by prohibition of commercial trade in potato tubers. The risk of introduction with breeding material is reduced by the fact that it is not carried by true seed of either potato or pepper.
author: CPC2006

management_info: The importation of potato tubers from countries where APMoV occurs should be prohibited (see Phytosanitary Risk). The virus is one of the group of South American pests of potato which justify strict post-entry quarantine procedures in the EPPO region, together with equivalent checks before export. Only material for scientific purposes, in quantities limited to what is strictly necessary and subject to import permit, should normally be imported from countries where APMoV occurs. Because of the probability that any wild tuber-forming Solanum spp. originated from South America may carry the virus, the same tests should be applied whatever their origin. EPPO's specific quarantine requirements (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) outline suitable quarantine measures, while EPPO's phytosanitary procedures lay down the test procedures to be followed both before export and in post-entry quarantine after import (OEPP/EPPO, 1984b).^p^pControl of APMoV depends primarily on the use of high-quality seed potatoes produced from virus-free nuclear stocks, which are initially obtained by meristem-tip culture and in vitro clonal propagation. (Schilde-Rentschler and Schmiediche, 1984). Plantlets are tested for freedom from the virus using nucleic acid spot hybridization and nitrocellulose membrane ELISAs (Dodds and Horton, 1990). Healthy material is further multiplied under greenhouse and field conditions following the usual schemes of seed certification (Bokx and Van der Want, 1987).^p^pRoguing out of diseased plants during the growing season can be effective, as infected plants show conspicuous symptoms (Fribourg and Jones, 1980). Cultivation when plants are small will reduce the hazard of spreading the virus by contaminated equipment.^p^pThe wild species Solanum brevidens and S. etuberosum are resistant to potato Andean mottle comovirus, which opens possibilities for resistance breeding (Valkonen et al., 1992).

potential_eco_desc: 该病毒危害性一般。

该病毒在马铃薯上引起有破坏性的症状，并广泛分布于它所发生的地区。对产量的直接影响目前没被研究，但大概在敏感马铃薯品种上影响严重(Jones et al., 1982)。在中美的实验显示，在辣椒上，APMoV联合其它病毒（如烟草蚀刻病毒，辣椒花叶病毒）的混合侵染能引起严重的症状（如花叶和矮缩）和明显的产量下降(Valverde, 2003)。 The virus causes damaging symptoms in potato and is widespread in its area of occurrence. Direct effects on yield have not been studied, but are probably severe in sensitive potato cultivars (Jones et al., 1982). Experience in Central America has shown that in pepper, mixed infections of APMoV with other viruses (e.g., Tobacco etch virus, Pepper mottle virus) can lead to severe symptoms (e.g., foliar mosaic and stunting) and substantially lower yields (Valverde, 2003).
author: zhangjianjun

management_info:
在生长季节去除生病植株是有效的，因为感染植株会表现明显的症状(Fribourg and Jones, 1980)。当植物还是幼小的时候栽培会减少病毒通过污染工具传染的危险。
野生品种Solanum brevidens和S. etuberosum对安第斯马铃薯斑驳病毒有抗性，这样，增加了抗性育种的可能性(Valkonen et al., 1992)。 Roguing out of diseased plants during the growing season can be effective, as infected plants show conspicuous symptoms (Fribourg and Jones, 1980). Cultivation when plants are small will reduce the hazard of spreading the virus by contaminated equipment.
The wild species Solanum brevidens and S. etuberosum are resistant to potato Andean mottle comovirus, which opens possibilities for resistance breeding (Valkonen et al., 1992).
author: zhangjianjun

description:
APMoV是豇豆花叶病毒属的一个种，是典型的甲虫传病毒；然而，该典型的品系Lm是由跳甲（Epitrix sp.）传播的(Fribourg et al., 1977)。辣椒上该病毒的一个分离种是由Diabrotica balteata 传播的(Valverde et al., 1995)。叶甲种类在发现该病毒的地区普遍存在(Smith and Lawrence, 1967; Avila et al., 1984)。
APMoV在植物间也很容易通过接触传播，它不能由真实的种子传播，但它能由马铃薯的块茎携带(Fribourg et al., 1977)。
一些马铃薯的野生品种对该病毒敏感，而且可能是病毒的重要天然储存库，因为传播媒介能携带病毒到马铃薯田中去(Fribourg et al., 1977)。 APMoV is a species of the Comovirus genus, members of which are typically beetle-transmitted; however, the type strain Lm was transmitted by the flea beetle Epitrix sp. (Fribourg et al., 1977). An isolate of the virus from Capsicum is transmitted by Diabrotica balteata (Valverde et al., 1995). Diabrotica species are prevalent in regions where the virus is found (Smith and Lawrence, 1967; Avila et al., 1984).　　
APMoV is also readily transmitted by contact between plants and is not transmitted by true seed, but is carried by potato tubers (Fribourg et al., 1977).　　　
Several wild potato species are susceptible to the virus and may be important as natural reservoirs from which the vectors could carry the virus to potato fields (Fribourg et al., 1977).
author: zhangjianjun

野生品种Solanum brevidens和S. etuberosum对安第斯马铃薯斑驳病毒有抗性，这样，增加了抗性育种的可能性(Valkonen et al., 1992)。 Roguing out of diseased plants during the growing season can be effective, as infected plants show conspicuous symptoms (Fribourg and Jones, 1980). Cultivation when plants are small will reduce the hazard of spreading the virus by contaminated equipment.
The wild species Solanum brevidens and S. etuberosum are resistant to potato Andean mottle comovirus, which opens possibilities for resistance breeding (Valkonen et al., 1992). APMoV的防治最初要依靠从无毒的核原料上产生的高质量的种子马铃薯的使用，这最初是由顶端分生组织培养物和试管无性繁殖里获得。幼苗用核酸斑点杂交和硝化纤维膜ELISAs来测试其不带毒性(Dodds and Horton, 1990)。健康的材料要用通常的种子检验方案接着在温室和田间条件下进一步繁殖(Bokx and Van der Want, 1987)。 Control of APMoV depends primarily on the use of high-quality seed potatoes produced from virus-free nuclear stocks, which are initially obtained by meristem-tip culture and in vitro clonal propagation. Plantlets are tested for freedom from the virus using nucleic acid spot hybridization and nitrocellulose membrane ELISAs (Dodds and Horton, 1990). Healthy material is further multiplied under greenhouse and field conditions following the usual schemes of seed certification (Bokx and Van der Want, 1987).

description: During September 2015, we observed orange to dark-brown algal leaf spots on leaves of Manilkara zapota (L.) P. Royen (sapodilla, lamoot) in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand. The disease was found on 20% of surveyed M. zapota, caused necrotic leaf lesions. The samples were collected and colonies were isolated, the pathogen was identified as Cephaleuros virescens by morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of algal leaf spot on M. zapota caused by C. virescens in Thailand.

host_range: CRSV has a moderately broad natural and experimental host range. It has been experimentally transmitted to 133 species in 25 families (Hollings and Stone, 1970; Kleinhempel et al., 1980). The virus was originally isolated from commercial carnations (Dianthus caryophyllus) in 1951 (Kassanis, 1955), but has since been found to infect a wide range of orchard trees, including plum, pear, apple, sour and sweet cherry and grapevines (Richter et al., 1978; Fritzsche et al., 1979; Kleinhempel et al., 1980; Kegler et al., 1983). CRSV has also been identified in several weed species particularly Stellaria media growing within infected fruit orchards (Rudel et al., 1977; Fritzsche et al., 1979; Kegler et al., 1983). The experimental host range of the Dianthoviruses is much broader than that found in nature (Hollings and Stone, 1970). CRSV is easily mechanically transmissible to a wide range of herbaceous species. The virus can systemically infect members of the Solanaceae, Leguminosae, Cucurbitaceae and the Compositae. It infects an even larger number of species locally (non-systemically) (Hollings and Stone, 1970).
potential_eco_desc: CRSV was once widespread and a major economic disease of both cut and pot carnations. In addition to the foliar symptoms described, CRSV infections also cause distorted flowers which are unmarketable (Hakkaart, 1964). Based on this, a rigorous effort to control CRSV by sanitation, indexing and meristem tip culture was instituted throughout the world in the 1970‘ s. As a result, CRSV infections in carnations are a rarity today, and the virus probably does not have a significant economic impact. It should be noted that indexing for CRSV and meristem-tip culture must be continued to ensure that CRSV does not reappear. The economic impact of CRSV on stone fruit and other orchard crops in Central Europe is uncertain. No studies determining the effect of CRSV in the absence of other viruses on these hosts have been performed.

description: There is no evidence that CRSV is seedborne, with the exception of a study in which somatic embryos of carnation cultivars were infected with CRSV, based on dot blotting and ELISA assays (Young et al., 1997).

remark: All Dianthus species are quarantined and assayed for CRSV in Chile, China, Hungary, Korea and Sri Lanka. management_info: The most effective control for CRSV is sanitation during plant propagation. In vegetatively propagated hosts such as carnation and fruit trees, eradication of CRSV in plant shoots or meristems by chemo- and thermotherapy is routinely accomplished to produce certified virus free nuclear stocks which are then commercially propagated under a strict sanitation regime. Production from virus-free nuclear stocks coupled with constant monitoring for CRSV infection by ELISA has ensured the production of CRSV free commercial carnations (van Ruiten, 1987). The nearly worldwide establishment of a virus-free certified carnation propagation program has ensured that CRSV has not returned in epidemic forms (Ebbels, 1979).

potential_eco_desc:
飞机草是我国危害特别严重的外来入侵物种之一，是世界公认的恶性有毒杂草。由于原产地中南美洲有大量的专一性昆虫取食及病原菌侵染，飞机草在当地并没有造成危害。但是在其入侵地区，由于缺乏天敌的控制，飞机草生长繁茂，密集成丛，具有极强的侵袭能力。它能迅速繁殖、扩散，通常以成片的单优势种群里出现，能通过遮阳作用排挤本地物种，严重影响了入侵地区农林牧业生产，并威胁到本土植物的生长及入侵地区的生物多样性资源，恶化环境。在我国西南地区，尤其是云南省，飞机草已经对当地宝贵的生物资源构成巨大威胁。因飞机草生物量高，在我国广东某林场每年对桉树追施的肥料多半被其利用，从而降低了桉树的生长量，造成较大的经济损失。飞机草干枯植株极易燃烧，成为火灾的隐患，然而火烧只能毁坏其地上部分，雨季来临后其根部又可发芽再生，成为火烧后第一种在生长的优势植物。飞机草在成功入侵后大暴发，生长难以控制，对生态系统造成不可逆转的破坏。对农业、森林、人、畜等造成严重的危害。
当飞机草高度达15cm或更高时，就能明显地影响其他草本植物的生长，并使昆虫拒食，严重破坏生态稳定。一般的牧草大都会被排挤出局，2~3年后草场就会失去利用价值。据统计，仅四川省凉山州每年损失牧草就可使畜牧业经济损失达数千万元。
飞机草倡议成片的单优势种群落出现，侵占益林荒山和椰林、橡胶林等经济林地。在林区，飞机草已能够沿着道路两侧逐渐向纵深处传播，占据每一块伐木迹地和林间空隙，影响林木的生长与更新。
飞机草入侵耕地后，造成农作物大面积减产。飞机草入侵耕地后，危害多种作物，造成粮食减产3%~11%，桑叶、花椒减产4%~8%，香蕉植株少2~3片叶、矮1m左右，幼树难以成林，经济林木推迟投产。据不完全统计，由于飞机草的危害，云南省大部分地区的农民每年要歉收两成以上的粮食，同时为防除和根除飞机草，每年每户要多投入100~500元的资金。
飞机草对畜牧业的危害。飞机草侵占草场，造成牧草严重减产，以致载畜量下降。有的乡村农户甚至出现无草放牧的现象，坡鹿、家畜等误食嫩叶会引起中毒，给畜牧业造成极大的危害。
飞机草对人的危害。据研究报道，飞机草的叶擦人的皮肤会引起红肿、起泡，误食嫩叶会引起头晕、呕吐。人接触飞机草过多，会引起头痛、头晕，甚至更重的中毒症状。
description: 飞机草即可进行有性繁殖又能进行无性繁殖，并且这两种繁殖方式的能力均较强。飞机草进行有性繁殖时，每棵植株产生的种子数高达7.2万~38.7万粒，种子极小而轻，千粒重仅0.17~0.19g，适于风传播，在风速1m/s时能飘至2.5~3m高、5~10m远的区域，并且其果实顶端的刺状冠毛能粘附在人、畜体表传播到风所不能及的角落。同时，飞机草也通过引种、货物运输、水流、交通工具进行长距离的传播扩散。
management_info:
严格进行杂草检验检疫制度，精选播种材料，特别是国内没有或尚未广为传播的杂草必须严格禁止输入或严加控制，防止扩散，以减少生态环境中飞机草种子来源。
防治方法：
（1）生物学方法：杂草生物防除是利用农业生态系统中的昆虫、病原微生物等生物通过其相生相克的关系，将杂草控制在其经济危害允许水平以下的一种治理措施，是杂草综合治理体系中的重要组成部分。杂草生物防除的主要途径：①阻止杂草结实，减少土壤种杂草种子库的容量。②减少杂草的萌发出苗数量，将其群体控制在经济危害水平以下。③抑制杂草生长，将其群体生长量控制在经济危害允许水平以下。例如，用香泽兰灯蛾、香泽兰瘿实蝇和安婀珍蝶，其均对防除飞机草有良好的效果。或采用替代防治方法，替代防治是指利用植物间的相互竞争原理，用一种或多种植物的生长优势来抑制害草，用其他植物覆盖的方法防治害草，种植生命力强、覆盖性好的作物，如牧草或速生桉等植物。
（2）农业措施：在那些刚刚传入、定居，还没有大面积扩散的地区可以进行人工清除。但是飞机草无性繁殖能力比较强，如果有根系残留在土壤中，在适宜的温度和土壤湿度条件下，从埋于土中的多年生根系中迅速再生，长成灌丛，再继续扩散危害，随整个生态系统的结构和功能造成更为严重的破坏。因此，必须彻底拔除，对拔除后的植株可用火烧处理，清除后的土壤必须压实防止其成为残留根系和飞机草种子新的萌发源。由于水分胁迫对飞机草的生长有明显抑制作用，因此，在季节性干旱时期，对飞机草采用人工拔除等多种方法，可防止飞机草群落的恢复，防除效果也更好。
（3）化学措施：喷洒化学除草剂是目前主要的、见效快的防除措施。如用2,4-二氯苯氧乙酸（2,4-D）、草甘膦、百草枯、吡氟禾草灵、敌草快等除草剂防除，2,4-D对飞机草幼苗防除有效，而对成熟草丛则需2,4-D与2,4,5-三氯苯酚代乙酸（2,4,5-T）或毒莠定与麦草畏混用进行防除才有效。但需要注意除草剂的合理使用，避免对环境造成二次污染。

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pC. odorata can be considered as a very serious weed in all types of perennial crops in the humid areas of the Palaeotropics. In low-growing plantations such as coffee and cocoa, C. odorata can completely smother the crop, whereas in taller plantations such as rubber or teak, as soon as the canopy is closed the weed is no longer a problem.^p^pIn shifting cultivation, C. odorata replaces the natural secondary succession and becomes the dominant fallow species (De Foresta and Schwartz, 1991; De Rouw, 1991; Gautier, 1992a; Roder et al., 1995; Slaats, 1995). It is often considered as beneficial by local farmers (Baxter, 1995) because it is easier to clear than the secondary vegetation, helps to suppress Imperata cylindrica, and is believed to accelerate the recovery of soil fertility. This last aspect is still a matter of debate among scientists, but there is an increasing requirement for further studies on the influence of the C. odorata fallow system before any biological control programme is launched (Herren-Gemmil, 1991; De Foresta, 1996).^p^pC. odorata causes severe problems in pastures in the Central African Republic (Audru et al., 1988), Java (Indonesia) and the Philippines because it invades overgrazed areas. Due to the high nitrate content of the leaves, C. odorata is poisonous to cattle and generally not grazed (Sajise et al., 1974).^p^pC. odorata can also transmit pathogenic fungi (Vayssiere, 1957; Esuruoso, 1971; Oritsejafor, 1986), and act as a host for insect pests including Zonocerus variegatus (Modder, 1984; Chapman et al., 1986), whose nymphs feed on leaves, flowers and fruits in Africa; Aphis citricola and Rhopalosiphum maidis in India; as well as various other polyphagous insects.^p^p^Environmental impact^pDepending on the length and the intensity of the dry season, C. odorata represents a serious fire hazard because of the presence of volatile oils in stems and leaves. Uncontrolled fires can destroy plantations, villages and infested natural vegetation. This problem is particularly acute in Natal, South Africa, where C. odorata is reported to burn even when green in the growing season (Macdonald, 1983).^p^p^Social impact^pIn some regions, such as southwestern China, the appearance of C. odorata has allowed a shortening of fallow periods in shifting cultivation and thus the species is welcomed by these traditional agriculturalists (Momose, 2002).^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pC. odorata invades natural vegetation such as forest margins and savannahs in Africa (Macdonald, 1983, Macdonald and Frame, 1988;Gautier, 1992a, 1996). In South Africa it is posing a very serious threat to the continued survival of the Nile crocodile (Leslie and Spotila, 2001).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>environment; livestock production; forestry production; native fauna; native flora
description: C. odorata was first introduced to Asia to the Calcutta Botanical Garden in the 19th century as an ornamental. It had spread to Malaysia, Sumatra and Indo-China by the 1920s. Burkill (1935) reported that on the Malay Peninsula it was "spreading in from Siam". Further spread of C. odorata in southern Asia and western Pacific was associated with the movement of military personnel and equipment during World War II. New foci of invasions have been identified as locations where key military bases were established, for instance Rabaul in New Britain and Jayapura in Irian Jaya (McFadyen, 2002). Similarly, troop movement appears to be responsible for the introduction of the weed to East Timor after 1975. It is very likely that much of the spread of the species in Indonesia resulted from the 1960s transmigration programme.^p^pIt reached the Philippines by the 1960s and was first reported from Laos in 1960. In recent decades it has carried on spreading and it is now reported as growing rampantly in southern Taiwan (Peng and Yang, 1998).^p^pIn 1994 small infestations of C. odorata were found in Queensland, Australia and it is suspected that the introduction resulted from contaminated pasture seeds from overseas (Waterhouse, 1994). After years of efforts the species can now be viewed as eradicated, but the threat of re-introduction from neighbouring islands is high (Waterhouse and Zeimer, 2002).^p^pIn West Africa the plant was accidentally introduced with forestry seeds in Nigeria in 1937 and was deliberately introduced to Cote d'Ivoire in 1952 to control Imperata spp. and other coarse grasses following a recommendation by the famous botanist Auguste Chevalier (1952) despite the fact that he regarded the species as a weed (Chevalier, 1949). The current distribution in West and Central Africa roughly extends from Guinea/Sierra Leone (12°W) to central Zaire [Congo Democratic Republic]/Central African Republic and northern Angola (23°E). It was introduced to South Africa near Durban around 1940 and has since spread to Natal, Transvaal, and central Swaziland.^p^pComparing the present distribution of C. odorata with a climatic map of the world, it is obvious that all the regions with a suitable climate are not yet invaded, especially in Africa and Oceania. Cruttwell McFadyen and Skarrat (1996) have predicted the potential distribution using a climate-matching program. C. odorata can be expected to reach the following areas:^p^pWest Africa^pSierra Leone, Guinea-Bissau, Gambia, southern Senegal, southern Mali, southern Burkina Faso^p^pEast and Central Africa^pSouthern Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi^p^pSouthern Africa^pAngola, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, northeastern Botswana^p^pAtlantic Ocean^pFernando Po, Sao Tome, Annobon^p^pArabia^pEastern side of Asir, Masquat area^p^pIndian Ocean^pComoros, Reunion^pAll other islands in the Indian Ocean, with the exception of Socotra^p^pPacific Ocean^pAll the islands included in the pentagon: Hawaii, Galapagos, Easter Islands, New Caledonia^p^pOceania^pIndonesian islands that are not yet affected

remark: In the early 1990s C. odorata was declared a prohibited species in Australia and became a primary target of weed surveys conducted in northern Australia, Papua New Guinea and eastern Indonesia. When Australian troops were deployed in East Timor in 1999, the Australian Quarantine and Inspection Service instigated an assessment of the quarantine risks associated with movements of troops and equipment between Australia and East Timor, and the risk of introduction of C. odorata seeds was identified as a primary threat. As a result, all equipment and personnel returning to Australia was systematically inspected and cleaned (Waterhouse and Zeimer, 2002).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pSlashing C. odorata stems manually or mechanically is not a solution, because the plants coppice profusely from the root. The root itself must be dug out, which can sometimes be done by hand if the soil is moist, or by mechanized equipment. This type of control must be conducted at least twice during the growing season (Liggit, 1983; Audru et al., 1988; Muniappan and Marutani, 1991).^p^pCultural practices involving other competitive species have been proposed: using Leucaena leucocephala in pastures in the Philippines (Castillo et al., 1977); Tephrosia purpurea in cocoa plantations in Sri Lanka (Salgado, 1972); and signalgrass (Brachiaria decumbens) in Yunnan, China (Wu and Xu, 1991). For perennial plantations, a ground-cover crop such as Pueraria phaseoloides, Calopogonium mucunoides, Centrosema pubescens or Vigna unguiculata can control C. odorata in the first years, before the crop canopy is closed (Liggit, 1983; Audru et al., 1988; Muniappan and Marutani, 1991).^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pSeedlings and young plants can be removed by hand-pulling, but follow-up clearance every 2-3 months is necessary because of rapid regrowth (Zachariades and Goodall, 2002). In South Africa an annual burning regime can effectively control the plant in grassland situations by killing mature plants and preventing new seedlings from establishing (Goodall and Zachariades, 2002).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pC. odorata is most susceptible to chemical control when it is growing vigorously, such as at the beginning of the rainy season. Best control is usually obtained when herbicides are applied to young shoots after slashing.^p^pFor control of germinating C. odorata, the following pre-emergence herbicides may be used: in yams and cassava, diuron or metribuzin; in cassava, oxyfluoren; in maize, cyanazine+atrazube or atrazine+terbutryn; in groundnuts and cotton, dipropetrin.^p^pThe following chemicals may be used as post-emergence treatments: 2,4-D; 2,4,5-T; glyphosate; asulam; paraquat; triclopyr; imazapyr; metsulfuron; tebuthiuron; atrazine (which also inhibits germination); picloram and classical combinations such as picloram+2,4-D; picloram + 2,4,5-T; dicamba+2,4-D; dicamba + 2,4,5-T. Some of these, such as 2,4-D, atrazine and paraquat, are only likely to be effective on seedlings or young plants. For mature plants, glyphosate or combinations including picloram, dicamba or triclopyr will be needed, and even then, repeat treatments are likely to be necessary. More detailed suggestions for the use of herbicides are provided by Goodall and Erasmus (1996), Utulu (1996) and Ikuenobe and Ayeni (1998). Ferrar et al. (1998) provide a valuable update on many aspects of controlling this weed. Vermeulen et al. (1996) give the latest South African recommendations including use of granular formulations of tebuthiuron and cut stump treatments with imazapyr and triclopyr. In Australia the herbicides used were picloram + triclopyr, or fluoxypyr, in combination with a wetting agent. Picloram + triclopyr was used where a residual action is desired (Waterhouse and Zeimer, 2002).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pAs C. odorata is found in forests, pastures and on wasteland as well as in arable areas, biological control is an attractive approach, especially where use of herbicides is uneconomic. Biological control in the Neotropics was pioneered by the Commonwealth Institute for Biological Control [IIBC] in the mid-1970s and work has been continued by other agencies, notably research teams from South Africa and Australia. Pareuchaetes pseudoinsulata was selected as the first agent for trial in West Africa and has been widely released there, in South and South-East Asia and the Pacific. Initial results were disappointing because establishment was hampered by poor climatic matching and predation of the larvae feeding exposed on the leaves.
