potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pS. halepense is listed by Holm et al. (1977) as one of the world's 10 worst weeds occurring as a principle weed of maize, cotton and sugarcane in tropical and temperate climates, and reported as a weed in 30 different crops in 53 countries. Considered in 1969 to be one of the 10 worst weeds of field crops in the USA (Anderson, 1969) its range has continued to expand in eastern and northern America, particularly in association maize and soyabean monoculture (Warwick, 1990). In the southern States, however, the weed declined in importance between 1974 and 1995 (Webster and Coble, 1997). Crop yield reductions due to S. halepense are reported to be 25-59% in sugarcane (McWhorter, 1972) 12-40% in maize (Holm et al., 1977, Mikulas and Sule, 1979) and 23-42% in soyabean (McWhorter and Hartwig, 1972). Losses in soyabean in Argentina were reported as $300 million per year as a result of S. halepense infestation (Colbert, 1979). In the USA, S. halepense has often caused the abandonment of row-crop cultivation on good soils once it has become dominant; Holm et al. (1977) suggest that the poor germination and growth of some crops on infested land is the result of toxic exudates from roots or decaying vegetation.^p^pThe species serves as an alternative host for several pests of sorghum and maize most notably sorghum midge (Contarinia sorghicola) in California and Mississippi, USA, the leaf hopper Graminella nigrifrons, the vector of corn stunt disease in South Carolina, USA, a corn leaf aphid Rhopalosiphum maidis in New York, USA, and the aphid Schizaphis graminium, the vector of sugarcane mosaic potyvirus in California and New York, USA. It is also the host of many nematode species including Meloidogyne incognita and numerous fungal pathogens including the leaf spot diseases (Cercospora sorghi and Helminthosporium sorghicola [Bipolaris sorghicola]), leaf blight (Helminthosporium turcicum [Setosphaeria turcica]), downy mildew (Sclerophthora macrospora), and loose and covered kernel smut (Sphacelotheca cruenta and S. sorghi). S. halepense is also an alternate host of viruses which cause rice leaf gall, corn leaf gall, stripe disease of rice, maize dwarf mosaic, sugar beet yellows and wheat streak mosaic. Further details of the crop nematodes, pathogens, bacteria and viruses associated with S. halepense are provided by Holm et al. (1977) and Warwick and Black (1983).^p^pIn Australia road verge infestations of S. halepense have been reported to constitute a safety hazard by restricting visibility on curves and corners (Monaghan, 1978). In the USA the pollen is said to contribute to hayfever (Wodehouse, 1971)^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; environment; crop production; livestock production; forestry production; fisheries / aquaculture; human health; rare / protected species; native fauna; native flora; animal / plant collections; animal / plant products; trade / international relations; transport / travel; tourism

remark: The rapid spread and establishment of S. halepense as a serious weed problem in the subtropics since its widespread introduction for forage from the mid 19th century demonstrates the need for vigilance to prevent its introduction to other areas. Phytosanitary inspectors of grain, particularly maize and sorghum, shipped from infested areas should always check for the presence of S. halepense seeds. Australian legislation prohibits the sale of crop seed contaminated with S. halepense seed (Genn, 1987).
author: CPC2006

management_info: An integrated weed management programme, in which crop rotation, repeated tillage, competitive crops and appropriate herbicides are combined, is needed for sustained suppression of S. halepense. Useful discussions of control options have been prepared by McWhorter and Hartwig (1965) Warwick and Black (1983), Parsons and Cuthbertson (1992) and Labrada (1994).^p^pBecause of its capacity to regenerate from rhizome fragments, control of S. halepense by tillage alone is difficult. A summer fallow combined with regular shallow tillage may be employed to prevent rhizome growth, but heavily infested areas have to be tilled up to six times at intervals of no more than 2 weeks to achieve eradication (Timmins and Bruns, 1951; McWhorter, 1973). Repeated tillage exposes rhizome fragments to desiccation at the soil surface, but limited early season tillage or harrowing produces an ideal seedbed for S. halepense regrowth. ^p^pIn annual crops selective control can be obtained with a number of herbicides including: propachlor, bifenox and metolachlor in grain sorghum; cloproxydim, fenoxaprop-p-ethyl, fluazifop-p-butyl, haloxyfop-methyl, imazaquin, imazethapyr, sethoxydim, trifluralin and quizalofop-ethyl in soyabeans; trifluralin, fenoxaprop-p-ethyl, fluazifop-p-butyl, haloxyfop-methyl, fluometuron and diuron in cotton; bifenox in sunflower; and propanil/thiobencarb mixtures in rice (Barrentine, 1987; Bridges and Chandler, 1987; Ignatov, 1989; Riley and Shaw, 1989; Frans et al., 1991; Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992; Labrada, 1994).^p^pSulfonylureas are particularly effective, with three consecutive seasons use of either nicosulfuron or primisulfuron achieving eradication of the weed in maize (Tweedy and Kapusta, 1995). Pre-sowing control of S. halepense with glyphosate is an important component of weed management for no-till crop systems including soyabean and sorghum (Defelice et al., 1987; Brown et al., 1988). With the expansion of the area planted to glyphosate tolerant cotton, maize and soyabeans in the Americas, S. halepense control should become much easier. Differences have been reported, however, in the susceptibility of different ecotypes of the weed to a number of herbicides including dalapon, fluazifop and glyphosate (McWhorter, 1971b; Fernandez et al. 1987). Asulam and directed application of glyphosate both provide effective control in sugarcane (Mehra et al., 1994; Bruff et al., 1996). ^p^pCrop rotation, particularly when a grazing component is included, provides the opportunity to combine a number of control practices including; herbicides with a number of different modes of action, control in different seasons of the year and chemical and cultural weed management methods. Diawara and Banks (1990) reported reduced S. halepense infestation in no-till grain sorghum following winter barley in which the herbicide programme had included oryzalin. A summer maize-winter wheat-grazing oat rotation can bring the weed under control over a relatively short period (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992). The same authors describe a programme used to eradicate S. halepense in which infested land is sown to a perennial pasture grass following a period of cultivations, to allow the control of regrowth by MSMA to which the fodder species, including Rhodes grass, are resistant. However, several applications of MSMA are needed over a period of years before the Rhodes grass becomes dominant enough to limit establishment of S. halepense seedlings.^p^pRegular mowing, cultivations or herbicides are effective in both orchard and non-crop situations, choice of weed control method depending largely on the accessibility of the site. Fluazifop or sulfosate are useful options in vineyards (Hearn, 1988; Trouslard, 1991). host_range: P. minor infests almost all crops grown in winter. It is a serious weed in wheat in most parts of India and Pakistan, the Mediterranean countries, the Arabian Peninsula and the Middle East, Central America, Australia and South Africa.
potential_eco_desc: P. minor is a very competitive weed in several winter crops in many Mediterranean countries, the Middle East, India, Pakistan, Nepal, Mexico, Australia and South Africa. Yield losses vary depending on crop, climate and management practices. The losses are maximum in crops of short stature such as chickpea, lentil, peas, etc. ^p^pIn India, yield losses ranging from 15-50% have been reported (Gill et al., 1978). Cudney and Hill (1979) recorded 40-60% reduction in wheat yield with P. minor at 108-915 plants per square metre. Afentouli and Eleftherohorinos (1996) reported 36-39% reduction in wheat yield in Greece with 304 canarygrass plants per square metre. ^p^pP. minor has been listed as amongst the top ten weeds in Pakistan (Shad and Siddique, 1996) and in central Greece (Damanakes, 1982). In Spain, several species of Phalaris are known to infest wheat and barley in the west Andulasian region, of which P. paradoxa and P. minor are the most serious (Saavedra et al., 1989). The problem has taken a new turn in some countries with reported development of resistance to herbicides. Vast wheat areas in the fertile north-western parts of India are faced with the problem of resistance to isoproturon - the herbicide recommended for its control (Malik and Singh, 1995). An extremely heavy population build-up, in the order of 2000-3000 plants per square metre, is frequently seen. Yield reductions in the region of 60-100% have been reported from these areas. A similar problem, albeit at a lesser intensity, has been documented in Israel (Tal et al., 1996).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pMechanical removal is very effective and useful if done during the initial growth stages of the crop. However, this is not always practical because of the morphological similarities of P. minor to wheat, in which it is a major weed. The stale seed-bed technique involves encouraging emergence of P. minor by irrigating the field, then later eliminating the weed either by shallow cultivation or by use of non-residual foliage-acting herbicides. Competitive crops such as rape, mustard, barley, etc. are useful. Rotations with fodder crops such as oats or berseem (Trifolium alexandrinum) and cultivation of sugarcane have been found to be effective in checking weed growth (Banga et al., 1997). Employing a higher seed rate, narrow row spacing, criss-cross sowing, etc. in wheat offers P. minor control to some extent, but these methods are inconsistent and cannot be relied upon. In India, P. minor has been found to be very sensitive to soil solarization carried out for a short period during summer, but its practical use in the field is unlikely due to economic considerations. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pP. minor is highly sensitive to phenylureas. Clorotoluron, isoproturon, methabenzthiazuron and metoxuron have been widely used in India, Pakistan and the Mediterranean countries (Gill et al., 1978; Catizone and Viggiani, 1980). Isoproturon, however, has remained as the most stable and reliable herbicide available for use in India. Excellent control of several species of Phalaris including P. minor has been reported with post-emergence application of diclofop-methyl (Breidert, 1978; Catizone and Viggiani, 1980). Continuous use of herbicides has, however, resulted in the development of P. minor populations resistant to isoproturon in India (Malik and Singh, 1995) and for some aryloxyphenoxypropionate herbicides in the Mediterranean region (Tal et al., 1996).

description: Over recent years, grapevines (Vitis vinifera) with symptoms similar to grapevine yellows disease have been observed in vineyards from different regions of Iran, especially Zanjan province. A survey was conducted in 2018 to identify possible phytoplasma agents. The samples were collected from vineyards in the Darsajin, Khoramdareh and Zanjan areas in Zanjan province. DNA was extracted, PCR products were obtained, the result of BLAST analysis and phylogenetic analysis showed that phytoplasma agents were 'Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii' and 'Ca. P. solani'. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a 'Ca. P. trifolii'-related strain associated with grapevine yellows disease in Iran.

description: During the investigation of the sudden and early onset of yellowing, followed by mortality of American elm (Ulmus americana L.) trees at the USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station in Delaware, Ohio, a phytoplasma of the clover proliferation group (16SrVI) was detected as the putative causal agent of the disease outbreak. Onset of symptoms was rapid and widespread, occurring in late July 2016 and affecting ～60 trees across two elm research plantations. Samples were collected from symptomatic and asymptomatic American elm trees. Based on PCR and sequences analysis, the sequence similarity between the Delaware elm phytoplasma and ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma trifolii’ is 99.9% in the 16Sr region, which places in the 16SrVI-A group. This is the first report of ‘Ca. P. trifolii’-related strain of 16SrVI-A Phytoplasma subgroup associated with elm yellows disease in American elm in Ohio, U.S.A.

potential_eco_desc: The diseases caused by ESFYP on apricot and Japanese plum are among the most important infectious disorders of these hosts and the predominant causes of decline and death of productive trees. Apricot trees are killed 12-24 months after first appearance of symptoms. This period may be reduced in duration to weeks if the rootstock source is peach. Spontaneous recovery is rare for apricot, but does occur more often with Prunus salicina. In France, ESFYP is probably responsible for 60-70% of cases of apricot decline. Serious problems begin to arise when trees first start bearing fruit after 5 years; 5% of trees may then be killed every successive year. In other countries where the ESFYP occurs, P. salicina seems to be more important as a host. In France, Molieres disease at one time killed thousands of plum and cherry trees but seems to be rare at present.

potential_eco_desc: 多毛碎木长蠧是咀嚼式口器，主要在寄主植物茎干、枝条等木质部部位取食，木材内部被破坏，蛀道成网状，并且充满着粉末状蛀屑。受害原木严重时，通常在木质表面10cm处会被蛀空，造成原木的经济价值严重受损。其危害习性隐蔽，开始受害时往往不易被发现，成虫最初将卵产在木材裂缝或微孔内，卵孵化成幼虫后，幼虫即在木材内部，特别是富含淀粉和其它营养物质的边材部分蛀道取食，当木材表面有成虫羽化孔出现时，木材内部往往已被破坏至相当程度，蛀道成网状，并且充满着粉末状蛀屑。可随木质包装、木制品和木材远距离传播扩散，且可长期危害，有较高的潜在经济重要性。
description: 该虫幼虫或成虫可从受感染植株转移到健康植株。人类使用的机械、设备、工具会有助于携带多毛碎木长蠧传播和扩散；货物贸易中，装运货物的运输工具或交通工具跨境运输携带该蠹虫的木材等可造成多毛碎木长蠧的远距离传播。

potential_eco_desc: 粗点平海小蠹是平海小蠹属内危害性最大的种类，该种具有一定的攻击性，侵染过熟林和不健康植株可致死，也可侵染被风吹倒的植株。粗点平海小蠹的经常与真菌Ophiostoma subannulatum 伴随发生，该菌被认为是导致植株死亡的原因。植株被粗点平海小蠹侵染之后一年内可发生顶枯，死亡一般发生在侵染一年之后；被侵染后的植株可愈合但会留下伤口，也可能会在几年之内反复受到该虫侵染从而导致死亡；伤口可使植株更容易受真菌如Armilaria ostoyae和Phellinus weirii的侵染并导致树木死亡。粗点平海小蠹一般仅攻击单颗植株或一小群植株，大规模暴发为害比较罕见。1947年至1955年间，俄勒冈州一场由干旱引发的大规模疫情导致100多万英亩的温哥华冷杉死亡。
description: 粗点平海小蠹有一定的飞行能力，自然条件下可进行短距离扩散；可随原木贸易、种苗调运等进行远距离传播和扩散。

potential_eco_desc: 红翅四眼小蠹作为一种次生害虫，因其对云杉的聚集危害可导致云杉大量死亡而广受关注。受侵染的寄主由于其防御系统被破坏而有利于小蠹共生真菌Ophiostoma piceaperdum 的侵染和发生。在纽芬兰，被色卷蛾(Choristoneura fumiferana) 严重危害的黑云杉(Picea mariana)有33%会受到红翅四眼小蠹侵染并导致树木死亡。除了导致树木死亡外，红翅四眼小蠹侵染会使木材含水率降低，硬度和纸张白度降低。同时由于红翅四眼小蠹导致树木死亡加速，增加了防治成本。

potential_eco_desc: 胡桃木细小蠹是细小蠹属内危害性最大的种类，大量的胡桃木细小蠹聚集取食可导致健康的树枝和树干的韧皮部溃烂死亡，受侵染的植株表现出变黄萎靡不振和枯萎等症状，并在3-4年后死于病原体侵害。胡桃木细小蠹是真菌Geosmithia morbida 迄今已知的唯一携带者，目前认为胡桃木细小蠹及其携带的 G. morbida 与一种能使胡桃木感染致死的疾病有重要关系，这一疾病名为thousand cankers disease，因患病植株枝干上布满小而分散的溃疡区而得名。植株最初患病时常伴随有树叶枯败的现象，随后出现树冠疏黄、顶梢枯死等症状，最后可导致植株死亡。这种昆虫-真菌复合侵染正威胁着美国东部价值约5000亿美元的黑核桃林。

host_range: G. sulcatus infests many North American conifers, including those in the genera Abies, Chamaecyparis, Larix, Picea, Pinus, Pseudotsuga, Sequoia, Thuja and Tsuga (Prebble and Graham, 1957; Bright, 1976; Furniss and Carolin, 1977; Wood, 1982).Affected Pl
potential_eco_desc: G. sulcatus is one of a complex of three ambrosia beetles that cause an estimated annual loss of $CAN 95 to 189 million in degrade of stored timber in British Columbia (Lindgren and Fraser, 1994). In addition other unquantified losses have been incurred in the modified manufacturing of infested timber, export restrictions and altered harvesting, storing and shipping practices (Gray and Borden, 1985; Orbay et al., 1994). ^p^pTrypodendron lineatum is the most damaging species because of its intense attacks and unsightly galleries in the spring and G. retusus is the least important because of its sporadic attack habits and single flight period in the spring. However, G. sulcatus flies throughout the summer and well into the autumn. This extends the period when the timber is vulnerable by 3-4 months after the risk of attack by the other two species has passed. It is much more inclined to attack unseasoned lumber than the other two species in British Columbia, Canada McLean and Borden, 1975a, b. Therefore, along with T. lineatum, it is a major target of a semiochemical-based integrated pest management (IPM) programme that has run continuously in British Columbia since 1981 (Borden, 1995; Borden et al., 2003).
author: CPC2006

description: The most common mode of introduction of ambrosia beetles into new areas is in galleries in unseasoned raw logs, lumber and dunnage. G. sulcatus has been intercepted in New Zealand in sawn wood imported from British Columbia, Canada (Bain, 1974). It is a strong flyer and was readily caught in rotary traps in Oregon, USA, mainly between 13.00 and 20.00 h (Daterman et al., 1965). Its dispersal capacity from a point of introduction is probably at least 1 km per year.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Adults; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Eggs, Larvae, Nymphs, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Wood: Eggs, Larvae, Nymphs, Pupae, Adults; borne internally; visible to naked eye.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Leaves.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Conveyances (transport Vehicles): Ships (Bain 1974)
author: CPC2006

remark: G. sulcatus has been included in the EPPO quarantine pest category 'non-European Scolytidae' (EPPO/CABI, 1992). If it becomes established in countries with substantial conifer-based timber industries, G. sulcatus could intensify the damage above that caused by native species and could extend the period of vulnerability well into the autumn. ^p^pIt readily breeds in unseasoned timber and can even complete its life cycle in unseasoned lumber (McLean and Borden, 1975b). One conifer-infesting congeneric species, Gnathotrichus materiarius, is already established in Europe (Wood, 1982) and it is probable that G. sulcatus could also become established. A concerted trapping programme in British Columbia, Canada, disclosed the presence of four exotic ambrosia beetles that were not previously known to be established (Humble, 2003) and it is possible that similar exotic species exist undetected elsewhere in the world. ^p^pFinally, the recent outbreak of Trypodendron domesticum and Trypodendron signatum in living beech trees in Europe, indicates that other ambrosia beetles, or their symbiotic fungi, could adapt under changing environmental conditions to become primary attackers (Gregoire et al., 2003). For these reasons, the phytosanitary risk of G. sulcatus is high.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Integrated pest management (IPM) of ambrosia beetles has three potential components, any or all of which may be employed depending on the species concerned and the product at risk (Borden and McLean, 1981).^p^p^ Habitat management^p^pThis eliminates a potential or occupied habitat. It can be accomplished by 'hot logging' (removing vulnerable logs from the forest before they can be attacked), minimising the storage time in log yards and disposal or burning of logging slash and debris at mill sites. ^p^p^ Protection of the product at risk by deterring attack^p ^pPreviously this was effectively accomplished by using chemical insecticides and water misting of log decks, both of which were terminated because of environmental concerns. Biologically-based repellents show promise, but are far from operational readiness (Borden et al., 2003). Thus, in all but very critical situations, e.g. the use of chemical insecticides to attempt to eradicate a newly-introduced pest, protection of the product from attack is not a viable management option at this time. ^p^p^ Suppression of beetle populations by intercepting and killing host-seeking beetles^p ^pThis is operationally accomplished by mass-trapping, through the use of semiochemical-baited traps and baited bundles of cull logs that can be disposed of, for example, by chipping, before brood beetles emerge (Borden and McLean, 1981; Lindgren and Fraser, 1994; Borden, 1995).^p^pThe exclusion of unseasoned logs, lumber and dunnage at ports of entry may not prevent introduction of all G. sulcatus because brood beetles may persist in apparently seasoned host material. Debarked logs may also harbour infestations. Therefore, the only reliable means of excluding this species is that all imported timber products and dunnage are kiln-dried. Traps baited with 'sulcatol' are highly effective in capturing G. sulcatus and could be used in sensitive areas. However, the pheromones of only two members of the genus are known and it is possible that other parapatric or allopatric species also use 'sulcatol'. Therefore, any captured Gnathotrichus must be identified to species.

potential_eco_desc: This is a late-season disease of widespread incidence and severity in Egypt, with 100% infection reported in some fields (Samra et al., 1962; Galal et al., 1979). The disease has also been found in India (Payak et al., 1970). It does not occur in the USA, but is considered to be a potentially important pathogen (Warren, 1983).
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pA. maydis was detected in 42 out of 43 seed samples in Egypt, at infection levels up to 11% (Mohamed et al., 1967). Seed infection was induced in plants inoculated at planting time (Samra et al., 1963). Michail et al. (1999) detected A. maydis in a higher percentage of white maize seeds (1-9%) than in yellow cultivars (1-3%) in Hungary. The fungus was detected in different ear parts, i.e., ear branch, cob, seeds, ear husks and silk of naturally infected maize cultivars. It was mostly manifested in the branch followed by cob, seeds, husks and silk. A. maydis is internally and externally seedborne in maize as it was detected at higher levels in the embryo and in both the endosperm and coat of the 13 tested seed samples, with the exception of seeds of cv. Amon in which the fungus was confined to the seed coat.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pSeed rot and reduced emergence resulted from infesting soil with A. maydis (Payak et al., 1970). This effect has not been demonstrated with natural seedborne inoculum.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pThere is no evidence for transmission by seeds. A. maydis is soilborne, with sclerotia surviving on maize debris (Dawood et al., 1979).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pSeed treatment with carbendazim or captan gave effective control of late wilt of maize in India (Satyanarayana and Begum, 1996). Actinomycetes and yeast fungi isolates, individually or in combination, were antagonistic to A. maydis and significantly reduced the incidence of late wilt disease when applied by seed inoculation under controlled greenhouse conditions (El-Mehalawy et al., 2004).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pCulture plate (Mohamed et al., 1967)^p^p1. Wash seeds in tap water.^p2. Surface disinfect seeds in 0.1% mercuric chloride, 2 min. ^p3. Rinse in sterile water. ^p4. Incubate on PDA at 27°C, 10 days.^p^pCulture plate (Michail et al., 1999)^p^p1. Maize seeds were plated on potato dextrose yeast extract agar medium. ^p2. A. maydis could be detected after 2 days of incubation at 20°C under 12 h alternating cycles of near ultraviolet light (NUV) and darkness.

description: In 2017, soybean (Glycine max) plants (cv. 24-10RY, R1 growth stage) with dead brown leaves associated with light to dark reddish-brown lesions and necrosis of the lower half of the stem, especially at the base of branches, were collected at Carman, Manitoba. Reddish-brown discoloration was observed inside stems when split in half. Severely infected plants wilted and desiccated. These symptoms are typical of Northern stem canker, the pathogen was identified as Diaporthe caulivora by molecular diagnostics and pathogenicity tests. This is the first report of Northern stem canker on soybean in Western Canada.
reference_name: First Report of Northern Stem Canker Caused by Diaporthe caulivora on Soybean in Western Canada

description: In August 2015, dry rot symptoms of wrinkled, shrunken roots with brownish lesions and carbonaceous black tissues beneath the surface of the infected lesions were observed on sweetpotatoes (‘Juwhangmi’) supplied by the Bioenergy Crop Research Center, RDA, Muan, Korea. description: Northern stem canker of soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.), incited by Diaporthe caulivora (Athow & Caldwell) J.M. Santos, Vrandecic & A.J.L. Phillips 2011, is an economically important disease commonly found throughout the North Central region of the United States and Canada where it can be a major contributor to yield loss in years with conducive weather conditions. In August 2014, soybean plants were submitted from Ontario, Seneca, and Wayne counties of New York for diagnosis. In addition to dead leaves attached to the stems, many of the plants exhibited necrosis of the terminal meristem. Each plant had visible cankers on the lower stems, typical of those caused by northern stem canker. The causal agent was be confirmed as Diaporthe caulivora by biological detection and molecular diagnostics. To the best of our knowledge, northern stem canker has not been reported previously on soybean in New York. Since this initial confirmation, northern stem canker was also been confirmed in Jefferson, Livingston, Niagara, and Orleans counties in 2014, suggesting that it may be widespread in New York. Northern stem canker can have a significant impact on soybean yield, potentially resulting in up to 50% loss.

potential_eco_desc: Human consumption of cooked soyabeans and soy flour may help to alleviate a global deficiency in protein, especially in highly populated developing countries (Circle and Smith, 1975). Soyabean seed quality, determined by germination and the general appearance of the seed, is therefore of great importance in many soyabean-growing areas of the world. Tropical areas have high rainfall and high temperatures, which favour the development of seedborne D. phaseolorum var. sojae. The pathogen is generally considered a weak parasite, but its wide distribution and high frequency suggest that it deserves careful attention.^p^pPod and stem blight has frequently been cited as a common disease in Illinois, Iowa and Indiana in the USA and Ontario in Canada (Athow and Caldwell, 1954; Gerdemann, 1954; Dunleavy, 1956; Hildebrand, 1956). Later, in the midwestern states of Maryland and Delaware, D. phaseolorum var. sojae was considered to be the predominant organism associated with low seed quality (Athow and Laviolette, 1973). Seed lots from Louisiana, bioassayed for internally-borne pathogens, showed 97% infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae (Ellis et al., 1974a). ^p^pPods infected with D. phaseolorum var. sojae are unsuitable for vegetable use (Mehlembacher et al., 1977) and soyabean oil must be colourless for acceptance in food products (Bailey, 1964). In Illinois, soyabean seeds showing symptoms of D. phaseolorum var. sojae infection were smaller in size and volume, lower in density, produced lower quality oil and flour, and had lower viability and durability than symptomless seeds. Oil from infected seeds had a rancid, off-odour and a high peroxide value indicating oil deterioration (Hepperly and Sinclair, 1978). ^p^pPod and stem blight, Phomopsis seed decay and stem canker are the diseases that most severely affect soyabean seed quality and yield. These diseases are present in almost every soyabean-producing region of the world (Athow, 1987).^p^pIn Europe, D. phaseolorum var. sojae was found for the first time in Romania in 1972 (Hulea et al., 1973), then in Hungary in 1975 (Ersek, 1978; Kovics, 1982) and later in the Serbo-Croatian region (Dimitrijevic and Jurkovic, 1982; Vrataric et al., 1991). It was isolated from soyabean plants and seeds in Senegal and Cameroon in the 1970s (Girard, 1979; Bernaux, 1979). ^p^pIn South America, D. phaseolorum var. sojae was identified on naturally infected soyabean plants in Argentina (Anon., 1979) and Brazil (Castro and Kimati, 1981; Almeida, 1981; Berger and Hinson, 1984) and pathogenicity was confirmed in Venezuela (Sanabria de Albarracin, 1993). Other studies have reported the importance of Phomopsis spp. (D. phaseolorum var. sojae, P. longicolla, Phomopsis spp.) as seedborne pathogens associated with green seed soyabean (eda mame) (Pioli et al., 1997). Pioli et al. (2000) discuss the epidemiological role of Phomopsis spp. through the progress of infection and the tissues colonized by the fungus in core soyabean-growing areas (Pioli et al., 2000).

potential_eco_desc: Stem canker caused major crop losses in the north-central region of the USA in the 1950s, with up to 80% of plants infected and yield reductions of 50% in individual fields. The epidemic was attributed to the widespread use of two highly susceptible cultivars, Hawkeye and Blackhawk (Athow, 1987). The disease declined in importance with reduced plantings of these cultivars (Kulik, 1983), and has remained as a minor problem in the region. In 1987-88, less than 5% of plants were infected in experimental field plots in Minnesota (Whiting and Crookston, 1993).^p^pA second epidemic of stem canker developed in the southern states of the USA in the early 1980s, was shown to be caused by a different pathogen and the disease was name southern stem canker (McGee and Biddle, 1987; Morgan Jones, 1989). Southern stem canker has been a major problem in Brazil since 1989 (Yorinori, 1990). ^p^pA significant epidemic of stem canker broke out in Europe in the 1980s (Vidic and Jasnic, 1988a). Yield was reduced by 50-62% when stem canker infection by the fungus occurred early, with premature wilting and desiccation of the plants. Yield was reduced by 9-20% in plants that were less infected, with spots on the stalk. Yield reductions were dependent on the cultivar; late maturing cultivars were more susceptible than early maturing ones. A highly significant negative correlation was found between yield and severity of infection (R = -6.697), and between 1000-grain weight and degree of infection (R = -0.565) (Vidic and Jasnic, 1988a). In a study of European isolates of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora, seedlings of soyabean varieties Mandarin, Harosoy and Tracy-M and the line J 77-339 were inoculated with five isolates collected in different areas of Vojvodina, Serbia. The reaction of Tracy-M soyabean indicated that the isolates were similar to the northern race, but different from the southern race. A study of Italian isolates of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora reached the same conclusion (DC McGee, Iowa State University, USA, personal communication, 1996).^p^pDuring the 2001-2002 growing season, isolates of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora were obtained from stems of soyabean, exhibiting symptoms of soyabean stem canker, grown in Marcos Juarez, Cordoba; Salto, Buenos Aires; and Diego de Alvear, Santa Fe. Disease incidence in the fields was 10-60, 5-15 and 10-20%, respectively. The isolates were classified as D. phaseolorum var. caulivora on the basis of morphological analysis and pathogenicity tests on cultivars Tracy M, Crockett, Hutchenson and RA 702 (Pioli et al., 2002).

potential_eco_desc: Significant stem canker damage to soyabean has been reported in the southern states of the USA from 1970s to the early 1980s. The earliest observations were in Mississippi (1973), followed by reports from Alabama (1977), Tennessee (1981), Georgia (1982), Florida, Arkansas and Louisiana (1983) and Texas (1984) (Backman et al., 1985). Southern soyabean stem canker was reported in 1981 in Tennessee (Hilty, 1981). In Georgia, the mean incidence of stem canker, caused by southern isolates of D. phaseolorum, increased from 1.6% of plants in 1983 to 74.2% in 1984, showing that the disease can increase from negligible to epidemic levels in 1 year (Rothrock et al., 1985). An epiphytotic stem canker occurred in South Carolina (Krausz and Fortnum, 1983) and severe outbreaks were also observed in Louisiana during 1983 and 1984 (Snow et al., 1984). A survey in Florida in 1983 detected the disease in 15 out of 18 counties, with 81% of fields affected in one county (Ploetz et al., 1986). At 25 locations in Mississippi in 1984, infected plants occurred in 84% of fields with incidences ranging from 0 to 50% and averaging 10% (Roy and McLean, 1984). In one county of Texas, 25% of the acreage was heavily damaged in 1985 with total losses reported in some fields (Whitney and Bowers, 1985). In all of these states, plantings of some cultivars were almost destroyed, whereas others were unaffected or only slightly damaged (Backman et al., 1985). From the start of this epidemic, the frequency and severity of disease was erratic (Smith and Backman, 1989). To a large extent, the problem was related to growing susceptible cultivars. A 10-50% reduction in the sales of seed from susceptible cultivars that were severely affected in Florida counties in 1983, was followed by a major decline in the incidence of the disease in these counties in 1984 and 1985 (Ploetz et al., 1986). In 1989, soyabean crop losses due to stem canker were estimated at 7.0, 3.1 and 15% in Arkansas, Mississippi and Tennessee, respectively (Sciumbato, 1993).^p^pStem canker has become a major problem in several areas of Brazil since 1989 (Yorinori et al., 1989; Yorinori, 1990) and in northern Argentina and Bolivia (Yorinori, 1996). In Brazil, the accumulated loss from 1989 to 1995 was estimated at more than US$ 350 million. In the 1994/1995 growing season alone, loss reached US$ 170 million (Yorinori, 1996). In Paraguay, stem canker was detected on more than 10 cultivars in three locations of Itapua prefecture and in 13 locations of Alto Parana prefecture. About 150 isolates obtained from diseased plants were morphologically identified as D. phaseolorum var. meridionalis (Sato et al., 1993).^p^pIn Argentina, D. phaseolorum var. meridionalis was reported in Pergamino, Buenos Aires Province, in 1992 (Ivancovich et al., 1992). During the 1992/1993 growing season, a survey conducted on 66 soyabean field plots in several localities of Santa Fe Province detected an incidence level of 5-8% (Pioli et al., 1993). Later, stem canker outbreaks occurred in the Santa Fe Province in 1996/1997 (Pioli et al., 1997a) and in north-west Argentina in 1996/1997 and 1997/1998 (Wrather et al., 1997; Ploper et al., 1999a) causing severe damage reaching 70-100% in some fields.

description: Natural dispersal^p^pPerithecia develop during late winter and the ascospores are released during the spring, while the soyabean crop is at early vegetative stage. These ascospores are exuded in a sticky matrix and dispersed by the splaying of raindrops and by wind-borne-rain, and are responsible for primary infections. A period of rain is also necessary for infection although all the predisposing conditions for infection have not been defined (Backman et al., 1985). The direction of disease spread was related to field slope, prevailing wind, row direction and water movement (Damicone et al., 1990). In order to correlate climatic factors with the occurrence of some diseases, including soyabean stem canker, Ponti and Cavanni (1992) used a spore-trap to assess the presence and levels of phytopathogenic fungal propagules in the air. However, airborne spore monitoring was only useful as a disease control strategy for Venturia inaequalis and Phytophthora infestans. It was suggested that this aerobiological monitoring system could not be employed for prediction of stem canker. On the other hand, studies made by Skripka and Podkina (1990); Lee and Subbarao (1993) reported that D. phaseolorum var. caulivora isolates from different regions of USA colonised and produced perithecia on non-host species. It probably means that these plants constitute sources of inoculum multiplication and dispersal centres in the field.^p^pSeedborne spread^p^pThere is evidence that infected seeds constitute a source of primary inoculum of some pathogenic fungi; although the efficiency of spread is a controversial subject (Kmetz et al., 1978; Schmitthenner and Kmetz, 1980). Even with low incidence values of infected seeds, severe cases of stem canker have developed with seed as the only apparent inoculum source. Although this observation supports the possibility that the seedborne fungus infects the plant through a secondary cycle and not by direct penetration from the cotyledon, no physical evidence of a secondary cycle originated from seeds (pycnidia or perithecia formation) has been reported (Backman et al., 1985). Typically, neither pycnidia nor perithecia are observed on infected plants during the growing season, although Hildebrand (1956) has reported it.^pThe effect of moisture and temperature on the infection of soyabean seeds by P. longicolla, D. phaseolorum var. sojae and D. phaseolorum var. caulivora, from physiological maturity (R7) to harvest maturity (R8) was investigated. Higher seed infection occurred in pods incubated at 85-100% RH for 7 days when they were detached at R7 than at R8 (Balducchi and McGee, 1987). Anderson et al. (1995) made field trials, over 3 years, with the cultivar Coles (susceptible) and the breeding line OX615 (moderately resistant) and evaluated the time and percentage of pod and seed infection caused by P. longicolla, D. phaseolorum var. caulivora and D. phaseolorum var. sojae. Pod infection increased linearly with time, averaging 15% less in the resistant genotype at each sampling date. Seed infection increased curvilinearly during seed development, with marked increases between the fifth and seventh weeks after flowering. At maturity, average seed infection was 69% in Coles and 28% in OX615 (Anderson et al., 1995).^p^pAgricultural practices ^p^pThe infected seeds can be responsible of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora movement trough longer distance, and the splaying of raindrops account for the primary infection in the fields on shorter distances. The movement of infected debris by agricultural equipment also spread the disease from field to field or among regions (Backman et al., 1985). D. phaseolorum var. caulivora was recovered from soyabean crop residues which had over-wintered in the northern states of the USA (Dunleavy, 1958). description: Incidence^p^pD. phaseolorum var. sojae was detected in soyabean seed samples from several states of the USA in 1970 and 1971. Less than 25% of any seed lot tested contained Phomopsis spp. (Nicholson et al., 1972). Another study showed that the percentage occurrence of D. phaseolorum var. sojae varied with harvest year, location and variety. When the percentage occurrence in a single lot approached 25% or more, in vitro germination and field emergence was reduced (Ellis et al., 1974a).^p^pIn Indiana, USA, an 8-10 week delay in harvest increased the incidence of D. phaseolorum in seed of 14 varieties belonging to MG I, II, III and IV. As a result of delayed harvesting, seedling emergence was reduced by, on average, 36% in MG I and II, 10% in MG III and 6% in MG IV. Only the variety Williams (MG III) and several varieties of MG IV germinated above the acceptable 80% level (Wilcox et al., 1974). In Illinois, USA, D. phaseolorum var. sojae was the predominant organism isolated from soyabean seeds in 1972, and low germination was associated with a high percentage of infected seeds (Chamberlain and Gray, 1974).^p^pIn Brazil, Phomopsis sojae [D. phaseolorum var. sojae], Cercospora kikuchii and Fusarium semitectum [F. incarnatum] were the principal fungi isolated from seeds of 10 cultivars. Up to 37% infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae and 15% by other fungi was recorded in one cultivar, with 50% germination (Dhingra et al., 1979a). The incidence of infection increased with a delay in harvesting and high relative humidity. D. phaseolorum var. sojae was isolated most often, but Alternaria, Fusarium spp. and C. kikuchii were also found (Castro and Kimati, 1981). In a survey during 1982-1992, Colletotrichum dematium and D. phaseolorum var. sojae were consistently found in soyabean germplasm from field collections and research centre accessions (Faiad et al., 1996). In Argentina, the incidence of Phomopsis spp. (D. phaseolorum var. sojae, P. longicolla and Phomopsis spp.) was 13.3 and 27.7% on carpels and seeds, respectively, on plots with soyabean as a precedent crop, and 7.2 and 19.4%, respectively, on plots with maize as a precedent crop (Pioli et al., 2000).^p^pIn Cuba, D. phaseolorum var. sojae, Fusarium spp., C. kikuchii, Xanthomonas campestris pv. glycines, Penicillium, Aspergillus, Alternaria, Cladosporium, Rhizopus spp., Colletotrichum dematium f.sp. truncata [Colletotrichum truncatum], Macrophomina phaseolina and Rhizoctonia solani [Thanatephorus cucumeris] were reported from seeds of soyabean variety R-315 (Garcia et al., 1988).^p^pIn Senegal, D. phaseolorum var. sojae and C. truncatum were isolated from seeds, and their pathogenicity verified by inoculating soyabean plants in the glasshouse (Girard, 1979). ^p^pIn Russia, 34 taxa of fungi and nine taxa of bacteria were isolated and identified from soyabean seeds. The isolates included D. phaseolorum var. sojae, Fusarium spp. and Peronospora manshurica, all of which cause harmful diseases of soyabean (Shchelko et al., 1982).^p^pD. phaseolorum var. sojae, C. kikuchii, C. truncatum and Fusarium oxysporum were isolated from 14 soyabean seed samples in the Korea Republic. Germination was reduced in seeds infected by D. phaseolorum var. sojae, C. truncatum and F. oxysporum (Lee, 1984). Another Korean study reported that 20 genera of fungi were isolated from 60 soyabean seed lots from 53 geographical locations. description: Incidence^p^pD. phaseolorum var. caulivora is commonly found in seeds in association with Phomopsis seed decay. Infection levels averaging 12.5% have been reported (Kmetz et al., 1978; Anderson, 1985). It was also isolated from 22% of the seeds from cultivars with the top dieback symptom of stem canker (Hobbs et al., 1981). ^p^pSeed infection by the southern stem canker pathogen, D. phaseolorum var. meridionalis,  occurs at lower levels. It was isolated from 5/50 southern seedlots in 1984, 12/47 in 1985, and 5/50 in 1986, with 1% the highest infection level found (Phillips and Pinnow, 1987). Also, less than 1% seed infection occurred in 12 seedlots from Mississippi (Roy and McLean, 1984). Another report stated that seed infection in southern fields does not exceed 5% (Backman et al., 1985).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pD. phaseolorum var. caulivora is part of the complex causing Phomopsis seed decay in the northern states of the USA, in which severely infected seeds are shrunken, light, with a white-chalky appearance (Lehman, 1923; McGee and Nyvall, 1984) and germination is reduced (Kmetz et al., 1978). Culture filtrates of northern isolates inhibited seed germination (Ivanovic and Sinclair, 1989). Reduced vigour has been reported in infected seeds from southern states (Omer et al., 1989).^p^p^Seed Transmission ^p^pSeed^pThere is no conclusive evidence that D. phaseolorum var. caulivora is transmitted by seeds (McGee, 1983). ^p^pOther sources ^pD. phaseolorum var. caulivora  was recovered from soyabean crop residues which had overwintered in northern states (Dunleavy, 1958; Kmetz et al., 1979). The pathogen has been recovered from Abutilon theophrasti, a common weed in soyabean, in Croatia (Vrandecic et al., 2005).^p^p^Seed Treatments^p^pCarboxin-thiram and carboxin-thiram-captan treatments reduced, but did not eliminate, D. phaseolorum var. meridionalis from seeds (Backman et al., 1985).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pBlotter (McGee, 1986; USDA National Seed Health System, Standard Method, www.seedhealth.org)^p^p1. Seed are surface sterilized in 0.5% NaOCl for 1 min. and then rinsed in sterile water. ^p2. Plate seeds on PDA adjusted to pH 4.5. ^p3. Seeds incubation at 25°C for 7 days under continuous light. ^p4. Seeds are evaluated for the presence of the three fungi associated with the Phomopsis/Diaporthe complex in soyabeans according to the following descriptions. ^p^pNote: There is considerable controversy regarding the taxonomy of this group. These descriptions should, therefore, only be used to identify the Diaporthe/Phomopsis complex and not the individual pathogens. ^p^pPhomopsis longicolla, previously known as Phomopsis sp. are floccose, dense and white, with occasional greenish-yellow areas on PDA. In reverse, colonies are colorless, with black, spreading stromata. Pycnidia are black, stromatic, solitary or aggregated, unilocular or multilocular, with prominent necks, more than 200 μm long. Alpha conidia are hyaline, ellipsoid to fusiform, guttulate, and measure 5-9 x 1.5-3.5 μm. Beta conidia, which are rarely formed, are hyaline, filiform and hamate. No perithecia are formed on PDA. ^p^pD. phaseolorum var. caulivora cultures on PDA are white, closely appressed, with tufted aerial mycelium. description: Natural Dispersal^p^pThe dispersal of the fungus over long distances occurs through infected seeds, crop harvest debris transported by agricultural machines, and climatic factors. Ascospores, the main primary inoculum, are released from perithecia on crop debris at the time of seedling emergence. Ascospores may be carried for short distances by rain drops, or over long distances by wind (Yorinori, 1996).^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pAlthough the incidence and severity of stem canker can reach high levels, the incidence of seeds infected with D. phaseolorum var. meridionalis is usually lower than 2%. However, infected seeds are the main and most efficient source of primary infection in plots that are free of the disease (Backman et al., 1985; Sinclair and Backman, 1989; Sato et al., 1993). In Brazil, the intensive movement of seeds, combined with extensive areas sown with susceptible cultivars and monoculture, are important factors for the dissemination of stem canker (Yorinori, 1996).^p^pAgricultural Practices^p^pThe bulk of the primary inoculum appears to originate from over-wintering or over-summering crop debris (Roy and McLean, 1984). Some studies on southern stem canker of soyabean in Georgia, USA, indicated that burying crop residues resulted in less disease incidence and severity. The pathogen was isolated more frequently from the stems and petioles of plants grown in no-tillage plots than from plants grown under conventional tillage (Tyler et al., 1983; Rothrock et al., 1985). Disease severity was higher with wheat/soyabean double cropping than with soyabean monoculture. The wheat residues may affect the disease by altering the amount of inoculum produced by the pathogen and the environment for the host (Rothrock et al., 1985). In Argentina, a soyabean stem canker outbreak reported in 1996/1997 in Santa Fe Province was due mainly to the wide diffusion of susceptible cultivars, predisposing weather conditions and high inoculum availability from no-tillage fields (Pioli et al., 1997a). There have also been reports from Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay on an increase in the incidence of several soyabean diseases including stem canker in monoculture conditions combined with no-tillage or minimum tillage practices (Yorinori, 1996; Vallone and Kokubun, 1998). In Brazil, the teleomorph of the fungus survives in harvest debris and is able to infect soyabean plants in more than one growing season, depending on climatic conditions. The degradation of crop debris is slower in southern regions of Brazil (with lower temperature and humidity) than in northern regions; the fungus can, therefore, survive for a longer period on the soil surface, resulting in the disease often being more severe in the south (Yorinori, 1996).^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pD. phaseolorum var. meridionalis was assumed to be introduced to Paraguay with a large quantity of soyabean seed imported from Brazil (Sato et al., 1993).Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - True Seeds (inc. Grain): Hyphae; borne internally; borne externally; invisible.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural dispersal^p^pSoyabean seeds and crop residues are recognized as sources of inoculum for D. phaseolorum var. sojae and Phomopsis spp. (Lehman, 1923; Kmetz et al., 1979). All colonized tissues are potential sources of primary inoculum, but the bulk of primary inoculum appears to originate from overwintered or oversummered crop debris (Kmetz et al., 1979; Garzonio and McGee, 1983; Athow, 1987).^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pAlthough little control of the disease can be achieved by planting Phomopsis-free seeds in soyabean-growing areas where pod and stem blight is endemic, Phomopsis-infected seeds may be of practical significance in introducing the fungus to new areas (Garzonio and McGee, 1983). Seeds infected with D. phaseolorum var. sojae, D. phaseolorum var. caulivora or Phomopsis longicolla are important in terms of seedling infection and long-range dissemination of these fungi (Roy and McLean, 1989).^p^pAgricultural Practices ^p^pSeveral studies have been conducted to estimate the relationship between levels of soyabean pod and stem blight and different agronomic practices. In Iowa, USA, marked differences in Phomopsis infection were observed among cropping systems, with the most severe disease occurring in continuous-soyabean rotations compared with maize-soyabean or continuous-maize rotations (Garzonio and McGee, 1983). Similar results were obtained in Santa Fe, Argentina, where a continuous-soyabean rotation increased the incidence of Phomopsis compared to a maize-soyabean rotation (Pioli et al., 2000). However, no significant relationship was detected between the amount of seedborne inoculum and disease severity on seedlings or on stems, pods or seeds of mature plants. The finding that seedborne inoculum, even on 77% of the seeds, could not be related to infections on either seedlings or mature plants in fields with continuous-soyabean or maize-soyabean rotation indicates that seeds are a minor source of inoculum (Garzonio and McGee, 1983). The most probable explanation is that soyabean residues infested with Phomopsis are the major source of inoculum for pod and stem blight (Kmetz, 1975; Kmetz et al., 1979; Garzonio and McGee, 1983).^p^pIn subsequent studies, the survival of the mycobiota on pod and stem debris of soyabean produced in a no-tillage system with cover crops of lucerne, rape, rye or wheat, or with no cover, was studied during 1994/95 in Indiana, USA. Fibreglass mesh bags containing pods and stems were assayed every 28-31 days to determine the isolation frequency of fungi. Common soyabean pathogens were Colletotrichum spp., Diaporthe spp. and Cercospora kikuchii. Fusarium graminearum [Gibberella zeae], which is responsible for several diseases of maize and wheat, was also isolated during this study. Of the Diaporthe spp., 87% were identified as D. phaseolorum var. sojae; the Colletotrichum spp. was identified as C. truncatum in 85% of the isolates; C. destructivum [Glomerella glycines] in 12% of isolates and both species in 3%. C. kikuchii was more commonly isolated from pods than stems and Colletotrichum spp. occurred more frequently on stems. Isolation frequencies for Diaporthe spp. were greater in May of both years than in the preceding months. No-tillage soyabean debris was shown to harbour numerous fungi pathogenic to soyabean, and producers who grow soyabean continuously may find more disease and lower yields in this crop. Fungi that attack crops such as maize and wheat were commonly isolated from soyabean debris in both years, and a no-tillage rotation, which included maize or wheat, could increase disease in these crops. Isolation frequencies of the fungi from cover crops varied with the sampling date, but no consistent patterns could be determined for a particular cover crop or fungal species. This was the first detailed study of survival rates of soyabean, maize and wheat pathogens that overwinter on soyabean debris in a no-tillage system (Baird et al., 1997). ^p^pOther studies have evaluated t
author: CPC2006

remark: Before 1960, D. phaseolorum var. sojae was considered of little importance to soyabean production (Sasaki, 1929; Luttrell, 1947; Athow and Caldwell, 1954; Hildebrand, 1956). Significant germination losses have since been reported in heavily infected seed lots in the USA and Canada Ellis et al., 1974a, 1976; Wallen and Seaman, 1963). D. phaseolorum var. sojae was later recognized as a major cause of mouldy, poorly germinating soyabean seeds in Brazil, Canada and the USA (Wallen and Seaman, 1963; Crittenden and Svec, 1974; Chamberlain and Gray, 1974; Bolkan et al., 1976). Phomopsis seed infection often exceeds 50% on susceptible cultivars when the harvest is delayed (Wilcox et al., 1974; Ellis et al., 1976; Sinclair, 1977). Latent infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae has been found in symptomless soyabean plants (Kmetz et al., 1974). This contributes to the fungus' capacity to overwinter on crop debris and is therefore of epidemiological importance. Seeds are also an important source of inoculum that can perpetuate the pathogen. Seed treatment is considered necessary, even for good quality, asymptomatic seeds (Hepperly and Sinclair, 1978).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pD. helianthi is considered by OEPP/EPPO (2001) as the most damaging pathogen of sunflower. Its control is essential for successful cultivation of the crop.^p^p^Environmental impact^pD. helianthi has only been recorded to attack sunflower, and this plant is an exotic annual crop, grown as a monoculture, in Europe. Possibilities for any effect on the environment are therefore limited. Fungicides are in any case used on sunflower against other pathogens, so any impact through pesticide load on the environment is difficult to evaluate. The impact of the disease has not been such as to reduce its cultivation, and thus affect land use.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pIn the absence of any knowledge of where D. helianthi is native, or of any records of it attacking wild plants, it is impossible to assess any effect on biodiversity. As sunflower is native to North America, such effects could exist there, but their significance would depend on whether the fungus is or is not native to North America, and whether it does have other hosts. The subject is not apparently under study in North America.
description: D. helianthi 'appeared from nowhere' in Europe in the late 1970s. Its successive appearance in different countries did not follow any obvious pattern of geographical spread, and it may therefore be conjectured that it moved with infected seeds. Its rise in importance coincided with a substantial increase in the cultivation of sunflower in western Europe, but the crop was previously cultivated, without the disease. It is not known where the fungus is native, or on what host, and it is impossible accordingly to say where it is exotic. There is a presumption that its later appearance in Asia and South America must be secondary.

remark: Although D. helianthi, when it first appeared, could have been considered to present a considerable phytosanitary risk to sunflower cultivation in Europe, in fact no phytosanitary measures were taken. This may possibly be explained by the fact that the pathogen rapidly established in several countries, with the possibility of further natural spread, that tolerant cultivars are available, that fungicide treatment is possible, and that controls on the trade of seeds might have been necessary. In Russia (Savotikov and Smetnik, 1995), D. helianthi is a quarantine pest and measures are taken to prevent its further spread within the country. D. helianthi certainly presents a risk to sunflower-growing countries in other continents, though the subject is not apparently researched in North America, despite the fact that the fungus has been recorded there.

management_info: EPPO has proposed good plant protection practice for control of the disease (OEPP/EPPO, 2001). Careful and proper ploughing of infected plant residues into the soil (deeper than 5 cm) prevents overwintering of the pathogen, and eliminates the primary inoculum from infected areas. Less dense planting (about 50,000 plants per hectare) reduces humidity and limits spread. Growing tolerant or resistant hybrids, use of healthy seeds, keeping a 5-6 year crop rotation, with good weed control are also recommended. The pathogen infects volunteer sunflower plants and their elimination is essential. Fungicides may be sprayed if conditions are favourable to the disease. They are most effective when 6-8 leaves have developed and at the beginning of flowering. A forecasting model (ASPHODEL) has been developed in France (Delos and Moinard, 1997). Resistance to D. helianthi is an important concern in sunflower breeding in Europe.

description: In September 2012, about 90% of M. sativa in grassland suffered severe black root rot in Kunming, Yunnan Province, China. Chlorosis symptoms of M. sativa first appeared on leaves, then black rot on roots, and finally the whole plant wilted and died in just a few days. Based on morphological characteristics showed the fungus was Cylindrocladium parasiticum Crous, M.J. Wingfield, & Alfenas (teleomorph Calonectria ilicicola). By DNA sequencing of the ITS rDNA region, the identity of the isolate was confirmed to be C. ilicicola. This fungus was previously cited in China on soybean and peanut . To our knowledge, this is the first report of C. ilicicola as a root rot pathogen of M. sativa in China.

In southern Florida, USA, canker incidence in coppiced Eucalyptus increased from ca 15 to 57% over 4 years (Barnard et al., 1987), with much of the damage attributed to Cryphonectria cubensis. The disease has been assessed as more severe in Brazil than that caused by Valsa ceratosperma (Auer and Kruger, 1993). In Kerala, India, the severity of infection varied with location and host species: it was more severe at high altitudes, where there was high rainfall, and in Eucalyptus grandis. In one plantation of E. grandis, infection was 0.8% in 1980 increasing to 27.5% in 1982. Overall mortality in the state was estimated at 3% of the infected trees (Florence et al., 1984). There is sometimes considerable infraspecific variation in host susceptibility (Conradie et al., 1992b), and fungus strains vary in virulence (Alfenas, 1986). Loss evaluation has been carried out in Brazil (Ferrari et al., 1984).

potential_eco_desc: Pine-oak rust causes economically significant disease throughout the northern temperate zone, resulting in malformation, reduced vigour and ultimately the death of plantation and nursery Pinus spp. stock. In North America, 25% losses to Pinus sylvestris have been recorded. C. fusiforme causes severe damage and significant financial losses to plantations of loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) and slash pine (Pinus elliottii var. elliottii) throughout the south-eastern USA (Schmidt, 2003). Annual losses to C. fusiforme have been estimated at $35 million in five southern states (Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia) and $8 million alone in Florida (Schmidt, 2003). Significant losses due to rust also occur in Alabama, Mississippi and eastern Texas.^p^pLosses occur mostly due to mortality in young Pinus spp. When 1-5-year-old trees develop stem galls, they often die before rotation age (harvest) or become deformed and unsuitable for sale, or are reduced in value. C. fusiforme is abundant in young, rapidly growing plantations of susceptible Pinus spp., especially when established in areas with a high risk of rust. Young plantations are extremely vulnerable to the disease in high-risk areas and more than 90% of susceptible trees can be infected by the age of 5 years. For more information on the pest significance of Cronartium spp., see also Sinclair et al. (1987), Tainter and Baker (1996), Chen (2003) and Schmidt (2003).

remark: As C. quercuum is one of the non-European species of Cronartium it should be stressed that the potential risk from introduced species of Cronartium is much affected by the indigenous Pinus and Quercus and the pathosystem concerned. In North America, the telial hosts of C. quercuum are mainly species of Quercus indigenous to that continent. No information has been published on the susceptibility of these European species of Quercus. The most widespread European oaks are 'white oaks' (subgenus Quercus), and thus belong to the group which is not susceptible to C. quercuum in North America. North American red oaks are planted to a limited extent in Europe (especially Quercus rubra). The European evergreen oaks could be susceptible, but there is no direct evidence of this. The Asian telial host Quercus serrata is a rarely cultivated garden ornamental in Europe. It is clear that several other Asian oak species can act as telial hosts, but in general Asian oaks are little grown in Europe.^p^pIn favour of the importance of C. quercuum as a quarantine pest for the EPPO region is the fact that the most important European pine species, Pinus sylvestris, has suffered serious losses from C. quercuum at the nursery stage in North America. On the other hand, the other significant Pinus spp. hosts of C. quercuum (in North America or Asia) have no importance in Europe, and no European species have been specifically recorded as telial hosts. Successful establishment of C. quercuum in Europe would thus depend on the conjectural susceptibility of some European Castanea or Quercus species. Accordingly, C. quercuum can be considered to present only a moderate risk for the EPPO region (CABI/EPPO, 1997).^p^pThe uredinial rust, Uredo quercus, is widely distributed on Quercus spp. throughout Europe, especially in the Mediterranean region where infection is more common. This rust may represent the alternate, uredinial form of the oak-pine rust (see Taxonomy and Nomenclature), which for reasons unknown fails to complete its life cycle on Pinus spp. in Europe at the present time. There is, however, no guarantee that the full life cycle will continue to be truncated in the future as climatic change becomes more pronounced and possibly other strains of C. quercuum become introduced in Europe.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control can be effected by removing infected material. Replanting, pruning limb galls and sanitation/salvage thinning have been suggested as control measures in infected plantations. Eradicating the alternate host is not a practical possibility for C. quercuum because the alternate Quercus spp. hosts are ecologically and economically important forest trees. However, if possible, Pinus spp. nurseries should be located away from potential infection sources. Research into genetically resistant Pinus spp. cultivars may ultimately lead to successful control of C. quercuum (Burnes et al., 1989).^p^pThe more rapidly a tree grows, the more it is at risk from C. quercuum. Thus, most practices which improve Pinus spp. growth (e.g., fertilization, control of competitive vegetation, genetic growth rate improvement, and intensive site preparation) favour rust development. This presents a dilemma to forest landowners when rapid reforestation and increased productivity are management goals (Schmidt, 2003).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe first efforts to control C. fusiforme began in the 1930s, when the first forest tree nurseries were put into operation (Lamb, 1937). Under forest conditions, the disease was not a significant problem at that time, but in forest tree nurseries, cultivation, fertilization and irrigation provided optimum conditions for disease development. One of the first control attempts was to use fungicidal sprays, including Bordeaux mixture (Lamb and Sleeth, 1940). Eradication of the alternate Quercus spp. hosts in, and adjacent to, the nursery area was also tried but was not successful, because basidiospores spread further than expected (Sleeth, 1943). In time, ferbam became the standard fungicide for rust control in nurseries (Siggers, 1951) and for over 30 years these recommendations remained unchanged. When applied as recommended, ferbam provided good control; infection in forest tree nurseries usually averaged less than 5%.^p^pOver the years researchers have tried new, promising chemicals such as antibiotics and systemic fungicides. Antibiotics were not very effective, and until recently neither were systemics. However, the systemic triadimefon has proven to be very effective (Snow et al., 1979), and it is now used in almost all nurseries in the southern USA. Triadimefon has replaced the older, protectant sprays because it acts as both a protectant and an eradicant. It therefore needs to be applied only three or four times a year, as compared to 35 to 40 times per year for ferbam. Early studies with triadimefon showed that foliar sprays alone will prevent infection for up to 14 days after spraying and will eradicate infections that occurred up to 14 days before spraying (Rowan, 1984).^p^p^Phytosanitary Methods^p^pBecause symptoms may not be apparent for many years after infection, the only practical safeguard is to prohibit the entry of Pinus spp. hosts from countries where C. quercuum occurs. Castanea and Quercus spp. should only be imported in a dormant state, without leaves. Pine wood and bark should have been appropriately treated (heat-treated, fermented, kiln-dried; EPPO quarantine procedures are in preparation).

management_info: Cultural ControlSluder (1996) reported on progeny-tested first-generation slash pine (Pinus elliottii) selections that were crossed in a half diallel to study inheritance patterns of their rust resistance. At age 10 years, the 15 progenies in the half diallel averaged 23% rust-infected compared with 54% for the control susceptible lots. Kuhlman et al. (1995) found that loblolly (Pinus taeda) and slash (P. elliottii) pine seedlings from C. fusiforme resistant orchards developed co-operatively by the USDA Forest Service and the Georgia Forestry Commission had significantly less rust 7 to 8 years after planting on four of five sites in Georgia and South Carolina than seedlings of the same species from orchard sources developed primarily for silvicultural improvement. This finding supports the hypothesis that mixes of resistant families will limit fusiform rust infections more effectively than single family plantings. Schmidt et al. (1995) described the influence of oak control and pine growth on C. fusiforme incidence (percentage trees infected) on rust-susceptible slash and loblolly pines (Pinus elliottii and P. taeda) by evaluation at age 5 years at seven potentially high-rust-incidence locations in the Coastal Plain of Florida, Georgia and Mississippi. Rust-susceptible oaks (predominantly Quercus nigra and Q. laurifolia) were reduced or eliminated in a 9 acre treatment block and the surrounding 500 ft border zone of an oak-free (OF) area; oaks were not controlled in an adjacent oak-present (OP) area. At four of seven locations, rust incidence was significantly greater on the OF areas compared with the OP areas, and among all locations average rust incidence on pine was greater on the OF areas (51.4%) than on the OP areas (40.0%). Greatly reducing rust-susceptible oak stems in the treatment blocks and in a surrounding 500 ft border did not reduce rust incidence on rust-susceptible slash or loblolly pine. Inoculum to infect pine came from beyond the 500 ft border zone. Greater pine height, associated with reduced competition from oaks, probably contributed to the greater rust incidence on pine in the OF areas. Schmidt et al. (1988) analysed the relation of soil drainage, soil surface texture, site preparation methods and site index to the incidence of C. fusiforme. In a combined analysis of all management areas, rust incidence in both pine species was greatest on sites with well- or moderately well-drained soils with loamy sand or sandy loam surface texture and least on sites with poorly or somewhat poorly drained soils with a sandy surface texture. It was concluded, however, that a definitive rust hazard model at the stand level would require quantitative data on alternate host (oak) abundance and dispersal of inoculum. ^p^p^Chemical ControlHaywood et al. (1994) reported results from four cultural treatments (control (no weed control or fertilizer); weeded (spraying with several herbicides plus periodic manual hoeing); weeded, applied inorganic fertilizer (triple superphosphate) and bedded before planting; and weeded, bedded and inorganic fertilizer applied in the sixth season. Fungicide applications of triadimefon greatly reduced rust damage in 10-year-old plantations, and resulted in higher survival, fewer trees with stem galls, fewer galls below 5 ft of tree height, fewer trees with galls encircling 76-100% of the stem, greater total volume per acre, and smaller volume among infected trees. Weed control and fertilizer application increased rust incidence. Fungicide-treated plots receiving delayed fertilizer application yielded the greatest volume after 10 years. McNab et al. (1990) reported that in clear felled pine/broadleaved sites prepared by burning or drum chopping and regenerated to loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) by planting (1 + 0 seedlings) or direct sowing (broadcast or row sowing) that site preparation had little effect on soil physical properties but that after 12 years, trees were larger in diameter at breast

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pC. coleosporioides kill seedlings and cause branch dieback and resinous, perennial trunk cankers that girdle and kill trees of all ages and degrade the quality of the trunk for sawnwood and pulp. They cause greatest damage in western forests of North America (Leaphart, 1955; Peterson, 1959; Sinclair et al., 1987; Tainter and Baker, 1996).^p^pOn large trees elongate cankers form on the main stem, reducing the value of the trees for poles and pilings.^p^pAlthough cronartium rusts cause very important diseases throughout the world, the abundance and pathogenicity of the pine cow wheat rust depends primarily on the abundance of suitable hosts. C. coleosporioidesis can damage young seedlings in nurseries rapidly, but when 2- and 3-year-old nursery trees were artificially inoculated, less than 1 percent infection was obtained with each rust. It appears that jack pines (P. banksiana) are most susceptible to infection during their first year of growth, but field observations indicate that C. coleosporioides can infect trees of all ages.^p^pThere is no particular indication of economic importance in Asia and Europe. C. coleosporioides is of no direct practical importance on its telial hosts. For more information on the pest significance of Cronartium spp., see Leaphart (1955), Peterson (1959), Sinclair et al. (1987), Tainter and Baker (1996).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pLimb rusts are so named because they kill branches in the crown without girdling the tree. As the disease progresses rapidly more branches are killed; the remaining crown can no longer meet the tree's needs, so the tree then dies. More often, however, these weakened trees are attacked by bark beetles. Even though some stands have less than 20% of the trees infected, the aesthetics of the area are severely degraded because it is the larger trees that are usually infected (Tainter and Baker, 1996).^p^pThis rust is a costly disease throughout North America. It causes reduced vigour and ultimately death of plantation and nursery pine stock. So far it has not been a problem in European plantations; there is, however, no guarantee that the full life cycle will continue to be truncated in the future as climatic change becomes more pronounced and possibly other strains of C. coleosporioides are introduced to Europe. Pine rust breeders are currently attempting to produce rust-resistant cultivars of pine; such programs are still at an early stage and rust-resistance has not yet been observed in trials. The pine-Scrophulariaceae species rust relationship is currently not well known among horticulturalists. The breeding of the alternative hosts has historically caused epidemics of pine rust.

remark: C. coleosporioides is one of the non-European species of Cronartium. The danger presented by these fungi to the EPPO region is classically exemplified by reference to the quarantine pest C. ribicola (Phillips, 1988). The telial hosts of C. coleosporioides are, in North America, mainly species of Scrophulariaceae indigenous to that continent. No information seems to be available on the susceptibility of European species of these genera. On the other hand, the other significant Pinus hosts of C. coleosporioides (in North America or Central America) are not significant in Europe, and no European species has been specifically recorded as a telial host. Successful establishment of C. coleosporioides in Europe thus depends on the conjectural susceptibility of some European species of Castilleja and Melampyrum, Orthocarpus, Pedicularis, Rhinanthus. Accordingly, C. coleosporioides can be considered to present only a moderate risk for the EPPO region.^p^pSince symptoms may not be apparent for many years after infection, the only practical safeguard is to prohibit entry of the Pinus hosts from countries where C. coleosporioides occurs. It should only be imported in a dormant state, without leaves. Bark and wood of Pinus should have been appropriately treated (heat-treated, fermented, kiln-dried; EPPO quarantine procedures are in preparation).

management_info: Introduction^p^pIntegrated pest management is the key control strategy, particularly in tree nurseries as cultivation, fertilization and irrigation provide optimum conditions for disease development.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pPine-cowwheat rust can be controlled in the nursery with fungicides such as ferbam.^p^p^Silvicultural Methods^p^pRemoving rust-infected trees as rapidly as practicable will reduce the volume of spore material capable of resulting in new infections and also should favour any resistant individual trees. Diseased stock should not be planted.^p^pEradicating infected hosts around nurseries would be of benefit.^p^pEradicating the alternate host is not practical, as the alternate hosts are weeds that are ecologically widespread. If possible, however, pine nurseries should be located away from potential infection sources. Eradication of alternate hosts adjacent to nurseries may be economically feasible. Pine cow wheat rust requires considerable shade, and if the nursery is located away from stands with the alternate host, incidence of the disease would be reduced.^p^pCutting strategy^p^pIn stands, diseased trees can be detected in early stages and eliminated. Shortening cutting cycles in affected stands to 25 years will allow salvage of diseased trees (Tainter and Baker, 1996). Research into genetically resistant pine cultivars may lead to successful control of C. coleosporioides.

potential_eco_desc: South American national average yields of cocoa vary from 750 to about 200 kg/ha. Unfortunately, there are few reliable estimates of losses to witches' broom over entire regions. In Colombia and Brazil, good yields can be maintained even in areas with high disease pressure. Average losses in these regions are probably about 30%, though up to 90% losses can occur where no cultural control is applied. Yields in Ecuador, Trinidad and Venezuela could probably be greatly improved with better disease management (Rudgard et al., 1993).^p^pAn estimate of growers' receipts calculated in 1985 in countries affected by the disease was US $788 million, calculating from a world market price of $2400 per ton at that time. The price then fell to about $980 per ton in the autumn of 1992, although it rose to stand at above $1600 per ton in April 1996. With losses fixed at an oversimplified estimate of 30% overall, this would mean that $120 million of potential earnings were lost in 1985, and about $49 million at prices prevailing in the autumn of 1992. These global losses will have increased as the disease continues to spread steadily through eastern Brazil (Bahia State) where it was first recorded in 1989. ^p^pThere is also an unquantifiable, but nonetheless important, indirect loss of yield due to debilitation of trees by M. pernicosa.
