description: Incidence^p^pCocoa pods infected with M. perniciosa can contain diseased seeds (Cronshaw and Evans, 1978; Frison and Feliu, 1989).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pAlmost all seeds from diseased pods with extensive lesions are killed or are not viable (Frison and Feliu, 1989).^p^p^Transmission^p^pThe pathogen can be transmitted in the hypocotyl of an ungerminated seed and it will remain viable as long as the seed is alive. Disease symptoms only become apparent once the seed has germinated (Cronshaw and Evans, 1978). Discharged basidiospores germinated and were infectious to pre-germinated cocoa seeds causing hypocotyl hypertrophy plus root and shoot reduction (Almeida et al., 1997).
author: CPC2006

remark: RISK CRITERIA 	 	CATEGORY^p^pECONOMIC IMPORTANCE	Moderate^pDISTRIBUTION 		Western Hemisphere^pSEEDBORNE INCIDENCE	Low^pSEED TRANSMITTED	Yes^pSEED TREATMENT	None^p	^pNotes on Phytosanitary Risk^p^pThe existence of recognized pathotypes with different levels of virulence means that movement of germplasm between different regions/countries with witches' broom should only be undertaken with great care to avoid transmission of the disease (Frison and Feliu, 1989). Diseased material and isolates of the fungus should also not be exchanged for the purposes of research between regions/countries for the same reason. M. perniciosa is declared a notifiable pest in Guyana.^p^pWitches' broom is absent from the major cocoa-growing regions of Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Spores are not sufficiently long-lived to be disseminated naturally over the huge distances between the present distribution and these new areas, so the disease will not enter these regions unless introduced by human activity. Introduction will only occur through the movement of diseased cocoa material which is then able to produce basidiomata sufficiently close to a cocoa-growing area to allow infection. On this basis, post-entry quarantine is advisable in cocoa-growing regions where the disease is currently absent.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe methods of controlling M. perniciosa fall into three broad groups; phytosanitation (or sanitation), spraying with chemicals, and the use of resistance, but in operation they often entail modifications in the way cocoa is grown. Each method or combination of methods needs to be appraised in terms of cost and benefit, and against a background of fluctuating cocoa prices this presents other problems. If witches' broom is controlled, then other pod diseases in the plantation must also be taken into consideration or their incidence may increase, thereby reducing the economic benefit of successful witches' broom control (Rudgard et al., 1993).^p^p^Cultural Control or Phytosanitation^p^pSanitation is based on the concept that by removing infected plant parts the production of inoculum will cease, or at least be reduced to low levels, depending on the efficiency of the removal. This approach has remained the basis of witches' broom control since it was first proposed at the beginning of the twentieth century. In practice, sanitation entails the pruning of brooms as diseased pods generally contribute little inoculum and can be removed during harvesting. The frequency of pruning is related to broom formation, basidioma production and cropping period in the particular area and takes advantage of any dry season when flushing is low and dry brooms can be seen more readily. Essentially it depends on the long (induction) period for basidiomata to develop on brooms which means that the latent period can be several months. There is generally only one disease cycle per rainy season; that is, within the span of one year the disease is monocyclic.^p^pIn cases where removal of individual brooms is feasible, vegetative brooms should be cut off at least 15-20 cm below the point of infection. Diseased material on cushions should be carefully removed by cutting it off as close as possible to the bark. Diseased pods together with their peduncles should be removed whenever healthy pods are harvested.^p^pDiseased tissues are distributed through the branches and canopy of the trees, with the bulk of brooms (both cushion and vegetative) and diseased pods found generally in the high canopy, with only relatively few on the trunk and lower branches. The removal must be as thorough as possible to have any chance of success.^p^pIt is important to ensure that all removed brooms and diseased pods reach the ground and do not remain suspended on branches within the canopy. Elimination of the diseased tissues from the plantation after pruning is optional in some circumstances but necessary in others. The practice is recommended if annual sanitation has lapsed for more than one year, because older brooms on the ground could produce basidiomata within a few days of rainy conditions if not removed. Where sanitation is regular, pruned tissues can be left in the plantation, provided that removed diseased material should not be heaped or left uncovered on the ground in plantations, and leaf-litter should be allowed to accumulate naturally, or should be placed over the removed diseased material. If phytosanitary removal is combined with structural pruning, it is likely that branches with brooms will be cut off the tree, in which case such material should be cut into small pieces. The material can then be spread on the ground so that it is all in contact with the leaf litter, as this speeds up decomposition.^p^pPhytosanitation must be correctly timed, and the choice of times can be determined using epidemiological studies which show the duration and the timing of the climatic and disease cycles. In many cases, additional (secondary) removals would be required to supplement a main (primary) sanitation pruning to ensure effective disease management. Phytosanitation should not be attempted where it is not possible to complete the primary removal at the recommended time. No secondary removal should be applied without a primary removal. 热带平刺粉蚧危害较大，现有的鉴定方法鉴定较为困难，防治成本较高。中国地域广阔，复杂多样的生物地理气候，频繁的对外贸易，为其入侵创造了有利条件。根据其现阶段分布和寄主植物分析，我国南方广大地区适宜该虫生长、发育和繁殖，为其潜在为害地区。风险评估结果表明，热带平刺粉蚧的危险性综合评估风险值为2.29，属于高风险有害生物，应加强入境口岸管理，特别是对来自疫区的相关产品的检疫监管，防止热带平刺粉蚧入侵我国。目前，美国已将该虫列为进境植物检疫性有害生物。一旦传入，将会对我国南方地区农、林业生产、园林绿化等造成重大影响。
根据以上，该有害生物经济、生态影响评估结果为高。
description: 热带平刺粉蚧于2004年由著名蚧虫学家Williams定名，原产马来西亚、菲律宾、泰国、越南等南亚国家，近年传入印度尼西亚，并于2020年爆发，对印度尼西亚重要经济植物A. excelsa和重要观赏植物海杧果造成严重危害。据Zarkani et al.（2021）推测，该虫可能是无意中通过国际运输和贸易从其已知地区进入印度尼西亚的，也有可能是风和台风把它从马来西亚带到了印度尼西亚。该虫在印度尼西亚明古鲁省不同寄主植物上为害，其为害程度表明，该虫很可能在数年前已经入侵印度尼西亚。我国广西口岸曾截获过该虫。热带平刺粉蚧分布于马来西亚、菲律宾、泰国、越南和印度尼西亚等南亚地区。该虫的寄主植物较多，已记录寄主植物为8科11种（属）。在印度尼西亚种植的经济植物A. excelsa和观赏植物海杧果受其严重危害，我国广泛种植的芒果、海杧果、榕属、柑桔属、龙眼等水果和观赏植物均为其重要寄主。该虫主要为害寄主植物的叶、芽、茎、枝、果柄等部位。以口针刺入寄主植物，吮吸汁液。近年来，美国多个口岸从菲律宾、泰国和越南进境的红毛丹、柑桔等植物上截获该虫。通过热带平刺粉蚧分布情况和寄主植物种类及栽培情况分析，我国南方广大地区均为其潜在分布区。热带平刺粉蚧在植株上的扩散危害，依赖若虫和成虫的爬行迁移；林间较远距离的传播，主要是靠风力、鸟类、人和昆虫携带；苗木、接穗、果实调运，则是远距离传播的主要途径。
reference_name: 热带平刺粉蚧（Rastrococcus tropicasiaticus Williams） 风险评估报告

potential_eco_desc: 病轻时造成枯梢，影响高生长；重时树冠呈扫帚状丛枝，不能成材，甚至死亡。
description: 借助风力、雨水飞溅、残枝扩散、侵染。
management_info:
1.检疫：为控制扩大被害面积，应在已发病地区进行普查，摸清病害分布及发生规律，在此基础上建立检疫制度。并宜培养无病苗木上山造林，防止形成发病中心，继而扩大蔓延。
2.消灭侵染来源：在重病区剪除病枝，伐除重病木，应在病原孢子成熟扩散前进行，把清理下来的枝梢就地烧毁。
3.营造混交林及防护林带：不仅枯梢病，其他病害也是纯林病重，营造针阔混交林是防病的一项有利措施。此外鉴于林缘发病重，则相应的保留或营造阔叶树保护林带。
4.药剂防治可试用30～50ppm放线菌酮，200倍代森铵，20～60ppm的春雷霉素，在7～8月份每15～20天喷洒1～2次，药剂必须喷洒到树冠上部才能起到防治作用。
5.日本已有两种抗生素——放线菌酮和多氧菌素用于苗圃中进行防治。7月到9月一般喷洒两种药剂的溶液，春季多用多氧菌素浸种。重病疫区应及时移除烧毁病株及病残体，并补种其他非易感品种。
reference_name: 中国进境植物检疫性有害生物(菌物卷)
author: cpqis.zhangxiling

management_info:
1.普查病情，严格检疫。在普查的基础上，确定无病区和发病区，对造林苗木或调出（或调入）木材进行检疫。以落叶松苗木、接穗、原木和小径木为检疫对象，清除罹病个体及原木和小径木上的枝梢，防止病害外传。
2.请初侵染源。苗圃周围有感病的落叶松防风林时，要及时防治，或改换其他树种。对被害严重的10年生以下的落叶松林，应根据当地条件考虑采伐烧毁，以便减少侵染源。
3.避免在风口处造落叶松林。在砍伐阔叶树营造落叶松林时，应保留部分阔叶树做保护带。大面积皆伐后造落叶松林时，也应栽植保护带。营造针、阔叶树带状混交林能防止该病害及其他一些病虫害发生。
4.选育抗病树种。
5.药剂防治。苗木发病可喷75%百菌清500~1000倍液，或喷浓度为3×10-6放线菌酮，或再加上浓度为150×10-6有机锡（TPTA）混合液（每10ml药剂加6ml展着剂），1平方米喷150~200ml。出圃苗木未发现病害要烧毁，也可以在放叶前，将苗木地上部分浸泡在有机汞EMP浓度为10×10-6药液中10分钟，取出后用塑料薄膜覆盖3小时，可杀死苗木内隐藏的病菌。幼林发病时，可施用克菌丹、五氯酚钠、百菌清等烟剂，也可喷福美砷、代森锌、百菌清、甲基托布津等液剂防治。或者用放线菌酮（浓度5×10-6），或加上TPTA（浓度200×10-6）混合液，每10L药液加6ml展着剂，每公顷约需300L，3~4次即可。
author: 张希玲

potential_eco_desc: 落叶松枯梢病于1970年代初期在中国开始发生以来，十几年间即已遍布东北三省的广大林区，是危害严重、蔓延迅速地危险性病害。病轻时造成枯梢，影响高生长；病重时树冠呈扫帚状丛枝，不能成材，甚至死亡。这种毁灭性病害已成为我国北方地区落叶松人工林的一种主要病害。已列为国家检疫病害之一。
description: 该病菌1938年发现于日本北海道，1950年泽田兼吉作为新种发表：Botryosphaeria laricina Sawada。后因病害发展迅速，仅北海道即达7.5万公顷，对其进行了全面研究，山本和伊藤于1961年将其重组为Guignardia laricina (Sawada) Yamamoto et K. Ito。1970年代开始，我国东北林学院等单位对其进行了研究，内蒙古林学院尚衍重先生将其组合为现在名称。  孢子借风雨传播
author: 张希玲

host_range: The main natural host is Larix kaempferi. Other Asian species (L. gmelinii and L. olgensis var. koreana) are reported to be resistant. The European L. decidua, and the North American L. laricina and L. occidentalis, are reported in Japan to be very suscep
potential_eco_desc: B. laricina causes the most serious disease of Larix forests and nurseries in Japan. It had long been known locally, but started to cause large-scale damage in Larix plantations after 1959; at which time Larix areas were increasing rapidly. In 1963, more than 80,000 ha of plantations were diseased, with 100% of the trees affected. Although young diseased trees do not usually die, their subsequent growth is retarded or stopped.^p^pNotwithstanding the above, little has apparently been published on this pathogen since the 1970s. The serious problems of the 1960s may have been associated with a rather specific situation.
author: CPC2006

remark: B. laricina is regulated by the European Union (EU, 2000), and by some EPPO countries (Turkey, but not Russia where it has a limited distribution in the Far East). Because Larix decidua has been found to be susceptible in Japan, B. laricina presents a serious risk to this species in its native Europe. A similar situation applies for the North American L. laricina and L. occidentalis.^p^pEPPO recommends (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) prohibition of the import of plants for planting and cut branches of Larix from countries where B. laricina occurs.
author: CPC2006

management_info: In Japan, two antibiotic fungicides (cycloheximide and polyoxin) have been used against this disease in nurseries. A solution of cycloheximide or polyoxin is applied during July-September. Dipping of Larix seedlings into polyoxin solution in spring is also used in highly infested nurseries. Removal and burning of the infected trees, and reforestation by other species, is also carried out in heavily diseased stands. Selection of resistant clones is in progress (Kobayashi, 1980).
author: CPC2006

potential_eco_desc: 落叶松枯梢病是我国北方新发现的一种危险性林木病害。虽然1970年以前就已发生，但到1973年才普遍流行。现在已知黑龙江、吉林、辽宁的中东部林区，以及山东烟台地区落叶松（Larix）人工林，都有不同程度的发生。据1973年不完全统计，全国发病面积已达19.8万公顷。吉林省的发病面积占全省落叶松人工林总面积的20％，因该病所造成的损失严重。

host_range: 小麦属Triticum、雀麦属Bromus、鸭茅属Dactylis和早熟禾属Poa。
potential_eco_desc: 在美国的内布拉斯加州发病率高达100%，引起小麦损失50～70%。

management_info: 以玉米、豆类、苜蓿、燕麦和中耕作物等轮作3年以上，避免过早种植，销毁病残体，去除杂草，选育抗病品种。

potential_eco_desc: A. pinicola is important on Pinus contorta on which it can cause extensive branch and stem cankers leading to malformation and consequent lowering of wood quality. It is seldom important on other pines, and generally never sufficiently severe to cause tree death. For additional information see also Baranyay et al. (1973).
author: CPC2006

description: Under natural conditions, Atropellis spp. spread by ascospore dispersal within pine stands. In international trade, logs of Pinus with bark attached may carry cankers on wood of appropriate age. Even after debarking, cankered tissue may remain in the wood. Plants for planting of Pinus may also carry cankers.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.^p - Wood: borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. Pods)^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx^p - Leaves^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants^p - Roots^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain).
author: CPC2006

remark: Atropellis spp. are regulated by the European Union (EU, 2000) and by various EPPO countries (Russia, Turkey) as A1 quarantine pests. They present a hazard to exotic Pinus spp. such as P. contorta and P. strobus, which are hosts in North America and have been planted in other continents. The European species P. nigra and P. sylvestris have been observed to be susceptible when planted in North America, and so are certainly at risk in their native range. ^p^pPhytosanitary measures: EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) recommends that importing countries should prohibit import of plants for planting, and isolated bark, of Pinus from North America. If isolated bark of Pinus is imported from North America, the consignment should have been heat-treated. If wood of Pinus is imported from North America, the consignment should have been debarked or kiln-dried.^p^pThere is no evidence that Atropellis spp. have ever been carried by wood packing. However, wood is liable to carry these pests in international trade.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural methods such as thinning of overcrowded stands may help to prevent infection, but no chemical control methods have been worked out.
author: CPC2006

potential_eco_desc: 受侵染的最初几年，果树失去活力。黑节绕茎可引起个别枝叉死亡，但最严重的还是果树的矮化，次生菌可通过节侵染。在未进行防治的果园损失通常是毁灭性的。

host_range: Black knot is a serious threat to the economic production of certain stone fruit crops, mostly in northeastern North America. The crops affected include varieties of European plums (Prunus domestica), Japanese plum (P. salicina) and tart or sour cherries
potential_eco_desc: A low incidence of knots that may have been overlooked during the winter pruning could induce as many as 400 knots/tree within one season (Koch, 1933; Rosenberger and Gerling, 1984; Northover, 2000). When the extent of the infection becomes apparent one year later, there may be no alternative to orchard removal. The cost of extensive pruning is prohibitive, and major limb surgery and removal would result in badly misshaped trees of greatly reduced productivity. The experiment described by Rosenberger and Gerling (1984) involved 1416 knots on unsprayed inoculated trees in their fifth year. The initial crop loss and crop reduction over the following two years equalled $US 8533/ha in 1984. The economic benefit of a zineb-captan protection program was clearly demonstrated. The usual maintenance programme in orchards at risk to black knot involves increased inspection and winter pruning of trees, and the use of extra fungicide sprays primarily for the control of black knot. These measures increase the cost of production by approximately 10% per year. Crop losses from black knot on plums and cherries were estimated by the USDA as being 10% and 1%, respectively (Cramer, 1967).
author: CPC2006

description: A. morbosa moves within parts of orchards as ascospores and conidia, which are released primarily by rain and dispersed by wind (Koch, 1933; McFadden-Smith et al., 2000). Ascospores were trapped 9 m from knot-infected trees by Koch (1933) and Smith et al. (1970), using a Hirst trap, trapped ascospores 3-4 m from a large supply of knots. Over longer distances and particularly between regions or countries, the greatest risk of spread is through the trade of nursery stock carrying either small knots or latent infections. Lodeman (1894) reported that in 1850 a grower in western New York state, USA, attributed the appearance of black knot in his Buffalo area orchard for the first time in thirty years, to his importation of infected plum trees from Massachusetts, 600 km away.
author: CPC2006

remark: Phytosanitary Risk^p^pA. morbosa is listed as an A1 quarantine pest by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1979) and is also of quarantine concern for IAPSC. In the EPPO region, it is potentially dangerous to plums (and probably other Prunus species), wherever grown. ^p^p^Phytosanitary MeasuresOEPP/EPPO (1990) recommends that plants for planting of Prunus from Canada and the USA should come from a place of production intensively treated (by chemical treatments and pruning) against A. morbosa, and found free from A. morbosa during the last two growing seasons.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Sanitation is the principal means of disease prevention. New knots that develop in the spring and produce conidia during the summer, are generally removed in late winter before the start of the next growing season. Pruning cuts are made at least 10 cm below the base of the knot. Infections that have spread into major limbs or tree trunks are removed surgically, by cutting into healthy tissues at least 1.5 cm from the knot margin. All infected wood is removed immediately from the orchard and burned.^p^pA high degree of biological control occurs from the very conspicuous cream-coloured overgrowths of Trichothecium roseum (Cephalothecium roseum), and less obviously from Coniothyrium sp. (Koch, 1934a). These hyperparasites may reduce ascospore production by as much as 80%, judging from the surface areas of knots that are colonized and the extent of sterile perithecia. The degree of hyperparasitism is not sufficient to provide a commercially acceptable level of disease control, and hyperparasitized knots must be removed.^p^pChemical control is used to complement sanitation practices. Bordeaux mixture and lime sulfur were the first fungicides used for protection against black knot (Lodeman, 1894; Koch, 1933). Zineb, dichlone, sulfur, chlorothalonil and the early formulations of captan have been very effective for controlling black knot (Rosenberger and Gerling, 1984; Northover and McFadden-Smith, 1995). Iprodione was ineffective (Northover and McFadden-Smith, 1995) and the benzimidazoles were of variable efficacy (Ritchie et al., 1975; Rosenberger and Gerling, 1984). Among the DMI group, triforine and myclobutanil were ineffective but fenbuconazole, flusilazole and propiconazole were of intermediate and variable performance, possibly related to marginal use rates (Northover and McFadden-Smith, 1995). The period of protection coincides with those of several other diseases of stone fruits including blossom blight/brown rot (Monilinia fructicola, M. laxa), powdery mildew (Podosphaera clandestina) and cherry leaf spot (Blumeriella jaapii). It would be most economical if materials could be used to simultaneously protect against several diseases in an integrated, resistance management programme.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Eradication was attempted but was not feasible as wild or volunteer Corylus plants in adjacent woodland provided an unmanageable reservoir of inoculum. Sanitation measures include destruction of infested wood, but are of little value because of the length of the latent period in the life cycle of the fungus. Chemical control has been applied, but was not very successful as the biology of the fungus was not well known (Pinkerton et al., 1992). Experiments have only recently been carried out to determine efficient chemical treatments. Johnson et al. (1993) found that chlorothalonil, flusilazole and fenarimol are potentially valuable components of a programme for control of A. anomala. Four or five applications during the period of potential infection can completely control the disease. However, such a programme may not be economically feasible for all growers. Genetic resistance is the only viable disease control strategy. Cultivars range in susceptibility from highly susceptible to immune. Corylus cornuta var. cornuta, C. cornuta var. california, C. heterophylla and C. sieboldiana were highly resistant, as were most C. americana genotypes and one C. colurna clone (Coyne et al., 1998). Breeding programmes are being conducted. Some European cultivars showed high susceptibility to the disease (Pinkerton et al., 1993).^p^pPhytosanitary measures^p^pA. anomala can be introduced with planting material of hazel. In the USA, spread of the disease to the West is thought to have been due to the importation of infected C. avellana nursery stock or of wild C. americana seedlings from the Eastern regions. Corylus planting material should be imported only from areas free from A. anomala.

host_range: The main hosts of A. triticina are bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) and durum wheat (Triticum durum). Durum wheat is more severely attacked by the pathogen compared with bread wheat (Prasada and Prabhu 1962; Prabhu and Prasada, 1966; Singh et al., 1990). I
potential_eco_desc: Leaf blight has caused serious damage on wheat crops, particularly in eastern and central parts of India. It is now considered as one of the most important foliar diseases of wheat grown in the major states of India (Nema, 1986). Mexican cultivars and their derivatives are relatively more susceptible. Disease incidence is higher in durum wheat compared with bread wheat (Prabhu and Prasada, 1966; Nema, 1986). The disease was first reported by Kulkarni (1924) from Maharashtra and later from other states of India. It caused heavy yield losses in the early 1960s in Kenphads cultivars that were developed in the Maharashtra state for resistance to rust. This resulted in the withdrawal of these cultivars from cultivation. During the 1963-64 wheat season the outbreak of the disease was so severe at the Botanical Sub Station, Pusa, Bihar that not a single genetic stock under cultivation escaped the disease (Prasada and Prabhu, 1964). ^p^pIn severe epidemics the yield losses may exceed 60% (Prabhu and Singh, 1974; Sokhi, 1974). A severe epidemic in a wheat crop grown on 300 ha in the Vidarbha region of India caused a 75% reduction in grain weight (Raut et al., 1983). The extent of damage depends upon the cultivar and the stage at which infection occurs. The disease can appear in severe forms in experimental plots under artificial epiphytotic conditions causing severe losses. Estimated losses revealed that there can be almost total loss of yield in a highly susceptible cultivar such as NP 830 when plants are infected at booting stage (Chenulu et al., 1970). According to Sokhi and Joshi (1974), the extent of damage may reach 33% if the top second and third leaves are badly blighted at heading stage. Ram and Joshi (1979), under artificial conditions of infection, observed that when the disease appears at the flag leaf stage the loss in number of grains was up to 26.4%. The ear-head length is considerably reduced which in turn affects the number of grains. Infection causes a significant decrease in growth parameters, especially in susceptible cultivars (Beshir, 1994). It decreases the number of grains per ear, 1000-grain weight and yield (Ram and Joshi, 1981). A culture filtrate of A. triticina inhibited seed germination, root elongation and induced symptoms on the leaves of wheat plants similar to those induced by the fungus (Kumar and Rao, 1979b). A. triticina has also been shown to produce alternariol, tenuazonic acid and altenuene mycotoxin (Logrieco et al., 1990; Bilgrami et al., 1995).

description: Incidence^p^pA. triticina has been shown to be seed transmitted in wheat Prabhu and Prasada, 1966, 1967; Kumar and Arya 1973a, 1973b; Dash and Narain, 1989). The pathogen can survive as conidia on the seed surface or as deep seated mycelium inside the seed coat, pericarp and embryo (Kumar and Arya, 1973a). Infection of plants at the dough stage results in glume infection, awn infection and infection of the seed (Prabhu and Prasada, 1966). A correlation between adult plant susceptibility and seed infection has been observed by Sharma et al. (1983). The extent of infection in seed varies from cultivar to cultivar and on average as high as 12.2% seed infection has been reported (Kumar and Arya, 1973a). It has been suggested that the pathogen may have been transmitted through infected seed in the Kalimpong hills of West Bengal, India (Kasier and Aslam, 1994). In addition to detection of the pathogen in wheat seeds in India it has also been isolated from wheat seeds in Bangladesh (Ahmed et al., 1994), France, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Turkey and Macedonia (Logrieco et al., 1990). It has also been isolated from seeds of barley in Greece, Lebanon, Macedonia and Turkey (Logrieco et al., 1990), and oat and rye in Greece (Logrieco et al., 1990).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pSeeds infected with A. triticina are shrivelled, with a brown discoloration spreading over the seed surface (Prabhu and Prasada, 1967). Infected seeds are small with a 46-75% reduction in weight (Raut et al., 1983). Seeds that appear normal in colour have also been shown to harbour the pathogen (Agarwal et al., 1972). Germination rate and seedling height are reduced due to seedborne inoculum (Dash and Narain, 1989).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pA. triticina has been shown to be both soil and seedborne in nature. However, the soilborne inoculum may not play a role in the perpetuation of the inoculum under hot conditions until the next planting. Thus, infection is initially perpetuated by conidia on the seed surface and as mycelium inside the seed (Kumar and Arya, 1976). Seedborne inoculum, therefore, plays a major role in the perpetuation of the disease (Kumar and Arya, 1973a). The initial inoculum carried with the seed may build up in the soil with the passage of time to such an extent that the soil itself can become infested (Prabhu and Prasada, 1966). The pathogen has been shown to survive in seed for 10 months (Kumar and Rao, 1979c).^p^p^Seed Treatments^p^pFungicidal seed and hot water treatments have been used to control seedborne inoculum. Seed treatment with iprodione (Raut et al., 1983), thiram (Raut et al., 1983), 2-methoxyethylmercury chloride (Raut et al., 1983) and phenylmercury acetate (Ahmad and Ahmad, 1985) have been shown to effectively control the seedborne inoculum. Seed treatments have also been shown to improve seed germination (Raut et al., 1983). Pre-soaking of seed in water for 4 h. followed by hot water treatment at 52-54°C for 10 min is also effective in the control of seedborne inoculum without adversely affecting seed viability (Prabhu and Prasada, 1970).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pAn agar plate method has been suggested for the detection of A. triticina from wheat seeds. A number of media have been used for detection. Seedborne infection can be determined on standard nutrient agar (SNA). Seeds are first surface sterilized for 5 min in a mild disinfectant followed by three washings with sterilized water. Five seeds are plated on SNA in a Petri dish and incubated for 8 days at 25°C in darkness. The colonies of the fungus appear olive-buff with a velvety surface covered with conidia. SNA medium is effective for sporulation because the formation of aerial mycelium is greatly reduced and sporulation is abundant only in darkness. Sporulation does not occur in continuous light. Partial sporulation also occurs when colonies are exposed to diurnal light and darkness (Prabhu and Prasada, 1965; 1967; Agarwal 1970; Agarwal et al., 1993). ^p^pPotato su

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe control of leaf blight has been attempted through seed treatment, fungicidal sprays and use of resistant cultivars. For details on Seed Treatments, see the section on Seedborne Aspects of Disease.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pWheat genotypes differ in their degree of resistance or susceptibility to leaf blight infection (Prasada and Prabhu, 1964; Prabhu and Prasada, 1966: Sokhi et al., 1973; Kulshrestha and Rao, 1976; Singh et al., 1977; Singh and Tyagi, 1979; Ahmad and Singh 1983; Serrone and Porta Puolia, 1985; Das et al., 1989; Singh 1990; Singh et al., 1992; Borkar and Patil, 1995; Chowdhury and Roy, 1995; Singh, 1995; Singh et al., 1995). Durum wheat and cultivars having durum derivatives are more susceptible than bread wheat cultivars (Prasada and Prabhu, 1962; Prabhu and Prasada, 1966; Serrone and Porta Puolia, 1985). Resistance has been identified in some cultivars of wheat but many cultivars and genotypes including the dwarfs are susceptible. There is abundant material available for the development of wheat cultivars resistant to A. triticina. Some of the highly resistant strains are Hope (E 41), H-44 (E48), Ceres (E50), Thatcher (E 124), Gobo (E 569), Cometa Klein (E 671), Frondoso (E 771) and La Prevision (E 928) (Prabhu and Prasada, 1966). Of 70 cultivars tested against A. triticina none was immune but three cultivars, HP 1163, HD 1941 and M-134, were resistant (Ahmad and Singh, 1983). The old Indian wheat cultivars namely NP 4, 52, 200, 809 and 824 were resistant to the disease whereas cultivars NP 710, 761, 988 and 790 were tolerant (Singh, 1990). Singh et al. (1977) reported that lines/cultivars Arnautka, E 6160 and K 7340 were immune whereas resistance was shown by E 8682, HB 384, HD2157, HS 74, HW 2449, K 401, K 899, K 7333 and VL 417. Cultivar HP 1209 has been shown to be resistant to A. triticina (Das et al., 1989).^p^pThe physiology of infected leaves of resistant and susceptible cultivars has been studied. Following inoculation with A. triticina the amount of sugar and starch decreases in both resistant and susceptible cultivars. Phenol content increases in resistant leaves and decreases in susceptible ones. Free amino acids, especially those involved in aromatic metabolism, increase markedly in resistant cultivars. The chlorophyll content decreases with infection. In resistant cultivars disease progress ceases after 5 days and changes in phenol and nitrogen content continue for up to 10 days (Kumar and Rao, 1980). ^p^pSusceptible cultivars contain larger amounts of sugars than resistant cultivars (Kumar et al., 1974a; Kulshrestha and Rao, 1977). There are also more phenolic compounds in resistant cultivars. Phenolic compounds accumulate more rapidly in resistant cultivars than susceptible cultivars as a result of infection (Beshir, 1994). The physiochemical properties of the leaf surface are partly governed by the presence of wax. Kumar (1974) reported quantitative variations in wax content of wheat leaf surfaces which was high in NP 4, a cultivar resistant to A. triticina, and low in the susceptible cultivar NP 83. Of the constituents, an acetate of n-w hydroxy acid was only found in the wax of resistant cultivars. The susceptible cultivar was characterized by the absence of n-w hydroxy acid, n-secondary alcohol and an unidentified lipid. ^p^pOn highly resistant T. sphaerococcum, A. triticina failed to penetrate the leaves; on moderately resistant cultivars although penetration did not occur spore-germ tube growth and branching occurred. In susceptible cultivars, penetration and appressorial formation occurred. In the highly susceptible cultivar almost all conidia in contact with the callus germinated and germ tubes directly penetrated the cells. Mycelial growth was intercellular and intracellular (Kumar et al., 1974b). host_range: 小麦Triticum aestivumb（麦穗） Fusarium sacchari is the cause of an important disease of sugar cane, pokkah boeng, and has been reported to produce the mycotoxin beauvericin, which causes toxicosis in human and other animals. To our knowledge, this is the first report of F. sacchari causing wheat head blight.
description: Fusarium head blight（FHB）epidemics in wheat occur frequently in China, especially along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, including Jiangsu and Shanghai. In 2013, wheat spikes showing clear FHB symptoms were collected from fields in Jiangsu and Shanghai. Based on morphological identification, molecular detection and the pathogenicity test showed that the causal agent was Fusarium sacchari. This pathogen is the cause of an important disease of sugar cane, pokkah boeng, and has been reported to produce the mycotoxin beauvericin, which causes toxicosis in human and other animals. To our knowledge, this is the first report of F. sacchari causing wheat head blight in China. The report contributes to an improved understanding of the composition of Fusarium species on wheat in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River in China, which will be useful for exploring appropriate disease management strategies in this region.
reference_name: First Report of Fusarium Head Blight of Wheat Caused by Fusarium sacchari in China

description: In 2013, while surveying for five-needle white pine cone crops in northeastern Nevada, we observed white pine blister rust, caused by the rust pathogen Cronartium ribicola Fisch., infecting branches and stems of limber pines (Pinus flexilis James) on Pine Mountain (41.76975°N, 115.61622°W), Humboldt National Forest, Elko County, Nevada. Nearby whitebark pines (P. albicaulis Engelm.) were also infected. In mid-June 2015, we returned to Pine Mountain and collected several vials of rust aeciospores from sporulating single-branch infections on three limber and two whitebark pines. We also noted active urediniospore production on infected leaves of nearby alternate host Ribes cereum Dougl. Based on tracking survey and molecular diagnostics confirming that the fungus collected at Pine Mountain is C. ribicola.
reference_name: First Report of the White Pine Blister Rust Fungus, Cronartium ribicola, Infecting Pinus flexilis on Pine Mountain, Humboldt National Forest, Elko County, Northeastern Nevada

potential_eco_desc: Cronartium ribicola J. C. Fisch., causal agent of white pine blister rust (WPBR), is one of the most damaging pathogens of five-needle pines, forming aecial states on the trunk and branches and causing cankering, topkill, and branch dieback.
description: Since 2010, a Cronartium sp. has been observed producing uredinia and telia on R. odoratum ‘Crandall’ H.L. Wendl. leaves in an urban environment in West Lafayette, Indiana. Both morphological and molecular methods indicate this species to be C. ribicola, making this a first report of white pine blister rust on R. odoratum in Indiana. This fungus has been observed previously on R. odoratum in the northeastern United States (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont, and New Hampshire), the Rockies (Colorado), northwestern United States (Washington), and Canada. In Indiana, C. ribicola has also been reported on R. cysnobati. There are no other reports of this fungus on any other host within the state. However, the aecial host, Pinus strobus, does grow within the state, and within West Lafayette. To our knowledge, WPBR has only been observed (not reported) once in Indiana in the past 30 years (Paul Pecknold, personal communication).
reference_name: First Report of the White Pine Blister Rust Fungus, Cronartium ribicola, on Ribes odoratum in Indiana

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe identification of C. ribicola as the same rust as that infecting cultivated Ribes virtually eliminated cultivation of Pinus strobus in Europe after 150 years (Laundon and Rainbow, 1971). In North America, its impact on all susceptible pine species has been severe The identification of C. ribicola as the same rust as that infecting cultivated Ribes virtually eliminated cultivation of Pinus strobus in Europe after 150 years (Laundon and Rainbow, 1971). In North America, its impact on all susceptible pine species has been severe (Boyce, 1961; Kliejunas, 1985; Hummer, 2000; Smith and Hoffman, 2000). Bega and Scharpf (1993) declared that white pine blister rust caused more damage and cost more to control than any other conifer disease in North America. The epidemic on Pinus monticola (Neuenschwander et al., 1999) was described as 'the world's most spectacular epiphytotic' (Bingham, 1983), causing a reduction of the gene pool of P. monticola (Hunt et al., 1985) and decimating regeneration of the threatened P. albicaulis (Tomback et al., 1995). However, Harvey (1967) found that branch cankers on P. lambertiana grew slower and died earlier, creating a lesser threat to survival, than similar cankers on P. monticola. Its impact on P. albicaulis and P. strobiformis is under recent study (Brown, 1978; Keane and Arno, 1993; Smith and Hoffman, 1998; Campbell and Antos, 2000; Zeglen, 2000). However, in mid-1980s C. ribicola caused trunk cankers in a sugar pine (P. lambertiana) plantation in the mid-Sierra Nevada mountains, killing 95% of the total number of trees (Chen, 2004). Susceptible Ribes species, especially R. nigrum, suffer reduced vigour and fruit yields.^p^p^Environmental impact^pAs the white pines of the western USA are killed, the associated ecosystems also decline, altering the forest landscapes. In addition, these white pines are all moderately to greatly fire dependent, and have declined from past fire exclusion policies and the resulting successional replacement (Sniezko et al., 2004).^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pEast Asia and North America were seriously attacked by C. ribicola during the 20th century, especially the western USA. There are nine white pine species native to the USA that are at risk and these include some of the oldest, and ecologically or culturally significant pine species in the USA. C. ribicola threatens the stability and survival of white pine ecosystems in 40 states of the USA. Without white pines, these forest communities would be altered dramatically (USDA-FS, 2004).
description: Accidentally introduced to North America in 1910, white pine blister rust has spread across the range of the five-needled white pines. All eight of the western North American species of white pines are susceptible to this pathogen. These pines occur in ecosystems from near sea level to the tree-line. Six of these eight species have already been affected, several severely. Prior to 2003 there were no known cases of bristlecone (Pinus aristata, P. longaeva) with blister rust infection in natural stands, but blister rust was known to occur dangerously close to both the ancient Great Basin bristlecone pines (P. longaeva) in California, USA, and the Rocky Mountain bristlecones (P. aristata) in Colorado, USA. In 2003, a Rocky Mountain bristlecone with infection was discovered (J Blodgett, USDA Forest Service, USA, personal communication, 2004).^p^pNon-native invasive pathogens such as white pine blister rust (C. ribicola) are killing trees and disrupting forest ecosystems in western North America. Populations of western white pine (P. monticola), sugar pine (P. lambertiana), whitebark pine (P. albicaulis), and limber pine (P. flexilis) are declining precipitously from damage by blister rust (Sniezko et al., 2004).

remark: Ribes cultivation is banned in some states of the USA (McKay, 2000). Importation of Ribes plants to North America is banned (Dale, 2000). Phytosanitary certification is required for shipments between Canada and the USA of Ribes plants and foliage or seedlings of susceptible pines. West Virginia, USA, prohibits cultivation of Ribes nigrum throughout the State, and of any Ribes species in 23 named counties (Gibson, 2000). Quarantine and Ribes eradication laws also exist in Pennsylvania (Hall, 2000); in New York State Ribes cultivation is regulated (Denham, 2000). Quarantines against importing the rust are established in Turkey, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and the USA (EPPO, 1999). Although not found in Macedonia, C. ribicola is listed as 'economically important' and a separation of 2 km is suggested for the planting of Ribes and susceptible pines (Pinus peuce and P. strobus) (Papazov et al., 2000).

management_info: Introduction^p^pWhere the alternate hosts exist, control is necessary. Control measures differ to protect the most-important hosts.^p^pGenetic resistance and species selection can be used as a means to control some rusts, and infected branches can be eliminated by pruning. Site hazard ratings based on habitat type and elevation are available. Ongoing research is evaluating ways to manage rust diseases in ways that maximize their benefit to forest ecosystems while limiting their detrimental effects on forest resources (Parks and Flanagan, 2001).^p^pBecause resistant individuals in all these species are rare, genetic variation may be reduced to the point where future populations may not be viable without active management (Sniezko, 2004).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pUnderstanding host-pathogen interactions is important in managing yield loss and can aid in the identification of disease-resistant trees. Several resistance mechanisms to C. ribicola have been identified in pine. At the molecular level, several defence responsive proteins and their genes have been characterized. Some of these are identified to be potential candidates for markers associated with resistance or susceptibility (Ekramoddoullah and Hunt, 2002).^p^pProgrammes of screening and genetic improvement of pines are active in Canada (Corriveau and Lamontagne, 1977; Meagher and Hunt, 1985; Zsuffa, 1985; Hunt, 1999), the USA (Miller,1973; Hoff and McDonald, 1980; Murphy, 1982; Samman, 1982; Franc, 1988; Eramian, 1999; Kitzmiller and Samman, 1999; Sniezko, 1999; Meier, 2000), Romania (Blada, 1994) and Korea (Hyun and Koo, 1981). Field testing of second-generation Pinus monticola seedlings has begun (McDonald et al., 1994). North American trials of species from Asia and Europe indicated potential gain in rust resistance (Heimburger, 1972), but eventual problems with adaptation to climatic differences. Rust resistance generally was higher in species closer to the Asian centre of the rust and least in North American species (Bingham, 1972), whether conducted in Europe (Soegaard, 1972) or North America (Bingham, 1972). Most activity now is in North America, mainly in P. strobus, P. monticola and P. lambertiana. ^p^pHeritability and gain estimates have been developed: for example, "spots only" (McDonald and Hoff, 1971), reduced needle-lesion frequency (Meagher and Hunt, 1996), leaf shed (of infected leaves) (Hoff and McDonald, 1971), bark reaction (Hoff, 1986b), and tolerance (Hoff, 1986a; Hunt, 1997) in Pinus monticola. Rust-resistance heritability estimates have been determined for Pinus wallichiana in Romania (Blada, 1994). Dominant genes stopping rust in pine foliage are identified (Kinloch et al., 1999; Kinloch, 2000) and a linkage map is constructed to facilitate cloning (Harkins et al., 1998). Laboratory techniques have identified a protein associated with defence in pines (Ekramoddoullah et al., 1998), and cloned a resistance gene analogue (Kim and Brunsfeld, 2000). Peptides with a potential for use in genetic engineering have affected spore germination and morphology (Jacobi et al., 2000; Rioux et al., 2000).^p^pThe aim of the pine genetic improvement programmes is generally to reduce the impact of the disease so that commercially-useful wood can be obtained without exerting such selective pressure on the rust's gene pool that would increase the frequency of rare alleles (Samman, 1982; Meagher and Hunt, 1985).^p^pRibes hybrids and cultivars are being screened in Russia (Ravkin and Litvinova, 1976), Siberia (Kuminova, 1980), Ukraine (Sherengovyi, 1979), Slovakia (Kozmenko and Invanicka, 1994), Poland (Tylus et al., 1981; Zurawicz et al., 1996; Pluta and Broniarek-Niemiec, 2000), Denmark (Pedersen, 1998) and the USA (Keep et al., 1975; Hummer, 1997; Dorrance and Bergdahl, 1990). host_range: The aecial hosts of C. comandrae in North America are two- and three-needled Pinus spp. (hard pines), of which the most important in practice are jack pine (P. banksiana) across Canada and lodgepole pine (P. contorta) and western yellow pine (ponderosa pi
potential_eco_desc: The Cronartium rusts cause very important diseases in North America, resulting in malformation, reduced vigour and death of trees and seedlings. However, their abundance does depend primarily on the abundance and localization of the alternate host (Gross et al., 1983).^p^pC. comandrae became epidemic from 1910 to 1945, then subsided for 10 years, but is now increasing in importance again, particularly on Pinus taeda in southeastern USA; seedlings may be killed within a few years after infection. Serious injury, in the form of basal infections on young P. contorta, has caused considerable reduced growth and mortality in Canada (Alberta, northern British Columbia and Yukon Territory) where Geocaulon lividum, the alternate host, is locally abundant. Hiratsuka et al. (1988) found that in northern Canada C. comandrae lesions spread more aggressively to girdle young trees than those of the other 'blister rusts'. Geils and Jacobi (1993) made a quantitative evaluation of losses of P. contorta var. latifolia due to C. comandrae in Montana and Wyoming, USA. Mean annual increments of total cubic bolewood volume after canker establishment were reduced 32% for trees with crown tops killed by C. comandrae and 9% for trees not yet girdled.^p^pThere is a suggestion that C. comandrae infection may predispose P. contorta to attack by the bark beetle Dendroctonus ponderosae in Utah, USA (Nebeker et al., 1995). For more information on the pest significance of C. comandrae, see Boyce (1961), Peterson and Jewell (1968), Ziller (1974), and Sinclair et al. (1987).

description: Cronartium spp. can be carried considerable distances as wind-borne aeciospores and can survive considerable periods in the airborne state (Chang and Blenis, 1989). More importantly, these rusts can also be carried into new areas on plants for planting of the coniferous aecial hosts, as has occurred in parts of the USA (C. comandrae was introduced into Tennessee on nursery trees of Pinus ponderosa). The long incubation periods of Cronartium spp. mean that latent infections easily go undetected unless post-entry quarantine is applied. remark: C. comandrae is one of the non-European Cronartium spp. of the EPPO A1 list (OEPP/EPPO, 1979). The danger presented by these fungi to the EPPO region is classically exemplified by reference to the quarantine pest C. ribicola (Phillips, 1988), which has made it almost impossible to grow Pinus strobus commercially in most areas in Europe and North America where the fungus was introduced from Asia. However, it should be stressed that the potential risk from introduced Cronartium spp. is much affected by the status of the alternate hosts concerned. While the Ribes hosts of C. ribicola are widespread cultivated plants, the telial hosts of C. comandrae are wild plants that do not occur in Europe. There is only a single related European wild plant (Comandra elegans), uncommon and occurring only in the Balkans, and this species may not be infected by the rust. On this basis, the risk of establishment of C. comandrae in the EPPO region is practically nil.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Removing infected material and eradicating the alternate host can effect control, although this is rarely economically viable. Geils and Jacobi (1990) found that C. comandrae cankers develop slowly and predictably, so that removal of infected plants is a workable strategy. Nurseries should be located away from possible infection sources. The use of certified fungicides is feasible in nurseries. Research into resistant cultivars has led to successful control of some Cronartium spp., including Cronartium ribicola and Endocronartium harknessii.^p^pC. comandrae can be carried alive only in live Pinus stem tissue. As a phytosanitary measure the entry of live planting stocks of Pinus hosts (see List of Hosts) should be prohibited from countries where C. comandrae is present.

management_info: Chemical ControlKavanagh et al. (1986) reported that of six fungicidal treatments tested on strawberries (chlorothalonil, dichlofluanid, iprodione flowable, vinclozolin and vinclozolin + maneb or + metalaxyl) all gave very large increases in yield of healthy fruit, averaging 65% more, but did not differ from one another in yield. Increases in yield worth >4000/ha were obtained for an expenditure on fungicides of approximately 200/ha. In the first season of a new experiment on the control of P. fragariae fosetyl-al improved growth of Cambridge Favourite when used as a root soak. Other treatments had no visible effect.^p^pO' Neill and Griffin (1987) reported that fosetyl-Al applied once, as a spray in the autumn after fruit picking, gave very good control of P. fragariae and significantly increased the number of healthy roots and marketable fruit yield in 2-year-old Redgauntlet strawberry plants. Fosetyl-Al applied twice, after fruit picking and in spring, further increased the number of healthy roots, but yields were not significantly better than the single treatment. A spray of fosetyl-A1 plus a drench of captafol applied after picking and in spring gave good disease control and a yield significantly better than all other treatments. In the same crop the following year, both of the twice-yearly treatments gave a significant reduction in red core recorded in September and the two fungicides together gave a significant increase in fruit yield. In a second trial, fosetyl-A1 plus a drench of captafol applied after picking and in spring again gave good disease control and significantly increased fruit yield. Timing fungicide application, both after fruit picking and in spring according to root development (5 mm or 15-20 mm), had no effect on the level of red core control and little effect on fruit yield. The fosetyl-A1 plus captafol treatment was significantly less effective when captafol was applied as a spray rather than as a drench. Seemuller and Sun (1989) discovered the occurrence of metalaxyl tolerance in P. fragariae. Severe symptoms of red core disease were observed in two fields that had regularly been treated with a fungicide containing metalaxyl. Several isolates of P. fragariae were obtained from diseased plants in these fields that exhibited a strongly reduced sensitivity to metalaxyl both in vitro and in inoculation experiments. Nickerson et al. (1991) concluded that the problem of metalaxyl tolerance and the lack of alternative fungicides is likely to result in increased emphasis being placed on the development of resistant cultivars.^p^pAnon. (1990) provides guideline for the efficacy evaluation of fungicides to control P. fragariae. Guidelines on experimental conditions, application of treatments, mode of assessment, recording and measurements and presentation of results for trials on the control of P. fragariae on strawberry are given. Harris (1990) found that red core (P. fragariae) and crown rot (P. cactorum), which occurred unexpectedly in the trial on Verticillium wilt and other soilborne diseases, were reduced significantly by dazomet treatment. There was no significant effect of treatment on crown number, but yield was significantly improved by two rates of dazomet and by chloropicrin. Yields from the metham-sodium and 1,3-dichloropropene treated beds were 92 and 68% of those from untreated beds. Yields in the second season were most closely correlated with red core severity. Harris (1991) provides a comparison of dazomet, chloropicrin and methyl bromide as soil disinfestants for strawberries. Results of broadacre treatment determined from samples were superior to those from bed-only application of methyl bromide for all criteria, while results determined from whole-plot data were inferior to those from bed-only application, reflecting the effects of soil movement between adjacent plots during bed construction. management_info: Cultural control methods that can reduce the severity of disease caused by P. erythroseptica var. erythroseptica include the use of healthy potato seed tubers; incorporation of organic matter to improve poor soil drainage; the use of greening potato seed tubers; the avoidance of excessive irrigation late in the growing season; crop rotation every 4 years, and avoiding planting in heavily infested soil.^p^pSome native potato clones are reported to be resistant to P. erythroseptica var. erythroseptica (Fernandez-Northcote et al., 1972), but resistance is conditioned by greening and the age of tubers (Chattopadhyay, 1955; Fernandez-Northcote et al., 1972). Some varieties of sugarcane are also resistant.^p^pThe application of fumigants such as methyl bromide and dazomet to heavily infested soils before planting, complemented with metalaxyl treatment at planting time, controls pink rot of potatoes (Torres et al., 1986), but some insensitivity to metalaxyl has been reported (Lambert and Salas, 1994; Goodwin and Mc Grath, 1995).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pIt is hard to assess the damage caused by P. cambivora because the host range varies between continents. In Australia, P. cambivora severely damages fruit trees such as apple, cherry and almond (Wicks et al., 1984; Wicks and Lee, 1985). Apple trees are affected in Japan and Korea (Nakazawa et al., 1981; Jee et al., 1997). In North America, P. cambivora infects orchards of apple and cherry (Bielenin and Jones, 1988; Browne and Mircetich, 1988) and Chastagner et al. (1995) reported that some plantations of Noble fir (Abies procera) Christmas trees were also susceptible to the fungus, with a net loss of production.^p^pP. cambivora has been detected on apple grafts and cherry together with other species of Phytophthora in Switzerland (Bolay, 1992) and causes severe damage to red raspberry in Scotland, UK, negatively influencing the economy of these crops (Duncan et a1., 1987). The production of nuts and timber was reduced on walnut plantations in Italy as a result of P. cambivora and other species of Phytophthora Belisario et al., 1997, 2001; Vettraino et al., 2003). Rhodendron and horse chestnut are damaged by the fungus, negatively influencing the economy of nursery growers. Beech stands are damaged in the UK and Germany (Day, 1938; Hartmann and Blank, 1998) and chestnut trees are damaged in Italy, France, Spain, Portugal and Greece. The economic repercussions on the timber and fruit trade are evident. Edible mushrooms are reported to decrease in number in stands severely infected with P. cambivora.^p^pP. cambivora and other species of Phytophthora particularly affect ornamental plants and the nursery industry. As the symptomatology of P. cambivora is similar to that of other species of Phytophthora, it is difficult to value losses attributable specifically to P. cambivora, particularly those from root and collar rot of apple, pear and other fruit trees.^p^p^Environmental impact^pP. cambivora, like other species of Phytophthora, can cause genetic erosion of different species and cultivars of fruit trees, but this risk can be overcome by using resistant rootstocks.^p^pThe decline of eucalyptus in Australia and oak forests in Europe due to P. cambivora is fortuitous, and its importance marginal. The impact of P. cambivora on beech and chestnut forests is significant because it puts the stability and evolution of these ecosystems at risk. Trees killed as a result of P. cambivora on mountain slopes or crests can compromise the stability of soils, leaving them exposed to erosion from runoff rainwater. In some stands in Italy, P. cambivora infection has led to the natural replacement of chestnut trees. Dead chestnut stands have gradually been invaded by more resistant oaks (Quercus pubescens), leading to the formation of new oak woods (Turchetti, 1986). Chestnut is also the main ectomycorrhizal host in most of these stands, and when it disappears the mushroom population suffers. P. cambivora, like other species of Phytophthora, colonizes anaerobic soils that are unfavourable to other fungi including Phytophthora antagonists, which suffer a great decrease in such soils.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; crop production; environment; forestry production; native fauna; tourism; animal / plant products; rare / protected species; trade / international relations
description: P. cambivora is widespread in all continents as a result of international trade. It was imported into Europe in the 18th century and was described for the first time by Puccinelli (1859), causing 'ink disease' on chestnut trees, where the disease was most prominent. In 1876 it was observed in France, in the Pyrenees and some parts of Cevennes (Allain, 1935).

management_info: Introduction^p^pControl of P. cambivora is difficult to achieve because the fungus can survive for several years as resting oospores in the soil or in infected host tissues (Biraghi, 1953; Turchetti, 1986, Vettraino et al. 2001). The aim of control strategies is to limit the damage caused and to prevent the natural spread of the fungus. These goals must be met in different ways:^p^p^Cultural ControlPetri (1918) suggested pruning infected chestnut trees to stimulate the root system to produce new lateral roots, a method that has proved suitable for other hosts, especially fruit trees. Felling severely infected trees at ground level is another possibility, as the tree stump will produce new shoots indicating that the root system has recovered. Other treatments specific to chestnut have been proposed, for example, Gandolfo, which consists of stripping the collar and roots of infected trees and leaving them exposed to low winter temperatures. This kills the mycelium of P. cambivora and enables the trees to recover. A similar method was proposed by Urquijo-Landaluze (1941) in Spain, consisting of exposing and cleaning the collar and roots and treating them with copper salts. However, these methods are difficult to employ in chestnut stands and orchards.^p^pDisease prevention is very important, especially in nurseries. Forest and fruit seedlings must be grown in pathogen-free soils and the residual roots of seedlings must be completely eliminated before they are grown. Soil must be well drained and water stagnation prevented, because excess soil moisture favours the fungus. Seedlings must not be watered with water originating from infected areas. It is advisable to use of pathogen-free planting material, potting mixes and containers.Jeffers and Aldwinckle (1988) found P. cambivora and P. cactorum in apple rootstock from nurseries in the USA and Europe. Both soil and seedlings should be sampled regularly for diagnosis using baits, isolation from host tissues and PCR-based technologies to improve detection. Infected seedlings must be eliminated at a primary stage and any remaining healthy seedlings treated with metalaxyl or fosetyl-Al.^p^pMulches have been tested against some species of Phytophthora including P. cambivora (Merwin et al., 1992; Fraser et al., 2001). In Australian forest sites dominated by Acacia pulchella, P. cinamomi was significantly reduced and mulching investigations carried out by D'Souza et al. (2001) are continuing. The use of chicken manure to control P. cinnamomi was tested in Australia by Aryantha et al. (2000). In Italy, control trials, in which mulching was combined with organic amendments to treat chestnut trees over 3 years, recovered most of the trees (Turchetti et al., 2000). Mixtures of amendments (cow manure, chicken manure and biological amendment) can provide effective biological control that will preserve the environment of chestnut stands (Turchetti et al., 2003).^p^pMychorrhizal fungi may prove effective in controlling P. cambivora and may help in soil sanitation and the production of healthy seedlings, especially chestnut seedlings (Branzanti et al., 1999).^p^p^Physical Methods^p^pSoil solarization, in which the soil is heated to 8-10°C above ambient temperature by covering with transparent plastic sheeting, was studied as a means of controlling P. cambivora in naturally infected almond and cherry orchards. In field experiments, soil temperatures above 40°C were rarely reached at a depth of 10 cm in solarized soil. This treatment controlled P. cambivora in an irrigated cherry orchard but not in non-irrigated almond orchards. Although solarization did not control established P. cambivora infections, it significantly increased the growth of the trees (Wicks, 1988b).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe use of resistant rootstocks is another means of controlling P. cambivora. In chestnut, high levels of resistance have been reported for Asiatic chestnut (Castanea crenata) and the hybrids C. sat

host_range: 经几十年来的研究，陆续发现多主瘤梗孢的寄主范围极广。据文献记载，它能为害双子叶植物在2000种以上。在这2000多种寄主植物中具有较大经济价值的大田作物就有31种，蔬菜58种、18种包括柑桔在内的果树与浆果类、35种林木与灌木、7种草本观赏植物和20种杂草。大田作物中以棉花和苜蓿受害最为严重。
potential_eco_desc: 根腐病是一种毁灭性病害，可以是棉花在成熟前死亡，或造成一部分死铃，因而减产并降低品质。在收获前三个星期枯死的棉花，品质降低一级，棉籽含油量常降低18%-35%；早期感病棉株的种子蛋白质含量低，含油量少于18%，且发芽率大大降低。1920年美国曾因此病而使棉花减产15%。另据美国棉花病害委员会1951年的记载指出，得克萨斯州棉花每年平均减产3.45%，而重粘土壌的棉花则减产在一半以上。Hervey曾报道，1959年在得克萨斯州的Temple地区附近的一些棉田发病率竟高达74%。另有资料称，亚利桑那州Mesa地区附近的一些实验棉田小区在1958年和1959年都曾因此病而全部失败、病害的危害性，还表现在受病菌污染严重的大田，大大降低了土地使用的价值。据Lyda的资料(1978年)，美国得克萨斯州大约有4655.8公顷棉田受根腐病菌污染严重，不能再种棉花或其他寄主植物。
management_info:
我国尚未发生此病，以下措施仅供参考。
1.轮作倒茬 与禾本科作物或豆科牧草、冬季绿肥植物轮作，尤以与高粱进行不少于4年的轮作效果较好。
2.棉田休闲 特别是夏季休闲，可以减少早期侵染，推迟发病。据McNamara的资料，休闲一年后，可使根腐病发病率从69%降到22%。
3.秋季深耕棉田 可将病根残土翻到深层使其分化，以减少其越冬的菌量。
4.施用绿肥，改良土壤 施用豆科绿肥植物，改良土壤，促进根际微生物群体的繁殖与活动，有利于控制菌核和菌索的萌发和残存，刺激植物生长。绿肥作物分解产生有机酸，可增加土壤酸度，从而降低棉根腐病的发病率，有效地增加棉花的产量。另外，施用化学氮肥，也可增强根的活力，并降低病菌的危害。
5.种植隔离带 在病田内种植禾本科作物，如高粱、玉米等，做隔离带，可控制病菌在田间的扩展蔓延，如每两行棉花间隔种一行高粱能有效地组织病菌在土壤中的传播。美国得克萨斯州的黑粘土棉田至少种有9.1m宽的高粱作为有效的隔离带。
6.选用抗(耐)病品种 种植早熟的棉花品种及培育抗病品种是病区防治该病的一个较可靠的防病保产的有效措施。美国曾用海岛棉与陆地棉的种间杂交及回交的方法，获得能兼抗根腐病等5种病害的棉花品系。由于缺乏对该病的抗源资料，目前在实际生产上，比较强调种植耐病品种和利用品种的早熟避病性。我国因未存有此病，因而在抗病育种上不考虑对此病的抗性。
remark: 由于此病害只在局部棉区发生，防治难度很大，加之病原菌随土壤和寄主苗木病根传播的特点，所以首先应加强检疫，防止该病的传入。世界上许多国家都非常警惕该病的入侵，并且采取了严格的植物检疫措施。如包括原苏联、保加利亚和希腊等35个成员国或地区在内的欧洲与地中海区域植物保护组织就把该病列为该区域性组织第一类检疫对象名单之内。阿尔及利亚、土耳其和南非等地也作为检疫性病害。我国自1950年代至今一直都把该病列为检疫对象。

potential_eco_desc: The most extensive disease loss surveys have been conducted on cotton in Texas and Arizona where average loss of raw fibre has been estimated to be 3.5 and 2.2%, respectively (Streets and Bloss, 1973). An intensive aerial survey conducted in several regions in Texas illustrated that 25% of the cotton-producing areas (6429 ha and 3339 ha in 1979 and 1981, respectively) were infested with the pathogen (SD Lyda, Department of Plant Pathology and Microbiology, Texas A&M University, Texas, USA, personal communication, 1991). Field surveys combined with aerial photography and image analysis have been used to estimate losses on the basis of loss per hectare, hectares affected and fibre quality and marketability in Upland and Pima cotton in Arizona (Mulrean et al., 1984). Yield loss was 10 and 13% for infested fields of Upland and Pima cottons, respectively, compared to healthy plants. In the case of orchard crops (e.g. apples, almonds), mortality exceeding 50% of the established trees has been found on some sites.

management_info: For most crops and soil types, there are no control measures that are both effective and economically justified. Soil fumigants such as 1,3-dichloropropene have been shown to provide control of the pathogen. These treatments are cost prohibitive for annual row crops, but may be justified as pre-plant treatments for orchards or vineyards established in soils that allow for adequate gas penetration. The fungus is highly sensitive to the triazole fungicides, but these compounds have herbicidal activity in cotton if applied to the seed (Whitson and Hine, 1986; Riggs and Lyda, 1988). Propiconazole and triadimenol applied in subsurface drip irrigation have been demonstrated significantly to reduce plant mortality in cotton (Olsen and George, 1987). The application of a systemic triazole fungicide deep in the soil near the root appears to offer the potential for disease reduction. ^p^pCurrently, other control measures (e.g. resistant varieties, biological, cultural) have not yielded adequate or sufficiently consistent reduction in plant mortality to be useful (Kenerley and Jeger, 1992).

host_range: In Greece, a disease of Citrus spp. caused by the fungal pathogen Phoma tracheiphila, which mainly affects lemon trees (Citrus limon) causing significant yield reductions of up to 60%. It has been estimated that 60-100% of the trees can be affected within 20 years after planting. In addition to lemon (and other citrus species/hybrids), mandarin (C. reticulata) and some of its hybrids can also become affected by the pathogen. Among rootstocks, sour orange (C. aurantium), the most widespread lemon rootstock in Greece, is considered to be very susceptible to infection. This is the first report of Phoma tracheiphila causing severe mal secco disease on a mandarin hybrid (cv. Ortanique) grafted onto Citrumelo rootstock in western Greece.
description: During surveys in citrus orchards in Katohi, western Greece in 2014, decline of a mandarin hybrid (Citrus reticulata x sinensis, cv. Ortanique) grafted onto Citrumelo rootstocks was observed, with approximately 90% of the trees being affected in an area of 20 ha. Based on biological detection and molecular diagnostics, the pathogenicity test showed that the causal agent was Phoma tracheiphila. This is the first report of Phoma tracheiphila occurring on cv. Ortanique grafted onto Citrumelo rootstocks.
remark: Phoma tracheiphila is listed as a II/A2 quarantine organism by the European Commission as it is absent from citrus plantations in some EU Member States.
reference_name: First report of Phoma tracheiphila causing severe mal secco disease on a mandarin hybrid (cv. Ortanique) grafted onto Citrumelo rootstock in western Greece

host_range: Almost all citrus plants are susceptible to artificial infections of P. tracheiphila. In the field, hybrids of citrus, related genera (Eremocitrus, Fortunella, Poncirus and Severinia) and other species have different degrees of resistance to the disease.
potential_eco_desc: In the Mediterranean region, P. tracheiphila is the most destructive fungal disease of lemons. Up to 100% of trees in a lemon orchard of a susceptible cultivar can be affected. Destructive outbreaks of P. tracheiphila may occur after frost spells and hail storms in spring (Perrotta and Graniti, 1988). In general, injury to the tree through severe cold weather may predispose it to fungal attack. The symptoms of the disease are most severe in spring and autumn; at high summer temperatures, spread in the host vascular system ceases and the symptoms do not develop further (Ruggieri, 1953). The disease reduces the quantity and quality of lemon production in the areas where the pathogen is present, and limits the use of susceptible species and cultivars.

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pP. tracheiphila can be kept under control by pruning infected twigs as soon as the first symptom appears (Salerno and Cutuli, 1982). Common practices aimed either at saving the affected trees or at eradicating the inoculum include cutting of whole branches and grafting the pollarded tree with resistant cultivars or species. Burning of the pruned branches is recommended in order to eliminate possible sources of inoculum. Injury during cultural practices must be avoided. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control is not widely used except in nurseries. Copper fungicides and ziram are the most common products used. Systemic products are effective only as preventives (Solel and Salerno, 1989). ^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe best method of controlling the disease would be to grow resistant clones but unfortunately this is not easily achieved. In some areas of Sicily the resistant lemon cultivar Monachello has replaced the susceptible cultivar Femminello but it is of inferior quality. Resistant clones of cv. Femminello have been selected but they either do not adapt to different environmental conditions or have still to be tested in the field (Gentile et al., 1992; Salerno and Cutuli, 1992).^p^p^Regulatory Control ^p^pIn countries or areas where the disease has not yet been reported, great care must be taken not to use plants from nurseries located in infected lemon areas for new plantings or replantings.

potential_eco_desc: Phoma medicaginis var. pinodella, together with Mycosphaerella pinodes and Ascochyta pisi, is part of a complex of seedborne fungi associated with Ascochyta spp. infection of peas. Ascochyta leaf diseases are widespread throughout the world, particularly in temperate regions in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand (Hagedorn, 1984).^p^pP. pinodella causes both yield and quality to be reduced. author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pP. pinodella, together with Mycosphaerella pinodes and Ascochyta pisi, is part of a complex of seedborne fungi associated with Ascochyta spp. infection of peas. P. pinodella is extensively seedborne on peas. In a survey of 214 samples of commercial field pea seed in South Australia, 31% of the samples were infected (Ali et al., 1982). In another survey of pea seed lots in Australia, the Ascochyta blight complex of field peas was isolated from 436 of 691 seed lots tested. P. pinodella was recovered from 4.2% of isolations, whereas M. pinodes was recovered from 94.8% and A. pisi from 1.0% of isolations (Bretag et al., 1995). In seed health tests of a range of pea seed samples, the three Ascochyta spp. were most frequently located in the seed coat, less so in the cotyledons and least frequently in the embryo. P.  pinodella and M. pinodes were also isolated at greater frequencies than A. pisi from plant debris mixed with pea seeds (Abd-El-Rehim et al., 1997). ^p^pP. pinodella has been isolated from seeds of Medicago spp. (Mebalds, 1987a), bean (Dhyani et al., 1989), faba bean (Simay, 1994) and soyabean (Erzurum and Iren, 1987). ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pNot recorded.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pSeedborne P. pinodella can enter the roots and lower stem of peas at the point of seed attachment (Hagedorn, 1984). Mebalds (1987b) stated that the pathogen was transmitted by Medicago truncatum seeds to plants. ^p^pThe pathogen also persists as chlamydospores in soil (Maude, 1996). ^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pA field trial was carried out in Beauvais, France, to compare the efficiency of seed treatments for the control of the Ascochyta complex in peas. The treatments tested were cymoxanil + oxadixyl + carbendazim + thiram and cymoxanil + oxadixyl. Treated pea seeds were grown in soil inoculated with Fusarium solani f.sp. pisi which also contained F. oxysporum and Phoma medicaginis var. pinodella. The seeds treated with cymoxanil + oxadixyl + carbendazim + thiram showed less rotting than the cymoxanil + oxadixyl treated seeds (Sanssene et al., 1998).^p^pIn field tests fungicides gave good control of: the most effective being benomyl, mancozeb, captafol, mancozeb + copper oxychloride + sulphate and chlorothalonil (Fadl et al., 1985).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pCulture Media (Hewett, 1987)^p^p1. Pretreat seeds in 1% sodium hypochlorite for 10 min.^p2. Incubate for 7 days at 21°C in darkness or under alternating light and dark 12/12 cycles in containers sealed to maintain humidity.^p3. Examine for colony characteristic of P. pinodella.^p^pNotes on methods^p^pAlthough specifically designed to detect seedborne Ascochyta pisi, the culture media method can also be used for P. pinodella (Hewett, 1987).

Isolates of B. exigua have been obtained from over 200 genera of plants and this report expands the list with a new host.
potential_eco_desc: The disease, at present, is limited to a few gardens and may spread to other areas.
description: During the fall of 2014, in a mountain garden located near Biella, northern Italy (45.6121660° N; 8.0562970° E; elev. 850 m), a leaf spot was observed on 12-month-old Salvia greggii plants. All plants grown in the garden were affected, with 20 to 30% of leaves showing symptoms. Infected plants rarely died, but the presence of lesions on mature plants decreased their aesthetic quality. The disease started from basal leaves on plants grown in shade and at higher relative humidity, progressing up and outward on the plants, until they were almost completely defoliated. The samples were collected and identified, the pathogen was identified as Boeremia exigua var. linicola (syn. = Phoma exigua var. linicola)  by morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests.
reference_name: First Report of a Leaf Spot Caused by Boeremia exigua var. linicola on Autumn Sage (Salvia greggii) in Italy and Worldwide

potential_eco_desc: Phoma exigua var. exigua, a soil-borne facultative parasite, has been obtained so far from over 200 plant genera, causing an array of symptoms, e.g., leaf and stem necrosis, root rot, and seedling blight.
description: During February 2015, a 1.5-ha commercial crop of oregano located in Nicosia, Cyprus, was severely affected with over 20% of the plants exhibiting a wilting appearance. Isolations from the infected stems of numerous oregano plants, based on fungal morphology and sequencing data, the causal agent was identified as the coelomycete Boeremia exigua var. exigua. Numerous species of the genus Phoma have been previously reported as pathogenic to plants of the Lamiaceae family. Phoma exigua var. exigua, a soil-borne facultative parasite, has been obtained so far from over 200 plant genera, causing an array of symptoms, e.g., leaf and stem necrosis, root rot, and seedling blight. To our knowledge, this is first report of B. exigua var. exigua causing stem rot of O. dubium in Cyprus and globally.  Phoma exigua var. exigua is a soil-borne facultative parasite.
reference_name: First Report of Boeremia exigua var. exigua Causing Stem Rot of Origanum dubium in Cyprus

description: Incidence^p^pP.exigua var. linicola is present as mycelium in the seed coat of flax, and has been shown by Colhoun and Muskett (1948) to remain viable for up to 27-43 months under typical seed storage conditions. Other authors have also demonstrated that the fungus is seedborne (Kumud et al., 1997).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pNot recorded.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pNot recorded.^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pSeed treatment is possible (Mercer et al., 1988). Decognet et al. (1994) found a number of seed treatment chemicals that gave some protection to young seedlings but not sufficient to provide season-long protection to the crop against foot rot.^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pBlotter Test (Malone, 1982)^p^p1. Seeds are placed on moist blotters and incubated for 10 days at 20°C under near ultraviolet (NUV) light in a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle.^p^p2. Following incubation, seeds are examined under a stereoscopic microscope (x12-x50) for thin-walled pycnidia with one ostiole measuring 100-300 x 70-300 μm. Pycnidiospores, which are extruded through the ostiole in a creamy tendril, are unicellular, hyaline and often biguttulate, measuring 5-8 x 2.5-4 μm.^p^pCulture Plate (Malone, 1982)^p^p1. Seeds are incubated for 5 days at 22°C in darkness on malt extract agar.^p^p2. Following incubation, plates are examined for dense, dark-grey to almost black colonies with smoky-grey aerial mycelium; the reverse is chocolate-brown to almost black. Pycnidia are rarely present but pycnidia production can be induced by exposure to NUV light.

management_info: Control can be achieved by burning down the haulms using chemical desiccants as soon as possible, and then harvesting the tubers as soon as practicable and before soil temperatures become cold. Some desiccants may increase gangrene. Physical damage to tubers should be minimized. Fumigation with sec-butylamine 1-3 weeks after lifting can control gangrene, as can dipping in organomercury solutions or spray application of thiabendazole or a mixture of thiabendazole and a salt of sec-butylamine. management_info: This disease is seedborne, and as such, the primary means of control should be the production of disease-free seed. Maddens (1987) described a number of suitable seed treatments. description: Since 2014, an increase of sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.) crop wilt diseases has been observed in Russia. potential_eco_desc: Brown stem rot can have a significant impact on soybean yield, potentially resulting in 25% loss. This confirmation of brown stem rot in New York indicates that soybean growers in this state should consider planting varieties with resistance to this disease in areas where it has been identified.
description: Brown stem rot of soybean (Glycine max), incited by Cadophora gregata is an economically important disease commonly found throughout the north-central region of the United States and Canada. This disease can be a major contributor to yield loss in years with conducive weather conditions. In late August 2013, soybean plants were submitted from Herkimer County, NY, for diagnosis to determine the cause of interveinal chlorosis of the foliage. When the stems were split, the diseased plants exhibited dark brown discoloration of the pith and vascular system, especially at the nodes, which is typical of brown stem rot. The fungus was isolated from the diseased soybean and confirmed to be Cadophora gregata based on morphological characteristics and ITS sequence analysis. To our knowledge, brown stem rot has not been reported previously on soybean in New York. Brown stem rot was confirmed in four additional counties, Cayuga, Montgomery, Niagara, and Yates, in 2014, suggesting that it may be widespread in New York.
reference_name: First Report of Brown Stem Rot Caused by Cadophora gregata in Soybean in New York
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 大豆 Glycine max
description: During late September 2010, soybean (Glycine max L.) plants exhibiting interveinal leaf necrosis and internal stem browning were received from Brookings (44°17.915′ N, 096°55.393′ W), Aurora (43°41.540′ N, 098°34.195′ W), and Hand (44°29.407′ N, 099°00.464′ W) counties for diagnosis. The strains were identified as Phialophora gregata by biological detection and pathogenicity test. Brown stem rot is favored by cool weather conditions and widespread across the northern tier of the U.S. soybean producing states. In South Dakota, although P. gregata was previously detected in soybean fields, the causal agent was never confirmed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first definitive report of P. gregata causing brown stem rot on soybeans in South Dakota.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pThe most effective fungicides of a range which were tested on fruit and leaf spot of citrus in Cameroon were copper oxide and benomyl (Menyonga, 1971; Rey et al., 1988). Others which were found to be effective were mancozeb, tridemorph, triadimenol, captafol.^p^pTreatment with benomyl, alternated with copper-based fungicides, should be carried out as follows. Sprays should be applied a week after the onset of rains at fortnightly intervals. A further three fortnightly applications with copper-based fungicides followed by benomyl should be made when the fruits are the size of golf balls.^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pThe following disease management methods have been recommended (Seif and Kungu, 1989).^p^p- Collection and destruction by burying and/or burning of all fallen fruit and leaves in affected orchards. This may drastically reduce the innoculum pressure in the field.^p^p- Planting of windbreaks around the citrus orchards to minimize the impact of wind, which is the primary dispersal agent for infective propagules.^p^p- Discouraging inter-planting in affected orchards with mature producing trees to prevent creation of a microclimate of relatively cool temperatures and high relative humidity (RH), which is conducive to disease development.^p^p- Judicious pruning of shoots, particularly those which have died back, to allow light penetration into, and free aeration within, the tree canopy, thus making the environment in the phyllosphere less conducive (short leaf wetness period, low RH, moderate temperatures) to disease development.
