host_range: The main hosts of O. wageneri (L. wageneri var. ponderosum) are the conifers Pinus contorta, P. jeffreyi and P. ponderosa (Harrington and Cobb, 1984). P. monophylla and P. edulis are the primary hosts for L. wageneri var. wageneri, and Pseudotsuga menzies
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pO. wageneri colonizes the sapwood of the roots and lower stem. Affected trees grow poorly for several years and then usually die. The disease typically occurs in enlarging foci, spreading at rates averaging 1 m per year. It is considered a major threat to managed crops of Pseudotsuga menziesii and Pinus ponderosa because of the vectored spread, and the responsiveness of the vectors to forest management practices. Its potential for damage in the forest regions of the northern hemisphere is considerable.^p^pThe disease has become important in the Douglas-fir region of North America since the 1970s, coinciding with the plantation of large areas of susceptible species as well as the increased use of heavy machinery in forestry (Hansen et al., 1988). Losses in scattered individual plantations reach 50%, mostly in southern Oregon and northern California, USA. Even in this area, losses in most plantations seldom exceed 1%. Regionwide, losses are much lower. Most infection centres cease to expand after a few years and cumulative losses are negligible. The rate of disease increase of active centres within a plantation may be alarming in the first 20 years, but even these usually slow as the stand ages (Hansen and Goheen, 1988). On a few sites, however, usually where obvious risk factors (soil compaction, pre-commercial thinning) are highest, losses are devastating although seldom quantified.^p^p^Environmental impact^pThis is a native pathogen, so far operating on its natural hosts. There is little or no information on the environmental impact of Douglas-fir and hard pine varieties of Leptographium wageneri, because disease occurs almost exclusively in managed stands. The pinyon pine variety, however, occurs in wild forests. Some of the best studied cases are in National Parks. Individual infection centres are often very large (up to several hectares). Blackstain selectively kills the pine from these pinyon juniper woodlands, transforming the structure and composition of the ecosystem. Many animals use the seeds of the pine (pine nuts) for food.
author: CPC2006

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pNatural spread of O. wageneri occurs locally via root grafts between adjacent trees and through the transport of the fungus by insects (Hessburg and Hansen, 2000). In addition, and somewhat surprisingly, the fungus is capable of growing freely through the soil for a few centimetres (Hicks et al., 1980). The disease normally appears in patches or centres which extend approximately 1 m per year (Hansen and Goheen, 1988) or up to 7 m per year (Cobb et al., 1982; Cobb, 1988).^p^pVector Transmission^p^pRoot-feeding bark beetles (Hylastes nigrinus) and weevils (Pissodes fasciatus and Steremnius carinatus) are the chief insect vectors in Douglas-fir (Harrington et al., 1985; Witcosky et al., 1986b; Jacobi, 1992). They breed readily in diseased roots and are able to create new infection courts by their feeding activities on healthy roots. Vector relationships are strongly suspected but not proven with the other varieties of L. wageneri (Landis and Helburg, 1976; Goheen and Cobb, 1978).^p^pSeedborne Spread^p^pThis disease is not known to be seedborne.^p^pSilvicultural Practices^p^pSilvicultural practices are not thought to spread the disease, but they do influence vector activity and thus the probability of disease establishment and intensification in a stand. Activities that lead to increased soil moisture (Goheen et al., 1978) or soil compaction (ground-based harvest, road construction and maintenance), or fresh stumps and injured trees (thinning, pruning) lead to higher populations of vector beetles, and greater probabilities of disease (Goheen and Hansen, 1978; Hansen, 1978; Harrington et al., 1985; Witcosky et al., 1986a).^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pInternational spread would most readily occur by transport of raw logs, or living coniferous host plants. The fungus is not likely to be carried in processed wood, unless adhering bark is infested by bark beetles and weevils acting as vectors.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Roots: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; visible to naked eye.^p - Wood: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; visible to naked eye.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark^p - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. Pods)^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain).
author: CPC2006

remark: O. wageneri is an EPPO A1 quarantine pest. A study carried out by Webber and Hansen (1990) examined the possibilities of establishment of L. wageneri in Europe, and especially the UK, and concluded that host plants as well as climatic conditions would permit the fungus to establish. Besides the host and climatic conditions, the fungus could be vectored by European Hylastes spp. and spread further. It could cause considerable economic and ecological damage in Europe if introduced.^p^pThe specific quarantine requirements for O. wageneri are currently being revised by EPPO (2003). In general, strict control is required over the importation of coniferous plants from North America, and appropriate precautions should be taken for wood. EPPO's recommended specific quarantine requirements for non-European Scolytidae could probably be easily adapted for O. wageneri (OEPP/EPPO, 1990).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Phytosanitary measures (e.g. quarantine and certification) can be effective in limiting the likelihood of long-distance transport of the pathogen. If detected, L. wageneri can be killed in wood using standard heating and fumigation methods rigorously applied (Rhatigan et al., 1998).^p^pHost-plant resistance has not been exploited, although field observations suggest that some trees can limit the development of the pathogen within the xylem. Non-host resistance is an important part of cultural control.^p^pCurrently there are no control methods available based on chemical or biological products. Cultural control is the key to managing blackstain root disease. O. wageneri causes most damage in areas which are disturbed by human activities, such as roadsides, pre-commercially thinned plantations of Pseudotsuga, and areas logged with heavy machinery with consequent soil compaction or interference with soil drainage. Avoiding or mitigating these activities will greatly reduce the risk of disease in future stands. ^p^pRecommended practices for cultural control include: planting non-host trees in high-risk areas, such as roadsides and along skid trails; careful logging practices to minimize soil disturbance; and scheduling thinning and pruning activities for mid-summer, after the main insect flight period, and early enough for slash to dry and be less attractive by the next flight the following spring (Hansen et al., 1988). Initial planting should be planned as much as possible to avoid the later need for pre-commercial thinning. Mixed species stands will slow the spread of the pathogen and provide value if susceptible species are killed.

potential_eco_desc: This moth is a serious pest of citrus in Southern Africa and of cotton in many parts of Africa. It also affects maize in West Africa. In South Africa, citrus crop losses of 10-20% are common (Glas, 1991). Reed (1974) described losses of between 42 and 90% in late crops of cotton in Uganda. It has also become a significant pest of macadamia in Israel (Wysoki, 1986). Blomefield (1989) reported losses of up to 28% in a late peach crop in South Africa. Begemann and Schoeman (1999) calculated citrus crop loss in South Africa specifically due to T. leucotreta was 1.6% in Navels and 0.3% in Valencias.

management_info: Introduction^p^pControl is difficult because the moth has many alternative hosts so reinfestation is likely to occur.^p^p^Cultural ControlReed (1974) and Byaruhanga and De Lima (1977) showed that late sown crops of cotton in Uganda are worst affected, but the difference is not great. As T. leucotreta is primarily a fruit feeder, it is suggested by Glas (1991) that crops of cotton grown close to fruit trees may be less affected. In areas with a prolonged dry season the moth, which needs a continual source of food, is less likely to reach pest proportions, conversely irrigation allows populations to build up to levels which cause damage.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pParasitoids of T. leucotreta have been identified, and mass release of Trichogrammoidea spp. has been practised with effect (Newton and Odendaal, 1990) but is unlikely to be cost effective. Fritsch (1988) reported on the successful use of a granulosis virus, which has been further identified by Jehle and Backhaus (1994). The use of pathogens was reviewed by Moore (2002). Jehle et al. (2003) examined the results of combining two genotypes of the virus.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe larva gains some protection from insecticides by living within a fruit or boll Although insecticides have often been used in the past, they seldom control populations effectively. Chitin inhibitors (Newton, 1987) are more likely to be effective.^p^p^Pheromonal Control.Hofmeyr and Burger (1995) describe a pheromone disperser whilst Newton et al. (1993) identify the compound. Pheromones have been much used for mating disruption of this species and constitute one of the most targeted control methods.

potential_eco_desc:
主要以球状鳞茎繁殖，具有极强的分生能力和竞争力。据实验，4枚鳞茎母球在一个生长周期能繁殖115~136枚子球，一旦定植后根除防治很难，会排斥其他作物和植物，易形成单一生长优势，严重影响生态环境。
茎叶含大量草酸盐，牲畜误食后会使血中非蛋白氮明显升高，伤害肾脏。
该杂草能危害热带、亚热带地区的重要作物生长，如木薯、玉米、旱稻、茶叶、马铃薯、咖啡、谷物、甘蔗果树和蔬菜等。据印度报道，在不防治的情况下，会导致玉米产量减产56%。为此，中国和澳大利亚都将其列为检疫性杂草，新西兰、南非、印度、乌干达等国家将其列为农田重要杂草。
description: 在原产地之外的宽叶酢浆草很少结实，主要依靠鳞茎的大量繁殖和传播扩散。农耕活动、农产品调运、灌溉水流都能导致传播扩散；花卉贸易活动、引种夹带也可导致跨境传播。
management_info:
（1）农业防治：一般的农田杂草防除措施反而会刺激宽叶酢浆草繁殖和扩散，必须配合化学方法使用以达到根除目的。根据实验，鳞茎深埋至土壤20cm以下，萌发率只有20%，因此，深埋25cm以下有一定的防治效果。
（2）化学方法：鳞茎萌发后的42~56d，使用除草剂草甘膦、噁草酮、乙氧氟甲草醚、氟乐灵最有效果。或定植后，在5个生长季连续每月施用百草枯（0.8kg/hm2）或杀草快（0.4kg/hm2），并结合25cm深埋处理可有效根除该杂草。
（3）生物控制：印度发现一中昆虫烟粉虱Bemisia tabaci会携带病毒，可引起宽叶酢浆草叶子；酢浆草柄锈菌Puccinia oxalidis可减少鳞茎数量和生存力。

potential_eco_desc: Holm et al. (1997) record that O. latifolia is a weed of at least 37 countries in at least 30 crops. It is listed as a major weed in India, New Zealand, Australia, South Africa and Uganda, particularly in cassava, maize, upland rice, tea, potato, coffee, cereals, sugarcane, orchards and vegetables. It can achieve dominance under certain intensive cultivation systems which remove other competing weeds, and spread of bulbs. Reports on the competitiveness of, and hence yield reducing potential of O. latifolia are somewhat contradictory. Atwal and Gopal (1972) recorded 56% reduction in maize yield from uncontrolled O. latifolia. However, Thomas (1991) reported no apparent effect on maize yield from populations of 33-50 plants/m2 in four successive seasons, when all other weeds had been controlled by a mixture of pre-emergence herbicides. The weed is of undisputed importance in horticultural nurseries where it may infest the produce sold and lead to loss of reputation and occasionally to business closure.^p^pO. latifolia is an alternate host of Puccinia sorghi.
author: CPC2006

remark: O. latifolia is a prohibited import to Australia.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pO. latifolia is exceptionally difficult to control by manual or mechanical means. Superficial hoeing or hand-pulling does nothing to destroy the bulbs, while harrowing and rotary tillage helps only to disperse them. A combination of deep tillage and desiccation can be helpful. Thomas (1991) noted that chisel ploughing followed by mouldboard and/or disc ploughing resulted in more suppression than chisel ploughing alone. Defoliation by mowing has to be repeated many times to have substantial effect. Chawdhry and Sagar (1974b) showed that clipping was needed at least five times to reduce growth by 90%, while Esler (1962) showed that monthly defoliation had almost no useful effect. The surest form of cultural control is by the use of smothering crops or mulching. Ingle et al. (1995) confirmed the effectiveness of black polythene or 'weed matting' over one and two year periods in New Zealand, while Ochoa and Zaragoza (1981) refer to the use of fodder crops in Spain. There are no reports on solarization, but there seems no reason why this would not be effective under suitable high temperature/clear sky conditions.^p^pChemical Control^p^pThe most successful chemical treatments have been with fumigants. Apart from methyl bromide, which is no longer available for this use, soil drenches with metam-sodium have given good results (Hunter and Over de Linden, 1958), though control is not always complete (Preest, 1964).^p^pMany standard herbicides fail to control O. latifolia and tend to favour it. These include most triazines and metolachlor. However, Marshall (1987) lists a range of compounds suitable for specific crop situations. These include trifluralin, oxyfluorfen, oxadiazon, terbacil, EPTC and diuron as pre-emergence treatments. Other compounds with potential include pendimethalin and imazethapyr. Chlorsulfuron, metribuzin and methabenzthiazuron are effective against O. pes-caprae and could be useful on O. latifolia (Parsons and Cuthbertson, 1992). Among post-emergence treatments 2,4-D is only effective at high doses, whilst paraquat needs repeated application. Glyphosate is especially valuable in tree and fruit crops, preferably at the bulb exhaustion stage.

potential_eco_desc: The disease was observed in India in 1962, but not described until 1967 (Payak and Renfro, 1967). It is a common and destructive disease in India, with losses ranging from 20 to 90% (Payak, 1975). It tends to be most severe in areas with 100 to 200 cm rainfall, declining in severity as rainfall declines (Frederiksen and Renfro, 1977).^p^pThe losses that the disease may inflict on a crop in a given area varies in a complex way. In general, if three-quarters or more of the foliage is affected prior to flowering, then the loss may be total, ear formation is either totally suppressed or markedly attenuated. Grain yield reductions may vary from 20 to 90%. Losses above 70% occur only in highly susceptible cultivars grown in conditions favourable for the disease (Payak, 1975). Yield losses of up to 63% have been recorded in the tarai area of Uttar Pradesh (Sharma et al., 1993).McGregor (1978) established the parameter designated as Expected Economic Impact (EEI), which formed the basis for listing '49 top-ranking exotic pathogens' from a total of 551 that pose a significant threat to agriculture in the USA. S. rayssiae var. zeae was ranked 43rd with the EEI standing at US$ 53 million at 1978 prices.
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pS. rayssiae var. zeae has been found in embryos of maize seeds Singh et al., 1967, 1968). Sangam et al. (1989) reported viable oospores on the seed surface, and mycelium was found within seed tissues. ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pS. rayssiae var. zeae infection has been associated with smaller seed size (Sangam et al., 1989).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pBrown stripe downy mildew developed on seedlings grown in sterilized soil from seeds taken from infected plants (Singh et al., 1968). Other attempts to demonstrate seed transmission of S. rayssiae var. zeae were unsuccessful (Singh et al., 1970). ^p^pSoilborne oospores (Singh et al., 1970) and infected Digitaria sanguinalis (Bains et al., 1978) are sources of inoculum. The pathogen is transmitted by wind and rain (Singh and Renfro, 1971).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pSeed treatment with metalaxyl gave control of the disease up to 30 days after planting; when followed by a foliar application of metalaxyl, control was improved and yield increased (Lal et al., 1980; Sangam et al., 1989). A high rate application of metalaxyl to seeds was phytotoxic (Lal et al., 1980).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pEmbryo test: ^pSeed is digested in 2% sodium or potassium hydroxide for 15 min. to 12 h (depending on seed hardness) at 45-50°C, then washed several times in distilled water, stained in 0.1% cotton blue in lactic acid or glycerol for 15-20 min., squashed under a coverslip and examined microscopically Singh et al., 1967, 1968).

management_info: As the disease was recorded in the 1960s, the need for control through host resistance was deemed to be a priority for the All India Coordinated Maize Improvement Project. In the hybrid development programme a large number of inbred lines were evaluated to this disease and many promising lines were soon identified so that it was possible to release a resistant hybrid as early as 1968. This was one of the fastest answers to a disease problem identified in 1965. Subsequently, through cooperative work in the Asian region under the aegis of the Inter Asian Corn Programme, very promising resistance to all the prevailing downy mildews of maize in the region was identified in Philippine germplasm; Taiwan had already released hybrids resistant to sugarcane downy mildew (Peronosclerospora sacchari). Materials identified as resistant in the Philippines, Taiwan and Thailand to the prevailing downy mildews have also shown a high level of resistance to S. rayssiae var. zeae (Payak and Sharma, 1976).^p^pCoordinated work at a national level has been carried out to determine dosage, formulations, etc., for the systemic fungicide metalaxyl, which is specifically active as a seed treatment against oomycetous fungi including the downy mildews. Lal et al. (1980) found that seed treatment with the fungicide controlled brown stripe downy mildew for up to 30 days after planting.

host_range: This is the first report of a root rot caused by Rhizoctonia fragariae on rosemary. This fungus is associated with black root rot of strawberry.
potential_eco_desc: There were up to 60% of plants diseased with clear symptoms.
description: In winter of 2016, garden beds in a shopping center of Zaragoza (northeast Spain) planted with 6-year-old rosemary plants (both semierect and prostrate cultivars) exhibited up to 60% of plants diseased with clear symptoms of plant stunting, reflected in a progressive drying of loose branches and eventually the collapse of the whole plant. The samples were collected and fungi were isolated, the pathogen was identified as Rhizoctonia fragariae by morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge this is the first report of a root rot caused by a pathogenic binucleate Rhizoctonia species on rosemary.

management_info: Because P. splendens survives well in soil, once it has become established it can persist in soil for a long time. In the greenhouse, P. splendens can be eliminated from soil or growing medium by heating or pasteurization. In the field or nursery, soil fumigation with methyl bromide has been standard practice for many years. Fungicides such as etridiazole, fosetyl-aluminium and metalaxyl are effective and are commonly used to control Pythium root rot (Chase, 1987). In addition, pathogen-free propagating material should be used to prevent disease transmission.

potential_eco_desc: D. saccharalis is generally considered to be a pest of substantial economic importance. The extent of economic losses may vary depending on factors such as environmental conditions and sugarcane varieties. Losses to the sugarcane borer often vary across geographic regions (e.g. crop losses to the borer in Louisiana, USA may range from 4-30% annually, possibly twice as high as in Florida (Ingram et al., 1951).^p^pThe amount of sugar lost due to borer damage may vary depending on factors such as the particular variety attacked, and when during the season the attack occurs. The correlation between borer damage and loss of sugar cane or sugar production have been estimated in different ways: an average of 1.86 kg sucrose lost per ton of cane (Wilson, 1942), 1% sugar lost with every 1% increase in internode bored, and 2.6 kg sugar lost per ton of cane (Ulloa et al., 1982). Other estimates of loss attributed to 1% increase in internode bored are: 0.38-0.54% (Long and Hensley, 1972), 0.75% (Williams et al., 1969), 0.023% in Cuba (Barreto, 1954) and 0.23% in Jamaica (Chinloy, 1954).^p^pWith respect to alcoholic fermentation of cane juice, an estimated average of 62 litres of alcohol per hectare was lost for each 1% bored internode (Lopes et al., 1983).^p^pOne approach used to make quantitative estimates of economic losses across different infestation levels of D. saccharalis in sugarcane has been to establish a quantitative relationship between yield and the number of stalk internodes damaged by borers; coupled with information on the average number of internodes a borer damages, the economic value of sugar, and the cost of control measures, economic injury levels or thresholds for the borer in sugarcane have been derived (Summers, 1976; Summers et al., 1977; Alvarez and Kidder, 1981). These economic thresholds have generally been in the range of two to eight borers per 100 stalks (Hall and Bennett, 1994). In conjunction with using economic injury levels, general sampling procedures have been developed for estimating infestation levels of the sugarcane borer (Summers, 1976; Summers et al., 1977; Hall, 1986).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Biological Control^p^pD. saccharalis is subject to control by a variety of parasitoids and predators, although the complex of beneficial organisms attacking the borer varies across geographical regions. Native and introduced tachinids have provided some degree of control of D. saccharalis in many countries. However, in Barbados no success was obtained and a programme of introductions of Asian parasitoids was begun. One of these was Cotesia flavipes, a parasite introduced from India into many sugarcane-growing areas in North, Central and South America. C. flavipes became established and brought the pest under control. Subsequently, C. flavipes was imported into most other affected countries and in many of them it became established and improved the level of control. In other countries, such as Brazil, it is released annually to maintain a high population so as to enhance control (Melo, 1990). Cock (1985) provides a detailed account of biological control efforts against D. saccharalis in the Caribbean. ^p^pC. flavipes, Lixophaga diatraeae, Metagonistylum minense and Paratheresia claripalpis are generally regarded as the most effective natural enemies in most countries, and for that reason they have been introduced into many new areas and have often been mass-reared and released as part of seasonal control programmes for the borer (Smith et al., 1993). Each of these four parasitoids was introduced a number of times into Florida (USA), but only C. flavipes became established. C. flavipes has been perhaps the single best parasitoid in most areas, although it has failed to become established in some areas (e.g. Louisiana) and may only be effective in some areas during certain times of the year, notably late summer and autumn. Trichogramma minutum has been regarded as an important egg parasitoid in some areas. A study in Florida showed 67% parasitism of field-collected egg masses by T. minutum (Ingram et al., 1938). Some reports indicate that inundative releases of this parasitoid have generally been unproductive Ingram et al., 1938, 1951) while other reports indicate that releases may sometimes boost control of the borer (Metcalfe, 1959). Teran (1980) reported that predation was the major component of egg mortality in Brazil. The earwig Labidura riparia is regarded as an important predator of larvae and perhaps pupae in some areas, including the USA. A wide range of predators have been reported to attack the borer in Louisiana (Negm and Hensley, 1969). Sugarcane growers in Louisiana consider the imported red fire ant Solenopsis invicta to be an important natural enemy of eggs and young larvae. Adams et al. (1981) reported increased damage by D. saccharalis in Florida after pesticides had been used to reduce population levels of ants (various species including S. invicta). Birds are considered of value in natural control of D. saccharalis (Ingram et al., 1951).^p^pResearchers in Brazil have experimented with a granulosis virus to control D. saccharalis, with some success (Pavan et al., 1983). Bacillus thuringiensis is effective against larvae (Charpentier et al., 1973) but may rarely be observed in the field. Certain strains of B. thuringiensis show fairly good activity against young larvae but may be easily washed off leaves or rendered inactive by UV light within a short period of time; it remains possible that a commercial formulation and application methodologies for better borer control will be worked out. Other bacterial and fungal pathogens are sometimes found attacking borer larvae and pupae, but Ingram et al. (1951) felt they provided little control of the pest in Louisiana. ^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pInfestations of D. saccharalis may be reduced by several cultural control methods. Avoiding the use of seedcane damaged by the borer is of benefit in preventing stand losses in plant cane. Soaking seed cane for 72 hours in water at 25.6°C killed 27-100% of the borers in seedcane; similarly, 96 hours soaking killed 50-100%.

management_info:
1．营林防治。对发病的枝条及时修剪、处理，对根部感病的树，施行毁根、嫁接，已死和濒死的树要彻底销毁。

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe introduction of O. novo-ulmi to North America, Europe and parts of Asia has resulted in a catastrophic pandemic in which most mature elms have died. Numbers are difficult to obtain, but in some areas of Europe 60-70% of the elm trees were killed (Tainter and Baker, 1996), with some 30 million elms killed in the UK (Brasier, 1996b). In North America the destructive impact of O. novo-ulmi has been even greater, with 46 million trees of urban Ulmus americana killed alone (Wallner, 1996). Losses caused by the two Dutch elm disease pandemics have been estimated to be over hundreds of millions of elms (Brasier, 2001). Although the disease does not reduce the value of the timber, a significant economic damage is caused. Leaving aside the aesthetic value of the trees in urban environments, the removal of diseased trees, replanting and disease management costs have been enormous. For example, the city of Winnipeg, Canada, spent Can $2,000,000 for Dutch elm disease management of its 200,000 elm trees in 2000 (Allen, 2000). The total economic loss caused by O. novo-ulmi is difficult to quantify because of the unequalled devastating impact of the pathogen on elm populations on three continents, but may go into hundreds of billions of US dollars (Heybroek, 1993b).^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe environmental impact of O. novo-ulmi is even greater than that of its predecessor O. ulmi and can only be compared to that of Chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) in North America (Tainter and Baker, 1996). O. novo-ulmi has strongly affected elms in the forest and has changed the species composition of several forest communities, for example, floodplain forests in Europe. Although elm coppice is still relatively common in these forests, because elms are prolific seed producers, they have largely vanished from the canopy and other species have taken over their niche in the ecosystem (Hall et al., 1996). Before the introduction of DED fungi, wild elm populations had already suffered from human influences such as lowering of the groundwater table, intensification of harvesting operations, and habitat destruction, but the two pandemics of DED have resulted in a dangerous loss in genetic diversity within the genus. A European project, in which nine countries are working together, was initiated to save this diversity  (Collin et al., 2000).^p^p^Social impact^pThere is no other disease of trees that has become so well known to the public as Dutch elm disease. Elms were once a premier kind of tree planted in urban landscapes in Europe but were, and are, even more common in cities throughout the north-east and mid-western USA. In particular, the American elm (Ulmus americana) had been extensively planted there and, with its vase-shape, gave the streets and boulevards a distinct appearance. Dutch elm disease has had an enormous social impact and huge efforts are being made in many cities to save their elms, fully supported by the public. Large urban elm populations have been preserved in this way in many American cities (e.g. Minneapolis; Stennes, 2000). Elms are very prominent in the capital, Washington DC, and form an important part of the parklands at the Monumental Core and along the National Mall, where they provide a unique American cultural statement (Sherald, 1993). The US national park service is implementing an elaborate management plan to protect this important plantation.^p^pThe association of elm and man goes back to prehistoric times and elms have always played an important role in cultural history (Heybroek, 1993b). For example, elms were used for fodder and in agricultural systems, and the wood was important for tools and wheels as well as archery (Richens, 1983). It is especially tragic that a tree that has had so many uses for man is so severely affected by a disease brought about by man.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pThe disappearance of mature and old elm trees caused by Dutch elm disease has certainly had a nega
description: Because O. novo-ulmi appeared when O. ulmi was still very active in some areas, especially in North America, the introduction event(s) were not immediately recognized. Today it is believed that the second pandemic of Dutch elm disease, caused by O. novo-ulmi, probably began, more or less simultaneously, in the 1940s at two different locations: the Moldova-Ukraine area of Eastern Europe (subsp. novo-ulmi) and the southern Great Lakes area of North America (subsp. americana) (Brasier, 1990). Subsp. novo-ulmi steadily moved westwards across Europe, reaching the Netherlands by the mid-1970s. It also spread eastwards into south-west and central Asia, the latter almost certainly through a separate introduction during the 1970s and 1980s. At the same time subsp. americana spread across the North American continent, reaching both the east and west coasts by the 1970s and 1980s (Brasier, 1990; Brasier and Mehrotra, 1995). In the early 1970s subsp. americana had been accidentally introduced from the Windsor area (Canada) into the UK with a shipment of Ulmus thomasii logs and started the second pandemic there (Gibbs and Brasier, 1973;Brasier, 1979, 1990). Subsequently subsp. americana spread into the Netherlands, France, Spain and most other western and central European countries. As a result of this development in central and other parts of Europe, the ranges of the two subspecies overlap and hybrids between them have been identified (Jeng et al., 1988; Konrad et al., 2002). O. novo-ulmi is currently extending its range into western Canada and the eastern states of the USA as well as into Central Asia (Brasier and Kirk, 2001). The most recent event in the spread of O. novo-ulmi was the introduction of O. novo-ulmi to New Zealand in 1989 (Gadgil et al., 2000).^p^pAlthough the spread of DED has been studied for more than 80 years it is still unclear where O. ulmi and O. novo-ulmi have their origin. The most plausible theory is that the fungi were accidentally introduced from an east Asian origin, because some Asian elm species show high resistance to the disease (Smalley and Guries, 2000). During a survey of China in 1986, which included areas of central and eastern China and Xinjiang, no Dutch elm disease pathogens were found on elms, not even an Ophiostoma species (Brasier, 1990). In 1993 a further survey was carried out in the western Himalayas, which led to the discovery of a third DED fungus, Ophiostoma himal-ulmi (Brasier and Mehrotra, 1995). This species proved to be a very aggressive pathogen to European and American elm species, but caused no wilt symptoms on Ulmus wallichiana, its native host. The discovery of this closely related species has led to the suggestion that the eastern Himalaya/Burma region, which is still unsurveyed, could be the origin of O. ulmi and/or O. novo-ulmi, or other DED pathogens (Brasier and Mehrotra, 1995).

description: Natural Dispersal^p^pIn addition to dispersal by its vectors, O. novo-ulmi is only known to be spread to new hosts via root grafts, which frequently occur between neighbouring trees, especially in rows of planted trees. This way of dispersal is very effective, because the inoculum goes directly into the stem and is carried upwards with the sapstream, affecting the whole tree simultaneously. Usually no countermeasures can be taken and the elm tree will be killed soon after infection (Stipes and Campana, 1981; Stipes, 2000). ^p^pVector Transmission^p^pVector transmission is the most important means of dispersal for O. novo-ulmi. It is associated with bark beetles of the genus Scolytus and Hylurgopinus. The main vectors in Europe and western Asia are Scolytus scolytus, S. multistriatus, S. pygmaeus and S. triarmatus. Other, less important or potential vectors of O. novo-ulmi in Europe and western Asia include Scolytus laevis, S. mali, S. kirschi, S. orientalis, S. ensifer, S. sulcifrons, S. zaitzevi, S. schevyrewi semenor, S. jacobsoni, S. japonicus, Pteleobius vittatus and P. kraatzi (Stipes and Campana, 1981). In North America only two species of bark beetles are known to be vectors of O. novo-ulmi: S. multistriatus (introduced from Europe) and the American elm bark beetle Hylurgopinus rufipes. Three North American species of ambrosia beetles have also been named as probable occasional vectors of the disease: Xylosandrus germanus, Xyloterinus politus and Monarthrum mali (Stipes and Campana, 1981).^p^pThe bark beetles breed in the inner bark of cut, diseased, or otherwise weakened elm stems. The dispersing adult beetles fly to healthy elms where they feed (maturation feeding) or directly to declining elms for breeding. During feeding on healthy elms the spores of O. novo-ulmi are introduced into a new host. Scolytus beetles usually feed on twig crotches and prefer vigorously growing young twigs at the crown periphery. Scolytus spp. produce two or more generations each year. The overwintering brood will emerge in May to June and the second brood follows in August. In H. rufipes, one or one-and-a-half generations are produced each year depending on the climate. H. rufipes overwinters either as adult or as larva. For hibernation the adults enter the bark at the base of healthy elm trees, where they are well protected against the cold (Tainter and Baker, 1996). Transmission of the pathogen by H. rufipes occurs either in autumn, when feeding on the lower boles, or more commonly during spring, when feeding in the branches (Stipes and Campana, 1981). Although the endemic H. rufipes is the main vector of DED in northern areas of North America (with winter temperatures below -21°C), the introduced S. multistriatus is the main vector of O. novo-ulmi and O. ulmi in other regions (Haugen, 1998).Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Spores, Hyphae, Fruit Bodies; borne internally; borne externally; invisible.^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants: Spores; borne externally; invisible.^p - Leaves: Spores; borne internally; invisible.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; invisible.^p - Roots: Spores, Hyphae; borne internally; invisible.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Spores, Hyphae, Fruit Bodies; borne internally; invisible.^p - Wood: Spores, Hyphae, Fruit Bodies; borne internally; borne externally; invisible.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. remark: Most of the distribution range of elms today is affected by Dutch elm disease in Europe, western and central Asia and North America. O. novo-ulmi is not yet established in Alberta, Canada, and not present in some states of the USA and some counties of California. These areas have quarantine regulations to prevent introduction of the pathogen Anon., 1995, 2002b). All countries with native or introduced elm populations not already affected by the disease are in danger of becoming infested with O. novo-ulmi in the future. This is emphasised by the recent introduction of the pathogen to New Zealand (Gadgil et al., 2000). The introduction of O. novo-ulmi into eastern Asia is a serious threat, because at least some of the elm species there have been reported to be susceptible and none is immune (Gibbs, 1978; Brasier, 1990). ^p^pO. novo-ulmi is already listed as a quarantine pest in several countries. Countries which list only O. ulmi as quarantine pest are also considered here because not all countries have changed to the new nomenclature. Despite the fact that the pathogen is well established in Europe, it is listed as a quarantine pest in several European countries (Switzerland, Hungary, Poland, Norway, Iceland) (OEPP/EPPO, 1999). Other countries which list it as quarantine pest are Algeria, Morocco (OEPP/EPPO, 1999), Canada (Anon., 2003b), China (Anon., 1991), Australia (Anon., 2003a) and New Zealand (Anon., 2002a). However, O. ulmi and O. novo-ulmi are not listed as quarantine pests in any country of the European Union (OEPP/EPPO, 1999) and are not mentioned on the APHIS list of regulated pests for the USA (Anon., 2000). This may pose a significant risk, because the fact that a particular fungal species has been recorded in a given region does not mean that there is nothing to fear from further introductions of what is believed to be the same species elsewhere (Gibbs, 2001). This is emphasised by the example of O. novo-ulmi, which was introduced into the UK when O. ulmi was already established there. The discovery of the endemic O. himal-ulmi in the Himalayas shows that a number of highly aggressive Dutch elm disease fungi or other pathogens of elm may still be undiscovered in some parts of Asia, awaiting their introduction. ^p^pMost danger of introduction of DED fungi comes from logs and branches with the bark attached (including firewood), loose bark used for mulching and especially elm wood (with the bark attached) used for crates. The latter goes mostly unrecognized and has been the source of introduction in many cases (Sinclair and Campana, 1978). The fungus may also be present in all parts of an infected elm (except for the seeds), but the highest risk for spread of the disease comes from the bark, as it also harbours the vectors of O. novo-ulmi. To date, there have been no reported cases of deliberate introduction of O. novo-ulmi, but this is theoretically possible. International mail may be used for such an intention.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Phytosanitary Measures^p^pThe import of elm wood with the bark attached is not allowed into countries with a quarantine for O. novo-ulmi or O. ulmi (e.g. Anon., 2003a). Debarked elm timber has to be properly treated for import. Treatments can consist of kiln drying, ethyl bromide fumigation or other methods able to disinfect the logs (e.g. Anon., 2003b). All shipments of elm wood have to carry a phytosanitary certificate (FAO, 1997) and are subject to inspection. The shipment of live plants of Ulmus is prohibited to some countries such as China (Anon., 1991). The same quarantine regulations apply to Zelkova spp. in some countries (OEPP/EPPO, 1999), and also to Planera sp. (Anon., 2002b). Although seeds have not been shown to carry the disease, the import of elm seeds is prohibited into India with reference to DED fungi (Anon., 1989).^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pSanitation is the most effective way of controlling the Dutch elm disease fungi and may account for 80% of the total effort in urban control programmes (Stipes, 2000). This method is directed against both the pathogen and its vectors. Sanitation can reduce the probability of infection significantly, but cannot eradicate the pathogen or vector. It involves the destruction (burning) of all elm wood attractive to beetle infestation, such as any elm stems and branches weakened, dying, or dead from the disease or any other cause (Stipes and Campana, 1981). ^p^pRemoval of the entire vascular lesion by pruning can be sufficient for an infected elm to recover from DED. For this approach to be effective, two prerequisites should be taken into account: the elm may not wilt before mid-summer, and early disease detection is necessary, i.e. the elm may not have more than 5% crown damage (Himelick and Ceplecha, 1976). Wilt symptoms observed early in the season are indicative of a DED infection that occurred in a previous year. In this case, the disease will be far more established than is apparent from foliar symptoms, and therapeutic pruning will probably fail. All branches showing characteristic streaking in the outer sapwood are removed. However, if the streaking has reached the stem, the infection will persist in the tree. Cutting tools should be sterilized between different trees. The success of eradicative pruning is limited when bark beetle populations are large, and is most effective in areas where multiple or successive infections are rare (Sinclair and Campana, 1978). Eradicative pruning is mostly used in urban areas, often together with the application of other (chemical) disease treatments, but is not practical in the forest (Haugen, 1998; Stennes, 2000).^p^pRoot grafts have been shown to spread O. novo-ulmi infection between trees, especially in hedgerows (Haugen, 1998). Root severance between infected and healthy trees is therefore a common control measure. A spade or trench-digging machine may be used for the purpose, depending on the size of the tree (Burdekin and Gibbs, 1974).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pExtensive work has been done in Europe and North America to exploit resistance in the host. Most clones developed for resistance to O. ulmi later proved susceptible to O. novo-ulmi. Today a broad range of elm cultivars is available which show at least some resistance to O. novo-ulmi (Heybroek, 1993a; Smalley et al., 1993a; Townsend and Santamour, 1993). However, resistance, especially in American elm (Ulmus americana) is not yet satisfactory. In addition to the slow progress connected to generation period in elms, the main problem of elm breeding is the fact that the basic mechanisms for disease resistance are still not known (Guries and Smalley, 2000). Genetic transformation has been successfully established in several elm species and may lead to the allocation of resistance genes against O. novo-ulmi as well as to the production of resistant elm cultivars (Gartland et al., 2000).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pSeveral attempts have been made for

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe introduction of O. ulmi to North America, Europe and parts of Asia resulted in a severe epidemic of Dutch elm disease during the first half of the twentieth century. Quantitative information on the extent of the damage is rare. For example, no control measures were applied in England but relatively few trees were killed. According to one estimation, 10-20% of the English elm population were killed by O. ulmi (Gibbs, 1978). However, the epidemic caused by O. ulmi in continental Europe was more severe. Between 1930 and 1943, 421,000 of 1,228,000 elms in the Netherlands had to be felled during a control attempt. In some locations in Italy (e.g. near Parma) over 50% of the trees had died by 1935 (Gibbs, 1978). On the whole, between 10 and 40% of the European elm population was killed by O. ulmi (Brasier, 2001). In North America the epidemic caused by O. ulmi started slowly with only a few affected trees, but infection rates reached 50% when control programmes were discontinued during the Second World War (Gibbs, 1978). A proportion of the elm population similar to the one found in Europe may have been killed by O. ulmi in North America, but assessment is difficult because of the overlap of O. ulmi and O. novo-ulmi outbreaks.^p^p^Environmental impact^pMost research on the impact of O. ulmi has focused on urban elms. The environmental impact of the fungus, compared to that of O. novo-ulmi, may be considered only minor. O. ulmi has mostly attacked susceptible trees (clones) in the urban environment which were probably predisposed by other (abiotic) stress factors. The effect of the pathogen on wild elm populations was much lower, as is shown by an example from Austria (Mayer and Reimoser, 1978). ^p^pBefore the introduction of DED fungi, wild elm populations had already suffered from human influences such as lowering of the groundwater table, intensification of harvesting operations and habitat destruction, but the two pandemics of DED have resulted in a dangerous loss in genetic diversity within the Ulmus genus. A European project, in which nine countries are co-operating, was initiated to save this diversity (Collin et al., 2000).^p^p^p^Social impact^pThere is no other tree disease that has become so well known by the public as Dutch elm disease. Elms were once a premier kind of tree planted in urban landscapes in Europe, but they were, and are, even more common in cities throughout the north-east and mid-western USA. In particular, the American elm (Ulmus americana) had been extensively planted there and, with its vase-shape, gave  the streets and boulevards a distinct appearance. Dutch elm disease has had an enormous social impact in these areas and huge efforts are being made in many cities to save their elms, fully supported by the public. Large urban elm populations have been preserved in this way in many American cities (e.g. Minneapolis, Stennes, 2000). Elms are very prominent in the USA, especially in the capital Washington, DC, and form the backbone of the parklands at the Monumental Core and along the National Mall, where they provide a unique American cultural statement (Sherald, 1993). The US national park service is implementing an elaborate management plan to protect this important plantation.^p^pElms have always played an important role in cultural history; the association goes back to prehistoric times (Heybroek, 1993b). For example, elms were used for fodder and in agricultural systems, and the wood was important for the production of tools and wheels as well as for archery (Richens, 1983). It is particularly tragic that a tree that has had so many uses for man is so greatly affected by a disease introduced by man.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pThe disappearance of mature and old elm trees has had a negative effect on biodiversity; however, only few data are available in this respect. remark: C. rosa is of quarantine significance for EPPO, JUNAC and OIRSA. Although C. rosa has only established adventive populations in Mauritius (since ca 1953) and Reunion, it has become a more important pest than C. capitata in Mauritius, suggesting that it could be at least as serious a threat as C. capitata in other areas; C. rosa displaced C. capitata within a few years of its introduction (Orian and Moutia, 1960).

management_info: Very little specific information has been written about the control of C. rosa. Most of the information given here is general information applicable to a large number of fruit fly species. When detected, it is important to gather all fallen and infected host fruits and destroy them. Traps containing male lures should be used to monitor population size and spread continuously (Ramsamy, 1989). Insecticidal protection is possible by using a cover spray or a bait spray (Schwartz, 1993). A bait spray consists of a suitable insecticide (for example, malathion) mixed with a protein bait. Both males and female fruit flies are attracted to protein sources emanating ammonia. Insecticides can therefore be applied to just a few spots in an orchard and the flies will be attracted to these spots. The protein most widely used is hydrolysed protein, but some supplies of this are acid hydrolysed and are highly phytotoxic.Smith and Nannan (1988) have developed a system using autolysed protein; in Malaysia this has been developed into a very effective commercial product derived from brewery waste (developed for Bactrocera spp.).^p^pPhytosanitary Measures^p^pConsignments of potential host fruits from countries where C. rosa occurs should be inspected for symptoms of infestation and those suspected should be cut open in order to look for larvae. It is recommended that such fruits should come from an area where C. rosa does not occur, or from a place of production found free from the pest by regular inspection for 3 months before harvest. By analogy with C. capitata, fruits may also be treated in transit by cold treatment (for example, 18, 20 or 22 days at 0.6, 1.1 or 1.7°C, respectively) or, for certain types of fruits, by vapour heat (for example, keeping at 43°C for 4-6 h) (USDA, 1994).^p^pEthylene dibromide was previously widely used as a fumigant but is now generally withdrawn because of its carcinogenicity. Methyl bromide is less satisfactory as it damages many fruits and reduces their shelf life, although treatment schedules are available (for example, 40 g/m3 for 2 h at 21 29.5°C; USDA, 1994).^p^pPlants of host species transported with roots from countries where C. rosa occurs should be free from soil, or the soil should be treated against puparia. The plants should not carry fruits. The importation of such plants may be prohibited.^p^pBiological Control^p^pIntroductions of parasitoids for biological control of C. rosa and other fruit flies have been made in Mauritius during 1939 and 1957 (Greathead, 1971) and in Reunion during the 1960s and 1970s (Greathead, 1971; OPIE, 1986) but none became established.

potential_eco_desc: 该病是北半球具毁灭性的病害之一，本世纪两次大流行。第一次始于本世纪初至40年代，法国首次报道，从西北欧迅速蔓延到中欧、南欧，至英国、美国，又到中亚和西南亚，造成榆树大面积死亡。美国1930－1935年，处理了250万株死树。第二次在70年代，起源于英国和北美中西部，随后在北美、欧洲、中亚和西南亚蔓延，引起大部分榆树死亡。英国南部1970－1978年230万株榆树有75％死亡，在葡萄牙1979年引起80％榆树损失。

description: 1918年在比利时、法国、荷兰，1930年在北美（俄亥俄州）首次报道了榆枯萎病。20世纪40年代在俄亥俄州榆枯萎病和榆黄化病同时爆发；50年代、60年代在伊利诺斯州的Champaign-Urbana爆发；70年代在纽约州的Ithaca爆发。在Syracuse东部（A区），1975-1985年间，A区所列出的118株榆树中有33％的榆树受到榆枯萎病的侵染。然而由于成功防治，在11年中只有21％的榆树因榆枯萎病而毁灭。1977-1980年间A区榆枯萎病发生率大大降低，归功于1975年开始的诱捕小蠹虫和1979年开始的诱虫树技术。近似发病率（r）从1975-1977年的0.50减少到1977-1980年的0.12。如果1977-1980年的发病率保持不变，到1990年榆枯萎病毁灭的榆树还不到1075年开始时榆树的50％。

description: 以芽孢形式通过空气或雨水传播，繁殖材料与病残体可行远距离传播，但非种传病害。
management_info:
1．农业防治。改善栽培条件，减少遮阴。
2．化学防治。喷洒磷酸盐、丙环唑、氯氧化铜等药剂，可抑制芽孢，减轻病害。最近研究发现，病菌在叶片组织内，产生大量的草酸，它与叶组织中的钙结合成草酸钙，而引起叶组织的分解、落叶，因此可施用熟石灰，以中和病菌产生的草酸，防止落叶，达到防治目的。
3．生物防治。在哥斯达黎加采用木霉或寄生细菌对病菌芽孢进行防治。

management_info: Cultural control measures aimed at reducing inoculum sources such as badly diseased trees and infected shade trees have had some success (Wellman, 1950). As the disease spreads slowly sanitation methods should have a significant impact but may be difficult to execute effectively in smallholder coffee. Application of fungicides continues to be used in areas where the disease is problematic. Bordeaux mixture and other copper fungicides are effective, but lead arsenate sprays were shown to have an eradicant effect (Echandi and Segall, 1958) and became commonly used in Central America. Triazole systemic fungicides are now most effective (Vargas et al., 1990) and application of calcium hydroxide has been shown to suppress symptoms due to the neutralization of oxalic acid produced by the pathogen (Rao and Tewari, 1988). There have been several investigations of the use of biological control agents; Vargas (1984) reduced the disease by applying coffee grindings inoculated with Trichoderma harzianum, antagonistic bacteria isolated from diseased coffee were used by Calvo and Vargas (1989) and Mora et al. (1989), and a Bacillus species was used by Quesada and Jimenez (1996).

host_range: 甜瓜Cucumis melo.
description: In September 2014, a root rot and vine decline was observed on melon (Cucumis meloL.) growing in several greenhouses with 85% disease incidence in Zhejiang Province in eastern mainland China. The samples were collected and identified, based on morphology and molecular diagnostics, the pathogen was identified as Monosporascus cannonballus. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. cannonballus on melon in eastern mainland China, extending the known range of the pathogen in China.  The wide distribution of melon cultivation and the loose transport policy to plant materials, there is a potential risk for disease spread throughout the country. Grafting of melon onto Cucurbita spp. more tolerant to the pathogen would be an effective disease management.
reference_name: First Report of Root Rot and Vine Decline of Melon Caused by Monosporascus cannonballus in Eastern Mainland China

remark: The OEPP/EPPO (1982) quarantine list for plant pests lists N. aberrans sensu lato as not yet introduced into the EPPO region and requiring zero tolerance for all countries. N. aberrans is considered to be an A1 quarantine organism for the EPPO region (OEPP/EPPO, 1984). The evidence suggests that the Andean populations of N. aberrans would be able to survive in north European and other temperate potato-growing areas (Jatala, 1979; Jatala and Kaltenbach, 1979). The wide host range of N. aberrans sensu lato suggests that it could also threaten a number of other temperate crops. Thus, N. aberrans sensu lato infesting sugarbeets in the USA may also be of potential importance in the EPPO region, although perhaps mainly in the southern, warmer areas.^p^pPhytosanitary measures^p^pN. aberrans sensu lato belongs to the group of South American potato pests that justify post-entry quarantine procedures in the EPPO region, together with equivalent checks before export (OEPP/EPPO, 1990). Only material for scientific purposes should normally be imported from South America. From other countries where N. aberrans sensu lato is known to occur, the simplest practical measure is to restrict the importation of soil, including that accompanying plants.^p^pUK plant health measures are based principally on the Plant Health (Great Britain) Order 1993 and the similar Order covering forestry pests, both implementing EU Directive 77/93/EEC. N. aberrans is a nematode species of quarantine status. EU marketing schemes require visual freedom from quality affecting nematodes. Soil samples normally comprise 500 g of soil from 100 cores per 4 ha (or less) (Ward and Hockland, 1996).^p^pN. aberrans is regarded as a high risk nematode species in Taiwan (Tsay, 1997).

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe control of Nacobbus aberrans sensu lato is described by Inserra et al. (1985), Stone and Burrows (1985) and in the review of the genus by Manzanilla-Lopez et al. Soil fumigation and granular nematicides gave good control of N. aberrans sensu lato (Inserra et al., 1985; Brodie, 1993), but their high cost and pollution risk makes them unsuitable. The use of soil fumigants such as 1,3 dichloropropene and aldicarb was suggested by Ambrogioni and Tacconi (1992). In sugarbeet fields in Wyoming, USA, aldicarb reduced galls caused by N. aberrans sensu lato by nearly half compared with untreated controls, although the reduction was not significant. Significant reduction of nematode galling occurred with combined aldicarb and iprodione drench treatment, aldicarb and iprodione spray treatments did not significantly reduce galling (Beaupre et al., 1990).^p^pAldicarb, carbofuran or Telone treatments of sugarbeet fields in Nebraska, USA, significantly reduced the infection level of N. aberrans sensu lato. Imilla Negra in Peru (Cornejo Quiroz, 1977).^p^p^Resistant Varieties^p^pBreeding for resistance has shown some promising preliminary results (Cahuana et al., 1975; Finetti Sialer, 1990; PROINPA, 1991), but resistant potato cultivars are not yet available (see Manzanilla-Lopez et al., 2002).^p^pWhen tested by inoculation, five varieties of Capsicum annuum showed no resistance to N. aberrans sensu lato (Sisler and Casuarang, 1983). In the roots of the resistant (incompatible) hybrid B 25 from S. tuberosum ssp. andigena, development was inhibited by the formation of necrotic cells surrounding the invading nematode. The clone of Solanum sparsipilum 7601217.7 showed the presence of physical barriers that delayed nematode invasion; however, development of the syncytium and of the nematodes were almost the same as observed in the susceptible potato cultivar Revolucion (Finetti Sialer, 1990).^p^pA list of world potato germplasm collections giving resistant, moderately resistant and susceptible accessions with respect to N. aberrans sensu lato has been provided by Huaman (1982). Among the potato varieties introduced into Argentina from the Netherlands, Blanka, Estima and Baraka were found to be tolerant of N. aberrans sensu lato, while some native species of the series Andigena were immune (Anon., 1979). potential_eco_desc: 该线虫为分布广、寄主多和为害严重的内寄生线虫，其危害可造成皮层坏死、根瘿，严重影响植物生长。主要为害的农作物有马铃薯，甜菜、大白菜、黄瓜、甘蔗、番茄，产量损失可高达20％。

在安第斯山脉和玻利维亚和南部的秘鲁，异常珍珠线虫是三种主要对马铃薯有害的线虫之一。
在玻利维亚和南部的秘鲁，很大部分的马铃薯区域都被异常珍珠线虫所侵袭。
在内布拉斯加州30%的旷野地区，被异常珍珠线虫所侵袭。同时，蒙大纳，怀俄明州，南部的达科他，美国科罗拉多州，堪萨斯州，也有更多的其他害虫侵袭。异常珍珠线虫可能引起某些作物常量降低高达90%。
在英格兰和联合王国，在温室大棚里发现异常珍珠线虫侵袭马铃薯，茄属植物，甜菜植物，生菜。然而，在波兰和俄罗斯的温室大棚里没有发现异常珍珠线虫对作物的明显影响。 N. aberrans is one of the three main nematode pests of potato in the Andean regions of Peru and Bolivia (Anon., 1973), and the most important in the Puno Department of southern Peru. Most potato fields in southern Peru and Bolivia are heavily infested with N. aberrans (Jatala, 1979).
About 30% of sugarbeet fields in Nebraska are infested with N. aberrans, with more scattered infestations in Montana, Wyoming, South Dakota, Colorado and Kansas (Caveness, 1959; Thorne and Malek, 1968). Yield reductions caused by N. aberrans may be as high as 90% in some crops.
Populations of N. aberrans attacking tomatoes, Solanum nigrum, mangold and lettuce under glass in England, UK (Franklin, 1959) and under glass in Holland and Russia have not assumed economic importance.

host_range: This is the first report of Monilinia fructicola causing postharvest fruit decay of strawberry in the United States.
description: In early summer of 2016, signs of Monilinia spp. decay were observed on ‘Monterey’ strawberry (Fragaria × ananassaDuch.) fruit, harvested from organically grown plants in a high tunnel at the USDA-AFRS in Kearneysville, WV. The harvested, asymptomatic strawberries were incubated on metal screens in plastic boxes in the laboratory for 5 days at which time abundant production of sporodochia occurred. Both morphological and genetic data were confirmed the pathogen was Monilinia fructicola. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. fructicola causing postharvest fruit decay of strawberry in the United States.

description: In June and July 2016, nectarine (Prunus persica var. nectarina) fruit (cv. Adriana) with symptoms of brown rot were collected from a 19-year-old commercial orchard (3.8 ha) located in the Podgorica region in Montenegro. Symptoms could be found throughout the orchard and included twig blight and rotted fruit with large, brown lesions covered by grayish brown sporodochia that consequently resulted in fruit mummification, which caused considerable yield losses. The pathogen was identified as Monilinia fructicola by morphological characteristics, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. fructicola in Montenegro. Peach and nectarines are among the most important fruit trees in Montenegro, with cultivated area of 92.5 ha in 2015. The spread of M. fructicola could have a great impact to peach and nectarine production of the country.
remark: Monilinia fructicola is listed in the EPPO A2 list of quarantine organisms for Europe; however.

description: In August 2015, brown rot was observed on the fruit of ‘Pristine’ apples at Meig’s Farm, at the Throckmorton Purdue Agricultural Center in Lafayette, IN, and was responsible for over 50% crop loss. host_range: 樱桃Cerasus pseudocerasus.
description: In April 2014, mature cherry fruit (Cerasus pseudocerasus cv. Wupi) displaying fruit rot symptoms were observed in five cherry orchards in Chongqing Municipality in Southwestern China. At each orchard, the incidence of fruit rot symptoms on mature fruit exceeded 2%. Based on morphological characteristics, PCR identification and the pathogenicity test showed that the causal agent was Monilinia fructicola. To our knowledge, this is the first report of brown rot caused by M. fructicola on Chinese sour cherry in Chongqing and represents a considerable threat to the regional cherry industry. The closest report of M. fructicola on cherry is in Liaoning Province, located more than 2000 km away, in northeastern China.
reference_name: First Report of Brown Rot Caused by Monilinia fructicola on Chinese Sour Cherry (Cerasus pseudocerasus) in Southwestern China

host_range: 苹果（果实） Malus (fruit)
description: In September 2013, a ‘Jonamac’ apple was found with brown rot symptoms on a tree at harvest in a commercial orchard in Lancaster County, PA, which has a history of brown rot disease on stone fruit. Approximately 1% of the apple trees within walking distance of affected stone fruit had at least one apple on the tree with brown rot symptoms. Based on biological detection, molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity test showed that the causal agent was Monilinia fructicola. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. fructicola causing brown rot on apple fruit in Pennsylvania. Although M. fructicola is a common pathogen in the United States, other Monilinia sp., such as M. fructigena and M. polystroma, are regulated pests. As a result, monitoring brown rot pathogens, especially infecting apple both pre and postharvest, could lead to early detection of these regulated pests if introduced.
reference_name: First Report of Brown Rot on Apple Fruit Caused by Monilinia fructicola in Pennsylvania

potential_eco_desc: In 2010 and 2013，in one location, brown rot was observed on fruit of the cornelian cherry cultivar Elegans. description: Monilinia fructigena is the only Monilinia species reported to infect cornelian cherry, but there is only a single report of it occurring in the United States. In August of 2010 and 2013, in one location, brown rot was observed on fruit of the cornelian cherry cultivar Elegans. In both instances, only ‘Elegans’ fruit was infected while neighboring ‘Sunrise’ exhibited no symptoms in the field, and lesions did not appear to develop into shoot blight. The samples were collected and identified. Pathogen was confirmed to be M. fructicola on the basis of morphological characteristics and sequence analysis. To our knowledge, this is the first fulfillment of Koch's postulates demonstrating that M. fructicola can infect cornelian cherry. A previous report by H?hnel in 1918 described infection by Lambertella corni-mas of a cornelian cherry in Austria; however, the taxonomic details presented are consistent with M. fructigena.
reference_name: First Report of Brown Rot (Monilinia fructicola) on the Dogwood, Cornelian Cherry (Cornus mas)

management_info: 欧李果园中发病后期的果实变得皱缩干瘪，成为僵果。僵果是一团被菌物菌丝完全穿透的干的果实组织，在地上或留在枝条越冬，它们是来春最好的侵染源，僵果中的分生孢子很容易脱落并随风雨传播，因此，彻底清除越冬菌源，注意果园的卫生，及时喷施杀菌剂是进行防治的必要措施。
remark: M. fructicola为世界上的检疫性真菌。

remark: M. fructicola is an EPPO A1 pest (OEPP/EPPO, 1988) and is also a quarantine pest for IAPSC. This corresponds to two major stone fruit-growing areas (Europe and the Mediterranean area, South Africa) where the fungus does not occur, but it also presents a risk for the Middle East and China. Monilinia laxa already occurs in most areas at risk from M. fructicola and it is difficult to predict what would be the consequence of the presence of the two fungi. In North America, where both occur, there are complex interactions of host species and climate with the result that each of the fungi is more damaging on particular hosts in certain areas. On this basis, the total impact of the two species could be expected to be greater than that of M. laxa alone.

management_info: Zehr (1982) reviewed control methods in North America. Control can be achieved by chemical and biological means as well as by the utilization of resistant cultivars.^p^pBenomyl and thiophanate-methyl (Montero et al., 1985), vinclozolin (Brackmann et al., 1984), iprodione and triforine (Harman and Beever, 1987), and bitertanol (Takamura and Ochiai, 1989) have been reported to be very effective against M. fructicola. However, the need to spray several times during the growing period in stone fruit orchards has led to a build-up of fungicide resistance in M. fructicola. Strains resistant to most of the commonly used fungicides can be found, especially to benzimidazoles (Elmer and Gaunt, 1986) and dicarboximides (Elmer and Gaunt, 1988). Studies in New Zealand showed that out of 1292 naturally sampled isolates of M. fructicola, 19% were tolerant of dicarboximides (Elmer and Gaunt, 1986). In laboratory studies, strains were selected which showed resistance to sterol biosynthesis inhibitors, demethylation inhibitors and morpholine (Nuninger-Ney et al., 1989).^p^pIn many countries, fungicides are only authorized for preharvest use on stone fruits but, where authorized, a postharvest dip is also a possibility, preferably using a fungicide different from that applied in the field. Various alternative methods are being tested for postharvest control. Bacillus subtilis gives as effective control as benomyl for postharvest treatment of brown rot (Pusey, 1989). Spotts et al. (1998) propose a combination of preharvest iprodione, postharvest treatment with the yeast Cryptococcus infirmo-miniatus and modified atmosphere packaging to control storage rot in sweet cherry. Other treatments examined include various kinds of ultraviolet irradiation, hot water treatments and use of short-chain fatty acids (acetic, propionic) as fumigants.^p^pSeveral cultivars are available which are especially resistant to fruit infection by M. fructicola (Layne, 1985; Feliciano et al., 1987).^p^pBecause symptoms on planting material are likely to be insignificant, it may be prudent to prohibit its entry from countries where M. fructicola occurs. Alternatively, such planting material should come from a recognized certification scheme (OEPP/EPPO, 1991/1992) in a region where M. fructicola does not occur.^p^pFruits of species of Prunus from infested countries in the Northern Hemisphere will arrive in Europe at a time when there is a relatively low risk that fruit trees might be infected. However, fruits from the Southern Hemisphere will arrive at a high-risk period and particular care should be given to their inspection. The same considerations apply reciprocally for countries at risk in the Southern Hemisphere. Fruits should come from an area where M. fructicola does not occur or the consignment should come from a source found free from M. fructicola six weeks before harvest and treated according to a recommended procedure such as OEPP/EPPO (1990).

马铃薯孢囊线虫侵染寄主根系后，地 上 部 无 特殊识别症状。由于根系受 害，植 株 对 水 分 和 营 养 物质的吸收能力降低，地上部表现矮化、黄化和缺水缺肥等 症 状，在干 旱 条 件 下 叶 片 表 现 凋 萎 症 状，中午时刻凋萎症状表现更加明显。田间病株分布不均匀，有发病 中 心，随着马铃薯的连续种植和农事操作，发病团连年扩大，最后全田发病。马铃薯孢囊线虫危害后常常使马铃薯植株早衰和侧根增生。在马铃薯开花期，受害植株的根部可见到金黄色或白色的球形雌虫，马铃薯金线虫雌虫成熟后逐渐呈金黄色，最后变成深褐色，而受害植株根部的马铃薯白线虫雌虫直至死亡仍为白色，在马铃薯块茎上也能观察到白雌虫。马铃 薯 收 获 后，根 系 上 的 孢 囊遗落到土壤中。
人类活动是马铃薯孢囊线虫远距离传播和扩散的唯一途径。马铃薯孢囊线虫远距离传播到一个新
的国家或地区最可能的途径是孢囊随粘附在马铃薯种薯、苗木、花卉鳞球茎或马铃薯块茎上的土壤传播。在田间自然条件下，马铃薯金线虫和白线虫可通过水流、灌溉水和雨水传播，也可以通过农机具和农事操作等传播，大风也有传播作用。

host_range: Globodera pallida  were observed on the roots of Ro1-resistant potatoes (Solanum tuberosum L.) in Abashiri, Hokkaido.
description: In August 2015, mature Globodera females and cysts were observed on the roots of Ro1-resistant potatoes (Solanum tuberosum L.) collected from a field in Abashiri, Hokkaido. Females adhered to roots were white or pale yellow, and were clearly distinguishable from G. rostochiensis females, which are brilliant gold. The eggs and second-stage juveniles (J2s) obtained and inoculated to Ro1-resistant potatoes, new cysts were observed on the potato roots after two months. Morphological and molecular analyses established the identity of the species as the pale potato cyst nematode G. pallida. This is the first report of the detection of G. pallida in Japan.
reference_name: First Report of the Pale Potato Cyst Nematode, Globodera pallida, on Potato in Japan

description: Up to now, only G. rostochiensis was reported from Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2011. A systematic survey on the presence of PCN on entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina started in 2011. During the PCN survey, each year 120 soil samples of 1.5 liters were collected in the Republic of Srpska, one of the two entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The samples were collected by soil auger 10 cm in length with a diameter of 1.5 cm consisting of 100 cores. Entire samples were processed by Seinhorst elutriator. In autumn of 2012, PCN viable cysts were found in two soil samples originating from one field. From one sample, 12 cysts were extracted, and 2 from another sample. The morphology of cysts and second stage juveniles and molecular analysis established the identity of this species as pale cyst nematode G. pallid. To our knowledge, only one field was found infested with G. pallida during the 3-year PCN survey in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
reference_name: First Report of the Pale Potato Cyst Nematode Globodera pallida from Bosnia and Herzegovina

remark: Potato cyst nematodes are A2 quarantine pests for EPPO (OEPP/ EPPO, 1978, 1981). They are also of quarantine significance for APPPC and NAPPO. Virtually all areas within the EPPO region that grow potatoes are already contaminated with potato cyst nematode. These areas are generally closely monitored. It is important to keep seed potato areas free of potato cyst nematode. Domestic measures and import controls are justified as they help to reduce spread and introduction of new pathotypes into already colonised areas. Globodera rostochiensis still seems to be the dominant species throughout Europe with the exception of England, UK, where G. pallida is common.^p ^pPhytosanitary measures^p ^pTo prevent further spread of potato cyst nematode into uninfested areas, several methods are used. These include international and national legislation on the movement of seed potatoes, nursery stock, flower bulbs and soil (CEC, 1969).^p ^pThe specific EPPO quarantine requirements (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) for these nematodes are that fields in which seed potatoes or rooted plants for export are grown are inspected by taking soil samples according to an EPPO-recommended method (OEPP/EPPO, 1991) and must be found free from viable cysts of both species of potato cyst nematode. The sampling must be performed after harvest of the previous potato crop.

management_info: Crop Rotation^p^pCrop rotation is frequently used to reduce population densities of potato cyst nematode. The major commercial hosts of the two potato cyst nematode species are in the plant family Solanaceae, namely potato, tomato and aubergine, all important cash crops. Where these crops are grown in monoculture for several seasons in infested soil, nematode densities increase to extremely high levels and crop yields become uneconomic. To reduce nematode population densities, non-host crops such as barley are grown between host crops (Whitehead, 1995). The length of the rotation and the crops used can have variable effects on the yield and the potato cyst nematode density. In South American countries, slightly different regimes are used and may include fallow, with intervening crops of lima beans, maize, barley or wheat. The annual decline rate in soil of Globodera pallida is, in general, slower than that of Globodera rostochiensis. When the reduction of potato cyst nematode is too slow by rotation alone, other additional methods can be used; for example, trap cropping can hasten the reduction of population densities. ^p^p^Trap Cropping^p^pTrap cropping is a simple method that has been used successfully for the reduction of cyst nematode populations (Halford et al., 1999). Sufficient crop growth time is allowed for the nematodes to penetrate the roots and develop into young adults (5-6 weeks), but not enough time for them to form new eggs. Potato cyst nematode populations can be reduced very quickly as long as the grower removes and destroys the crop, including the nematodes in the roots. If left too late, the nematode density will increase but, if the crop is removed in time, the nematode density is reduced and there will be a significant yield benefit for any subsequent potato crop. G. pallida can be reduced by as much as 80% per annum and even greater reductions were found when ethopropos was used in the soil before the first of two potato trap crops; almost 100% control  was achieved (Mugniery and Balandras, 1984). The use of other non-tuberous solanaceous plant species to stimulate hatching has proved very efficient in Dutch studies. Non-hosts that are well adapted to temperate conditions, in this case Solanum sisymbrifolium, proved capable of inducing large hatches of potato cyst nematode juveniles. Solanum sisymbrifolium is fully resistant to potato cyst nematode, therefore eliminating the risk of increasing potato cyst nematode density (Scholte, 2000).^p^p^Soil Solarization^p^pSolarization is a good method of killing nematodes in hot climates. The soil is covered with two layers of polyethylene sheeting, allowing the soil underneath to heat up to temperatures of 60°C or more. In cooler climates solarization is much less effective.^p^p^Resistant Cultivars^p^pCertain European cultivars of potato have resistance (often only partial) to European pathotypes of potato cyst nematode but some South American populations are more virulent than European populations and are able to overcome the resistance in European cultivars (Kort and Jaspers, 1973; Turner et al., 1995). Thus, strict quarantine measures remain essential. Studies at the International Potato Centre (CIP) in Lima, Peru, on 3000 accessions of potato, have focused on the two locally predominant pathotypes of G. pallida: P4A and P5A. A more virulent pathotype (P6A) has emerged and been selected in some areas. Variety of cultivars (tolerant, resistant and partially resistant) has an important part to play in maintaining an acceptable balance of pathotypes. For example, Maris Piper is a popular potato cultivar in the UK and has full resistance to UK populations of G. rostochiensis but no resistance to G. pallida. Its widespread cultivation has selected G. pallida and it is now recognized that other types of cultivars (e.g. tolerant ones) should be included in the rotation to avoid this problem. The soil is covered with two layers of polyethylene sheeting, allowing the soil underneath to heat up to temperatures of 60癈 or more. In cooler climates solarization is much less effective. Kuhn第一次应用化学方法防治线虫在1881年，但直到1943年才被广泛应用。最初用D-D，随后利用EDB，DBCP等防治。它们能有效地接触杀线剂，但必须在适宜的天气条件才能有最大影响。这些高水溶性物质能被轻松地淋洗出土层。免熏杀线剂需要的剂量少于熏剂，但在土壤中保持的时间与熏剂差不多。它们以颗粒状在植物栽培季节通过撒播，行播，条播施入土中。有时在作物生长中期需二次施入。 Kuhn first used chemicals as a nematode control method in 1881, but chemicals were not used extensively for this purpose until 1943 (Carter, 1943). The first attempts used D-D (1,2-dichloropropane - 1,3-dichloropropene mixtures). This led to other chemical control agents, such as ethylene dibromide (EDB), 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP), chloropicrin and methyl bromide.The granular oximecarbamates oxamyl and aldicarb are more effective on cyst nematodes that produce only one generation a year. They are effective contact nematicides but must be applied in appropriate weather conditions to have maximum impact. They are highly water soluble so can easily be leached out of the soil layers in which they are required.Non-fumigant nematicides are used in smaller amounts then fumigants but usually persist in the soil as long as fumigants. They are applied as granules in broadcast, row or narrow band treatments at the time of planting. In some cases a second application may be made at mid-season. 生物防治方法抵抗马铃薯包囊线虫是当前研究的热点。20世纪90年代晚期，多数的研究都集中在真菌和细菌防治。一些研究人员利用盆钵研究马铃薯金线虫的生物防治。将这种方法应用到大田上是困难的。原因如下，实施防治的尺度必须事先决定，接种菌对大田中存在的微生物群落的影响必须知道。黄萎病菌侵染盆钵中的雌性幼虫，但对于线虫密度较低的马铃薯田则影响较小。生物防治领域的进步要求更好地了解马铃薯包囊线虫的种群动力学和它们的寄生物。许多影响的因素，如寄主植物，根系分泌物的作用，土壤类型以及防治的寄生微生物在某一时刻相互影响。同样，马铃薯包囊线虫在不同的生活史阶段更易受真菌的侵染。 Biological control agents active against potato cyst nematode are currently the subject of intense study.The majority of studies in the late 1990s have concentrated on the fungal control agents Verticillium, Hirsutella and Arthrobotrys, and the bacterium Pasteuria. Several workers (e.g. Roessner, 1986) have studied biological control of G. rostochiensis in pots and in vitro. This work is difficult to transfer to the field for several reasons. For example, the form and volume in which to apply the control agent must be decided, and how the inoculum reacts to the microbial population already present in the field must be determined. Verticillium chlamydosporium will infect young females in pots but is less effective when potatoes are grown in the presence of low nematode population densities. Progress in the area of biological control requires a better understanding of the population dynamics of potato cyst nematode and their parasites (Davies, 1998; Davies et al., 1991). A number of factors interact, such as plant host, the action of root exudates, soil type and the mode of parasitism of the control micro-organism at any one point in time. Also, potato cyst nematode may be more susceptible to infection by any one fungus at different points in its life- cycle.

据估计，每年与植物病原线虫有关的损失达1000亿美元。英国每年由马铃薯包囊线虫引起的损失大约几千万美元，整个欧洲的损失是英国的几倍。马铃薯是五种最重要的食物和作物之一。马铃薯包囊线虫尤其在气候温和区和失去抵抗性的病毒病变发生区分布及其广泛。而马铃薯白线虫引起的结果更糟，具有较好抵抗性的出口栽培作物也常被侵染。伤害与每单位土壤的可孵化线虫卵的数量和畸形块茎的重量有关。最初描述这种关系的模型是Seinhorst 的模型。模型后来被改进能够适应大田中不同样品，环境和种群密度等条件。其他研究也表明了线虫引起的作物产量损失。 It has been estimated that plant parasitic nematodes are responsible for losses of $100 billion annually (Lilley et al., 1999). For potato cyst nematodes (PCN) in the UK, loss is estimated at around ?0 million per annum and for Europe several times this amount. Potatoes are one of the top five important food and cash crops. PCN cause extensive damage, particularly in temperate areas and particularly when virulent pathotypes occur and any resistance has failed. The situation is worse with G. pallida, where commercial cultivars with good resistance are still few and often have undesirable characteristics. Damage is related to the number of viable eggs per unit of soil, and is reflected in the weight of tubers produced. One of the first models to describe this relationship was that of Seinhorst (1965). This model has subsequently been improved upon and adapted to take into consideration the various soil types, environments and population densities that occur in field situations (Been et al., 1995.) Studies by other workers (Elston et al., 1991; Phillips et al., 1991) have also provided information on how nematodes cause yield losses. 在英国，马铃薯白线虫引起严重损失。密度为0-24粒卵每克土，损失为6.25吨每公顷，密度为40-160粒卵每克土壤，损失为1.67吨每公顷。最大粮食损失量为每公顷22吨。
