potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pX. fastidiosa precludes a profitable commercial production of susceptible bunch grapes (Vitis vinifera) in most of the south-eastern USA, where the pathogen is endemic in natural vegetation, vectors abound, a mild winter climate allows good bacterial survival, and temperatures during the spring and summer support rapid bacterial growth. It causes severe localized losses in California and western Texas, USA, and Mexico. Peach and plum crops in the coastal plain of the Gulf of Mexico and the southern Atlantic states (Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana) in the USA are severely affected by phony disease.^p^pLosses to X. fastidiosa caused by tree leaf scorches in a growing number of tree species (oaks, mulberry, maple, sweet gum, sycamore (plane), elm) do not ordinarily include direct mortality and have not been calculated, but are probably substantial. Sycamore leaf scorch has destroyed young plantations for sycamore pulp wood (Leininger et al., 2001). During the 1990s, a strain of X. fastidiosa that causes a lethal disease of oleander in California (Hendson et al., 2001), and the rapid dissemination of citrus strains in Brazil illustrated the rapidity with which new strains can spread. ^p^pCitrus variegated chlorosis causes major losses in Brazil and the Missiones district of Argentina. According the Fundecitrus sampling (http://www.fundecitrus.com.br/english/est_cvc_us.html#inc_cvc), three major citrus regions had 44-63% of commercial trees with fruit symptoms in 2005. It will probably ultimately affect citrus production in all South American citrus east of the Andes. Plum leaf scorch causes the loss of entire orchards in Brazil and Paraguay within several years after the disease first appears in orchards. ^p^pCoffee leaf scorch has caused uncalculated losses, especially in some newer coffee cultivars. It has the potential to become a major new problem in regions with high populations of xylem sap-feeders, all of which are likely to be vectors. ^p^pIn the USA, within the main areas where X. fastidiosa occurs naturally (coastal plains of the Gulf of Mexico), Vitis vinifera and V. labrusca cannot be cultivated because they are rapidly infected due to high rates of natural spread. As a consequence, only selections of V. rotundifolia (muscadine) and specially bred resistant hybrids can be cultivated. The same situation exists throughout tropical America. In California, however, X. fastidiosa occurs only in 'hot spots'. V. vinifera has to be cultivated outside these hot spots. There have been considerable losses in the past, before this situation was clarified. Vector habitats can be eliminated as a preventative measure, but this is not possible in all situations. Insecticide treatment against its vectors has been only partially successful (Purcell, 1979). Antibiotic treatment of grapevines against X. fastidiosa is not effective enough for commercial use and has unfavourable health and environmental characteristics. The recent establishment in California of an invasive species, Homalodisca coagulata, dramatically increased the risks of Pierce's disease losses (Blua et al., 1999; Purcell and Saunders, 1999a). ^p^pPierce's disease is thus a major constraint on grapevine production in the USA and tropical AmericaIt does not occur in all grapevine-producing areas of the USA largely because of climatic constraints. However, the incidence of the disease can dramatically increase with the introduction of new vectors, as illustrated in California with Homalodisca coagulata.^p^pBy contrast, phony disease of peach does not kill trees or cause dieback, but it does significantly reduce the size and number of fruits. An analysis of biophysical effects on peach trees (Anderson and French,1987) found the disease was extremely important in the south-eastern USA in the 1940s, when about half of the trees in 5-year-old orchards were often found to be affected and older orchards entirely so. However, t
description: Phony disease of peach spread within the south-eastern USA from the 1890s until about 1930 (Turner and Pollard, 1959), and the spread of citrus variegated chlorosis disease of orange throughout Brazil in the 1990s (Laranjeira, 1997) was documented. The origins of these strains are unknown but are likely to be endemic to unknown regions of the Americas.
author: CPC2006

description: X. fastidiosa is dispersed by its vectors on a local scale. Vectors could also be carried internationally on plants, or fruits, of grapevine, peach or other plants. Tests of grape fruit clusters as an acquisition source for feeding vectors resulted in no transmission by an efficient vector (Purcell and Saunders 1995). Vector eggs are inserted into plant tissues, making visual detection difficult. The bacterium is not passed through the eggs of the vectors. Immature vectors (nymphs) do not retain infectivity after moulting but can rapidly reacquire the bacterium by feeding on infected plants. The bacterium could be spread in planting material, but this has not been considered a major risk for grapevine in North America, where such material does not survive long enough to present a hazard (Goheen and Hopkins, 1988). Hot-water treatments (50°C for 20 min, 45°C for 180 minutes) eliminates viable bacteria from dormant cuttings (Goheen et al., 1973). X. fastidiosa has presumably reached the limit of its natural distribution in America, so that infected planting material presents a relatively minor risk of introduction and establishment. The situation in the EPPO region is quite different, since large areas of susceptible grapevines are at risk, and the bacterium could readily be introduced on grapevine planting material or in a wide range of species of symptomless plant hosts from which vector spread may be possible. Of greatest importance in preventing the establishment of X. fastidiosa diseases in Europe is to prevent the introduction and establishment of a vector that overwinters as an adult, thus being able to carry the pathogen through the winter and establish infections during spring. A prime candidate is the leafhopper Homalodisca coagulata, which rapidly invaded California, USA, and shortly thereafter became abundant in French Polynesia and Hawaii. This sharpshooter has an extremely wide host range, and climate-matching models predict it could become established in southern Europe and in subtropical and tropical Africa and Asia (Hoddle, 2004).^p^pVector transmission^p^pIntroduction of new vectors can radically change the epidemiology of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa, as demonstrated in southern California in the late 1990s (Blua et al., 1999; Purcell and Saunders, 1999a). Vector abundance, host plant preferences, and other behaviour (flight, transmission efficiency) are key components of the rate of spread of X. fastidiosa. ^p^pAgricultural practices^p^pPlanting of X. fastidiosa-free trees in new citrus groves is a key control component of citrus variegated chlorosis in Brazil. Movement of vegetative propagative materials may introduce the bacterium over long distances.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Fruits (inc. Pods): borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Leaves: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Roots: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain): borne internally; visible under light microscope.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - Wood.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Conveyances (transport Vehicles): Bacteria In Living Vector Insects (Purcell and Saunders 1995)^p - Mail: Bacteria In Living Vector Insects Or Plants (dormant Or Non-dormant). Cultured Bacteria Are Highly Infectious To Plant Wounds That Introduce Bacterial Cells Into Xylem Tissues^p - Travellers And Baggage: Bacteria In Living Vector Insects Or Plants (dormant Or Non-dormant)

remark: The greatest threats are to mild winter regions with one or more of the following crops: grapevines, citrus, almond, stone fruits (Prunus spp.), coffee, oleander, lucerne or where the tree species that can be potentially affected by leaf scorch diseases occur.^p^pEPPO considers X. fastidiosa as an A1 quarantine pest (OEPP/EPPO, 1989) and it is also a quarantine pest for COSAVE. In the EPPO region, it is clear that the grapevine strain of X. fastidiosa has the potential to kill large numbers of grapevines and to make areas unfit for growing V. vinifera. Its vectors in North America do not occur in the EPPO region, but vector capacity is so non-specific that one could certainly expect European Cicadellinae (e.g., Cicadella viridis) or Cercopidae to transmit the bacterium if introduced. After the recent introduction and spread of the vector Homalodisca coagulata in California, USA, this leafhopper has become extremely abundant on citrus and other crops in southern California (Sorensen and Gill, 1996). This illustrates that this exotic vector species can become abundant in Mediterranean climates, despite originating in a humid subtropical region (south-eastern USA). The main danger in the long term in Europe is that X. fastidiosa could become established in natural vegetation which would then act as a reservoir for infection of vineyards or other susceptible crops or forest trees. It is less likely that Pierce's disease would become a problem in the production of planting material, for it is easily detected, can be prophylactically eliminated by hot-water treatment, and is rapidly self-eliminating if introduced into fields. Nevertheless, infected planting material could introduce the disease to new areas. X. fastidiosa is only likely to establish as a serious problem in the warmer parts of the EPPO region such as the southern Iberian and Italian peninsulas and the lowlands of Greece, which have winter temperatures approaching those of the southern USA. Its persistence in the cooler climate of Kosovo, former Yugoslavia, over several years suggests Pierce's disease could also become established in coastal parts of southern France, and northern Italy. Information on the incidence and severity of the disease in the former Yugoslavia was not available as of early 1998. The potential natural range and severity of Pierce's disease in Europe may depend on the distribution and biology of potential vectors and is accordingly rather difficult to assess. ^p^pThe South American strain on citrus also presents a major risk, for the climatic conditions of Mediterranean countries seem favourable to its development. The reported damage in Brazil suggests potential damage even greater than for the grapevine disease. No critical evaluation of possible European vectors has yet been made, but the arguments developed above for grapevine should certainly also apply to citrus.^p^pThe peach strain is relatively less important, but X. fastidiosa still presents a definite danger for peaches, plums, almonds, oaks and, sensu lato, for other fruit and amenity trees (see Hosts) (Dunez, 1981).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Phytosanitary Measures^p^pGrapevine-growing countries should prohibit or severely restrict importation of grapevine planting material from countries where X. fastidiosa occurs. As recommended by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1990), if planting material is imported under licence, it should be maintained in post-entry quarantine for 2 years and shown to be free from the pest. Imported plants and fruits should be free from vectors, possibly by use of an appropriate treatment. A temperature treatment has been shown to eliminate the bacterium (45°C for at least 3 h) (Goheen et al., 1973), and may have potential as a phytosanitary measure. ^p^pCitrus-growing countries should similarly prohibit or severely restrict importation of citrus planting material from South America. Peach and other Prunus material from a country where the peach or plum strain occurs should come from a reliable certification scheme, with particular emphasis on preventing re-infection of healthy material via the vectors.^p^pWhile the hazard presented by X. fastidiosa in other hosts (oak, plane, maple and others) still has to be evaluated, inspection services should be aware that these hosts and the many symptomless hosts also present a certain risk.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control of Xylella diseases has not been successful in the field. Tetracycline drenches cause a temporary remission of symptoms in potted grapevines (Hopkins and Mortenson, 1971).

potential_eco_desc: Leaf scald caused by Xanthomonas albilineans is a destructive disease of sugarcane, as it causes severe economic losses. In Beihai, Laibin, and Baise, Guangxi Province, the average disease incidence of cultivars Guitang46 and Guitang06-2081 were 44.6 and 50.1%, respectively.
description: In June 2016, symptoms of leaf scald were observed on the newly-bred sugarcane cultivars Guitang46 and Guitang06-2081 in Beihai, Laibin, and Baise, Guangxi Province, China. Diseased plant samples were collected and bacterial colonies were isolated. The pathogen was identified as Xanthomonas albilineans by sequences analysis and the pathogenicity tests. To our knowledge, this is the first report of X. albilineans causing plant disease in mainland China.  Xanthomonas albilineans can be easily transmitted by vegetative propagation of sugarcane.
remark: Xanthomona albilineans is a quarantine pathogen for sugarcane germplasm imported into China.

potential_eco_desc: Leaf scald was responsible for heavy losses in sugarcane at the beginning of the century when noble canes, Saccharum officinarum, was cultivated (Ricaud and Ryan, 1989). The impact of the disease is reduced by the cultivation of interspecific hybrids but susceptible varieties may be rapidly destroyed. Yield losses of 15-20% were recorded in sugarcane variety B 69379 in Guadeloupe (Rott et al., 1995). Cochereau and Jean-Bart (1989) estimated a loss of 13 tonnes of cane per hectare of infected plants compared with healthy cane. In Mexico, leaf scald destroyed 800 hectares under variety Mex 64-1487 (Rott, 1995), while in Mauritius, a sugar yield-depressing effect of up to 31% was observed in variety M 695/69 (Anon., 1990).

management_info: Leaf scald may be controlled effectively by the simultaneous use of several methods. The cultivation of resistant varieties should be supplemented with the use of disease-free cuttings from nurseries. These cuttings should be established using sets which have undergone a cold soak/long hot-water treatment in which the cuttings are soaked in cold running water for 48 h followed by hot-water treatment at 50°C for 3 h.^p^pIt is necessary to disinfect cutting instruments regularly when cuttings are prepared and during harvest because X. albilineans is transmitted by knives and harvesters. potential_eco_desc: S. citri causes the serious stubborn disease of citrus which under hot, dry conditions can greatly reduce the quality and quantity of the yield. The fact that it is vector-transmitted, unlike most other graft-transmissible pathogens of citrus, makes it more difficult to control by use of healthy planting material. In California, USA, the main economic hosts are orange, grapefruit and tangelo, of which 5-10% of trees are estimated to be affected. In the Mediterranean area, stubborn is very serious in some countries, especially in Syria where the vector Neoaliturus haematoceps is common and introduced healthy budwood was rapidly reinfected (Bove, 1986). The Syrian practice of rebudding imported healthy stock has also favoured reinfection (UNDP/FAO, 1988). The disease is also reported to be widespread and important in Iraq and Turkey. In other Mediterranean countries (Cyprus, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco) the disease is present, but only rarely on certain cultivars. In others (Algeria, Libya, Tunisia), stubborn was reported to be common in the past but the survey of UNDP/FAO (1988) found few or no trees with characteristic symptoms. Importance no doubt depends largely on the presence or abundance of vectors. N. haematoceps occurs throughout the Mediterranean area, while Circulifer tenellus occurs mainly in its southern and eastern parts. Newly planted citrus orchards are readily invaded by leafhoppers from surrounding crops, and can suffer serious attacks, which then decline as the trees become older and less attractive to the insects (Bove, 1986). Stubborn also tends to occur only in certain years, when the vectors are abundant.^p^pAlthough S. citri naturally infects many other hosts and some of these are crop plants, it is not reported to have any economic impact on these. Their main significance would be as reservoirs of S. citri for infection of citrus. Horseradish brittle root is of purely anecdotal interest.
author: CPC2006

remark: In its Mediterranean area of origin, stubborn occurs only sporadically in many countries. Accordingly, use of disease-free planting material (OEPP/EPPO, 1995) is still recommended to prevent further spread, despite a certain possibility that newly-planted citrus will be reinfected by leafhoppers having fed on other hosts.^p^pMany citrus-producing areas in the rest of world (i.e. most of sub-Saharan Africa, Australia, most of South America and eastern Asia) are free from stubborn and from its vectors (although other local leafhoppers could possibly become vectors). S. citri should certainly be considered as a quarantine pest for those areas, as it is by CPPC, COSAVE and IAPSC.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Production of healthy budwood is the only practical means of control, but it must be accompanied by suitable siting of orchards to avoid reinfection during the first years of development. In practice, this means that S. citri should be covered by disease-free certification schemes for imported or nationally-produced citrus (OEPP/EPPO, 1995).^p^pTrees showing symptoms should be rogued and replaced, not so much because they constitute a risk to neighbouring trees, but because they will never bear fruit satisfactorily. Insecticide treatments against the vectors are not effective, because S. citri can be transmitted very rapidly after arrival of infective vectors in an orchard. It has been suggested (Gumpf, 1988) that trap plants (attractive to the vector, but not hosts of S. citri, such as sugarbeet) should be planted in the vicinity of orchards. Gumpf (1988) summarizes the main elements recommended for stubborn control in North America.

host_range: Tomatoes are the sole host of the pathogen.Affected Plant Stages: Flowering stage, fruiting stage, post-harvest, seedling stage and vegetative growing stage.Affected Plant Parts: Fruits/pods and leaves.
potential_eco_desc: Bacterial speck is a significant source of economic loss in the tomato industry. Lesions may make fruit unfit for fresh market. On tomatoes for processing, lesions may be deep enough to cause considerable grading or loss in quality (Goode and Sasser, 1980). The severity of bacterial speck of tomato is closely related to weather conditions in the field. The disease develops and spreads only at temperatures between 13 and 28°C and at high relative humidity when there is free water on the leaves. In the field, yield losses varied from 75% in plants infected at an early stage of growth to 5% in plants infected later in the season (Yunis et al., 1980).^p^pA serious outbreak of a leaf spot disease was observed on tomato transplants grown in commercial seedling companies in southwestern Turkey (Antalya) during the springs of 2002 and 2003. Disease incidence was more severe in the western mediterranean region of Turkey. Occurrence of the outbreak resulted in approximately 20 and 25% seedling losses in 2002 and 2003, respectively. In addition, in 2003, the disease incidence was approximately 5% in 142 commercial greenhouses. Tomato production was unaffected as significant outbreaks did not occur on greenhouse plants (Basim et al., 2004).

description: IncidenceChambers and Merriman (1975) found tomato seeds contaminated by P. syringae pv. tomato. Bashan and Assouline (1983) detected the pathogen in 7 of 38 pepper seed lots at levels higher than 10,000 c.f.u./g seeds.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pNot reported.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pTomato plants grown in sterile soil from seeds, artificially infested with P. syringae pv. tomato developed speck symptoms when incubated under greenhouse conditions (Devash et al., 1980). ^p^pP. syringae pv. tomato can persist in the soil for long periods in the absence of tomato (Schneider and Grogan, 1977).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pPartial control of seedborne infection was achieved with copper compounds (Chambers and Merriman, 1975). Immersion of seed in hot water at 48°C for 1 h eliminated the bacterium from the seed without affecting the germination ability of the seeds (Devash et al., 1979).^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pLiquid enrichment (Bashan and Assouline, 1983)^p^p1. 4000 tomato seeds are soaked in liquid King's B medium at 28°C and shaken vigorously for 4 h (250 strokes/min).^p2. Viable bacterial counts from the leachate were estimated by spreading 0.2 ml of 10-fold dilutions on agar plates with ND and KFT media.^p3. Colonies of P. syringae pv. tomato have wrinkled margins and produce a typical fluorescent pigment. Colonies are oxidase negative.^p4. Suspect colonies were tested for pathogenicity by spraying leaves on two plants with a washed bacterial suspensions (10,000 c.f.u./ml) supplemented with carborundum.^p5. Plants were incubated in partial must chambers for 5 sec mist every 15 min at 22°C for 10 days.^p^pNotes on methods^p^pThe liquid enrichment method (Bashan and Assouline, 1983) detected P. syringae pv. tomato to 1000 c.f.u./g tomato seeds. A method developed by Kritzman (1989) was able to detect the pathogen to a level of 10,000 c.f.u./g tomato seeds.^p^pA semi-selective medium was developed for detection of P. syringae pv. tomato from tomato seeds. Growth tests of the pathogen were carried out with five isolates collected in tomato-producing fields of Brazil. A semi-selective medium based on King's B medium was developed that gave abundant growth of P. syringae pv. tomato but repressed most other bacteria (Soares et al., 2001).

potential_eco_desc: Damage to the plant is caused by necrotic spots and streaks which may occur on all above-ground parts, and infection of seeds. Necrosis results in a reduction of the assimilating surface and, when severe infections occur on peduncles, flowers and pods wither and die. Pre- and post-emergence damping-off has been observed. ^p^pSevere infections (reaching 100% disease incidence) and substantial crop losses have only recently been reported from winter-sown peas in southern France, New Zealand and South Africa (Boelema, 1972; Taylor, 1972b), when hail, rainstorms and frost prevail. It has been shown, however, that another pathogenic bacterium, Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae, may also be involved in disease development under these conditions (Taylor, 1972b). Epidemic outbreaks (without severe crop losses) in Europe occur in pea cultivars sown in early spring under conditions of night frost and high humidity. A marked influence of these weather conditions was also established in Australia (Harris, 1964). Serious damage to Vicia sativa was reported from Greece in 1965 (Anon., 1965) and in Victoria, Australia, a 70% yield loss was observed (Forbes and Bretag, 1991). It should be noted, however, that other (leaf) pathogens such as Ascochyta and Mycosphaerella pinodes contribute to yield losses in natural epidemics of pv. pisi (Cruger, 1984). Individual pea plants showed a 24-71% reduction in seed yield upon artificial inoculation (Roberts, 1993). In field trials, the effects of pea blight were difficult to estimate, partly because of bird damage, but they appeared to be within the range of normal annual variation for a pea crop (Roberts et al., 1995).^p^pEconomic losses arise from the reduced marketability of the crop, the presence of diseased pods and seeds, possible yield reduction and indirectly through the application of phytosanitary restrictions. The disease as such, however, does not appear to be of great economic importance in the European area. In the state of New York, USA, the disease was observed in 1979 after an absence of 25 years (Hunter and Cigna, 1981).

description: Incidence^p^pP. syringae pv. pisi is extensively seedborne. In the UK there has been a steady increase in the incidence of infection of pea seed stocks from 8.2% infected in 1987 to 36.5% in 1994. The most significant increase followed removal of statutory certification controls in 1993 (Reeves et al., 1996). Roberts et al. (1991) also noted an association between incidence and regulatory controls in that the prevalence of disease in UK-produced seed stocks initially declined from 1986 to 1987 then increased steadily from 1987 to 1989 but declined again in 1990. The prevalence of disease was consistently greater in seed which was not subject to statutory testing.^p^pA survey for P. syringae pv. pisi in winter pea seed lots submitted for disease testing in the UK showed that Race 6 was the most commonly occurring pathogen race in each of the 3 years of the study, with races 2 and 4 also being found in most years. Race 1 was not found in any of the samples tested. All the winter pea cultivars tested were resistant to pathogen races 1 and 7 and susceptible to races 4 and 6. For the other three races, the cultivars were mixed in their reactions but most were resistant to races 2, 3 and 5 (Kenyon et al., 1999).^p^pWhen pods have been infected the pathogen may contaminate the seed coat. It can also be present under the seed coat when it enters the seed through the funiculus (Skoric, 1927). The bacterium can survive on or within seeds for at least 10 months (Skoric, 1927). Seed infection can occur in the apparent absence of field symptoms (Stead and Pemberton, 1987).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pPea seeds within infected pods may show a water-soaked spot near the hilum and/or are shrivelled, with a brownish-yellow discoloration.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pSeed^p^pP. syringae pv. pisi can multiply with no (or cryptic) symptoms on seedlings grown from contaminated seed. High populations of the pathogen may be observed on all plants in a field and, when the right climatic conditions are fulfilled, disease can occur in a whole field within 14 days (Grondeau et al., 1996).^p^pThe most important means of spread from season to season and over long distances is infected seed. An equation was developed to predict transmission rates of the pea blight pathogen from seed to seedling (Roberts, 1992). Sowing in a dry seed bed will not prevent transmission of P. syringae pv. pisi to seedlings. However, seed transmission is significantly reduced at low soil water contents (Holloway et al., 1996).^p^pOther sources^p^pThe bacterium can survive for several months on diseased plant debris in the field (Harris, 1964; Grondeau et al., 1996). Volunteer plants maintain high levels of bacteria for at least 8 months after harvesting of a diseased crop. An epiphytic, race dependent life cycle on pea (where multiplication takes place) and the epiphytic presence of the pathogen on weeds for as long as 8 months after harvest has been reported by Grondeau et al. (1996). The importance of soil and field pea (Pisum sativum cv. Dun) debris as sources of P. syringae pv. pisi inoculum for infection of field pea was investigated both in a controlled environment and in the field. Studies of the survival of P. syringae pv. pisi in soil using autoclaved and non-autoclaved soil found that P. syringae pv. pisi is unlikely to survive in soil from one season to the next, suggesting that soil is an unlikely source of inoculum in the field. However, P. syringae pv. pisi was able to survive on buried pea debris for at least 29 weeks and on pea debris positioned on the soil surface for at least 78 weeks. In a field trial, the presence of pea debris naturally infected with P. syringae pv. pisi caused significant bacterial blight and reduced grain yield of a field pea crop by 25%. management_info: Introduction^p^pThere is no suitable method to eliminate the bacterium from the seed. Resistance to P. syringae pv. pisi is present in peas, and this appears to have a gene-for-gene relationship with pathogenicity in P. syringae pv. pisi. Seven races have been identified by inoculation into a range of differential pea cultivars and race 2 is predominant. No resistance has been found to race 6 (Taylor et al., 1989). Many cultivars are resistant to more than one race.^p^pDisease prevention can be obtained through production of disease-free seed by growing seed under semi-arid conditions and/or certification (Harris, 1964), through late sowing and avoidance of frost-pockets to reduce infection chances or by sanitation.^p^p^Seed Testing^p^pOne method of control is seed testing. Removal of statutory certification controls in the UK resulted in a substantial increase in seed infection. This may lead to the cyclic reoccurrence of pea blight epidemics when weather conditions are favourable (Reeves et al., 1996). However, Roberts et al. (1991) found, for the years 1988 and 1989, that the number of infected seed stocks was not limited by seed testing.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pSeveral pea varieties show resistance to one or more races of the pea blight pathogen. When planting these, races of pv. pisi may increase in the natural population. This was observed in the UK. Race 6 can mutate from race 2 (the race most commonly found and against which several UK varieties are resistant) following the loss of the avirulence gene A2 (Bevan et al., 1995; Reeves et al., 1996). Resistance breeding concentrates on the combination of six specific resistance genes and a race non-specific resistance gene (from Pisum abyssinicum) in commercial peas (Taylor et al., 1994).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pFoliar sprays of streptomycin have been shown to reduce bacterial blight incidence by 62% (Forbes and Bretag, 1991).^p^p^Physical Control^p^pHeat treatment of pea seed is described under Seed Treatments in the section on Seedborne Aspects of Disease.

Yellow-fleshed nectarine cultivars appear to be of moderate susceptibility (Luisetti et al., 1976).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pIn countries and regions where P. syringae pv. persicae is not present, new plantings should be made using nursery material which is from disease-free sources. In affected regions, where winter frosts are severe, the most important aspects of control are connected with soil management. In regions with light sandy, acidic, shallow soils, or soils with a tendency to form pans, elevation of pH above 5.5, the breaking of pans or the mounding of soil to increase depth are considered efficacious (Young, 1987).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pCopper sprays in autumn during leaf fall will reduce bud and stem die-back in spring (Luisetti et al., 1976). However, this treatment does not ameliorate main leader and trunk injury occurring in winter (JM Young, Landcare Research, Auckland, New Zealand, personal communication, 1998) and may not be efficacious. Calcium amendments to soil may limit disease (Vigouroux et al., 1987).

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pCopper-containing compounds such as Bordeaux mixture and fixed coppers may be of value for preventing infection at critical times. Protective-copper compounds are applied in spring and again in autumn. The timing and number of applications depend on the sensitivity of each stone fruit species to injury from copper. Spring treatments on sweet cherry are applied before bud break. On Montmorency sour cherry, spraying trees weekly with a low rate of copper from bud break to about the shuck-split stage of bud development is used for disease control (Olson and Jones, 1983).^p^pAutumn leaf-scar infections are controlled on sweet cherry with a series of copper sprays covering the period of leaf fall from the beginning to the end. Mixing rapeseed oil or other vegetable oils with Bordeaux mixture helps to reduce the premature defoliation of trees in autumn caused by the copper spray (Allen and Dirks, 1979).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pAvoiding susceptible cultivars when planting new orchards is the best horticultural practice for preventing bacterial canker. Sour cherry cultivars Stevnsbar, Kelleriis 16 and Schattenmorelle seldom become infected under natural conditions when Fanal, Nefris and Rexelle are severely infected (Bech, 1992). Sweet cherry cultivars also show a range in susceptibility, but because the two pathovars can vary in their virulence towards particular cultivars, cultivar selection in regions where both pathovars occur together is particularly difficult (Allen and Dirks, 1978). In addition, the rootstock can alter the resistance of sweet cherry cultivars to infection (Garrett, 1986).

potential_eco_desc: Halo blight is a major disease of bean crops throughout the world. Epidemics have been recorded in Wisconsin and other parts of the USA (Walker and Patel, 1964). In four plot experiments in which various Phaseolus vulgaris lines were infected by inculation with P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola, losses in seed yield were in the range 2.8-55.4% (Anon., 1980).^p^pYield losses of 43% in the UK and between 23 and 43% in Michigan, USA have been obtained under experimental conditions (Allen et al., 1998). In the UK, green beans are mainly used for processing. Reduction in quality due to pod lesions can thus be considered economically important (Taylor and Dudley, 1977b). Allen et al. (1998) observed crop losses as a result of halo blight in Lesotho, Rwanda and Zimbabwe.
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pP. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola is extensively seedborne in beans. Of eight test samples of bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) seeds from Germany, six contained seeds infected by P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola. Routine laboratory testing of 710 seed lots of P. vulgaris of various origins for P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola with immunofluorescence (IF) showed that 27.5% of the seed lots were infected (Vuurde et al., 1991). Analysis of ungraded single seeds from these samples revealed between 1.8 and 3% of all seeds to be infected. Seeds with greasy spots (1-2 per 1000 seeds) showed >80% infection, whereas P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola was detected in only 0-3% of symptomless seeds (Naumann and Karl, 1989).Zaumeyer (1932) showed that P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola  is systemic in the bean plant and can enter the seed by way of the raphe or micropyle and thus can occur in or under the seed coat. Transmission of the bacterium from plant to seed in P. vulgaris was mainly by the penetration of bacteria from external pod lesions to the seeds. There was no evidence for translocation from other parts of the plant to the seed, and symptomless pods contained only healthy seeds (Taylor et al., 1979a). The pathogen is internal to the seed and as a surface contaminant (Grogan and Kimble, 1967). Surface contamination of seeds occurs during threshing and other harvesting and conditioning operations (Grogan and Kimble, 1967). Taylor et al. (1979a) showed that the viability of bacteria in seed stored under relatively uncontrolled conditions (10-27°C) declined by a factor of 250 per annum over the first 3 years, extrapolation predicting effective extinction after ca 5 years. The pathogen survived longer under controlled conditions (7-10°C and 45-50% RH) but no viable bacteria were detected in seed stocks that were 10 years old.^p^pRelationships have been reported between the incidence of seed infection of P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola and host-plant resistance (Katherman et al., 1980; Bovenkamp et al., 1991).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pHeavily infested white seeds are discoloured and wrinkled with longitudinal grooves or have intense yellow spots with an entire edge (Jansing and Rudolph, 1990).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pTransmission of P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola to plants grown from seeds was demonstrated by planting seeds infested with dust obtained from pulverized, dried, infected bean leaf tissue (Grogan and Kimble, 1967; Guthrie, 1970). Transmission of the pathogen was also was demonstrated from seeds with internal infection (Grogan and Kimble, 1967) and from seeds with slight or no symptoms and seeds obviously infected (Taylor et al., 1979a). Development of halo bight disease, resulting from seedborne inoculum is greatly exacerbated under sprinkler compared to in-furrow irrigation due to secondary spread of the pathogen (Snyder et al., 1965). ^p^pA correlation between the level of seed infection estimated by laboratory tests and the disease index in the fields was established. This defined 1:20,000 as the tolerance level of infection under which no symptom appears even under the most favourable climatic conditions. Seed stocks, free from infected seeds at an estimated level of 5:10,000, may cause significant spread of halo blight (Trigalet and Bidaud, 1978). A range of tolerances, ranging from 0 seeds infected in samples of 4000-45,000, are used in seed quality programmes in US seed companies to ensure that the pathogen is not transmitted by commercial seed lots (Maddox, 1997).^p^pInfected crop residues are sources of inoculum for P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola (Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1957).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pSeed treatment techniques using antibiotics or steam-air treatment were unsuccessful in controlling seedborne P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola Ralph, 1977a, b.^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pSelective Media (Jansing and Rudolph, 1997)^p^pExtraction of the bacterium ^p^pDivide the bean seed sample into subsamples of 1000 seed

description: Natural dispersal (non-biotic)^p^pHalo blight disseminates rapidly between leaves and plants by water-splash directed by prevailing winds during rainfall (Walker and Patel, 1964). Studies indicated that the disease spreads as far as 26 m from the initial inoculum source. No evidence of spread by cultivation equipment could be detected (Walker and Patel, 1964). The pathogen is also spread with sprinkler irrigation (Grogan and Kimble, 1967; LeBaron et al., 1977).^p^pVector transmission^p^pNo records of vector transmission of halo blight could be found. It has, however, been indicated that fresh manure from sheep, feeding on blighted bean plants, may contain halo blight bacteria for up to 9 months (Starr and Kercher, 1969).^p^pSeedborne spread^p^pSeed infection is the most important means of halo blight transmission. The first report of seed transmission was by Burkholder in 1930 (cited by Allen et al., 1998). Severe epidemics have occurred under favourable conditions from as few as 12 infected seeds (Walker and Patel, 1964). management_info: Biological Control^p^pLupinine extracted from Lupinus albus and L. luteus showed some bactericidal effect against P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola (Muzquiz et al., 1999). Erwinia herbicola applied to seed inhibited growth of P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola from infected seed onto agar (Downes and Duggan, 1978). In vitro studies indicated that garlic extract inhibited growth of P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola (Gondwe et al., 1996).^p^p^Agricultural Practices^p^pDeep-ploughing or removal of infected debris and volunteer beans is essential to reduce initial inoculum sources (Schwartz, 1989). Crop rotation with cereals such as wheat, barley, oat and maize for 3 or more years is recommended (Schwartz and Otto, 2000). Reduced halo blight incidence has been reported in bean-maize intercropping (Schwartz, 1989). This was confirmed in Kenya (van Rheenen et al., 1981) and Malawi (Msuku and Edje, 1982). Mabagala and Saettler (1992c) however, indicated that halo blight severity and seed infection were higher when beans were intercropped with maize.^p^pClean seed production contributes greatly to the control of halo blight. In the USA, pathogen-free seed production depends upon field inspection, laboratory inoculation, serology testing and quarantine to prevent importation of infected seed (Schwartz, 1989).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pAlthough the efficacy of copper compounds for bacterial disease control is generally low (Menkissoglu and Lindow, 1991), it is widely applied to control halo blight (Taylor, 1972; Taylor and Dudley, 1977b; Schwartz and McMillan, 1991). Time of application is important in effectively controlling the disease (Taylor and Dudley, 1977b).^p^p^Disease Resistance^p^pHost-plant resistance is considered the most effective control strategy for halo blight (Allen et al., 1998). Several sources of resistance have been reported (Innes et al., 1984; Beebe and Pastor-Corrales, 1991). Patel and Walker (1965) identified the dry bean line PI 1505414, which has race non-specific resistance. It is therefore an important source of resistance and widely used in breeding programmes (Beebe and Pastor-Corrales, 1991). Similar resistance occurs in Great Northern Nebraska #1 sel 27 (Beebe and Pastor-Corrales, 1991). A combination of race-specific and race non-specific resistance enhances the chances of developing cultivars with durable resistance (Allen et al., 1998).

host_range: D. abbreviatus is best known in the Caribbean area as a pest of citrus and sugarcane, but the adult weevil is polyphagous with a wide host range, attacking a wide variety of economically important plants. ^p^pHost plants associated with D. abbreviatus (15
potential_eco_desc: D. abbreviatus is an insidious pest of citrus, sugarcane and other economic crops of subtropical and tropical areas of the USA and several Caribbean island nations. As a result of inadequate management strategies and a wide range of adult and larval food plants, D. abbreviatus can be considered a major long-term threat to the survival of several agronomic crops (Simpson et al., 1996).^p^pIn the French Antilles, the recently established citrus crop has been declining since 1984, and D. abbreviatus infestations are one of the main causes. The setting up in 1985 of a multidisciplinary programme for integrated control of the weevil was reported by Mauleon and Mademba (1988).^p^pLosses attributed to D. abbreviatus on citrus in Florida, USA, was estimated at US $73 million during 1995. In Barbados, Metcalf (1959) estimated that larvae were responsible for sugarcane losses of 4.4 tonnes/ha in first ratoon cane and 2.0 tonnes/ha in second ratoon crops.^p^pFeeding by larvae on roots can result in significant damage to citrus and sugarcane. An infestation of larvae can rapidly kill a young citrus tree. As few as two or three weevil larvae can remove the entire bark from the root system of a containerized citrus seedling within 4-5 weeks. Older trees may also be killed if enough larvae are present. Little is known regarding economic injury levels of larvae in either citrus or sugarcane, but there is some evidence that relatively few larvae may sometimes cause substantial damage. Older citrus trees infested by larvae do not always die, but generally become unproductive.^p^pExperiments performed by Schroeder and Sutton (1977) concerning larval feeding damage in citrus groves in Florida, USA, revealed that larvae placed at the base of the tree caused both the most severe type of damage (on the taproot and at the insertion of the major lateral roots) and the highest proportion (80%) of severely damaged trees. Larvae placed at the tree drip line fed mostly on lateral roots, causing severe damage to only 20% of the trees, whereas larvae placed 20 cm from the trunk caused intermediate levels of damage.^p^pIn Puerto Rico, nursery citrus trees are often affected more severely than mature grove trees (Woodruff, 1964). Jackson (1963) reported that adults fed on female flowers and fruits (Kimri stage) of the date palm, causing the fruit to abort within 48 to 72 hours.^p^pThe weevil may increase the potential for Phytophthora rots to invade the roots of citrus, if present in the soil.
author: CPC2006

remark: D. abbreviatus was intercepted three times in Puerto Rico on plants from Haiti during 1963 (Mumford, 1964).^p^pThe discovery of immature stages in the soil of plants shipped to other areas and of adults clinging to tractors used in infested citrus groves in Florida, USA, suggests that mechanical transportation is an important factor in the dispersal of D. abbreviatus (Beavers and Selhime, 1978).^p^pIn 1977, quarantine inspectors intercepted eggs of D. abbreviatus on ornamental species of Dracaena intended for export from Puerto Rico to Florida, USA. In view of the damaging effect on the export of ornamental plants due to restrictions subsequently imposed, experiments were carried out in Puerto Rico to identify those species of ornamental foliage plants on which this weevil would oviposit, in the hope of derestricting ornamental plants shown not to be used for oviposition (Abreu and Perez, 1983).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pThe chances of D. abbreviatus being introduced into a non-infested citrus grove can be lessened by planting trees free of weevil adults, eggs and larvae. Vigorous washing and careful inspection of nursery citrus stock have aided the control of infestations in Florida, USA (Simanton and Bullock, 1973). Barriers placed under infested trees may help prevent neonate larvae from reaching the soil.^p^pRemoving wild host plants growing between infested and non-infested plantings of citrus and sugarcane may be of some value in preventing the pest from moving into new areas. In Puerto Rico, D. abbreviatus is sometimes a problem along the edges of sugarcane fields near other, more preferred adult food sources. Therefore, controlling wild host plants in the vicinity of infested cane may limit larval infestations. Hand removal of adults and eggs has been used with limited success.^p^pDepending upon water availability and environmental considerations, sugarcane growers may be able to reduce damage caused by D. abbreviatus infestations by flooding infested fields for several weeks, providing flood waters are above 24°C Shapiro et al., 1996, 1997).^p^pMinimizing water stress and maintaining adequate plant nutrition can help reduce the impact of feeding damage.^p^p^Biological ControlSirjusingh et al. (1992) reviewed the biological control potential of natural enemies of D. abbreviatus in the Caribbean. During the 1970s, hymenopterous egg parasitoids, Aprostocetus gala, and Quadrastichus haitiensis (Jamaica, St. Vincent and Montserrat), Brachyuferus osborni (Florida, USA) and Fidiobia citri (Jamaica) were introduced into Barbados. These parasitoids did not attack eggs on sugarcane. Q. haitiensis was also introduced into Florida, USA, for biological control during the 1970s, but has failed to provide evidence of establishment (Beavers and Selhime, 1975a; Beavers et al., 1980). Cruz and Segarra (1991) suggested that they do not become significantly established on sugarcane due to the difficulty in parasitizing eggs of D. abbreviatus through the leaves.^p^pEntomophagous nematodes have shown promise as control agents for D. abbreviatus under some conditions. A review of nematodes for root weevil control was presented by Schroeder (1988). Considerable research efforts were made during the 1980s and early 1990s with Steinernema carpocapsae. More recently, interest has shifted toward the related nematode S. riobravis (Duncan and McCoy, 1996), as this nematode may be able to move further into soil in search of hosts. In the mid-1990s, a company called Biosys was marketing this nematode in the USA. These nematodes enter larvae and release a bacterium which is lethal to the host. The nematodes are applied into the soil beneath citrus trees using low-volume irrigation systems or by boom spraying when soil moisture levels are high. Entomophagous nematodes can provide from 40 to 80% control of young larvae in the soil (Beavers et al., 1983; Roman and Beavers, 1983; Roman and Figueroa, 1985), although most researchers believe that >95% larval mortality is required to reduce the economic importance of the pest in citrus. See Martin and Miller (1994), Schroeder (1994) and Bullock and Miller (1995) for further details of entomopathogenic nematodes and control of D. Abbreviatus.Adair (1995) monitored the use of entomopathogenic nematodes to control larval stages and grower acceptance in grapefruit groves in Florida, USA. Little difference was observed in the number of trapped adults or in the incidence of tree decline from root damage due to larval feeding between the treated and the untreated areas. Consecutive annual reductions of 45-48% in captured adult weevils in 1993 and 1994, respectively, was speculated to be due to a high population of endemic parasites found in the soil. host_range: Flavescence doree phytoplasma is transmitted by the leafhopper vector Scaphoideus titanus, formerly Scaphoideus littoralis (Schvester et al., 1963) which is an ampelophagous species. Thus, flavescence doree phytoplasma is restricted to species of Vitis un
potential_eco_desc: Flavescence doree causes symptoms that are detrimental to infected vines. Depending on the intensity of infection the yields may decrease dramatically. Their vitality is affected, yields are reduced, and the quality of wine is decreased by high acid and low sugar contents of infected clusters. When no control of the vector has been undertaken, the number of infected vines may increase steadily about 10 times every year and may reach 80-100% within a few years. The economic viability of maintaining a vineyard ceases when the productive plants are less than 25% of the total.^p^pIn France and Corsica, where it is considered a major disease of grapevine, flavescence doree has destroyed large viticultural areas and suppressed this crop from these regions since the 1950s. It is still progressing in spite of mandatory uprooting of the diseased stocks and mandatory insecticide control of S. titanus.^p^pSeveral cultivars which are used for the production of high-quality products such as Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon blanc, Semillon, Grenache, Barbera, Trebiano toscano (syn. Ugni blanc), Soave, Prosecco, Garganega, are highly susceptible to flavescence doree. Furthermore, the culture of several varieties which are of regional importance only but are essential for the production of unique specialities, is endangered (Sancassani and Posenato, 1995; Posenato et al., 1996). Cultivars such as Sangiovese (syn. Nielluccio) and Garganega are extremely susceptible and killed immediately by flavescence doree. Biodiversity of vine germplasm is endangered.
author: CPC2006

remark: Flavescence doree phytoplasma is a quarantine organism in the EU (Directive EEC 77/93). Multiplication and plantation vine material must be free of the organism. Certification cannot be obtained by mere diagnosis on the material, due to the uneven distribution of phytoplasma in the canes and in the mother stock which makes sampling uncertain. Rootstock varieties are an additional hazard, because they may be tolerant to the phytoplasma and serve as symptomless carriers of the disease agent that they will distribute by grafting to V. vinifera scions (Caudwell et al., 1994). Unpublished data indicate that incubation of the disease for as long as several years before any overt expression of symptoms may occur in scions grafted onto infected rootstocks. Certification must include indexing on susceptible varieties and observation in quarantine nurseries of scions and grafted plants.^p^pA curing method involving soaking of dormant material for 45 min in 50°C hot water Caudwell et al., 1990, 1997) kills phytoplasmas in situ and ensures healthy material. This method should be applied to all planting material in flavescence doree-free regions, especially those inhabited by the leafhopper vector.
author: CPC2006

management_info: The improvement and maintenance of the phytosanitary quality of planting material by certification procedures and the protection of mother plots and nurseries from inoculation is an important prevention strategy for the establishment of healthy vineyards. This is even more important for planting material that is shipped into areas that are not yet affected. ^p^pTwo principles of controlling the spread of flavescence doree can be distinguished. One is decreasing the inoculum density and the second is controlling the vector. Inoculation pressure may be reduced by the destruction of sources of infection consisting of infected vines. Vector control is accomplished by the use of insecticides since no biological control of the vector is available.^p^pIn France, control of flavescence doree is subject to several legislative directives. One reason is the high importance of this disease for viticulture. Furthermore, the successful control of flavescence doree is only possible as a joint activity for a particular area, due to the high mobility of the vector. In France, all mother plots for propagation material have to be treated with insecticides against S. titanus three times a year. All nurseries have to be treated throughout the time when larval stages or adults of S. titanus are likely to occur. Directives from the local authorities regulate the mandatory control of flavescence doree and its vector for particular areas where flavescence doree is present. They also regulate the obligate control of S. titanus by insecticides and the measures to be taken in order to reduce inoculum. ^p^pProphylactic measures include the destruction of infected vines to remove sources of flavescence doree phytoplasma, destruction of abandoned vineyards and wild Vitis plants, which serve as sources of inoculum and breeding hosts for the vector. These measures, as well as the obligate uprooting of all plants in vineyards when the disease incidence is excessive, are subject to prefectorial directives in France.^p^pAlthough removal of infected stocks is useful to reduce the inoculum of flavescence doree, pruning of diseased wood of flavescence doree-infected grapes is not advisable. In contrast, this kind of pruning as well as cutting of the trunk and rebuilding the stock can be dangerous for vineyards. Pruning can mask the infection while the vines are still sources of inoculum, since they are infected systemically by flavescence doree phytoplasma. The frequency of obvious symptoms of flavescence doree may be decreased but the epidemic spread, nevertheless, goes on.^p^pControl of the vector depends on insecticide treatments, which are applied either against the eggs during winter or against larvae and adult leafhoppers during the growing season. Pruning wood that carries the eggs of S. titanus should be burned. The number of viable eggs can be reduced by a treatment of wood in March before bud-burst. Insecticides based on oleo-parathione are used for these applications. A wide range of insecticides, mainly organophosphates and pyrethroids, are available for summer treatments, which are usually carried out three times. The first treatment is usually in June and should not be done later than one month after the beginning of hatching: the delay is the period of time necessary for the first insects to become infective if they could feed on infected vines soon after hatching. The time of the second treatment depends on the stability of the compound used, but it is usually applied in combination with the control of the second generation of grape berry moth. Adult leafhoppers immigrating into the vineyards from surrounding areas are the target of a third treatment in August. ^p^pFor further information see Caudwell (1965), Caudwell et al. (1971, 1974), Boudon-Padieu and Maixner (1998) and Anon. (1999).

host_range: 该虫为寡食性害虫，寄主主要为栗属（Castanea spp.）和栎属（Quercus spp.，栎树又称橡树，其果实被称作橡实），具体包括西班牙栗（C. sativa），欧洲板栗（C. vesca），夏栎（Q. robur）和欧洲栓皮栎（Q. suber），冬青栎（Q. ilex）
potential_eco_desc:
幼虫在果实内部取食，消耗大部分营养物质，通常情况下，果肉几乎被蛀食干净，降低种子生命力和发芽率，阻碍栗树和橡树林的再生。受害果实一般会提前脱落或感染真菌病害，不能被正常食用，不耐储存，严重减产，降低板栗的食用价值和市场价值。

在土耳其，欧洲栗象可为害欧洲板栗和多种栎树。寄主植物总的平均受害率为9.5%，不同地区受害程度差异很大，Bahkesir地区林木受害率为20.5%，Tavsanh、Istanbul地区的受害率分别为20.9%和29.1%。发生严重的地区，平均每个果实内有3-4头幼虫，甚至可高达8头  欧洲栗象具有重要的经济重要性，可以为害板栗和橡树果实。该虫是为害欧洲板栗最重要的害虫之一，根据不同板栗品种，危害程度不同。成虫取食可造成20%的幼果脱落；成虫和幼虫的共同为害可造成栗实90%的损失。幼虫取食可影响板栗或橡树种子的发芽力。葡萄牙橡实的受害率据估计为50-63%，被害橡实中约有89-95%由欧洲栗象取食引起。虽然有些被害橡实、栗实仍能发芽，由于欧洲栗象取食消耗了大部分营养物质，种苗发育大多受阻，严重阻碍了橡树林和栗树林的再生。除直接造成损失外，由于欧洲栗象产卵和取食孔口，果实还容易感染栗疫菌Endothia parasitica。
西班牙调查欧洲栗象和Cydia fagiglandana对人工橡树林和野生橡树林橡实的危害，果实平均受害率为16.6%，受害率变化较大，两种橡树林每棵橡树果实的最低和最高受害率分别为2-72%和0-32%）。橡实受害后发芽和出苗率降低15%
description:
欧洲栗象有翅能飞，但主动扩散能力有限，成虫羽化后钻出地表，飞到羽化孔附近的寄主植株果实上取食并交配。成虫多停留在寄主植株或果实附近，一般来说，该虫几乎整个成虫期都呆在寄主植株上。
感染有该虫的寄主植物的贸易往来、土壤基质及运输工具等是其长距离扩散的主要途径，该虫可以卵、幼虫、成虫随寄主植物果实贸易进行扩散，以各种虫态随寄主植物调运及其土壤基质运输进行传播。由于该虫是内部取食，肉眼难以直接观察。到达新的领地后，该虫在一个生长季内，群体迅速扩大。
management_info:
检疫或存储期处理：该虫主要在果实内部为害，杀虫剂等化学药剂难以扩散到果实内部杀死该虫。冷处理对于欧洲栗象的处理效果有限，温热处理可以很好的杀死欧洲栗象。意大利研究人员将冬青栎、栓皮栎果实在45℃、含水量40%条件下处理2小时，橡实的平均发芽率为62%，平均发芽时间为19.1天，幼虫杀死率为100%；45℃、含水量38%条件下处理半个小时，橡实发芽率为71%，平均发芽时间为19.1天，幼虫杀死率为100%  化学防治：欧洲栗象主要以幼虫在果实内部取食造成危害。由于栗实和橡实被有坚硬的外壳，喷洒化学药剂可能对在果实表面取食的成虫有一定作用，对在果实内部取食的幼虫效果甚微。  生物防治：生防真菌白僵菌Beauveria bassiana (Balsamo) Vuill可用于防治该虫。Paparatti于1993–94，1994–95和1997–98 年间在意大利Viterbo进行3次试验，每次重复3次，利用白僵菌商用菌株(Naturalis-L，Fermone Corporation，Phoenix，AZ)进行2个重复，意大利实验室提供的菌株重复1次。前两次试验效果良好，表明该菌防治欧洲栗象取得良好结果；第3次试验处理过的欧洲栗象与对照组无明显差别，表明该菌的杀虫效果受降雨量影响很大。  由于该虫在果实内部取食，单一的防治措施效果有限，化学药剂难以直接有效地接触或杀死该虫，应当采取有害生物综合防治技术。
农业防治：良好的农事操作和抗虫品种可以有效降低欧洲栗象种群。私家花园或小的种植园中，可以每天及时收集提前落下的果实，阻止老熟幼虫钻入土壤，打断该虫的越冬，防止再侵染。重复此操作3-4年，可将欧洲栗象的种群密度降低到可承受水平。
remark: 欧洲栗象Curculio elephas (Gyllenhal)属鞘翅目Coleoptera、象虫科Curculionidae、象虫亚科Curculioninae、象虫属Curculio。在欧洲南部大部分地区、非洲北部均有分布。该虫是栗树上的重要害虫，降低板栗的食用价值、市场价值，减缓橡树林的再生，严重影响这些地区寄主植物及其产品的国内调运和对外贸易。1983年，美国将该虫列入《美国尚未发生或局部分布的有害生物》。该虫是我国进境检疫性有害生物，一旦传入我国，将对我国的板栗生产、橡树林等带来毁灭性危害。
author: cpqis.zhouxian

management_info:
检疫管理措施 
1   将玫瑰蜗牛增补为进境植物检疫性有害生物鉴于国际自然保护联盟(IUCN)已将玫瑰蜗牛列为全球100种最具破坏性的外来人侵物种名录和中国大陆没有该螺分布以及该螺在入侵地造成的生态灾害情况，为最大限度地降低该螺传人中国大陆的风险，建议将该螺增补为进境植物检疫性有害生物，加强检疫。 
2  禁止引种 
世界各国的实践证明，引进玫瑰蜗牛作为天敌控制螺害，将对当地的生态平衡造成严重破坏，因此，有关部门必须明令禁止引进玫瑰蜗牛作为天敌用于生物防治。 
3  加强口岸检疫 
对来自疫区的木质包装材料、集装箱应该重点检查，仔细观察集装箱的底部和四角部位以及所装货物的木质包装材料是否有蜗牛，玫瑰蜗牛昼伏夜出，尤其要注意阴暗蔽光处的检查，用手电筒仔细寻找蜗牛的行迹。蜗牛爬行过后，会留下银灰色的丝带状黏液痕迹，这是判定是否有蜗牛污染的重要依据。发现蜗牛标本，随时装入塑料自封袋或标本瓶带回实验室做进一步的检验鉴定。发现盆景等携带土壤或其他细碎衬垫材料时，需过筛检查是否有卵或幼螺。对可能被蜗牛污染的物品可用高压水枪冲洗或做熏蒸灭蜗处理。 
4  加强口岸监测 
每年监测l～2次，用密达(Meta)、梅塔等优良杀螺剂与炒香的米糠等混合制成可回收的绿色毒饵，于傍晚时施于口岸码头、车站、货场周围的阴暗处，诱杀蜗牛。第2天早上回收毒盒，捡取中毒蜗牛，并进行鉴定或集中销毁，达到监测与除害的双重效果。
author: cpqis.wuchen

potential_eco_desc:
从已有的文献分析，玫瑰蜗牛主要是对入侵地的无脊椎动物区系构成威胁，特别是侵害本地蜗牛，引起种群数量的锐减，造成本地蜗牛的物种灭绝。第二次世界大战前后，非洲大蜗牛在太平洋地区危害成灾，为了防治螺害，玫瑰蜗牛和三叶扁平虫(Platydemus manokwari De Beauchamp，1962)被作为非洲大蜗牛的天敌引进到这些地区，虽然非洲大蜗牛得到了一定的控制，但也导致一些本土有益蜗牛灭绝。如1955年，玫瑰蜗牛引人夏威夷用于控制非洲大蜗牛，结果当地的一些树栖性蜗牛种群数量锐减，大量物种灭绝，成为本意引进天敌控制有害生物，引进后反而捕食有益生物最为典型的负面事例之一。
太平洋岛屿是陆生软体动物最丰富的地区之一，引进玫瑰蜗牛和三叶扁平虫后，其陆贝的物种多样性正在迅速消失。Endodontidae可能是太平洋岛屿中最大的科，似乎已经完全灭绝，或者缩小成为稀疏的残余种群。法属玻里尼西亚(Moorea)上的所有Partulidae已在野外灭绝。在夏威夷，750种蜗牛中高达90％的物种已经灭绝。在马里亚纳群岛北部(Rota)，43种蜗牛中68％已经灭绝或者种群下降，而在萨摩亚群岛，几乎全部蜗牛种群都在下降，面临灭绝的境地。

host_range: E. rosea is native to the south-eastern USA, and is found in South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana. In 1955 it was introduced to the Hawaiian islands in an attempt to control the spread of the introduced herbivorous snail Ac
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe economic impact of E. rosea is difficult to determine. Whilst it appears to have had no effect on the control of Achatina, it has had a devastating impact on the endemic snail faunas of many of the islands to which it has been introduced (Cowie, 2001; Gerlach, 2001). This in turn has been damaging to scientific investigations of those species, notably the work carried out by Clark and others on the genetic diversity of Partula on Moorea (Civeyrel and Simberloff, 1996). A considerable international effort is underway to conserve these threatened island snails, which includes captive breeding programmes and the creation of reserves free from Euglandina.^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe introduction of E. rosea has resulted in changes to the endemic snail fauna. Thirty-three species of Partula were lost from Raiatea, one of the Society Islands, French Polynesia, destroying one of the finest examples of island evolutionary radiation (Coote and Loeve, 2003). According to Cowie (1998), the modification and destruction of indigenous snail habitats in Hawaii has helped the spread of non-indigenous molluscs.^p^p^p^Social impact^pOn Huahine, one of the Society Islands, French Polynesia, the shells of Partula rosea and Partula varia were used for making lei (jewellery). The extinction of these snail species has had a detrimental economic and social effect on the local community, with the women in many villages losing their livelihoods (Coote and Loeve, 2003).^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pIn many cases, E. rosea has had a serious, negative impact on endemic snail species, such as Partulidae and Achatinelliae, in the countries to which it has been introduced in order to control the spread of Achatina fulica. Many of these endemic species have either been eradicated or vastly reduced in number. In French Polynesia there are now conservation programmes in place aimed at breeding and releasing Partulid species that have evaded extinction by E. rosea predation (Mace et al., 1998).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>native fauna
description: E. rosea was deliberately introduced into Bermuda (in 1958-1960), French Polynesia (in 1974-1977), Guam, American Samoa (1980), Hawaii (in 1955-1958) and the Northern Mariana Islands as a biological control agent against Achatina fulica. It is probable that E. rosea was similarly introduced into the other countries where it is listed as an exotic species (Cowie, 2003). In all cases it has failed as a biological control agent but succeeded in impacting upon native mollusca, frequently resulting in the loss of endemic species. E. rosea was introduced into New Caledonia (1974-1978) and Vanuatu (1973). It was also introduced into Papua New Guinea (1952-1961) but failed to establish there (Cowie, 2000).

description: Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants: invisible.

remark: The potential for further spread of E. rosea is primarily through further deliberate introductions. The IUCN ISSG has listed E. rosea amongst 100 of the world's worst invasive species and condemned its use as a biological control agent. However, Cowie (2000) stated that intense pressure from Pacific Islanders to resolve the problem of Achatina fulica may lead to its deliberate official or unofficial release. Increasing trade between countries could also lead to the introduction of E. rosea into new habitats (Cowie, 1998).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pIn the Mediterranean region, T. pityocampa is considered one of the most important forest pests (Cadahia et al., 1975). It is very common in pine forests. It also commonly occurs in the cedar forests of North Africa. Defoliation damage is extremely serious in young reforested areas where it may lead to death of trees, directly or as a consequence of attack by bark beetles or other wood-boring insects. In mature forests trees are rarely killed but significant losses occur in volume growth.Calas (1897) estimated a 60% reduction in height growth of Pinus nigra trees. In young reforestations of Pinus radiata, Cadahia and Insua (1970), by controlling infestations on young trees, demonstrated losses of wood volume increment between 14 and 33% for light and high infestations, respectively. Bouchon and Toth (1971) showed by dendrochronological techniques that forests of P. nigra periodically subject to heavy attacks lost about 45% of their volume in 50 years. Lemoine (1977) found a reduction of 30% in circumference growth after an attack on Pinus pinaster in Les Landes, France. Defoliation of P. nigra on Mont Ventoux by T. pityocampa caused a missing growth ring the year after a severe attack, resulting in radial growth reductions of 35% (Laurent-Hervouet, 1986). In Corsica, radial growth losses on P. nigra were 20% for the 28 years studied, but the attacks only took place every other year.^p^pDefoliation damage and the presence of caterpillars are important on amenity trees in recreational and residential areas, where defoliation may also cause severe deterioration and greater maintenance costs.^p^p^Environmental impact^pT. pityocampa is most conspicuously damaging on pine plantations, or amenity pines. Such plantations are readily invaded, including those of Pinus spp. originating in other areas. On this basis, it could be said that T. pityocampa is not invasive in its native area, but has a clear potential to become so on other Pinus spp. in any area of Mediterranean climate. It may also have the potential to be invasive as a result of climate change; for example, in France, Pinus nigra forests in the centre of the country have been more severely damaged by the pest in the recent series of warm years (Goussard et al., 1999), whereas in Italy Pinus sylvestris and Pinus mugo are now attacked in mountain areas (Benigni and Battisti, 1999).^p^p^Social impact^pThe caterpillars have urticating hairs from the third instar onwards (Demolin, 1963), which may cause allergies resulting in conjunctivitis, respiratory congestions and asthma (Ziprkowski and Roland, 1966). Domestic and farm animals may also be affected. These effects occur not only when the caterpillars are present, but also during the following summer because of the persistence of allergenic hairs in the remains of winter nests. This problem not only affects recreational and residential areas but also hinders sylvicultural operations and grazing in forests (Marti Morera and Barri Baya, 1959).^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pLarval feeding weakens and disfigures pine trees. Semi-natural forests in the Mediterranean area of, for example, the native Pinus halepensis or P. pinaster are affected, but not to the extent of damaging their biodiversity. T. pityocampa could potentially affect the biodiversity of natural forests of native Pinus spp. in areas with a Mediterranean climate where the pest does not now occur.^p^pIn Spain, Pinus sylvestris persists naturally as an ice-age relict in small mountain forests. Their survival is threatened by T. pityocampa, which damages them especially in warmer years (Hodar et al., 2003).
description: T. pityocampa is widespread in the Mediterranean region, but is missing from some smaller islands. Thus, it is present in Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily and Crete, and the larger Balearic Islands, but the European Union maintains a 'protected zone' for the island of Ibiza. There are no records for Malta.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pChemical control treatments are mainly applied by ULV aerial spraying with rotary atomizers, with petroleum oil or vegetable oils as solvents. Dosages of active substances (diflubenzuron, cypermethrin, deltamethrin) are given by Robredo (1980) and Robredo and Obama (1987). All larval instars are susceptible to these treatments, but the fourth and fifth instars need the highest dosages. At this stage of development, during the winter months, the impact of pyrethroids on the beneficial insect fauna is minimized (Robredo and Obama, 1991). ^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pIn small areas or at low population density, mechanical control is also recommended, by cutting and burning of winter nests. Sex pheromone traps may be used, both for monitoring and for mass trapping (Cadahia et al., 1975;Montoya, 1984, 1988).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pNumerous natural enemies occur naturally on T. pityocampa (see Notes of Natural Enemies) and regulate populations to a certain degree. They are not specifically used as biological control agents. ^p^pBacillus thuringiensis can be used successfully as a 'microbial insecticide', under the same conditions as the substances mentioned under Chemical Control. Recently, entomopathogenic nematodes have been evaluated to control overwintering larvae (Triggiani et al., 2003), and the Argentine ant Linepithema humile has been found to be a very active predator of larvae (Way et al., 1999).^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pThe measures used for 'protected zones' in the European Union are to require plants for planting of Pinus to be produced in nurseries, which should with their immediate vicinity be found free from the pest. Because the pest is conspicuous, such requirements are probably easier to implement than inspection of traded plants for eggs and larvae, or of accompanying soil for pupae, which would be a more direct approach.

management_info:
As with other bacteria, available chemicals are rarely effective against D. chrysanthemi. Streptomycin sulphate or kazugamycin can be applied (in countries where antibiotics are allowed) to control soft rot in propagation beds. Streptomycin sulphate and iodine gave better control of Dickeya paradisiaca on plantain than copper oxychloride (Salazar and Duque, 1994). Chlorination of water reduced infection on maize. Calcium hypochlorite was effective as a soil drench and streptomycin was effective in sprays (Thompson, 1965; Lal et al., 1970; Thind and Soni, 1983; Thind et al., 1984).
In general, control relies largely on the integration of prophylactic measures: adoption of cutting indexing schemes for dahlia, carnation (Nassar et al., 1996b), certification of pathogen-free potato seed tubers (Pérombelon and Hyman, 1992; Cazelles et al., 1995; Wolf et al., 1995) and reduction of the rates of nitrogenous fertilizer (on maize, Saxena and Lal, 1981).    Host-Plant Resistance: The use of resistant cultivars is effective for a number of host plants (MacFadden, 1959; Goto, 1992). For chrysanthemums, the cultivars Goldsmith, Masterpiece, Mary Lennon Hall and Blazing Gold were considered the most tolerant (Burkholder et al., 1953). For maize, differences in susceptibility have been detected among maize lines in India after artificial inoculation (Lal et al., 1970; Thind and Payak, 1978). Resistance has been identified in hybrids that have higher amounts of total phenols present. For Dieffenbachia, the cultivars Camille, Compacta and Parachute showed the broadest resistance toward all pathogens, and would permit selection (Norman et al., 1997). For potato, susceptibility is often performed on tubers, and ranking of cultivars appears to be the same with all pectolytic Erwinias (Wolters and Collins, 1994; Lebecka and Zimnock-Guzowska, 1996; Haynes et al., 1997). Breeding programmes would be most efficient when directed to clonal differences for stem base resistance (Allefs et al., 1996). A somatic hybrid of Solanum brevidens and S. tuberosum, resistant to degradation by D. chrysanthemi, was shown to have the advantage of a high methylated pectin (MacMillan et al., 1993; Dorel et al., 1996). For sweet potato, selection provided high resistance to D. chrysanthemi (Chen et al., 1994; Rolston et al., 1995).

potential_eco_desc: P. chrysanthemi causes destruction of many flower and ornamental crops, particularly carnation and chrysanthemum in rooting beds. Losses from P. chrysanthemi are also recorded in potato and Dahlia tuber production. On potatoes, it causes soft rot and blackleg like E. carotovora (Perombelon and Kelman, 1987), but the symptoms tend to be expressed at higher temperatures. Seed potato certification schemes producing material for warmer countries should take account of E. chrysanthemi (Perombelon et al., 1987). Other E. chrysanthemi pathovars affect different glasshouse ornamentals (Saintpaulia ionantha, Kalanchoe), as well as in the banana pseudostem rot which can be very destructive.

D. chrysanthemi strains have been isolated from a number of different hosts in different countries. The list of all susceptible plants after inoculation by D. chrysanthemi would be far longer than the natural host range, and difficult to establish.
potential_eco_desc: Corn stalk rot is one of the four major diseases of maize in India. Incidences of 80-85% have been observed in natural cases and yield losses of 98.8% recorded in artificial epiphytotics (Thind and Payak, 1985). A sweetcorn population grown during the 1979/80 growing season in Brasilia (Brazil) was heavily attacked by E. chrysanthemi (Reifschneider and Lopes, 1982). In temperate regions, the disease is often linked to overhead irrigation but not exclusively (Kelman et al., 1957; Hartman and Kelman, 1973; Otta and Wood, 1977; Lopes et al., 1986). ^p^pHollow stalk of chrysanthemum causes rapid and serious losses in the greenhouse for the cut flower market. Young plants may be destroyed in propagation beds under favourable environmental conditions. However, the economic importance of this pathogen is not clear. This is partly due to confusion with E. carotovora, which is also capable of soft rotting stem cuttings of chrysanthemum.^p^pSlow wilt of carnation occurs in protected and field-grown crops. Symptoms appear 3 to 6 months after planting. This was a major carnation disease in the 1950s and 1960s due to the persistence of the bacteria in stock mother plants and the absence of cutting indexing schemes (Lelliott, 1988).^p^pWhen potato soft rot, due to E. chrysanthemi, is tuber-transmitted, tuber breakdown appears very soon after planting giving dwarfism, wilting and sometimes no plant at all.

remark: E. chrysanthemi pv. dianthicola is subject to control within the European Union (Community Legislation in Force Document 392L0103) under Section II, harmful organisms known to occur in the community and relevant for the entire community. As it is not at this time known to occur within Lithuania, E. chrysanthemi pv. dianthicola is also considered a sufficiently harmful organism that must be prohibited (Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Lithuania, 1998). Pathovars of E. chrysanthemi are listed as A2 quarantine pests by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1982). This arose historically from the earlier listing of the carnation pathogen and it does not appear that plant quarantine authorities had other hosts in mind. When bacterial nomenclature was revised in 1980, EPPO specified that the quarantine pests concerned were pathovars dianthicola and chrysanthemi (OEPP/EPPO, 1988). It was accepted that the major means of infection of these crops, at least in some countries, was the use of infected planting material which, according to current trade practice, was mostly imported. Thus, the local presence of E. chrysanthemi was irrelevant (since it could be excluded by very simple precautions), and protection against this pest was perceived as a plant quarantine problem.^p^pSince then, argument has continued on the infraspecific forms of E. chrysanthemi that are supposed to be covered by the quarantine pest classification. This debate has been further complicated in two ways: (1) many authorities consider E. chrysanthemi is so widely distributed in the EPPO region that it cannot classify as a quarantine pest: (2) the existence of host-specific pathovars is queried (Samson et al., 1987), at least with respect to carnation and chrysanthemum, which increases yet further the possibility that these crops might be infected from sources other than imported planting material. It is now accepted within EPPO that the risk from E. chrysanthemi can be adequately covered by national nuclear-stock certification schemes for the crops concerned (see Phytosanitary Measures) and that E. chrysanthemi will be deleted from the EPPO A2 list as soon as such schemes have been agreed for carnations (OEPP/EPPO, 1991) and chrysanthemums. No other regional plant protection organization considers E. chrysanthemi to be a quarantine pest. ^p^pAs a phytosanitary measure, EPPO recommends (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) that plants for planting of carnations or chrysanthemums should come from mother plants found free from E. chrysanthemi (by testing in the case of carnations). However, now that nuclear-stock certification schemes are recommended for carnations (OEPP/EPPO, 1991) and chrysanthemums (in preparation), it is simpler to recommend that planting material of these crops should originate from such schemes. No particular recommendations are needed for other crops.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pAs with other bacteria, available chemicals are rarely effective against E. chrysanthemi. Streptomycin sulphate or kazugamycin can be applied (in countries where antibiotics are allowed) to control soft rot in propagation beds. Streptomycin sulphate and iodine gave better control of E. chrysanthemi pv. paradisiaca on plantain than copper oxychloride (Salazar and Duque, 1994). Chlorination of water reduced infection on maize. Calcium hypochlorite was effective as a soil drench and streptomycin was effective in sprays (Thompson, 1965; Lal et al., 1970; Thind and Soni, 1983; Thind et al., 1984).^p^pIn general, control relies largely on the integration of prophylactic measures: adoption of cutting indexing schemes for dahlia, carnation (Nassar et al., 1996b), certification of pathogen-free potato seed tubers (Perombelon and Hyman, 1992; Cazelles et al., 1995; Wolf et al., 1995) and reduction of the rates of nitrogenous fertilizer (on maize, Saxena and Lal, 1981).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe use of resistant cultivars is effective for a number of host plants (MacFadden, 1959; Goto, 1992). For chrysanthemums, the cultivars Goldsmith, Masterpiece, Mary Lennon Hall and Blazing Gold were considered the most tolerant (Burkholder et al., 1953). For maize, differences in susceptibility have been detected among maize lines in India after artificial inoculation (Lal et al., 1970; Thind and Payak, 1978). Resistance has been identified in hybrids that have higher amounts of total phenols present. For Dieffenbachia, the cultivars Camille, Compacta and Parachute showed the broadest resistance toward all pathogens, and would permit selection (Norman et al., 1997). For potato, susceptibility is often performed on tubers, and ranking of cultivars appears to be the same with all pectolytic Erwinias (Wolters and Collins, 1994; Lebecka and Zimnock-Guzowska, 1996; Haynes et al., 1997). Breeding programmes would be most efficient when directed to clonal differences for stem base resistance (Allefs et al., 1996). A somatic hybrid of Solanum brevidens and S. tuberosum, resistant to degradation by E. chrysanthemi, was shown to have the advantage of a high methylated pectin (MacMillan et al., 1993; Dorel et al., 1996). For sweet potato, selection provided high resistance to E. chrysanthemi (Chen et al., 1994; Rolston et al., 1995).
