host_range: Notholithocarpus densiflorus, Abies grandis and Pseudotsuga menziesii growing in the mixed conifer forest of Curry County, OR were infected by Phytophthora ramorum.
potential_eco_desc: Phytophthora ramorum EU1 lineage is considered more aggressive than the NA1 lineage and is of opposite mating type to NA1, thus potentially resulting in establishment of sexual populations.
description: In the winter of 2015, a symptomatic Notholithocarpus densiflorus Manos, Cannon & S.H.Oh (tanoak) was identified during a SOD helicopter survey in Curry County, OR. Phytophthora ramorum was isolated from symptomatic bark tissue. Subsequently, the isolate was determined to be of the EU1 lineage based on 14 microsatellite loci. Continued monitoring of the area in 2016 and 2017 has identified symptomatic Abies grandis and Pseudotsuga menziesii saplings growing near infected tanoak trees in the mixed conifer forest of Curry County, OR. Based on the presence of chlamydospores, characteristic hyphae, and sporangial morphology, the isolates were identified as Phytophthora ramorum, and sequences analysis confirming that the pathogen was P. ramorum EU1 lineage.
reference_name: First Report of Phytophthora ramorum Lineage EU1 Infecting Douglas Fir and Grand Fir in Oregon

host_range: Rhododendron（a rhododendron var. Trilby ）
description: In July 2012, we collected a rhododendron var. Trilby with twig dieback symptoms in the lower canopy, consistent with the disease “ramorum blight” caused by Phytophthora ramorum. The symptomatic plant had been planted a year earlier to replace a dead rhododendron in a landscape setting in Placer County, California (Lat: 39.036216°; Long: –120.999274°), Sierra Nevada foothills at ~600 m elevation. The test demonstrated that the pathogen was Phytophthora ramorum, the isolate belongs to the NA2 lineage of the pathogen. This is the first report of P. ramorum from the Sierra Nevada eco-region in the interior of California. It is also the first report of a NA2 isolate from a plant outside of commercial nurseries in California. The mating type of the isolate was not determined, but NA2 isolates are normally A2, the same mating type of NA1 isolates. The only other report of a NA2 isolate found outside of a nursery is from Washington State. Although there is no evidence the pathogen may have infected other plants, the infected rhododendron was found at a location situated over 100 km east of the closest known infestation (www.sodmap.org). Additionally, this is the first report of the pathogen outside the coast mountain range of California.
reference_name: First Report of the NA2 Lineage of Phytophthora ramorum from an Ornamental Rhododendron in the Interior of California
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: 地中海荚蒾Viburnum tinus
description: In spring 2013, pot-grown Viburnum tinus plants shipped to an ornamental nursery in Pescia (Pistoia, central Italy, 287 m a.s.l., 43°54′0″ N, 10°41′0″ E) from another local nursery were found to bear disease symptoms. The test demonstrated that the causal agent was P. ramorum, it was reported in Italy in 2003 on the exotic Rhododendron yakushimanum. This is the first report of the pathogen on a native species (V. tinus) in this country.
reference_name: Foliar Blight and Shoot Dieback Caused by Phytophthora ramorum on Viburnum tinus in the Pistoia Area, Tuscany, Central Italy

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe overall economic impact of P. ramorum in California, USA, is hard to assess. Californian oaks (Quercus spp.) and tanoaks (Lithocarpus densiflorus) affected by the pathogen are not commercial timber species. The addition of redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) to the list of hosts poses a potential economic cost to the timber industry. Symptoms on these hosts are somewhat limited and the pathogen has only been found on plant parts with a diameter of less than an inch. Impact is generally limited to only small trees, such as regeneration trees.^p^pDead tree counts are probably in the thousands, but the extreme patchiness of the disease makes any assessment of tree mortality extremely difficult (Kelly and Meentemeyer, 2002). Oaks in particular are known to increase the real estate value of property: large numbers of landscape oaks have been infected, with significant financial repercussions for property owners. Mortality of oaks is likely to have doubled and that of tanoaks quadrupled (Swiecki and Bernhardt, 2001; McPherson et al., 2002), due to this disease. Costs of removal of dead trees and of disposal of the infectious green waste are also significant. The need for precautionary and sanitary practices is an added indirect cost to arborists and other tree professionals. ^p^pSome industries have been particularly affected by P. ramorum, including the ornamental plants industry (Linderman et al., 2002; Parke et al., 2002) and the composting industry (Garbelotto, 2003). It is not only Californian growers that are affected, but also those outside California due to the decreased availability of Californian-grown propagative material. Edible mycorrhizal mushrooms are reported to have decreased in numbers in areas highly affected by the disease.^p^pDeath of large numbers of trees in popular parks and recreation areas, and the partial closure of some infested areas during the rainy season, are having an impact on the recreational value of open spaces. The cost of tree removal and disposal for agencies, public or private, running large open spaces can be extremely high. The need to lower the risk of spread in industries affected by Sudden Oak Death will translate into management practices with a significant price tag (e.g the washing of logging trucks, the closure of some roads and accesses, the need to process bay leaves to ensure the pathogen is dead, the need to ensure mature compost does not become contaminated by the green waste in fresh compost piles, and so forth). These expenditures can be considered indirect economic costs of P. ramorum.^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pOaks and tanoaks are extremely susceptible to the disease. Tanoak (Lithocarpus densiflorus) is probably the most susceptible species in California, USA. Some local populations, e.g. some canyons in the Big Sur area (Monterey County), have lost all of their adult trees because of Sudden Oak Death (SOD). The disease has the potential to cause a significant genetic bottleneck in this tree species. The demise of entire tanoak populations is changing the nature of those forests, in general moving towards pure redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) stands with marginal presence of oaks and Douglas firs. All life depending on tanoaks is likely to be locally affected. Tanoak is also the major ectomycorrhizal host of most of these stands and its disappearance is likely to have a significant impact on ectomycorrhizal populations. Abundance of dead and fallen woody material constitutes a significant fire hazard: although fires are probably a good thing in these fire-adapted forests, it is likely that the intensity of these fires may be much higher that the norm because of the large accumulation of woody debris. The presence and incidence of coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia) is also bound to change, and some local strong shifts towards Douglas fir forests may be observed. The extremely adaptable and drought-resistant woodlands

management_info: Recommendations for silvicultural practices to control P. ramorum have not yet been made. It has been shown that fresh wounds will be optimal infection courts. In restoration projects, avoid bay laurel (Umbellularia californica) if possible, especially in areas where oaks may be growing. Eradication has been attempted in southern Oregon, USA, via the burn-and-slash technique (Goheen et al., 2002b).^p^pKnowledge to support a complete control program is still limited; however, significant results have been achieved, considering the relatively short period of time since the pathogen was discovered:-^p^p- Kiln drying: 55°C for 30 minutes was insufficient to kill the pathogen. At least one hour required.^p^p- Composting following guidelines prescribing piles to be kept at 55°C for at least 2 weeks is successful in eliminating the pathogen (oospores not present).^p^p- P. ramorum is susceptible to label-dosages of copper sulfates and copper hydroxides. In different formulations it is moderately susceptible to mancozeb. The pathogen is sensitive to phosphites or phosphonates. Phosphite injections are effective in oaks and tanoaks (Lithocarpus densiflorus). Phosphite foliar sprays are not effective on oaks and tanoaks. The pathogen is extremely sensitive to metalaxyl, but drenches and foliar sprays are ineffective in oaks (Garbelotto et al., 2002b).^p^p- Water and moisture management are extremely important, especially when temperatures are between 15 and 20°C. Infection on bay (Umbellularia californica) leaves requires 9-12 hours of leaf wetness.^p^p- Natural contagion from oaks is estimated to be low: susceptible oaks should not be planted near foliar hosts like bays, madrones (Arbutus menziesii) and rhododendrons.^p^p- Early infection can be detected on foliar hosts: new infection on bay leaves and Pacific madrones, or infection on new maple (Acer macrophyllum) and buckeye (Aesculus californica) leaves are good signs of inoculum level.^p^p- Sites, soil and streams can be monitored by baiting with live rhododendron or madrone plants (air), or by baiting with rhododendron leaves and pears (Davidson et al., 2002c).

description: 发病植株上的果实中的病菌可以侵入种子，病菌粘附在种皮或种毛上，如果种植了这种带菌的种子，即可将病菌传开。有报道认为：种子的带菌率达到1%时，即可以引起田间50%植株发病。番茄溃疡病在国家之间，多半都是通过种子的流通或新品种的引进传播开的。病菌在田间主要依靠雨水飞溅进行传播，如果一块地被传入番茄溃疡病，在3～4周后田间极有可能出现病株，这些病株病斑上可产生大量病原细菌，除继续由雨水飞溅传播外，还可随灌溉水、整枝、打杈、绑蔓等农事操作以及昆虫危害的途径在田间进行多次再侵染，引起大面积的发病。带病的土壤和种苗也是病害的主要侵染源。

potential_eco_desc: Severe outbreaks of the disease were recorded in the central and northwest parts of the Russian Federation.
description: Yellow-pigmented clavibacteria were isolated from diseased potato plants and tubers from five regions of Russia between 2011 and 2017. Severe outbreaks of the disease were recorded in the central and northwest parts of the Russian Federation. Samples were collected and colonies were isolated from diseased potato plant. The pathogen was identified as Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis (Cmm) by molecular diagnostics and the pathogenicity tests. This is the first report of Cmm affecting potato in Russia.
reference_name: First Report of Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis Infecting Potato in Russia

description: 该病原菌的远距离传播主要靠带菌种子，番茄种子内外层都可带菌。在田间和温室，该病菌主要通过灌溉水、雨水、修枝剪、培养料等传播，由伤口、气孔和自然孔口侵入寄主组织。该病菌在土壤和病残体组织中可存活 2 ～ 3年。

先将番茄种子在凉水中浸泡10分钟，捞出后将种子放入55℃温水浸泡30 min，不断搅拌并随时补充热水，然后把种子捞出后放入凉水中，室温条件下浸泡4～5 h；或将充分干燥的番茄种子放人70℃恒温箱中灭菌72 h；或用200毫克/公斤农用硫酸链霉索浸种2小时后播种。
及时拔除田间发现的病株，并带出田外深埋或烧毁，然后每穴浇灌20%石灰水0.25公斤，或每穴扑石灰0.25公斤。也可用50%墟胶肥酸铜叫湿性粉剂500信液灌根，每株用药液0.5公斤。
在田间发病初期，可喷1:1200的波尔多液，或72%农用硫酸链霉素4000倍液，或77%可杀得可湿性粉剂500倍液，或40% DT杀菌剂400倍液进行喷雾，或14%的络氨铜水剂300倍液，间隔期7～10天，连施3～4次。

potential_eco_desc: Since the first report of the disease in the USA in 1910, bacterial canker has spread throughout the world and causes serious losses to both greenhouse and field tomato crops either by killing the young plants or reducing marketable yields. Reduction in yield may be associated with direct plant loss, reduced numbers of fruit or fruit size. Field experiments have recorded yield losses of 20% or more in Ontario, Canada (Dhanvantari, 1989; Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993); 20-30% in France (Rat et al., 1991); 46% in Illinois, USA (Chang et al., 1992c); and a 10-fold yield reduction after plant loss in Queensland, Australia (Dullahide et al., 1983).
author: CPC2006

description: Incidence^p^pThe incidence of infection of tomato seeds by C. michiganensis subsp. michiganensis reported in the literature varies from (dayuhao)1 to 97% (Strider, 1969; Chang et al., 1991; Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993). This variability may be attributed to the age of seed stocks and seed storage conditions. In storage at room temperature, the viability of seed infection in naturally infected seeds harvested from the field declined from 82 to (dayuhao)1% in 18 months and to 0% in 2 years. In storage at 4°C and 60% RH, the general seed storage conditions and viability of seed infection declined from 100 to (dayuhao)5% in 3 years and 6 months (Dhanvantari, 1993). Indirect evidence from seed disinfection studies indicate that a small percentage of seed infection may be deep-seated within the seed tissue (Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993).^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pInfected tomato seeds are usually indistinguishable from healthy seeds. Germination of infected seeds and the ensuing seedling stand also appear normal (Dhanvantari, 1989; Gitaitis et al., 1991; Chang et al., 1992a).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pStudies on transmission of seedborne C. michiganensis subsp. michiganensis were carried out with seeds harvested from naturally-infected tomato plants (Dhanvantari, 1989); seed from artificially-inoculated plants (Dhanvantari, 1989; Chang et al., 1992a; Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993); and artificially-infested seeds (Tsiantos, 1987). Infection levels in plants grown from infected seeds varied from ca 1% (Tsiantos, 1987; Chang et al., 1992a), 24-53% (Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993) and 80-90% (Dhanvantari, 1989), depending upon the proportion of infected seeds in the seed batches and seed storage conditions (Dhanvantari, 1993). Even low seed transmission rates may result in increased disease incidence as a result of trimming, packaging and transportation of transplants (Chang et al., 1991; Gitaitis et al., 1991); pruning and tying of trellis and staked tomato plants; or deleafing, suckering and tying operations in the greenhouse. Kritzman (1991) reported a seed health assay that enables the determination a minimal threshold of C. michiganensis subsp. michiganensis that is related to the percentage of diseased seedlings that develop from the same seed lot.^p^pThe pathogen may survive in infected plant debris or on stakes and trellises for long enough to establish a resident population on newly planted tomato seedlings in the following season. This leads to infection via broken trichomes on the leaves or through wounds (Layne, 1967; Gleason et al., 1991; Shirakawa et al., 1991; Chang et al., 1992a). Entry of the bacteria into the leaf may also be gained by withdrawal of contaminated guttation drops through hydathodes (Carlton et al., 1992) or by injury caused by chemical sprays (Farley and Miller, 1973).^p^pIn nutrient film technique (NFT) culture of tomatoes growing in recirculating nutrient solution, it was shown that low populations of the bacterium are sufficient to infect the plants via roots at all stages of development (Griesbach and Lattauschke, 1991). Canker was shown to spread from infected transplants to other plants in recirculating NFT culture with a lag of ca 4 weeks before brown necrotic spots on the leaves and wilt symptoms began to appear on other plants (Dhanvantari, 1995).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pSeed treatments for the eradication of C. michiganensis subsp. michiganensis from seeds include fermentation, hot water, hydrochloric acid, calcium hypochlorite and sodium hypochlorite, and o-hydroxydiphenyl (o-phenylphenol). Fermentation is routinely used to extract tomato seeds while reducing the population of the canker bacteria, but it can take as long as 96 h to eradicate them. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) has been reported to be consistently effective in eradicating the canker bacteria from tomato seeds. It is used to treat the tomato pulp in seed extraction at 0.6% for 45 min (Thyr et al., 1973) or to soak the seeds at 1.9%

management_info: Improved management of bacterial canker in tomato has been shown to be possible by the use of healthy seeds, seed treatment, appropriate cultural practices, chemical sprays where needed, hygiene and sanitation (Gleason et al., 1993).^p^pRecent advances have introduced more efficient techniques to aid seed health testing, and many seed companies are using one or more of them. A substantial reduction of infection can be achieved by acid extraction of seeds or treatment of seeds with acid or other disinfectants or hot water (Shoemaker and Echandi, 1976; Dhanvantari, 1989; Fatmi et al., 1991; Dhanvantari and Brown, 1993; Dhanvantari, 1994).^p^pCultural practices such as deep ploughing to bury infected crop residue after harvest to accelerate decomposition, and crop rotation away from solanaceous crops for at least 2 years, are recommended to reduce the incidence of canker (Gleason et al., 1991). Production of tomato transplants in greenhouses planted in soilless medium in plastic trays, has been found to be feasible and more reliable than field-grown transplants for reducing the risk of bacterial canker (Gleason et al., 1993). They form part of the current production recommendations in Canada and the USA. Copper-based chemicals are usually sprayed on tomato for controlling bacterial diseases but their effect on canker is poorly documented. However, under conditions of frequent rainfall and prolonged wet periods, chemical sprays with copper-containing compounds have been found useful in reducing foliar blight and fruit spotting (Shoemaker, 1992).^p^pSources of resistance are available (Gardner et al., 1990; Poysa, 1993; van Steekelenberg, 1985) but have not yet been introduced into commercial cultivars.^p^pIn protected crops, strict hygiene measures such as early detection, isolation and eradication of infected plants, destruction of crop residues, rinsing hands/gloves and pruning tools with a disinfectant after working each row, and disinfection of structures and equipment are essential to manage canker. See Jarvis (1992) for general greenhouse hygiene.

host_range: P. medicaginis has a narrow host range in nature and is primarily a pathogen of the family Fabaceae. It is only known as an agricultural pathogen. Lucerne (Medicago sativa) is the primary host (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996). Other species of Medicago, notably
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThere is apparently no specific information available on the economic impact of P. medicaginis on a regional scale. It is widespread in many lucerne production areas and reduces stand density, winter hardiness (Tu, 1980; Basu and Butler, 1991; Wiersma et al., 1997) and forage yield of individual plants and entire fields (Lowe et al., 1987). A 75% stand reduction in the first year after sowing a susceptible cultivar in naturally infected fields (Gray et al., 1983) is perhaps representative of severe damage. In a different study, individual infected and healthy plants were monitored for 2 years; forage yield of root-rotted plants was reduced by 68% (Gray et al., 1988). In Wisconsin, USA, lucerne cultivars with good field resistance to Phytophthora root rot yielded 40% more than susceptible cultivars and combined resistance to Phytophthora and Aphanomyces increased yield still more (Wiersma et al., 1995). Estimating damage from comparisons of susceptible and resistant cultivars probably underestimates total loss, because even 'resistant' cultivars may be infected and damaged, especially under very wet conditions (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996). ^p^pIn eastern Australia, Phytophthora root rot caused by P. medicaginis is regarded as one of the major constraints to lucerne production on poorly drained soil types (Irwin, 1974; Rogers et al., 1978). ^p^pP. medicaginis is a major disease of chickpea in Australia (Vock et al., 1980; Irwin and Dales, 1982; Brinsmead et al., 1985; Knights et al., 2003). Large areas of chickpea in a field can be killed causing growers to abandon part or all of affected crops (Dale and Irwin, 1990b). Yield losses can exceed 50% for individual crops and reach 20% on a regional basis in years with above average rainfall (Knights et al., 2003).^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe impact of P. medicaginis on the natural environment has not been reported. However, it is likely to be minimal because of its narrow host range of agricultural plants within the Fabaceae.   Lucerne and chickpea are the primary hosts (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996; Irwin and Dales, 1982). Annual species of Medicago are also susceptible under field test conditions (Haan et al., 1996). Annual medics and many other legumes are common in the natural environment. However, the effect of P. medicaginis on many of these legumes and the interaction of these effects with other plants are unknown.^p^p^p^Social impact^pThere are no documented studies of the social impact of P. medicaginis on human activities which would indicate a low impact.  However, root rot of lucerne and chickpea caused by this pathogen can result in high economic losses on individual farms and, logically, this reduces the livelihood of these primary producers. ^p^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pThere are no reported impacts of P. medicaginis on biodiversity. P. medicaginis does not hybridize with other Phytophthora spp. such as P. sojae (Layton and Kuhn, 1988; Nygaard et al.,1989) and P. megasperma (Hansen, 1987).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>crop production; livestock production
description: The centre of origin of P. medicaginis is unknown. However, because this pathogen has a narrow host range of chickpea and lucerne, it has been suggested that it has co-evolved with these hosts in Transcaucasia (Irwin et al., 1995). Single introductions from this centre may have resulted in the Australian and USA populations of P. medicaginis. These introductions were most likely of an accidental nature involving the transport of contaminated soil or infected plant material.

remark: The spread of P. medicaginis is by survival structures (oospores and chlamydospores) in infected plant tissue and in soil and by zoospores in water. Oospores and chlamydospores may be spread short distances within fields during tillage, or further to different fields in soil adhering to vehicles, tillage implements or animals' feet. Zoospores in their encysted state may spread even greater distances during flood events (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996). In regions where P. medicaginis is already present and damaging, it is usually not found in every field (Aguirre et al., 1983; Basu, 1983; Dale and Irwin, 1990; Munkvold and Carlton, 1995).^p ^pSoil contaminated with oospores of P. medicaginis adhering to tillage implements or to the footwear of travellers or the feet of live export animals are the most likely means of accidental introduction of this pathogen. These carriers may travel vast distances with modern transport, particularly air transport, and oospores can survive for 3.5 years in the soil (Pratt and Mitchell, 1975; Stack and Millar, 1985b).  ^p^pFloodwaters carrying zoospores also are a likely means of accidental introduction to new areas (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996). However, the spread by this means is restricted to areas below the source of infection in the local geomorphic drainage system.^p^pAlfalfa seedlings (sprouts) infected with P. medicaginis also may pose a potential threat in the introduction of this pathogen to new regions. Alfalfa sprouts used in the food industry may be transported great distances by air, rail or road transport and P. medicaginis infecting such plants would readily survive these journeys. Although it may be very unlikely for alfalfa sprouts to be infected with P. medicaginis because this pathogen is not seedborne and water used for their germination should not be contaminated, the possibility remains.  Alfalfa or lucerne seedlings are very susceptible to infection by P. medicaginis and are used to bait the fungus in the isolation of this pathogen (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996).^p^pIt is unlikely that P. medicaginis would be deliberately introduced into a region because it has a narrow host range of mainly agricultural plants and would not be a suitable candidate for the biological control of weeds, other pathogens or animal pests.^p^pP. medicaginis is not known from Europe, and is potentially damaging to lucerne and chickpea if introduced there. In both international and local situations, sanitary precautions, aimed at limiting transport of infected plants and infested soil, will greatly reduce the risk of introduction or local spread.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control of Phytophthora root rot of lucerne is possible in most situations by combinations of improved water management, use of resistant cultivars and crop rotation. Assuring good drainage is the first step in almost all situations. This can be accomplished by selecting well-drained soils for establishment of lucerne crops or grading fields to eliminate low spots (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996), by installing drainage tile or ditches to remove water, by subsoiling to break up impervious soil layers, and by avoiding excessive irrigation (Lehman et al., 1968).^p^pPhytophthora root rot in chickpea in Australia has been partially controlled by using moderately resistant varieties, by seed applications of fungicides such as metalaxyl, by alternative crop rotations and by reduced irrigation regimes (Myatt et al., 1993).^p^pLucerne and chickpea cultivars vary widely in their tolerance of Phytophthora root rot, and selections with useful field resistance are available in most regions where root rot is a problem (Lehman et al., 1967; Irwin, 1974; Irwin and Maxwell, 1980; Frosheiser, 1980; Brinsmead et al., 1985; Lowe et al., 1987; Dale and Irwin, 1991a; Ansar et al., 1995). However, resistance is relative and losses may still be heavy in seedling stands and in chronically poorly drained soils (Erwin and Ribeiro, 1996). If Aphanomyces euteiches is also present, then it may be necessary to use cultivars with dual tolerance (Holub and Grau, 1990b). In the future, new resistant cultivars produced by genetic engineering may be available (Masoud et al., 1996). A genetic linkage map has been developed for lucerne grown in northern Australia (Musial et al., 2005). Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) involved in resistance to P. medicaginis were identified in a backcross population. This genetic linkage map provides an entry point for future molecular-based improvement of disease resistance in lucerne in Australia.^p^pThere has been a recent advance in chickpea breeding for resistance to Phytophthora root rot with the evaluation of wild Cicer species for resistance to P. medicaginis. Cicer echinospermum accessions have shown significantly greater resistance to P. medicaginis than chickpea genotypes, both in the glasshouse and in the field (Knights et al., 2003). C. echinospermum accessions can be readily crossed with chickpea to give fertile progeny and so provide a readily available source of resistance for this pathogen. However, while this source of resistance provides extended scope in breeding programmes, it is incomplete and chickpea with this resistance remain partially susceptible under extreme disease pressure. Thus, other disease control methods in conjunction with plant resistance should not be overlooked.  ^p^pCrop rotations of 3 years or longer are necessary to reduce P. medicaginis populations in fields because of the long-lived oospores (Pratt and Mitchell, 1975; Stack and Millar, 1985b). Populations may quickly recover to damaging levels after a rotation unless drainage is improved and resistant cultivars are employed. Chemical control of Phytophthora root rot is possible, but is seldom economically feasible. The Oomycete-active fungicides will limit development of root rot in seedlings and in established plants, but will not eradicate the pathogen from infested soil. It may be feasible to provide critical short-term protection to seedling stands by fungicidal seed treatments before sowing (Rhodes and Myers, 1989). The usefulness of metalaxyl to control P. medicaginis may soon be reduced with the discovery of an isolate of the fungus insensitive to this fungicide (Stack and Millar, 1985a). Protection of seedlings can be obtained under experimental conditions by seed treatment with biological agents such as the bacterium Bacillus cereus (Silo-Suh et al., 1994). Myatt et al. (1993) found that Pseudomonas cepacia (7 strains) and Pseudomonas fluorescens (2 strains) were able to limit or delay chickpea seedling disease caused by P. medi

description: Incidence^p^pSeed infection by C. michiganensis subsp insidiosus occurs in seeds of lucerne (Cormack and Moffatt, 1956) and has been shown to survive there for at least 3 years (Cormack, 1961). Using a PCR assay in which individual seeds were analysed from infected seed lots, approximately 2.5 to 8.7% of seed contained C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus (Samac et al., 1998). Cormack and Moffat (1956) observed cells of C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus in varying numbers in the vascular system of the flowering rachis and pedicel portions of infected plants. They were also observed in the vascular and parenchymous tissues of several seed pods. Masses of bacteria were observed near aborted seeds. Bacteria were relatively scarce in apparently normal seeds. In premature seeds, bacteria were found in the parenchymatous tissues below the Malpighian cells. In mature seed, bacteria were mainly confined to the aleurone layer of the endosperm. They were not observed in the cotyledons. Erwin and Khan (1987) confirmed seed infection by recovery of the bacterium from seeds harvested from artificially-inoculated plants.^p^pC. michiganensis pv. insidiosus was identified in rice seed by whole cell fatty acid analysis using gas chromatography (Hossain et al., 2003). ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pDiseased plants generally produce relatively few seeds. The seeds which are produced are of low quality, usually shrunken and shrivelled. These seeds are difficult to detect in large seed lots and are usually removed during the seed cleaning process (Cormack and Moffatt, 1956).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pThere is no evidence for transmission of the pathogens from seeds to the plants grown from the seeds.^p^pC. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus can survive in lucerne crop debris for several years (Cormack, 1961).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pNone reported.^p^p^Seed Health Tests^p^pCulture Plate (Sheppard, 1991)^p^p1. Randomly select 5000 seeds; 5 replicates of 1000.^p^p2. Wash thoroughly in running water to remove chemical seed treatment.^p^p3. 2 g (1000 seeds) samples are ground to a fine powder using a ball mill.^p^p4. The ground seed is added to 30 ml sterile nutrient broth and incubated with shaking for 20 min.^p^p5. A 3-fold serial dilution series of this seed slurry is prepared and 100 μl plated from each dilution onto duplicate plates of Glucose-Yeast-Carbonate Agar (GYCA), supplemented with antibiotics to reduce the numbers of contaminating bacteria.^p^p6. Incubate samples at 22°C in the dark for 7-10 days. Examine after 5, 6 and 7 days for colonies typical of the pathogen.^p^p7. Colonies of the pathogen are mucoid, pale yellow to greyish, convex and entire. Frequently a brilliant blue to jet-black pigment forms in the colonies of C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus. This pigmentation appears to be enhanced by the antibiotics in the media. Pseudomonas corrugata, a species associated with symptomless lucerne plants (Lukezic, 1979) produces a transient brilliant blue pigment on this media. This pigmentation fades after 2-4 days whereas the pigment produced by C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus, intensifies over time.^p^pSuspect colonies are removed from the original test plates and pure colonies prepared for use in further tests to confirm identity of the suspect isolates. management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe most effective means of control of bacterial wilt is through the use of resistant cultivars. Resistance to this pathogen was recognized early (Brink et al., 1934; Weimer and Madison, 1936; Viands et al. 1979). Most lucerne varieties currently being developed are resistant to bacterial wilt. Some recent North American registrations include: highly resistant, Victory (Viands et al., 1995c), Sabre (Viands et al., 1995b), WL323 (Kugler et al., 1995); moderately resistant, ABT-805 (Bouton et al., 1997a), AmeriGraze 702 (Bouton et al., 1997b), WL 525 HQ (Cluff et al., 1995); resistant, Majestic (Viands et al., 1995a), and AC Blue J (Acharya et al., 1995).^p^p^Biological ControlJohnson et al. (1971) studied the interactions between Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. medicaginis and C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus during disease development in the field and found that F. oxysporum produced a substance that appeared to inhibit C. michiganensis subsp. insidiosus and reduce severity of bacterial wilt in lucerne.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pCultural practices such as harvesting young stands before old stands when using the same equipment, and avoiding harvesting when the crop is wet can reduce the spread of the disease within and between fields (Graham et al., 1979).

host_range: A. ritzemabosi is a major and widespread pest of chrysanthemum in Europe, North America, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, and has been reported on this host from several other countries including Brazil (Curi and Pitta, 1971), Mexico (Cid del Prad
potential_eco_desc: A. ritzemabosi is a major and widespread pest of chrysanthemum in Europe, North America, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, and chrysanthemum is regarded as the major host in Europe (Juhl, 1978; Farkas et al., 1985).^p^pA. ritzemabosi is a serious pest of strawberry in Ireland, where yield reductions up to 60% due to A. ritzemabosi and A. fragariae infestations have been recorded (Duggan, 1969). The crown weight of strawberry cv. Senga Sengana was reduced by 51% by A. ritzemabosi and by 41% by A. fragariae. Fruit yield in the first year was reduced, owing largely to a decline in fruit number, by 65% and 54%, respectively, by these two species. The number of runners was reduced by 25-30% by A. ritzemabosi, but only by 11-15% by A. fragariae. Damage to the plant crowns and reduced yield were related to population density in winter and spring, but reduced runner production was due to the summer population density (Bohmer, 1981). Due to infection by A. ritzemabosi, average yield losses of the strawberry variety Korallovaya 100 were estimated as 53.4%. The variety Yasna seems to be somewhat less susceptible to A. ritzemabosi than Korallovaya 100 or Muto (Lebedeva et al., 1972). In Poland, A. ritzemabosi infestation destroyed 45% of chrysanthemum plants on a holding, and for the most susceptible varieties the number could be as high as 92% (Baranowski, 1976).

management_info: Introduction^p^pSymptoms and control of diseases in strawberry due to infestation by A. ritzemabosi and Aphelenchoides fragariae are described in an advisory leaflet (MAFF, 1970). Siddiqi (1974) reviewed control of A. ritzemabosi.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pDipping chrysanthemum stools infested with A. ritzemabosi in parathion solution effectively controlled the nematode (Hesling and Peachey, 1963); spraying chrysanthemum plants with parathion also proved effective (Dimock and Ford, 1950; Bryden and Hodson, 1957). In Poland, parathion and parathion-methyl gave good control on strawberry (Szczygiel, 1969). On begonia in Denmark, parathion and mevinphos gave effective control (Rasmussen, 1971). Spraying with demeton (superseded) and with sodium selenate also gave good control (see Siddiqi, 1974).^p^pIn lucerne, carbofuran granules applied around the seeds at sowing in spring 1988 in a clay loam at Rothamsted, inoculated with A. ritzemabosi and Ditylenchus dipsaci, increased lucerne herbage yields on average by 17 and 59%, respectively, in the first and second years of a 4-year experiment (1988-91) (Whitehead, 1994).^p^pStrawberry runners treated with aldicarb and fensulfothion (superseded) were less susceptible to attack than the untreated ones (Hirling, 1970). Aldicarb gave good control (Szczygiel, 1970). In a trial comparing aldicarb and oxamyl, applied protectively once before inoculation or as eradicants, both nematicides were equally effective applied by either method. Neither nematicide is phytotoxic (Strider, 1979). ^p^pIn Germany, application of aldicarb controlled A. ritzemabosi in strawberry runner beds, and 10 months later nematode-free plants were available for replanting (Heide, 1976). Aldicarb gave good control of A. ritzemabosi infesting strawberry in Germany, producing 55.6% higher yield than the controls (Blank, 1985). Good control of A. ritzemabosi and A. fragariae in strawberry plants grown for production of runner plants was achieved by application of granular aldicarb in September or October in southern Germany. However, autumn-treated plants were not resistant to re-infestation the following spring. More and larger runners were produced in spring by the treated plants (Krczal and Burckhardt, 1972). ^p^pOf several pesticides tested in Poland, parathion-methyl or liquid malathion gave the best control of A. ritzemabosi on bedded-out chrysanthemums (Baranowski, 1974). Of the granulated chemicals, aldicarb, oxamyl or fenamiphos gave the best control of A. ritzemabosi, and of the spray chemicals fenitrothion, triazophos or oxamyl gave the best control (Baranowski, 1985). ^p^pCarbofuran was effective in controlling A. ritzemabosi on chrysanthemum mother plants (Wojtowicz and Labanowski, 1995). Treatment of chrysanthemum nursery soil with methomyl or an organophosphorous nematicide was very effective in control of this nematode (Fukazawa and Kobayashi, 1971; Kobayashi et al., 1971). On chrysanthemum, treatments with parathion-methyl aimed at catching the newly hatched larvae gave effective control (Janowicz, 1976). ^p^pSuggested control measures include cleaning and burning infested leaves, submerging infected cuttings in hot water, treatment of seedlings with phorate and aldicarb, and spraying of foliage with parathion-methyl and chlorpyrifos (Gill, 1981). Foliar sprays of quinalphos and parathion-methyl, and an aldicarb or phorate soil application, successfully controlled A. ritzemabosi on Zinnia elegans, reducing both the symptoms of infestation and the final nematode population (Gill and Walia, 1980). ^p^pGuidelines have been given for the efficacy evaluation of nematicides against A. ritzemabosi and A. fragariae on susceptible cultivars of ornamentals such as Chrysanthemum indicum [Dendranthema indicum], Begonia elatior [B. hiemalis], Primula denticulata, Verbena hybrida, Saintpaulia ionantha or Weigela spp. (EPPO, 1994). potential_eco_desc:
A. ritzemabosi是一种植物寄生虫，抑制叶子、芽、生长点和枝干的外表层：在土壤中不能完成其生活史，不能在冬天存活。它取食叶子的细胞、芽和生长点(Southey, 1952; Siddiqi, 1974).。这线虫不进入枝干组织内，而是通过植物表面的水膜，进入叶子和芽内。叶子表面有水滴有利于线虫的再侵染和传播(Wallace, 1959).。它通过气孔侵入叶子。线虫区食寄主组织并且破坏植物细胞，在寄主表面容易看见导致叶子斑点和小孔。线虫通过气孔离开褐色组织，通过寄主表面的水膜侵染顶端的花朵，从而导致花的畸形。在一个菊花叶子上可能可以发现15,000条线虫(MAFF, 1969)。每14 g紫苑种子可以提取出300多个线虫(Brown, 1956)。A. ritzemabosi侵染的柠檬组织也表现出强的侵染性，每2.5 g叶子组织大约有100多条线虫(Bohm and Aruta, 1985)。
菊花上的典型症状包括特征的纹理限定的褐色斑点和整个叶子的黄化。这些症状主要是由线虫和其它生物体互作引起的(Cayrol and Combettes, 1972)。侵染的菊花叶子最多症状包括：在叶子较少的小植物上表现出一个红黄的伤害；而随着它们的成长，这些叶子明显表现出变色病的病斑，叶子表明大部分区域坏死。从而造成植株的叶子变少、开的花很少并切造成花的畸形。植株上部叶片与下部叶片相比，明显表现出较好的抗性(Cid del Prado and Sosa-Moss, 1978)。直接的影响是由口针引起的机械化损伤，还有生长分裂激素造成的损伤(Cayrol and Combettes, 1972).。
侵染的紫罗兰表现明显的矮小，使枝叶向下卷曲、枯萎和死亡；在叶子的背面明显表现出典型的水侵状大斑点(Thomas, 1968).。在侵染的Crassula coccinia 表现出矮化和发芽迟缓的症状(Atkinson, 1964).。
总体的症状：整个植株：矮化；叶子：坏死，畸形，萎焉，黄化或者死亡；枝干：粗缩。 A. ritzemabosi is an obligate plant parasite, inhabiting leaves, buds, growing points and outer layers of stem; in soil it does not complete its life cycle or survive the winter. It feeds endoparasitically on mesophyll cells of leaves, and ectoparasitically on buds and growing points (Southey, 1952; Siddiqi, 1974). The nematodes move in the water film over plants, not within the stem tissue, to reach the leaves and buds. Rain splashes and leaf contacts contribute to re-infestation and spread (Wallace, 1959). The leaves are invaded through the stomata. The nematodes feed on the parenchymatous tissue of the mesophyll and destroy the cells, resulting in leaf spots or blotches, easily seen on the under surface. The nematodes leave brown tissue through the stomata and migrate in the water film on the surface to infect terminal flower buds which produce deformed and under-sized blossoms. as 15,000 nematodes may be found in one leaf of chrysanthemum (MAFF, 1969); over 300 individuals per 14 g of infested aster seeds have been recovered (Brown, 1956). Limonium sinuatum attacked by A. ritzemabosi also showed a high level of infestation, more than 100 individuals per 2.5 g foliar tissue (Bohm and Aruta, 1985). 
The symptoms on chrysanthemum include characteristic brown spots limited to the veins, and a progressive yellowing of the whole leaf. These symptoms are due to combined action of the nematode and other organisms (Cayrol and Combettes, 1972). Leaf symptoms on infested Chrysanthemum maximum include reddish-yellow lesions on the lower leaves of young plants; in older plants these leaves are markedly chlorotic and a large area of the leaf surface becomes necrotic. The foliage is scanty and the flowers are few and deformed. Leaves in the upper part of plants have shown slightly higher resistance than those in the lower part (Cid del Prado and Sosa-Moss, 1978). Direct effects are mechanical damage caused by the stylet, and damage due to hormones of growth and division (Cayrol and Combettes, 1972). 
Attacked violets are stunted, and affected leaves curl down, wither and die; under surfaces of leaves showed typical water-soaked blotches (Thomas, 1968). Stunting and shoot blindness occurred on attacked Crassula coccinia (Atkinson, 1964).

description: Since 2010, a new emerging citrus decline disease (CDD) widely spread in the southern Kerman region of Iran, killing around 10% of cultivated citrus species trees. During field surveys, carried out in March 2017 in southern Kerman, one leaf and root sample was collected from citrus (Citrus sinensis [L.] Osbeck) trees showing early (three trees) and late (three trees) CDD symptoms. Extracted total nucleic acids from the samples were used as templates in PCR reactions carried out to amplify 16S rRNA gene of liberibacters  and phytoplasmas. Both 16S rDNA fragments were amplified indicating a coinfection. Based on sequence identity, CDD-associated liberibacter strains attributed to the species ‘Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus’ and CDD-associated phytoplasma strains attributed to the species ‘Ca. Phytoplasma aurantifolia’. Phylogenetic analyses confirmed the species affiliation of CDD-associated liberibacter and phytoplasma strains.
reference_name: First Report of a New Citrus Decline Disease (CDD) in Association with Double and Single Infection by ‘Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus’ and ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma aurantifolia’ Related Strains in Iran

host_range: M. gibsonii affects many species of Pinus. It is particularly associated with old seedlings in tree nurseries, but is also quite common on older trees of highly susceptible species such as Pinus radiata and P. roxburghii. It also occurs on senescing folia
potential_eco_desc: M. gibsonii causes a serious needle blight of both exotic and native pines, particularly at the later nursery stage, and has become a major obstacle to production of pine seedlings (especially P. pinaster, P. thunbergii and P. densiflora) in Japan and Taiwan. The disease causes slow growth of seedlings, a high cull rate, and in some cases mortality up to 85% (Ivory, 1987). Severe defoliation in young plantations of P. radiata occurs in Tanzania, resulting in reduced growth and sometimes even death of the trees (Mulder and Gibson, 1972). The disease is important on P. merkusii and P. caribaea nurseries in West Malaysia (Ivory, 1975).^p^pMost species develop effective resistance by 2-3 years of age; however, trees which are severely affected initially may remain stunted and severely blighted for many years. Such trees often succumb to competition from healthier trees or weed growth. In a few cases, such as P. radiata and P. canariensis, infection may occur on much older trees, especially on highly susceptible individuals (Ivory, 1987).

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pIt is unlikely that the fungus could spread from Africa and Asia as wind-borne spores.^p^pSilvicultural Practices^p^pInfected needle pieces in uncleaned seed or mycorrhizal soil inocula probably enabled the disease to spread to various tropical countries (Ivory, 1987).^p^pMovement in Trade^p^pM. gibsonii could be spread on infected seedlings and on cut branches of Pinus and, in view of the long incubation period, latent infections present a hazard.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Spores; borne externally; invisible.^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants: Spores, Hyphae; borne externally; visible to naked eye.^p - Leaves: Spores, Hyphae, Fruit Bodies; borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants: Spores, Hyphae, Fruit Bodies; borne internally; borne externally; visible to naked eye.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Spores, Hyphae; borne externally; invisible.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Soil, Gravel, Water, Etc.: Mycorrhizal Soil Inocula (Ivory 1987)

remark: M. gibsonii is listed as an A1 quarantine pest by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1980). It is also of quarantine significance to the Andean Community (CAN) and South Cone Plant Protection Committee (COSAVE) (Brazil, Ministerio da Agricultura e do Abastecimento, 1996; COSAVE, 2002). In the EPPO and COSAVE regions it is potentially dangerous to Pinus spp. wherever grown.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pSome measures for control of M. gibsonii were listed by Ivory (1987). General nursery hygiene measures to minimize the risk of infection are described: removal of all pines in and around the nursery, cleaning out the nursery between annual production cycles, the physical separation of young seedlings from older plants where the nursery cycle is >12 months, banning transfers of plants between nurseries, and taking care with mycorrhizal-soil introductions.^p^pThere is some evidence of edaphic factors (soil pH, organic matter and nutrient content of soil) affecting the incidence of needle blight (Cruz et al., 1984).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pIn nurseries, control can be obtained by using maneb (or mancozeb) or copper-based fungicides applied to the current year's and 1-year-old seedlings at 2-weekly intervals during the growing season (Reddy and Pandey, 1973). It is important that all diseased seedlings are removed and burned early in the season when infection occurs. Apply foliar sprays of fungicides at 2-4 week intervals during conditions favourable for the spread of the fungus. Recommended fungicides are benomyl, chlorothalonil, mancozeb, zineb, tridemorph and thiophanate applied with effective wetting agents (Singh et al., 1983; Ivory, 1987). Copper fungicides have been reported to be effective only in Japanese nurseries (Ivory, 1987).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pReplace highly susceptible species with a more resistant, but equally productive species, such as P. elliottii in place of P. massoniana (Ivory, 1987). Resistant Pinus spp. may have a small portion of their foliage affected, but suffer little growth reduction and no mortality.

management_info: Phytosanitary Methods^p^pIn areas where the disease is not present, effective quarantine measures are essential to prevent the introduction of the huanglongbing (HLB) organism or the vector. Furthermore, the possibility exists that the vector could be introduced 'naturally' or through alternative hosts (da Graca and Korsten, 2004).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pIn the absence of hyperparasitic wasps, the parasitic wasp Tetrastichus dryi significantly reduced populations of Trioza erytreae,  the vector of HLB, on the Indian Ocean island of Reunion, leaving a strongly limited population of the vector (Aubert and Quilici, 1984).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThere are no chemical controls that specifically target the bacterium. Several antibiotics have been trialled to treat the tree via trunk injection methods. However, this was not sustained as a commercial treatment because the method proved expensive, remission was temporary, treated trees were inclined to produce small fruit, there were phytotoxic effects at the injection site and high levels of residues were found in the fruit of treated trees. Treatment then turned to control of the vector (Buitendag and von Broembsen, 1993). ^p^p^IPM ProgrammesBuitendag and von Broembsen (1993) recommended a three-pronged strategy of the provision of certified greening-free nursery trees to commercial growers, a reduction of inoculum through an ongoing programme of removing plant parts showing greening symptoms and the implementation of effective measures to control the psylla vector, T. erytreae. This has brought about a distinct reduction in the incidence of greening-infected trees in commercial plantings in South Africa.

description: Bacterial panicle blight (BPB) emerged recently in epidemic proportions in rice-growing areas of northern India including Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Delhi, and National Capital Regions during September to November of 2014. B. glumae was documented as a serious pathogen of rice from the United States, China, Vietnam, Taiwan, and the Philippines. The significance of this pathogen to rice production in India was not known until this report; thus, this constitutes the first report of BPB caused by B. glumae in India.

description: 1956年在日本九州发现水稻细菌性谷枯病，1967年首次将病原定名为Pseudomonas glumae Kurita et Tabei(颖壳假单胞菌)，1994年改名为Burkholderia glumae(颖壳伯克氏菌)。20世纪70年代前该病一直是日本水稻上的次要病害，到70年代后期由于实行机械化生产而进行大面积的工厂化育秧，导致B．glumae引起的水稻苗腐病大流行，成为水稻上最严重的病害之一。目前该病已经蔓延到印度尼西亚、泰国、越南、韩国、斯里兰卡、马来西亚、菲律宾等东南亚国家及南美洲的哥伦比亚等国。最近，非洲的坦桑尼亚及美国的路易安那州相继报道有该病发生。我国台湾地区1983年报道水稻细菌性谷枯病的发生。  水稻细菌性谷枯病可经由稻种传播，带菌种子是主要的初侵染源。

host_range: 水稻细菌性谷枯病菌的寄主范围很广,除水稻外, 还危害燕麦、扁穗雀麦、狗尾草、牛筋草、芦苇、苏丹草、早熟禾、鞘糠草、看麦娘、升马唐、薏苡、狼尾草、弯叶画眉草、梯牧草、雀稗属的双穗雀稗和毛花雀稗、黍属的秋稷和羊草以及须芒草属的一些杂草等。叶部接种表明禾本科、菊科、豆科、蓼科和车前科的20 多种植物都感病。
potential_eco_desc: 是一种严重的种传病害。它不但侵害谷粒, 而且还引起水稻秧苗腐烂。  水稻细菌性谷枯病主要引起水稻种子和苗床种苗的腐烂, 易造成重大的经济损失。用喷雾法接种, 即可引起稻穗谷粒严重受害,其谷粒饱实率仅有29% ~ 39% 。此病在日本已造成极大的损失, 是日本水稻上最主要的细菌病害; 1982 年在台湾省中南部首次发现此病害, 危害就非常严重; 1992 年在越南发现该病害, 10 万公顷的水稻被侵染, 严重地区损失达75%。
description:
20 世纪50年代在日本被发现，到20 世纪70 年代后期，由该病菌引起的水稻苗腐病大流行, 成为日本水稻上最严重的病害之一。  水稻细菌性谷枯病菌可以通过胚芽鞘和叶片的气孔侵入寄主, 另外也可以通过由第一片叶子或次生根的出现造成的伤口侵染寄主, 一些昆虫咬食造成的伤口也可为病原菌的入侵提供方便。水稻细菌性谷枯病可经稻种传播, 其寄主范围较广, 可随寄主种子做远距离传播,带菌种子是主要的初侵染源。浸种催芽时污染健康种子, 在育苗期间感染发病, 腐烂枯死或带菌苗再移栽本田, 其病菌潜伏到孕穗开花时再侵染谷粒, 形成轻重不同的谷枯病状和带菌种子; 播种带菌谷粒, 遇有适宜的发病条件, 即抽穗期高温多日照, 降雨量少易发病。土壤里病谷和病草中的病菌可存活到次年的7~ 8 月间, 秧苗移栽后进行侵染。据日本报
告, 将被害稻谷埋在田间越冬, 下期作稻种秧苗时, 被害谷粒的病原细菌可感染稻株发病;1987 年台湾简锦忠等也通过试验证实稻种上带有该病原, 播种后可引起严重的腐败症。

description: Incidence^p ^pB. glumae was recovered at a rate of around 100 million c.f.u./g fresh weight from seeds from plants which had been inoculated at the booting stage and stored at room temperature for 3 years. However, B. glumae was not recovered from seeds kept outdoors for 5 months. It is suggested that seed stored at room temperature is a possible source of infection in the field, resulting in seedling rot and grain rot (Tsushima et al., 1989). ^p^pOn rice inoculated at the booting stage, the total population of the bacterium was less than around 10 million c.f.u./g fresh weight of grain by heading time, increasing to 100 million to 1000 million c.f.u./g fresh weight during the next 6 days after heading. Under the scanning electron microscope, cells of B. glumae were seen densely colonizing the surface of the basal part of the lodicule and the inner surface of the lemma. Invasion of the interspaces of host epidermal cells and the spongy parenchyma of the lemma was observed under the transmission electron microscope (Tsushima et al., 1987).^p^pB. glumae entered rice lemmata and paleae via the stomata and multiplied in the intercellular spaces of the parenchyma. Stomata are opened mainly on the inner surfaces of lemmata and paleae and are connected through the parenchymal intercellular space. The bacteria multiplied on albumen and embryo surfaces but never invaded them (Tabei et al., 1989).^p^pRice plants were spray inoculated with B. glumae at different times before heading to study population dynamics of the pathogen on rice sheaths in the field and the relationship between population size and disease incidence. The bacterial population on the uppermost leaf sheaths and flag leaf sheaths was detected using the selective S-PG medium. The results suggested that the number of leaf sheaths with a pathogen population of more than 103 c.f.u./g fresh weight, which was the detection limit of the selective medium, decreased greatly with internode growth. Bacterial populations on individual leaf sheaths varied from leaf sheath to leaf sheath showing approximately lognormal distribution by plotting data sets on the cumulative probability scale. It is suggested that the bacterial populations on uppermost leaf sheaths in the field may be estimated from lognormal value of population size on individual leaf sheaths more accurately than from bulked leaf sheath samples. Correlation coefficients between detection frequency of the pathogen on flag leaf sheaths and disease incidence on panicles a week after heading time was high (r=0.78, P=0.01), but not significant 2 and 3 weeks after heading time, suggesting that the pathogen on flag leaf sheaths is important in primary infection of the disease. It is concluded that the value of frequency was applicable for estimation  of disease incidence of bacterial grain rot of rice in the field (Tsushima et al., 1996) .^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p ^pB. glumae is a pathogen that primarily attacks grains, but other bacteria causing diseases of leaves or leaf sheaths may also infect rice grains at panicle emergence (Goto et al., 1988).^p^pIn diseased grain, brown to dark-brown lesions are first observed on the basal part of the hulls. The lesions gradually enlarge upward. As soon as lesions appear on the grain, the hulls assume a faded green appearance and begin to wither. Affected grains are either sterile or carry brown rice with dark-brown discoloration at the base (Goto et al., 1988).^p^pBacterial grain rot of rice was found at the milky stage of the second crop in 1982 in central and southern Taiwan and the pathogen was identified as B. glumae. In severe infestations more than half of the grains in a panicle may be attacked. The sterile lemmata of infected grains were purplish-brown but the branches remained green. management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pMethods for controlling seedling rot caused by B. glumae in nursery boxes have been investigated in Japan. Cultural control methods include the following (Goto, 1982): ^p^p* Eliminate infected seeds by saltwater selection with a specific gravity of 1.18.^p^p* Keep the bed surface even and level to avoid localized standing water.^p^p* Avoid overwatering.^p^p* Maintain temperatures between 15°C and 30°C.^p^p Symptoms of bacterial grain rot of rice (caused by B. glumae) vary considerably, depending on the temperature and the amount of nitrogen applied prior to panicle emergence (Kan, 1985).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThere was significant interaction between varieties and isolates in inoculation studies, suggesting the existence of differential strains (Chien et al., 1987). When rice seeds were dipped in a water suspension of 100,000,000 c.f.u./ml of B. glumae for 30 minutes before sowing, germination was unaffected but c. 98% of seedlings died. Inoculation at the booting stage by injection with a similar suspension caused infection and discoloration of all panicles and sheaths. Inoculation at booting or heading by spraying caused infection of panicles but not sheaths and resulted in >60% unfilled grains. Susceptibility to isolates B24 and 01 was greatest from 4 days before to 2 days after heading; to isolates B15 and B23, it was greatest from 4 days before to 4 days after. When 21 varieties of rice were inoculated with four isolates 10 days before heading, isolate B89 was the most virulent and B88 the least. Tainan 6 was the most susceptible variety (65% incidence of bacterial grain rot) and Kaohsiung S.7 the most resistant (28%). ^p^p^Chemical Control ^p^pEffective compounds for chemical control of B. glumae include: kasugamycin, thiram, benomyl, nonyl-phenyl-sulfonic copper, ammonium ethylenebis(dithiocarbamate), and NaOCl. Care should be taken in the application of NaOCl in order to avoid seedling phytotoxicity (Endo, 1985, Isogawa, 1986). The soil fungicide, methasulfocarb, controlled B. glumae when applied as a dust (Ohmori and Watanabe, 1986).^p^pChemical spraying is expected to be effective only when it is applied at or a few days after panicle emergence (Yasunaga et al., 1985; Isogawa, 1986).^p^pThe greater the population of B. glumae on rice plants at the stage of maximum tiller number, the greater the bacterial population on the upper leaf sheaths and spikelets and the more severe the bacterial grain rot. Treatment with oxolinic acid at heading stage inhibited an increase in the bacterial population on spikelets and was effective in the control of the disease (Hikichi, 1993a). This synthetic bactericide, developed from quinoline derivatives, completely inhibited the development of Gram-negative bacteria, including B. glumae, Pseudomonas plantarii, Pseudomonas avenae, Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora and Erwinia carotovora subsp. atroseptica in vitro. Oxolinic acid was effective against various isolates of B. glumae from rice grains collected from different districts in Japan. Activity varied according to the growth phase of the bacterium, being bactericidal at the lag phase and bacteristatic at the early logarithmic phase, with a decrease after the middle logarithmic phase. Oxolinic acid sometimes induced abnormal elongation of B. glumae cells at the early logarithmic phase (Hikichi, 1993b). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pPre-treatment of rice seeds with avirulent strains of B. glumae reduced the incidence of seedling rot caused by virulent strains. The suppression varied depending on the combinations of both avirulent and virulent strain used. A high concentration (c. 10,000,000,000 c.f.u./ml) of the avirulent strain was the most effective. Killed cells of avirulent B. glumae or other bacteria in the genera Agrobacterium, Erwinia, Bacillus and Clavibacter did not suppress the disease. potential_eco_desc: A. fragariae and A. ritzemabosi reduced yield of strawberry by up to 60% in nematode-infested areas in Ireland (Duggan, 1969). A. fragariae is involved in strawberry decline in France (Clerjeau et al., 1983).^p^pThe weight of the crown of strawberry, cv. Senga Sengana, plants was reduced by 51% by A. ritzemabosi and 41% by A. fragariae. The number of runners was reduced by 25-30% by A. ritzemabosi, but only by 11-15% by A. fragariae. Damage to the plant crowns and reduced yield were related to population density in winter and spring but reduced runner production was due to the summer population density (Bohmer, 1981).^p^pThe susceptible strawberry cultivars Macherauchs fruhernte and Cambridge favourite showed 65% and 82% reduction in yield, respectively, after 2 years infestation in Poland (Szczygiel, 1963)^p^pHeavy losses of bird's-nest fern (Asplenium nidus) have been recorded in California, USA (Ark and Tompkins, 1946).^p^pA foliar blight of anthurium (Anthurium andraeanum) in Hawaii which is often lethal in young plants was found to be caused by Aphelenchoides fragariae. The nematode also invades and destroys anthurium seeds (Hunter et al., 1974).

management_info: Chemical control^p^pStrawberries^p^pIn Germany, application of aldicarb controlled A. fragariae in strawberry runner beds and, 10 months later, nematode-free plants were available for replanting (Heide, 1976). Good control of A. fragariae and A. ritzemabosi in strawberry plants grown for production of runner plants was achieved by application of granular aldicarb in September or October in southern Germany. However, autumn-treated plants were not resistant to re-infestation the following spring. More and larger runners were produced in spring by the treated plants (Krczal and Burckhardt, 1972). Strawberry runners of Senga Gourmella taken from plants heavily infested with nematodes were treated with aldicarb. Of these plants, 76% remained healthy compared with 36% of control plants, and they produced a 55.6% higher crop (Blank, 1985) ^p^pSymptoms and control of diseases in strawberry due to infestation by A. fragariae and A. ritzemabosi are described in an advisory leaflet (Anon., 1972a). Immersion of fresh strawberry plants in thionazin before freeze preservation virtually eliminated A. fragariae infection. Washing the plants after treatment reduced the nematicidal effect at lower concentrations (Tacconi et al., 1982). Redgauntlet and Tioga strawberry plants infested with A. fragariae in New Zealand were soaked in a solution of fenamiphos. Healthy plants of both cultivars produced higher yields, crown weights and fruit numbers/plant than treated plants and untreated infested plants (Soteros, 1985). ^p^pBegonias^p^pTwo foliar applications of oxamyl, with a 2-week interval, gave excellent control of A. fragariae in 2 begonia cvs and completely suppressed symptom development. Granular applications of Bay 68138 (ethyl 4-(methylthio)-m-tolyl isopropylphosphoroamidate) and oxamyl were also effective. Benomyl was ineffective and aldicarb, although giving control, was phytotoxic (Riedel et al., 1973). Oxamyl as a soil drench followed in 10 days with a top application eradicated A. fragariae on Schwabenland Red begonia. Single applications of oxamyl as a drench or as a foliar spray and aldicarb applied 1 week before inoculation prevented infection. Aldicarb was also effective but did not give complete eradication. Three applications of parathion severely reduced populations (Strider, 1973). Parathion, mevinphos, thionazin and a carbamoyl compound were effective in controlling A. fragariae in begonia (Hansen et al., 1972). ^p^pAgainst A. fragariae infesting Begonia X elatior in Sweden, the best effect after one month was given by oxamyl. Temik 10 G (aldicarb) gave phytotoxic symptoms except when used in low dosages, but then had no nematicidal effect. Oxamyl and mevinphos were the least phytotoxic of the compounds tested (Banck, 1988). ^p^pFerns^p^pFerns have been successfully treated with parathion (Sachs, 1950; 1952; Olisevich, 1956) and demeton (Hirschmann, 1953). Good control and improved growth were obtained by treating fern, Pteris cretica, infested with A. fragariae with soil drenches of aldicarb or methomyl; aldicarb giving the better control and methomyl better growth (Heungens, 1971).^p^pThe Hawaiian tree fern, Cobotium chamissoi, which is used as a planting medium, is the source of infection to other plants (Hunter et al., 1974).^p^pOther hosts^p^pThe best results in controlling heavy infestations of A. fragariae on azaleas in Holland were obtained with aldicarb granules applied in May, followed by 1 or 2 soil-drench applications of oxamyl 1 or 2 months later (Heungens, 1985). ^p^pPractical control efficacy was obtained by dipping the infested lily bulbs in a  solution of methomyl. No control was obtained by foliar sprays of methomyl at 10 day intervals during the growing season (Yamada and Takakura, 1989). Foliar sprays of lilies with demeton were effective (Jensen and Caveness, 1954).^p^pAbamectin applied to Lamium maculatum foliage infested with A. fragariae significantly reduced the numbers of A. fragariae recovere

management_info: There are no direct control measures against B. caryophylli. Disease-free mother plants should be used and rooting beds and soil should be fumigated. potential_eco_desc: L. ulmi is often found infesting apples in many regions, and heavy populations may cause serious damage to the fruit. This species is also considered an occasional pest of fruits and nuts. However, it was reported to be among the most frequently encountered pests out of 25 species of scale insects infesting fruit trees in European orchards (Kozar et al., 1979; Kozar and Konstantinova, 1981). Konstantinova (1976) and Korchagin (1987) considered it to be one of the most important pests of apples in northern Russia. Abramovic (1980) found this pest occurred on over 17% of apple trees infested with scale insects in Belgrade, Yugoslavia. L. ulmi was reported to be the most important pest of apples in Turkey (Kozar et al., 1979). In addition,  it was considered among the most important species infesting forest and ornamental trees and shrubs in Belgrade Kozarzevskaja and Vlainic, 1981, 1982). It was reported to be a serious pest of walnuts in California, USA (Ebeling, 1959; Gill, 1997). Koteja (1983) found that this species caused serious damage to bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) in Poland. Tsachev (1978) reported that this species is a widely distributed pest in Bulgaria where it prefers apple and willow. It has also been a problem on olives in Greece where it, along with Parlatoria oleae, causes serious injury to the tree and fruit (Argyriou and Kourmadas, 1981). Suresh and Mohanasundaram (1996) found that it infested species of Citrus in India.^p^pIf left uncontrolled, heavy infestations can weaken or stunt plants. In addition to reducing plant vigour (de Groot, 1967), heavy infestations reduce plant growth and lower frost resistance, endangering trees and possibly leading to death in 2-3 years. Infestations may cause leaf yellowing, fruit deformity, leaf drop and dieback of branches.  Helsen et al. (1996) noted that even minor infestations of fruit may cause major economic losses as a result of the zero tolerance policies for export produce.
author: CPC2006

management_info: The serious threat posed by outbreaks of L. ulmi often requires control efforts to be implemented against this pest. Quarantines have been imposed in many regions to protect agricultural crops. Mineral oil sprays and chemical insecticides, including permethrin, are used to suppress infestations of this pest on fruit and ornamentals (Sarkisyan, 1982; Djike and Frankenhuyzen, 1985; Korchagin, 1987; Alezsidze, 1995). Spray programmes are applied against the migratory nymphs or crawlers upon emerging from under the parent's cover. Regular spray programmes have been reduced or eliminated to lessen the impact on natural or exotic beneficials that can keep the pest below economic threshold levels in managed orchards and gardens. Injac (1980b) reported an increase in the pest population from 2 to 14% following chemical application in apple orchards. Argyriou and Kourmados (1981) proposed a spring treatment to protect the fruit, and a summer application in August to control the overwintering generation of L. ulmi.^p^pPhenological calendars were developed to provide the means for timing pest control applications within a particular region (Mussey and Potter, 1997). ^p^pIntegrated pest management programmes for protecting apples against infestations by the oystershell scale involve monitoring for pest occurrence, use of non-acaricidal fungicides to promote development of natural enemies, and a reduction in the number of insecticide applications (Easterbrook et al., 1985). A number of parasitoids and predators have been imported into regions where this species has attained pest status. Semyanov et al. (1996) reported that Chilocorus bipustulatus and C. renipustulatus fed on Lepidosaphes ulmi on apples in Russia. In Bulgaria, the parasitoid Aphytis mytilaspidis was reported to be the most important biocontrol agent against this pest, with Aphytis proclia and A. aonidiae providing less impact, along with the predators Chilocorus bipustulatus and C. renipustulatus (Tsachev, 1978). The parasitoid, Epitetracnemus zetterstedti, is used for biological control in several countries. ^p^pThe mite, Hemisarcoptes malus, was found to consume up to 40% of the eggs of L. ulmi in apple orchards treated with chemicals and 97% of the eggs in untreated orchards (Trenchev and Pavlov, 1981). Yasnosh (1995) reported that L. ulmit is often suppressed by aphelinid parasitoids  in forest environments and seldom becomes a significant problem.

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pDispersal of scale insects is predominantly through infected stock, thus imported and propagative material should be thoroughly checked for the presence of scales. Dispersal from plant to plant occurs through the activity of crawlers at points where adjacent plants touch. Thus pruning and allowing adequate spacing between plants throughout cultivation can reduce spread. Mechanical control can be achieved by scraping and scrubbing to remove scales.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pP. pergandii populations may be controlled by natural enemies and cultural control methods unless these predator and parasite populations are disturbed by the use of broad-spectrum insecticides. Limon et al. (1976) report that the increase in populations of P. pergandii in Castellon, Spain, is attributed in part to the reduction of parasite populations as a result of indiscriminate chemical control. Insect growth regulators used in the control of scales have been shown to disrupt the fecundity and egg viability of Chilocorus spp. (Hattingh and Tate, 1995). Carrero (1980) reports that the parasites Aphytis diaspidis, A. aonidae and Encarsia inquirenda were only moderately effective in controlling P. pergandii in orange groves in Valencia, and suggest that control could be reinforced by appropriate cultural practices. Hare and Morgan (1997) report on the mass priming of Aphytis spp. for biological control.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control is usually achieved by spraying with horticultural oils at critical points during the season. Mixtures of mineral oils and insecticide are often used. Regular monitoring programmes to detect the presence of adult scales and crawlers, and predict scale population intensity should be used to coordinate spraying. Care should be taken to avoid excessive pesticide use, to maintain populations of natural enemies of the scale.

potential_eco_desc: P. gossypiella is a worldwide pest of cotton and in some regions of the world, it is the key cotton pest. Oerke et al. (1994; modified from Frisbie, 1983) classify it as a key pest in North and South America and Asia, and an economically important pest in Africa, Europe and the former USSR, and Oceania. ^p^pBased on trials from 1945 to 1980, Schwartz (1983) calculated that the potential loss, without control, was 61% due to P. gossypiella in the USA. Estimated losses of 9% were suggested where the pest was controlled. For 1987, King et al. (1988) estimated that the area affected by P. gossypiella was 237,330 ha of which 131,949 ha were treated. The cost of treatment was $22/ha. The estimated crop loss was 0.13% or 4150 t. Green and Lyon (1989) said that P. gossypiella infested over 200,000 ha in the western USA. Frisbie et al. (1989) indicated that economically damaging thresholds were reached if boll infestation rose above 5-15%.Agarwal and Katiyar (1979) calculated the crop loss due to P. gossypiella based on field trials in Delhi. According to their data, the crop loss in the 1970s was 20.2% or 234,000 t of cotton.^p^pIn the Yangtze valley, China, Cai et al. (1985) reported that P. gossypiella reduced cotton yield by ca 10%. In the Wuhan region, it reduced fibre yield by 17-26% (Luo et al., 1986). Yuan and Lu (1986) estimated specific losses due to P. gossypiella of 0.0467 g/larvae due to direct injury and 0.0544 g of cotton due to indirect damage in the Shanghai region.^p^pIn Sudan, Darling (1951) estimated that 10.7% of the potential cotton yield could be lost following infestation by P. gossypiella.^p^pIn Egypt, in 1985, trial plots in the Nile Delta used a pheromone to control P. gossypiella. Losses of 2.2% were recorded, compared with 4.5% following insecticide treatments. The cotton yield from pheromone-protected crops was 3450 kg/ha while that from insecticide treated crops was 3100 kg/ha. Insect pests other than P. gossypiella were also controlled by these treatments (McVeigh et al., 1983; El-Adl et al., 1988).

management_info: Introduction^p^pAn account summarising the control methods most effective against P. gossypiella has been written by Graham (1980). A review of control in south-western USA was given by Hutchison (1999). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pP. gossypiella has been a target for biological control, particularly in the USA. Parasitoids were introduced there from India, from the Indonesia-northern Australia region and from several other countries, but only Bracon kirkpatricki became established (Greathead, 1989). Biological control agents were first obtained from India, in the belief that it was the origin of the pest. When these failed later introductions were from Indonesia-Australia as opinion shifted in favour of an origin in this region. However, the matter is not settled and Ingram (1994) suggested that it may have come from the Indo-Pakistan area because of the number of species recorded by Cheema et al. (1980) (Greathead, 1989). More recently nematodes have been used as control agents in the USA (Henneberry et al., 1996; Gouge et al., 1999).^p^p^Integrated Pest Management^p^pCombinations of biological and chemical controls have also proved successful. Tuhan et al. (1987) found that application of Trichogramma brasiliense in combination with chemical insecticides gave good control of pink bollworm in India, and Bacillus thuringiensis has been found to be effective in combination with chemical insecticides in Egypt (Hussein et al., 1990).^p^pThe Pectinophora gossypiella IPM project in California, USA, was reviewed by Walters et al. (1998). The project used the release of sterile insects, cultural controls, intensive monitoring with pheromone baited traps for adult males and boll sampling, pheromone applications for mating disruption, very limited use of pesticides and the widespread use of genetically engineered cotton.^p^pIn Pakistan, Ahmad et al. (2001) found a combination of Biological control and mating disruption techniques to be effective.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pInsecticidal control is hindered by the larvae being internal feeders; moreover, resistance to insecticides develops making it often more expensive than other methods. Nonetheless, there is an extensive literature on chemical control, especially from India. The efficacy of asymethrin has been tested in India by Dhawan et al. (1992), that of chlorpyriphos in India by Dhawan et al. (1989), of methomyl by Simwat et al. (1991), of synthetic pyrethroids by Dhawan et al. (1990) and Butter et al. (1990), of endosulfan, chlorpyrifos and fenpropathrin by Mahar et al. (1987), of chloropyrifos and teflubenzuron by Green and Lyon (1989), of pyrethroids and organic insecticides with high contact toxicity (chlordimeform hydrochloride and carbaryl) in China by Gao et al. (1992), of cyhalothrin and fluvalinate in India by Thangaraju et al. (1993) and of fenvalerate by Tadas et al. (1994). Application methods were assessed in Brazil by Ramalho and Jesus (1989). A strain in Arizona has been found to be resistant to permethrin (Osman et al., 1992). ^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pLate planting of crops has been used as a cultural control method where the end of diapause is triggered by day length. Larvae that emerge before the crop is ready then have no food supply (Frisbie et al., 1989). Methods have also been developed for reducing the number of overwintering larvae, including the chemical defoliation of crops and desiccation of the crop at the end of the season; removing immature late season bolls; and the use of short-season varieties. Beasley and Adams (1995) suggest eight cultural control methods following a study of pink bollworm in the USA. In essence, they recommend the use of short-season cultivars appropriate to the seasonal climate of the area, not forcing regrowth and a second flowering cycle, rotating crops and specific recommendations for harvesting and dealing with crop debris. potential_eco_desc: In north-western USA, C. longana is a pest of strawberry, while in Central Europe it is a pest of cereal crops. Glas (1991) described the economic threshold as varying from 40-50 larvae/m2 to about 200 first- and second-instar larvae/m2, although the density reduces with larval mortality and is therefore difficult to assess. Consequently the avoidance of continuous cropping of cereals will reduce infestation.^p^p^Biological ControlGlas and Hassan (1985) showed that it is possible to achieve control with a release of about 900,000 Trichogramma evanescens per solitary tree (on which eggs have been laid).Glas (1986) found that applications of Bacillus thuringiensis were not very effective against the early stages in cereals on account of the mining behaviour of larvae. Norton (1991) found the timing of application of B. thuringiensis to be crucial against the pest on grapes in California, USA.^p^p^Chemical ControlGlas (1986) stated that parathion and synthetic pyrethroids are effective insecticides.
