description: Incidence^p ^pA. pisi together with Phoma medicaginis var. pinodella and Mycosphaerella pinodes is part of a complex of seedborne fungi associated with Ascochyta spp. infection of peas. A. pisi is extensively seedborne on peas. In survey of pea seed lots in Australia, the Ascochyta blight complex of field peas was isolated from 436 of 691 seed lots tested. A. pisi was recovered from 1.0% of isolations, whereas M. pinodes was recovered from 94.8% and P. medicaginis var. pinodella from 4.2% (Bretag et al., 1995). In another report, seedborne infection by A. pisi varied from 6.6% in the pea cultivar Bonneville to 33.3% in cv. Lincoln (Sandhu and Sharma, 1988). Hewett (1987a) reported incidences of seed infection as high as 46%. In seed health tests of a range of pea seed samples, the three Ascochyta spp. were most frequently located in the seed coat, less so in the cotyledons and least frequently in the embryo. P. medicaginis var. pinodella and M. pinodes were also isolated at greater frequencies than A. pisi from plant debris mixed with pea seeds (Abd-El-Rehim et al., 1997). Maude (1996) indicates that intracellular mycelium of the fungus occurs in the cotyledons and that the pathogen infects the outer layers of the embryo. In a study of the infection of nine pea genotypes by A. pisi in various regions of Poland, seed infection by A. pisi was correlated with infection of leaves, stems and pods of plants from which seeds were harvested (Marcinkowska, 1996). ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality ^p^pInfected seeds may have brown areas on the seed coat (Hewett, 1987b). ^p^p^Pathogen Transmission Maude (1996) showed that transmission of the pathogen to the seedling occurs by contamination of the plumule from the infected seed coat. The importance of seed transmission of A. pisi has resulted in several countries implementing regulations for incidences of seed infection to minimize transmission to the planted crop. These tolerances range from 1 to 20% seed infection, depending on the grade of the seed and country (Hewett, 1987a; Maude, 1996). ^p^p^Seed Treatment^p ^pCaptan and thiram, applied as dry powders to infected pea seeds, effectively reduced transmission of A. pisi (Maude, 1996). Seed treatment with benomyl gave acceptable levels of control of seedborne infection with A. pisi, whereas thiram, mancozeb or captan gave only poor disease control ((dayuhao)50%) (Girsch, 1990). ^p^p^Seed Health Tests ^p^pCulture Medium (Hewett, 1987b) ^p^p1. Pretreat seeds in 1% sodium hypochlorite for 10 min. ^p2. Incubate on PDA for 7 days at 21°C in darkness or under alternating light and dark 12/12 cycles in containers sealed to maintain humidity. ^p3. Examine for colonies characteristic of A. pisi. ^p^pNotes on methods^p ^pInternational comparative tests showed that the agar plate method provides reliable results for the detection of A. pisi on pea seed samples (Hewett, 1987a).

host_range: A. viennensis is generally considered as a pest of Rosaceae. Gotoh and Takayama (1992) tested the development success of this mite on various plants. Over 50% maturity of this mite was obtained from Amelanchier asiatica, Chaenomeles speciosa, Crataegus la
potential_eco_desc: A. viennensis is an important pest in apple, peach, pear, apricot, plum, hawthorn, cherry, sweet cherry and raspberry in China, Georgia, Japan, Russia, Turkey, Ukraine and other European countries. However, Panonychus ulmi (Koch) may compete with A. viennensis and reduce its importance (Galetenko, 1978; Loladse, 1989).^p^pA. viennensis may cause particular damage in dry years (Chepurnaya and Myalova, 1981), and photosynthesis is also sensitive to mite damage. Qin et al. (1990) recorded a significant decrease in photosynthesis in apple when leaf damage reached or exceeded 15% in China. Skorupska and Tomczyk (1988) detected a 30% reduction in photosynthesis in apple seedlings after 7 days infestation by A. viennensis, although photosynthesis recovered thereafter.^p^pHeavy infestation of A. viennensis may cause water loss, premature leaf drop, impair fruit formation, and lower the resistance of the host to winter conditions (Sepasgozarian and Schruft, 1975). In apple, pear, and peach, a density of 31.8, 32.3, and 19.5 mites per leaf with indices of damage 61.3, 60.1, and 58.0%, respectively, may cause early leaf fall (Li et al., 1998).^p^pThe mite causes a reduction in fruit size and weight, but not in the number of fruit produced (Bulgak, 1979; Cai et al., 1992), however flower and fruit production in the following year are reduced (Cai et al., 1992). In apple, 100 or more mites per leaf may result in a yield loss of 40-65% (Bulgak, 1979). An accumulation of adult females with a mite day of 12.0, 104.9, 167.1, 245.4, 433.0 and 501.8 may generate a yield loss of 0.5, 6.4, 23.8, 25.6, 38.7, 38.4%, respectively (Cai et al., 1992). ^p^pThe economic threshold for applying acaricides to apple is 4-5 individuals per leaf during the first half of the vegetative period, which is more sensitive to mite damage, and 7-8 mites per leaf during the second half of the vegetative period (Bulgak, 1979).
author: CPC2006

description: Natural dispersal^p^pCrawling is the main means of dispersal on a host plant, from leaf to leaf and eventually to spread over the whole tree. The mite may also crawl from tree to tree, or to a neighbouring field. Aerial dispersal by wind over longer distances involves two different launching behaviours: spinning down from the foliage on a thread until the wind breaks the thread; and facing into the wind with the forelegs upright. ^p^p^Vector transmission^p^pBirds, large insects, or animals may transfer the mites from plant to plant accidentally - this process is known as phoresy.^p^p^Agricultural practices^p^pHumans may transport mites on their clothes, or they may deposit plant material which is infected by mites.^p^p^Movement in trade^p^pA host plant carrying either mites on the leaves or diapausing adult females under the bark has potential to distribute this mite to a new region or country.Plant parts liable to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bark: Adults; borne internally; visible under light microscope.^p - Leaves: Adults; borne externally; visible under light microscope.^p - Stems (above Ground)/Shoots/Trunks/Branches: Adults; borne externally; visible under light microscope.Plant parts not known to carry the pest in trade/transport - Bulbs/Tubers/Corms/Rhizomes^p - Fruits (inc. Pods)^p - Growing Medium Accompanying Plants^p - Flowers/Inflorescences/Cones/Calyx^p - Seedlings/Micropropagated Plants^p - Roots^p - True Seeds (inc. Grain)^p - Wood.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pNumerous acaricides have been recommended to control A. viennensis, however, resistance to acaricides has also been reported, such as to carbophenothion, chlordimeform, dichlorvos, dicofol, dimethoate, fenitrothion, malathion, parathion, parathion-methyl, and schradan in China (Anon, 1977; Cao et al., 1990); organophosphorus compounds in Azerbaijan (Parkhomenko, 1979); organophosphorus and chlorinated-hydrocarbon chemicals (Loladse, 1989), dimethoate, fenbutatin oxide, phosalone (Lobzhanidze and Ordzhonikidze, 1978; Lobzhanidze, 1980) in Georgia; and dimethoate, dicofol in the Ukraine (Galetenko, 1978).^p^pApplication of acaricide is recommended in the spring when the females are active (Galetenko and Opanasenko, 1971; Sepasgozarian and Schruft, 1975; Mamaladze, 1978; Chepurnaya, 1994); or in the pink-bud stage (Galetenko and Opanasenko, 1971); or when A. viennensis density reaches an action threshold. The action threshold differs among various researchers: 4-5 individuals per leaf during the first half of the vegetative period and 7-8 mites per leaf during the second half of the vegetative period (Bulgak, 1979); 3-5 mites per leaf in April and 7-8 mites per leaf in July and August (Loladse, 1989); or 0.2-0.3 mites per leaf after first application (Galetenko and Opanasenko, 1971). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pMost biological control studies are conducted on phytoseiid mites. Amblyseius longispinosus feeds on A. viennensis remaining active at 35°C in the laboratory, and is a promising biological control agent (Akimov and Kolodochka, 1981). If fed on A. viennensis below 26°C and at 75% relative humidity, Amblyseius fallacis completes development from egg to adult in 6.8 days, and adult females lay an average number of 49 eggs. If released in an apple orchard it demonstrates good control on a spider mite population (Zhang and Kong, 1986). Organophosphate resistant strains of Typhlodromus occidentalis released in apple orchards in Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia, and Xinjiang regions in China at a ratio of 1:26-1:64, also show good control of A. viennensis. However, several restricting factors are found: Typhlodromus occidentalis cannot survive the winter (-19.5°C); it fails if rainfall exceeds 600 mm or if the relative humidity is greater than 80%; or if other predators such as Orius sp., are present (Chen et al., 1986;Zhang et al., 1986, 1987, 1988). When fed on A. viennensis, Amblyseius orientalis develops from an egg to an adult in 5 days, and the longevity and fecundity of adult females are 20.5 days and 16 eggs. When released in an apple orchard at a ratio to prey of 1:57-73, it gives 93.4% control on the populations of A. viennensis and Panonychus ulmi (Zhang, 1990; Zhang et al., 1992; Wu et al., 1997). In Georgia, Euseius finlandicus at a ratio of 1:5 to prey, and Amblyseius aberrans at a ratio of 1:7-1:10 can prevent the density of spider mite populations reaching the acaricide-application threshold, 3-5 mites per leaf in April or 7-8 mites per leaf in July-August (Loladse, 1989).

(1987) and Ooi and Shepard (1994). description:
传播媒介提供了一个在一种作物或一种健康作物的初侵染之中病毒再次传播的方法。BCMNV能以非持久方式有一些蚜虫品种传播，这些蚜虫正常地不会迁移到菜豆，但传播BCMNV的是有翅的迁飞型，特别是豌豆蚜（Acyrthosiphon pisum）、蚕豆蚜（Aphis fabae）和桃蚜（Myzus persicae ）(Kennedy et al., 1962; Zettler and Wilkinson, 1966).。
一些传播BCMV的其他的蚜虫品种包括棉蚜Aphis gossypii、苜蓿蚜A. medicaginis、豆卫茅蚜A. rumicis、Hayhurstia atriplicis、Uroleucon ambrosiae、大戟长管蚜Macrosiphum euphorbiae 和豌豆蚜Acyrthosiphon pisum (Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1957)。
BCMV传播的效率是由桃蚜（Myzus persicae）取食行为之前和之后来决定的(Zettler and Wildinson, 1966)。 Vectors provide a means of secondary spread of BCMV within a crop or primary infection of a healthy crop. BCMV can be transmitted in the non-persistent manner by several aphid species which do not normally colonize P. vulgaris but transmit BCMV as winged migrants, especially Acyrthosiphon pisum, Aphis fabae and Myzus persicae (Kennedy et al., 1962; Zettler and Wilkinson, 1966).
Several other aphid species transmit BCMV including Aphis gossypii, A. medicaginis, A. rumicis, Hayhurstia atriplicis, Uroleucon ambrosiae, Macrosiphum euphorbiae and Acyrthosiphon pisum (Zaumeyer and Thomas, 1957).
The efficacy of BCMV transmission is determined by the pre- and post-feeding behaviour of Myzus persicae (Zettler and Wilkinson, 1966).
author: zhangjianjun

potential_eco_desc:
在整个非洲、欧洲、南美和拉丁美洲，BCMV在经济上是重要的。侵染水平可能达到100％，估计的产量损失范围为35％到98％(Galvez, 1980)。在美国俄勒冈州由BCMV引起的在菜豆作物上的产量减少从53％到达68％，这是由株系的严重程度决定的(Hampton, 1975)。
在1972年和1974年摩洛哥，BCMV严重爆发，所有菜豆植株中的50％显示由蚜虫传播的种传侵染的BCMV的症状(Lockhart and Fischer, 1974)；产量损失估计达到50％以及34％的收获种子被感染。 BCMV is economically important throughout Africa, Europe, North America and Latin America. Infection levels may reach 100% and estimated yield losses range from 35-98% (Galvez, 1980). Yield reductions in bean crops due to BCMV ranged from 53 to 68% in Oregon, USA, depending on disease severity (Hampton, 1975).
Severe outbreaks of BCMV occurred in Morocco in 1972 and 1974, in which 50% of all bean plantings showed BCMV symptoms from a seedborne infection spread by aphids (Lockhart and Fischer, 1974); yield losses were estimated at 50% and 34% infection of harvested seed.
author: zhangjianjun

management_info:
化学防治不能在田间规模上用作消除感染植株上的BCMV。然而，它们可用作防治病毒媒介和因此可减少感染的传播。1975年在CIAT的实验证明，杀蚜虫剂喷雾能减少BCMNV的传播(CIAT, 1975)。其他研究已显示，控制非持久性蚜虫传播病毒如BCMNV的杀蚜虫剂的使用可能是无效的(Walkey, 1991)。
Walkey and Dance (1979)利用稀释的矿物油来减少由温室中桃蚜（Myzus persicae）、甘蓝蚜（Brevicoryne brassicae）和蚕豆蚜（Aphis fabae）来传播的BCMV的蚜虫传播。然而，这矿物油在高浓度时会产生植物性毒素的作用，并且在田间，不引起危害植物的毒性时的浓度不能防治蚜虫。在非洲利用化学方法去防治蚜虫即使是有效的，但在财政上是不可实行的。对长期病害防治的最有效和经济的方法是提供对BCMV的抗性品种给农民。 Chemicals cannot be used to eliminate BCMV in infected plants on a field scale. However, it may be used to control the virus vectors and, consequently, may reduce the spread of infection. Experiments at CIAT in 1975 demonstrated that spraying with aphicide could reduce transmission of BCMV (CIAT, 1975). Other studies have shown that the use of aphicides to control the spread of non-persistently aphid-transmitted viruses such as BCMV may be ineffective (Walkey, 1991). 
Walkey and Dance (1979) reduced aphid transmission of BCMV by Myzus persicae, Brevicoryne brassicae and Aphis fabae in the glasshouse using diluted mineral oils. However, the mineral oils were phytotoxic at higher concentrations and, in the field, concentrations which did not cause phytotoxicity failed to control the aphids. The use of chemicals to control aphids in Africa is not financially practicable, even if effective. The most effective and economic method for long-term disease control is to provide farmers with cultivars with host resistance to BCMV.   BCMV的可能的防治方法包括种植健康种子、改善农业操作、防治传播媒介和寄主植物的抗性。 Possible control measures for BCMV include planting healthy seed, improving cultural practices, controlling the vector and host-plant resistance.

CMV has been identified as the causal agent of several recent epidemics in crops such as tomatoes in Spain, Italy, Iran and Japan, bananas in Morocco and Central America (Palukaitis et al., 1992), lupins and capsicums in Australia. description: Incidence^p Palukaitis et al. (1992) list 22 plant species in which CMV is seedborne. Since 1992, the following transmission rates of CMV from infected seeds have been reported in the following additional species: chickpea at a rate of 0.1-2%, lentil at 0.1-1% (Jones and Coutts, 1996), and spinach at 15%. CMV was present in all reproductive tissues of spinach, and it was identified as a member of subgroup II (Yang et al., 1997). A mean seed infection of 0.11% was reported in 97 seed lots of Lupinus angustifolius (Tapscott and Cowling, 1995). Seed lots with infection levels of 15% were recorded in lupins in Australia (Bwye et al., 1994). ^p^pThe process of seed infection of lupins CMV seems to begin first with infection of the megagametophytes (Geering, 1992). Later it can be found in the cotyledons and embryo and usually in or on the testa as determined by PCR assays (Wylie et al., 1993; Yang et al., 1997). In spinach all male and female parts of flowers were infected (Yang et al., 1997).^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pCMV is seed transmitted. An inoculum threshold of (dayuhao)0.5% seed infection is recommended to minimize infection sources for lupin production (Bwye et al., 1994; Jones, 2000). This threshold was based on a study (Bwye et al., 1994) in which narrow-leafed lupins  of cv. Gungurru, were grown in six field experiments in plots sown with healthy seed or seed that carried 0.5-5% infection with CMV. Seed-infected plants were the primary source for subsequent virus spread by aphids. The rate of CMV spread and the extent of infection in plots depended on the level of infection in the seed sown, the proportion of infected seeds that successfully developed into established plants and the time of arrival and number of aphid vectors. In the same study, significant yield losses (25-42%) always resulted when seed with 3-5% infection was sown. Sowing 1% infected seed resulted in significantly decreased yields in two experiments, while 0.75 and 0.5% infected seed caused significant losses in one experiment (16-19% losses). ^p^pIn studies of agronomic effects on the rate of seed infection of CMV in Lupinus angustifolius, Jones and Cowling (1995) showed that this was dependent on the cultivar and Geering (1992) indicated that seed infection was very low when plant infection occurs just before flowering. According to Bwye et al. (1999), greater competition occurred with other plants within wide than narrow rows; wide row spacing diminished the survival of seed-infected plants by 46%. Increased plant growth from banding superphosphate below seed did not significantly decrease the number of seed-infected plants that survived. Straw spread on the soil surface suppressed final CMV incidence by 25-40% and, when applied at different rates, diminished recorded CMV incidence more at 4 than at 2 t/ha, and least at 1 t/ha. Where there was no straw, CMV incidence increased faster with narrow spacing than wide spacing. Soil disturbance from sowing seed with double discs instead of tynes significantly increased incidences of both seedborne and current-season infection and diminished grain yield. management_info: Control measures for CMV are mainly preventive. Conventional methods of virus control are difficult to apply due to the wide host range of CMV which infects many weeds that can act as virus reservoirs and infect crops in adjacent fields. Seedlings derived from infected seeds can also serve as potential primary inocula. Infected bulbous ornamental plants can act as virus reservoirs. The application of thermotherapy coupled with tissue culture has greatly reduced the level of CMV in these crops. Developing new crop varieties resistant to CMV, either by conventional breeding methods or by gene technology, is gaining momentum.^p^pSince CMV is transmitted by over 80 aphid species, the diverse behaviour of various aphid vectors can greatly reduce the impact of insecticide sprays, which are more effective when the insects are a direct 'pest' rather than a 'vector'. A more sustainable approach will be the prevention of aphids reaching the crops. This can be achieved by planting barrier crops, applying sticky traps, or covering the ground with an aphid deterrent material like aluminium foil boards (Mansour et al., 2000). Spraying the crops with mineral oil is sometimes effective. The use of virus-free seeds together with the eradication of virus reservoirs can be effective in controlling CMV.^p^pControl strategies utilizing transgenic expression of the CMV coat protein, truncated replicase and/or other non-structural virus genes to protect crops from infection by CMV look promising. Broad-spectrum resistance against strains of both subgroups of CMV was induced in tomatoes transformed with the coat protein gene of a CMV strain from subgroup 1 (Gielen et al., 1996). Field trials have shown a 40% yield increase in tomato lines transformed with CMV coat protein gene compared to non-transgenic plants (Fuchs et al., 1996).^p^pAlthough the wide host range of CMV makes control measures difficult, new resistance strategies using pathogen-derived genes, which can be inheritable, are encouraging.

management_info:
CMV的防治方法主要是预防性的。由于CMV有广泛的寄主范围，它能侵染能作为病毒储存场所的许多野草和侵染在邻近田块的作物，所以病毒的防治的常规方法是很难去应用的，来自感染种子的幼苗也能作为可能的初接种体来源。感染的球根观赏性植物能作为病毒的储存场所。温热疗法与组织栽培的联合使用能大大地降低CMV在这些作物中的水平。通过常规育种方法或通过基因技术来发展新的抗性的作物品种的动力不断增加。
既然CMV能通过超过80个蚜虫品种传播，那带病毒媒介的不同的媒介能大大地减少杀虫剂喷雾的影响，当昆虫是一个直接的‘害虫’而不是‘媒介’时，杀虫剂喷雾会更有效。更可靠的方法可能是防止蚜虫到达作物。这能通过种植屏障作物、使用粘性陷阱或用蚜虫威慑材料如铝金属薄板来覆盖在地面上来达到(Mansour et al., 2000)。用矿物油来喷洒植物有时候是有效的。无病毒种子的使用以及病毒储存场所的根除一起能有效防治CMV。
利用CMV衣壳蛋白的基因、删短了的复制酶和/或其他的非结构病毒基因的转基因表达来保护免受CMV侵染的防治策略看来是理想的。对CMV的两个亚组的株系的广谱抗性已在一个来自亚组1的CMV株系的衣壳蛋白基因发生转变的番茄上产生(Gielen et al., 1996)。与非转基因植株相比，田间实验已显示40％的产量增加发生在转变了CMV衣壳蛋白基因的番茄系上(Fuchs et al., 1996)。
虽然CMV大范围的寄主使到防治方法有困难，但使用来自病原物的可遗传的基因的新的抗性策略是被鼓励的。 Control measures for CMV are mainly preventive. Conventional methods of virus control are difficult to apply due to the wide host range of CMV which infects many weeds that can act as virus reservoirs and infect crops in adjacent fields. Seedlings derived from infected seeds can also serve as potential primary inocula. Infected bulbous ornamental plants can act as virus reservoirs. The application of thermotherapy coupled with tissue culture has greatly reduced the level of CMV in these crops. Developing new crop varieties resistant to CMV, either by conventional breeding methods or by gene technology, is gaining momentum.
Since CMV is transmitted by over 80 aphid species, the diverse behaviour of various aphid vectors can greatly reduce the impact of insecticide sprays, which are more effective when the insects are a direct‘pest’rather than a‘vector’. A more sustainable approach will be the prevention of aphids reaching the crops. This can be achieved by planting barrier crops, applying sticky traps, or covering the ground with an aphid deterrent material like aluminium foil boards (Mansour et al., 2000). Spraying the crops with mineral oil is sometimes effective. The use of virus-free seeds together with the eradication of virus reservoirs can be effective in controlling CMV.
Control strategies utilizing transgenic expression of the CMV coat protein, truncated replicase and/or other non-structural virus genes to protect crops from infection by CMV look promising. Broad-spectrum resistance against strains of both subgroups of CMV was induced in tomatoes transformed with the coat protein gene of a CMV strain from subgroup 1 (Gielen et al., 1996). Field trials have shown a 40% yield increase in tomato lines transformed with CMV coat protein gene compared to non-transgenic plants (Fuchs et al., 1996).
Although the wide host range of CMV makes control measures difficult, new resistance strategies using pathogen-derived genes, which can be inheritable, are encouraging.

description:
1915年在澳大利亚首次发现。  昆虫介体传播：Thrips tabaci，Thrips setosus（烟蓟马），Thrips parmi， Frankliniella schultzei，Frankliniella occidentalis（西方花蓟马）， Frankliniella fusca（烟褐蓟马）,Scirtothrips dorsalis（茶黄蓟马）以持久性方式传播，这些蓟马只能由幼虫获毒，获毒时间10min或稍短，脱皮仍保留病毒，病毒在昆虫体内繁殖，可能不传给其后代。成虫不能获毒，但成虫能传毒，成虫保毒时间较长，也不能经卵传递。最近研究表明，当苜蓿蓟马的2龄若虫在病株上食毒24h后能有效传播病毒，而且80%的蓟马可由若虫传播病毒，当这些若虫羽化为成虫以后可恢复其传毒功能。
曾报道番茄（Lycopersicon esculentum）种传，千里光（Senecio scandens）种传率96%。但五十年代报道传毒率仅1％，病毒明显的携带在外种皮上而不是在胚里。
有报道认为种子、花粉和植株间相互接触均不传毒。
机械接种、嫁接传毒。
remark: 塞内加尔、南非、赞比亚、尼日利亚、罗得西亚、尼亚萨兰、东非、芬兰、以色列、智利、意大利、马耳他、新西兰等国家和地区将该病毒作为检疫性有害生物。1997年我国将其列入进境检疫三类有害生物名录；2007年我国将该病毒作为检疫性有害生物，对其依法实施检疫。

host_range:
Capsicum annuum, lettuce, pea, tobacco, potato, tomato, and a large number of ornamental plant species are the main hosts of TSWV. Groundnut is a host of TSWV in the USA (causing groundnut ring mosaic), whereas two other orthospoviruses, GBNV and PYSV, are common on groundnut in South-East Asia. TSWV is a real threat to the tobacco industry in the Balkans, to tomato in some regions in Brazil, South Africa and other countries.
TSWV has an extremely wide host range with more than 1300 plants including agricultural crops, wild and weed species (Parrella et al., 2003). This include plant species in 15 monocotyledonous and 69 dicotyledonous families and one family of the Pteridophyta (Turina et al., 2012).
Groundnut ringspot orthotospovirus (GRSV), Tomato chlorotic spot orthotospovirus (TCSV), Chrysanthemum stem necrosis orthotospovirus (CSNV) and TSWV were identified in tomato, lettuces, endives and pepper crops in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and TCSV was the most prevalent virus (Colariccio et al., 2001). In a study of the geographical distribution of orthotospoviruses affecting tomato crops in Argentina, 63% of samples were found to be GRSV, 28.2% were TCSV and corresponding to a restricted area only 8.8% were TSWV (Williams et al., 2001). In tomato and pepper fields in San Francisco Valley and Federal District, USA, 53.5% of samples analysed by ELISA were positive to GRSV, 11.6% to TSWV, 1.9% to TCSV; Impatiens necrotic spot orthotospovirus (INSV) was not detected in this survey (Lima et al., 2000). With 189 recorded susceptible host species, INSV is a specialist pathogen of ornamental plants (Daughtrey et al., 1997). Double infections with TSWV and INSV have been detected in several ornamentals (Daughtrey, 1996; Kaminska et al., 1997). CSNV is probably the main orthotospovirus species infecting chrysanthemum in Brazil, whereas TSWV is the most frequently found orthotospovirus in chrysanthemum in Europe and the USA. Watermelon bud necrosis orthotospovirus (WBNV) can cause severe yield losses in India in watermelon. Infections of Iris yellow spot orthotospovirus (IYSV) occur in onion in Iowa, USA, and in Bahia and Pernambuco, Brazil, where it causes a disease known as ‘ sapeca‘  (Ávila et al., 1998).
Weeds and cultivated species are hosts (Jorda et al., 1995); the role of weeds as possible inoculum sources has been stressed (Cho et al., 1987; Bautista et al., 1995; Lavina et al., 1996; Ochoa et al., 1999; Groves et al., 2001).
In Europe and the Mediterranean region, the principal vegetable and industrial host crops, susceptible to TSWV, are artichoke (Cynara scolymus), aubergine (Solanum melongena), Capsicum annuum, chicory (Cichorium spp.), cucurbit, faba bean (Vicia faba), lettuce, potato (Solanum tuberosum), tobacco and tomato. Some of the principal ornamental species are Alstroemeria, Anemone, Aster, Begonia, Calceolaria, Callistephus, chrysanthemum (Dendranthema morifolium), cineraria (Senecio cruentus), Cyclamen, Dahlia, Gerbera, gloxinia (Sinningia spp.), Pelargonium, Ranunculus, Tagetes and Zinnia. Impatiens hybrids are important hosts of TSWV and INSV in New Guinea. The latter is usually found on other ornamentals (for example, cyclamen, kalanchoe) although not on vegetable crops. In Portugal, it has only been recorded on ornamentals (Louro, 1996) and in the Netherlands on almost 40 ornamentals and only on one vegetable, C. annuum (Verhoeven and Roenhorst, 1998). In addition to several ornamentals, three vegetables: Cichorium endivia, Ocimum basilicum and Valerianella olitoria have been recorded as hosts in France (Llamas-Bousquet and Berling, 1993). This virus has been found occasionally in chrysanthemum in the USA (Daughtrey et al., 1997). It rarely infects and spreads in solanaceous greenhouse and field crops. Infections by INSV in sweet pepper in the Netherlands caused symptoms that were restricted to the fruits. Restriction of symptoms to fruits has also been observed in tomato in Brazil (Pavan et al., 1996). Ruter and Gitaitis (1993) report INSV from a number of woody ornamentals (TSWV is not known to infect any woody plants); it has also, unusually, been reported from a fern (Asplenium nidus-avis; Lavina and Battle, 1994) and from prickly pear cactus (Opuntia microdasys; Blockley and Mumford, 2001). Wild species, including Arctium lappa, Datura stramonium, Emilia sonchifolia, Senecio vulgaris, Solanum nigrum, Sonchus spp. and Stellaria media may be important reservoirs of TSWV (Bautista et al., 1995).
potential_eco_desc:
TSWV and other tospoviruses have become an increasingly important factor contributing to economic losses in many food and ornamental crops throughout the world; losses may be as high as 100% (Berling et al., 1990; Rodriguez, 1990; Rosello et al., 1996). TSWV incidence in Brazil, Hawaii, USA, and South Africa can be so high that farmers are forced out of production. Destructive outbreaks of TSWV have occurred in France and Spain in protected and field crops of tomatoes, Capsicum and Anemone, associated with the establishment and rapid spread of the vector Frankliniella occidentalis (OEPP/EPPO, 1989). In Liguria, Italy, Capsicum production can be severely affected while adjacent tomato and lettuce crops remain healthy. Devastating epidemics can occur in tobacco in Bulgaria, Greece and other south-eastern European countries. In some areas of Argentina, Brazil, Italy and South Africa, TSWV has become one of the most important diseases in tomato. In general, economic loss data are limited, but the following examples of economic impact have been obtained from the literature.
In groundnuts, TSWV has been shown to reduce yield in direct proportion to the intensity of infection. Healthy plants produced 50% more kernels than plants with maximum infection by TSWV (Saharan et al., 1983). The virus reduces height, root length and yield depending on the plant growth stage at the time of infection (Rao et al., 1979). In plants showing symptoms within 45 days of sowing, 100% losses were observed. Losses decreased with increasing age of plants at infection. Gopal and Uphadhyaya (1991) reported yield losses of 50% in Raichur, India. Field trials indicated that early infection with the virus caused a heavy yield loss compared with late infection. Siddaramaiah et al. (1980) reported a drastic reduction in dried pod weight, fresh fodder weight and shelling percent in plants affected at an early stage. Narendrappa and Siddaramaiah (1986) also reported that infection of plants up to 65 days old caused significant reductions in yield while no losses were recorded in plants infected after 95 days. The incidence of bud necrosis (caused by TSWV) has been shown to be lower in close plant spacings than in wide ones (Anon., 1981). Culbreath et al. (1992) reported that the number of seed produced, average weight per seed and total seed yield were lower for TSWV symptomatic plants than for healthy plants in Georgia, USA, in 1988, 1989 and 1990. TSWV has also been reported to reduce the oil content in groundnuts; earlier infection causing greater losses. Plants infected 15 days before harvest showed a 13.2% oil reduction (Ali and Rao, 1982).
Fiederow and Kralowska (1995) reported decreases in yields of tomatoes and Capsicum of 38.7 and 92.2%, respectively. In tomatoes, earlier infection has been shown to cause greater yield losses (Kumar and Irulappen, 1991). A lower number of fruits, fruits weight, and yield were recorded in tomato plants infected at an early stage than those infected at more mature stages; however, the quality of production was altered even in late-infected plants due to abnormal ripening and no difference in marketable fruit yield was obtained (Moriones et al., 1998).
The biochemical changes caused in tomato following infection with TSWV have also been studied. Chlorophyll, xanthophylls and carotene levels decreased in infected plants (Sutha et al., 1998).
In peas in India, TSWV-affected plants were pale-green and stunted with reduced leaf petioles, stipules and tendrils. Only a few pods were produced and these were necrotic. Disease incidence ranged from 10 to 25%, causing serious yield losses (Singh and Gupta, 1994). In greenhouse tests in Canada during 1989-1990 and 1990-1991, TSWV affected Lathyrus sativus and Pisum sativum var. arvense. In L. sativus, symptoms varied from loss of chlorophyll, wilting and drying-up of the foliage to bleaching and drying-up of stem segments at the nodes. In P. sativum var. arvense, purplish-brown streaks were prominent on the stems and petioles. Flower and pod abortion occurred in severely affected plants (Zimmer et al., 1992).
In cucurbit and solanaceous vegetables in Okinawa, Japan, severe losses have been caused by TSWV. Cucumber plants inoculated at the cotyledon stage were shorter, lateral shoots were fewer and shorter and yields were 40% lower than in non-inoculated plants (Hokama and Tokahashi, 1987).
Dahlias in the Netherlands in 1992, 1993 and 1994 had infection levels of 15, 5 and 2%, respectively. Yield of cuttings/tuber was reduced by up to 20% (Asjes et al., 1997).
In Hawaii, USA, TWSV has destroyed 50-90% of lettuce crops (Cho et al., 1987).
Potato crops have been affected by TSWV in India (Khurana et al., 1997), Portugal, Brazil and Argentina (Granval de Millan et al., 1998). Doubt exists as to whether infected tubers will produce healthy plants when they sprout.

remark: TSWV is not at present listed as a quarantine pest by EPPO, but is of quarantine significance. EPPO at one time considered potato strains as A1 quarantine pests under the heading non-European potato viruses, but this idea has now been overtaken by events: TSWV is much more immediately threatening on hosts other than potato than as a theoretical non-European strain on potato. The recent introduction and widespread occurrence of the vector Frankliniella occidentalis in the EPPO region has provided a means of rapid dissemination of the virus. Those affected parts of the region have shown the potential importance of the virus throughout, especially for glasshouse cultivation of ornamentals and vegetables. However, it should be noted that both vector and virus are now present in the majority of EPPO countries. Only a rather small group of countries is apparently free from TSWV.

management_info:
As there is no direct means of controlling the virus, the method of control must either be aimed at the thrips vectors or involve the application of sanitation measures. Seedling beds should be isolated from ornamental plants and susceptible crops and the surrounding areas kept free from weeds. The inside and outside of glasshouses should be kept free of weeds, thus reducing all possible sources of infection and reducing thrips populations. Fine-mesh netting may possibly be useful to exclude thrips (Lacasa et al., 1994). Susceptible decorative plants should preferably not be grown in the vicinity of the glasshouse. The glasshouse should be regularly and frequently inspected after planting. The presence of thrips in the crops should be monitored using yellow sticky cards. If the disease appears in a crop, infected plants should be rogued and destroyed immediately and the house treated with insecticide against thrips.
Similar precautions should be taken with field crops. Although chemical control is possible (Bournier, 1990), F. occidentalis has been found to develop resistant populations if certain insecticides are used repeatedly (OEPP/EPPO, 1989). It is, therefore, important to rotate insecticides with different active ingredients. For ornamental hosts (chrysanthemums, pelargoniums) for which virus-free certification schemes are applied, TSWV is now one of the most important viruses to be tested for (OEPP/EPPO, 1992). Promising results with biological and integrated control measures against thrips in glasshouses have been achieved in several countries (Gillespie, 1989; Ramakers et al., 1989; Trottin-Caudal and Grasselly, 1989; Sanchez et al., 2000). F. occidentalis, infesting plants and present in plastic houses, could be drastically reduced in number using UV-absorbing plastic sheets as cover (Antignus et al., 1996).
Reports about the virus-vector relationship and reduction in TSWV epidemics by chemical treatment are very limited. However, higher levels of control of TSWV were observed in dahlia with weekly sprays of mineral oil, polydimethylsiloxane and deltamethrin (Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 2001). Host-plant resistance, intensive insecticide treatment and the use of reflective mulch significantly reduced the incidence of thrips and TSWV (Riley and Pappu, 2000). In Louisiana, USA, aluminium-surfaced mulch reduced the numbers of trapped thrips by 33-68% and the incidence of TSWV by 60-78% in tomatoes and Capsicum (Greenough et al., 1990). These results support the general view that primary transmission during adult thrips dispersal and host seeking accounted for most observed incidences of TSWV in tomato and groundnut (Camann et al., 1995) and probably also in most crops.
Yudin et al. (1990) devised disease-prediction and economic models that enable growers with lettuce fields affected by TSWV to make management decisions early in the planting cycle. Early disease incidence was a better predictor of disease incidence at harvest than thrips abundance because the proportion of infectious insects is essential to analyse the epidemics. The incidences of TSWV in early transplanted tomato crops with the highest thrips population was comparable to those found in late transplanted tomatoes with very low population densities (Aramburu et al., 1997).
The effect of the groundnut variety, planting date, plant density, insecticides used and disease history on the incidence and severity of TSWV was assessed in groundnut fields in Georgia, USA. These effects can be evaluated for each field in a risk assessment index. This index can vary between 25 and 125 points for each field. Fields with an index of 25-55 were considered to have a low risk, those between 60-80 a moderate risk, and those with more than 85 a high risk (Brown et al., 1998). Previous crops, adjoining crops, tillage practices, row patterns and weather also have effects, but were not indexed as these factors are insufficiently defined.
Screening vegetative dahlia propagation material for TSWV infections resulted in an almost healthy dahlia crop and seed tubers in the Netherlands (Schadewijk, 1996).
The growth regulators gibberellic acid, naphthalene acetic acid and chlormequat sprayed once on tomato plants either before or after TSWV inoculation inhibited the infectivity of the virus (Sapatnekar and Sawant, 2001).
Several sources of resistance to TSWV have been found in species of Solanum (Kumar et al., 1995; Cho et al., 1996). Two dominant and three recessive genes were responsible for resistance in S. pimpinellifolium and two tomato cultivars (Finlay, 1953). Introduction of these genes in tomato lines did not result in field resistance (Watterson et al., 1989). Lack of success in introducing this resistance into commercial tomato cultivars may be due to the existence of different TSWV strains or pathotypes. The tomato cv. Stevens, obtained from a cross between S. lycopersicum and S. peruvianum, has broad resistance to different TSWV isolates (van Zijl et al., 1986) and has been preferred by breeders for incorporating resistance into cultivated tomatoes. This resistance, introgressed in cv. Stevens, is conferred by a single dominant gene denoted Sw-5 with a 98.7% penetrance (Stevens et al., 1992) and also provided a high level of resistance to other members of the genus orthotospovirus, including Groundnut ringspot orthotospovirus (GRSV), Tomato chlorotic spot orthotospovirus (TCSV) and Groundnut bud necrosis orthotospovirus (GBNV). TSWV isolates, breaking this resistance, have been found in field crops in South Africa, Australia, USA (California and Hawaii) and Spain (Thompson and van Zijl, 1996; Latham and Jones, 1998; Aramburu and Marti, 2003; Batuman et al., 2017). New and selected accessions from Solanum species showed high resistance to TSWV and other viruses and seem to be of interest for enhancing the durability of the resistance to TSWV in commercial varieties (Roselló et al., 1999; Picó et al., 2002).
In lettuces, two cultivars (Tinto and Ancora) are reported to be resistant to TSWV in Hawaii, USA (O‘ Malley and Hartmann, 1989). This resistance was not confirmed in later studies. In groundnuts, breeding lines with a lower incidence of spotted wilt and lower disease severity ratings have been, or will be, released (Culbreath et al., 1996). Some field tolerance to GBNV occurs in Indian cultivars (Nigam et al., 1990) and could be explained by mature and tissue resistance (Buiel and Parlevliet, 1996). In tobacco, Nicotiana sanderae was immune and N. alata and N. langsdorffii were highly resistant to TSWV (Palakarcheva and Yancheva, 1989).
A gene designated Tsw, which prevents systemic spread of TSWV by a hypersensitive response has been identified in several C. chinense accessions (Black et al., 1993; Boiteux, 1995). This resistance proved to be less stable when young plants became infected and were kept at high temperatures (Roggero et al., 1996; Moury et al., 1998; Soler et al., 1998); by contrast, INSV infection was restricted to the inoculated leaves in Capsicum annuum and C. chinense under high temperatures (Roggero et al., 1999). The Tsw gene has phenotypic and genetic similarities of resistance in pepper with tomato plants carrying the Sw-5 gene; however, distinct viral gene products control the outcome of TSWV infection (Jahn et al., 2000); so, TSWV isolates that overcome tomato resistance gene Sw-5 failed to overcome hypersensitive resistance to TSWV in C. chinense PI 152225 and PI 159236 (Latham and Jones, 1998). Line 159236 was not resistant to GRSV (Boiteux and Nagata, 1993).
High levels of resistance to TSWV has been obtained in inbred lines of tomato transformed with the nucleoprotein (N) gene (de Haan et al., 1996). Similar levels of resistance have also been found in Nicotiana tabacum and N. benthamiana (Vaira et al., 1995), and chrysanthemum (Sherman et al., 1998) containing the nucleoprotein gene of TSWV. This transgenic resistance to TSWV in N. tabacum is effective in reducing the incidence of the disease under field conditions (Herrero et al., 2000). Sense or antisense copies of the N or Nsm genes can confer resistance. Groundnut lines transgenic for the antisense nucleocapsid (N) gene showed a lower TSWV incidence in field assays (Magbanua et al., 2000). Other TSWV sequences, spanning 70% of the genome, appear not to be effective in inducing resistance in transgenic tobacco (Prins et al., 1996). A broad resistance to GRSV, TSWV and TCSV was found in tobacco plants expressing the N gene sequences of these viruses (Prins et al., 1995). Transgenic plants expressing the transgene with green fluorescent protein fused to segments of the nucleocapsid (N) gene of TSWV showed multiple virus resistance (Jan et al., 2000).
The ability of TSWV isolates to overcome the resistance conferred by Sw-5 gene in tomato and the resistance conferred by the nucleocapsid gene in transgenic tobacco has been associated with the M RNA segment (Hoffmann et al., 2001).
Phytosanitary Measures。Susceptible host plants in greenhouses should be regularly inspected for orthotospovirus infections and vectors. Removal or roguing of infected plants, especially when the incidence is low, is an option to control further spread. Application of this practise may depend on the crop and its age, and the question whether the infection will or will not spread in the crop. Vectors should be actively controlled at the place of production. In general, heavily infected crops should be destroyed. Where appropriate, healthy planting material should be used. All plant residues left after harvested crops in greenhouses and fields should be eliminated. The soil has to be disinfected after the removal or harvest of severely infected crops with a high infestation of thrips. The emerging of viruliferous adults from infected pupae may form a serious threat to the new crop.

management_info:
因为没有防治该病毒的直接的方法，所以防治的方法必需以蓟马媒介为目标或包括卫生方法的使用。苗床应与观赏植物和敏感作物隔离，周围的区域应保持没有野草。温室内外应保持没有野草，因此能减少所有可能的侵染来源和减少蓟马的种群数量。细孔的网可能对防蓟马有用(Lacasa et al., 1994)。易感的装饰植物最好不种植在邻近的温室内。在种植后，温室应定期地和常常地检查。蓟马在作物中的存在应利用黄色粘卡进行监测。如果病害在一个作物中出现，感染植株应被迅速根除和毁灭，温室应用对付蓟马的杀虫剂处理。
应对田间作物作出类似的防范。虽然化学防治是可能的(Bournier, 1990)，但被发现如果某种杀虫剂重复地被使用，苜蓿花蓟马（F. occidentalis）会产生抗性种群(OEPP/EPPO, 1989)。所以，轮换使用不同活性成分的杀虫剂是重要的。对于观赏性植物寄主（菊花、天竺葵），因为无病毒鉴定程序的使用，TSWV现在是需要测试的最重要的病毒之一(OEPP/EPPO, 1992)。对温室中蓟马的生物和综合的防治方法的理想的效果已在一些国家中达到(Gillespie, 1989; Ramakers et al., 1989; Trottin-Caudal and Grasselly, 1989; Sanchez et al., 2000) 。侵染植物和在塑胶大棚中存在的苜蓿花蓟马（F. occidentalis）应利用吸收UV的塑胶薄板覆盖来彻底地减少(Antignus et al., 1996)。
关于病毒与媒介的关系和通过化学防治减少TSWV流行的报道是有限的。然而，TSWV更高的防治水平在使用每周一次矿物油、聚二甲基硅氧烷和溴氰菊酯喷洒的大丽花上发现(Asjes and Blom-Barnhoorn, 2001)。抗性寄主植物、强烈的杀虫剂处理和反射物质的覆盖能大大地减少蓟马和TSWV的发生率(Riley and Pappu, 2000)。在美国路易斯安那州，在番茄和辣椒上铝平板的覆盖能减少捕获的蓟马的数量的33-68％以及TSWV发生率的60-78％(Greenough et al., 1990)。这些结果支持了在番茄和花生上(Camann et al., 1995)和可能在大多数作物上在成虫蓟马分散和寻求寄主时期占有最大TSWV观测发生率的主要传播这个一般的观点。
Yudin et al. (1990) 设计的病害预测和经济模式，这能够使受TSWV感染的莴苣田块的种植者在种植周期的早期制定管理的决策。病害的早期发生率比起蓟马的丰富来说能更好地预测收获时病害的发生率，因为传染性的昆虫的比例是分析该流行的必要因素。有最高蓟马种群数量的早期移植的番茄作物中的TSWV发生率比得上那些有非常低蓟马种群密度的晚期移植的番茄作物中的发生率(Aramburu et al., 1997)。
花生品种、种植日期、种植密度、杀虫剂使用和病害历史对TSWV发生率和严重程度的影响已在美国乔治亚州的花生田块中作出了估计。这些影响能估计每块田地的一个危险估计指数。这指数在每块田地25点和125点之间作变化。25-55点指数的田地被认为有低危险性，而在60-80之间有中等危险性，在85以上的那些有高危险性(Brown et al., 1998)。之前的作物，邻近的作物、耕地实践、播种类型和天气也有影响，但不在指数当中因为这些因素是不够详细的。
在荷兰，筛选对TSWV侵染的有生长能力的大丽花繁殖材料导致几乎都是健康的大丽花作物和种子块茎(Schadewijk, 1996)。
生长调节剂赤霉酸、萘乙酸和Cycocel (矮壮素)在TSWV接种前或后在番茄植物上喷洒一次能抑制病毒的侵染(Sapatnekar and Sawant, 2001)。
一些对TSWV的抗性来源已被发现在番茄属的种中(Kumar et al., 1995; Cho et al., 1996) 。两个显性和三个隐性基因引起醋栗番茄（L. pimpinellifolium）和两个番茄品种的抗性(Finlay, 1953)。这些基因在番茄品系中的引入不会导致田间抗性(Watterson et al., 1989)。对商业番茄品种引进这抗性的不成功可能是由于不同TSWV株系或病变型的存在。从番茄（L. esculentum）和秘鲁番茄（L. peruvianum）中杂交获得的番茄品种Stevens对不同的TSWV分离种有较广的抗性van Zijl et al., 1986)，而且是合并抗性进入栽培的番茄的育种的首先选择。基因渗入品种Stevens的这抗性是由一个表示98.7％外显率的Sw-5的单一的显性基因所给予(Stevens et al., 1992)，它也对番茄斑萎病毒属的其他成员有高度抗性，包括GRSV、TCSV 和 GBNV。破坏这抗性的TSWV分离种已在南非、澳大利亚、夏威夷（美国）和西班牙的田间作物中发现(Thompson and van Zijl, 1996; Latham and Jones, 1998; Aramburu and Marti, 2003)。新的和从番茄属种中挑选的添加物对TSWV和其他病毒表现高抗性商业品种中，并且似乎对TSWV抗性耐久性的增强有作用(Rosell?et al., 1999; Pic?et al., 2002)。
在莴苣中，两个品种(Tinto and Ancora)在美国夏威夷被报道对TSWV有抗性(O’Malley and Hartmann, 1989)。这抗性在后来的研究中没有被证实。在花生中，有较低斑萎发病率和较低病害严重性等级的育种品系已经或将要被发表(Culbreath et al., 1996)。一些对花生芽坏死病毒的田间耐病性发生在印度品种中(Nigam et al., 1990)，而且能被成熟和组织抗性作解释(Buiel and Parlevliet, 1996)。在烟草中，美花烟草（Nicotiana sanderae）是免疫的，而花烟草（N. alata ）和 蓝格斯多夫烟草（N. langsdorffii）对TSWV有高度抗性(Palakarcheva and Yancheva, 1989)。
一个叫做Tsw的基因能通过一个敏感反应来预防TSWV的系统性传播，它已在一些C. chinense的添加物中被鉴别出(Black et al., 1993; Boiteux, 1995)。被证明当年幼植物受到侵染和保持在高温下时，这抗性具较低稳定性的(Roggero et al., 1996; Moury et al., 1998; Soler et al., 1998) ；与其对比的是，INSV侵染在高温条件下的辣椒（Capsicum annuum）和 C. chinense的接种叶片中受到限制 (Roggero et al., 1999) 。辣椒中的抗性的Tsw基因与携带Sw-5基因的番茄植物的相比有表型的和遗传的相似之处；然而，不同的病毒基因产物控制着TSWV侵染的结果(Jahn et al., 2000)；所以，克服番茄抗性基因Sw-5的TSWV分离种不能克服C. chinense PI 152225 和 PI 159236中对TSWV的敏感抗性(Latham and Jones, 1998)。品系159236对GRSV没有抗性(Boiteux and Nagata, 1993)。
TSWV分离种克服在番茄中由Sw-5基因给予的抗性和在转基因烟草中由核壳体基因给予的抗性的能力与M RNA片断有关(Hoffmann et al., 2001)。 As there is no direct means of controlling the virus, the method of control must either be aimed at the thrips vectors or involve the application of sanitation measures. Seedling beds should be isolated from ornamental plants and susceptible crops and the surrounding areas kept free from weeds. The inside and outside of glasshouses should be kept free of weeds, thus reducing all possible sources of infection and reducing thrips populations. Fine-mesh netting may possibly be useful to exclude thrips (Lacasa et al., 1994). Susceptible decorative plants should preferably not be grown in the vicinity of the glasshouse. description: 在自然界所有的番茄斑萎病毒属病毒是通过蓟马科 (缨翅目)属于花蓟马和蓟马的昆虫传播和散布的。它们包括Frankliniella bispinosa (Webb et al., 1998)、台湾蓟马（F. intonsa ）(Wijkamp et al., 1995)、烟褐蓟马（F. fusca）、苜蓿花蓟马（F. occidentalis ）(EPPO/CABI, 1992)、F. schultzei、节瓜蓟马（Thrips palmi）、粗毛蓟马（T. setosus）和烟蓟马（T. tabaci.）。亮蓟马（T. flavus ）(Singh and Krishnareddy, 1996)、玉米蓟马（F. tenuicornis ）(Lormelink, 1994)和茶黄蓟马（Scirtothrips dorsalis ）(Amin et al., 1981)被报道为传播媒介，但它们传播的地位目前还未被证实。 All tospoviruses are transmitted and spread in nature by insects of the family Thripidae (Thysanoptera), belonging to the genera Frankliniella and Thrips. They include Frankliniella bispinosa (Webb et al., 1998), F. intonsa (Wijkamp et al., 1995), F. fusca, F. occidentalis (EPPO/CABI, 1992), F. schultzei, Thrips palmi, T. setosus and T. tabaci. T. flavus (Singh and Krishnareddy, 1996), F. tenuicornis (Lormelink, 1994) and Scirtothrips dorsalis (Amin et al., 1981) have been reported as vectors, but their status as such has yet to be confirmed.

potential_eco_desc:
TSWV和其他的番茄斑萎病毒属病毒已成为在全世界范围内造成许多粮食和观赏作物的产量损失的一个日益重要的因素；损失可能会高达100％(Berling et al., 1990; Rodriguez, 1990; Rosell?et al., 1996)。在巴西、美国夏威夷和南非，TSWV的发生率非常高，这令到农民们被迫要放弃生产。TSWV毁灭性的爆发已在法国和西班牙的番茄、辣椒和银莲花的受保护和田间作物中发生，这与媒介Frankliniella occidentalis的建立和快速传播有关系 (OEPP/EPPO, 1989)。在意大利利古里亚，辣椒生产能受到严重的影响，而邻近的番茄和莴苣作物仍保持健康。毁灭性的流行能在保加利亚、希腊和其他欧洲东南部国家的烟草上发生。在阿根廷、巴西、意大利和南非的一些地区，TSWV成为了番茄上最重要的病害之一。一般而言，经济损失的数据是受到限制的，但经济影响的下面的例子是从文献中获得的。
在花生上，TSWV已被证明能与侵染的强度成正比地减少产量。健康的植株比受TSWV最大侵染的植株多产生50％的果仁 (Saharan et al., 1983)。该病毒根据侵染时的植物生长阶段而减少植物的高度、根长度和产量 (Rao et al., 1979)。在播种45天内表现症状的植物中，100％的损失被观测出。损失会随着植物受侵染时的年龄的增加而减少。Gopal and Uphadhyaya (1991)报道了在印度赖久尔50％的产量损失。田间实验证明：该病毒在早期的侵染比在晚期的侵染引起更重大的产量损失。Siddaramaiah et al. (1980)报道了在早期阶段受感染的植物中干燥荚果重量、新鲜草料重量和去壳百分比的一个急剧的减少。Narendrappa and Siddaramaiah (1986)也报道：超过65天大的植物的侵染引起产量的明显减少，而在95天后侵染的植物没有产量损失。芽坏死病害（由TSWV引起的）的发病率已被证明在较密的植物间距中比在较宽的间距中的要更低(Anon., 1981)。Culbreath et al. (1992)报道：在美国乔治亚州，在1988、1989和1990年，产生的种子的数量、每颗种子的平均重量和总的种子产量在表现TSWV症候的植株上比健康植株的更低。TSWV也被报道会减少花生的含油量；侵染越早引起的损失越大。收获前15天受感染的植物显示13.2％的油量减少(Ali and Rao, 1982)。
Fiederow and Kralowska (1995)报道了番茄和辣椒产量分别38.7％和92.2％的减少。在番茄上，更早的侵染已被证明能引起更严重的产量损失(Kumar and Irulappen, 1991)。在早期的阶段受侵染的番茄植物比在更成熟的阶段受侵染的植物产生更低的果实、果实重量和产量；然而，因为其不正常的成熟，生产的品质即使在晚期受感染的植物上也会有所改变，在可销售的果实产量上没有不同(Moriones et al., 1998)。
在TSWV侵染后番茄中的生物化学的变化也被研究。感病植株中的叶绿素、叶黄素和胡萝卜素水平有所降低(Sutha et al., 1998)。
在印度的豇豆上，受TSWV感染的植株是淡绿色和矮化的，叶柄、托叶和卷须有所减少。只有些豆荚产生，而且是坏死的。病害发生率从10％到25％，引起严重的产量损失(Singh and Gupta, 1994)。在1989-1990和1990-1991年的加拿大的温室实验中，TSWV侵染家山黧豆（Lathyrus sativus）和食用豌豆（Pisum sativum var. arvense）。在家山黧豆（L. sativus）上，症状从叶绿素的损失、叶片的萎蔫和干枯变化到节点上茎节的变白和干枯。在食用豌豆（P. sativum var. arvense）上，紫褐色的条纹明显地出现在茎和叶柄中。花和豆荚的败育发生在严重感染的植株上(Zimmer et al., 1992)。
在日本冲绳岛的葫芦和茄属蔬菜中，TSWV引起严重的损失。在子叶阶段接种的黄瓜植物愈非接种植株相比是更矮的、侧枝是更少和更短的，产量也低40％(Hokama and Tokahashi, 1987)。
在1992、1993和1994年，在荷兰，大丽花的侵染水平分别是15％、5％和2％。插条/块茎的产量减少超过20％(Asjes et al., 1997)。
在美国夏威夷，TWSV毁灭了50-90％的莴苣作物(Cho et al., 1987)。
在印度(Khurana et al., 1997)、葡萄牙、巴西和阿根廷，马铃薯作物受到TSWV的侵染(Granval de Millan et al., 1998)。感染的块茎当它们萌发时是否会产生健康的植株是令人怀疑的。 TSWV and other tospoviruses have become an increasingly important factor contributing to economic losses in many food and ornamental crops throughout the world; losses may be as high as 100% (Berling et al., 1990; Rodriguez, 1990; Rosell?et al., 1996). TSWV incidence in Brazil, Hawaii, USA, and South Africa can be so high that farmers are forced out of production. Destructive outbreaks of TSWV have occurred in France and Spain in protected and field crops of tomatoes, Capsicum and Anemone, associated with the establishment and rapid spread of the vector Frankliniella occidentalis (OEPP/EPPO, 1989). In Liguria, Italy, Capsicum production can be severely affected while adjacent tomato and lettuce crops remain healthy. Devastating epidemics can occur in tobacco in Bulgaria, Greece and other south-eastern European countries. In some areas of Argentina, Brazil, Italy and South Africa, TSWV has become one of the most important diseases in tomato. In general, economic loss data are limited, but the following examples of economic impact have been obtained from the literature.
In groundnuts, TSWV has been shown to reduce yield in direct proportion to the intensity of infection. Healthy plants produced 50% more kernels than plants with maximum infection by TSWV (Saharan et al., 1983). The virus reduces height, root length and yield depending on the plant growth stage at the time of infection (Rao et al., 1979). In plants showing symptoms within 45 days of sowing, 100% losses were observed. Losses decreased with increasing age of plants at infection. Gopal and Uphadhyaya (1991) reported yield losses of 50% in Raichur, India. Field trials indicated that early infection with the virus caused a heavy yield loss compared with late infection. Siddaramaiah et al. (1980) reported a drastic reduction in dried pod weight, fresh fodder weight and shelling percent in plants affected at an early stage. management_info: Chemical Control^p^pB. theobromae disease on Citrus spp. is checked by standard fungicidal treatment in the packing house. Brown et al. (1970, cited in Holliday, 1980) found that stem-end rot was reduced in fruit from trees sprayed with benomyl at the rate of 0.25 of the product. Applications to dormant trees in the USA in February reduced this rot in Hamlin oranges harvested in the following November and December.^p^pThiabendazole has been recommended for the control of B. theobromae infection in banana and yam (Amusa and Ayinla, 1996). Benomyl or captan prevented rots in sweet potato (Arinze et al., 1975). A reduction in disease progression was reported for gummosis in cashew by benomyl or benomyl in combination with copper oxychloride (Cardoso et al., 1998). Control of damping off in cotton was achieved with carbendazim with tolylfluanid and carboxin-thiram in Brazil (Araujo et al., 1999). Kuo and Liu (2000) reported a reduction in the severity of seedling stem blight of Phaseolus caused by B. theobromae after treatment with benomyl, procymidone, tebuconazole and iprodione.^p^p^Physical Control^p^pQuimo et al. (1974, cited in Holliday, 1980) described control in mango fruit by hot-water treatment at 53°C for 10 minutes. Stem canker of mulberry was reduced by soil solarization (Gupta et al., 1999). ^p^p^Post-Harvest Treatment^p^pControl of the potentially more serious rots that are caused after harvest must vary with local conditions. Sensible, cultural precautions at harvest and post-harvest fungicidal treatment should reduce incidence (Holliday, 1980). Post harvest fruit rot of mango caused by B. theobromae was controlled by carbendazium (Waskar et al., 1997) and carbendazim and thiophanate-methyl (Banik et al., 1998; ). Hot-water treatment of fruits has been reported for control of stem-end rot of papaya (Yaguchi et al., 1998; Kodikara et al., 1998) and mango (Bugante et al., 1997). Majumdar and Pathak (1997) reported effective control of fruit rot of guava using imazalil in the pre-inoculation and benomyl in the post-inoculation treatment. Treatment with growth regulators such as 2,4-D, GA3 and NAA along with prochloraz increased the efficiency of fungicides against B. theobromae in mango (Tang YouLin et al., 1997). Precooling of mango fruits resulted in no incidence of B. theobromae for up to 13 days of storage and reduced incidence was recorded until the end of the storage period (Kapse et al., 1997). Significant reduction in the incidence of storage rot of kolanut was achievbed using Milton solution and wood ashes prepared from Vernonia amygdalina, Tectona spp., Gliricidia sepium and Cassia siamea (Agbeniyi, 1999).^p^pSaprophytic yeast isolate LM-5 demonstrated great potential as an agent for postharvest control of mango rot (Michereff et al., 1997).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pIn maize, resistance has been reported by Payak and Sharma (1979) and Vasantha Kumar (1986). Among the inbred lines, CM-202, CM-500, CM-400, B-57Htn, DIARA and CM-600 showed moderate resistance to cob and stalk rot caused by B. theobromae. Among composites, Phil.DMR-Comp., NLD Comp. and 400175 showed moderate resistance.Banik et al. (1996) identified the mango cultivars Alphonso, Krishnabhog and Totapuri Red Small as sources of resistance. In forage legumes, the genotypes CIAT 10136 and FM 9405 parcela 1 were reported to be most resistant to die back (Kelemu et al., 1997). Batista et al. (1997) recommended the castor bean cultivar Preta Pernambucana as the donor of tolerance to rot caused by B. theobromae, while Lima et al. (1998) identified Espada and Manguito to be resistant to three isolates of B. theobromae. The yam cultivars TDa  84/093, 176, 382 and TDr 608 and 81/453 were mildly susceptible to the rot pathogen B. theobromae (Osai et al., 1996).^p^p^Biological ControlKrauss et al. (1998) identified eight mycoparasites to have traits of biocontrol agents of crown rot of banana.

potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pL. maculans occurs throughout the world and causes leaf spotting and stem rot of vegetable brassicas, swede and raddish and stem canker or blackleg of oilseed rape (canola) (Brassica napus var. oleifera or B. rapa). ^p^pStem infections can reduce seed yield if the infection becomes severe enough to cause early senescence or lodging. In the distant past, the disease has caused marketable yield losses on vegetable crops by infecting leaves and stems (Henderson, 1918), and more recently on seed crops of vegetable brassicas (Humpherson-Jones, 1983). ^p^pThe vast majority of yield losses caused by this disease have been recorded on the most economically important and most widely grown host, oilseed rape. Currently in Europe, North America and Australia, total devastation of the crop can occur due to seedling death, although this is rare. In harvested crops, yield losses are usually 0-10% but can often reach 30-50% in individual fields (Gladders and Musa, 1979; Gugel and Petrie, 1992; Hall et al., 1993; Barbetti and Khangura, 1999; Zhou et al., 1999).^p^pThere is confusion over the importance of the B group (L. biglobosa) in crop protection. In Canada, the B group generally is not considered to be a serious pathogen. The structure of populations of L. maculans in different regions, the climate, cultivar resistance and cultural practices influence the economic impact of the disease.^p^pThe following table shows the type of oilseed rape grown in different regions and the typical yields, which vary considerably - an important consideration in deciding whether the impact of L. maculans is significant and whether it is economic to apply fungicides.^p^pType of oilseed rape and typical yields in different regions (1999/2000 data)^p^p^p	Type of oilseed rape	Typical yield^p^pCanada	West: spring B. napus and       1.5 t/ha^p	some B. rapa	^p^p	Ontario: B. napus of both          2.2 t/ha^p	winter and spring type	^p^pEurope	West: winter B. napus	 4 t/ha^p^p	Central: 60% winter, 40%          1.5 t/ha ^p	spring B. napus	^p^pAustralia	>95% B. napus (spring type      Western Australia 1.1 t/ha ^p	grown over winter period          South east 1.6 t/ha^p	<5% B. juncea	^p^p^Crop Losses In Oilseed Brassicas^p^pNorth America^p^pOilseed rape or canola is grown extensively in the western Canadian provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and also in Ontario, plus a few states of the USA. The disease was not important until the mid-1970s when the damaging A group began to spread in Saskatchewan, western Canada, causing estimated losses of 20% in one field by 1977 (Petrie, 1978). However, the disease was not considered to be widespread in that province until 1982 when the estimated average yield loss was 6% (reaching 56% in individual fields) (Gugel and Petrie, 1992). Gugel and Petrie (1992) reported yield losses in Saskatchewan of 7.2% in 1984 and 5.2% in 1985 (over 30% in some individual fields). The disease continued to spread west into Alberta by 1983 and east into Manitoba by 1984. By 1988, 62% of fields in southwest Manitoba were infected with an average plant incidence of 30% leading to a 10% yield loss (Platford and van den Berg, 1989) while the province-wide yield loss was 5% (Gugel and Petrie, 1992). By 1991, the yield loss for Alberta was 1% with substantial losses in some areas (Evans et al., 1991).^p^pIn Ontario, Peters and Hall (1987) found the A group in 1986 and 1987 in 92% and 100% of fields, respectively. The mean disease incidence increased from 32 to 69% with estimated yield losses 5% and 7.5% respectively. Hall et al. (1993) found that winter oilseed rape was more heavily infected than spring crops. They found infection in 60-100% of fields of winter oilseed rape, and 27-31% of fields of spring rape. Mean annual seed yield losses were 1.1-7.5% (maximum estimated loss per field was 29.2%) for winter rape, and 0.3-1.6% (maximum estimated loss per field was 8.8%) for spring rape. description: Incidence^p^pL. maculans is seedborne on several cruciferous crops. Jacobsen and Williams (1971) detected it in crucifer seed as dormant mycelium within the seed coat or even within the embryo. Reported incidences of seedborne infection were 0.3-1.5% for cabbage (Mannerucci et al., 1982), 0.08-5.9% on rapeseed in Australia (Stovold, 1977; Wood and Barbetti, 1977) and up to 5.1% on rapeseed in Canada (Chigogora and Hall, 1995). Virulent strains of the pathogen have been implicated in economic losses (McGee and Petrie, 1978). In Canada, virulent strains predominate in isolates recovered from rape seeds. They were found in 17 of 570 rapeseed samples from Saskatchewan. Fourteen of the 17 samples had (dayuhao)0.5% infected seeds and three had >2%. A more geographically widespread, weakly virulent strain occurred in 13% of the Saskatchewan samples (Petrie, 1979). Of 61 isolates of  L. maculans obtained from seed in Ontario, 50 were highly virulent and 11 were weakly virulent (Chigogora and Hall, 1995). A survey of L. maculans (Phoma lingam) contamination in Brassica napus seed samples from England, UK, and Poland shpwed that P. lingam contamination in Polish and English seed samples reached 0.5 and 0.6%, respectively, of which 7.1% of the Polish isolates and 12.3% of the English isolates were classified as Tox+pathotype (Wang et al., 2003).^p^pInfections on siliques of cabbage plants were localized, suggesting that infection of L. maculans did not progress systemically from basal crown cankers. No infected seeds were recovered from symptomless siliques, but they were found in infected siliques (Bonman and Gabrielson, 1981). One report found a correlation between silique infection and seed infection of rape (Chigogora and Hall, 1995), but another  (Wood and Barbetti, 1977) revealed no correlation between levels of silique infection and seed infection at maturity.^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pNot recorded.^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pIn field tests in Western Australia, a rapeseed plot grown from 5.9% infected seed resulted in 19% of plants developing blackleg crown cankers, whereas one containing 0.08% infected seed resulted in 1% infected plants. The following year, at a different location, a sample with 0.5% infection produced only 0.06% of plants with crown cankers and 0.08% infected seed yielded 0.08% infected plants (Wood and Barbetti, 1977). McGee (1979), on the other hand, found no differences in infection of seedlings or in crown cankers in field plantings of seeds with 3 and 0% infection with L. maculans. However, the field contained black leg-infected crop residues from which extensive ascospore inoculum overwhelmed that from infected seeds. The conclusion of this study was that seedborne L. maculans was a minor source of inoculum compared with that from infected crop residues. However, this is not the case for seedborne infection of cruciferous vegetable crops which include a transplant bed phase in the growing practice. Under these circumstances, low incidences of seed infection greatly multiplied under the high humidity, high density planting in the seed bed, resulting in epidemics when contaminated transplants are taken to the production fields (Sherf, 1968; Williams, 1980). The importance of the amount of seedborne inoculum in the infestation of transplant beds is indicated in the result that black leg failed to develop in beds grown from seed lots containing 0.6% seedborne L. maculans, but did appear in beds grown from lots with 1.5% or more infection, suggesting that eradication of seedborne inoculum may not be necessary for field control (Gabrielson et al., 1977).^p^pA study was conducted to investigate the infection routes of cabbage black leg in a plug nursery. Seed and plug tray sterilizing methods, irrigation methods and chemical control for preventing disease spread were also examined. management_info: Host Plant Resistance^p^pResistant cultivars are important in the integrated management of this pathogen. However, due to the variability in the virulence of L. maculans, cultivars which are resistant in one part of the world may be susceptible in other areas. Until 1997 the cultivar Jet Neuf was widely used as a resistance source in Europe (Ferreira et al., 1995), but its efficiency is diminishing in some locations. In Canada, the cultivar Quantum is considered to have the best resistance (Ansan-Melayah et al., 1995). A great deal of research is underway to find new sources of resistance (from brassicas or other plants) which can be engineered or conventionally bred (using double haploids) into rape. To cope with the variability of L. maculans, breeding for resistance must be given a high priority since cultural and chemical control measures are generally insufficient (Somda et al., 1996). In Australia, the cultivar Hyola 60 has proven to be extremely resistant to L. maculans (Sosnowski et al. 2001b). This resistance originated from a wild accession of B. rapa var. sylvestris which was collected in Sicily and then crossed with B. oleracea var. albogabra to produce a hybrid (Crouch et al. 1994).^p^pThe physical strength of a cultivar is also important as this increases the tolerance to infection, i.e. infection occurs but does not reduce the yield greatly. Thicker, tougher stems with a high lignin and calcium content are thought to have greater tolerance.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pTo prevent serious attacks of stem canker in infected areas it is essential to control early infection of rape plants by airborne ascospores. Good crop rotation to reduce exposure to inoculum and to improve plant vigour through improved nutrition requires at least 3 seasons before replanting with rape (Petrie, 1986).^p^pAdditionally, deeply ploughing rape stubble followed by a minimal tillage the following year and sowing of a non-brassica crop minimises spore release from infected residue. Gladders and Musa (1980) reported that severe leaf spot infection of seedlings near unploughed oilseed rape stubble resulted in complete crop loss and that ploughing infected rape stubble was effective in reducing the amount of debris on the soil surface and apparently reduced the spread of infection to newly sown crops. Field selection, planting date and weed control are also important factors to reduce inoculum (Hall, 1992). It has also been suggested that a separation of 5 to 8 km from infested stubble is necessary to avoid severe stem canker in rape (Bokor et al., 1975).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pResearch is currently assessing the potential of several organisms such as Bacillus bacterium (Yang et al., 1997) and species of bird's nest fungus, Cyathus striatus and C. olla (Tewari et al., 1997), as biocontrol agents (see Natural Enemies).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control is most efficient when directed at critical points in the disease cycle (Hall, 1992). The most sensitive period for infection of oilseed rape plants by L. maculans is from emergence to the 8th leaf stage in terms of subsequent canker development and related yield loss. For winter oilseed rape crops, epidemics occur when there is particularly wet weather just before and during crop establishment (autumn in western Europe). Until 1995 in the UK, few crops were sprayed in the autumn against stem canker (Gladders et al., 1997). Experiments applying fungicides at different times in the season have suggested that at least 2 sprays (autumn and spring) are necessary to obtain adequate control of severe stem canker epidemics. In the autumn, sprays may be needed against the leaf spot phase of stem canker to prevent the spread of the pathogen from the leaves into the stems (Hammond and Lewis, 1986). management_info: Introduction^p^pDiseases caused by V. dahliae can be controlled through the use of disease-resistant cultivars when they are available. For effective management, an integrated approach is necessary. This usually involves a combination of cultural practices which minimize disease, such as crop rotation and manipulation of fertility and irrigation, planting pathogen-free seeds or stock, use of available resistant cultivars and sometimes pre-plant soil treatments such as soil fumigation or solarization that reduce the viability of microsclerotia in soil (El-Zik, 1985; Shen, 1985; Bell, 1992; Powelson and Rowe, 1993; Jeger et al., 1996).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pResistant or tolerant cultivars have been useful in controlling Verticillium wilt in many crops worldwide. Tomato cultivars containing the Ve resistance gene (Diwan et al., 1999) are widely employed to combat Verticillium wilt, although strains of the pathogen capable of overcoming this resistance (Race 2 strains) have appeared in North America (Dobinson et al., 1996), Australia (O'Brien and Hutton, 1981), Japan (Nagao et al., 1997), South Africa (Ferreira et al., 1990) and several European countries (Tjamos, 1980; Montorsi, 1986; Ligoxigakis and Vakalounakis, 1992). The development of resistant cultivars has been the mainstay of wilt control in cotton, particularly where cotton defoliating strains have become established. The usefulness of some resistant types has been curtailed by the evolution of strains able to overcome their resistance (Bell, 1992; Melero-Vera et al., 1995; Ma and Shezeng, 2000). In potato, truly resistant commercial cultivars are not yet available, but considerable work is underway to identify disease-resistant germplasm (Powelson and Rowe, 1993; Pavek et al., 1994; Corsini et al., 1996). Host resistance is also an important wilt management factor in strawberry (Shaw et al., 1996), horseradish (Atibalentja et al., 1998), hop (Romanko et al., 1996), aubergine (Cirulli et al., 2000) and sunflower (Sackston et al., 1992). The application of genetic engineering techniques may increase this potential greatly (McFadden, 2000), particularly approaches aimed at activating natural defence mechanisms (Li et al., 1996). Resistance to V. dahliae in transgenic potatoes has recently been achieved by transfer of an antifungal defensin peptide from lucerne (Gao et al., 2000).^p^pGrafting wilt-susceptible cultivars to resistant tomato rootstocks has been used to manage Verticillium in tomato (Granges et al., 1996) and aubergine (Ginoux and Dauple, 1982). Grafting to Verticillium-resistant rootstocks is also used in woody plants such as pistachio (Morgan et al., 1992).^p^p^Cropping Systems^p^pAlthough there are many reports of the value of crop rotation in controlling wilt diseases, there is considerable disagreement as to its overall effectiveness. Rotation with paddy rice has proven particularly effective in eliminating V. dahliae from soil as a result of flooding (Pullman and DeVay, 1981) and reducing wilt in subsequent cotton crops. Cotton wilt has been reduced by rotations with cereals, legumes and crucifers (Egamov, 1976; Mannapova, 1976; Butterfield et al., 1978) and with lucerne (Sezgin et al., 1982). However, there are reports that rotation systems have not been effective in providing control (Huisman and Ashworth, 1976). Studies of the effects of various rotations on potato early dying also have shown variable results (Busch et al., 1978; Joaquim et al., 1988; Easton et al., 1992; Powelson and Rowe, 1993; Chen et al., 1995). The inclusion in the rotation of crops intended to be ploughed down, so called green manures, has shown some effectiveness in Verticillium management (Lazarovits et al., 2000), particularly with sudan grass in potato (Davis et al, 1996) and broccoli and other crucifers in several crops (Subbarao et al., 1999). 细菌性溃疡病是猕猴桃的毁灭性病害，其发生具有适生范围广、发生迅猛、致病性强、根除难度大等特点，可在短期内造成大面积树体死亡，已被列为我国森林植物检疫性病害．是目前猕猴桃生产中面临的重大问题。  该病害在报道的国家都曾造成了严重的产量和经济损失，比如上世纪80年代在日本静冈市初次发生时，35％的种植面积受到侵染，造成许多果园毁园[3]。我国首先于1985年在湖南东山峰农场发现此病．发病面积为13 hm2，当年造成猕猴桃植株成片死亡，此后该病连年流行，致使133 hm2人工栽培猕猴桃基地濒临毁灭[11]。1989年，四川三溪口林场发生此病，当年被害面积达5.93 hm2．数月内园中6000多株结果树全部病死，产量由1988年的15万kg猛跌到5万kg[12]。
    近年来，随着猕猴桃栽培面积的不断增加，溃疡病快速蔓延，自2005以来已在世界主要猕猴桃栽培地造成严重危害，已成为猕猴桃栽培过程中最具毁灭性的病害，严重威胁世界猕猴桃的安全生产。据报道．2006～2009年间在韩国济州岛的H0n16A品种上溃疡病发生大流行．从2006年发病率低于1％，到2009年调查的11个果园中4个果园发病率100％[13]。同样的情况亦发生在世界第二大猕猴桃生产国意大利。2008—2009年的调查结果显示．在意大利中部及北部的猕猴桃主栽区的2～8年生的品种Hortl6A．和金桃上，溃疡病的发病率为50％一80％，该病害造成的经济损失约200万欧元[14]。在我国该病害已经在安徽、四川、湖南、福建以及陕西等省的猕猴桃栽培区域发生，并造成了严重的经济损失。陕西
省作为猕猴桃人工栽种起步早、发展最快、规模最大的省份，在1992—2002年的10年间．溃疡病的发病面积从0.13 hm2扩大到311.5 hm2．平均发病株率从3.6％迅速增加到20％以上[15]。本研究小组2009年春季调查发现．该病害在陕西省普遍严重发生，病株率普遍达到30％以上，严重果园达到80％以上，而且所有品种、砧木。不同树龄、地域的果园均受感染，很多果园因死树率太高而导致农民砍树毁园．损失惨重。

remark: The different sources of inoculum and spread of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora cited, such as infected seed, movement of infected debris by agricultural equipment, and factors dependent on climate, constitute a great epidemiological risk of introducing the disease to new areas or increasing its severity in established soyabean-growing areas (Backman et al., 1985). Studies by Lee and Subbarao (1993) showed that D. phaseolorum var. caulivora isolates from different regions of USA colonized and produced perithecia on non-host species, indicating that these plants could constitute inoculum sources in the field. An additional problem is that the fungus has been isolated from asymptomatic mature plants (susceptible and resistant cultivars) infected later during the growing season. Debris derived from these plants can support the development of perithecia and, therefore, increase the level of disease (Backman et al., 1985).^p^pMoreover, pathogenicity trials conducted in Argentina confirm that some cultivars selected for their resistance to var. meridionalis are susceptible to var. caulivora. This fact, together with recent reports confirming the coexistence of var. caulivora and var. meridionalis in the core soyabean-producing area of Argentina, increases the phytosanitary risk to commercial cultivars in the field Pioli et al., 1997a, 2001, 2003).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pCrop rotation, deep ploughing and seed disinfection are recommended for control of stem canker in the Caucasus region, Russia (Skripka and Podkina, 1990). ^p^pThe extent to which a soyabean-maize rotation is able to limit the build-up of host-specific pathogens of soyabean and the involvement of plant diseases in the rotation effect was investigated. The incidence and severity of seven diseases and seed yield were recorded at two field locations in Minnesota, USA, in 1987 and 1988. Stem canker, caused by D. phaseolorum var. caulivora, was noted in 1987 at both locations in less than 5% of all plants monitored. It was concluded that, within the conditions of the study, the yield benefit to soyabean from rotation with maize did not appear to be due to the reduced incidence of plant diseases (Whiting and Crookston, 1993).^p^pIn the Korea Republic, the effect of field sanitation was investigated for controlling Phomopsis seed decay in soyabean. Field sanitation included removing host debris, petioles and cotyledons from the field. It markedly reduced infection of pods and seeds by Phomopsis sp. However, seed infection was 28.7% in the sanitised field. This control strategy was effective in controlling Phomopsis seed decay when infection pressure was low. D. phaseolorum var. sojae, D. phaseolorum var. caulivora and Phomopsis longicolla were mostly identified from soyabean seeds; Colletotrichum truncatum and Cercospora kikuchiana were also isolated. Field sanitation did not significantly increase soyabean yield but a routine application schedule did (Oh JeungHaing, 1998).^p^p^Host-Plant ResistanceHildebrand (1952) reported pathogenic specialization among D. phaseolorum var. caulivora isolates on seedlings of different soyabean cultivars from Ontario.^p^pIn northern USA, soyabean stem canker has essentially been under control since highly susceptible cultivars were withdrawn in the late 1950s (Athow, 1987). A limited amount of screening for resistance has been done since then, but resistance is not generally considered to be at a high level (Tisselli et al., 1980). Two isolates of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora, one from Ohio and other from Indiana (northern USA) were non-pathogenic to the soyabean line J77-339, whereas isolates from Tennessee and Mississippi (southern USA) were severely pathogenic to this line (Keeling, 1985; 1988a). Moreover, the cultivars Blackhawk, Harosoy, L4404, Nathan, Tracy-M and Williams were all susceptible to one isolate from Iowa, and resistant to two isolates from Mississippi; whereas J77-339, Clark and Pike were susceptible to all three isolates. It was proposed that the Iowa isolate be designated race 1 and the Mississippi isolate race 2 (Higley and Tachibana, 1987). Similar results were reported for the behaviour of Blackhawk, Hawkeye, and Tracy-M, cited as susceptible to northern isolates of D. phaseolorum var. caulivora, but were highly resistant to the southern isolates (Backman et al., 1985; Keeling 1985, 1988a, b).^p^pMonoascosporic isolates from Maryland, north-eastern USA, exhibited dimorphism associated with their degree of pathogenicity to soyabean seedlings. Isolates that were fast growing on APDA were largely non-pathogenic to seedlings of the soyabean cultivars Blackhawk and Zane, whereas slow-growing isolates were largely pathogenic. In contrast, Alabama and Florida (south-eastern USA) isolates did not exhibit a sharply defined separation into two groups on the basis of their culture morphology. A clear association of pathogenicity with colony diameter, as seen in the Maryland isolates, was not evident in the Alabama isolates. Inoculation of Blackhawk seedlings with Alabama isolates failed to produce cankers, whereas inoculation of seedlings of the same cultivar with the Maryland isolates produced many cankers (Kulik, 1989).^p^pSeedlings of soyabean varieties Mandarin, Harosoy, Tracy-M and the line J 77-339 were inoculated with five isolates
