management_info: Cultural Control^p^pThe diseases caused by the Diaporthe/Phomopsis complex can be partially controlled by cultural practices such as clean tillage and crop rotation with non-host crops. Knowledge of the inoculum sources is basic for these control strategies (Athow, 1987).^p^pIn Brazil, the incidence of D. phaseolorum var. sojae on seeds increased with delayed harvesting (Dhingra et al., 1979a). Heavy rainfalls during August in central Illinois, USA, favoured an epidemic of soyabean pod and stem blight. Even under these severe weather conditions, the quality of seeds harvested from the upper portions of soyabean plants was not reduced. Selective harvest would therefore be feasible and may avoid seed quality losses (Hepperly and Sinclair, 1980a).^p^pDelayed planting decreased infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae and increased germination rates. Late season cultivars showed less infection and greater germination of seeds than early season cultivars. As plant density increased, infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae increased and germination decreased. Seeds treated with benomyl germinated better at 15°C than at 25°C. An increased level of N induced greater infection by D. phaseolorum var. sojae and lower germination. A delay in harvest caused a reduction of seed germination and increased the occurrence of abnormal germination and seed decay. This trend was more conspicuous in seeds from soyabean plants that had not been treated with benomyl than in those that had been sprayed with the fungicide (Chin et al., 1993a). Infection of seed by D. phaseolorum var. sojae, Glomerella glycines and Fusarium spp. was lowest, and germination percentages highest, on late-maturing cultivars that were harvested early (Alexander and Hinson, 1973). However, the physiological quality and health of seeds were decreased in Goias, Brazil, by early sowing due to adverse moisture conditions, mechanical damage at harvesting and fungal infection, mainly by D. phaseolorum var. sojae (Pereira et al., 2000).^p^pField sanitation, including the removal of host debris, fallen petioles and cotyledons from the field, reduced the infection of pods and seeds by Phomopsis spp.; however, seed infection was 28.7% in the sanitized field. Fields sanitized by the application of benomyl around the soyabean plant decreased seed infection by Phomopsis spp. Total seed infection caused by various pathogens was 75-79% without benomyl application compared to 34-42% with a routine fungicide application schedule. Field sanitation was effective in controlling Phomopsis seed decay when infection pressure was low. However, it did not significantly increase the yield of soyabean, whereas a routine fungicide application schedule did (Oh Jeung Haing, 1998).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pIn the USA, seed treatment with thiram and carboxin + thiram against D. phaseolorum var. sojae and Fusarium spp. generally improved germination and field emergence but did not increase yields in the field. Benomyl + thiram was most effective in increasing laboratory germination and field emergence of soyabean. In the field, yields from seed treated with the latter combination were 11% higher than those from untreated seeds or seeds treated with thiram or thiram + carboxin (Nedrow and Harman, 1980). Metham-sodium fumigation and benomyl sprays effectively controlled the major pathogens, reducing sporulation of D. phaseolorum var. sojae on pods and stems, vascular discoloration in roots and stems and rate of leaf loss, and increasing seed quality. Neither treatment alone increased yield consistently, but together they produced a large increase in yield, averaging 26% (Kittle and Gray, 1982). ^p^pIn Brazil, the effect of foliar fungicide applications on the control of seedborne disease was evaluated in field trials against D. phaseolorum var. sojae on soyabean. Benomyl, thiophanate-methyl, chlorothalonil, thiabendazole and captafol all reduced incidence of the pathogen on the seed coat and embryo tissue a

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pA survey of 25 locations of Mississippi, USA, showed that the disease was more severe under no-till than under other tillage practices (Roy and McLean, 1984). In Georgia, USA, the disease was more severe in no-till than in conventional tillage plots for moderately resistant and highly susceptible cultivars. However, yield reduction under no-till only occurred in a highly susceptible cultivar in a year in which disease pressure was severe. Although the incidence and severity of the disease were reduced by burying crop debris with conventional tillage, this can only be considered as one part of the control strategy, which should also include crop rotation and the planting of resistant cultivars Rothrock et al., 1985, 1988). In Mississippi, under conditions of natural infection, the disease was more severe in soil with a high organic matter, pH and soil moisture, and low potassium fertility (Rhoton, 1989). Harville et al. (1986) reported that, in Louisiana, the correlation between yield and disease rating was lower in early maturing than in later maturing cultivars. Another study indicated that disease severity was primarily dependent on plant growth stage at the time of exposure to inoculum and was relatively independent of planting date (Smith and Backman, 1989). Backman et al. (1985) and Omer et al. (1989) reported that, in Alabama, yield and seedling vigour of most susceptible cultivars were higher at delayed sowing dates and similar results were obtained in Tucuman, north-west Argentina, where highly susceptible and short cycle cultivars showed highest yields with late sowing dates due to the shorter duration of exposure to the disease (Ploper et al., 1999b).^p^pIn Brazil, no-tillage and crop rotation are necessary strategies in regions with low levels of nutrients and low organic matter. However, susceptible cultivars grown under no-tillage systems in fields with a history of the disease constitute a high risk. In areas where resistant seeds are limited, rotation with maize or other crops could be adopted. However, this alternative requires additional infrastructure related to storage and commercial processes (Yorinori, 1996). Cultural practices that can be used to decrease the incidence and severity of soyabean diseases are: crop rotation, sowing date, appropriate row spacing and plant population, weed control, improvement of soil fertility, use of resistant or tolerant varieties, use of fungicides, selection of high quality disease-free seeds, and use of disinfected (treated) seeds (Yorinori, 1996; Vallone and Kokubun, 1998).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pThe use of genetic resistance is the best strategy for controlling soyabean stem canker. Early in an epidemic in the southern USA, cultivars were screened for susceptibility and classified as resistant, moderately resistant, moderately susceptible and susceptible (Weaver et al., 1984; Berggren et al., 1985; Keeling, 1985). There is variability in the reaction of cultivars to the pathogen in different south-eastern states of the USA, and also within areas of a particular state, possibly due to variability in the pathogen (Moore, 1984;Keeling, 1982, 1985). Backman et al. (1981) reported a complete range of cultivar reactions for southern isolates collected in Alabama, USA, from no disease on cv. Tracy-M to severe infection on cvs. Hutton and RA 800; most cultivars showed an intermediate reaction. Tracy-M and Braxton cultivars were reported as immune when evaluated over 2 years in fields naturally infested by D. phaseolorum (Weaver et al., 1984). These results were later confirmed by using 60 cultivars of different maturity groups (Backman et al., 1985). Cultivars Tracy-M and CNS were included as resistant controls in screening tests, and their inclusion in breeding programmes for stem canker resistance was suggested (Keeling, 1985). host_range: P. adamsoni feeds on a number of Eucalyptus species. It is also known to attack Pinus radiata (Monterey pine), which is widely planted in southern parts of Australia. It infests stumps, decayed logs and living trees.Affected Plant Stages: Vegetativ
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pP. adamsoni is considered to be an important pest of forests in New South Wales, Tazmania and Victoria, Australia (Harris, 1971; Elliot and Bashford, 1984). This termite feeds on the heartwood of living trees and can cause severe damage to them. Infestations are initiated through injured roots or stems. They develop slowly but can eventually result in the degradation or destruction of approximately 50% of the tree volume in a stand (Browne, 1968). In a study in Tasmania, this insect damaged 60% and 43% of the trees in two areas. All species of Eucalyptus occurring in the two sites were attacked; Eucalyptus sieberi, Eucalyptus obliqua, Eucalyptus amygdalina, Eucalyptus viminalis, Eucalyptus globulus and Eucalyptus tenuiramis. There was no detectable difference between the species in the proportion of trees attacked. The incidence of damage increased with increasing tree diameter. Ninety percent of the trees with a stump diameter of over 105 cm were affected. Defects in the logs, mainly 'pipes' with concentric galleries, sometimes associated with decay, resulted in the downgrading of trees from sawlogs to pulpwood or waste (Elliot and Bashford, 1984).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pBecause P. adamsoni colonies feed in the heartwood of host trees, the infested trees lose structural integrity and are more prone to breakage. Wind-thrown host trees could alter the species composition and accelerate plant succession. Alternatively, this species is instrumental in the decomposition of wood. Moreover, the hollows they sculpt in the trees can serve as homes for birds and mammals.

remark: Termites typically spread slowly (approximately 20 to 350 m per year) because they are poor flyers and only approximately 1% of those that fly are likely to establish a new colony (Williams and La Fage, 1979). Humans may physically move the infested wood. However, because of their moisture requirements, the probability of dampwood termites of the genus Porotermes surviving an ocean voyage in logs or other wood products is low.
author: CPC2006

management_info: The prevention and control of dampwood termites consists of the same measures taken against subterranean termites and dry rot. For example, wooden constructions should be designed to avoid contact with the soil, excessive moisture conditions should be eliminated and an effective insecticide should be used in soil treatments. ^p^pThe removal and destruction of infested wood has been used to eradicate introduced populations in New Zealand (Ross, 1999). ^p^pWood in-use can be protected from infestation by dampwood termites through the periodic inspection and elimination of sources of moisture that could make the wood attractive to these insects. This could involve channelling water drainage away from wooden structures and the appropriate placement of irrigation sprinklers. ^p^pGeneral control measures for termites in wood in-use are available, but they are expensive. Termite colonies in logs destined for export, can be destroyed by rapid processing and kiln-drying. Guidelines prepared by the International Plant Pest Convention (IPPC) recommend that wood and wood products destined for export should be heated to a minimum internal wood core temperature of 56°C for 30 minutes. Kiln-drying, chemical pressure impregnation or other treatments may be used as a means of achieving heat treatment, provided that the above temperature and time requirements are met (IPPC, 2002).

potential_eco_desc: Pre- and post-harvest losses of many high-value crops are substantial in the tropics because of various diseases caused by C. gloeosporioides. ^p^pFlower infection on mangoes (blossom blight) can destroy flowers and young fruit and cause complete crop failure. Fruit infection may cause premature fruit drop, but major fruit losses occur during ripening when quiescent infections break out and cause spreading black lesions. Anthracnose of other fruits also causes major post-harvest losses. Heavy infections cause rapid rotting, and even light infections which cause mainly cosmetic damage will shorten fruit storage life. Because of variability between seasons and locations, overall figures for losses are difficult to give, but it is clear that in many mango-growing areas, unless expensive chemical control applications are not used, losses of up to 50% of the crop to the various stages of the disease would not be uncommon.^p^pOf the foliage diseases caused by C. gloeosporioides, yam anthracnose can be one of the most economically damaging and may prevent significant growth of tubers if the disease strikes early. Reductions of 10% of latex flows have been reported from rubber affected by secondary leaf fall. Major reductions in fodder and consequential effects on cattle growth and productivity result from Stylosanthes anthracnose.

description: Incidence^p^pG. cingulata has been detected on seeds of several plants species including kenaf (More and Moniz, 1969), Dalbergia sissoo (Hiremath and Hiremath, 1991), guava (Pandey and Dwivedi, 1987), chilli (Basak et al., 1994), Stylosanthes hamata (Davis, 1987), pepper (Juangbhanich and Chana, 1975), Bixa orellana (Peregrine, 1970) and Lupinus angustifolius (Wilson, 1947). Incidences of infection by G. cingulata were 1.5 and 18% in two seed lots of Stylosanthes hamata, respectively (Davis, 1987). ^p^p^Effect on Seed Quality^p^pThe majority of seeds in infected pods of S. hamata failed to germinate on moist blotters in laboratory tests (Davis, 1987). ^p^p^Pathogen Transmission^p^pSome symptoms of anthracnose were found on seedlings grown on moist blotters from seeds taken from infected pods of S. hamata (Davis, 1987). In August 1994, severe anthracnose was found on Lupinus albus in plots at four sites in Western Australia. G. cingulata was isolated from lesions on collapsed stems. The primary infection was traced to seed lines of L. albus imported from Germany. In September 1994, procedures to eradicate the disease were introduced (Sweetingham et al., 1995).^p^p^Seed Treatment^p^pThe application of benomyl dust at 500 g/kg eliminated G. cingulata on S. hamata seeds (Davis, 1987). Treatment of pepper seeds with methoxyethyl-mercury chloride at 0.16% or Delsine methyl 2-benzimidazole carbamate at 0.8% of seed weight gave complete control of the disease on Colletotrichum piperatum [G. cingulata] and C. capsici (Juangbhanich and Chana, 1975).^p^p^Seed Health Testing^p^pCulture plate (Davis, 1987)^p^p1. Surface sterilize seeds of S. hamata with 0.1% mercuric chloride and rinse three times in sterile water.^p2. Dry seeds on a sterile blotter in a laminar flow hood.^p3. Plate seeds on oatmeal agar and incubate for 10 days.

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe applicability of control strategies depends as much on the characteristics of the crop on which they are being used as on the diseases at which they are aimed. For perennial cash crops, the long-term investment involved and the value of the produce increases the need for adequate disease control Waller, 1988, 1992).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pThe ubiquity of inoculum sources of C. gloeosporioides and its often rapid epidemic development under suitable conditions reduce the effectiveness of many general phytosanitary practices. Although general orchard hygiene has a place in integrated disease control, examples of good field control of Colletotrichum diseases effected solely by measures aimed at reducing inoculum sources are hard to find. Greater knowledge of the specificity of strains of the pathogen may enable effective phytosanitary practices to be developed. Options for integrated control of the disease on mango have been discussed by Arauz (2000).^p^pThe necessity for wet conditions to coincide with susceptible crop stages for development of Colletotrichum epidemics should offer an opportunity for disease control through manipulation of cropping patterns. Chemical methods can also be used to change growth patterns: application of potassium nitrate sprays can stimulate mango flowering; defoliants have been used to modify the wintering pattern of rubber and avoid secondary leaf fall (Rao, 1972). Application of calcium salts can enhance resistance to bitter rot in apples (Biggs, 1999). Cultural practices such as spacing and pruning can reduce the suitability of environmental conditions for Colletotrichum disease development by assisting more rapid drying of the tree canopy, as well as allowing better penetration of fungicide sprays. The worst effects of Colletotrichum diseases may also be avoided if susceptible crops are grown in drier environments.^p^pBecause C. gloeosporioides is an opportunistic pathogen, the avoidance of predisposing conditions such as mechanical or physiological damage is particularly significant. Control of other pests and diseases, and avoidance of harvesting damage to fruit, all help to offset secondary infections.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBiological control methods for Colletotrichum diseases are now receiving increasing attention, although the potential of biological control through the effect of phyllosphere antagonists has been realised for some time (Lenne and Parbery, 1976). Jeger and Jeffries (1988) have recently discussed the possibilities of biological control of post-harvest fruit diseases. However, there is still much to achieve before practical methods for field use can be established; given the epidemiological versatility of Colletotrichum diseases on perennial crops, biological control will need to be integrated with other control techniques for maximum effect.^p^pInitial experiments with an antagonistic strain of Pseudomonas fluorescens against anthracnose on mango have been encouraging, and control was achieved in unfavourable conditions for the biocontrol agents (Jeffries and Koomen, 1992). While the post-harvest situation offers the greatest potential for success, there are still advantages in considering a pre-harvest approach to the biological control of anthracnose disease. For example, pre-harvest agents can interact directly with the spore or germination hypha rather than with an established appressorium. Modifications to the surface microflora through cultural manipulation of plants in the field may also help to control these pathogens on plant shoots. In some countries, notably the USA, there are now considerable problems in finding suitable effective chemicals that are still permitted for agricultural use, and alternatives are urgently required (Jeffries and Koomen, 1992).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pGenerally, Colletotrichum diseases can be controlled by a wide range of chemicals such as copper compounds, dithiocarbamates, and benzamidazole and triazole

potential_eco_desc: Economic impactHolm et al. (1979) list C. europaea as a 'serious' weed in Afghanistan and Poland, and a 'principal' weed in Czechoslovakia and the former USSR. It is rarely a major weed over large areas, perhaps because of the lack of attack on Gramineae [Poaceae], and the cleaning effect of cereal crops in rotation. But once contact is established with the host phloem, Cuscuta becomes a powerful sink for metabolites, causing a severe drain on host resources and often completely preventing normal fruit development, as shown by Wolswinkel (1979) for C. europaea on faba bean (Vicia faba). Owing to this powerful metabolic sink effect, studied and described in detail by Wolswinkel and Ammerlaan (1983), the damage to infected hosts can be severe, to the extent of total crop loss. Less dry matter and ash were found in the leaves of parasitized Urtica dioica and Aegopodium podagraria than in those of healthy plants. Leaves of parasitized U. dioica plants contained 8.5% less chlorophyll than uninfested ones (Gal'vidis, 1993). Perhaps the crop most seriously affected is sugarbeet in Italy, the former Yugoslavia and eastern Europe. There is also further economic loss when crop produce, such as clover or lucerne seed, intended for export, is rejected or has to be expensively cleaned.^p^pThere are occasional reports of toxicity to livestock from Cuscuta species, including toxicity to horses from C. europaea  (Pergat and Stolyarova, 1961).^p^p^Environmental impact^pC. europaea is not known to have caused any significant environmental impact.^p^p^p^Social impact^pC. europaea is not known to have caused any significant social impact.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pC. europaea is not known to have caused any significant impact on biodiversity.^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>crop production; trade / international relations

(1997) indicate that 25 countries have declared Cuscuta spp. as noxious, and that the movement of Cuscuta-infested material is prohibited in every state of the USA.^p^pDry heat at 100°C for 15 minutes has been shown to selectively kill seeds of Cuscuta spp. in nigerseed (Guizotia abyssinica) (Strasser, 1988) providing a means of de-contaminating contaminated imports, but it is not certain that this is being used in practice.

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pUse of clean crop seed is vital. Seed crops which might have been infested should be inspected and cleaned if necessary, or seed should be obtained from a source known to be reliable. Separation of Cuscuta seeds from lucerne is quite successfully achieved by equipment comprising felt- or velvet-covered rollers to which the rough seeds of Cuscuta stick while the smoother crop seeds pass over (see Dawson et al., 1994).^p^pRotation with non-susceptible crops can be helpful. Cereals are virtually immune, but some broad-leaved crops may also be sufficiently resistant, including soyabean, kidney bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), squash (Cucurbita sp.), cucumber and cotton (see Parker and Riches, 1993).^p^pDeep shade suppresses the coiling and attachment of Cuscuta; hence encouraging a dense crop canopy is a valuable component of any integrated control programme.^p^p^Mechanical Control^p^pThe young seedlings of Cuscuta, with rudimentary roots, are readily destroyed by shallow tillage before or after crop establishment. Hand-pulling is suitable only for scattered infestations as the infested crop plants have to be removed with the parasite. Scattered infestations of C. campestris have also been controlled by heat, using a hand-held flame gun. More extensive infestations of that species in lucerne are also sometimes treated with overall flaming, as the crop is able to recover. Close mowing is an alternative means of control in lucerne and clovers. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThere is relatively little information on the use of herbicides against C. europaea but good results have been reported for ethofumesate in sugar beet; propyzamide in sugar beet and onions; and a mixture of chlorthal-dimethyl with chlorpropham in onions and carrots (Foschi and Rapparini, 1977; Rapparini and Campagna, 1998). Other herbicides of value in the control of other Cuscuta species, especially C. campestris, include metham-sodium and dazomet as pre-planting fumigants, trifluralin and related compounds, pendimethalin, fluchloralin, butralin etc, in lucerne and some other legumes. These might be expected to be equally effective against C. europaea.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBiological control of C. europaea has been attempted in Kazakhstan, by augmentative release of Melanagromyza cuscutae but the outcome is not certain (Julien and Griffiths, 1998). This insect has also failed to give convincing results on other Cuscuta spp. The biology and host range of M. cuscutae were studied by Baloch et al. (1967) and reviewed by Spencer (1973). ^p^pOther attempts at biological control of Cuscuta spp. by insects have mainly involved the gall-forming weevils Smicronyx spp.; S. tartaricus has given encouraging results for control of C. europaea in Kazakhstan when introduced from one region to another (Shinkarenko, 1982b), while among pathogens, Alternaria cuscutacidae and a form of Colletotrichum gloeosporioides [Glomerella cingulata] have given helpful results against C. chinensis and C. australis (Parker and Riches, 1993; Julien and Griffiths, 1998). ^p^pProspects for biological control of C. europaea and other Cuscuta spp. have been reviewed by Girling et al. (1979).^p^p^Integrated Control^p^pIntegrated methods for control of Cuscuta species generally involve the all-important use of clean seed; good field hygiene to eradicate scattered infestations before they get out of control; good control of other weeds which might act as reservoirs of infestation; timing of tillage and planting to maximize destruction of parasite seedlings before sowing; and optimum planting arrangement and growing conditions for a good crop canopy to suppress development of the weed.

host_range: This is the first confirmed report of a member of the FIESC on Cucurbita pepo in Jamaica. Recent reports describe FIESC infecting cucurbits in Asia, such as Cucumis trigonus in India and muskmelon in China.
potential_eco_desc: Symptoms have been observed on about 60% of farms in the major production areas.
description: Since 2012, chlorotic or necrotic leaf spot symptoms have been observed on about 60% of farms in the major production areas (Clarendon, Portland, St. Ann, St. Catherine, St. Elizabeth and St. Mary). To determine the causal agent, total genomic DNA was extracted and ITS1/ITS4 primers were used in PCR amplification and sequencing of the rDNA internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region. The resulting sequences of two representative isolates were identical to Fusarium incarnatum-equiseti species complex (FIESC) sequences present in the FUSARIUM-ID database. To our knowledge, this is the first confirmed report of a member of the FIESC on C. pepo in Jamaica.
reference_name: First report of leaf spot on Cucurbita pepo caused by Fusarium incarnatum-equiseti species complex in Jamaica

description: During June and September of 2018, bacterial necrosis and root rot disease surveys were conducted in sugar beet (Beta vulgaris) fields in Yozgat province in the Central Anatolia region of Turkey. From 33 fields surveyed, 19 sugar beet plants exhibiting vascular necrosis with blackened petioles, root rotting varying from wet to dry and wilting symptoms were collected for bacterial isolation. The bacterium was identified as Pectobacterium betavasculorum by sequence analysis and BLAST analysis. This is the first report of P. betavasculorum causing bacterial vascular necrosis and root rot disease on sugar beet in Turkey.

host_range: Xanthomonas citri pv. citri Pathotype A has the widest host range comprising most citrus cultivars and citrus relatives.
description: Asiatic citrus canker (ACC) has been considered endemic in Réunion Island since the 1970s, but was likely present earlier and was not subjected to any eradication attempt. Most citrus growers on the island frequently apply copper-based pesticides as part of integrated pest management programs. A recurring lack of ACC control in several citrus groves was investigated in 2014 using our lab collection of authenticated Xanthomonas citri pv. citri strains. The test strain was identified as copper-resistant strains (CRS)  X. citri pv. citri Pathotype A by phenotypic tests and PCR assays. CRS were widespread in most citrus production areas of the island where they coexisted with copper-susceptible strains (CSS). The oldest CRS dated from 2010. Because no extreme hurricane hit the island between 2010 and 2014, the fast spread of CRS over the island was very likely related to their presence in a major citrus nursery, as confirmed by our data. This is the first report of copper-resistant X. citri pv. citri Pathotype A causing Asiatic citrus canker in Réunion, France.
reference_name: First Report of Copper-resistant Xanthomonas citri pv. citri Pathotype A Causing Asiatic Citrus Canker in Réunion, France

The pathogen was identified as Xanthomonas citri pv. citri pathotype A strains.
potential_eco_desc: Asiatic canker, caused by Xanthomonas citri pv. citri, is a major threat to worldwide citriculture. X. citri pv. citri pathotype A infects a broader range including most commercial citrus species and hybrids and can cause important economic losses in tropical and subtropical areas.
description: Martinique (France) is an outermost region of the EU in the eastern Caribbean Sea. Canker lesions were first observed at Morne Rouge, Martinique in June 2014 on grapefruit (Citrus paradisi), mandarin (C. reticulata), Tahiti lime (C. latifolia), and Valencia and Washington Navel oranges (C. sinensis). Official diagnostics, including bacterial isolations on YPGA or KC semiselective medium, PCR-based identification with 4/7 primers, and pathogenicity tests, were performed following the EPPO standard PM7/44 and identified isolates as Xanthomonas citri pv. citri. Using MLVA-31 targeting 31 minisatellites, Martinique strains were assigned to lineage 1 composed of pathotype A strains. This is the first report of X. citri pv. citri in Martinique and to our knowledge in the Caribbean region.
remark: Xanthomonas citri pv. citri is listed as a quarantine pathogen in the European Union (EU) – Directive 2000/29/EC annex II A1.

potential_eco_desc: L. japonica attacks all citrus severely, multiplying rapidly to cover the trunk, branches and young shoots with dense colonies. Individual trees are killed by heavy infestations, while neighbouring trees may be virtually unaffected. In Azerbaijan and Georgia, L. japonica has caused serious problems, especially on satsumas (Citrus unshiu), mandarins, lemons (C. limon) and the citrus rootstock Poncirus trifoliata; also on other fruit crops and ornamentals (Konstantinova, 1992; Yasnosh, 1994; Tabatadze et al., 1997). When it was recently introduced, it also caused problems on Laurus nobilis in southern Russia (Konstantinova, 1992). In Georgia, tea is also attacked (Yasnosh and Tabatadze, 1997).Danzig and Pellizzari (1998) describe L. japonica as a dangerous pest. In the USSR, it was recorded damaging citrus, Japanese persimmon, pears and other plants (Danzig, 1980). Miller (1985) records that L. japonica is able to kill the branches of maples in the USA (Maryland).

remark: The cryptic habit and appearance of L. japonica makes it difficult to detect on fruit tree planting material at quarantine inspection. Before the break-up of the USSR, L. japonica was subject to internal quarantine constraints within the USSR (Danzig, 1980; Konstantinova and Gura, 1986) and is still in the quarantine regulations of Ukraine and Belarus. Lemon production in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan remain at risk, and in the EPPO region L. japonica could attack citrus and other fruit crops throughout the Mediterranean basin, from the Middle East to Spain (Balachowsky, 1953). It also presents a threat to woody plants grown under glass throughout Europe. L. japonica is a quarantine pest for Europe (Pellizzari and Vettorazzo, 1999).^p^pIt should be noted, however, that the introduction of L. japonica to various countries has not been followed by any rapid spread or very significant damage. Generally there is little information in the literature about this pest, which usually indicates that it is of relatively minor importance.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Introduction^p^pIn Georgia, the economic threshold of L. japonica on citrus is 20-25 scales per cm on trunks or branches (Yasnosh and Tabatadze, 1997). An express method of counting arthropods (including L. japonica) on citrus is given by Orlinskii (1990) (in Russian).^p^p^Cultural ControlKonstantinova (1992) gives a range of cultural measures available for the control of L. japonica.^p^p^Integrated Pest Management^p^pIn Georgia, integrated pest management was used to control L. japonica on citrus (Tabatadze et al., 1997). Natural enemies were of great value in controlling the pest, reducing the population by 50%. If required, spraying with mineral oil (1% in summer, 2% at other times of year) or 0.5-1% buprofezin to first- or second-instar larvae gave an effective level of control. Yasnosh (1986) reported on a five-year trial in Georgia, using three mineral oil and fungicide sprays, and augmentative release of Cryptolaemus and Lindorus if pest populations exceeded the economic threshold. This maintained L. japonica populations below the economic threshold on all but one occasion, when a corrective spray of organophosphate insecticide was required.^p^p^Chemical ControlKonstantinova (1992) gives a range of chemical measures available for the control of L. japonica. Chemical control of L. japonica in the USSR using organo-phosphorous pesticides was discussed by Alan and Katsitadze (1974). Where natural enemies failed to give satisfactory control on integrated pest management schemes on citrus in Georgia, spraying with mineral oil (1% in summer, 2% at other times of year) or 0.5-1% buprofezin to first- or second-instar larvae gave effective control (Tabatadze et al., 1997). Zheng et al. (1993) gave a method of predicting the optimum control date for control measures against the first generation each year, based on average maximum January temperature, average temperature in the last 10 days of April, and the temperature/RH coefficient in April in China. In the period 1982-1991, this method had a 90% success rate and the forecast could be given at the beginning of May, allowing 20-30 days of preparation of control measures.^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pWoody plant material (both rooted plants and budwood material) from countries where L. japonica is established should be carefully inspected. They should also be fumigated before export.

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pGood store hygiene plays an important role in limiting infestation by Z. subfasciatus. The removal of infested residues from last season's harvest is essential, as is general hygiene. When small amounts of beans are stored, sunning periodically in a thin layer for periods up to 4 hours can give substantial protection.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pZ. subfasciatus may be controlled by fumigation treatment with methyl bromide or phosphine. Admixture of approved grain insecticides, especially organophosphates, protects against Z. subfasciatus. When grain pulses are stored on the farm, admixture of vegetable oil is known to give good protection against Callosobruchus spp. and would be expected to be effective against Z. subfasciatus (Don-Pedro, 1989).

description: It is believed that X. volvulus is native to the Americas (Wood, 1982). It probably arrived in Africa hundreds of years ago, and is now well-established in many parts of the Afrotropical region, although less common than X. perforans (Schedl, 1963). In Asia and the Pacific, X. volvulus was probably accidentally introduced through commerce. It is not clear whether the species is established in Australia, although it has been intercepted there (Schedl, 1964). No specimens have been seen in extensive collections of Scolytidae from Queensland (RABeaver, Chiangmai University, Thailand, unpublished data). Although established on the main islands of Japan (apart from Hokkaido),  X. volvulus has often been intercepted at Japanese ports from timber imported from countries from Indonesia to the Solomon Islands (Schedl, 1966;Ohno et al., 1987, 1988, 1989; Ohno, 1990). It has also been intercepted in certain European countries and New Zealand, but has not established there, probably because it is unable to survive winter conditions.

remark: Like most of the species in Xyleborus and related genera, X. pseudopilifer should be considered a quarantine pest. This is because members of the tribe Xyleborini (Xyleborus plus related genera) are all inbreeding, with the males generally mating with their sisters within the parental gallery system before dispersal.Thus the introduction of only a few mated females may lead to the establishment of an active population if suitable host plants can be found and environmental conditions are satisfactory. Because X. pseudopilifer is basically restricted in its hosts to Dipterocarpaceae, it is unlikely to be able to invade areas outside the geographical range of this plant family.
author: CPC2006

management_info: When Xyleborus species are detected in imported plant material, all of the infested material should be destroyed. When they are detected in traps, plant material in the vicinity of the trap should be actively inspected, with special attention directed towards imported woody products such as timber, crating, dunnage and lumber milling scraps. If an active infestation is detected, control using insecticides is possible but of limited effectiveness. Chemical control is not generally effective since the adult beetles bore deep into the host material. The following insecticides were effective against a species of Euwallacea destructive to tea: fenvalerate, deltamethrin, quinalphos, cypermethrin and dichlorvos (Muraleedharan, 1995); these insecticides may also be effective against other ambrosia beetles.^p^pThe concealed habitats in which these species feed and reproduce, the difficulties and high costs of insecticide application, and environmental concerns all limit the effectiveness of chemical control. In plantation and reforestation areas, care needs to be taken to avoid damage to the trunks of trees during thinning or other forest operations. X. pseudopilifer can attack living trees through wounds (Browne, 1961).  In logging areas, fast removal of the felled timber from the area will reduce attacks, and rapid conversion to sawn timber will reduce the depth of such attacks as have occurred. Attacks on sawn timber are much less frequent, and can be further reduced if the timber is seasoned and its moisture content falls (Roberts, 1987).

remark: Several other species of Xyleborus with similar habits to X. fallax have been imported to tropical and subtropical areas around the world. A few have become important pests, either because they may attack living or stressed trees, or because of their abundance in disturbed forest areas, and their very wide host range. X. fallax seems to be solely a secondary borer, but it can be very abundant in felled timber. An increased tendency for secondary species of ambrosia beetle to attack living trees in recent years has been noted (Kuhnholz et al., 2003). The risk of introduction outside its present geographic range must be considered high.  X. fallax is not specifically listed as a quarantine pest, but Xyleborus spp. are included in the APHIS Regulated  Pest List in the USA, and as quarantine pests in New Zealand.

If an active infestation is detected, control using insecticides is possible but is of limited effectiveness. Chemical control is not generally effective since the adult beetles bore deep into the host material. The following insecticides were effective against a species of Euwallacea destructive to tea: fenvalerate, deltamethrin, quinalphos, cypermethrin and dichlorvos (Muraleedharan, 1995); these insecticides may also be effective against other ambrosia beetles.^p^pThe concealed habitats in which these species feed and reproduce, the difficulties and high costs of insecticide application, and environmental concerns all limit the effectiveness of chemical control. In logging areas, fast removal of the felled timber from the area will reduce attacks, and rapid conversion to sawn timber will reduce the depth of such attacks as have occurred. Attacks on sawn timber are much less frequent, and can be further reduced if the timber is seasoned and its moisture content falls (Roberts, 1987).

description: Natural Dispersal^p^pThe adult females fly readily and flight is one the main means of movement and dispersal to previously uninfected areas. Of more importance, however, is the movement of infested woody material in timber, ship dunnage and crating. Numerous species of Xyleborus and related genera have been taken in port cities from raw logs destined for saw mills, from discarded ship dunnage, and in similar circumstances.^p^pVector Transmission^p^pX. emarginatus, like other members of the Xyleborini is dependent for food on a symbiotic ambrosia fungus or fungi. The fungus is transmitted by the female in a mycangial pouch. The position of this is not known in X. emarginatus. Both the adults and larvae are dependent on the growth of the fungus on the walls of the gallery system in the wood for their food (Beaver, 1989). No studies of the ambrosia fungus have been made in X. emarginatus, but the typical staining of the wood around the galleries can easily be observed. Some ambrosia fungi are pathogenic to the host tree. remark: Several other species of Xyleborus with similar habits to X. emarginatus have been imported to tropical and subtropical areas around the world. A few have become important pests, either because they may attack living or stressed trees, or because of their abundance in disturbed forest areas, and their very wide host range. X. emarginatus seems to be solely a secondary borer, but it can be very abundant in felled timber. The risk of introduction outside its present geographic range must be considered high. X. emarginatus is not specifically listed as a quarantine pest, but Xyleborus spp. are included in the APHIS Regulated Pest List in the USA, and as quarantine pests in New Zealand.

potential_eco_desc: X. rivesi is a parasite of peach and apple, and causes economic loss due to direct damage. The individuals appear to be attracted to young, growing roots, where they feed by puncturing several successive layers of cells and extracting cytoplasm. However, its economic importance is greatly enhanced because it is a vector of important plant viruses. X. rivesi is the principal vector of Tomato ringspot virus in Ontario, Canada (Allen et al., 1988), but has not been associated with virus transmission in Europe. In the Great Lakes area, especially Michigan and Ontario, Peach rosette mosaic virus causes substantial damage in Prunus species, grapes and blueberry (Brown et al., 1993). ^p^pThe weed dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) is a major natural reservoir of Tomato ringspot virus in Pennsylvania, USA, and has potential importance in the epidemiology of orchard diseases due to this virus, especially Prunus stem pitting in peach and apple union necrosis in apple (Mountain et al., 1983). ^p^pX. rivesi is most important as a vector of the following American nepoviruses (Taylor and Brown, 1981), which are important mainly on fruit crops.^p^p- Tomato ringspot virus (an EPPO A2 quarantine pest; EPPO/CABI, 1996c); transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. bricolensis and X. californicum, and also by X. rivesi (Forer and Stouffer, 1981).^p^p- Tobacco ringspot virus (on the EPPO A2 list; EPPO/CABI, 1996b), transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. californicum and X. rivesi.^p^p- Cherry rasp leaf virus (an EPPO Al quarantine pest; EPPO/CABI, 1996a), transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. californicum and X. rivesi.^p^pStudies have been reported on the virulence of Tomato ringspot virus in apple (Forer et al., 1984) and grapevines (Allen et al., 1988). The apparent lack of specificity in the transmission of North American nepoviruses by the X. americanum group species markedly contrasts with the specific associations between European nepoviruses and their vector nematode species (Brown et al., 1993).

remark: EPPO constituted an ad hoc committee to devise taxonomic and identification tools for these species so that proper phytosanitary regulations can be enforced (Brown et al., 1993). As X. americanum group species are known to transmit North American nepoviruses, they have been included in the EPPO A2 quarantine pest list. EPPO recommends (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) that soil from non-EPPO countries where X. americanum sensu lato occurs should be prohibited. Plants with roots may also be prohibited; if not, precautions should be taken to ensure that the nematodes will not be carried in the roots. The field from which the plants originated must have been tested and found free from the nematodes, and if the plants were in a growing medium that must be either inorganic or have been tested or treated against nematodes. In addition, plants can either be bare-rooted (having had the growing medium removed 2 weeks previously), or have had the growing medium changed within the previous 2 weeks, or have been kept under special conditions avoiding the risk of reinfestation. Soil or growing medium can be treated to kill nematodes by heating to 60°C and maintaining at that temperature for 1 h.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pThe application of fenamiphos, carbofuran or carbosulfan to peach trees infested with X. americanum and X. rivesi resulted in a significant increase in yield over controls (Jaffee and Shaffer, 1985). ^p^pFenamiphos has been used for control of X. americanum sensu lato in vineyards (Olsen, 1984) and in blueberry production Olsen and Nelson, 1986, 1988).^p^pOxamyl, fenamiphos or Soilbrom 90 [?ethylene dibromide] applied to apple orchards in South Carolina, USA reduced populations of X. rivesi and X. americanum; carbofuran reduced populations only after the second application (Thompson et al., 1984). Carbofuran and Tenekil (a chlorinated petroleum hydrocarbon) were effective in controlling populations of a complex of nematodes including X. rivesi on apple in Pakistan (Khan et al., 1996).^p^pRaspberry soils infested with X. rivesi, Pratylenchus penetrans and Meloidogyne hapla in Quebec, Canada, were treated with 1,3-dichloropropene or 80% chlorinated C3 hydrocarbon + 20% methyl isothiocyanate. Soil fumigation increased raspberry yield by 98, 59 and 18% in the first, second and third years of production, respectively, although this increase in yield was related mainly to control of P. penetrans, the most abundant nematode present (Belair, 1991).

host_range: X. index is a pest of cultivated and wild grapevines and a number of other crops and ornamentals.Affected Plant Stages: Vegetative growing stage.Affected Plant Parts: Roots.
potential_eco_desc: High population levels of X. index (above 50 specimens per litre of soil) negatively affected grape yields (Lamberti and Melillo, 1991). In California, USA, X. index significantly reduced root and shoot growth of the grape cultivar French Colombard. Bud break was delayed by X. index and buds were less vigorous than in the control (Anwar and Van Gundy, 1989). Grapevine plants grown at 16.6°C and inoculated with 500 X. index had, in the first year, 23% increased abscission of oldest leaves, and in the second year, 65 and 38% reduction in top and root weights, respectively, 60% fewer inflorescences and 89% reduced fruit size (Kirkpatrick et al., 1965; see also Boubals et al., 1971).^p^pA survey on the distribution of X. index in the traditional vine-growing areas of Cyprus revealed that the nematode is widely spread, while its average percentage of occurrence, out of the 1185 soil samples examined, reached 22.2%. It is believed that the major factor influencing the spread of this nematode is the presence of its natural host plant, grapevine, as shown by historical documentation on the island's vine cultivation since the 12th century (Philis, 1993). In Iran, X. index was recorded from 105 of 170 vineyards (maximum population=500/250 ml soil), from eight provinces (Mojtahedi et al., 1980).^p^pThe impact of X. index is increased by its transmission of grapevine fanleaf nepovirus and grapevine chrome mosaic nepovirus (see Biology and Ecology). An 11-year-old Thompson Seedless vineyard in the central area of Chile had a mean population of 250 X. index and was infected with grapevine fanleaf nepovirus. The effect of the virus infection was seen in differences between infected and healthy plants in the rate of photosynthesis, stem and berry diameter, yield and soluble solids (Auger et al., 1992).

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pSee Siddiqi (1974) for the control of X. index.^p^pA single, deep placement of 1,3-dichloropropene has prevented re-infection of replanted vines with grapevine fanleaf nepovirus and controlled the vector, X. index, for 5 years. In another trial, in an old vineyard which had been planted with sudangrass prior to replanting, soil fumigation with methyl bromide virtually eliminated X. index at all levels down to 8 feet within 2 months (Raski et al., 1971; Raski and Schmitt, 1972); X. index was more susceptible than other parasitic nematodes to methyl bromide. Increasing soil temperature increased X. index susceptibility (Abdalla and Lear, 1975). Methyl bromide and 1,3-dichloropropene reduced nematode numbers and disease incidence; carbon disulphide (superseded) was ineffective. Wet soils and those with a high clay content prevented successful control of the nematode-virus complex by any treatment (Lear et al., 1981). Good control of X. index and grapevine fanleaf nepovirus on grapevines in France was obtained by soil fumigation with 1,2-dichloropropane with 1,3-dichloropropene ('D-D', superseded) with ethylene dibromide and 1,3-dichloropropene (Boubals and Dalmasso, 1968). La Red and Vega (1970) found that treatment of grapevines with 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP, superseded) in irrigation water reduced X. index populations in Argentina and increased fruit yield for 2 years, after which the nematode populations reverted back to previous levels. Phytotoxicity to some grapevine stocks due to DBCP (superseded) at over 100 p.p.m. has been reported (Lider et al., 1967).^p^pIn California, USA, good control of X. index on grapevines was obtained with aldicarb, carbofuran and fenamiphos applied once in February. Grape yield responses were variable but were usually positive in the 2 years after treatment (Raski et al., 1981). X. index inoculated to Vitis vinifera cv. Thompson Seedless at time of nematicide application was effectively controlled by aldicarb, fenamiphos and oxamyl (Hafez et al., 1981). Methyl bromide (under a polyethylene cover or without a cover) and 1,3-dichloropropene reduced the population of X. index and increased the yields of grapevines in California (Raski and Goheen, 1988).^p^pGerman vineyards with high X. index populations were treated with 'D-D' (superseded). On the untreated plots, more than 50% of the vines were infested by the 4th year after planting and over 90% by the 10th year, whereas on the treated plots only 5.3 and 22.4% were infested in the 4th and 10th years after planting, respectively. After the 2nd year, yields from treated plots were higher and the higher yields from treated plots compensated for the fumigating costs by the 4th cropping year. The graft combination Traminer/SO4 became infested more slowly than Traminer/5C and yielded better (Rudel, 1978). ^p^pIn France, treatment of plots of grapevines (cv. Ugni Blanc on 41B) with aldicarb; 'sulfocarb' (oxidation metabolite of aldicarb); 'D-D' (superseded)+aldicarb; and 'D-D' alone gave about 20% higher yields than control plots. The best control of X. index was obtained with 'D-D'+aldicarb (Cuany et al., 1980). In South African trials for eliminating grapevine fanleaf nepovirus from old vineyard soils by applying 'D-D' soil fumigation against the vector, X. index, no re-infection was observed after deep fumigation, but shallow treatment was ineffective (Anon., 1978b). ^p^pField and greenhouse studies showed that split treatments of aldicarb gave better control of X. index than a single treatment, but that virus transmission to indicator plants interspersed among infected grapevines was higher with split treatments than with a single treatment (Esmenjaud et al., 1988).^p^pIn Moldavia, granulated DBCP (superseded) gave a good control of X. index on grapevines (Koev and Polinkovskii, 1976).^p^pMethyl bromide can control X. index (the most important nematode vector of courtnoue disease in France) for a year or so in nur

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pAs a result of the extensive plant host range of X. diversicaudatum little evidence is available of the satisfactory control of the nematode by cultural methods.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pLittle information is available of the satisfactory biological control of X. diversicaudatum (see Natural Enemies).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pLittle information is available of plant resistance directly affecting X. diversicaudatum, although some work has been successful in developing transgenic resistance to arabis mosaic (ArMV) and strawberry latent ringspot (SLRSV) nepoviruses (Brown et al., 1995; Kreiah et al., 1996; Taylor and Brown, 1997).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe application of chemical nematicides has proved effective in controlling virus-vector nematodes, including X. diversicaudatum, with commercial application rates of nematicides achieving an 80-90% reduction of nematodes in the upper 40-60 cm of soil (Thomason and McKenry, 1975). As a result of the long life-cycles and slow reproduction rates of virus-vector nematodes such chemical treatments provide protection to annual and short term perennial crops from direct damage by these nematodes. However, control is much shorter when the crop is affected by either of the nepoviruses transmitted by X. diversicaudatum, as even very small numbers of the vector species are sufficient for efficient transmission of these viruses. ^p^pFumigant nematicides such as 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP); 1,3 dichloropropene; 1,2 dichloropropane-1,3 dichloropropene mixture (DD); methyl bromide; methyl isothiocyanate precursor compounds such as dazomet and metham sodium; and methyl isothiocyanate mixtures have been reported to give good control of X. diversicaudatum (Harrison et al., 1963; Peachey and Brown, 1965; Peachey et al., 1965; Thresh et al., 1972; McNamara et al., 1973; Pitcher and McNamara, 1973; Scotto la Massese et al., 1973). Virus transmission by X. diversicaudatum has been prevented in pot experiments by application of carbamate chemicals such as aldicarb and oxamyl, probably as a result of the temporary nematostasis induced by these chemicals (Taylor and Gordon, 1970).^p^pThe phytoalexin rishitin, produced in potato tissue challenged by the bacterium Erwinia carotovora pv. atroseptica, has been shown to have repellent and nematicidal effects against X. diversicaudatum in laboratory tests (Alphey et al., 1988). Also, the plant-derived sugar analogue (2R, 3R, 4R, 5R)-2, 5-bis(hydroxymethyl)pyrrolidine-3, 4-diol, also known as DMDP (2,5-dihydroxymethyl-3, 4-dihydroxypyrrolidine), from tropical legumes in the genera Lonchocarpus and Derris, applied as a soil drench to pots inhibited virus acquisition, transmission and root galling by X. diversicaudatum Birch et al., 1992, 1993).

management_info:
化学杀线剂的应用被证明是控制带病毒线虫的很好的方法，其中包括裂尾剑线虫，此杀线剂能使土壤上层40-60 cm 处的线虫减少80-90% (Thomason and McKenry, 1975)。它可以延长带病毒线虫的生活周期及减缓繁殖率，此化学方法能减少线虫对一年生和短期多年生作物的直接损害。然而，对于携带线虫传多面体病毒的裂尾剑线虫，杀线剂起不到很好的作用，因为少量的线虫就能传播大量的线虫传多面体病毒。

杀线虫熏剂，例如：二溴氯丙烷;；1,3-二氯丙烯；1,2二氯丙烷和1,3-二氯丙烯的混合物；威百亩、棉隆及硫氰酸甲酯的混合剂对裂尾剑线虫的防治很有效(Harrison et al., 1963; Peachey and Brown, 1965; Peachey et al., 1965; Thresh et al., 1972; McNamara et al., 1973; Pitcher and McNamara, 1973; Scotto la Massese et al., 1973).。在盆栽实验中，对携带病毒的裂尾剑线虫，可以使用氨基甲酸脂的化学药剂，例如得灭克和欧杀灭，它能使线虫暂时性的死亡(Taylor and Gordon, 1970)。

马铃薯块茎受到大白菜软腐病菌侵染后，产生一种植物保卫素-日齐素，通过实验鉴定此植物保卫素能起到杀死裂尾剑线虫的作用(Alphey et al., 1988)。
同样，(2R, 3R, 4R, 5R)-2, 5-（二羟甲基) 吡咯烷-3, 4- 二醇,又叫 (2,5-二羟甲基-3, 4-二羟基吡咯烷)简称DMDP，这是从热带和亚热带的鱼藤属、尖荚豆属提取出来的，用它浸湿盆栽中的土壤，这样能抑制病毒的传播同样也能被裂尾剑线虫侵害后根的损伤(Birch et al., 1992, 1993)。 The application of chemical nematicides has proved effective in controlling virus-vector nematodes, including X. diversicaudatum, with commercial application rates of nematicides achieving an 80-90% reduction of nematodes in the upper 40-60 cm of soil (Thomason and McKenry, 1975). As a result of the long life-cycles and slow reproduction rates of virus-vector nematodes such chemical treatments provide protection to annual and short term perennial crops from direct damage by these nematodes. However, control is much shorter when the crop is affected by either of the nepoviruses transmitted by X. diversicaudatum, as even very small numbers of the vector species are sufficient for efficient transmission of these viruses. 

Fumigant nematicides such as 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP); 1,3 dichloropropene; 1,2 dichloropropane-1,3 dichloropropene mixture (DD); methyl bromide; methyl isothiocyanate precursor compounds such as dazomet and metham sodium; and methyl isothiocyanate mixtures have been reported to give good control of X. diversicaudatum (Harrison et al., 1963; Peachey and Brown, 1965; Peachey et al., 1965; Thresh et al., 1972; McNamara et al., 1973; Pitcher and McNamara, 1973; Scotto la Massese et al., 1973). Virus transmission by X. diversicaudatum has been prevented in pot experiments by application of carbamate chemicals such as aldicarb and oxamyl, probably as a result of the temporary nematostasis induced by these chemicals (Taylor and Gordon, 1970).

The phytoalexin rishitin, produced in potato tissue challenged by the bacterium Erwinia carotovora pv. atroseptica, has been shown to have repellent and nematicidal effects against X. diversicaudatum in laboratory tests (Alphey et al., 1988). Also, the plant-derived sugar analogue (2R, 3R, 4R, 5R)-2, 5-bis(hydroxymethyl)pyrrolidine-3, 4-diol, also known as DMDP (2,5-dihydroxymethyl-3, 4-dihydroxypyrrolidine), from tropical legumes in the genera Lonchocarpus and Derris, applied as a soil drench to pots inhibited virus acquisition, transmission and root galling by X. diversicaudatum (Birch et al., 1992, 1993). 到现在为止对裂尾剑线虫还没有合适的生物学防治方法 Little information is available of the satisfactory biological control of X. diversicaudatum (see Natural Enemies).

potential_eco_desc: 裂尾剑线虫的取食导致了根尖的损伤，从而使整个植株矮化。植物生长变缓，作物的减产。它还可以携带南芥菜花叶病毒和草莓潜隐环斑病毒，给植物带来间接的损害. Feeding by X. diversicaudatum causes characteristic root-tip galling which can result in dwarfing of the whole plant. This reduction in growth can reduce plant crop yield. Indirect damage can result from the nematodes ability to transmit arabis mosaic (ArMV) and strawberry latent ringspot nepoviruses (SLRSV) (Pitcher et al., 1974; Taylor and Brown, 1997 裂尾剑线虫传播时通常携带南芥菜花叶病毒和草莓潜隐环斑病毒，它在欧洲、东欧及前苏联西部有着广泛的分布。此种线虫和南芥菜花叶病毒现在在新西兰也有分布。它通过在果实、观赏植物和蔬菜的直接取食，给它们带来了直接的损害。而更造成重要的经济影响是因为裂尾剑线虫传播时携带南芥菜花叶病毒和草莓潜隐环斑病毒，这些病毒又对作物有直接的影响，例如可以直接杀死被感染的植株或者通过这个非主要的病原菌也给植株带来直接的影响。 X. diversicaudatum, frequently in association with arabis mosaic (ArMV) and strawberry latent ringspot (SLRSV) nepoviruses, is widespread throughout Europe, Eastern Europe and western regions of the former Soviet Union. The nematode and ArMV are present in localized areas of New Zealand (Taylor and Brown, 1997). The nematode causes direct damage by feeding on a wide range of fruit, ornamental and vegetable crops. However, X. diversicaudatum is of most economic importance due to its ability to transmit ArMV and SLRSV, with these viruses able to render some infected crops as unmarketable and in some instances to kill infected plants directly, or through subsequent infection by secondary pathogens.
description:
裂尾剑线虫广泛分布在欧洲的西部、东部和俄罗斯的西部，但是在芬兰，罗马尼亚和南地中海国家却没有(Brown, 1983; Brown and Taylor, 1987; Brown et al., 1990)。Cohn (1969)报告说此物种在以色列被发现，但是这些被怀疑的线虫被鉴定为X. israeliae(Luc et al., 1982).此外，X. paraelongatum现在被认为是裂尾剑线虫的幼虫(Luc and Tarjan, 1963).这是一份来自希腊科斯岛的裂尾剑线虫的报告，它还有待确认(Brown, 1983)。

在欧洲以外的国家这种物种已经被确认，它只被发现出现在新西兰和美国的加利福尼亚(Brown, 1983)。在加利福尼亚，这种物种只在3个区域发现，这三个区域的土壤随后用杀菌剂处理。 然而，在20世纪80年代，裂尾剑线虫被发现在这三个区域的其中一个区域里恢复过来了，这是从在圣地亚哥的一个私人花园的土壤里发现的(Brown, 1983)。 Thorne (1939)报道裂尾剑线虫来自美国犹他州、维吉尼亚，但是这些样本或许鉴定的不正确，只有来自犹他州的样本才可能是裂尾剑线虫(Brown, 1983)。 此外，Schindle (1957)报告裂尾剑线虫广泛分布在种植玫瑰花的暖房里，位于美国东北部的14个州。但是现在它已经被根除了(Brown, 1983)。Riffle (1968, 1970) 报告在新墨西哥和美国有类似的裂尾剑线虫.，但是后来这些线虫被鉴定为X. sahelense(Brown, 1983).。

在加拿大的安大略省，裂尾剑线虫被发现在草莓和温室里的玫瑰上(Townshend, 1961; 1966)，但是在20世纪80年代采样却没有此线虫。裂尾剑线虫被断定已经从这个地区根除，因此在加拿大已不存在(Brown, 1983)。 在澳大利亚，裂尾剑线虫被发现出现在维多利亚和昆士兰(Colbran, 1964; Stubbs, 1971)，但是后来国家的官方说法却认为此为X. basiri，而且在第一个报告后，此物种在维多利亚没被发现。 因此，裂尾剑线虫或许在澳大利亚已经不存在(Brown, 1983)。最初从赤道几内亚(Luc，1958)和马拉维(Saka和Siddiqi，1979)得来的样本被认为是裂尾剑线虫，在几内亚后来又把它描述成X. seredouense(Luc, 1975)，在马拉维把它描述成X. limbeense and X. malawiense(Brown et al., 1983)。这种物种在欧洲以外的国家也有发现，例如阿根廷，印度和特立尼达，关岛(Reinking and Radewald, 1961; Moreno, 1968; Singh, 1968; Acharya et al., 1988),，这些发现还有待去证实，它或许是他种类。 
 X. diversicaudatum is widespread in western and eastern Europe and western Russia but has not been reported from Finland, Romania and southern Mediterranean countries (Brown, 1983; Brown and Taylor, 1987; Brown et al., 1990). Cohn (1969) reported that the species occurred in Israel, but susbsequently these nematodes were identified as X. israeliae (Luc et al., 1982). Also, X. paraelongatum is now recognized as a junior synonym of X. diversicaudatum (Luc and Tarjan, 1963). A report of X. diversicaudatum from the island of Kos, Greece (Terlidou, 1967) requires confirmation (Brown, 1983).

Outside Europe the species has been confirmed as being present only in New Zealand and California, USA (Brown, 1983). In California, the species was known to exist at three sites which were subsequently treated with soil sterilants. However, during the early 1980s specimens of X. diversicaudatum were recovered from one of these sites, from soil in a private garden in San Diego (Brown, 1983). Thorne (1939) reported X. diversicaudatum from Utah and Virginia, USA, but some of these specimens were probably incorrectly identified and only those from Utah may represent X. diversicaudatum (Brown, 1983). Also, Schindler (1957) reported X. diversicaudatum to be widespread in glasshouse roses in 14 states in northeastern USA but the species has probably been eradicated from these cultures (Brown, 1983). Riffle (1968, 1970) reported X. diversicaudatum associated with Pinus ponderosa in New Mexico, USA, but subsequently these nematodes were identified as X. sahelense (Brown, 1983).

In Ontario, Canada, X. diversicaudatum was reported associated with strawberry and glasshouse grown roses (Townshend, 1961; 1966) but sampling during the 1980s failed to detect the nematode. It is concluded that X. diversicaudatum has been eradicated from this region and thus no longer exists in Canada (Brown, 1983). In Australia, X. diversicaudatum was reported from Victoria and Queensland (Colbran, 1964; Stubbs, 1971) but specimens from the latter state were subsequently identified as representing X. basiri and the species has not been detected in Victoria since the first report. Therefore, X. diversicaudatum probably no longer exists in Australia (Brown, 1983). Specimens originally identified as X. diversicaudatum from Equatorial Guinea (Luc, 1958) and Malawi (Saka and Siddiqi, 1979) were subsequently used to describe X. seredouense from the former country (Luc, 1975) and X. limbeense and X. malawiense from Malawi (Brown et al., 1983). Reports of X. diversicaudatum occurring in countries outside Europe, for example Argentina, Guam, India and Trinidad (Reinking and Radewald, 1961; Moreno, 1968; Singh, 1968; Acharya et al., 1988), require the species identification

potential_eco_desc: Direct damage to strawberries, fruit trees, forage legumes and forest trees has occurred in the USA. X. americanum is thought to be a major factor in the unthriftiness of the shelterbelt trees of South Dakota (Malek, 1968) and of red clover (Trifolium pratense) in Iowa (Norton, 1967). Yields of some French-American hybrid grapevine cultivars in Michigan were significantly reduced by four species of nematode including X. americanum (Ramsdell et al., 1996).^p^pThe nematode is most important as a vector of the American nepoviruses, which are important mainly on fruit crops (Taylor and Brown, 1981). Peach rosette mosaic nepovirus (PRMV), which is prevalent in Michigan, USA, causes severe crop loss and death to Vitis labrusca cultivars Concord and Niagara. Because of the high cost of soil fumigation, combined with the removal of most soil fumigants from the market, three types of grapevine cultivars (American Vitis labrusca cvs Concord, Delaware and Niagara; French-American hybrid rootstock cvs Couderc 1202 and 1616, Teleki 5A and 5C; and French-American hybrid scion cvs Chancellor, Foch, Seyval and Vignoles) were tested for resistance to PRMV. Over a period of 4 years, PRMV was detected in less than 5% of the vines of Chancellor and Couderc 1616, 7% of the vines of Couderc 1202 and Foch, 18.2% of the vines of Niagra and Delaware, 20% of the vines of Teleki 5C and 50% or more of vines of Vignoles, Teleki 5A and Concord. Seyval remained uninfected for the duration of the experiment. The greatest reduction in yield and growth (up to 40 and 60%, respectively) was in Concord. Chancellor, Couderc 1202 and 1616, Foch, Teleki 5A and Vignoles also showed reduced yield, growth or both when PRMV-infected and healthy vines were compared (Ramsdell et al., 1995). ^p^pA combination of results of the application of fenamiphos, carbofuran or carbosulfan to peach trees infested with X. americanum and X. rivesi showed that there was a significant increase in yield over controls (Jaffee and Shaffer, 1985). Preplant soil fumigation resulted in increased tree growth and eliminated X. americanum, providing effective control of Prunus stem pitting induced by tomato ringspot nepovirus. There was no significant re-invasion of treated areas by the nematode during the first three growing seasons, but they were present in low numbers in succeeding years (Stouffer and Mowery, 1980).

remark: In the EPPO region, X. pachtaicum and other Xiphinema spp. of the americanum group are not reported to cause any significant damage (Lamberti and Siddiqi, 1977), nor to transmit virus diseases. Even X. rivesi, which has been reported to transmit ToRSV in North America, has not been associated with virus transmission in Europe. The report from the former USSR on the transmission of tomato ringspot nepovirus (ToRSV) and of a virus causing a leaf crinkle disease in blackcurrant (Koev et al., 1970) can presumably now be discounted, as the methods used were subsequently shown to be open to misinterpretation (Trudgill et al., 1983). The species of the americanum group present in North America have still not been fully characterized for their identity, geographical distribution and vector ability, and because the ability to transmit virus is defined in relation to nematode population rather than species, it has been argued that the phytosanitary risk for the EPPO region is presented by "North American populations of X. americanum sensu lato". These are the only ones which are liable in practice to carry the nepoviruses concerned, since the latter are mostly confined to North America (for exceptions, see EPPO/CABI, 1996a, b, c, d). So populations of X. americanum sensu lato from other parts of the world should not be considered to be quarantine pests for the EPPO region.^p^pUK plant health measures are based principally on the Plant Health (Great Britain) Order 1993 which lists X. americanum sensu lato (non-European populations) (Ward and Hockland, 1996). EPPO (1982) lists X. americanum as present in some countries of the EPPO region but requiring a zero or stated tolerance; a list of synonyms and hosts is given in this bulletin.^p^pThe nematode is most important as a vector of the following American nepoviruses (Taylor and Brown, 1981), which are important mainly on fruit crops.^p^pTomato ringspot nepovirus (an EPPO A2 quarantine pest; EPPO/CABI, 1996d). Transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. bricolense and X. californicum, and also by X. rivesi (Forer and Stouffer, 1981).^p^pTobacco ringspot nepovirus (recently added to the EPPO A2 list; EPPO/CABI, 1996c), transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. californicum and X. rivesi.^p^pCherry rasp leaf nepovirus (an EPPO Al quarantine pest; EPPO/CABI, 1996a), transmitted by X. americanum sensu stricto, X. californicum and X. rivesi.^p^pPeach rosette mosaic nepovirus (recently added to the EPPO A1 list; EPPO/CABI, 1996b), transmitted only by X. americanum sensu stricto. This virus is rather less important than the first three listed. Soybean severe stunt nepovirus is a relatively minor North American pathogen also reported to be transmitted by X. americanum.EPPO (1990) recommends that soil from non-EPPO countries where X. americanum sensu lato occurs should be prohibited. Plants with roots may also be prohibited, but if not then precautions should be taken to ensure that the nematodes will not be carried in the roots. The field from which the plants came must have been tested and found free from the nematodes and, if the plants were in a growing medium, that must either be inorganic or should have been tested or treated against nematodes. In addition, the plants can either be bare-rooted (having had growing medium removed 2 weeks previously), or have had the growing medium changed within the previous 2 weeks, or have been kept under special conditions avoiding the risk of re-infestation. Soil or growing medium can be treated to kill nematodes by heating to 60°C and maintaining at that temperature for 1 h.

management_info: Introduction^p^pControl of X. americanum, particularly of viruliferous nematodes in the field, presents problems. Treatment of the soil with nematicides can give good control of the nematodes (over 95% control) but the nematodes that remain can still transmit virus to the roots of the crop. At best, soil treatment can slow the spread of virus through the crop. Leaving the soil free of any plant growth for over 2 years will rid the nematode population of virus.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pControl methods are reviewed by Siddiqi (1973) who stated that nematicidal treatments in orchards, vineyards and on other perennials may enable the plants to become well established, but nematodes deep in the soil may escape and cause damage a few years later. ^p^pX. americanum was one of the commonest nematodes in samples of damaged Zoysia japonica lawns in Maryland, USA; application of prophos [ethoprophos] directly to the lawns provided a marked improvement in the condition of the lawns within 2-4 weeks, and the population density of nematodes was greatly reduced (Feldmesser and Golden, 1972). Preplant treatment with 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (superseded) decreased the nematode population and increased the growth of cherry trees (Knierim, 1964). Seedlings of loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) grown in plots treated with 1,3-dichloropropene, ethylene dibromide, 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (superseded) and methyl bromide/chloropicrin before planting showed significantly greater height and stem diameter and much more extensive lateral roots, and gave a larger plantable stock than the seedlings in non-treated plots (Hansbrough and Hollis, 1957). Application of fenamiphos to vineyards in Michigan controlled Meloidogyne hapla, Pratylenchus penetrans and X. americanum, but was less effective against Hoplolaimus galeatus and Criconemella xenoplax (Olsen, 1984). Oxamyl, fenamiphos or ethylene dibromide applied to apple orchards in South Carolina, USA, reduced populations of X. americanum and X. rivesi. Fenamiphos was applied as a split application or as a spring or autumn application to Vaccinium corymbosum infested with X. americanum - 70-80% control of X. americanum was achieved whether the nematicide was applied in the spring, autumn or as a split application (Olsen and Nelson, 1988). Carbofuran only reduced populations after the second application (Thompson et al., 1983). Fumigation with 1,3 dichloropropene successfully controlled X. americanum (Burlando et al., 1978). Control of nematodes on Concord grapes (Vitis labrusca) with 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (superseded) decreased X. americanum populations, but had no apparent effect on other plant parasitic nematodes in two field trials in Washington State, USA. author: CPC2006

remark: T. variabile is under quarantine restriction in New South Wales (Australia).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pGrain may be protected from T. variabile attack by the admixture of insecticide. As far as is known, T. variabile is susceptible to all the insecticides normally used on stored food. Grain stocks may be fumigated with phosphine or methyl bromide to eliminate existing infestation, but these treatments provide no protection against reinfestation. The diapausing larvae are about nine times less susceptible to phosphine than active larvae and have about the same resistance as eggs. All life stages appear to be substantially more susceptible to phosphine than Sitophilus granarius (Banks and Cavanaugh, 1985). Thus, complete kill should be achieved using 'normal' fumigation procedures and the tolerance of diapausing larvae does not have to be taken into account.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBiological control has not been practised against T. variabile. However, there may be some potential for the development of pest management strategies that favour the action of natural parasites and predators.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pGood storage hygiene plays an important role in limiting infestation by T. variabile. The removal of infested residues from last season's harvest is essential. General hygiene in stores is very important, for example by ensuring that all spillage is removed and cracks and crevices are filled.

host_range: T. fuscum primarily infests Picea and Pinus (BilY and Mehl, 1989), but Abies, Larix and hardwoods are also potential hosts (CFIA, 2003b). In North America, T. fuscum was reared from Picea rubens, Picea mariana, Picea glauca and Picea abies (Smith and Humb
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pIn Europe and Asia, T. fuscum attacks dead or dying trees except during outbreak periods. During population outbreaks, T. fuscum can attack living trees and reduce the quality of the timber (CFIA, 2003b). These outbreak populations can persist for 10 years (CFIA, 2003b). In North America, red spruce (Picea rubens) is an important tree for lumber, pulp and paper, and T. fuscum has been shown to infest apparently healthy stands of P. rubens. A serious insect pest of P. rubens could have significant economic implications for North American wood industries (Locke, 2001). In addition to causing feeding damage to trees, a wood-staining fungus, Ophiostoma tetropii was introduced into Nova Scotia, Canada, with T. fuscum. Although this species of fungus is not pathogenic, it may further depreciate the value of the infested timber (Jacobs et al., 2003).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe spruce tree is a major component of the North American boreal forests (Locke, 2001). Although T. fuscum is thought to typically only attack dead or dying trees in its native habitat, established populations in North America infested healthy Picea rubens. The environmental implications of the establishment of a wood-boring beetle that infests spruce could be severe to the North American boreal ecosystem.

host_range: T. inconsequens is polyphagous. Teulon et al. (1994) provide extensive lists of host-plant associations for pear thrips. Breeding hosts were identified from 35 species, 17 genera and 12 families, with incidental records from at least 207 species, 138 gene
potential_eco_desc: During the first half of this century T. inconsequens was considered one of the more important insect pests of pear, prune, and other deciduous fruit tree crops in North America. Serious outbreaks occurred in California, British Columbia, New York, Oregon and Washington but there has been little damage in recent years (see Bailey 1944; Teulon et al., 1994). T. inconsequens is an irregular and occasional, but sometimes serious, pest of deciduous fruit trees in Europe and Asia (Teulon et al., 1994). ^p^pSince 1979, repeated attacks by T. inconsequens have occurred on sugar maple (Acer saccharum) and associated hardwood forest tree species in the north-eastern United States and adjacent areas of Canada. Sugar maple is an important component of indigenous forests and is vital to three rural industries: the hardwood lumber industry, the maple syrup industry, and tourism associated with foliage colours during autumn. Damage has been most severe in New England, New York and Pennsylvania with a significant outbreak in 1988 causing over 500 000 hectares of foliar damage in Pennsylvania alone (Teulon et al., 1993). The impact of pear thrips on sugar maple in terms of defoliation, sap volume and sugar content is summarized in Teulon et al. (1993), with further information on pear thrips impact in relation to photosynthesis and water-use efficiency reported by Ellsworth et al. (1994).
author: CPC2006

remark: Considering that the pear thrips has not colonized tropical regions and is primarily a pest of deciduous fruit and forest tree species it should be considered a quarantine pest in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, northern India and parts of China. ^p^pT. inconsequens was probably spread around the world in soil contaminated with thrips. As thrips inhabit soil for up to 10 months of their life cycle, soil poses the greatest risk for dispersal in terms of national or international trade and transport. Pear thrips eggs and young larvae could also be transported in young buds of host plants.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pDeciduous Fruit Orchards^pHistorically, control of T. inconsequens in fruit orchards was obtained with insecticides directed against the adult and larval stages in the tree (see Teulon et al., 1993). Recently applications of diazinon, azinphosmethyl, malathion, and oxamyl have all been effective on thrips attacking apple. ^p^pNorthern Hardwood Forests^pThe use of synthetic pesticides for pear thrips control in forest environments is not considered a suitable option because of a number of technical, economic and environmental concerns (Teulon et al., 1993). At this point in time other control options such as biological control and cultural controls are only in the development stage (see Brownbridge et al., 1993; Teulon et al., 1993; Brownbridge, 1995). Stanosz (1994) reports on potential chemical control for sugar maple seedlings.^p^p^Regulatory Control^p^pAs T. inconsequens was probably distributed around the world in thrips-contaminated soil adhering to the roots of fruit tree nursery stock, appropriate disinfestation actions (e.g., pesticide dips, fumigation) should be taken to kill thrips in the soil.
