potential_eco_desc: Economic impactHolm et al. (1979) list S. asiatica as a serious or principal weed in Pakistan, India, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Mauritius; also in USA and in Uganda, though it has now been all but eradicated in USA and the record for Uganda is dubious. It is also known now to be serious in parts of Togo (Agbobli and Huguenin, 1987), in S. Ethiopia (Matiyas Mercuria, 1999), in Tanzania (Mbwqaga, 1996), in Botswana (Riches, 1989), in Malawi (Kroschel et al., 1996), in Mozambique (Davies, 1999) and in Madagascar (Elliott et al., 1993). The main host crops parasitized by S. asiatica are sorghum, maize, millets, rice and sugarcane in both Africa and Asia. The millets attacked include pearl millet mainly in West Africa but also locally in Sudan, East Africa, southern Africa and western India; finger millet (Eleusine coracana) in East Africa and India; and the minor millets Setaria italica, Paspalum scrobiculatum, Panicum miliare and Panicum miliaceum locally in India. Irrigated crops are not generally attacked; hence, rice is only attacked when being grown as an upland rainfed crop. Crop damage is especially severe under conditions of marginal rainfall and low soil fertility, and can lead to total failure of any of the above crops. Estimating crop loss has always proved difficult but data from India (Vasudeva Rao et al., 1989) and Togo (Agbobli and Huguenin, 1987) suggest that loss may often be equivalent to 1% of crop yield for each plant of S. asiatica per m2, though it may sometimes be much lower than this. Overall losses in infested fields of southern India were estimated to be about 21%. Average losses of maize due to S. asiatica in Malawi were estimated at 28% in infested fields and 4.5% for the country as a whole (Kroschel et al., 1996).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pS. asiatica is not known to have any significant impact on natural vegetation.^p^p^Social impact^pS. asiatica is not thought to have any significant social impact beyond the farmers involved.^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pS. asiatica is not believed to have any significant effect on biodiversity.

remark: There is considerable scope for further spread of S. asiatica, especially to semi-arid regions of North and South America. management_info: Integrated Control^p^pIntegrated programmes have been devised for the control of S. hermonthica in countries such as the Gambia, but have not been widely proven or adopted. A programme for control of that relatively large species in a peasant-farming situation almost inevitably relies on hand-pulling as a final means of removing plants after the infestation has been reduced by the use of other methods such as crop rotation, growing less susceptible varieties, manuring, intercropping and delayed planting. In the case of S. asiatica, effective hand-pulling is much less feasible as the plant is so much smaller and the seed matures and sheds rather faster. Hence, there has tended to be greater reliance on single control approaches such as the use of resistant varieties (of sorghum) or herbicides.^p^pAn eradication programme for S. asiatica, which has been employed in the USA, could be seen as an IPM system, albeit a very expensive one. Here, the main method of control was the application of herbicide, supplemented by the application of ethylene gas or methyl bromide fumigation and the enforcement of a strict local quarantine. This eradication programme is more fully discussed under the section on Regulatory Control.^p^pIPM programmes must ensure that S. asiatica is not allowed to set seed because of the very large numbers of seed produced and their longevity in the soil. The range of possible measures to be incorporated into systems of control, according to infestation level, are discussed by Parker and Riches (1993). Other discussions of integrated control, and the problems of educating farmers and designing and introducing control methods appear in the volume edited by Kroschel et al. (1999).^p^p^Regulatory Control^p^pRegulatory control has been enforced in the USA for the past 20 years and is finally nearing success with 93% of the originally infested area declared Striga-free by the end of 1994 (English et al., 1995).^p^pThe eradication programme employed in the USA involved the application of herbicide, not only to kill the emerged weed in the cereal crop (maize) but also to control alternative grass hosts in the rotational broad-leaved crops such as tobacco and soyabean. The spraying programme in maize, which was repeated several times per season, was based on an intensive survey procedure and was supplemented by the injection of ethylene gas into the soil to boost suicidal germination in some situations and by methyl bromide fumigation in others. A strict local quarantine was enforced, including vehicle washing and restriction on the movement of many classes of agricultural produce.^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pThe complex germination requirements, and specialized physiology of S. asiatica, together with certain ecological preferences, can be exploited to some degree in cultural control methods.^p^pPreference for relatively dry conditions can be countered by using irrigation wherever available. Preference for infertile soil conditions can be countered by improving soil fertility via the use of nitrogenous manures, green manuring (see Chibudu, 1998) or rotation with leguminous crops. Treatments providing longer-term improvement in soil fertility are generally preferable to the use of inorganic fertilizers, but modest doses of di-ammonium phosphate have provided good results when applied in the ridge before planting, for example, in Malawi (Shaxson and Riches, 1998). Preference for low humidity and high transpiration rates can be countered by dense crop planting, inter-cropping with leafy species or later planting when rains have set in more fully and continuously, provided care is taken not to prejudice the growth of the major crop to any great extent. Conversely, early planting may be beneficial in more temperate zones when temperatures are sub-optimal for the weed.^p^pSome crop species can act as 'trap-crops', stimulating germination of the parasite but failing to allow parasitization. potential_eco_desc: S. hermonthica is almost certainly responsible for more crop loss in Africa than any other individual weed species. Over 5 million ha of crops - mainly sorghum, millets and maize - are affected in six countries of West Africa alone (Sauerborn, 1991), possibly 10 million ha in Africa as a whole. One plant of S. hermonthica per host plant is estimated to cause approximately 5% loss of yield (Parker and Riches, 1993) and high infestations can cause total crop failure. Overall yield losses are estimated at 21% of all sorghum in northern Ghana, 10% of all cereals in Nigeria, 8% in Gambia and 6% in Benin (Sauerborn, 1991). Other countries seriously affected include Cameroon, Cote d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso, Niger, Mali, Senegal, Togo, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.^p^pThe damaging effect of S. hermonthica on the host plant derives not only from the direct loss of water, minerals, nitrogen and carbohydrate to the parasite, but from a disturbance of the host photosynthetic efficiency (e.g. Press and Graves, 1991) and a profound change in the root/shoot balance of the host, leading to stimulation of the root system and stunting of the shoot. ^p^pAs S. hermonthica occurs mainly under conditions of low fertility, it is also associated with some of the poorest farming systems in Africa, in which farmers have few resources and very few options in terms of control measures.

management_info: Varietal Resistance/Tolerance^p^pNo completely immune cereal varieties have yet been developed, but many sorghum varieties show high levels of resistance, at least under local conditions. Selection and breeding programmes in India and Africa have led to the development and release of many lines with at least reduced susceptibility, and these may be valuable as components of an integrated control approach (e.g. Carsky et al., 1996; older literature reviewed by Parker and Riches, 1993). However, traditional varieties in Striga-infested areas often show relatively high tolerance, and these may yield well in spite of heavy infestation. ^p^pIn maize there are no effectively resistant varieties, though some show partial resistance, such as var. Katumani in Kenya (Baltus et al., 1994), and some more tolerant lines have been developed by the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (Kim and Adetimirin, 1997). Work is now in progress to transfer high-level resistance into maize from wild relatives including Zea diploperennis (e.g. Lane et al., 1997). ^p^pLittle progress has been possible with the out-crossing pearl millet, but there are promising results from work in progress to select and develop rice varieties with resistance to Striga species (e.g. Riches et al., 1996). ^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pCharacteristics/weaknesses in S. hermonthica which may be exploited in cultural control measures include the following.^p^p- Dependence on a susceptible host for establishment. Crop rotation avoiding a susceptible cereal will prevent new seeding and allow decline of the soil seed bank. In some areas, there may be alternative cereals which are not attacked (e.g. sorghum in a millet-growing area, or vice versa). Among the non-cereal crops, many are known to exude germination stimulant, though they cannot be parasitized. These trap crops, such as cotton, groundnut, cowpea and soyabean, are especially beneficial in causing suicidal germination and accelerating a decline in the soil seed bank. But they need to be sown at a time when Striga germination is likely to be high, usually early in the rainy season, before the onset of any secondary dormancy. Catch crops are susceptible cereals which may be grown at the beginning of the season or in short rains prior to the main season, to stimulate germination of the Striga. However, they need to be destroyed before the weed can mature and set seed. ^p^p- Preference for low nitrogen. Additional nitrogen fertilizer usually reduces Striga incidence, though not always, especially when applied as a single dose (see Parker and Riches, 1993). However, improved soil fertility is a vital key to long-term control, whether by organic, inorganic or green manuring, rotation with legumes, or agroforestry techniques involving mulching.^p^p- Preference for dry conditions. Irrigation is rarely an option, but moisture conservation techniques may be beneficial. Any means of raising humidity will reduce Striga transpiration and its ability to draw nutrition from the host. Hence leafy crop varieties, dense, uniform planting and mixed cropping (see e.g. Carsky et al., 1994) all tend to suppress the weed.^p^pNone of the methods described above will, alone, provide complete control, and without complete control there is the certainty that surviving plants will mature and replenish the soil seed bank. It is therefore essential that manual, mechanical or chemical methods are used to destroy surviving plants. Hand-pulling is the commonest traditional technique, though a late hoeing or ridging may also be effective. ^p^p^Chemical Control^p^p2,4-D may be used to kill emerged S. hermonthica or to prevent it from maturing and setting seed in sole-crop cereals, but not where mixed with legumes. management_info: S. densiflora is not known to differ from S. asiatica in its response to cultural control methods, and it can be presumed that rotation with non-host crops and improvement in soil fertility are likely to be helpful. (1977) reported unsatisfactory results with 2,4-D both pre- and post-emergence, other reports suggest it can be helpful at either stage (Kumar et al., 1949; Uppal, 1952).  ^p^pVarieties of sorghum resistant to S. asiatica have generally been found to be resistant to S. densiflora as well. Although the African variety Boganhilo, resistant to S. asiatica was reported susceptible to S. densiflora in Anon. management_info: There are few reports of specific control measures for S. angustifolia but the opportunities and limitations of methods for control are largely comparable with those for S. asiatica. Of the cultural methods it is likely that improvement of soil fertility will be one of the most effective. As germination is independent of host root exudates, the use of trap crops is unlikely to be effective, but crop rotation with non-susceptible crops will reduce the build-up of infestations and allow a reduction in the soil seed bank. Although it survives under wet conditions, there is evidence that continuous irrigation may suppress germination and establishment.^p^pAmong the herbicides that have been tested on S. angustifolia, the best results have been obtained with 2,4-D applied to sorghum 4 weeks after crop sowing, before emergence of the parasite. With this treatment, the weed was suppressed and yields increased. Post-emergence 2,4-D killed the weed but failed to improve yields.  Sprays of sodium chloride or urea post-emergence caused only temporary damage. Ethephon was ineffective (Rao and Reddy, 1982c).

host_range: Complete development of S. mangiferae is only achieved on mangoes. Oviposition was obtained in the laboratory on potatoes, peaches, Litchi chinensis, plums, Phaseolus vulgaris and several cultivars of apples, but none of the resulting larvae reached matur
potential_eco_desc: All cultivars are susceptible to mango seed weevil attack but no external symptoms of attack are readily visible on infested fruits, apart from the brown hardened secretion remaining attached to them at the sites of oviposition. Marketability is not directly affected because the weevil resides inside the seed within a thick husk in mature mangoes and is rarely encountered. However, emerging adults cause post-harvest damage to the pulp of late-maturing cultivars in South Africa (Kok, 1979).  The adults tunnel through the fruit, leaving scars on the outside which serve as sites for secondary fungal infection. Also, mango seed weevil infestation may increase fruit drop during early fruit development (Follett 2002), and may reduce the germination capacity of seeds. In Hawaii, germination rates for infested seeds were equal to that of uninfested control seeds in a polyembryonic cultivar ('Common'), whereas germination was significantly reduced for infested seeds of a monoembryonic cultivar ('Haden') compared with uninfested control seeds but germination of infested seeds was still >70% (Follett and Gabbard, 2000). Probably its greatest significance as a pest is to interfere with the export of fruit because of quarantine restrictions imposed by importing countries. In India, all cultivars are susceptible and levels of infestation vary from 48 to 87% (Bagle and Prasad, 1985).
author: CPC2006

management_info: Introduction^p^pThere is little incentive for growers to attempt control because the eating qualities of the fruit are usually unaffected. In nursery beds, more seeds than are required for the projected number of seedlings can be planted to allow for a lower percentage of germination. Alternatively, the seed may be shelled and only sound kernels planted (O'Connor, 1969).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pGood orchard sanitation involves the destruction of scattered stones (Kok, 1979) and the removal of fallen fruits and their stones (Villiers, 1987).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pLarval penetration of the seed of the variety Itamaraca is impossible (Balock and Kozuma, 1964).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control has been used with some success and a wide range of insecticides have been recommended (see, for example, Shukla and Tandon, 1985; Villiers, 1987). The main strategy is to attack diapausing adults by trunk applications or to use foliar sprays at the time of oviposition.^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pLong-range dispersal occurs largely through the transport of fruit and seeds containing larvae, pupae or adults. S. mangiferae has been intercepted in mango fruits and seeds in international trade (USDA, 1988; SPC, 1989).^p^pThe fruit and seeds of mangoes containing larvae or pupae present the main risk of introducing S. mangiferae, although mango plants with diapausing adults could also be a danger, and such material from countries where the pest occurs may be prohibited by mango-growing countries. Mango plants for planting (including seeds) may be imported if they derive from an area where the pest does not occur and the place of production has been found free from infestation by inspection during the previous growing season.^p^pImported mangoes from countries where S. mangiferae occurs can be subjected to a quarantine treatment. Methyl bromide fumigation gave complete kill of all stages but injured the fruit (Balock and Kozuma, 1964). Irradiation is the most effective method of killing or sterilizing weevils within fruit (Follett, 2001). An irradiation dose of 300 Gy is approved for control of mango seed weevil in mangoes exported from Hawaii to the continental USA (US Federal Register, 2002). In South Africa, irradiation of ripe, marketable fruit protected it from damage and prevented adult emergence (Kok, 1979). Hot and cold treatment of fruit has also been tried but gave unreliable results and proved phytotoxic (Balock and Kozuma, 1964; Seo et al., 1970; Shukla and Tandon, 1985).

当芒果果实长到30-35mm时，成虫开始在果实上产卵。幼虫在果肉内钻蛀取食，使果肉内形成纵横交错的隧道，并将粪便堆积在隧道内，使芒果失去食用价值。一个果实内可有l-2头幼虫，多时可达6头。每个坑道一般有1头虫，也有的一坑道内有2头虫。虫子坑道与坑道互不相通，各坑道都分布在果肉内部，其深度不达果核。坑道最大处的直径为7-l0mm。越靠近果皮越缩小，到达果皮的地方只剩一点点痕迹。从外表看不到入侵孔和危害状，整个果皮呈青绿色完好无损。芒果受害后，严重影响果品质量。  据印度尼西亚报道，雅加达和万隆地区果实受害率达30%-80%，在苏门答腊的比例更高。小芒、野生芒、印度芒Mangifera indica和M. foetida芒受害最重，其他芒果品种次之。在云南西双版纳虫害严重的年份，不抗虫品种，芒果受害率达50%以上，一般年代也达20%。

management_info: 46.5℃的温度条件下，处理40分钟，果实中的芒果骨肉象甲可完全被杀死。其他防治方法：保持果园清洁，清除芒果果肉象甲的越冬场所。开花前在树干上涂以胶带，防止成虫上树，或涂煤油乳剂于树干以杀灭成虫。也可用1:600倍乐果加入1.5%-2%的牛皮胶喷树干，防止成虫产卵。结果期每周2次清除受害果并集中销毁。

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pClean cultivation of mangoes in Tripura, India reduced attack on the fruit from 87% (for no treatment) to 68%. Disturbing the soil under the trees reduced the attack to 78%. Hand-picking adult S. frigidus as they ascended the trees was less effective. In combination, the three treatments reduced attack to 24% (De and Pande, 1987a)^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pField trials conducted at Tripura, India with 11 insecticidal sprays at flowering and when the fruits were marble-sized and half grown showed that, in general, persistent insecticides with contact action were more effective in reducing infestations than systemic insecticides. All the insecticides were more effective when applied to marble-sized fruits than at the other two stages. It is suggested that a single foliar application of an effective persistent insecticide with strong contact toxicity is given at the onset of fruit-setting to keep infestations below economic injury levels (De and Pande, 1987c).

host_range: The host range of S. littoralis covers over 40 families, containing at least 87 species of economic importance (Salama et al., 1970).^p^pIn many of the published reports of host plants, it is difficult to distinguish between S. littoralis and S. litura bu
potential_eco_desc: S. littoralis is one of the most destructive agricultural lepidopterous pests within its subtropical and tropical range. It can attack numerous economically important crops throughout the year (EPPO, 1997). On cotton, the pest may cause considerable damage by feeding on the leaves, fruiting points, flower buds and occasionally on bolls. When groundnuts are infested, larvae first select young folded leaves for feeding, but in severe attacks, leaves of any age are stripped off. Sometimes, even the ripening kernels in the pods in the soil may be attacked. Pods of cowpeas and the seeds they contain are also often badly damaged. In tomatoes, larvae bore into the fruit, which is thus rendered unsuitable for consumption. Numerous other crops are attacked, mainly on their leaves.^p^pIn Europe, damage caused by S. littoralis was minimal until about 1937. In 1949, there was a catastrophic population explosion in southern Spain, which affected lucerne, potatoes and other vegetable crops. At present, this noctuid is of great economic importance in Cyprus, Israel, Malta, Morocco and Spain (except the north). In Italy, it is especially important on protected crops of ornamentals and vegetables (Inserra and Calabretta, 1985; Nucifora, 1985). In Greece, S. littoralis causes slight damage in Crete on lucerne ^pand clover only.^p^pIn North Africa, tomato, Capsicum, cotton, maize and other vegetables are affected. In Egypt, it is one of the most serious cotton pests.
author: CPC2006

remark: EPPO has listed S. littoralis as an A2 quarantine pest (OEPP/EPPO, 1981). CPPC, NAPPO and OIRSA also consider it to be of quarantine significance. It is a potential pest of areas where the average annual minimal temperature is not below -10°C. S. littoralis is already fairly widespread in Mediterranean countries and does not present a phytosanitary risk there. The most significant phytosanitary risk for S. littoralis is the possible introduction into glasshouses in most parts of Europe, where it could damage many ornamental and vegetable crops. Although control with insecticides is possible, there have been many cases of resistance and the lack of available biological control methods means that introduction of S. littoralis into glasshouses could necessitate insecticide treatments that could interfere with existing biological control of other pests (EPPO, 1997). ^p^pS. littoralis first appeared in UK glasshouses in considerable numbers in 1963. It was found that the eggs were being introduced on imported cuttings, especially chrysanthemums and carnations.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Biological Control^p^pNumerous studies have been carried out on possible biological control of S. littoralis. Parasitoids (braconids, encyrtids, tachinids and ichneumonids) and predators have been extensively documented. A nuclear polyhedrosis virus has been evaluated against S. litura (Elnagar and El-Sheikh, 1990; Jones et al., 1994), whereas fungi and microsporidia have also been recorded as pathogens. Parasitic nematodes such as Neoaplectana carpocapsae have also been evaluated. However, direct use of these biocontrol agents has not been commercailized. Treatment with Bacillus thuringiensis has been used (Navon et al., 1983), but only some strains are effective as S. littoralis is resistant to many strains (Salama et al., 1989).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pThe chemical control of S. littoralis has been extensively reported, especially in relation to cotton in Egypt. Until 1968, S. littoralis was held in check by methyl-parathion, but then resistance to this compound developed. Since then, numerous other organophosphorus, synthetic pyrethroid and other insecticides have been used, with appearance of resistance and cross resistance in many cases (Issa et al., 1984a; 1984b; Abo-El-Ghar et al., 1986). However, compulsory limitation of the application of synthetic pyrethroids to one per year on cotton in Egypt has stopped the appearance of new resistance (Sawicki, 1986).^p^pChemicals used against species of Spodoptera also include insect growth regulators. There is interest, especially in India, in various antifeedant compounds or extracts, and in natural products, such as azadirachtin and neem extracts.^p^p^IPM^p^pIntegrated pest management techniques, favouring beneficial arthropods, are applied against S. littoralis on cotton in Egypt. These involve hand collection of egg masses, use of microbial pesticides and insect growth regulators and slow-release pheromone formulations for mating disruption. If these measures are taken, relatively few applications of conventional insecticides are necessary (Campion and Nesbitt, 1982; Hosny et al., 1983; Campion and Hosny, 1987). Damage thresholds have been established by Hosny et al. (1986). Pheromones have also been used for mass trapping using a lure and kill strategy (McVeigh and Bettany, 1987) and for monitoring populations. Souka (1980) experimented with irradiation for sterile-insect release, but this technique has not been widely applied in the field.^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pFor planting material, EPPO recommends (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) absence of the pests from the place of production during the last 3 months, or treatment of the consignment. For cut flowers, pre-export inspection is considered sufficient.^p^pCold storage of chrysanthemum and carnation cuttings for at least 10 days at a temperature not exceeding 1.7°C will kill all stages of S. littoralis, but may damage the plants. Storage at slightly higher temperatures or shorter durations does not eradicate S. littoralis, but differences in response to cold have been observed both between strains and within developmental stages of the pest (Powell and Gostick, 1971; Miller, 1976). The standard treatment now used in the UK is cold storage for 2-4 days at (dayuhao)1.7°C, followed by methyl bromide fumigation at 15-20°C (Mortimer and Powell, 1988). This has also been adopted as an EPPO quarantine procedure (OEPP/EPPO, 1984). Irradiation has been investigated as a treatment for cut flowers (Navon et al., 1988). For cut chrysanthemum flowers, Wang and Lin (1984) suggest enclosing buds in perforated polythene bags to exclude the pest and dipping the cut stems in insecticide solutions.

至少危害87种肯经济重要性的植物。该种是极其严重的有害生物。它的幼虫能够使许多经济重要的作物落叶。
在印度大豆上进行的对照实验，不进行防治的田块，产量少42％以上。
在印度烟草上，据估计，每棵植株上如有2、4、8头幼虫，该株产量可分别减少23－24％、44.2%、50.4%。在芋头上，每棵植株上有4、8头4龄幼虫，则其产量减少10％。

一年生草本，具较强的竞争优势，能严重影响作物的产量，其植株多刺影响牧场的放牧价值。它还是茄属有害生物的替代寄主，能帮助有害生物建立和维持种群，因此，许多国家将其列为有害杂草并加以控制。如美国将其列为有害杂草、加拿大列为入侵杂草、俄罗斯列为境内限制传播的检疫杂草等。
刺萼龙葵在其各生育期均含有茄碱，对动物有毒。茄碱在动物体内含量达到体重的0.1%~0.3%即可致毒，可对马、绵羊、山羊、牛产生毒害，症状主要为运动失调、多涎、急喘、颤抖、恶心、腹泻、呕吐等。
description: 通过风、水流、人和动物的活动进行近距离传播，通过动物皮毛、谷物、草料、土壤等携带进行远距离传播。
management_info:
（1）机械防除：刺萼龙葵生长初期（4叶前的幼苗期）生长缓慢，之后生长速度显著加快。因此，在幼苗期将其彻底铲除最为安全和有效。随着植株成熟，全株具刺，给铲除工作带来很大的困难，如进入花果期，铲除时可能造成种子散落，加大危险性。另外，由于刺萼龙葵种子具有休眠特性，当年未萌发的种子可能在数年后仍能萌发，因此，需要连续几年进行追踪观察。
（2）化学防除：国外使用2,4二氯苯氧乙酸开花前进行防治。将2,4二氯苯氧乙酸和麦草畏联合使用，防治效果会更好。

description: 在我国，最早报道日本双棘长蠹S．japonicum 分布于云南昆明（曹一诚，1981），1984和1985年又发现于山东泰安和河南郑州（赵杰，2005），1986年又发现于江苏南京和河北沧州（刁彩华和袁克，1986）。随后在北方多个地区报道了日本双棘长蠹的发生与危害（图1）：天津蓟县（1990），河南洛阳（1995），陕西丹凤、商南和山阳县（1997年以前），北京（1997），甘肃天水（1997），江苏镇江（1998），河北石家庄（1999），山西运城（2002以前），内蒙古鄂尔多斯（2009）（陈君和程惠珍，1997；毛春英等，1997；束兆林等，1998；党风锁和张乐平，1999）。  作者推测日本双棘长蠹的这种分布格局与国槐在我国南北方地区的种植状况有关，人类活动可能是其种群扩散的主要原因。调查发现山西临汾2002和2003年从河南调入苗木时带入了日本双棘长蠹，2004年从河南调入全缘栾树Koelreuteria integrifoliola时亦发现了此虫(张旭萍，2007)。2009年从河北省定州调入内蒙古鄂尔多斯市的绿化用苗中发现日本双棘长蠹。作者认为日本双棘长蠹具有较大的适宜生态空间和潜在地理分布范围，人类活动导致植被景观改变使其局部地区种群增长，地区间的苗木转运加快了其种群的扩散。

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pIn the twentieth century the association between Dutch Elm Disease and elm bark beetles (including S. scolytus) caused the disappearance of elms in almost all European towns. In addition, wood attacked by scolytids and colonized by the fungus loses its mechanical, physical and aesthetic characteristics, with serious consequences for commercialization. In this respect, S. scolytus causes both tree death and wood loss.^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe death of millions of elms throughout Europe has had an environmental impact at the landscape level. Elm bark beetles changed the appearance of all European towns and their parks. In several European (and American) towns there are 'Elm Streets' with no more elms. S. scolytus has been one of the major protagonists, beside other species, in killing trees that were hundreds of years old.^p^pFor breeding, S. scolytus needs thick bark to bore maternal tunnels and lay eggs (see section on Biology and Ecology). Only old elms have barks thick enough to allow S. scolytus colonization. Although smaller Scolytus species, such as S. multistriatus or S. pygmaeus, can colonize both young trees and the upper part of old trees, larger species (e.g. S. scolytus, S. triarmatus, S. sulcifrons and S. laevis) need old elms with thick bark. The strong competition for breeding substrate occurring between larger and smaller species, especially S. multistriatus, leads to a progressive disappearance of S. scolytus, which becomes unable to find suitable hosts.

management_info: Introduction^p^pControl strategies are aimed at reducing the population density of S. scolytus below an economic threshold. Several control methods can be listed. The action, advantages and restrictions of the various methods are discussed in the following sections.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pInsecticides can be spread to kill beetles when they arrive to feed or breed in elm trees (Campana and Stipes, 1981). Two different kinds of insecticides can be used: contact insecticides (sprayed directly onto the tree) and systemic insecticides (injected into the tree).^p^pOver the years, a number of contact insecticides have been shown to protect healthy elm trees against twig-crotch feeding and bark colonization by elm bark beetles (Sinclair and Campana, 1978; Karnosky, 1979; Owen and Lownsbery, 1989). However, different compounds show differing toxicity to elm bark beetles. Contact insecticides appear to be most effective when the treatment of the host tree occurs during the winter just before spring flight. In this way two targets could be reached at the same time: spraying uninfested elm logs completely prevents elm bark beetle colonization (Lanier et al., 1984); in addition, chemicals completely eliminate broods when the new adults emerge from elms attacked before the winter. The insecticides must remain operative throughout the entire flight period of the insects, or be periodically reapplied. In particular, thorough spray coverage of all tree surfaces is necessary for successful insect control. To protect trees from scolytids, all twig crotches 1- to 4-years-old should be covered. Crown application of these chemicals may increase host tree protection (Campana and Stipes, 1981). ^p^pThe method used to apply the insecticides is important for the effectiveness of the insecticide (Hubbes, 1999). Spraying insecticides from a helicopter results in top coverage of the trees. This treatment will protect the elm against beetles feeding in the upper crown. Similarly, hydraulic sprayers provide coverage throughout the crown. Finally, mist blowers should be used only for small trees (Sinclair and Campana, 1978). Contact insecticides may also be used to poison elm wood that has been cut and not debarked (Campana and Stipes, 1981). Jin and Webster (1998) report that some contact insecticides (pyrethroids) remain 100% effective for approximately 60 days after spraying on elm bark. However, an important disadvantage of the broad-spectrum contact insecticides (i.e. pyrethroids) is that they are also toxic to non-target species (i.e. natural enemies). The drift of contact insecticides during application is an additional disadvantage restricting their use (Sclar and Cranshaw, 1996). For these reasons, despite their effectiveness with respect to bark beetle control, their application is not always the best control strategy, especially in urban areas.^p^pTreatment of elm trees with systemic insecticides, which can be injected directly into the trunk, provides an attractive alternative to foliar sprays and their associated drift (Faccoli, 2001). Injection of insecticide and the subsequent spread of the chemical through the tree prevent bark beetles both from feeding and breeding. The timing of application appears to be crucial and needs to take place in the Dutch Elm Disease (DED)-susceptible period (spring). In this respect, studies carried out on the smaller elm bark beetle show that only a low percentage of adults emerged at the end of the summer (second flight) are DED vectors (Faccoli and Battisti, 1997). However, several chemicals or their high concentrations can injure the elms (Faccoli, 2001), although new classes of systemic insecticides for elm insect control have been recently developed (Sclar and Cranshaw, 1996). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pBiological control programs include the single or combined use of different antagonists and volatiles able to modify the beetle behaviour. host_range: S. multistriatus primarily inhabits elm (Ulmus spp.) trees, but can occasionally be found on poplar (Populus spp.), plum (Prunus spp.), lime (Tilia spp.), blackthorn (Rhamnus spp.) and oak (Quercus spp.) trees.Affected Plant Parts: Stems and whole
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pS. multistriatus and S. scolytus (larger elm bark beetle) are the two principal vectors of the pathogenic fungus Ophiostoma ulmi, which causes Dutch elm disease (DED). DED was described by Spierenburg (1921) and is a major cause of elm death in Europe and North America. All elm bark beetles are secondary pests which generally attack attenuated and weak elm trees. When populations of bark beetles increase, they can also be considered as primary pests because of the damage to young twig crotches during feeding. Feeding on twig crotches is the most important means of infestation of healthy elm trees.^p^pDED originated around 1910 in the area between France and Barabant (the Netherlands). The disease spread throughout Europe and caused extensive elm death, reducing elm numbers by 10-40% by the 1940s in most European countries (Brasier, 2000). The first epidemic of DED was caused by a relatively non-aggressive race of O. ulmi, whereas the second DED pandemic was caused by the most aggressive fungus race, Ophiostoma novo-ulmi. It began simultaneously in the 1940s in Eastern Europe (Moldavia-Ukraine) and North America (southern Lakes) (Brasier, 1990). The second DED pandemic resulted in the widescale destruction of elm trees in continental Europe, as well in the UK where over 20 million elms were destroyed (Webber, 1981). Practically, all countries where DED has been registered suffered great losses in the elm population (Heybroek, 1967).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pDutch elm disease (vectored by S. multistriatus and S. scolytus) endangers populations of elm trees in all infested regions. It leads to disturbance of relationships in deciduous forest assemblies (Heybroek, 1967; Burdekin and Gibbs, 1974).

management_info: One of the most common practices for control of S. multistriatus is sanitary removal of infested elm trees in late autumn (Maksimovic and Motal, 1983). This method, combined with treatment of stumps and branches with insecticide, decreases the death rate of elms (Barger, 1977; Basset et al., 1992). Healthy trees can also be protected with insecticidal sprays, and pheromones can be used to detect and monitor beetle populations and to time chemical controls (Birch et al., 1981).^p^pBiological control of bark beetles has been investigated for control of Dutch elm disease. A number of hymenopterous parasites have been identified (Bushing, 1965), but from studies in Austria it was concluded that biological control was unlikely to have much effect on the spread of the disease (Schroder, 1974).^p ^pTreatment with fungicide has some effects (Webber, 1981) on Dutch elm disease vectored by S. multistriatus, but generally Dutch elm disease prevention is considered to be more effective than treatment of already diseased trees. Control strategies are based on interruption of various stages of disease progression and of the interaction between fungi and their vectors (Barger, 1976; Neely, 1984).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pS. populnea causes a high loss of timber. For a 2- to 4-year-old tree, one gall on the main shoot can decrease the increment in height by 25%. Two galls will decrease height increment by 45%, three galls by 70%, and four or more galls can prevent growth of the main shoot in that year or cause the whole tree to wither and die (Zhang and Zhang, 1990).^p^pIn Jilin Province, China, where S. populnea is a major insect pest of poplars, S. populnea occurs in more than 20,000 hectares of poplar forest and has much impact on the social economy and ecology. ^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pLarge areas of poplars and willows can be attacked by S. populnea outbreaks, causing significant enviromental impact. For example, in north-eastern China, pure poplar forests cover large areas in the Three-North Protection Belt for protection from wind and erosion damage. Destruction of poplars by S. populnea has had a significant effect on environmental protection.

management_info: Biological Control: ^p^pGood control of larvae and pupae of S. populnea was achieved by the release of Sclerodermus guani in conditions of sparse understorey vegetation, low altitude (200-300 m), high temperature (22-30°C) and low humidity ((dayuhao)90% RH) (Zhang, 1994). In an experiment conducted during 1996 in Jilin, China, the introduction of S. guani resulted in effective (64.5%) control of S. pupulnea. The financial cost of this control strategy, however, was high (Pi et al., 2001).^p^pIn a field trial, the application of Metarhizium anisopliae against S. populnea resulted in 94.1% mortality (Fan et al., 1988). Pilot tests with a conidial suspension of M. anisopliae subsp. anisopliae, strain Ma83, gave 70.8% control of S. populnea (Fan et al., 1990).^p^pThe protection and utilization of natural enemies such as woodpeckers may be a good way of controlling the pest. In a study in Finland, the few natural enemies of S. populnea together destroyed 29% of the eggs, larvae and pupae, and seemed to play a relatively large role in regulating numbers of S. populnea (Pulkkinen and Yang, 1984).^p^p^Silvicultural Control:^p^pThe occurrence of S. populnea is closely related to the environmental conditions, especially the silvicultural methods used. Planting large areas of pure poplar forest creates good conditions for the pest to thrive, and therefore planting mixed forests including resistant species suitable to the site is useful. When planting poplars, 3-year-old saplings with an obvious stem should be used. Existing pure forests should be restructured to improve the quality of the forest, as pure poplar forests are very liable to be infested by S. populnea. ^p^p^Chemical Control:^p^pSpray treatment with cyfluthrin, phenthoate or chlorpyrifos during the period of adult emergence produced high insect mortality (>91%) (Shin and Shung, 1987). ^p^pA programme comprising 5-8 applications of organophosphate insecticides with systemic, ovicidal or contact action against different stages is recommended as effective against S. populnea (Attard, 1979). The cost of the treatment was considerably lower than that for treatments used hitherto.^p^p^p^Other Control Methods: ^p^pSources of pest infestation should be cleared; infested branches, dead trees and wind-thrown trees should be removed, and weak trees should be regenerated. Galls can be cut from late autumn to early spring. ^p^pThe flight ability of S. populnea is poor, and artificial trapping can be used against the pest. During the peak period of adult eclosion, trapping adults can reduce the population. ^p^pThe eggs can be cracked with hammers or stones to decrease the quantity of larvae emerging.
remark: In China, S. populnea occurs widely and so is not listed as a quarantine pest. It is listed as an A1 quarantine species for the COSAVE region.

management_info: Cocoa-producing countries launched national mirid control campaigns as early as 1958-1960. Annual eradication of the pest by chemical control was ensured by State companies under the authority of the Ministries of Agriculture in the countries in question (Mature Spraying Scheme in Ghana, SATMACI in the Ivory Coast, LPAC in Cameroon, SRCC in Togo).^p^pThe first insecticide to be used was HCH, in the organochlorines group. It was quickly replaced by gamma HCH following transmission of a mouldy taste to the beans. Lindane 20, which is highly effective against mirids, has been used in most African countries, either by spraying or by hot fogging (Cameroon, Togo).^p^pWhen cases of mirid resistance to lindane were reported in Ghana (Telford, 1964), then in the Ivory Coast (Nguyen-Ban, 1977b), Lindane was superseded by organophosphorus products with a lower vapour effect (diazinon, fenthion, fenitrothion, etc.), then by carbamates (propoxur, BPMC, elocron, etc.). More recently, certain pyrethroids, including bifenthrin and an organochlorine, endosulfan, which have proved to be highly active against mirids (over 90% kill rate) have also come onto the market (Nguyen-Ban, 1977a).^p^pAs regards product application techniques, research on reducing the flow rate (Low Volume Treatment) has been undertaken and the results have been extended (Nguyen-Ban, 1977a). ^p^pInsect eradication operations begin in July-August, at the beginning of mirid population increases in the ecosystem. Complete treatment consists of two rounds one month apart. The second round is intended to reach neonatal larvae, which were not affected by the first spraying. In general, one treatment is carried out per year.^p^pThere can be no denying that this rational chemical control programme against mirids has been a success, since it has largely contributed towards economic growth in several African countries.^p^pIn the case of integrated pest management (IPM), cultural techniques (installing temporary shading in young plantings, upkeep and sucker removal in plots) have been routinely applied, in addition to the rational use of pesticides, with a view to minimizing pest damage to cocoa plantations. ^p^pIn terms of genetic control, hybrids have been obtained from clones with mirid tolerance (UPA). Other avenues of research currently being investigated are the study of molecular markers of resistance and an analysis of the biochemical components responsible for the attraction of mirids to cocoa clones.

host_range: R. vulneratus is essentially a pest of plants belonging to the Palmae family. Leong (1987) reported that young sago palms provided better conditions than older ones for reproduction of R. vulneratus. Kimura (1979) reported R. vulneratus as a major pest of
potential_eco_desc: Although R. vulneratus is a major pest of coconut and sago palms, there is not much information on the quantitative loss of palms due to this weevil. Observations by Sivapragasam et al. (1990) indicated an increasing incidence of R. vulneratus in both estates and smallholdings in an estate in Lower Park, Malaysia. In one estate the death of coconut palms was 11%, and 3% showed evidence of fresh attacks. In another estate, loss of revenue due to damaged palms, particularly tall palms, ranged from 21-59%. The problem of the weevil is particularly serious in tall palms as in such palms it is difficult to control the weevil using insecticides. Death of these tall palms, besides affecting the yield of coconuts per unit area, also affects the shade available for the underplanted cocoa trees.

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe control measures suggested for R. ferrugineus also apply for R. vulneratus. No specific integrated pest management programme has been reported. The following measures are suggested (based on Sivapragasam et al., 1990).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pSanitation^p^pIn severe weevil-prone areas, all dead palms which are standing and trunks on the ground should be removed and burnt. High beetle larvae populations have been observed in dead standing palms left to rot in situ in the field after poisoning. Such beetle populations might contribute to higher levels of palm damage and consequently increase the oviposition sites for R. vulneratus.^p^pFelling infested palms^p^pThe distribution of R. vulneratus within an area is usually scattered; it is not uncommon to see infested palms far away from the nearest infested neighbour. Sivapragasam et al. (1990) reported that inspection surveys at 45 day intervals in moderately affected fields appeared to be effective. In badly affected areas, at least monthly rounds of inspections need to be carried out in order to detect the infestation at an early stage. Palms which are badly affected, especially the tall ones which are currently not amenable to chemical treatment, should be felled, and the weevil within either destroyed by chemicals or collected and burnt; burial of the weevil might not be effective as suggested by Corbett and Ponniah (1924) who reported the escape of weevils buried in 3-foot-deep pits. The fronds and the affected parts of the stem should also be treated similarly to inhibit further development of the weevil as the freshly eclosed grubs could complete their development in stems of dead palms. More importantly, the felling of infested palms would reduce the spread of the weevil to other neighbouring palms to initiate fresh attacks.^p^pAvoid wounding palms^p^pAs R. vulneratus has been reported to kill young palms with or without beetle damage, the wounding of such palms should be avoided. Pruning wounds, for example on the cut portions of the frond, should also be treated.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control, using dieldrin and monocrotophos, has been found to be effective in short palms only, especially those 12 years old and younger. Here, the palm can be saved only during the early stages of attack and if the crown is not damaged irreparably. Arikiah (1988) reported complete mortality of all the visible stages of the weevil when dieldrin was used as a crown drench on moderately damaged (those with 'skirting' symptoms) 17-year old Dwarfs. Approximately 85% of the palms survived in spite of the initial weevil attack. It was not possible to treat taller palms using this method as the height of the palm posed problems in administering the chemical in the crown by the operator. Trunk injection using monocrotophos was also not effective although a dose three times the recommended rate for controlling other leaf-feeding insects was used. Other chemicals, such as carbaryl, had been suggested to be effective in injection trials elsewhere, but then this could be for relatively short palms. ^p^pBecause the detection of R. vulneratus is difficult during the early stages of infestation, prophylactic measures are sometimes undertaken for young palms. For example, Mathen and Kurian (1967) recommended placing gamma-BHC mixed with an equal volume of sand in the leaf axils of young palms to deter weevil attacks. It causes similar damage within palm plantations to R. ferrugineus in India and South-East Asia, and R. palmarum in Latin America.^p^pThe larvae burrow in the crowns of palms and feed on the shoot and young leaves. They sometimes destroy the growing point, causing the palm tree to die. Leaves turn chlorotic and die. Extensive tunnelling in the trunk weakens the tree, leaving it susceptible to storm damage (Hill, 1983).

management_info: Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pThe primary means of control is preventative, using cultural and sanitary methods. Adult R. phoenicis are attracted to the odour of feeding sites and to damaged palms, in which they lay their eggs. Therefore, the avoidance of wounds is important during plantation management. The passage of a tractor through a young coconut plantation, for example, can lead to serious weevil attack, as the slight damage to the leaf axils caused by tearing as the wheels run over leaves trailing on the ground can open up ideal egg-laying sites. The removal of all heavily attacked and wounded palms, along with those showing distinct growth disorders, discourages further infestations. ^p^pTraps made from thinned or wild palms that have been felled and split into longitudinal sections, divert weevils away from cultivated palms, because adults are attracted to the chemicals emitted from damaged wood. Trap heaps are frequently burnt and replaced with fresh trap wood. Older traps can be sprayed with palm sap to maintain their effectiveness. These sanitary methods have been shown to be more effective than insecticides in preventing weevil damage (Anon., 1990).^p^pCombined gas chromatographic (GC) and electroantennographic detection (EAD) studies have been carried out to try and identify the chemicals in freshly felled oil palms that are particularly attractive to male and female adult weevils. A number of compounds stimulated strong antennal responses, including ethyl acetate, ethyl propionate, isobutyl propionate, ethyl butyrate, and ethyl isobutyrate. These volatiles are all characteristic of fermenting oil and coconut palm trees. In addition to enhancing the attractiveness of trap wood, plant volatiles could be used for monitoring purposes, for both sexes of weevil, or to increase the effectiveness of pheromone traps that attract and capture male weevils (see Pheromonal control) (Gries et al., 1994).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pRecommended insecticides have included aldrin and dieldrin on crowns and trunks. Alternatively, demeton-S-methyl, carbaryl or similar insecticides can be injected into infested feeding galleries or into the trunk above infested regions (Hill, 1983).^p^p^Pheromonal Control^p^pA male-specific aggregation pheromone has been identified in R. phoenicis. Trapping studies in Cote d'Ivoire have demonstrated that synthetic blends of this aggregation pheromone are highly attractive in the field, and could be used for monitoring or even control purposes. The synthetic aggregate pheromone, 3-methyl-4-octanol, goes under the trivial or common name phoenicol. R. phoenicis produces and responds to only one of the four possible stereoisomers of 3-methyl-4-octanol (Gries et al., 1993; Rochat et al., 1993; 1995; Perez et al., 1994).^p^pVolatiles identified from freshly-felled palms have been added to synthetic aggregation pheromone to try and increase trapping efficiency. In field experiments, ethyl propionate significantly increased capture of R. phoenicis in pheromone-baited traps. However, no single host-plant volatile was as effective as palm tissue itself at enhancing pheromone attraction (Gries et al., 1994).

potential_eco_desc: Since the beginning of this century R. palmarum has been reported as one of the most important pests on ornamental palms and on oil palms, mainly in commercial plantations of Cocos nucifera and Elaeis guineensis (Griffith 1968, 1970; Dean 1979; Fenwick 1967; Sanchez and Cerda 1993).^p^pThe larvae feed on the growing tissue in the crown of the palm, during which it makes a gallery, often destroying the apical growth area and causing eventual death of the palm. Economic damage depends on the palm species and on the number of larvae infesting the plant. Fenwick (1967) and Griffith (1968) reported that populations of 30 larvae are sufficient to cause the death of an adult coconut palm.^p^pIn addition to the direct damage caused by this pest, R. palmarum is an active vector of the nematode Rhadinaphelenchus cocophilus, which in turn is an obligate parasite distributed in all tissues of the plant. This nematode causes the plant illness known as red-ring disease which has reached epiphytotic levels in the past (Griffith, 1968). Coconut palms of 3-10 years of age die during the first 2 months after inoculation (Griffith, 1987). Thurston (1984) and Brathwaite and Siddiqi (1975) reported that infested plants take 23-28 days to show the symptoms of red-ring disease, and die 3-4 months after showing the first symptoms.Esser and Meredith (1987) estimated that several millions of US dollars are lost annually due to the association of red-ring disease and R. palmarum. They estimated that 800 hectares of coconut plantations were abandoned in 1923 due to this disease, and that in Grenada 22% of the coconut palms were infested with red-ring disease. A similar situation seems to be common in other countries in America.
author: CPC2006

remark: R. palmarum has probably reached the limits of its natural distribution in the American continent, and seems unlikely to be able to displace closely related sister species in other parts of the world.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Control strategies have to take into account that R. palmarum is both a pest in its own right and a vector of the nematode Rhadinaphelenchus cocophilus. Bain and Fedon (1951) determined that contamination of healthy plants with red-ring disease occurs only if insect vectors are present. The most important vector in America is R. palmarum. At the moment, the control of red-ring disease is by control of the insect vector as no efficient control of the nematode exists. Chemical control of the insect, although often attempted, is not successful (Hagley, 1963). Cultural control consisting of the burning of affected trees reduces infestation. Chemical killing and drying of infected plants also reduces infestation (Victoria et al., 1970; Blair, 1970; Griffith, 1987), as larvae need living plant tissue in order to survive. The use of natural enemies against this pest may be possible, but has yet to be established. Moura et al. (1993) suggested that P. menezesi may be used to regulate populations of R. palmarum. ^p^pThe most widely used control methods are based on the capture of adults with traps baited with rotting plant materials, such as palm tissue, pineapple and sugar cane (Griffith, 1987; Dean, 1979; Morin et al., 1986; Genty, 1988; Moura et al., 1990). Various different types of traps have been proposed in order to attract the insects and kill them in the trap with chemicals (methomyl, triclorfon and pirimifos-ethyl) (Dean, 1979). Yellow traps seem to be more efficient than those of other colours (Camino, 1975).^p^pThe most modern versions of the trap use natural or synthetic aggregation pheromones to help attract the insects. Moura et al. (1989) and Rochat et al. (1991a) showed that males produce an aggregation pheromone, attracting males and females equally. Rochat et al. (1991a) identified the pheromone as 2(E)-6-metil-2-hepten-4-ol, calling it Rhynchophorol. It was found that male insects only release the pheromone when feeding. Jaffe et al. (1993) showed that it was the smell of the appropriate plant odours, mainly ethyl-acetate, that started the release by males of the aggregation pheromone, and that the aggregation pheromone alone only attracts insects up to a certain distance, after which plant odours are required to attract the insect into the trap. Oehlschlager et al. (1993) and Chinchilla and Oehlschlager (1992a, 1993) evaluated pheromone baited traps in the field. Various efficient trapping methods have been proposed Moura et al., 1990, 1993; Chinchilla and Oehlschlager 1992a, b;Oehlschlager et al., 1992a, b; Vera and Orellana, 1988; Jaffe et al., 1993; Sanchez and Jaffe, 1993), all based on containers which attract the insect with odours produced by plant tissue (mostly sugarcane) and the aggregation pheromone. The pheromone can be obtained either by commercial synthesis or by filling the trap with males, activating them with ethyl-acetate odours to induce production of the pheromone (Sanchez and Jaffe, 1993). Captured insects can then be killed with insecticide or by other means.

remark: R. pomonella has already shown its capacity to spread from its original range in eastern North America, to western states of the USA since 1979 (Foote et al., 1993) and it represents the most serious potential new tephritid pest for many apple producing temperate areas. Canada considers it as an internal quarantine pest (absent from the fruit-producing areas of British Columbia). R. pomonella is of quarantine significance for COSAVE, EPPO and OIRSA.^p^pConsignments of apples from countries where R. pomonella occurs should be inspected for symptoms of infestation and those suspected should be cut open in order to look for larvae. For example, EPPO recommends that such fruits should come from an area where R. pomonella does not occur, or from a place of production found free from the pest by regular inspection for 3 months before harvest. Fruits may also be treated, but specific treatment schedules have mostly not been developed for Rhagoletis spp., since there is no need for them in North America. Schedules developed for other fruit flies on apples will probably be adequate, for example treatment in transit by cold treatment (13, 15 or 17 days at 0.5, 1 or 1.5°C, respectively) (USDA, 1994). Ethylene dibromide was previously widely used as a fumigant but is now generally withdrawn because of its carcinogenicity; methyl bromide is less satisfactory, damaging many fruits and reducing their shelf life, but treatment schedules are available for apple (for example, 32 g/m3 for 2 h at 21-29.5°C; USDA, 1994).^p^pPlants of host species transported with roots from countries where R. pomonella occurs should be free from soil, or the soil should be treated against puparia, and should not carry fruits. Such plants may be prohibited importation.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Upon detection, fallen and infected fruit must be removed and destroyed. If possible, wild and abandoned host trees should also be destroyed. Boller and Prokopy (1976) noted that systemic organophosphates, such as dimethoate, are highly effective against most species, killing eggs, larvae and adults. Belanger et al. (1985) discussed the use of pyrethroids, but these were only of use when pest activity was low. More environmentally acceptable techniques have been tried; namely bait sprays (insecticide plus ammonia source) which can be applied as a spot treatment; soil application of insecticide to destroy pupae; juvenile hormone analogues which can be applied to the soil (Boller and Prokopy, 1976); pesticide-coated red spheres suspended on apple trees, which visually attract adult R. pomonella (Duan and Prokopy, 1995). However, it should be noted that bait sprays may not work well where natural sources of protein and ammonia abound, for example abundant brid droppings (Prokopy et al., 1993). An IPM approach is now generally recommended for apple pests in North America (Prokopy et al., 1990), for example Trimble and Solymar (1997) described a programme for Ontario. Monitoring to facilitate IPM of R. pomonella and other apple pests can be facilitated by computer software such as Bugwatch (Yee and Yee, 1990). Averill and Prokopy (1987) demonstrated that the application of the oviposition deterrent pheromone of R. pomonella deterred oviposition for up to 3 weeks, provided it was not rain-washed. Biological control has so far not been successful (Boller and Prokopy, 1976; Wharton, 1989), and Van Driessche et al. (1987) concluded that, of 15 apple pests, R. pomonella was one of only two for which biological control had no potential. It has been noted that if R. pomonella were to spread to British Columbia, Canada, the control measures required against it would conflict with the integrated pest management (IPM) of other apple pests (FL Banham, Agriculture Canada, British Columbia, Canada, personal communicaton, 1988). Behavioural management (use of oviposition detering pheromones, red spheres) is reviewed by Prokopy (1991).

(1985) discussed the use of pyrethroids, but these were only of use when pest activity was low. Use of soil insecticides to kill puparia has been considered (AliNiazee, 1974).^p^pMore environmentally acceptable techniques have been tried; namely bait sprays (insecticide plus ammonia source) which can be applied as a spot treatment; soil application of insecticide to destroy pupae; and juvenile hormone analogues which can be applied to the soil (Boller and Prokopy, 1976). Advanced IPM systems have been implemented in some areas, for example, Michigan (Edson et al., 1998).^p^p^Phytosanitary Measures^p^pConsignments of cherries (Prunus avium, P. cerasus) and of P. salicina from countries where R. cingulata or R. indifferens occur should be inspected for symptoms of infestation and those suspected should be cut open in order to look for larvae. The European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) recommends that such fruits should come from an area where R. cingulata and R. indifferens do not occur, or from a place of production found free from these pests by regular inspection for 3 months before harvest. Fruits may also be treated, but specific treatment schedules have mostly not been developed for Rhagoletis species, since there is no need for them in North America. Schedules developed for other fruit flies on cherries will probably be adequate, for example cold treatment in transit (11, 12 or 14 days at 0.5, 1.0 or 1.5°C, respectively) (USDA, 1994). Irradiation has been successfully tested as a quarantine treatment against R. indifferens (Burditt and Hungate, 1988).^p^pPlants of host species transported with roots from countries where R. cingulata or R. indifferens occur should be free from soil, or the soil should be treated against puparia, and should not carry fruits. 饵，并且最具吸引力的黄色粘板的波长为 500～550 nm，且在 300～400 nm 波长范围有一个二次峰。统计评价结果表明， 使用大规模诱捕技术的果园与喷施农药的果园之间果实侵染率的差异不显著，其果实侵染率分别为 0.22%和 0.33%，而不使用任何防控技术的果园的侵染率为 10.20%。当樱桃果实为绿色或红色时是不需要保护的， 因为欧洲樱桃实蝇只在呈黄色或略带粉红色的黄色樱桃上产卵。因此，合理的诱捕时间可根据果实的成熟情况而定。在欧洲， 欧洲樱桃实蝇最佳的诱捕时间为每年的 4月下旬—7 月下旬。

description: 欧洲樱桃实蝇的幼虫和卵可以通过寄主果实进行远距离传播，比如商品流转或人为携带。 其虫蛹可以随苗木携带的土壤、 运输工具等进行远距离传播扩散。成虫的飞行传播一般只发生在成虫找不到产卵果实的情况下，雌成虫会离开它出生地树木寻找合适的寄主植物，雄成虫随后跟随。扩散飞行的最大距离很难准确估计， 可能的飞行范围为100～500 m，在特殊情况下其迁飞距离可达 3 km。实验室内的飞行研究表明成虫为寻找寄主植物可在 24 h 内飞行数千米。 因此该虫定殖后扩散传播风险为高。
management_info:
目前， 国际上对欧洲樱桃实蝇采取的非化学防控措施主要包括：Naturalis-L （球孢白僵菌Beauveria bassiana）、作物网、粘板诱捕、利用性信息素或机械障碍来防止成虫产卵， 昆虫病原线虫防治， 饲养和释放寄生蜂Phygadeuon wiesmanni。 一些昆虫病原线虫可用于防治 3 龄老熟幼虫，研究表明由 Steinernema feltiae引起的致死率高 达 95%，Heterorhabditis marelatus
可达到 82%，H. bacteriophora 可达到 76%。 这些昆虫病原线虫可能成为防治欧洲樱桃实蝇的重要方法， 但目前该方法仍处于实验室研究阶段。 在自然条件下，寄生蜂 Phygadeuon wiesmanni 寻找并在实蝇幼虫上产卵寄生，致死率高达 72%，但目前这种措施的研究还很少。

potential_eco_desc: The internal chewing and tunnelling of the borer larvae within the stalk internodes directly decreases the amount of juice that can be extracted and the percentage of sucrose that is present in the juice. This leads to a corresponding decrease of juice purity and an increase in total organic non-sugars such as dextran (Allsopp et al., 1993; Kuniata, 1994; Tamanikaiyaroi, 1997). Further losses are caused by red rot, Colletotrichum falcatum, and related microbial decomposers that invade the damaged tissues. Damaged stalks are lighter and do not keep as well as undamaged cane after they are cut for milling.^p^pIn Fiji, 2% stalk damage in terms of length and weight causes a 1.5% loss in obtainable sugar, a 3.3% loss in purity and a 0.4% increase in dry matter and fibre. Overall, this caused a F$2 million loss (Tamanikaiyaroi et al., 1996), but decreases in cane weights and losses in cane that is not harvested may increase these losses to more than F$2.5 (Tamanikaiyaroi, 1997).^p^pIn Queensland, Australia, total losses to weevil borer exceeded A$3.5 million in the mid 1990s, but this does not include the cost to mills associated with removal of dextrans from the juice of damaged cane (Robertson and Webster, 1995). Up to 72% of blocks in some areas have been damaged by the pest (Pope and Johnson, 1996) and 32,000 tonnes of cane were lost to the pest in 1996 (Stringer et al., 1999). Frequency and severity of damage has increased in north Queensland with the cessation of preharvest burning, mechanical harvesting and a change in cultivars.^p^pIn Papua New Guinea, infestations are usually less than 2-8% of stalks bored, and normally only the lower internodes are damaged (Kuniata, 1994). Damage from caterpillar stemborers is an attractive site for oviposition and losses are confounded. However, up to 15% of shoots or stalks are lost when more than 30% of the rhizomes are damaged, especially when this occurs during the dry season.^p^pDamage in palms has not been quantified, although Halfpapp and Storey (1991) reported that damage was becoming more common with increases in plantings of ornamental palms.

management_info: Physical and Cultural Control^p^pPreharvest burning of crops and/or raking and burning postharvest residues reduce numbers of R. obscurus in the succeeding ratoon crop (Mungomery, 1954; Hitchcock, 1978; Robertson and Webster, 1995; Agnew, 1997). However, the change to harvesting crops green (without prior burning) and retaining crop residues as a mulch (trash blanketing) (practised for nutrient recycling and soil-water conservation) has seen increased numbers of and damage from this pest (Robertson and Webster, 1995). Environmental pressures are unlikely to see a return to widespread burning, so the use of trash mulchers or shredders to reduce crop residues to pieces too small to allow weevil breeding and the improvement in harvester efficiency to remove breeding material are advocated (Robertson and Webster, 1995; Anon., 1997).^p^pThe use of borer-free planting material is seen as important in restricting movement of the pest within farms or to uninfested areas (Mungomery, 1954; Kuniata and Young, 1993; Agnew, 1997).^p^pHigh rates of nitrogen fertiliser increased the severity of damage by weevil borer in Hawaii (Chang et al., 1973). High nitrogen levels can lead to lodging in sugarcane and may result in a softer rind; both can lead to better establishment of borer larvae (Robertson and Webster, 1995).^p^pControl of other pests that cause damage to cane, especially rats and stemborers, will reduce the amount of damage by weevil borer through reducing sites for entry of larvae (Kuniata, 1994; Robertson and Webster, 1995).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pThe parasite Lixophaga sphenophori has been distributed in Hawaii, Fiji and eastern Australia and has established in all areas. It appeared to exert more control in the Hawaiian sugar industry, where crops are harvested after 2 years' growth, than in Queensland where all crops are harvested annually. This appears related to habitat disturbance and the fly's ability to recolonise after harvest (Mungomery, 1954). Attempts to mass rear the fly are deemed uneconomical (Mungomery, 1954). Parasitism of weevil borer larvae in palms in north Queensland can reach high levels (60%) (Halfpapp and Storey, 1991). The fly may be encouraged by planting nectar sources close to the fields (Topham and Beardsley, 1973; Leeper, 1974), especially Euphorbia spp. and Crotalaria spp., and by judicious use of herbicides.^p^pOther natural enemies appear to exert little control (where they have become established).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pDifferences in cultivar susceptibility to weevil borer have long been recognised and used in control of the pest (Veitch, 1917; Bell, 1937; Mungomery, 1954; Robertson and Webster, 1995; Berding, 1996; Anon., 1997; Tamanikaiyaroi, 1997). Resistance has been researched extensively in Hawaii, Queensland and Fiji. In Hawaii, susceptible clones were shown to host 4-5 times as many larvae as resistant clones (Chang et al., 1971). Fewer eggs are laid and development of grubs is slower on resistant compared to susceptible clones (Chang et al., 1970). Larval development is retarded when reared on an artificial diet containing the juice of resistant clones (Chang et al., 1973). Establishment of larvae is lower on clones with higher hardness of the rind (Buzacott, 1938). Hence, both chemical and physical antibiosis is present within clones. Early generation screening within a high-infestation environment is recommended as a cost-effective breeding strategy (Berding, 1996) and has yielded resistant cultivars (Anon., 1999).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pControl of weevil borer in palm nurseries involves regular applications of chlorpyrifos sprays throughout the year (Robertson and Webster, 1995). A similar spray regime would not be acceptable in commercial sugarcane because of cost, access difficulties and environmental concerns.^p^pTwo applications by air of insecticide to cane, 2 months apart, reduced weevil borer numbers when organochlorines were used, but not when carbaryl was ap

description: 刺桐姬小蜂是一种新发生的害虫，直到2004年才被描述为新种。近两年陆续在美国夏威夷、中国台湾等地严重发生。2005年7月25日，深圳出入境检验检疫局在深圳一景区杂色刺桐上发现刺桐姬小蜂，这是在中国大陆首次发现该害虫。  可随刺桐属植物苗木、植株、栽培土、集装箱等运输工具远距离传播扩散。
management_info: 一是暂停从疫区国家和地区(毛里求斯、留尼汪、美国夏威夷、新加坡、中国台湾省)引进刺桐属植物；二是对刺桐姬小蜂采取检疫控制措施，予以扑灭，并在全国范围内开展疫情普查；三是各地出入境检验检疫机构加强对进出境刺桐属植物的检验检疫，防止刺桐姬小蜂传人和传出。
remark: 中国农业部、国家林业局和国家质检总局于8月29日联合发布公告，将刺桐姬小蜂列为我国进境植物检疫性和林业检疫性有害生物。

potential_eco_desc: 刺桐姬小蜂产卵于新叶和枝杆内, 幼虫在叶组织内发育, 并在叶片、新枝和叶柄处形成虫瘿。刺桐受到感染时, 叶片常会发生卷曲, 在叶的正背面和叶柄等处出现畸形、肿大, 幼虫在叶或茎杆组织内部化蛹, 蛹羽化时通过羽化孔飞出。虫瘦严重的叶片和茎杆造成生长迟缓和缺乏活力, 严重感染时能引起大量落叶甚至植株死亡。
description: 刺桐姬小蜂可随刺桐属植物的叶片、枝杆和植株、集装箱等运输工具远距离传播。

host_range: 除严重危害香蕉Musa paradisiaca var. sapientum、胡椒Piper nigrum和椰子Cocos nucifera外，还危害大豆Glycine max、玉米Zea mays、高粱Sorghum bicolor、甘蔗Saccharum officinarum、茄子Solanum melongena、咖啡Coffea、番茄Lycopersicon esculentum和马铃薯Solanum tuberosum等作物。
potential_eco_desc: ①主要侵害香蕉根部，穿刺皮层，引起根部外表出现暗红色的坏死斑，毗邻的坏死斑融合，形成红褐色至黑色的条状病斑，根部皮层组织萎缩、发黑，严重时坏死病斑可环绕根部一周；同时皮层坏死，诱发腐生菌侵入，加速病部组织发黑、坏死。可穿通香蕉根皮层，形成空腔，并聚集在韧皮部，形成层内取食、发育繁殖，使受害根死亡。②白色幼嫩的胡椒根被线虫危害后产生桔黄色至紫色的坏死斑，在老根上颜色为褐色，病根大量腐烂，须根和侧根大量坏死，使主根的生长越来越弱。侵染胡椒3～5年后．黄化的叶片、花序完全脱落主茎死亡。③线虫侵入椰子树白色的幼嫩根，在根表面形成桔色的坏死斑，线虫在此处寄生、繁殖，坏死病斑不断扩大融合，使根大面积廊烂、坏死椰子树苗被害严重时，幼嫩根组织呈海绵状+可导致桔色主根表面开裂，椰子树的根部皮层被线虫穿刺破坏形成空隙，最后空隙融台，形成大的空腔，导致根的死亡。  1969年苏里南香蕉种植园普遍发生香蕉相似穿孔线虫病，造成50％以上的经济损失。印尼邦加岛，在此病猖獗流行的20年内有2200万株胡椒树被毁，造成9O％以上的植株死亡。
remark: 是一种重要的危险性植物病原线虫，许多国家和地区如欧盟、葡萄牙科学发展协会(APPPC)、欧洲和地中海植物保护组织(EPPO)、土耳其、阿根廷、智利、巴拉圭、乌拉圭等国家和地区将其列为危险性植物检疫有害生物。有55个国家对其实施官方控制，是我国禁止入境的一类植物检疫危险性有害生物。
reference_name: 外来入侵生物香蕉相似穿孔线虫及其发生分布

host_range: 香蕉，花卉苗木。
potential_eco_desc: 是一种非常重要的植物病原线虫，引起香蕉猝倒病，花卉苗木发生衰退病，可造成4O%-80%的产量损失，严重时造成毁灭性损失。
description: 借助寄主植物根和所粘附的土壤进行远距离传播。入侵国家基本上是在引进疫区种苗或入境旅客携带疫区花卉苗木时传人该线虫的。
management_info: 严格审批管理，提高防范能力；加强部门沟通，实行信息共享；加大宣传力度，增强防范意识；加强检疫和阻截，防止生物入侵；设立管理机构，建立防控机制。
remark: 已有欧盟、智利、土耳其等55个国家对其实施官方控制。是我国一类检疫危险性有害生物，中国政府采取了严格的官方控制措施，严防其传人。

host_range: 香蕉穿孔线虫(Radopholus similis)为迁移性内寄生线虫，其寄主范围非常广泛，已报道的寄主超过350多种。主要危害香蕉、柑橘、可可树、棕榈树、生姜、茶树、鄂梨、咖啡、胡椒、甘蔗、花生、胡萝卜、番茄、马铃薯、西瓜、番荔枝等多种农作物和园艺植物 卜 ，是热带地区果树上最重要的线虫之一。
description: 主要危害寄主植物的根部，在世界范围内大多通过植物种苗根以及附带的土进行远距离传播。
remark: 香蕉穿孔线虫经济意义极大，多数区域国际植物保护组织和国家将其列为检疫线虫，也是我国的一类植物检疫性有害生物。

host_range: Radopholus similis (sensu lato) is very polyphagous, attacking hundreds of plant species notably those belonging to the Rustaceae (Citrus and related genera) but also many other families including the Arecaceae, Musaceae, Poaceae, Brassicaceae, Rubiaceae
potential_eco_desc: Bananas and Plantains^p^pIt is uncommon for bananas to be parasitized by monospecific nematode populations and the relative importance of the different species of other migratory endoparasites in mixed populations and their role in yield loss is not fully known. Most estimates of yield loss come from the use of nematicides that generally decrease populations of all species not only R. similis and can possibly cause other beneficial growth effects. ^p^pWhere R. similis is the only major nematode present, yield improvement based on gross yield per hectare or weights of harvested bunches following nematicide application can be as high as 267%. Increase in banana and/or plantain yield has been recorded as 86% in Panama and 15% in Honduras (Wehunt and Edwards, 1968), 207-275% in Puerto Rico (over a 3-year period) (Roman et al., 1977), 5-30% in Australia, 71% in Ecuador and 267% in St Vincent (Gowen and Queneherve, 1990; Gowen, 1995) and 38% in South Africa (Jones and Milne, 1982). When R. similis is the main nematode species present in association with other nematodes, the yield improvement over untreated plants after nematicide application can range from 16 to 263% in Ivory Coast (Sarah, 1989; Gowen and Queneherve, 1990), 20-40% in Cameroon (Melin and Vilardebo, 1973; Vilardebo et al., 1988; Sarah, 1989), 35-40% in Madagascar (Beugnon and Vilardebo, 1974), 29-35% in Martinique (Gowen and Queneherve, 1990) and 46% in St Lucia (Gowen, 1975, Gowen and Queneherve, 1990). ^p^p^Black Pepper (Piper nigrum)^p^pR. similis is notorious for being associated with 'yellows disease' of black pepper which caused the loss of 20 million pepper 'trees' on the island of Banka, Indonesia by 1953 (Hubert, 1957). It was commented  at the time that "this seems destined to become one of the instances in the history of agriculture where an important industry will be completely wiped out by a nematode" (Christie, 1959). The nematode is also involved in the same or a very similar disease in India known it that country as 'slow-wilt'. Subsequent publications have proven that R. similis is the primary causal agent of both yellows disease (Mustika, 1992) and slow wilt disease (Venkitesan and Setty, 1977; Mohandas and Ramana, 1991).^p^pPathogenicity tests under simulated field conditions on mature black pepper vines have given significant growth and yield reductions in vines inoculated with 100 or more nematodes. Yield reductions of 29, 50 and 59% are caused by initial R. similis populations of 100, 1000 and 10,000 respectively (Mohandas and Ramana, 1991). Glasshouse experiments on young black pepper plants have shown that all plant growth characteristics are reduced significantly by R. similis alone. After 4 months, initial populations of 1000 nematodes reduce plant heights by 26%, number of nodes by 31% and number of leaves by 39% (Mustika, 1992).^p^p^Ginger^p^pIn Fiji, R. similis has been reported on ginger at infection levels in farmers' fields of more than 50% resulting in yield reductions approaching 40% (Vilsoni et al., 1976). In glasshouse experiments, R. similis causes reduction in growth and rhizome weight. Even an initial population of 10 nematodes per plant can cause a 40% reduction in rhizome weight; 100 nematodes results in a 42% reduction and very high populations of 10,000 nematodes will result in a 74% reduction in rhizome weight after 6 months. At this population level the ginger plants are killed due to severe rotting of rhizomes and roots (Sundararaju et al., 1979).^p^p^Coconut^p^pR. similis causes non-specific general decline symptoms on coconut such as stunting, yellowing, reduction in number and size of  leaves and leaflets, delay in flowering, button shedding and reduced yield (Griffith and Koshy, 1990; Koshy et al., 1991). In pot experiments, soil population levels of 100 nematodes per seedling cause a 35% reduction in height and a 14% reduction in girth of coconut palms over a five year period (Koshy and Sosamma, 1987).
