remark: R. similis is spread on infested vegetative planting material such as rootstocks, corms and tubers. It is a tropical nematode and can become a pest of any of the susceptible host crops in subtropical and tropical climates. Crops in temperate climates are not at risk.^p^pBananas/Plantains^p^pR. similis now occurs in most tropical and subtropical areas of the world. It has been found to be widespread in almost all the banana- and plantain-growing regions of the world except Israel, the Canary Islands, Cape Verde Islands, Cyprus, Crete, Mauritius and Taiwan. It also appears to be absent from some of the important areas of production in the highlands of Eastern Africa.^p^pIts worldwide distribution is relatively recent (beginning of the 19th century) and is due to the transfer of infected plant material, particularly banana sets, from country to country for commercial purposes. The wide distribution of R. similis is correlated with the areas where banana sets of the sub-group Cavendish (AAA) were imported. Adaption may cause the development of a wider host range as it spreads on different AAA, AAB and ABB clones in Africa, and on ornamental plants which increasingly are being exported to regions outside the tropics.^p^pTea^p^p0ne of the most important means of spread of R. similis in tea areas is the dissemination of infested plants to fields from contaminated nurseries. The spread of nematodes could also occur through infested soil and water, poor soil conservation measures adopted in infested areas, use of contaminated irrigation water, use of infested planting material for intercropping tea areas, and the presence of alternative hosts in the vicinity of tea areas. Uprooting old tea fields from the bottom of the slope upwards could also cause a threat by exposing the newly planted, young tea to re-infestation from the infested soil above (Gnanapragasam, 1989a).
author: CPC2006

management_info: In Bananas and Plantains^p^pThe different practices used for controlling nematodes in bananas are summarized below. In permanent cultivation, the opportunities for control are limited to regular nematicide treatment; however, in subsistence cultivation, the only realistic or economically justifiable techniques for preserving losses from nematodes may be by applying large quantities of mulch to stimulate root growth, and by propping fruit stems. Several of the techniques used for nematode control are also appropriate for controlling the banana borer Cosmopolites sordidus, which is a widespread pest causing damage to banana corms.^p^pThe selection of appropriate control techniques will depend largely on the conditions, availability and reliability of workers, and economic considerations. Most control methods depend on the skill and experience of the operators and may be of little value if the work is not supervised.^p^pThe following are established practices for decreasing nematode populations in two different banana-growing systems (replanted systems and permanent plantations).^p^pReplanted System:^p- rotation with alternative crops for 2-3 years^p- flooding for 8 weeks after having destroyed previous banana crop^p- fallow in absence of banana volunteers for 10-12 months^p- selection of disease-free suckers^p- use of in vitro-produced plants^p- paring diseased tissue from corm^p- paring and leaving large corms in sun for 14 days^p- immersing corms in hot water^p- coating corms with nematicide in mud^p- applying nematicide to planting hole and in-fill soil^p- regular spot applications with granular or liquid nematicide formulations.^p- Planting resistant varieties^p- Biological control using endophytic fungi (e.g. Fusarium sp.) (Pocasangre et al., 2000) and mycorrhizal fungi (Koshy et al., 1998).^p^pPermanent Plantation:^p- regular spot applications with granular or liquid nematicide formulations^p- heavy mulches with organic wastes may have beneficial root growth effects ^p- propping fruiting stems with poles or with string guy ropes may prevent plants uprooting.^p- inoculation with mycorrhizal fungi^p^pFor further information see Gowen and Queneherve (1990).^p^p^In Black Pepper^p^pAt present there are no effective control measures for control of slow-wilt or pepper yellows disease. The price of black pepper is known to fluctuate greatly and with the fall in prices, the farmer often loses.^p^pIntegrated methods of nematode management that can be suggested are:^p^p- planting of nematode-free rooted cuttings^p- uprooting of affected vines and replanting after a period of 9-12 months^p- use of non-living supports or standards^p- exclusion of R. similis-susceptible trees as standards for trailing black pepper vines^p- exclusion of susceptible intercrops such as banana, ginger and turmeric^p- application of organic amendments, such as neem oil cake (Azadirachta indica), green foliage, or farm-yard manure^p- earthing-up after application of nematicides, NPK fertilizers and organic amendments^p- application of phorate with the onset of monsoon and again after 3 months (nematicide may be applied after removing the top soil without causing damage to the roots, followed by replacement of the soil; susceptible intercrops, such as banana, may also be treated with nematicides).^p^pFor further information see Koshy and Bridge (1990).^p^p^In Coconut^p^pThe following are suggested control measures in coconut:  ^p^p- application of cow dung, farm yard manure, oil cakes and green manures to the basins^p- applications of chemicals^p- avoiding use of banana as a shade crop in coconut nurseries^p- use of nematode-free planting material of coconut and other intercrops^p- use of tolerant or less susceptible cultivars^p^p^In Arecanut ^p^pControl of R. similis is difficult in arecanut. management_info: Cultural Control^p^pWater stress is considered to be a key factor in pest management in agroecosystems with Citrus limon (lemon) (Mineo, 1993). In Sicily, orchards submitted to water stress, resulted in total infestation in buds, flowers and set fruits below the economic threshold. However, in orchards with adequate water, the total registered infestation surpassed the economic threshold in the same period. ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pP. citri has many natural enemies, predators, parasites, and some polyphagous, which attack other species such us P. oleae (Mineo, 1967; OILB, 1971). The impact of biological control and use of natural enemies is considered negligible in some countries, because they are unable to control the moth effectivley (Garrido and Ventura, 1993; Uygun et al., 1995). However, Bacillus thuringiensis is a promising candidate for P. citri control with low toxicity to the natural enemies complex (Carvalho and Aguiar, 1997), and is recommended for control in integrated pest management programmes. Another pathogenic organism is the fungus Beauveria bassiana (Setata and Nasr, 1998).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pInsecticides commonly used against the citrus flower moth in lemon tree include azinphos-methyl, chlorpyriphos and methidathion.^p^p^Pheromonal Control^p^pThe synthetic sex pheromone (Z) - 7- tetradecenal showed a high degree of selectivity against P. citri, and affected only a few individuals of P. oleae in areas near olive groves. The relationship between male catches and the degree of infestation was largely influenced by locality, climatic and cultural factors, with no apparent correlation between catches and infestation. The use of pheromone traps appeared to be of little practical use for population monitoring (Mineo et al., 1980). Mass trapping and mating disruption have not proved to be promising methods for control of P. citri (Carvalho and Aguiar, 1997).

host_range: The winter (primary) host of M. persicae is almost invariably Prunus persica (peach), including var. nectarina; sometimes P. nigra in USA, and  possibly P. tenella, P. nana, P. serotina, P. americana and peach-almond hybrids.  It is not clear whether the
potential_eco_desc: M. persicae is the most important aphid virus vector. It has been shown to transmit well over 100 plant virus diseases, in about 30 different families, including many major crops. Persistent viruses transmitted include beet western yellows luteovirus (BWYV), beet yellows closterovirus (BYV), beet mild yellowing luteovirus (BMYV), pea enation mosaic enamovirus, bean leaf roll luteovirus, potato leaf roll luteovirus, and several viruses of tobacco (for example, tobacco vein-distorting, tobacco yellow net). Many more are transmitted by the non-persistent method, including cucumber mosaic cucumovirus, clover yellow vein potyvirus, alfalfa mosaic alfamovirus, pepper veinal mottle potyvirus, plum pox potyvirus, lettuce mosaic potyvirus and tobacco vein mottling potyvirus.^p^pDirect feeding damage can be of economic importance in some crops, an effect enhanced by toxic effects of aphid saliva (van Emden et al., 1969). Honeydew production is less than for many other aphids because dense colonies are not formed, but it may be economically important in greenhouse plants due to growth of black sooty mould.^p^pM. persicae is a major pest everywhere potatoes are grown. It is the most important vector of potato leafroll virus (PLRV), which causes leaf roll and tuber rot necrosis. Seed potatoes have low tolerance for PLRV and low aphid populations can be very damaging.^p^pYield losses in sugar beet due to beet yellows are more serious if infection occurs early in the season and can be up to 30-50%, with an increase also in the impurities present in the harvested sugar.

management_info: Chemical Control ^p^pControl of M. persicae by insecticides has had only limited or transient success. Resistance to a range of insecticides has developed world-wide (for example, Hockland et al., 1992; Gao et al., 1992; Herron and Rophail, 1994). The main mechanism of insecticide resistance is based on amplification of esterase-producing genes (for example, Field et al., 1994), but other mechanisms have recently developed (for example, Foster et al., 1998), necessitating use of new insecticides such as imadocloprid (Nauen, 1995).   Devonshire et al. (1992) compared methods for detecting insecticide resistance in field-collected M. persicae. Neem was effective against M. persicae (for example, Lowery et al., 1993), and antifeedants based on alarm pheromones are also being developed (Griffiths et al., 1989). ^p^p^IPM Programmes^p^pInsecticidal soaps have been found useful in greenhouses, where they have low toxicity to many beneficial organisms. The fungal pathogen Verticillium lecanii is effective against M. persicae in a wide range of crops, particularly in IPM programmes in greenhouses, where various extracts, strains and commercial preparations have been used against M. persicae.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pThe parasitoid, Aphidius matricariae, has been widely used as a biological control agent against M. persicae in greenhouses, for example, on aubergine in France, chrysanthemums in the UK, sweet pepper in the Netherlands and Russia, and tomatoes in Canada. These releases were often made in combination with the predatory aphid midge, Aphidoletes aphidimyza (for example, Granges and Leger, 1995). Aphidius gifuensis has been successfully mass-reared and released in greenhouse control of M. persicae and other aphids in China (Xin, 1986). Ephedrus cerasicola, Aphidius colemani and Aphelinus abdominalis have also been used in biological control against M. persicae (Hagvar and Hofsvang, 1991). ^p^pReleases of the aphid midge Aphidoletes aphidimyza against M. persicae in greenhouses and plastic tunnels in China were described by Cheng et al. (1992) and in greenhouses in Canada by Gilkeson and Hill (1987). This midge is also of importance in biological programmes in Eastern Europe and the former USSR.^p^pThe fungal pathogen Verticillium lecanii is effective against M. persicae in a wide range of crops, particularly in IPM programmes in greenhouses, where various extracts, strains and commercial preparations have been used against M. persicae.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pGlandular trichomes on potatoes are an important resistance factor. Gibson and Pickett (1983) described the release of the repellent aphid alarm pheromone chemical, (E)-?-farnesene, from these glandular hairs of wild potato. Trichomes also release a sticky exudate, which immobilizes aphids, and contains toxic sucrose ester compounds, shown to inhibit settling and probing. Glandular hairs have been bred into resistant potato cultivars. Vallejo et al. (1994) described the inheritance of resistance factors in potatoes, and Gatehouse et al. (1996) reported enhanced resistance to M. persicae in transgenic potato plants.  ^p^pIncreased waxiness in brassicas decreased aphid colonization, mainly due to a non-preference resistance mechanism. ^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pAmong the cultural control methods recommended against M. persicae are early sowing, weed management and the use of certified seeds, known to be virus-free (for example, seed potatoes). In peach orchards normal pruning procedures are effective control against overwintering eggs, beneficial to peach and also crops to which aphids migrate in summer. In potatoes, spraying sprout inhibitor is practised, to decrease emergence of infested volunteer plants which could serve as reservoirs of infection for the following year's crop. In sugar beet, where beet itself is the most important reservoir of infection, elimination of overwintering plants is important.

host_range: B. helichrysi has a wider host range in the tropics than in temperate regions. It has host alternation between species of Prunus (primary hosts), especially Prunus domestica and Prunus spinosa, and many different kinds of herbaceous plants (secondary host
potential_eco_desc: B. helichrysi is the major aphid pest of plum, and is also of considerable importance in the cultivation of glasshouse chrysanthemums.^p^pIn Norway, B. helichrysi is a pest of strawberry (Stenseth, 1989).Heie (1992) indicated the aphid can be a pest of plum trees, of plants in glasshouses and of ornamental plants in homes. It can also harm clover seed crops because of the sticky excrement deposited on seeds.Carlson (1972) reported that B. helichrysi occasionally causes economic damage to safflower (Carthamus tinctorus) in California, USA. Studies were carried out in several areas of the state in 1962-71 on the damage caused and control. B. helichrysi fed primarily on seedling terminals, developing buds and younger seed heads in spring. Attacked plant parts developed a spotty or mottled yellow coloration and sometimes became shrivelled and distorted, resulting in loss of seed. Infestations of B. helichrysi of about 2000/seed head severely affected seed production. Moderate infestations of 10 or more/leaf, or about 500/plant, sometimes caused enough stunting to result in a 69% seed loss. Infestations of about 1500/plant could destroy the plants. Infestation by aphids was generally irregular, being restricted to small or medium-sized areas of a field, but sometimes became quite widely distributed.^p^pB. helichrysi is one of the main pests of sunflower in Europe. Yield losses were assessed in open field conditions and natural infestations over a 3-year period in central western France. Field and cage experiments were conducted between 1985 and 1989 to assess the influence of aphids on the relationship between stem diameter at harvest and seed yield. As an indicator of plant vigour (size and yield), stem diameter at harvest was the best choice, as neither its relationship with seed yield nor its mean value was affected by aphid infestation. It was the used as a covariate to study yield losses. Aphid populations were quantified weekly from the beginning to the end of the infestations according to the leaf curling symptom and to the number of aphids per plant. It was found that when aphid populations reached >100/plant at the budding stage, yield losses occurred. When populations were <100 aphids/plant at the budding stage and then decreased, no yield loss was observed (Lerin and Badenhauss, 1995). In Hungary, an outbreak of aphids at the end of the growing period was followed by a 10.7% decrease in weight and 10.9% decrease in the germinating capacity of sunflower seeds (Bujski and Szalay 1995).^p^pB. helichrysi is able to transmit plum pox, cucumber mosaic, Dahlia mosaic and Cineraria mosaic viruses
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pIn Hungary, malathion was tested against B. helichrysi on sunflowers in 1995. Control after 2 and 7 days was over 90%, about the same as with standard treatments with deltamethrin and pirimicarb (Veszeika et al., 1997).^p^pThe incidence, injuriousness and chemical control of B. helichrysi on sunflowers in France were studied in 1988-89 and proposals are made for testing insecticides at various threshold levels of infestation in 1990. Trials in 1988 showed that populations colonizing young sunflower were the most injurious, and timing of infestation affected the results of trials. Pirimicarb gave the best results at temperatures of at least 25°C. Endosulfan plus thiometon was effective at all temperatures, and fluvalinate was effective when infestation levels were low ((dayuhao)50 aphids/plant). In 1989, the threshold of 30-50 aphids at plant stage B5 was not reached and the results of trials were inconclusive. In Himachal Pradesh, India, field experiments were carried out in 1980 and 1981 on the chemical control of B. helichrysi on peaches. Of the six insecticides tested, formothion, methyl demeton and momocrotophos gave effective control of the pest. Thiometon, phosphamidon and dimethoate were less effective.^p^pField tests were carried out in Udaipur, India, in 1972 to devise a suitable schedule for use of insecticides against insect pests of tomato, particularly B. helichrysi. Based on yield, two application of phosphamidon at a 2-weekly interval followed by an application of mevinphos 2 weeks later proved most effective, followed by the schedules: methyl demeton/carbaryl, endosulfan/malathion and jindane/dichlorvos (Agrawal and Kushwaha, 1978).^p    ^pCompounds containing oxamyl were tested on greenhouse rose pests at Elst and Wageningen in the Netherlands. The products showed good results against both mites and insects and remained effective for 4-6 weeks after spraying and no phytotoxic effects were observed (Schipstea, 1975).^p^pIn greenhouse tests in California, USA, using various insecticides against B. helichrysi on chrysanthemums in 1972, pirimicarb and acephate, were the most effective compounds, giving protection against B. helichrysi for up to 5 weeks (Oetting, 1977).^p^pTwelve insecticides were evaluated in sprays in three field tests in Egypt in 1967-69 against B. helichrysi. The mortalities given by omethoate, dimethoate, Bayer 6010 (of unstated composition), malathion, fenthion and formothion averaged 94.66-97.14, 89.09-95.12, 93.38, 91.97, 85.63 and 81.72%, respectively (Abdel-Salam et al., 1972).Carlson (1972) reported that sprays of mevinphos and a combination of malathion and dimethoate (applied by aircraft) gave good control of B. helichrysi in California, USA.^p^p^Biological Control^p^pA blastospore suspension of the fungus, Verticillium lecanii, at a concentration of 108 spores/ml applied in sprays to plants in the glasshouse was highly effective against B. helichrysi on cucumber (Khalil et al., 1983). Hall (1976) and Hall and Burgess (1979) indicated that aqueous sprays of the spores of Verticillium lecanii eliminated low populations of B. helichrysi on the apical growth of chrysanthemums in a small glasshouse in England, UK.^p^pIn Germany, three field trials were carried out in Berlin to determine the effects of a fermenting extract of stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) aqainst B. helichrysi infesting Callistephus chinensis. The extract was not effective against the aphids in any of the trials, while demeton-s-methyl showed levels of effectiveness between 97.98 and 99.95% (Kollner and Sauthoff, 1983; Kollner, 1985).^p        ^p^Host-Plant ResistanceGunenc and Gibson (1980) reported that sticky hairs on leaves of Solanum berthaultii hindered departure of vectors B. helichrysi, lessened probing and decreased acquisition of potato virus Y during 5 minute feeding periods.^p^pInterspecific sunflower hybrids resistant to B. helichrysi have been developed in Russia. management_info: Chemical control is possible, but may not be economic. Fumigation in heavy soils is not practicable. Adequate fertilizing of the soil, particularly nitrogen, reduces the effect of the nematodes by increasing host vigour. Crop rotation with poor or non-hosts has potential. Rotation with lucerne and sugar beet has reduced numbers in Utah, USA (Thorne, 1961) and flax, peas and potatoes have been reported as having a similar effect in the Netherlands (Oostenbrink et al., 1956). In Australia and some other countries, however, P. thornei is reported to attack potato. In sunnier climates solarization has been used and at least some of the major hosts are reported to have resistant varieties. Green manures have also been applied with some success.

description: In September 2017, five samples were collected for root lesion nematodes in a soybean field in Xuchang City of Henan Province, China. On average, 310 root lesion nematodes per kilogram of soil and 28 root lesion nematodes per gram of roots were extracted. Both morphological and molecular data confirmed the existence of Pratylenchus scribneri. To our knowledge, this is the first report of P. scribneri on soybean in Henan Province, China.

description: Five soil samples were collected in October 2014 from a potato field near Cogswell (Sargent Co.), ND, to investigate the occurrence of root-lesion nematodes. All of the samples contained root-lesion nematodes. Nematodes from soil and potato roots were examined morphologically and molecularly for species identification, it was Pratylenchus scribneri. potential_eco_desc: P. loosi is the most serious pest of tea in Sri Lanka (Gadd, 1939; Gadd and Loos, 1946; Loos, 1953; Sivapalan, 1972) and is a serious pest of tea in Japan (Kaneko and Ichinohe, 1963; Takaji, 1969).^p^pAlmost all detailed assessments of crop losses in tea, caused by plant parasitic nematodes, have been conducted in Sri Lanka. Although P. loosi has been recovered from several locations, significant damage to tea has been observed mainly at altitudes between 900 and 1800 m. Approximately 40-50% of the high altitude tea areas in Sri Lanka, covering about 55,000 to 60,000 hectares, is known to suffer obvious damage caused by P. loosi. Although decline in yield in such areas has been estimated at around 225-350 kg made tea/hectare/year (Gadd, 1939; Visser, 1959), this can vary from about 4 to 40% depending on the type of cultivar planted, prevailing climatic conditions, population density of nematode, age and vigour of plant, type and pH of soil, etc. (Gnanapragasam, 1988). The extent of damage is greater in young infested tea clearings and nurseries where damage ranging from 60 to 100% can occur if the proper sanitary measures are not followed.^p^pIn experiments conducted under controlled conditions in the greenhouse, the damage threshold of P. loosi was estimated to be 40 nematodes per 100 g soil at 24°C; this is the average temperature of areas between the altitude range of 900-1800 m in Sri Lanka (Gnanapragasam and Manuelpillai, 1984).^p^pPopulations of P. loosi are highest in areas with high and well distributed rainfall; this determines the severity of damage within the same altitude (Hutchinson and Vythilingam, 1963).^p^pIn Sri Lanka, P. loosi is widely distributed in tea fields at all altitudes but damage to tea is confined mainly to altitudes between 900 and 1800 m (Hutchinson and Vythilingam, 1963). In contrast, P. loosi damages tea throughout Japan, where the crop is cultivated at altitudes between 0 and 300 m, because Japan is located in the cooler temperate zone (Takaji, 1969).^p^pIn Bangladesh, P. loosi only causes damage symptoms to tea grown in nurseries.^p^pNematode damage varies with the type (texture) and physical condition of the soil. Damage caused by P. loosi is most severe in ill-drained, clay-type soils (Sivapalan, 1971).

management_info: Control measures recommended for P. loosi include leaving the ground fallow (not possible in tea) or growing non-host plants for a set period, removing old infested roots, and fumigating nurseries to obtain clean stock. P. loosi is controlled in tea-growing areas, especially in Sri Lanka, by an integrated control method involving the minimal use of pesticides. ^p^pExtensive investigations have been undertaken to identify clones which are tolerant or resistant to P. loosi. Tea clones have varying degrees of tolerance to P. loosi; over 40 tolerant clones have been identified including Tri 3049, Drayton DT95, Balangoda DG7, Mooloya 146 (Sivapalan and Gnanapragasam, 1990).^p^pCultural methods that enhance plant growth while simultaneously curtailing soil populations of the nematode, help to sustain productivity at economic levels. The tea fields which benefit most from these practices are those in which yields have declined, but not to an uneconomic level.^p^p^Cultural Methods^p^pIncorporation of organic matter^p^pIn addition to helping to retain essential soil nutrients and the nutrient status of the tea plant, large inputs of organic matter, including dung and well-decomposed plant residue, suppress the population level of P. loosi (Loos, 1953; Takaji, 1969). The incorporation of specific oil cakes, such as Margosa seed cake (Azadirachta indica), castor oil cake (Ricinus communis), Mahuva oil cake (Madhuca indica), Karanj oil cake (Pongamia glabra), decomposed poultry droppings, coconut copra residue, decomposed tea waste, and plant residues such as freshly harvested water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) helps curtail the pathogenicity caused by P. loosi (Gnanapragasam, 1991). ^p^pCultivation of cover crops^p^pGrowing grasses as cover crops for a 2-year period following uprooting is used to recondition the soil in old tea fields. These cover crops include Tripsacum laxum and Cymbopogon confertiflorus; both of which suppress populations of P. loosi (Visser, 1959; Hutchinson, 1962; Kerr and Vythilingam, 1966). Planting Eragrostis curvula, a grass used mainly to prevent soil erosion in steep sections and vacant areas in tea fields, also suppresses populations of P. loosi and serves as a trap crop (Gnanapragasam, 1981). Other trap crops that can be planted in vacant tea areas include Tagetes sp., Tithonia diversifolia, Wedeliya trilobata, Veti-veria zizanoides and Arachis pintoi (Gnanapragasam, 1995).^p^pFertilizer^p^pIncreasing the dosage of potash fertilizer has been found to be useful in reducing population levels of P. loosi and also in reducing pathogenicity to tea (Gnanapragasam, 1982).^p^pReplanting old tea^p^pTea fields that are uneconomical are uprooted and replanted. Large root fragments left in the soil harbour nematodes in the periphery of the lesions; such populations remain viable for up to 2 or 3 years. It is, therefore, necessary to ensure that all residual roots are removed following uprooting. Large-scale failures in newly-planted tea areas have been traced to re-infestations occurring from residual old roots (Sivapalan, 1967).^p^p^Physical Control^p^pThe only physical control method adopted for the control of nematodes in tea is used in nurseries. Nursery soil, used for propagating young tea plants in India, is sometimes spread on galvanized sheets and heated to temperatures ranging from 60-62°C for 5 minutes (Rao, 1976; Basu, 1978). This method of soil treatment is not practical for large nurseries.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical control is not generally economical in a perennial crop that is grown for as long as 50-60 years because repeat applications are necessary to maintain populations below economic thresholds. Chemical control is confined to the eradication of nematodes from nursery soils and the reduction of soil populations in the field at the time of planting young tea. Fenamiphos and carbofuran are routinely applied to planting holes in Sri Lanka (Sivapalan et al., 1980a).^p^p^Biological Contro

management_info:
在印度茶树线虫防治的唯一方法是被用在幼小的茶树上或者被用在传播发病的的幼小茶树上，有时被传播在电锌版上或者在60℃-62℃之间加热五分钟(Rao, 1976; Basu, 1978).。这种防治方法不适合大的幼茶树园。 The only physical control method adopted for the control of nematodes in tea is used in nurseries. Nursery soil, used for propagating young tea plants in India, is sometimes spread on galvanized sheets and heated to temperatures ranging from 60-62癈 for 5 minutes (Rao, 1976; Basu, 1978). This method of soil treatment is not practical for large nurseries. 化学防治在生长了50-60年的多年生植物上是不经济的，因为要想维持在经济阈值以下必须不断用药。在种植小树的时候可以将一些化学农药施在土壤中，这样可以减少线虫的数量，从而减轻危害。在印度细长植物上经常使用Fenamiphos和carbofuran(Sivapalan et al., 1980a). Chemical control is not generally economical in a perennial crop that is grown for as long as 50-60 years because repeat applications are necessary to maintain populations below economic thresholds. Chemical control is confined to the eradication of nematodes from nursery soils and the reduction of soil populations in the field at the time of planting young tea. Fenamiphos and carbofuran are routinely applied to planting holes in Sri Lanka (Sivapalan et al., 1980a). 在P. loosi中有一种内寄生的孢子，但是它的作用还不知道(Gadd and Loos, 1946)。最近几年，在印度细长植物的综合防治措施中，通过使用复合肥和土壤改善的方法抑制线虫的发生。另外这种办法也有利于增加捕食致病性P. loosi的自然天敌(Visser, 1959; Sivapalan, 1972; Gnanapragasam, 1991)。另外一些捕食线虫真菌被证实也可以减少线虫的数量(Mohotti et al., 1998).。 A sporozoan endoparasite was occasionally recorded from P. loosi, but its significance in control was not confirmed (Gadd and Loos, 1946). For several years, compost and soil amendments have been included in the integrated management programme to suppress P. loosi in Sri Lanka. In addition to other beneficial effects, these were known to help increase the natural predators and parasites of the pathogenic nematode (Visser, 1959; Sivapalan, 1972; Gnanapragasam, 1991). Pasteuria penetrans and nematode trapping fungi have also been found to reduce populations of this nematode (Mohotti et al., 1998). 尽管它们不能在一块田地中同时使用，但是这些防治措施对于使危害降到经济阈值以下从而改变降低生产力是很必要的。无论在种植幼小还是在老的茶树园中，减少线虫的数量从而降低到经济阈值以下，单个防治方法是不够的。在印度细长植物上，在特定环境中经常采用综合防治措施(Gnanapragasam, 1987)。最有用的防治措施包括：
-有限的环境内可以采用化学防治方法
-种植耐和抗线虫的植株
-合适的土壤管理，使土壤pH值维持在4.5-5.0范围之内。
-使用化学肥料，从而使含有丰富的碳酸钾
-使用各种有机物质使土壤肥沃
-使用合理的分支耕作土壤 Although they cannot be eradicated in a field, it is essential that populations of nematodes are reduced to below the economic damage threshold to help avert reduced productivity. Individual control methods may not be adequate to reduce the population level of nematodes below the economic damage threshold in fields planted to young and mature tea.
In Sri Lanka, the management strategy is directed towards the integration of the most appropriate methods of control for a given environment (Gnanapragasam, 1987). The most useful resources of management include:
- limited use of environmentally accepted chemicals with short soil persistence
- planting nematode-tolerant and resistant clones
- proper soil management to maintain soil pH within the range of 4.5-5.0
- using fertilizer mixtures enriched with potash
- enriching the soil with various organic matter
- cultivation of soils by regular forking

host_range: P. brachyurus is polyphagous, with a very wide host range including fruit trees, forest trees, cereals, vegetables, tuber crops, oil seed crops, fibre crops, woody ornamentals, plantation crops, grasses and medicinal plants.^p^pP. brachyurus is a pest of
potential_eco_desc: In many instances, although P. brachyurus has been found to invade the roots and multiply, its effect on the host is unknown. In some cases, the damage is accentuated due to the association formed with other pathogens, resulting in disease complexes.^p^pMany fields in the groundnut producing areas of the USA and several other countries are infested with P. brachyurus, causing severe damage to crop yield and quality (Oteifa, 1962; Alexander, 1963; Minton et al., 1963; Colbran, 1968; Dickson and Smart, 1971; Singh, 1972; Jackson and Sturgeon, 1973; Ibrahim and El-Saedy, 1976; Motsinger et al., 1976; Ingram and Rodriguez-Kabana, 1980; Wheeler and Starr, 1987). Severe infestations have been reported to reduce yield by as much as several hundred kg/ha (Minton and Baujard, 1990). Although damage threshold levels have not been well established, significant yield increases have been demonstrated in fumigated plots (Boswell, 1968; Minton and Morgan, 1974).^p^pPineapple is an important host for this species in the equatorial tropics and yield losses as high as 30% for the plant crop and 80% for the ratoon crop were demonstrated in the Cote d'Ivoire (Lacoeuilhe and Guerout, 1976; Sarah, 1986). A significant yield increase was demonstrated in fumigated plots by Minton and Morgan (1974).^p^pIn Nigeria, Egunjobi (1974) reported a 28.5% reduction in yield of maize which was correlated with a 50% increase in P. brachyurus density. Kimenju et al. (1998) also demonstrated a significant reduction in the growth of maize infestation with P. brachyurus.^p^pIn soyabeans, the nematode reproductive rate was found to be inversely correlated to the inoculum level and the fresh weight and top dry weights were decreased by 13.9-41.8% and 14.1-33.3%, respectively, at an inoculum level of 5000 nematodes per plant (Ferraz, 1995). Caveness et al. (1987) reported significant yield losses in the soyabean varieties TGx539-5E and TG 814-26D.^p^pP. brachyurus is also of economic importance to cotton. Treatment of infested cotton plants with nematicides was found to help improve fibre strength, fibre maturity and fibre length, thus improving quality (Lordello and Sabino, 1985).Boswell (1968) obtained a significant increase in yields of groundnuts treated with fumigant nematicide in which there were 242 or less P. brachyurus/g of shell, compared with untreated plots, with 2771/g of shell. Minton and Morgan (1974) obtained significant yield increases in fumigated plots in which there were 127 P. brachyurus/g of shell compared with 2280/g of shell in untreated plots. Larger yields were possible from irrigated groundnut grown in fumigated soil and harvested earlier than non-irrigated groundnut. P. brachyurus were 10 times more numerous in shell tissue in irrigated than in non-irrigated plots (Good et al., 1958; Good and Stansell, 1965; Boswell, 1968).^p^pIn South Africa, Koen (1967) found that P. brachyurus was a pathogen of economic importance to potatoes. The presence of lesions on tubers reduces their market value (Winslow and Willis, 1972).^p^pVery low initial population levels of P. brachyurus significantly reduced the growth of coffee plants in greenhouse experiments. The reproductive rate of the nematode was low, indicating that the varieties tested were intolerant hosts (Oliveira et al., 1999a).

management_info: ^Introduction^p^pControl of Pratylenchus species in the field is hampered by their wide host range and the presence of multiple species of nematodes in the field. The various methods of control involve pre-plant and post-plant strategies, including use of uninfested planting material, hot-water treatment, chemical dipping, fumigation, systemic nematicides and cultural methods such as the use of resistant varieties, soil amendments, crop rotation and fallowing.^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pChemical treatments that have been used to control P. brachyurus include fumigants, systemic nematicides and fungicides.^p^pP. brachyurus has been successfully controlled in dormant strawberry plants by dipping in ethoprophos, fensulfothion or thionazin. These chemicals are, however, toxic to actively growing plants (Christie, 1959; Smart, 1967). Dipping pineapple suckers in fenamiphos or carbofuran controlled P. brachyurus in the Cote d'Ivoire, although this treatment is not so effective as pre-plant fumigation (Guerout, 1975).^p^pPre-plant treatment with DBCP, followed by post-plant treatment with a systemic nematicide applied just before the build-up in nematode population during the rainy season was effective in controlling P. brachyurus in pineapple fields in the Cote d'Ivoire. DBCP was not effective on clay or stony soils or as a post-plant treatment (Sarah, 1980). Similar results were obtained by Guerout (1976), by treatment with DBCP followed by fenamiphos to control P. brachyurus in pineapple. Willers and Smart (1990) found isazofos, EDB or methyl bromide under gas-tight sheets to be very effective in controlling this nematode in pineapple. Pre-plant treatment with fumigants DD or EDB followed by the application of aldicarb postplant and cadusafos and aldicarb at root formation effectively controlled P. brachyurus, whereas aldicarb treatment pre-plant showed little difference to the control (Rabie et al., 1997).^p^pFenamiphos gave effective control of P. brachyurus in pineapple fields in the Cote d'Ivoire, provided it was not used after inflorescence, as it was found to be toxic to young plant tissues (Sarah, 1983). However, according to Sarah (1987), the optimum dosage recommended was effective only when combined with other cultural practices such as use of a non-host crop, catch crops or green fallows. Fenamiphos also controlled P. brachyurus in tobacco (Miller et al., 1970), Centipede grass (Eremochloa ophiuroides) (Johnson, 1970), sugarcane (Birchfield, 1972) and mango (McSorley and Parrado, 1984). DBCP also effectively controlled this species in sugarcane fields (Birchfield, 1972). Aldicarb and fenamiphos helped to suppress nematode population numbers in millet and sorghum-Sudan grass (Sorghum sudanense) hybrids (Johnson and Burton, 1973).^p^pFor groundnuts, fumigation of infested shells with methyl bromide was successful in eradicating P. brachyurus thus making them safe for use as a mulch in the field. Although nematodes in groundnut pods could also be eradicated, germination was affected at higher dosages (Minton and Gillenwater, 1973). Chemical treatments in infested groundnut fields are resorted to only when infestations are severe. Chemicals that control Meloidogyne sp. have also been found to be effective for P. brachyurus (Good and Stansell, 1965; Boswell, 1968; Jackson and Sturgeon, 1973; Minton and Morgan, 1974). In groundnut fields infested with P. brachyurus, yields were increased by applying fensulfothion, DBCP or carbofuran at various growth stages. Highest yield was obtained by treating with carbofuran (Jackson and Sturgeon, 1973).^p^pCarbofuran and aldicarb are effective in controlling P. brachyurus in soyabean fields in Brazil (Novaretti et al., 1982). remark: Endoparasitic nematodes of banana such as P. goodeyi are disseminated on banana vegetative planting material, and the presence of P. goodeyi in the Canary Islands, Crete and Egypt is almost certainly due to their introduction on planting material. Bananas were introduced to the Canary Islands in the 19th century, in part based on Cavendish banana plants raised in greenhouses in the UK. Banana in the Palm House at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, UK, is the type locality of P. goodeyi, which may therefore have been introduced to the Canaries and Egypt on infected plants from European greenhouses. Plant quarantine procedures should be followed to prevent the further dissemination of P. goodeyi to other warm, temperate banana-growing areas such as Spain or Turkey where it is not yet established (Price and Bridge, 1995).

management_info: Introduction^p^pThe different practices used for controlling P. goodeyi are the same as for other lesion nematodes of banana, Pratylenchus coffeae and Radopholus similis. In permanent cultivation, the opportunities for control are limited to regular nematicide treatment; however, in subsistence cultivation the only realistic or economically justifiable techniques for preserving losses due to nematodes may be by applying large quantities of mulch to stimulate root growth, and by propping fruit stems. Established practices for decreasing nematode populations in different banana-growing systems are described here (after Gowen and Queneherve, 1990; Queneherve, 1993).^p^p^Replanted System^p^p1. Rotation or break with non-host crops, e.g. cassava.^p2. Flooding for 8 weeks after having destroyed previous banana crop.^p3. Fallow in absence of banana volunteers for 10-12 months.^p4. Use of disease-free suckers (from nurseries or clean land) as planting material.^p5. Use of in vitro-produced plants.^p6. Paring diseased tissue from corms.^p7. Paring and leaving large corms in the sun for 14 days.^p8. Heat treatment (hot water, solarization) of corms before planting.^p9. Coating corms with nematicide in mud.^p10. Applying nematicide to planting hole and in-fill soil.^p11. Regular spot applications with granular or liquid nematicide formulations.^p^p^Permanent Plantations^p^p1. Regular spot applications with granular or liquid nematicide formulations.^p2. Growing resistant or tolerant cultivars.^p3. Heavy mulches with organic wastes.^p4. Propping fruiting stems with poles or with string guy ropes to prevent plants uprooting.

In a limited number of studies, attempts have been made to determine losses by actually comparing crop yields in soils with and without the nematode present, ie. where the nematode population was reared to a requisite level, rather than being depleted by nematicides (Olthof and Potter, 1973; Olthof et al., 1973;Potter and Olthof, 1974, 1977; Olthof, 1986). management_info: Introduction^p^pControl of P. penetrans is implemented most often with crops of high value per unit area, or for crops where failure to reduce the nematode population would result in unacceptably high yield losses. Crops like tobacco or ginseng have sufficient commercial value to allow for the expense of soil fumigation, whereas few field grains or forages generate such financial returns to the growers. Sustainable alternatives to chemical controls are still vitally needed.^p^pIPM programmes^p^pThe extremely large host range of P. penetrans poses a challenge to the development and use of IPM programmes for this nematode species, since control by rotation is considerably more difficult. Research on wild plant species and plant resistance screening, nematode population studies, soils and soil microorganisms, and effects of climatic conditions shows some promise toward producing information useful for IPM programme development. However, where several ecological variables can affect the nematode's life cycle, distinctions between cultural, biological and chemical control methods may become hazy. Integrating such cultural practices as winter fallowing in cool climates (Olthof, 1971) or herbicide treatments to suppress weed hosts in orchards (Marks et al., 1972b) with other farming operations would be beneficial in an IPM approach to managing lesion nematodes. ^p^pControl with Mulches and Covercrops^p^pThe result of adding an amendment to soil, or of growing a covercrop, or green-manuring the covercrop, may be seen in soil fertility responses, in direct suppression of nematodes by exuded products from the growing cover plants, or in noxious compounds released into the soil matrix. Stirling (1991) is especially eloquent on the topic of organic amendments for nematode control.^p^pIn Sweden, application of milled peat or green manuring of apple nurseries reduced populations of P. penetrans and eliminated replant disease (Kauri-Paasuke, 1973a); it was noted that nematode-preying tardigrades were stimulated by the milled peat, and nematophagous fungi by the green manure. Miller (1977) achieved an 85% reduction of P. penetrans populations with leaf mould plus sewage sludge; mycelial residues, alone or with leaf mould, and leaf mould plus ammonium sulfate were also effective. Malek and Gartner (1975) inhibited population development of P. penetrans with 2:1 mixtures of hardwood bark: soil for greenhouse container use. Saka (1978) used similar materials to Miller (1977). Valdez and Cowel (1979) discuss nematode control, including P. penetrans, using chicken manure. Rossner and Zebitz (1987) were successful in reducing P. penetrans by 8X in greenhouse and field soil using ground neem seed kernels and leaves. Shauer-Blume (1988) reduced P. penetrans in winter wheat roots to 7% and 20% of the control, using neem oilcake (crushed, de-oiled seeds) and a neem kernel extract (AZT-residue), respectively.^p^pGrowing Tagetes marigolds (T. erecta, T. minuta, T. patula and T. tenuifolia) has been shown to reduce Pratylenchus numbers by 90% (Oostenbrink, 1957). The chemistry of this suppressive effect has been studied by Uhlenbroek and Bijloo (1958); Gommers (1973); Gommers and Bakker (1988); Kyo et al. (1990), and Chitwood (1992). Experimental attempts have been made to use marigolds to manage P. penetrans in potato production in North America (Sieczka et al., 1991), in apple replant disease and field crops in Canada (Edwards et al., 1994; Kimpinski and Arsenault, 1994), in Japanese radish (Raphanus sp.) production (Ohbayashi and Chikaoka, 1973; Nakajima et al., 1985), in lettuce (Shibamoto et al., 1980), and in artichoke cultivation in France (Caubel et al., 1978). Suppressive cover crops in apple orchards may become a component of a nematode control programme with minimal pesticide use (Merwin and Stiles, 1989). management_info:
在澳大利亚和加拿大，将土壤暴晒可以成功控制穿刺短体线虫。在10厘米厚田间土壤中的线虫虫量充分降低或者完全被除去。 There has been some success in controlling P. penetrans by soil solarization (under transparent polyethylene sheets) in Australia and Canada. 对于很多穿刺短体线虫的一年生寄主来说，最有效的化防方法就是播种前的土壤熏蒸。现在在许多国家，土壤熏蒸剂是1,3-氯丙烯、甲基硫氰酸盐, metam-sodium或棉隆（后两种接触土壤水汽后产生？？）。这些产物可单独或混合使用。如果同时要求抗病则混合使用三氯硝基甲。溴甲烷是一种多用的土壤消毒剂，在一些国家也可以用以控制线虫危害，尽管现在溴甲烷的使用需要经过详细的审查并且考虑到大气质量可能将被禁止使用。因此一些新的原料，诸如sodium tetrathiocarbonate 和cadusafos近来已被引入使用。
在世界各地，系统的杀线剂被广泛使用，但在一些情况下由于水土污染而在商贸交易中被退回。一些常见的杀线剂包括：涕灭威、克百威、灭克磷、丰索磷、福赛绝和殴杀灭。 For many annual hosts of P. penetrans, the only effective chemical control is preplant soil fumigation. Currently, in many countries, the choice of soil fumigants is limited to 1,3-dichloropropene, methyl isothiocyanate, metam-sodium or dazomet (the latter two yielding methyl isothiocyanate when contacted by soil moisture). These products are used individually, or in mixtures. The mixtures may also contain chloropicrin, if fungicidal activity is also required. Methyl bromide, a general-purpose soil sterilant, is also used for control of lesion nematodes in some countries, although its use is presently under close scrutiny and will probably be terminated because of atmospheric quality concerns. A few new materials, such as sodium tetrathiocarbonate and cadusafos, have been recent introductions since the concern over methyl bromide was enunciated. 

Systemic nematicides have been widely used in many parts of the world, but in some cases have been withdrawn from commerce due to soil water contamination. Some of the more commonly used systemic chemicals include aldicarb, carbofuran, ethoprophos, fensulfothion, fosthiazate and oxamyl. 使用生物制剂防治穿刺短体线虫主要集中在各种真菌上，但也包含了一些对放线菌、细菌和土壤中取食线虫的动物的研究。Stirling认为所有的迁移型植物内寄生线虫都是很难用天敌防治的。如短体线虫和类穿孔线虫，它们生活史的大部分时间在根部，只有其寄主植物承受不住压力，开始衰老或患病，或者被收获犁耕时，这些线虫才可在土壤中被发现。所以生物防治的成果必定是极其有限的。
一个早期使用真菌诱捕线虫的成功例子是Rama Rao完成的，他发现葡萄串状节丛孢菌Arthrobotrys arthrobotryoides,指状节丛孢菌 A. dactyloides, 指状菌Dactylaria thaumasia 和小指菌Dactylella doedycoides可以显著减少穿刺短体线虫在紫花苜蓿根上的穿刺。A. dactyloides是最为有效的种类。Wimble和Young 详细描述了穿刺短体线虫被Dactylella lysipaga侵染的机制，Dactylella lysipaga的侵入钉与A. dactyloides的诱捕环无相似性。Timper和Brodie还发现了A. dactyloides与节丛孢菌Arthrobotrys oligospora、椭圆单顶孢Monacrosporium ellipsosporum 和柱捕单顶孢M. cionopagum一样，可以杀死大部分的穿刺短体线虫的成虫和幼虫。他们还发现Hirsutella rhossiliensis和M. ellipsosporum减少了53%沙土中的穿刺短体线虫。Miller和Anagnostakis使用不同的方法，将非诱捕型的真菌绿色木霉Trichoderma viride的菌丝体切碎，置于含有穿刺短体线虫的土壤中，3周内使得虫口密度降低了90%。最近，Kimura等人使用曲霉滤出液，活性物质是赭曲霉代谢物，杀线活性可达80%。
与之不同的是，Jansson和Nordbring-Hertz发现穿刺短体线虫只吸引13种供试食线虫真菌中的两种；Voss和Wyss发现在穿刺短体线虫的发育阶段不存在Catenaria anguillulae的寄生病；Jansson等人发现Drechmeria coniospora的分生孢子可粘附在穿刺短体线虫的头和尾部，但并不寄生。
Dicklow提供了使用放线菌防治穿刺短体线虫的明确例证，他从哥斯达黎加抑制线虫的土壤中分离得到一种特殊的链霉菌，应用于美国马萨诸塞州的田间实验，减少了草莓根部的线虫数量，并抑制了黑根腐病菌的侵染。温室也在用氮素材料如蟹壳质和煤泥等改良土壤后，使用放线菌控制线虫。这表明放线菌释放的毒素与氨和硝酸盐能够共同作用。

Nematodes such as Pratylenchus and Radopholus spend much of their lives in roots and tend to be found in soil only when their host plants are stressed, senescing or diseased, or when their hosts have been ploughed out after harvest. It is difficult to envisage biological control agents being of more than limited value against them.

description: During a survey in February 2011, root and soil samples were collected from 16 common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) fields in Paraná state, southern Brazil. potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pP. coffeae is a major pest of bananas, plantains and abaca, yams, coffee, ginger, citrus and other crops.^p^p^Bananas^p^pP. coffeae is of particular importance on bananas in the Pacific island countries (Bridge, 1988) and parts of Africa (Sarah 1989), and on bananas, plantains and abaca (Musa textilis) in Cuba, Central and South America (Gowen and Queneherve, 1990). P. coffeae rarely occurs as the only nematode pest on the roots of Musa species. Although localized in South Africa, where it is found as the main nematode pest, the estimated crop losses can be as high as 80% (Sarah, 1989). In Cuba, high population densities cause toppling of the plants and limit production of the crop; economic threshold densities of the nematode have been estimated at 5000-10,000 nematodes per 100 g roots in good soils but as low as 1000-5000 nematodes per 100 g roots in soils with low fertility (Fernandez and Ortega, 1998).^p^p^Yams (Dioscorea spp.)^p^pP. coffeae has been recorded as a parasite of yams in Barbados, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, and in the Pacific islands of Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Niue, Tonga, Vanuatu and Solomon Islands. P. coffeae is the cause of tuber dry rot disease of yams, known locally in Jamaica as burn. (Ayala and Acosta, 1971; Brathwaite, 1977; Coates-Beckford and Brathwaite, 1977; Bridge, 1988).^p^pP. coffeae is important as a parasite of the tubers reducing their edible portions, marketable value and, particularly, their storage qualities. In the regions of the world where the nematode occurs it can be very widespread. In Jamaica, 67 to 100% of D. rotundata and D. cayenensis tubers were found to be infected with P. coffeae (Thompson et al., 1973), and over 50% of D. alata tubers examined in Papua New Guinea had obvious signs of dry rot and were infested with P. coffeae sometimes in numbers in excess of 60,000 nematodes per 50 g tissues (Bridge and Page, 1984). Where there are obvious signs of dry rot in the tubers the likelihood of complete rot of tubers during storage is high. Dry rot of yams alone causes a marked reduction in the quality, marketable value and edible portions of tubers, and these reductions are more severe in stored yams.^p^pSoil populations of 600 P. coffeae per vine of D. rotundata can produce significant tuber damage, and 1000 nematodes/plant can cause complete deterioration and severe reduction in tuber quality (Acosta and Ayala, 1975). However, neither of these populations causes reduction in total weight of harvested tubers. If seed tubers are badly affected by dry rot but survive storage, they can be so weakened that sprouting does not occur (Acosta and Ayala, 1976; Coates-Beckford and Brathwaite, 1977). Control of P. coffeae in seed pieces by chemical treatment can increase the yield of high quality tubers from 0.03 to 6.09 tonnes per hectare (Roman et al., 1984). Similarly, disinfesting tuber planting material with hot water treatment to control P. coffeae can increase tuber yields by 23% (Hutton et al., 1982).^p^p^Coffee^p^pP. coffeae is found as pest of coffee in Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Puerto Rico, Costa Rica, Cuba and Brazil. P. coffeae also occurs on coffee in India, Southeast Asia, Barbados, Martinique, and Tanzania, Madagascar and in Indochina. In Java and India it is a very damaging and major pest of coffee (Campos et al., 1990). P. coffeae is the most destructive nematode of Coffea arabica in South India (Palanichamy, 1973). The use of nematicides to control P. coffeae can increase coffee yields by 28% (Figueroa, 1978).^p^p^Ginger, Turmeric^p^pP. coffeae is widely distributed on ginger and turmeric in Kerala and Himachal Pradesh in India (Koshy and Bridge, 1990) where it is the cause of 'ginger yellows' and infects both roots and rhizomes (Kaur and Sharma, 1990). management_info: Cultural Control^p^pIn yams, the use of plant material which is free of nematodes and dry rot disease is an effective means of controlling or reducing the damage caused by P. coffeae. Central or distal tuber pieces, which generally contain lowest number of P. coffeae, are recommended as propagative material. Seed tubers showing symptoms of dry rot (cracking and flaking) should not be used for planting.^p^pAny foliar material used for propagation should be completely free of P. coffeae. Yams, such as Dioscorea bulbifera and some forms of D. alata, can be readily propagated from bulbils or aerial tubers. A number of yams, such as D. alata, D. rotundata and D. dumetorum, can be produced from vine cuttings. Even true seed can be used for propagating D. rotundata.^p^pAlthough these methods of propagation are not a practical means of producing ware tubers, they can be used to produce nematode-free seed tubers. Producing large numbers of seed tubers from relatively few yams by growing 'microsetts' or 'minisetts' cut from mature tubers (IITA, 1984) effectively produces nematode-free propagation material if clean, healthy 'mother seed yams' are selected (Jatala and Bridge, 1990).^p^pIn bananas, planting nematode disease-free suckers is recommended. Some growers or organizations maintain 'disease-free' nurseries from which new planting material, usually sword suckers, is collected. More commonly, planting material is taken from existing banana fields and these are more likely to be infested with nematodes. If the external tissue of the corm has purple or reddish-brown lesions, these, together with root stumps and adhering soil should be removed with a machete (pared) until only white corm tissue is exposed.^p^pParing suckers should take place away from the field, and corms with severe lesions should be discarded. Although useful, the paring technique may never be totally effective in removing all nematode infection; this treatment is often complemented by dipping suckers in a nematicidal solution or, more effectively, by coating them with a nematicidal mud.^p^pIn Cote d'Ivoire, it is recommended practice to store large corms in the sun for 2 weeks prior to planting; populations of Radopholus similis in the corm tissue can decline by as much as 80%. The most reliable means of avoiding the introduction of the nematode is to use completely nematode-free banana plantlets grown from meristem cultures (Queneherve and Cadet, 1985; Gowen and Queneherve, 1990).^p^p^Hot-Water Treatment^p^pBananas^p^pThe immersion of banana suckers in water held at a constant 55°C for periods of 15-25 minutes has been a commercial practice in Australia and Central and South America (Stover, 1972). However, the technique is difficult to manage because of the critical balance that is required to achieve a temperature that is lethal to nematodes in the corm tissue but does not cause permanent damage to the plant. This factor can also be important if suckers are not of uniform size.^p^pYams^p^pIn yam tubers, theoretical, but not always practical, control of P. coffeae can be achieved by hot water treatment. The immersion of tubers in hot water can reduce tuber populations of P. coffeae considerably, but rarely eliminates them without damage to the tuber.^p^pHot water at 46-52°C for 15-30 minutes is recommended for control of P. coffeae in D. rotundata tubers. The use of seed tubers with extreme dry rot should be avoided as treatment of these tubers is less effective. Treatments in water at 51°C for 15-45 minutes also effectively suppresses populations of P. coffeae and dry rot in D. rotundata tubers, and also increases vine growth. However, hot water treatment can cause severe physiological damage (Acosta and Ayala, 1976; Coates-Beckford and Brathwaite, 1977; Thompson et al., 1973).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pNematicides are widely used by commercial banana growers producing fruit for the international export trade. potential_eco_desc: Stubby root nematodes (Paratrichodorus and Trichodorus) are migratory ectoparasites that feed on roots and vector tobraviruses. They are important to the potato industry as they transmit Tobacco rattle virus (TRV) causing corky ringspot disease, which has a direct economic impact on growers due to abandonment or rejection by processing or fresh markets.
description: In October 2014, three soil samples were collected from a potato field in Sargent Co., ND, to determine the occurrence of stubby root nematodes (SRN). Most of the field was harvested but a portion of the field was abandoned due to 80 to 90% of the tubers (cv. Milva) exhibiting the typical brown necrotic ring, arc, and spot symptoms of corky ringspot. Diseased tubers from this field were tested and found to be infected with TRV. Nematodes were extracted from soil using sugar centrifugal flotation and one of the samples was found to contain SRN (44/kg soil). In April 2015, 49 soil samples were collected from the same field and seven of the samples had SRN with population densities ranging from 135 to 300 (mean = 175) per kg of soil. Nematodes were examined morphologically and molecularly for species identification, the nematode species was identified as Paratrichodorus allius. potential_eco_desc: Stubby root nematodes, including P. minor, cause severe crop losses to a variety of vegetable crops (IFAS, 1989) but there is limited information available on estimated losses caused by P. minor (Brodie, 1984). P. minor is known to be responsible for stubby root symptoms on a wide variety of plants, but major pest status results from the known ability to transmit tobacco rattle virus [tobacco rattle tobravirus] and to a more restricted extent (only known from Brazil) pepper ringspot virus [pepper ringspot tobravirus] (Brown et al., 1989).^p^pP. minor is considered an important limiting factor on vegetable crops grown in light soils in the subtropical regions of the USA (Perry and Rhoades, 1982). Netscher (1970) reported that P. minor caused a 50% reduction in root weight of tomato in Senegal. P. minor is considered a major pest on corn where populations are large (Norton, 1984). The stubby-root nematode was more destructive than either reniform or root-knot nematode in the first 30 days after inoculation.^p^pP. minor and P. porosus are found abundantly associated with sugarcane crops. They are believed to cause much damage to sugarcane, but few experiments have been made to prove the pathogenicity of the genus, and the amount of tonnage and sucrose losses to sugarcane is unknown (Birchfield, 1984). Although P. minor had a sporadic distribution in Hawaii, it should be considered an important pest of sugarcane where it occurs in relatively large numbers (Apt and Koike, 1962). P. minor together with Helicotylenchus dihystera and Criconemella ornata was responsible for reduction in yield of sweet corn (Johnson, 1975).

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pP. minor is easily killed by nematicides. Both fumigant and non-fumigant nematicides, as pre-plant treatments of soil or when applied at planting time, have been effective in reducing initial damage and in giving the crop a head-start on the nematode (Streu, 1975; Rodriguez-Kabana et al., 1979). The species is, however, notorious for the ease with which it re-establishes itself after treatment with fumigants.Johnson and Chalfant (1973) considered non-fumigant materials such as aldicarb and carbofuran to be more effective in controlling P. minor than fumigants. Population re-establishment was slower, and onion yields higher, after treatment with fensulfothion, carbofuran, prophos [ethoprophos], aldicarb and phorate than with the fumigant 1,3-dichloropropene (Rhoades, 1969). P. minor was controlled for up to 8 months in the root zone of Japanese holly (Ilex crenata) with aldicarb (Benson and Barker, 1978). Prophos [ethoprophos] reduced numbers of P. minor in bermuda grass 1 month after treatment (Lucas, 1985). Also treatment with fenamiphos significantly reduced populations of P. minor on bermuda grass (Tarjan and Frederick, 1984) and on corn (Rhoades, 1985), but fenamiphos was found phytotoxic in sunflower field trials where it reduced plant emergence (Rich and Dunn, 1982). Herbicides, including EPTC on corn, peanuts, soyabeans and monosodium methancarbonate, do not significantly affect nematode population densities of P. minor on cotton (Johnson et al., 1975; O'Bannon and Stokes, 1978) or decrease populations of P. minor on peanut (Johnson et al., 1983).^p^pEvaluation of nematicides for control of P. minor indicates that nematicides should be used only with caution and where nematodes are present in significant numbers (Minton et al., 1976). Greenhouse tests showed significant damage on Thompson Seedless grape by inoculation with only 100 P. minor specimens (Hafez et al., 1981).^p^p^Cultural Control^p^pCrop rotation as a means of control is not generally suggested or practised because of the polyphagous nature of P. minor, though crop rotation may be advantageous under some circumstances (Johnson et al., 1983). P. minor populations usually appear unaffected by crop rotations, including turnip-corn-chickpea (Johnson et al., 1990), okra, sorghum-sudangrass followed by rye, squash or eggplant (McSorley and Gallaher, 1994b). Good et al. (1973) reported the greatest increase in population under cropping systems involving millet, Sudan grass and okra, whereas the smallest increase occurred in cropping systems involving crotalaria and fallow. The use of poor hosts or non-host crops reduced populations of P. minor (Haroon and Abadir, 1989). Asparagus officinalis is known to be antagonistic to many nematode species including P. minor due to toxic glycoside present in the roots (Paxton, 1975). Crotalaria spectabilis has been shown to be a non-host of nematodes, including P. minor, and when used as a cover crop will reduce nematode densities (Rhoades, 1964; Brodie and Murphy, 1975).^p^pControlling P. minor by fallow appeared effective. Six weeks of fallow between tomato harvest and the following cover crops (crotalaria or maize) was as effective as a continuous fallow in preventing an increase in the population of P. minor (Brodie and Murphy, 1975). Christie (1959) observed that fallow or fallow and dry tillage may be fairly effective, whereas flooding is not very effective. Overman (1964), however, found that flooding for 2 weeks reduced populations significantly and that this effect was improved if flooding was followed by 2 weeks of drying. Tillage practices and management of cover crop residues may have little effect on P. minor populations McSorley and Gallaher, 1994a, b.^p^pCrop loss in sugarcane due to P. minor can be significantly reduced by growing sugarcane on soils other than sands and loamy sands. host_range: P. quercivorus has a wide host range. It attacks many species of the family Fagaceae but it is also known to attack trees from other families including Aquifoliaceae, Lauraceae, Rosaceae and Cupressaceae (Wood and Bright, 1992).Affected Plant Stages:</
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pDirect damage caused by P. quercivorus is associated with galleries constructed in the wood of host trees during breeding attacks. This can result in the loss of structural integrity in the wood and loss of lumber quality. ^p^pSince the early 1980s, extensive mortality of oak forests has been reported from western Japan (Kaneko, 1995). This condition, referred to as Japanese oak disease, is now attributed to the fungus Raffaelea quercivora, an anamorphic Ascomycete, which is a fungal associate of P. quercivorus (Ito et al., unda). The mortality of oak trees, at a rate of more than 200,000 per year, has been observed in the western coastal areas of Honshu, Japan (EPPO, 2003). The deciduous species of oaks, Quercus serrata and Quercus mongolica are susceptible to the disease. Other trees of the family Fagaceae that are present in the area, e.g. Quercus acutissima, Quercus acuta, Quercus phillyraeoides and Castanopsis sieboldii, are apparently not affected by the fungus (Ito et al., unda). To date, the most severe tree mortality has occurred on the west coast of Honshu (Hamaguchi and Goto, 2003). ^p^pIt has been postulated that oaks, which are resistant or tolerant to Raffaelea quercivora, co-evolved under a stable relationship between the tree, fungus and beetle during a long evolutionary process. Q. mongolica may not have been part of this co-evolution. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that P. quercivorus has the least preference for Q. mongolica but exhibits the highest reproductive success in this species. Therefore, P. quercivorus could spread more rapidly in stands with a high composition of Q. mongolica. The present oak dieback epidemic in Japan may have resulted from the warmer climate that began in the late 1980s. This facilitated the encounter of P. quercivorus and Q. mongolica, by allowing the beetle to extend its range to more northerly latitudes and higher altitudes (Kamata et al., 2002).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pP. quercivorus, in combination with its associated ambrosia fungus, Raffaelea quercivora is capable of causing extensive tree mortality in oak forests dominated by Quercus mongolica and Quercus serrata. This could result in major environmental impacts such as the loss of biodiversity, changes in the species composition of forests, reduced acorn crops and the resultant adverse impacts on wildlife species that depend on these crops for food.

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pThe yearly incidence of attacks is typically 2-5% but may be as high as 30%. The cumulative incidence of attacks may be as high as 87% (Langor et al., 1992). Repeated attacks on the same tree cause a crooked or forked stem and bushy crown, thus reducing the tree's value as lumber (Salman, 1935). Leader loss can be recovered in 2-3 years if the tree is not attacked in succeeding years. The economic impact of P. terminalis is generally considered to be minor, even though infestations may be quite high in thinned plantations. However, there has never been a thorough examination of the economic impacts of this species. In forests managed for fibre or saw-logs, weevil-impact is minor, since the trees tend to recover their growth and form fairly quickly following attack. For high-quality Christmas trees, even light weevil damage is unacceptable as it affects the tree form. However, jack pine and lodgepole pine are not preferred species in the Christmas tree industry. Although P. terminalis vectors some fungi, there is no evidence that these fungi are pathogenic or cause significant degradation of lumber due to staining or other defects (Mallett and Langor, 1996).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pAs this species only affects tree form and to a small extent tree growth and is not a source of tree mortality, there is no evidence of environmental impact.

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pRepeated attacks on the same tree cause a crooked or forked stem and bushy crown, thus reducing the tree's value as lumber. Defects in wood due to wane, bark-encased knots and red rot due to vectored fungi can also result in significant cull. In Ontario, Canada, Brace (1972) estimated that timber value was reduced by an average of 25% due to P. strobi. Later, in the same province, Gross (1985) estimated annual growth losses at 8000 m3, annual volume loss due to cull at 15,400 m3 and an additional 15,600 m3 of timber which suffered a 25% loss in value. In 1967 in New Hampshire, USA, volume losses caused by weevils were estimated at 40% in the saw-log portion of saw-timber trees (Godwin and Reeks, 1967). Both planting programmes and management practices have been significantly affected by this weevil. However, studies have shown that trees more than 30 years old are seldom attacked.^p^p^Environmental impact^pAs P. strobi affects only tree form and to a small extent tree growth, and is not a source of tree mortality, there is no evidence of environmental impact.

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pP. strobi appears to be a fairly strong flier, and flight is the principal means of dispersal from stand to stand. Within stands beetles can also simply walk to nearby trees from overwintering sites in the duff (old litter). It appears that most individuals do not move far (Harman and Kulman, 1967; Harman, 1975). It is not known how far P. strobi can disperse on an annual basis. ^p^pMovement in Trade/Transport^p^pInternational spread would most probably occur via the shipment of living conifer plants, including Christmas trees. remark: P. strobi is an EPPO A1 quarantine pest (OEPP/EPPO, 1980), but no other regional plant protection organization has cited it as a quarantine pest. As a serious pest of the introduced Picea sitchensis and the native P. abies, two very important timber species in Europe, and with an obvious potential to establish in the conditions of northern Europe which resemble those of Canada, P. strobi clearly presents a serious risk for the EPPO region. It seems to have less potential importance on European Pinus spp., since P. strobus is no longer planted to any significant extent; however, it has successfully attacked several European Pinus species in plantations in North America.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Considerable recent effort has been invested in the exploration of genetic resistance as a management tool, particularly in Sitka spruce (Alfaro and Ying, 1990; Kiss, 1991; Klimaszewski et al., 2000; King and Alfaro, 2001). Cultural control tactics by manipulation of stand densities and shading hold some promise for reducing P. strobi impact (Berry and Stiell, 1976; Taylor et al., 1996). ^p^pChemical control has been achieved by using various insecticides (see references in Langor, 1998). Stem implants containing the systemic insecticides oxydemeton-methyl or acephate have been used successfully on P. sitchensis in British Columbia, Canada (Fraser and Heppner, 1993). Some experimentation with leader and systemic applications of neem EC formulations for control of P. strobi on jack pine (Pinus banksiana) and white pine (P. strobus) in Ontario have yielded good results (Helson et al., 1998). Control using juvenile hormone analogues shows some promise (Dimond and Bradbury, 1992). ^p^pThere is good potential for pursuing classical biological control tactics for this pest. In 1950, a braconid, Coeloides sp., was introduced from Europe and released in southern Quebec but it is unknown whether this became established (McGugan and Coppel, 1962). From 1986 to 1999, the braconids, Eubazus robustus and E. semirugosus were shipped to Canada from Europe and released in cages against P. strobi (Hulme and Kenis, 2002). E. semirugosus gave the most promising results but additional work is needed before open releases can be considered. Alfaro et al. (1995) describe an integrated pest management (IPM) system relying on accurate hazard rating of plantation sites and continuous monitoring of attack levels.^p^pPhytosanitary Measures^p^pTo prevent the introduction of life stages of P. strobi, EPPO recommends that the importation of plants and cut branches of host species of Picea and Pinus from North America should be prohibited (OEPP/EPPO, 1990). There is also a minor risk from conifer wood, which is effectively covered by the measures recommended by EPPO (OEPP/EPPO, 1990) for non-European Scolytidae (EPPO/CABI, 1992).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pP. piniphilus is considered to be among the most injurious insect pests in pine forests of some regions of eastern, northern and central Europe, particularly in the Baltic states, Finland and Russia (Kohh, 1939; Saalas, 1949; Maavara et al., 1961; Bogdanova, 1985; Ozols, 1985; Demakov, 1994, 1998; Voolma, 2000). The middle-aged stands of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), growing on dry sandy soils, are mostly affected. P. piniphilus first attacks trees that have been previously damaged by defoliating insects, root-rot or other diseases, or by abiotic factors. Subsequently the trees will be colonised by Tomicus piniperda, Tomicus minor and other bark and wood-boring insects that kill the tree.^p^pKohh (1939) and Riis (1975) provided a review of Estonian literature on the damage caused by P. piniphilus. A brief overview of the damage caused by the pine-top weevil in pine forests of Estonia is also given by Voolma and Luik (2001). In southern Estonia, an outbreak of P. piniphilus was reported at the end of the nineteenth century when more than 370 ha of pole-stage pine stands were destroyed and cut down (Knersch, 1901). In the 1930s, a large-scale outbreak occurred in south-east Estonia, where 3453 ha of damaged pine stands (average of 60 years old) were registered in 1937-1938 (Kohh, 1939). Some damage also occurred in northern Estonia. Altogether, more than 55,000 m2 of timber was cut in the damaged areas (Kohh, 1939). In 1971-1972, a small outbreak (43 ha) of P. piniphilus occurred almost in the same region of southern Estonia (Riis, 1975). At the beginning of the 1990s, P. piniphilus widely infested pine stands in southern Estonia again (Luik, 1993, 1994; Pilt, 1994). In particular, an outbreak of P. piniphilus occurred in pine stands infested by root-rot diseases, caused by Heterobasidion annosum and Armillaria spp. According to data from the Estonian Centre of Forest Protection and Silviculture, 209-699 ha of damaged pine stands were registered annually in 1992-2000 (Asi et al., 2002).^p^pDemakov (1996) described an outbreak of P. piniphilus in the Marii-El Republic, Russia, in 1981-1991, which covered 300,000-350,000 ha. The most severe damage was observed in dry boreal pine forests (Vaccinum vitis-idea and Vaccinum myrtillus-site types), where 57% of trees in middle-aged stands and 30% of trees in pre-mature stands died (Demakov, 1996). During the outbreak, P. piniphilus attacked 15- to 200-year-old pine trees. At the same time, a high population level of P. piniphilus was observed in other regions of central Russia (Moscow and Tver provinces) (Demakov, 1996).^p^pP. piniphilus is also one of the commonest curculionids in artificial Scots pine plantations of Western Siberia, where most of the damage is caused by the weevils during both maturation and renewal feeding in the crowns of growing pines (Bogdanova, 1985).^p^pP. piniphilus is considered to be a vector of Endocronartium pini, the fungus that causes resin-top disease of pines (Pappinen and von Weissenberg, 1994a, b, 1996; Pappinen, 1996). A possible role of P. piniphilus in the dispersal of the blister-rust fungus (Peridermium sp.) attacking P. sylvestris was suggested by Kangas (1938) and Rennerfelt (1943). Several species of insects were found in sections of infected stems, including P. piniphilus, Pissodes pini, and the Lepidoptera Dioryctria splendidella and Laspeyresia coniferana, but it is not known whether any of these plays a part in natural infection. Under laboratory conditions, the ability of P. piniphilus to carry E. pini spores and its ability to infect P. sylvestris in the field, were investigated in Finland. It was concluded that the weevil may carry spores and cause infection in healthy trees (Pappinen and von Weissenberg, 1994b).^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pThe ecological role of P. piniphilus was assessed by Demakov (1994), with special reference to the amount of tree mortality in stands. management_info: See Fuhrer and Kerck (1978a, b) for a discussion of forest-protection problems in wind-damaged pine pole forests in Luneburg Heath, Germany. Insect attack was assessed in 1973-1975 in standing trees in Pinus sylvestris stands, some damaged by windthrow in 1972, and some adjacent to damaged stands. In the summer of 1974, 30% of trees sampled within the windthrown areas contained larvae of a Pissodes species (probably P. piniphilus). Trees in stands adjacent to the windthrown areas were only slightly affected by bark-breeding insects. In uncleared windthrown areas, the frequency of Pissodes attack was similar for apparently healthy and for partially-uprooted trees. In areas that had been cleared before spring 1974, more healthy trees were attacked by Pissodes than in uncleared stands. It was recommended that if clearing of windthrown pine pole stands cannot be done before beetle emergence in the first summer after windthrow, then the stands should be left uncleared until the following May, to allow uprooted stems to act as trap trees.^p^pTo reduce losses caused by secondary bark-breeding insects, including P. piniphilus, sanitary felling restricted to infested and dead trees is recommended (e.g. Kohh, 1938, 1939; Kozak, 1978). P. piniphilus should be controlled by the removal of freshly colonized trees.^p^pIn addition, natural stands and plantations of P. sylvestris damaged by Heterobasidion annosum should be monitored, and weakened trees promptly removed to prevent outbreaks of P. piniphilus and other xylophagous insect pests (Bogdanova, 1998).

potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pP. castaneus is an important pest of Pinus spp. in France, UK, Russia, Finland and Spain where large numbers of young trees in new plantations may be killed. In addition, attacks by this weevil cause serious losses of young Pinus in both natural stands and plantations in southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean (Kailidis, 1964). In Portugal, P. castaneus shows a preference for grafted P. pinaster, tunnelling in small branches and endangering the success of the graft. In plantations grown for seed, infestation resulted in severe reductions in yield (Silva and Nogueira, 1967). It almost exclusively attacks 2- to 15-year-old trees, but even 100- to 120-year-old trees are not immune. Development may also occur in felled pine logs and split firewood. The most serious damage is caused by the larvae, whereas the adults cause little damage.^p^pUsually this weevil is a secondary pest of conifers which have been weakened in some way. Often it may be associated with or succeed another pest, for example Pityogenes bidentatus. In the south of France, P. castaneus is a principal pest of Pinus attacked previously by the coccid Matsucoccus feytaudi (Carle, 1974; Arzone and Vidano, 1981); however, Alauzet (1969) showed that from 1962 to 1963, 58% of trees were destroyed by P. castaneus alone and it may, therefore, also be a primary pest of P. pinaster in France.^p^p^p^Environmental impact^pAlthough P. castaneus is mainly a plantation pest, it also attacks young trees in natural stands. However, no serious environmental impact is reported.
