management_info: To decrease the incidence of pine wilt, insecticides such as fenitrothion and carbaryl are sprayed on the crown of trees by hand, sprinkler or helicopter twice during the M. alternatus adult emergence period. This is to prevent the beetles from feeding on pine twig bark and to reduce the number of nematodes transmitted to healthy trees. A simple simulation model for optimal spraying time is constructed using the emergence and survivorship curves of M. alternatus adults, the transmission curve of B. xylophilus, and mortality curves of M. alternatus after insecticide treatment (Togashi, 1980b). Insecticide application against M. alternatus adults shows a high efficacy (Kobayashi, 1988; Kishi, 1995) but three problems are pointed out in the aerial application of insecticides. First is the increased survival rate of immature M. alternatus due to an increased mortality of natural enemies. Second is the disturbance of the biological community in the pine forest ecosystem. Third is the diffusion of insecticide from the pine forests. When aerial applications are conducted twice in June, mortality due to predacious insects decreases for beetle cohorts produced in June and July but it increases for cohorts produced in August (Togashi, 1990d).^p^pA trap using a-pinene and ethanol as attractants has been developed (Ikeda et al., 1980). It can be used to monitor M. alternatus as trees surrounding the trap are likely to succumb to pine wilt disease, even if they have had insecticide applied.^p^pWhen Pinus densiflora and P. thunbergii were treated with paraquat dichloride or ethephon, they receive ten times as many oviposition scars as untreated, nematode-infected trees (Yamasaki et al., 1980). Volatile oil from paraquat-induced lightwood is attractive to M. alternatus (Yamasaki and Suzuki, 1982), (+)-cis-3-pinen-2-ol in the oil is attractive for male beetles only (Sakai and Yamasaki, 1991). Control measures using paraquat-treated trees as a lure have not yet been established.^p^pM. alternatus in dead trees are destroyed by burning, chipping, spraying insecticide or fumigation after felling (Kobayashi, 1988; Kishi, 1995). Burning and fumigation can be expected to eradicate the insects in dead trees. However, branches and the edges of logs sometimes break the plastic sheet used for wrapping for fumigation, resulting in incomplete eradication. Burning in pine forests induces the occurrence of a fungal disease by Rhizina undulata, a mortality factor of pine trees, in Japan (Sato et al., 1970). The efficacy of insecticide spraying fluctuates depending on season of application and insecticide formulation (Kishi, 1995). When logs infested with M. alternatus are buried in soil over 15 cm deep, no adults emerge from the soil (Matsubara and Yonebayashi, 1980). The greatest problem with the eradication of M. alternatus harboured in dead trees is that it is very difficult for workers on the ground to find all the dead pine trees in the forest.^p^pApplication of the entomophagous fungus, Beauveria bassinana, with nonwoven fabric strips induces an 80% mean mortality of M. alternatus larvae in the field (Shimazu et al., 1995). Beauveria brongniartii is less effective than B. bassiana in laboratory tests (Shimazu, 1994). Application of Steinernema carpocapsae in mid-April causes ca. 70 % mortality of larvae within the logs (Yamanaka, 1994) whereas the application of Steinernema kushidai to pine logs is ineffective (Mamyia, 1989). Release of approximately 20 Sclerodermus sichuanensis adults per infected tree resulted in parasitism ranging from 36.4 to 100% 2 weeks later. After 1 year infection rates had fallen by 57.7% compared to control areas with a mean parasitization rate of 69.7% (Yang et al., 1999). ^p^pInjection of nematicides such as mesulfenhos, morantel tartalic acid, and levamysol hydrochloride, into healthy tree trunks during winter prevents the development of pine wilt disease, resulting in a reduced reproduction rate of M. alternatus (K

management_info:
1 监测。 首先应对其进行较为准确的监测，结合气候、森林资源分布及遗传信息等情况对入侵物
种的潜在分布进行预判。
2 人工防除 在广东省，薇甘菊在 3—4 月开始萌芽，6—8 月进入生长旺盛期，9 月出现花蕾，此
时生长速度减缓; 10 月进入开花期，花期可以持续至 12 月，果期 1—2 月，2 月后种子成熟，花枝枯萎，生长期达 8 个月，茎枝每周生 30 cm 以上，一个节一年中所有分枝茎节生长 1007 cm。所以薇甘菊的最佳防治时期是每年 10—12月种子成熟前。利用人工割除、拔除或机械铲除，
先将植株割除，再耕翻晒根，必须尽可能连根拔起，尽量将残留在土壤中的根茎等集中焚烧销毁，务必做到斩草除根。
3 化学防除 目前对于有害生物灾害最有效的控制手段就是化学防治，可以采取喷洒除草剂进行防治。紫薇清( 24% 2，4－滴·二氯吡啶酸水剂)是一种比较好的防治薇甘菊的药剂，为内吸传导型
除草剂，可以通过茎叶吸收传导至植株的各个部位，引起植株枯萎、坏死，最终导致整株死亡，因此可以清理薇甘菊地下部分的根部; 并且其选择性强，对大部分硬阔叶类幼树安全。在薇甘菊大面积覆盖的非经济林地，使用 1000～1500 倍 24%紫薇清水剂进行非定向喷雾; 对薇甘菊与其他植物混合生长在一起的区域，应采用针对茎、叶定向喷药方法。此外，五氟磺草胺、噻吩磺隆、单嘧磺脂 、25%辛酰溴苯腈乳油、48%麦草畏水剂、80% 2，4－滴钠盐可湿性粉剂、氯氟吡氧乙酸乳油、20% 氯氟吡氧乙酸异辛酯乳油、10%草铵膦水剂、48%灭草松水剂和 41%草甘膦异丙胺盐水剂 等对薇甘菊也有一定的防效。
4 生物防治。已有大量关于利用菟丝子 Cuscuta chinensis Lam．强寄生能力来防治薇甘菊的报道，研究者认为菟丝子属 大花菟丝子 Cuscuta reflexa及田野菟丝子 Cuscuta campestris 能寄生并致薇甘菊死亡。但是利用菟丝子属植物防控薇甘菊目前仍存在一定的争议。在深圳 7 个森林公园的薇甘菊危害区投放田野菟丝子并开展野外监测，本地菟丝子对本土其他植物整体上的影响远远小于薇甘菊的影响，因此，可在薇甘菊高度覆盖( 覆盖度＞90%) 且无重要经济作物生长的空地内利用菟丝子防控薇甘菊(  。甘薯 Dioscorea esculenta在植物生长和养分利用方面都比薇甘菊具有竞争优势，因此，可在热带和亚热带地区种植甘薯从而减少薇甘菊的生长 。本地天敌昆虫艳婀珍蝶 Actinote thaliapyrrha 、小蓑蛾 Acanthopsyche． sp.、紫红短须螨 Brevipalpus phoenicis ) 等均被报道对薇甘菊具有一定威胁，但其侵扰能力有限。本土天敌昆虫薇甘菊颈盲蝽Pachypeltis micranthus对薇甘菊具有显著的控制效应 。薇甘菊挥发物对薇甘菊颈盲蝽具有引诱作用 ，薇甘菊颈盲蝽取食薇甘菊叶片，并破坏叶片正常生理功能，导致其最终的叶片萎蔫坏死。薇甘菊颈盲蝽具有取食能力强、取食量大、取食频率高等特点，对薇甘菊的茎、花生长均具有一定影响，抑制其无性繁殖、开花结实量，是一种有效控制薇甘菊传播、扩散的重要天敌昆虫。
5 营林措施 加强林间管理，及时对薇甘菊发生区域的生态系统进行修复。可以在造林时搭配种植一些阔叶树如 幌伞枫 Heteropanax fragrans、血桐 Macaranga tanarius 等，不仅可以提高郁闭度，还可抑制薇甘菊的生长，阻止其入侵 。也可以利用替代控制技术治理薇甘菊的危害，利用本土植物和具有一定生态价值的草本植物来抵御薇甘菊的入侵。黄花蒿 Artemisia annua、高羊茅 Festuca elata、黑麦草 Lolium perenne、杂三叶 Trifolium hybridum、紫花苜蓿Medicago sativa、柱花草Stylosanthes guianensias等不仅具有一定经济价值，还可被用作替代植物进行种植。

potential_eco_desc:
薇甘菊为多年生草质或稍木质藤本，具蔓生茎，攀缘并缠绕幼树、作物或其他植物，使其死亡。薇甘菊是危害经济作物和森林植被的主要害草，薇甘菊所到之处，植物被其攀缘、缠绕或覆盖，难以进行光合作用，可因饥饿而死，或是被重压、绞杀而死。对茶园、橡胶园、香蕉园、柚木林、森林等造成极大的危害，因而薇甘菊被称为“植物杀手”。
薇甘菊具有发生量大、繁殖迅速、传播快、危害重的特点，常在局部区域危害成灾。在其发生地，薇甘菊对土壤生态的影响明显高于本地植物对土壤生态的影响，薇甘菊的入侵使土壤养分和土壤酶活性（如有机质、全氮、全钾、硝态氮、铵态氮、有效磷、速效钾、脲酶和磷酸酶等）显著提高，薇甘菊在竞争过程中，不断通过直接或间接影响土壤微生物区系，进而改善土壤酶活性和土壤英粉含量，使得土壤环境条件向着有利于薇甘菊自身生长的方向发展，形成有利于其入侵繁殖的环境，抑制本地植物的生长，形成其不可替代的优势种群，这可能是薇甘菊在新生态系统的竞争方式之一，也是其成功入侵的重要原因之一。
马来西亚在用薇甘菊作为地面覆盖物时，橡胶树干的茎围比用豆科植物覆盖时少27%，乳胶产量减少27%~29%。20世纪40年代薇甘菊在印度出现后就迅速蔓延，致使茶园、蕉园、柚木林受到严重侵蚀，并造成人工林系统持续减产。在尼泊尔，薇甘菊已入侵到自然林，包括常绿林、半常绿林和潮湿的落叶林，威胁到当地自然生态系统和生物多样性。
薇甘菊对于6~8m高的天然次生林、人工速生林、经济林、风景林的几乎所有树种都具有严重威胁。典型的入侵事件是薇甘菊侵袭珠江口外的伶仃洋中伶仃岛，使该岛自然保护区内460hm2林木中80%受到薇甘菊的危害。在广东的荔枝园也发现有薇甘菊攀爬现象，种种危害现状表明，防控薇甘菊的任务刻不容缓。
在中国和新西兰，薇甘菊被认定为检疫性有害生物。
description:
由于薇甘菊的种子产量及丰富，细小且轻，易借风或动物、昆虫以及人类的活动而远距离传播，也可以通过与土壤接触的节间与匍匐茎蔓延，且生长迅速，单株植物在生长季节几个月内就能扩散蔓延。同时，人工防除时，选择的时期不对，有时甚至是在薇甘菊种子成熟时采取人工拔除、机械除草等，这反而有利于薇甘菊种子的扩散。
在薇甘菊发生区域，通过农产品的运输、园林花卉的交流、交通工具的往来等是薇甘菊远距离快速传播的主要途径。由于其蔓延速度极快，故有些学者称其为“一分种一英里的杂草”。
management_info:
防治方法：
（1）生物学方法：生物防治是控制、防治外来杂草的最有前景的防治方法之一，主要包括对外来杂草有控制作用的真菌、天敌昆虫等的引进。在薇甘菊的原产地热带美洲有9种主要天敌和22种次要天敌。9种主要天敌是：假泽兰滑蓟马Liothrips mikaniae 、半翅目的Telenemia sp.、鞘翅目的Desmogramma conjuncta、Echoma marginata、Echoma quadristillata、Physimerus pygmarus、Apion luterirostre、Pseudoderelomus baridiiformis，以及下毛瘿螨属的一种Acalitus sp.。但利用此类天地进行成功防控的案例很少。此外，也有利用真菌进行防除的报道，在病原菌防除研究方面，我国台湾学者发现齐整小核菌可侵染薇甘菊把造成其大面积死亡，这种病原菌对其他植物也可以致病，因此，用来防除薇甘菊还需要进一步研究。虽然菟丝子是一种危害性较强的杂草，但是有研究表明，田野菟丝子可以很好的防控薇甘菊，但最理想的是能够从相关研究中开发出新型、低成本、高效果、无污染、专一性强的生物源除草剂，已达到安全、有效地控制薇甘菊的目的。
（2）农业措施：在薇甘菊土壤种子库中，上层（0~3cm）土壤种子库密度显著高于下层（3~5cm），幼苗主要有上层土壤中的种子萌发而成。从地表向下对着深度的增加，活力种子逐渐减少。种子随雨水进入种子库时，总是先分布在种子库上层，而后由于动物活动、雨水冲刷、自身重力等原因逐渐下移，越是下层的种子，在种子库中存在的时间越长，种子丧失活力也越多。在经营较细致的农田或果园中，通过翻土等耕作措施，在一定程度上能减少薇甘菊的发生。从整体效果上看，作用不明显，因此农业措施的防控仅能作为辅助手段。但从某种意义上讲，人工防除时一种对环境无危害的较为清洁的一种放出方法。
（3）化学防治：化学防治由于见效较快，多在受害严重的地区采用。研究显示，25%森泰和70%嘧磺隆粉剂（森草净）都有显著杀灭薇甘菊的效果，但前者需要4~5个月见效，后者则能在2~3个月内彻底杀灭，且森草净用量低，0.01~0.001g/m2的森草净（有效成分）就已有良好的杀灭效果。以10%嘧磺隆水悬剂（草灌净）防治薇甘菊的研究显示效果较好，时，用药量在12L/hm2时，薇甘菊死亡率达95%以上。2,4-滴丁酯等对薇甘菊有极好的灭除效果，且作用快速，用药后7d枝条死亡率均在90%以上，14d后枝条死亡率可达100%。氯氟吡氧乙酸（使它隆）混用茶枯粉及一些表面活性剂喷于植株上、中部对薇甘菊的防治作用明显。
尽管有些地区薇甘菊危害严重，且大有向周围蔓延之势，但也并非在短期内就“遍地开花”。在防治上切记操之过急，尤其要慎用各种除草剂和外引天敌，以免造成新的难以预料的生态灾难。在重视生态环境建设的今天，防止外来入侵物种更应遵循自然生态规律，维护生态系统健康，逐步构建合理群落结构，提高生态系统自身免疫力，从而持续有效地抵御其侵害。

potential_eco_desc: 对农业生产及生态环境的危害  薇甘菊能通过大量繁殖幼苗占据空地，以蔓生茎缠绕、攀援、覆盖等多种方式绞杀其他植物，并争夺阳光、水分和养分，从而使其他植物无法正常生长与繁殖，危害农作物，轻者会使作物减产20％以上，严重者造成绝收。薇甘菊繁殖快，能形成密集成片的单优植物群落，快速覆盖生境，影响生物多样性。此外，薇甘菊还可以通过释放化感物质，抑制和危害其他植物的生长，并能降低土壤肥力，表现出争取生存机会的生态功能。据报道：薇甘菊能分泌具有强烈活性的化感物质阿魏酸，可以抑制植物、真菌、细菌的活性，对植物和水稻稻瘟病菌的抑制活性尤为显著；薇甘菊植株的乙醇提取物对水稻、萝卜、黄瓜、菜心具有不同程度的化感作用；其叶片和根的提取物能够抑制某些杂草，如蜈蚣草(Chrysopogon aciculatus)和两耳草(Paspahtm conjugatum)等的生长，导致其纵向生长和幼苗鲜重下降，且抑制作用随浓度的增高而增强。  薇甘菊能够入侵山林、侵占河、沟梗，绞杀其他植物和抑制其他植物的生长，导致植物种类减少，影响生态平衡和生物多样性；伤害植被，毁坏山林、园林景观，严重影响农林牧生产和旅游业发展；如果成为薇甘菊疫区，疫区的苗木、花卉和肥料基质等均不能外运，造成的直接和间接经济损失难以估算。
description: 薇甘菊的传播有自然扩散人为扩散两个途径，两者常相互关联，可借风力、水流畜活动、交通运输等途径传播。人为的农产品的运输物引种、园林花卉的交流、交通工具的往来等是薇甘菊距离快速传播的主要途径。薇甘菊的生长非常迅速殖力甚强，每年开花结果产生的种子数量很大，小而轻的凤媒种子极易扩散。每个节茎乃至节间均可产生不根，每个节的叶腋均可长出一对新枝，另生成新的植株现今公路、街道边土地开发利用增多，土壤裸露，适合甘菊生长的废弃地在增加，这些因素可能会促进薇甘的传播；此外，随着交通运输的日益发达，从疫区调运产品、苗木、土壤等的汽车、火车、船只等交通工具都有能成为薇甘菊的主要传播媒介，这一切都加剧了薇甘的扩散。
remark:
薇甘菊是国际上备受关注的杂草，也是国内外重视的入侵杂草。该种已被列入世界上最有害的100种外来入侵物种之一，也被列入中国首批外来入侵物种。2007年5月28 日，被列入我国进境植物有害植物名录。
如果成为薇甘菊疫区，则疫区的苗木、花卉和肥料基质等均不能外运，这将对国内某些地区发达的苗木花卉产业造成极大的损失。

host_range: M. micrantha is a serious weed of plantation crops including tea, teak, rubber, oil palm and coconut (Holm et al., 1977; Cock, 1982).  It is also a weed of bananas, coffee, and other tree crops, especially in moist locations.
potential_eco_desc: Economic impact^pM. micrantha is widespread throughout South and Central America, but is considered a weed in only a few places. Following its introduction to the Old World from South America, it has become a serious weed of plantation crops including tea, teak, rubber, oil palm and coconut, from India to Oceania (Holm et al., 1977; Cock, 1982). In India, M. micrantha is a serious weed of tea plantations, particularly in areas with high soil moisture. As a climbing vine, it quickly covers and smothers other plants, including other weeds (Dutta, 1977). The annual cost of controlling M. micrantha was estimated at US$9.8 million for rubber, oil palm and cocoa crops in Malaysia (Teoh et al., 1985). ^p^pImpact on Bamboo Plantations^p^pIn one study, 54 species of weeds were collected from a 3-month-old bamboo (Dendrocalamus asper) plantation in Lampung, Indonesia, which had been previously planted with cassava. The number of weed species decreased with the age of the bamboo plantation, from 28 at 6 months to 10 under a 1-year-old crop, probably because crowding by the bamboo leaves suppressed weed growth. By the end of one year, M. micrantha was the most dominant weed. Its climbing habit enabled it to cover the crop plants, suppressing their growth and in some cases killing them (Widjaja and Tjitrosoedirdjo, 1991).^p^pImpact on Tree Crops^p^pM. micrantha competes with teak, merkus pine (Pinus merkusii) and manila copal (Agathis loranthifolia = A. dammara) for nutrients, space and light and causes mechanical damage to the trees (Suharti and Sudjud, 1978). It is also a serious weed of rubber and oil palm plantations (Teoh et al., 1985).^p^p^Environmental impact^pM. micrantha has a major impact on forest communities once established. It smothers native vegetation and eventually kills much of the standing vegetation including trees. In southern China it is a considered to be a major threat to the local biodiversity (Xie et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2004).^p^p^Impact on biodiversity^pM. micrantha was observed in the Neilingding Island (Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China) in 1997, yet two years later it has covered 40-60% of the total land killing local plants. The site is famous for its large population of macaques (Macaca mulatta) and these are now under threat (Xie et al., 2001).^p^p^Impact descriptors^p(dayuhao)i>Negative impact on: (dayuhao)/i>biodiversity; environment; crop production; forestry production; rare / protected species; native fauna; native flora
description: M. micrantha originates in South and Central America where it is widespread but not often a significant weed problem (Holm et al., 1977). It has now been introduced in the Asia-Pacific region (though sometimes referred to mistakenly as M. scandens or M. cordata) (Adams et al., 1972; Holm et al., 1977; Ismail and Mah, 1993). Most of the records in Holm et al. (1977) for M. cordata and M. scandens in Asia almost certainly refer to M. micrantha, while those for M. cordata in West Africa are probably correct. Conversely, most of the records for M. micrantha in mainland Africa cited in EPPO (2005) probably relate to the indigenous M. cordata. The record for Mauritius may be correct but the occurrence of true M. micrantha in mainland Africa has yet to be confirmed.^p^pIn China it was introduced to Hong Kong in the early 20th century (first herbarium records date from 1919). After a long lag-phase it started to spread in the adjoining Guangdong Province in the early 1980s and rapid economic development of the last two decades appear to have assisted the spread of the weed. By the year 2000 the Chinese authorities recognised the species as a major threat and research projects were initiated. In Taiwan M. micrantha was introduced for soil conservation in the 1970s and is now found throughout the island. It was introduced into India and Indonesia as ground cover in the 1940s and then somehow spread to the Pacific Islands, New Guinea and much of South-East Asia (Sankaran, 1999; Zhang et al., 2004). In Malaysia it is believed that the plant was introduced in the early 1950s as non-legume ground cover for rubber plantations due to scarcity of legume seeds (Ismail, 2001). Although M. micrantha is widespread in Sri Lanka it does not appear to be posing a serious economic or ecological threat (Evans, 1999). The weed has recently been reported at a number of sites in northern Australia and M. micrantha is listed as a Northern Australian Quarantine Strategy target species because it has the potential to become a major weed (Anonymous, 2003).

description: Natural Dispersal (Non-Biotic)^p^pDispersal of M. micrantha is mainly by wind, but water dispersal is possible.^p^pVector Transmission^p^pNot documented, but highly likely that it is dispersal by animals.^p^pAccidental Introduction^p^pBeing wind-dispersed, the seeds may be carried on any article that is transported through an area where the weed grows. Vehicles and equipment moving through areas infested with M. micrantha are likely carriers that should be cleaned before travelling long distances to avoid spread of the weed.Transport pathways for long distance movement - Conveyances (transport Vehicles)^p - Soil, Gravel, Water, Etc.^p - Travellers And Baggage

remark: M. micrantha is classified as a Federal Noxious Weed in the USA (Westbrooks, 1989). Seeds, seedheads, stem fragments with seeds, and rootstocks may be intercepted in contaminated commodities. High-risk carriers include forest products, timber, etc. Dispersal is mainly by wind, but also on vehicles and equipment moving through infested areas; these should be cleaned before travelling to uninfested areas. Border clearance personnel with the US Department of Agriculture have intercepted M. micrantha as a contaminant of medicinal herbs from Mexico. Seeds of Mikania spp. have been intercepted as a hitch hiker on a truck entering the USA from Mexico (Westbrooks, 1989).

management_info: Cultural Control^p^pIn Malaysia, it was found that the use of Dorset horn sheep to graze infestations of M. micrantha and several other weeds resulted in cost savings of 15-25% for the overall weed control programme in rubber plantations (Arope et al., 1985).^p^pIn China it is suggested that the establishment of a herb layer in managed orchards, forests, perennial crops (tea and tree plantations), parks and on newly developed areas should somewhat hinder M. micrantha seed germination and by increasing understorey shade in forests it should make growing conditions unsuitable for the vine (Zhang et al., 2004).^p^p^Mechanical ControlIsmail (2001) reported that traditionally, manual control in newly infested crop areas have been carried out by rolling, drying and burning the plants but this proved to be unsustainable. In India manual methods (sickle weeding or uprooting) have been used but these are more expensive than chemical options (Sankaran, 1999).^p^pWhen the vines are cut near the ground once a month for three consecutive months in summer and autumn and then in winter and spring, 90% of the plants can be eliminated. Hand-pulling in southern China is most effective before the end of October, i.e. prior to seed maturity, or during  the March rainy season. A hand-pulling campaign by thousands of citizens was initiated by the Shenzhen government (Guangdong Province) in 2000 and proved quite effective, as many dying trees damaged by M. micrantha subsequently recovered (Zhang et al., 2004).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pYoung M. micrantha is susceptible to standard post-emergence herbicides, 2,4-D, paraquat and glyphosate, and these are the basis for chemical control in most plantation crops. ^p^pIn rubber^pIn Malaysia, field trials were conducted to compare the efficacy of three treatments (grazing by sheep, mechanical slashing and the use of glyphosate+picloram) for the control of M. micrantha (and several other weeds) in a 2-year-old rubber plantation. Two months after treatment, over 90% of weeds had regrown in plots that had been grazed or slashed, compared to (dayuhao)10% weed regeneration in chemically-weeded plots (Ahmad-Faiz, 1992).^p^pIn oil palms^pPreliminary surveys in Malaysia indicated that M. micrantha is associated particularly with rubber and oil-palm plantations. Weed competition was greatest in immature crops and declined as rubber and oil palms matured. Applying paraquat and/or 2,4-D amine was the preferred method of control in plantations. ^p^pA commercial preparation of a mixture of glyphosate and dicamba was evaluated for several years for weed control in >1-year-old oil palms on two plantations in Malaysia. This treatment resulted in a 90% weed control by 30 days after application and 40% by 120 days. Comparable treatment with a mixture of paraquat + diuron produced 95% control by 7 days and 0% by 120 days (Teng and The, 1990).^p^pComplete eradication of M. micrantha from immature oil palm is important to ensure normal growth of the trees. In Indonesia, field experiments were conducted to determine the effectiveness of four translocated herbicides to control M. micrantha in immature oil palms. In all cases, the initial application was followed by a second. The best control was observed on plots that received 2,4-D amine, 2,4-D-sodium and ioxynil, applied 6 weeks apart, hexazinone + diuron at 4 weeks apart, and 2,4-D-sodium followed 6 weeks later by glyphosate (Mangoensoekarjo, 1978).^p^pIn a similar study of M. micrantha in young oil palm plantations in Indonesia, picloram + 2,4-D gave the best results but glyphosate gave only moderate control after 4 weeks. Regrowth of the weed and phytotoxic symptoms on oil palm were not observed on any plots up to 6 weeks after treatment (Hutauruk et al., 1982).^p^pTriclopyr + picloram showed the best results in control trials of the weed in Indian forest plantations (Sankaran, 1999). The use of herbicide in China has been reviewed by Zhang et al. (2004).^p^p^Biologica

description: Root-knot nematodes (RKN) of the genus Meloidogyne are among the most economically important plant-parasitic nematodes infecting coffee in Latin America. Root samples were collected and nematodes were extracted. Meloidogyne izalcoensis Carneiro et al. 2005 was identified from infected coffee roots in Kenya (Kabete) and Tanzania (Mufindi), establishing the first record of this species in these countries on coffee. The same species was also detected on cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) from Benin (Cotonou), and on tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) in Tindini and Kianga, Tanzania, respectively. host_range: Tomato, aubergine, tobacco, pepper (Capsicum annuum) and watermelon are good hosts for Meloidogyne mayaguensis (Rammah and Hirschmann, 1988). Guava and Bidens pilosa are also good hosts and may occur side by side thus serving as alternative hosts (Willers
potential_eco_desc: M. mayaguensis parasitizes coffee in Cuba and occurs sympatrically with, and is more damaging than, Meloidogyne incognita, M. arenaria and M. javanica (Rodriguez et al., 1995). Severe root galling was observed on commercial guava in Nelspruit, South Africa. The attacked trees declined severely or died within 3 years (Willers, 1997b). Bidens pilosa, growing between guava trees, were heavily infested providing a source of infection (Willers, 1997b). M. mayaguensis was also reported causing galling to guava in Brazil (Carneiro et al., 2001). Carneiro et al. (2001) reported M. mayaguensis causing severe damage to commercial guava orchards in Pernambuco and Bahia states. Infested trees had a drastic reduction in growth, reduced leaf size and a decline in yield quantity and quality. Severely infested root systems were poorly developed and were distorted by multiple galls of various sizes. The authors speculated that the nematode had probably been spread from infected nurseries.^p^pM. mayaguensis is more capable of breaking resistance than other common tropical species. Following the use of resistant cultivars, the resistance-breaking lines, with the pVI esterase phenotype using RFLP, were shown to belong to the species M. mayaguensis. These were not lines selected from other existing species of Meloidogyne such as M. incognita, M. arenaria, M. javanica and M. hapla (Fargette et al., 1996). Resistance studies have been done by Maranhao et al. (2003) and Rubio-Cabetas et al. (1999) who reported that the Ma gene from Myrobalan plum (Prunus cerasifera) conferred resistance to M. mayaguensis.

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pIn South Africa, cadusafos used over a 3-year period gave effective control of M. mayaguensis in open pollinated guava seedlings Willers, 1997a,b. Moreira and Henriques Neto (2001) studied the control of M. mayaguensis on guava seedlings in Brazil. They used various nematicides but did not demonstrate a reduction in the development of the nematode population.^p^pBiological Control^p^pIn Senegal, the two local strains (ORS 18692 S7 and ORS 18692 S5) of the nematophagous fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora trapped 98% of groups of 7-day-old M. mayaguensis juveniles within 48 h; optimal growth occurred at 25-30°C and at pH 5.6, but salinity inhibited development. When the fungus was incorporated into compost blocks before sowing and transplanting tomato seedlings, it reduced M. mayaguensis populations and stimulated seedling growth in pot experiments during the cool season (28°C) and in field trials during the hot season (35°C). Both strains were efficient in reducing M. mayaguensis and other species of Meloidogyne populations (Duponnois et al., 1995). Duponnois et al. (2001) investigated the effects of organic amendments on the interactions between A. oligospora and M. mayaguensis parasitizing tomato plants.

management_info: Introduction ^p^pMethods for the control of Meloidogyne spp. Depend largely on crop plant, climate and economic considerations.^p^p^Cultural Methods^p^pFallows have been evaluated (Martin, 1967). Hot-water treatment of potatoes has been used (Martin, 1972). ^p^pCrop rotations with various non-host grasses are used to control M. javanica in tobacco (Shepherd and Barker, 1990). Various potential rotation crops, including Tagetes spp., guinea grass and maize have been assessed for the control of M. javanica on mung beans (Vigna radiata) (Toida, et al., 1991). In pot tests, Crotolaria ochroleuca, C. juncea (legumes) Tagetes erecta (African marigold), sesame and groundnuts were identifed as poor hosts for M. javanica (Madulu et al., 1994). ^p^pOrganic amendments have been assessed to control M. javanica on tomatoes and okra in India (Singh and Sitaramaiah, 1966; 1967) and tested against M. javanica on mung beans (Toida et al., 1994). ^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pRoot-knot resistance in tomatoes was evaluated against M. javanica in India (Sikora et al., 1973). Various vegetable varieties with resistance to M. javanica, including cowpeas, sweet peppers and tomatoes, have been developed in the USA (Lehman and Cochran, 1991).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pWhere cost justifies their use, nematicides can be applied. Many crops have potential for development of resistant or tolerant varieties.^p^pFor general information on the use of nematicides see Luc et al. (1990) and Evans et al. (1993). Both granular and liquid formulations have been used to control this nematode (for example, aldicarb, fenamiphos, carbofuran, ethoprophos and oxamyl). description: Araujia sericifera, is native to South America and was exported to many other countries as an ornamental plant. However, it is now considered an invasive, perennial, noxious weed in Italy. In September 2013, numerous plants of A. sericifera with chlorotic leaves and large root-galls were observed in agricultural fields, gardens, and uncultivated locations in Nocera Inferiore, Salerno Province, Italy. The samples were collected and identified, based on morphological identification and molecular detection showed that the causal agent was Meloidogyne incognita. Weeds are known to serve as hosts for nematodes in the absence of crop plants and to affect the success of nematode management programs. Meloidogyne spp. have been reported to survive and even thrive on weeds; among them, M. incognita is considered the most economically important agricultural nematode pest worldwide as it causes severe yield losses on many hosts. Thus, the invasive plant A. sericifera can be a potential reservoir for M. incognita in Italy and elsewhere. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. incognita parasitizing A. sericifera.
remark: Because of the ability of this plant to spread rapidly and invade natural ecosystems, A. sericifera has been included on the Alert list by the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO).

potential_eco_desc: Introduction^p^pThe root knot nematode species, M. incognita, is the most widespread and probably the most serious plant parasitic nematode pest of tropical and subtropical regions throughout the world (Sasser, 1979). It occurs as a pest on a very wide range of crops. Most estimates of yield loss come from the use of nematicides and it should be noted that these can possibly cause other beneficial growth effects. ^p^p^Cotton^p^pThe most accurate and detailed estimates of cotton yield losses due to nematodes have been undertaken in states of the USA where nematicides are regularly used. In Arkansas, where M. incognita is by far the most important nematode of cotton, yield losses after the application of nematicides are estimated at 1.5% annually; in South Carolina, M. incognita with other nematodes account for an estimated 5% loss annually Kirkpatrick, 1988, 1989). In Texas over a 16-year period of field experiments, the average cotton yield increase was 26% when fields infested with M. incognita were fumigated with nematicides. In six Texan counties, where over 47% of field soils were infested with M. incognita, it was calculated that the total annual yield loss was 10.2% or 85,600 cotton bales (Orr and Robinson, 1984). Disease complexes involving M. incognita and vascular Fusarium wilt on cotton are well recognized. Where the two organisms occur together, increasing the nematode population has a greater effect on wilt incidence and cotton yield loss than an increase in the Fusarium population (Starr et al., 1989; Hillocks and Bridge, 1992; Hillocks, 1997).^p^p^Tobacco^p^pRoot knot nematodes, mainly M. incognita and M. javanica, are always pests of economic importance in tobacco culture, wherever the climate favours them (Barker et al., 1981; Shepherd and Barker, 1990). In North America, losses to tobacco from root knot nematodes, mainly M. incognita, have been estimated to range from 1% to 14% annually in areas where control measures are the norm (Shepherd and Barker, 1990). Root knot nematodes, probably M. incognita, have been estimated to cause 50 to 60% yield losses in parts of Turkey and losses of 25% from field infestation and 50% if the infestation started in the seedbed in India (Shepherd and Barker, 1990). The percentage loss in tobacco yield is estimated to be 8 to 9% for each ten-fold increase in the initial population of M. incognita (Barker et al., 1981). In Cuba, in the region where the highest quality tobacco for cigars is produced, the losses due to M. incognita are estimated at 27.5% of the crop potential of flue-cured tobacco (Garcia and Perez, 1987; Fernandez and Ortega, 1998).^p^p^Food Legumes^p^pM. incognita is a major economic pest of food legumes in the tropics and subtropics (Sikora and Greco, 1990). Moderate soil populations of 1000 nematodes per plant in pathogenicity pot experiments can reduce pod yields of chickpea (Cicer arietinum) by 27% and very high soil populations of 10,000 per plant reduce pod yields by 87%. In M. incognita-infested field plots treated with nematicides, yield of chickpea can increase by 15 to 33% (Reddy, 1976). Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) is very badly damaged by Meloidogyne species in the tropics. Significant bean yield increases of 45 to 60% have been achieved in Kenya by reducing mixed soil populations of M. incognita and M. javanica with the application of nematicides (Ngundo and Taylor, 1974). Similarly in Peru and Colombia, in fields infested with mixed populations of  Meloidogyne species, mainly M. incognita, common bean seed yield can be reduced by 26 to 63% depending on the bean cultivar grown and other factors (Mullin et al., 1991). M. incognita is a serious pest of  Phaseolus vulgaris in the USA where there is a reduction of 66% in crop value in fields where the nematodes are not controlled. The reduced crop value is a result of a combination of reduced plant stands and a 27% lower average pod production by surviving plants (Smittle and Johnson, 1982). Cow

management_info: Methods for the control of M. incognita vary with the production system used and the value of the crop. Chemical control may be used on high-value crops, and a wide range of chemicals are available (Johnson, 1985a; Hague and Gowen, 1987). Strategies of cultural control are less well developed and crop rotations are difficult to design because of the wide host range of M. incognita. Groundnuts or maize, which are both poor or non-hosts to M. incognita, have been evaluated for use in cropping systems designed to manage this nematode (Raymundo, 1985). Systems of integrating cropping sequences and chemical control have been evaluated in the USA (Johnson, 1985b). Resistance to M. incognita exists in a number of commercial crop varieties, principally vegetables (Lehman and Cochran, 1991). These have generally been developed in the USA, but have been evaluated in other parts of the world (for example, see Krishnappa, 1985).

受到影响的植物阶段:  秧苗阶段，营养体生长阶段, 开花阶段, 和结果阶段.

受到影响的植物部份:  整个植物，树叶和根. Affected Plant Stages: Seedling stage, vegetative growing stage, flowering stage, and fruiting stage.

Affected Plant Parts: Whole plant, leaves, and roots. 在根结线虫的种中，在全世界范围，南方根结线虫在热带和亚热带区域中或许是最广和最严重的植物寄生线虫类害虫(Sasser, 1979).。作为一种害虫，它发生在广泛的农作物上。产量损失的大多数估计来自于杀线虫机剂的运用，并且应该注意，这些杀线虫剂可能对其它有益生长造成影响。

棉花

在美国杀线虫剂有规律运用的州中，由于线虫而对棉花造成的最精确和最详细的估计已经从事。    在阿肯色州，到目前为止，南方根结线虫是最重要的棉花线虫。在杀线虫剂运用后，每年的产量损失估计是1.5%， 在卡罗莱那州南部， 南方根结线虫与其它根结线虫每年造成估计5%的产量损失 (Kirkpatrick, 1988, 1989)。 在德克萨斯州的16 年期间的田间实验中，当被南方根结线虫侵染的田块用杀线虫剂熏蒸后，棉花的平均产量增产26% 。在德克萨斯州的六个县中，超过 47% 的土壤田块被南方根结线虫侵染，据估计造成的总年产量损失是10.2%或85.600棉花包(Orr and Robinson, 1984).。  在棉花上，由于南方根结线虫造成的混合病害和维管束镰刀菌萎焉也被肯定。两个生物体一起发生时，线虫量的增加给萎焉范围和棉花产量损失造成的影响远比镰刀菌的增加造成的影响大(Starr et al., 1989; Hillocks and Bridge, 1992; Hillocks, 1997)。

烟草

根结线虫, 主要是南方根结线虫和爪哇根结线虫，是烟草种植重要的经济害虫，无论在气候适合它们的什么地方(Barker et al., 1981; Shepherd and Barker, 1990)。在北美，根结线虫给烟草造成的损失，主要是南方根结线虫，在控制措施规范的地方，损失量估计范围是1—4%(Shepherd and Barker, 1990) 。在土耳齐，根结线虫 ，很可能是南方根结线虫，给烟草造成的产量损失估计是50—60%，25%的损失来自田间侵染，在印度，如果在苗床开始侵染可达到50的损失(Shepherd and Barker, 1990)。当南方根结线虫以最初量十倍增加时，给烟草产量造成的百分比损失估计可达到 8 —9 % (Barker et al., 1981)。在古巴, 在生产雪茄的最高质量的烟草区域中，由于南方根结线虫，给烤干烟草质量造成损失估计达到 27.5%  (Garcia and Perez, 1987; Fernandez and Ortega, 1998)。
 
食物豆类

在热带和亚热带，南方根结线虫是一种食物豆类的主要经济害虫 (Sikora and Greco, 1990) 。在致病性的盆栽实验中，每株植物 1000个线虫的适度群体土壤能减少鹰嘴豆(Cicer arietinum)的豆荚产量 27%， 而非常高每株植物10,000个线虫的适度群体土壤减少能达到87% 。在用杀线虫剂处理过的南方根结线虫侵染的块地中，鹰嘴豆的产量能增加15—33% (Reddy, 1976)。在热带中，一般的豆 (Phaseolus vulgaris) 被线虫种类破坏的非常严重。在肯尼亚，通过用杀线虫剂处理减少土壤中混合的南方根结线虫和爪哇根结线虫的量，重要的大豆产量增加达到45—60%(Ngundo and Taylor, 1974) 。同样地在秘鲁和哥伦比亚， 在根结线虫种混合群体的侵染地中，主要是南方根结线虫，依靠大豆培育植物生长和其它因子，一般的大豆种子的产量的损失可减少26—63%(Mullin et al., 1991)。 在美国，南方根结线虫是状态普通的严重害虫，在线虫没有控制的地方，造成的作物价值损失达到66% 。减少的作物价值是植物抵抗状态减少合并的一种结果，仍然活着植物的结荚量平均减少27%(Smittle and Johnson, 1982) 。[植]豇豆(Vigna unguiculata) 是南方根结线虫非常易受侵染的寄主植物。在尼日利亚，南方根结线虫是主要的线虫类寄生虫，杀线虫剂的运用能增加[植]豇豆产量达到95—222%(Babatola and Omotade, 1991) 。黄豆(Glycine max) 是另外一个豆荚严重地被根结线虫损害，而且在巴西产量减少能超过 55% 在南方根结线虫存在的地方(Antonio, 1988)。在印度，杀线虫剂运用到南方根结线虫混合侵染的农民的田中，大豆的产量增加达到19%(Prasad, 1999)。

蔬菜

在热带和亚热带地方，南方根结线虫是一种主要的蔬菜害虫。许多农作物，如蔬菜，易于线虫侵染的，特别是蕃茄，茄子，秋葵，黄瓜，甜瓜，胡萝卜，葫芦，生菜和胡椒粉。由于线虫类，主要是南方根结线虫和爪哇根结线虫 ，给蔬菜作物造成的损失，估计对茄子17—20%，对瓜18—33% ，            对蕃茄24—38% (Sasser, 1979).。 在印度，对秋葵 (Abelmoschus esculentus) 、蕃茄和茄子的产量损失估计分别是 91%、42—54% 和 18% (Bhatti and Jain,1977; Subramaniyan et al 1990)。在印度，运用杀线虫剂的其它实验中表明：南方根结线虫和爪哇根结线虫混合侵染的自然地块，对豌豆，秋葵, 蕃茄和瓶子葫芦 (Lagenaria siceraria) 造成的可避免的产量损失是 46-56%(Sharma and Baheti, 1992)。

山药

南方根结线虫对山药 (薯蓣属种) 的主要损害，是质量和由于根结线虫造成表面广泛膨大的可销售根的减少(Jatala and Bridge, 1990)。据估计，与健康的块茎相比，肿大的根的价格下降39—52% (Nwauzor and Fawole, 1982)。然而, 有例证是线虫对实际上减少的产量是知道，举例来说，在尼日利亚在 D. alata，重要的产量减少能由于南方根结线虫(Adesiyan and Odihirin, 1978)。 在马提尼克岛，据报道南方根结线虫对山药有完全的破坏(Kermarrec, 1974)。 在印度，盆栽实验已经证明：甚至在比较低的线虫群体，每株100 个南方根结线虫幼虫能在山药块茎重量上造成27%的减轻，比较大的线虫群体能造成超过55%的产量损失(Mohandas and Ramakrishnan, 1997)。   

马铃薯

马铃薯的损失由于线虫种造成的, 主要南方根结线虫，估计在 25% 或更多(Mai et al., 1981)。

香料

在许多国家，南方结接线虫是黑色胡椒粉的重要害虫，特别是在巴西和印度，据报道侵染水平达到90%以上(Koshy and Bridge, 1990)。像盆栽中的每株植物含10个幼虫那么少就能减少黑色胡椒粉生长16% (Koshy et al., 1979)。在印度，有南方根结线虫存在下， 小豆蔻 (Elettaria cardamomum) 遭受产量损失达到32—47%(Ali, 1986).。 在澳大利亚，南方根结线虫和爪哇根结线虫是姜害虫，根状茎部的严重损失能减少产量 57%(Pegg et al, 1974)。 在盆栽实验中，由于最初的含有10，000南方根结线虫土壤，对姜根茎重量的减轻达到74% (Sukumaran and Sundararaju, 1986)。

咖啡

南方根结线虫在全球的许多种咖啡种植地都有发现，但是它在巴西的影响效果是最严重的。在巴西，线虫对咖啡种植园造成了毁灭性的破坏，并且农业结构的改变，因为农民被迫选择可采用的作物(Campos et al., 1990)。

potential_eco_desc: M. graminicola can cause economic yield loss in upland, lowland and deepwater rice. In upland rice, there is an estimated reduction of 2.6% in grain yield for every 1000 nematodes present around young seedlings. The population levels which cause 10% loss in yield of upland rice are 120, 250 and 600 eggs/plant at 10, 30 and 60 days age of plants in direct seeded crops (Rao et al., 1986). In flooded rice, damage by M. graminicola is caused in nurseries before transplanting - the tolerance limit of seedlings is <1 J2 per cubic centimetre of soil (Plowright and Bridge, 1990). Damage also occurs prior to flooding where rice is sown directly in well-drained soils. Experiments have shown that 4000 juveniles/plant of M. graminicola can cause destruction of up to 72% of deepwater rice plants by drowning out. Losses as high as this in the field are unlikely as natural root populations vary considerably (Bridge and Page, 1982).

management_info: Introduction^p^pIncreasing soil fertility can compensate for some damage by M. graminicola. Resistant cultivars hold out the most promise for effective and economic control, and some resistance to the different species has been found. Chemical control on the field scale is generally uneconomic, particularly with low-yielding upland rice, but could be an economic proposition for nursery soils.^p^p^Flooding^p^pM. graminicola will survive normal flooding but damage to the crop can be avoided by raising rice seedlings in flooded soils thus preventing root invasion by the nematodes (Bridge and Page, 1982). Continuous flooding is highly effective in controlling M. graminicola in Vietnam (Kinh et al., 1982).^p^p^Resistance^p^pThe majority of rice cultivars are susceptible to M. graminicola. However, there are a number of cultivars from India, Thailand and USA which are reported to be resistant to this nematode (Bridge et al., 1990).^p^p^Crop Rotation^p^pCertain crops are resistant or poor hosts of M. graminicola and could be used in rotation to reduce nematode populations e.g. castor, cowpeaa, sweet potatoes, soyabeans, sunflower, sesame, onion, turnip, Phaseolus vulgaris, jute and okra (Rao et al., 1986). Long rotations, greater than 12 months, will be needed to reduce M. graminicola soil populations to low levels. Introducing a fallow into the rotation will also give control of the nematodes but, to be effective, it needs to be a bare fallow free of weed hosts and is therefore impractical in most circumstances (Roy, 1978). However, one weed, Eclipta alba, is toxic to M. and could be grown and incorporated into the field soil to kill the nematodes (Prasad and Rao, 1979).^p^p^Soil Amendments^p^pThe use of decaffeinated tea waste and water hyacinth compost as organic soil amendments has been suggested to control M. graminicola (Roy, 1976b).

potential_eco_desc: M. exigua is pathogenic to coffee, reducing coffee yield in many countries in Central and South America. It causes a serious disease of Coffee arabica in shady, humid valleys, resulting in yellowing and falling of leaves and death of the trees in heavy attacks. management_info: Chemical Control^p^pDBCP, fenamiphos and 1,3-dichloropropene controlled M. exigua on coffee (Gomez Tovar, 1972). Schieber (1968) recommended seedbed and nursery soil treatment with D-D followed by aeration of treated soil four weeks before seeding but treatment of established trees was difficult because of toxicity and expense. ^p^pOn coffee seedlings, oxamyl significantly reduced M. exigua egg production and the number of root galls. Of the other products tested, only the fungicide carboxin significantly reduced the numbers of eggs and galls (Pereira et al., 1980b). Dpx 1410 controlled M. exigua in 3 month old coffee cv. Caturra plants. Treated plants responded with increased height, leaf area and weight (Leguizamon and Baeza, 1972). In greenhouse trials with 17 compounds the best control of M. exigua was obtained with a dichloropropane dichloropropene mixture, fenamiphos, dazomet, fosthictan, Bunema, fensulfothion and Phosphos (Curi and Silveira, 1974). Of 12 chemicals tested, monocrotophos gave the best control of M. exigua on coffee seedlings (Moraes, 1977a). ^p^pWhen eggs of M. exigua were treated with aldicarb, ethoprop or carbofuran for 14 days and then transferred to distilled water for 19 days, hatch was significantly inhibited. Aldicarb and carbofuran significantly decreased the motility and life span of the second stage juveniles, aldicarb being more toxic than carbofuran. In a field test, aldicarb, ethoprop and carbofuran significantly decreased M. exigua populations on coffee (Huang et al., 1983). A significant negative correlation between the numbers of galls on coffee seedlings due to M. exigua and eggs/root system and the concentration of KCl in the soil was observed after 50 days (Dos Santos et al., 1981a). ^p^pCarbofuran, oxamyl, prophos, fensulfothion and fenamiphos gave good control of M. exigua but the highest rate was phytotoxic and decreased plant fresh weight (Baeza Aragon and Leguizamon, 1977). Carbofuran was applied to 3-year-old coffee trees infested with M. exigua and Pratylenchus coffeae in Sarchi, Costa Rica. It had no positive effect on yield during the first year, but at the end of the second year, all treatments produced significantly higher yields than the untreated controls (Figueroa, 1978). Foliar applications of oxamyl were more effective than root dip treatments. Treatment was effective in controlling nematode populations and nematode development was hindered at the higher concentration (Laughlin and Lordello, 1979). ^p^pAldicarb, carbofuran, oxamyl, disulfoton and phorate were all effective in reducing gall formation due to M. exigua on the treated part of coffee roots, although oxamyl and aldicarb were more effective than phorate. Oxamyl was the only compound to reduce gall formation on the untreated part of the roots, indicating lateral translocation of the nematicide (Pereira et al., 1980b). Applications of aldicarb, carbofuran and oxamyl to plastic bags containing coffee seedlings growing in soil naturally infested with M. exigua were effective, although no treatment completely eradicated the nematodes; after 45 days the roots of the treated seedlings had a gall index close to zero. Oxamyl and carbofuran produced phytotoxicity symptoms in seedlings (Pereira et al., 1979). Aldicarb with fertilizer on a coffee var. Mundo Novo plantation infested with M. exigua did not completely eradicate the nematode but increased coffee yields (Calafiori et al., 1988). In glasshouse experiments higher numbers of M. exigua galls were formed in plants fertilized with urea or calcium nitrate than in unfertilized controls. Plants fertilized with 'nitrocalcium' (a commercial mixture of ammonium nitrate and dolomitic limestone) or ammonium sulphate had lower numbers of galls than the controls, whereas sodium nitrate had no effect (Dos Santos et al., 1981b). ^p^p^Biological Control^p^pIn Colombia, Pasteuria penetrans was found to naturally parasitize the cuticle of juveniles of M. exigua on Coffea ara

management_info:
化学防治
DBCP、丁基苯基咪唑丙腈和1,3--二氯核黄素能防治咖啡上的短小根结线虫(Gomez   Tovar,1972) 。Schieber(1968)推荐用D-D处理的苗床和土壤，随后在播种之前对已处理的土壤通风四个星期，但是由于毒性和费用，对已确定树木的处理是很困难的。 Chemical Control
DBCP, fenamiphos and 1,3-dichloropropene controlled M. exigua on coffee (Gomez Tovar, 1972). Schieber (1968) recommended seedbed and nursery soil treatment with D-D followed by aeration of treated soil four weeks before seeding but treatment of established trees was difficult because of toxicity and expense. 生物防治
在哥伦比亚，在阿拉比卡种咖啡上，发现 Pasteuria penetrans能自然地寄生于短小根结线虫二龄幼虫的表皮。细菌侵染的比率变化范围是6—35%(平均17%)。侵染影响整个幼虫阶段,但是在二龄幼虫阶段最普遍(Baeza Aragon, 1978)。与防治的相比， Arthrobotrys conoides真菌的inocula 、A. musiformis, Paecilomyces lilacinus or Verticillium chlamydosporium作为孢子悬液或侵染小麦谷粒能大量地减少了二龄幼虫的数量、每克根上的卵块数量和短小根结线虫的总数量。当与线虫接种前运用相比较，线虫接种后真菌的运用能大量地减少短小根结线虫卵块数量和总群体数量(Campos and Campos, 1997)。 Biological Control
In Colombia, Pasteuria penetrans was found to naturally parasitize the cuticle of juveniles of M. exigua on Coffea arabica. The rate of bacterial infection ranged from 6 to 35% (mean 17%). The infection affected all juvenile stages, but was commonest in second stage juveniles (Baeza Aragon, 1978). Fungal inocula of Arthrobotrys conoides, A. musiformis, Paecilomyces lilacinus or Verticillium chlamydosporium as spore suspension or infested wheat grains significantly decreased the number of second stage juveniles, the number of eggs per gram of roots and total population of M. exigua compared with the control. Application of fungi after the nematode inoculation significantly reduced the number of eggs and total population of M. exigua when compared with application before the nematode (Campos and Campos, 1997). 栽培防治
抗性寄主植物
Lordello(1972)注意到巴西与圣保罗咖啡上短小根结线虫的三个生理小种，Chitwood and Berger (1960) 在危地马拉发现2个株系。在危地马拉, Schieber and Sosa (1960)发现Coffea robusta对短小根结线虫与Pratylenchus coffeae是有抗性的。在比较低的影响下嫁接受影响高的C. robusta，但能对C. canephora根茎产生抗性达到防治措施(Flores and Yepez, 1969)

去除和燃烧受侵染的咖啡树,只种植健康苗木，作为防治措施，N 和 P 肥料被推荐使用(Schieber,1968)。 Curi and Silveira(1978)建议：作物轮作、咖啡地的检查与登记作为控制措施。受侵染咖啡根的消灭能猛烈地减少土壤中线虫的数量，    5个月后线虫群体是无法发觉的，在处理后22个月的新种植咖啡苗木地中根结和二龄幼虫是不能观察到的(Almeida and Campos, 1993)。

Schieber 与 Grullon(1969) 和 Schieber(1968) 发现： N 和 P 肥料有助于咖啡抵抗病害。大豆、棉花、落花生或调味瓶豆子能有助于土壤侵染，作为改善在8个月后减少咖啡苗木上短小根结线虫的群体是有效的。油渣的较高浓度是植物性毒素的。在巴西，为了防治咖啡种植园中的短小根结线虫，咖啡豆子包装运用作为肥料产生了积极的防治效果，总的防治线虫的水平是75—100%。当它们与土壤合为一体,而不是在土壤表面时，包装将会起到更好的防治效果(Tronconi et al., 1986)。 

种植水稻、高粱属植物、makueni (Panicum maximum) 、豆子、 大豆 、 Crotalaria spectabilis 和 Stilozobium aterrimum 作为咖啡后的轮作植物, 6个月后能大幅地减少土壤中短小根结线虫幼虫的数量。9个月后在玉米地中也能观察到。轮作23个月后，种植咖啡上二龄幼虫的缺乏证实用于本研究中所有植物的功效(Almeida and Campos, 1991)。 Cultural Control
Removal and burning of infected coffee trees, planting of only healthy seedlings and the use of N and P fertilisers are recommended as control measures (Schieber, 1968). Curi and Silveira (1978) suggest crop rotation and registration and inspection of coffee nurseries as control measures. The elimination of infected coffee roots allowed a drastic reduction of the second stage juveniles in soil; the nematode populations were undetectable after 5 months and galls or second stage juveniles were not observed in newly planted coffee seedlings in the area 22 months after treatment (Almeida and Campos, 1993).

Schieber and Grullon (1969) and Schieber (1968) found that that N and P fertilizers help coffee plants to fight the disease. Soyabean, cotton, groundnut or castor bean cakes added to infested soil as an amendment were effective in reducing M. exigua populations on coffee seedlings after 8 months. Higher concentrations of oil cake were phytotoxic. Increased application levels of coffee bean casings applied as fertilizer to control M. exigua in coffee plantations in Brazil gave increased control; total inhibition of the nematodes occurring at levels of 75 to 100%. The casings gave better control when they were incorporated into the soil, rather than layered on the soil surface (Tronconi et al., 1986).

potential_eco_desc:
在美洲南部和中部的许多国家，短小根结线虫是咖啡的病原物，并减少了咖啡产量。在暗又潮湿的山谷，它造成阿拉比卡种咖啡的重要病害，并导致树叶变黄、落叶，严重时会促使树的死亡。在巴西，它侵染所有的州的咖啡(Lordello,1971)，在哥伦比亚，发现在来自三个不同区域的 48% 的咖啡根样品中都含有(Gomez, 1980)。  在咖啡树附近生长的许多杂草能隐藏线虫和有助于病害的传播(Moraes et al., 1972; Lima et al., 1985; Lopez and Vilchez, 1991)。玉米、 棉花或大豆在清扫干净的曾被短小根结线虫侵染的旧咖啡耕园种植1 或 2 年，建立一个新的种植园，玉米的产量是 6.68 t 谷粒/每年，于大豆2.51 t 种子/每年，但是棉花没有产量；平均产量是4.94-5.92 t 玉米谷粒/每两年, 0.92 t 种子棉花/每两年和 1.94 t 大豆种子/每两年(Moraes et al., 1977)。

关于短小根结线虫、南方根结线虫和花生根结线虫的组织病理学说，是从巴西几个咖啡种植地收集到的（see Vovlas et al. 1987)。 M. exigua is pathogenic to coffee, reducing coffee yield in many countries in Central and South America. It causes a serious disease of Coffee arabica in shady, humid valleys, resulting in yellowing and falling of leaves and death of the trees in heavy attacks. In Brazil, it attacks coffee in all states (Lordello, 1971) and in Colombia it was found in 48% of coffee root samples from three different regions (Gomez, 1980). Many weeds growing near coffee trees serve as reservoirs and help to spread the disease (Moraes et al., 1972; Lima et al., 1985; Lopez and Vilchez, 1991). Maize, cotton or soyabeans were grown for 1 or 2 years between clearing an old coffee plantation infested with M. exigua and establishing a new plantation; yields for crops grown for 1 yr were 6.68 t grain/ha for maize and 2.51 t seed/ha for soyabean but cotton gave no yield; for crops grown for 2 years average yields were 4.94-5.92 t maize grain/ha, 0.92 seed cotton/ha and 1.94 t soyabean seed/ha (Moraes et al., 1977).

For the histopathology of M. exigua, M. arenaria and M. incognita collected from coffee soils in several sites in Brazil, see Vovlas et al. (1987).

potential_eco_desc: Meloidogyn enterolobii has a well-documented ability to overcome many crop resistance genes that are effective against the more cosmopolitan M. incognita group (MIG) species endemic to the southern United States. It was first reported in Florida (Brito et al. 2004) and more recently in North Carolina (Ye et al. 2013) infecting root-knot nematode resistant varieties of cotton and soybean. This is the first detection of this nematode infecting root-knot nematode resistant sweetpotato in South Carolina.
description: In February 2018, a soil sample was collected as part of a Cooperative Agricultural Pest Survey for root-knot nematode species from a soybean field in Darlington Co., SC. The surveyed field had been rotated between soybean and sweetpotato for several years. Soil was sent to the USDA-ARS Laboratory in Beltsville, MD, for analysis. Nematodes were isolated from samples, and based on morphological and molecular analysis it was identified as Meloidogyn enterolobii. This is the first detection of this nematode infecting root-knot nematode resistant sweetpotato in South Carolina. Greenhouse tests demonstrated that M. enterolobii is highly virulent on the widely used MIG-resistant sweetpotato cultivar Covington.
reference_name: Meloidogyne enterolobii Found Infecting Root-Knot Nematode Resistant Sweetpotato in South Carolina, United States

These symptoms were accompanied by numerous root galls. Based on morphological measurements and PCR test showed the nematodes was Meloidogyne enterolobii. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. enterolobii in Niger.
reference_name: First report of the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne enterolobii parasitising sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) in Niger

host_range: Meloidogyne enterolobii is considered an economically important agricultural nematode globally as it causes severe yield losses for many crops such as tomato, pepper, and guava. This is the first report of M. enterolobii parasitizing weed Solanum pseudocapsicum.
description: During the summer of 2015, Jerusalem cherry (Solanum pseudocapsicum) exhibiting multiple galls in the roots but no above-ground symptoms were detected in Cachoieira do Sul County (29°35′ S, 51°06′ W), Rio Grande do Sul State, Brazil. The nematodes were identified as Meloidogyne enterolobii according to morphological and molecular analysis. The weed S. pseudocapsicum can act as a potential reservoir for M. enterolobii in Brazil and elsewhere when crops are absent. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of M. enterolobii parasitizing S. pseudocapsicum in Brazil.  The weed Solanum pseudocapsicum can act as a potential reservoir for Meloidogyne enterolobii in Brazil and elsewhere when crops are absent.
reference_name: First Report of Meloidogyne enterolobii Infecting the Weed Jerusalem Cherry (Solanum pseudocapsicum) in Brazil

host_range: Meloidogyne enterolobii  is known to be present in West Africa and other continents affecting a range of crops, but not yam, this is the first record of M. enterolobii infecting yam and causing galling damage.
description: During a taxonomic nematode survey, galled yam tubers were collected from markets and farmers’ fields between November 2012 and February 2013 in Nigeria. Nematodes were isolated from galled tubers, biochemical and molecular identification demonstrated that the nematodes belonged to Meloidogyne enterolobii . To our knowledge, this is the first record of M. enterolobii infecting yam and causing galling damage.
reference_name: First Report of Meloidogyne enterolobii Causing Tuber Galling Damage on White Yam (Dioscorea rotundata) in Nigeria

host_range: This is the first report of Meloidogyne enterolobii parasitizing Solanum scabrum in Keny.
potential_eco_desc: Meloidogyne enterolobii is considered to be a highly pathogenic plant-parasitic nematode species because it is able to reproduce on varieties of tomato, tobacco, watermelon, and pepper that are resistant to other RKN species. In addition, the pathogenicity and reproductive potential of M. enterolobii is higher when compared with other tropical RKN such as M. javanica, M. incognita, and M. arenaria.
description: Root-knot nematodes (RKN; Meloidogyne spp.) are belowground pests capable of parasitizing many hosts including African nightshades, leading to severe yield loss and sometimes total crop failure. A survey was carried out in Kenya between May and July 2015 to determine the presence and incidences of RKN infecting the African nightshade Solanum scabrum. Symptomatic African nightshade plants showed very large galls isolated from Yatta, Machakos County, population densities of infective second stage juveniles in the soil ranged from 100 to 750 individuals per 100 cm3 soil. Morphological and molecular identification demonstrated that the nematodes belonged to Meloidogyne enterolobii. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. enterolobii in Kenya.
reference_name: First Report of the Root-Knot Nematode Meloidogyne enterolobii Parasitizing African Nightshades in Kenya
author: cpqis.wangnaiyang

host_range: This is the first report of Meloidogyne enterolobii infecting both a plant in the genus Stenocereus and also S. queretaroensis in Mexico and worldwide.
description: In April 2015, plants of Stenocereus queretaroensis exhibiting root galling, yellowing stems, a reduction in numbers of fruit, and in some cases plant death were found in a pitaya-growing area in Amacueca County (20.00317° N; 103.58968° W) in Jalisco State. Some heavily galled root samples were collected for morphological and molecular analysis. The nematode was identified as Meloidogyne enterolobii. This result expand the distribution and host range of this nematode species. The discovery of M. enterolobii in this arid agroecosystem in the state of Jalisco represents a serious threat to crop production in this region. To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. enterolobii infecting both a plant in the genus Stenocereus and also S. queretaroensis in Mexico and worldwide.
reference_name: First Report of Meloidogyne enterolobii Infecting Columnar Cacti Stenocereus queretaroensis in Jalisco, Mexico

potential_eco_desc: Meloidogyne enterolobii is polyphagous and has a wide host range, including cover and vegetable crops, fruit trees, herbs, and ornamental and weed plants. Moreover, it displays virulence against several sources of Meloidogyne resistance genes and is considered particularly aggressive.
description: In September 2014, several jackfruit trees in an orchard in Wanning, Hainan Province, China were observed with symptoms of decline including wilting and trunk cracking. Partial roots of the affected trees (n = 12) were collected, and showed symptoms of root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne spp.) infection, were heavily galled, and were beginning to rot. This population of Meloidogyne sp. isolated from jackfruit trees was identified to be M. enterolobii based upon morphological and molecular characteristics. To our knowledge, this is the first report worldwide of jackfruit as a host of M. enterolobii and the first record of M. enterolobii parasitizing a plant in the Artocarpus genus of the mulberry family (Moraceae) in China.

description: In midsummer 2014, several Jackfruit(Artocarpus heterophyllus) plants (age 3 years old) grown in the ground of a tropical plant nursery in Collier County, Florida, were exhibiting severe root galling (large and bead-like galls), yellowing leaves, and stunted growth. Heavily galled root samples were collected and identified. Morphological and molecular identification demonstrated that the nematodes belonged to Meloidogyne enterolobii. To our knowledge, this is the first report worldwide of A. heterophyllus as a host of M. enterolobii.

host_range: 辣椒Capsicum annuum
description: In March 2014, hot pepper (Capsicum annuum) plants growing in a commercial field in Yuanmou County, Yunnan Province, China, were observed with stunted growth and yellowing leaves. Examination of root systems of symptomatic plants revealed the presence of heavily galled and rotting roots similar to damage caused by root-knot nematodes. Dissection of galled root tissue revealed mature root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne sp.) females. Nematodes were extracted from soil and root samples and identified to species morphologically, molecularly, and by esterase and malate dehydrogenase isozyme phenotyping. Meloidogyne enterolobii was determined to be the causal agent. M. enterolobii was first reported on pacara earpod tree (Enterolobium contortisiliquum) in China. In China, M. enterolobii has been reported in the eastern provinces (Hainan, Guangdong, and Fujian). To our knowledge, this is the first report of M. enterolobii parasitizing hot pepper and also the first report of this nematode in Yunnan Province, China.
remark: Due to M. enterolobii wide host range and ability to develop and reproduce on several known crops carrying resistance genes, it is currently considered an emerging, highly pathogenic, root-knot nematode species with the potential to cause great economic damage. Consequently, several countries and regulatory agencies have designated M. enterolobii a quarantine pathogen.
reference_name: First Report of Meloidogyne enterolobii on Hot Pepper in China

potential_eco_desc: Although the African coffee root-knot nematodes have been known in Tanzania for many years there is no information available on the actual yield losses caused by these pests. It is clear that mature coffee trees exhibit a certain amount of tolerance to the nematodes (Bridge, 1984) and infested plants are able to survive in optimal growing conditions even though growth and yield will be affected. On the basis of figures with similar nematodes from other coffee growing countries, particularly in South America, and the amount of root damage caused by the nematodes in Tanzania, it is estimated that yield losses of severely infested trees will be in the region of 20% in optimum conditions with the percentage loss increasing under adverse conditions to the point of non-productivity. The stress to which trees are subjected because of nematode damage will also cause premature fruit drop, twig dieback and defoliation, nutrient deficiency symptoms and stunted growth.

Necrotic spots in the flesh of tubers of as little as 5% of a crop make it commercially unacceptable. Overall yields of tubers are also reduced. This species is considered to be the major nematode pest of potatoes in the Pacific Northwest states of the USA and the annual predicted loss there would be ca $40 million if control measures were not applied (Santo, 1994). No information is available on the economic impact of this pest in European countries.^p^pEffects on other crops are not as marked nor as well documented, but yields of cereals (wheat, barley, oats and maize) have been shown to be significantly reduced by infestation (Santo and O'Bannon, 1981).^p^pIn the Netherlands, M. chitwoodi has recently been found to have damaged potato crops (and certain vegetables) in a limited area in the east of the country. This damage is apparently associated with sandy soils and a succession of warm summers. It is possible that M. chitwoodi has been present in the area for many years, undetected because it caused no significant damage (see Geographical Distribution).^p^pM. chitwoodi has also caused damage to potatoes in Germany (Muller et al., 1996). The multiplication rate and damage probability of M. chitwoodi seems to depend mainly on weather conditions in spring and temperature accumulation during the vegetative period (Braasch et al., 1996).Chaves and Torres (2000) reported the presence of M. chitwoodi on golf courses in Buenos Aires province, Argentina. remark: M. chitwoodi has been added to the EC Plant Health Directive 77/93/EEC.^p^pA comparison of the air temperatures found in Finland with those found across the present distribution of the pest indicated that the nematode could survive and produce two generations per year in the southern part of Finland. Baker and Dickens (1993) concluded from their PRA that M. chitwoodi would be likely to produce three generations in the UK. They did not feel capable of predicting the likely economic impact of the pest, as this could depend on a number of other unknown factors such as soil wetness, varietal susceptibility and quality control thresholds. A recent PRA for Germany (Braasch et al., 1996) led to the conclusion that M. chitwoodi was most likely to be damaging on potatoes in the north-west of the country, in the area adjoining the Netherlands. Countries further south in the EPPO region would provide climatic conditions suitable for as many as four generations per year.^p^pPotato crops would be most at risk from M. chitwoodi in the EPPO region. For a number of reasons, it represents a greater threat than other Meloidogyne species already widespread in the EPPO region, in particular M. hapla with which it often forms mixed populations. M. chitwoodi is less easily controlled by nematicides, it has a wider host range, it produces more severe tuber symptoms and is tolerant of lower soil temperatures. In fact, the soil temperature requirements for population development of M. chitwoodi are similar to those of Globodera rostochiensis (Tiilikkala et al., 1995), suggesting that the former species could occupy the same geographical distribution as the latter.
author: CPC2006

management_info: Chemical Control^p^pControl measures currently used against other root-knot nematodes have proved to be less effective against M. chitwoodi. For example, treatment trials with the nematicides aldicarb, dichlorpropene, ethoprop and metham-sodium have not been as consistently successful as against M. hapla (Pinkerton et al., 1986; Santo and Wilson, 1990). In north-western USA, crop failures in several potato fields have been attributed to M. chitwoodi despite the use of spring soil fumigations. Hafez and Sundararaj (2002a,b) evaluated applications of ethoprop for the management of M. chitwoodi on potato.^p^p^Cultural Control and Sanitary Methods^p^pRecent work on sugarbeet suggests that late drilling and reduced irrigation can play a part in reducing damage to crops (Heijbroek, 1996).^p^pCrop rotation with cereals is often used to reduce populations of M. hapla. However, M. chitwoodi reproduces well on wheat, oats, barley and maize. Therefore, rotation with any of these crops will favour a build-up rather than a decrease of M. chitwoodi populations in infested soils. There are, however, other crops which will reduce populations (see Host Range) which can be used in rotations. Brinkman et al. (1996) suggested that chicory cultivars (Cichorium intybus), Dahlia (cv. Vuurvogel) and borage (Borago officinalis) supported low populations of M. chitwoodi and can offer alternatives in crop rotations. However, further studies are necessary to collect more information on crops which can be used in rotation to reduce nematode populations.^p^pSome success has been achieved by the incorporation of green manure into the soil, which reduces population densities of M. chitwoodi Mojtahedi et al., 1993a, b Suloiman and Hafez, 1996).^p^pMeasures similar to those for potato cyst nematodes (EPPO/CABI, 1992) would appear relevant, i.e. that consignments of rooted plants should come from areas where the pest does not occur or from fields found free from the pest. Suitable survey and test methods have still to be established. Freedom from M. chitwoodi should be specifically assured by certification schemes for seed potatoes.^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pPotato cultivars differ in their tolerance of M. chitwoodi (van Riel, 1993). There is interest in breeding for host resistance to M. chitwoodi, for example, in potatoes, using resistance from Solanum bulbocastanum and other sources (Brown et al., 1991; Austin et al., 1993; Janssen et al., 1997) and cereals (Jensen and Griffin, 1994). Yu (2001) and Yu and Lewellen (2004) registered nematode-resistant sugarbeet germplasm; Zoon et al. (2002) discussed durable resistance against M. chitwoodi and M. fallax whilst Brown et al. (1999, 2003, 2004) investigated resistance to M. chitwoodi in potato and evaluated several wild Solanum species as sources of resistance. Tovar-Soto et al. (1997) reported on the response of five potato genotypes to M. chitwoodi race 2 in Mexico. Berthou et al. (2003) characterized virulence in populations of M. chitwoodi by challenging with Capsicum annuum line PM217. Their results demonstrated great polymorphism in M. chitwoodi populations and the existence of a major gene in pepper controlling a specific resistance against some nematode populations.^p^p^IPM Programmes^p^pGuidelines for integrated pest management in potatoes are still being devised in those countries affected by this M. chitwoodi (Ferris et al., 1994a,b; Santo, 1994; Hafez et al., 1997).

management_info: Host-Plant Resistance^p^pMuch progress has been made in the use of resistant plants for reducing the damage caused by M. arenaria on various crop plants (Sasser and Kirby, 1979). Plants with some level of resistance include cultivars of cowpea, crown vetch, soyabean, passionfruit, okra, cassava, tomato, sweet potato, cucumber, guava rootstock, pepper, tobacco and various grasses (Sasser and Kirby, 1979). No useful source of resistance has been found in peanut.^p^p^Crop Rotation^p^pMeloidogyne species are obligate parasites and populations decline rapidly in the absence of a host. Rotation of susceptible host crop plants with those that are immune or poor hosts is a useful way to reduce the effect that M. arenaria has on plant growth. Unfortunately, the non-host, when it does occur, is usually less profitable than the susceptible crop. M. arenaria has a very large host range and non-hosts or cultivars that have been reported resistant should be used with caution because of the innate variability that occurs in the root-knot nematodes. Other agronomic and economic factors are also important in the selection of a rotation crop. An adequate weed control programme is absolutely necessary for a crop rotation scheme to be effective because many weed species serve as suitable hosts (Taylor and Sasser, 1978).^p^p^Chemical Control^p^pNematicides have often been used for limiting the damage that nematodes cause on plants. Nematicides are usually used as a soil treatment before planting. However, a few nematicides can be applied after planting. These chemicals are relatively expensive and they require costly equipment and trained personnel to apply them.^p^pHigh-value crops that are good hosts of M. arenaria can be protected with a soil fumigant. These chemicals volatilize and kill the nematodes on contact. Less valuable crops can be protected with cheaper non-fumigant nematicides that dissolve in water and act as nerve poisons. They prevent nematodes from feeding on plants for 2-3 weeks, but their effect is reversible. Often they do not kill the nematodes. Because they are water soluble, their effectiveness is dependent on an adequate amount of soil moisture. If an optimum amount of water is available, the optimum effect is achieved; if too much or too little water is present, very little control is achieved (Bunt, 1987).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pNumerous attempts have been made to control root-knot nematodes with parasitic and predacious organisms or various organic amendments, with varying degrees of success. Naturally occurring organisms, such as Pasteuria penetrans, which are obligate parasites of Meloidogyne, may prove to be effective for biological control.

host_range: 其原始营养植物是匍匐冰草，主要为害小麦。另外还为害大麦、黑麦、冰草属、葡萄龙牙草等。 但根据国外资料报道，黑森瘿蚊除为害上述植物以外其寄主还有冰草属（Agropyron）、野麦属（Elymus）、大麦属（Hordeum）、小麦属（Triticum）、雀麦属（Bromus）、山羊草属（Aegilops）等属中的一些种及牧梯草(Phleum pretense)、加州猬草（Hystrix califrnica）等牧草和杂草。
potential_eco_desc: 黑森瘿蚊对冬小麦和春小麦都能造成严重危害。  1980年伊犁州发生面积9410多亩，博尔塔拉州重灾田8万多亩，翻耕改种超过3000余亩。1981年博州发生面积将近44.6万亩，占小麦播种面积的78.9%，翻种超过10000亩，损失产量1400万斤。某兵团农场，春季田间受害率为21.4%，麦收前麦茎折倒率为55.6%，不但产量降低，也不便机械收割。小麦拔节后，由于幼虫侵害节下的茎，阻碍了养分向顶端输送，麦穗发育不良，千粒重减少，一般要减产25％-30％。受害茎秆脆弱倒伏，严重田块折秆率可达50％-75％。黑森瘿蚊幼虫危害作物除侵害叶片外，它还能分泌一种物质，可干扰第2和第3叶片代谢产物及其运输，间接阻止叶片后期的伸长而严重影响产量。
description:
黑森瘿蚊的传播方法除成虫迁飞做近距离扩散外，主要借助围蛹随原粮或包装充垫的麦秸杆进行远距离传播，其次是随混有围蛹的种子传带。成虫随气流自然传播的能力较弱。
根据1991年在伊犁对黑森瘿蚊的为害部位、为害高度调查以及饲草带虫情况的调查，原粮和饲草调运是其传播的及为重要途径。
management_info: 其中包括土壤处理、种子处理、喷雾、喷粉、熏蒸及使用驱虫剂或引诱剂、茎秆涂药以杀死转移的幼虫等。土壤和种子处理是比较有效的，但成本较高，目前很少大面积使用。此外，在成虫羽化高峰时，过去曾用过林丹喷粉，也可喷洒植物性杀虫剂如除虫菊、鱼藤和尼古丁。  黑森瘿蚊的天敌主要是寄生蜂和寄生蝇等。最主要的是小广腹细腰蜂，寄生在卵内，此外还有Merisus属的寄生蜂可寄生在蛹内。保护和利用寄生蜂和寄生蝇，对防治黑森瘿蚊是一种非常有效的措施。  根据当地黑森瘿蚊成虫的发生期，调节小麦播种期，以避开成虫产卵，减轻危害，具体日期每年要做调整。也可应用遗传防治和选育抗虫品种。遗传防治是利用不同小种的黑森瘿蚊进行杂交，以便产生危害性弱的小种。目前在美国各地育种者培育的小麦品种都是抗黑森瘿蚊的品种。这些品种降低黑森瘿蚊危害的机制主要是由于具有抗性和耐性，如有些品种表现的抗性是低危害率，它使植株上幼虫的发育受到影响，形成的围蛹个体很小；耐性的表现是，虽然植株受害，但受害程度很轻，产量损失不大。

potential_eco_desc: M. destructor has been a major pest of wheat in the USA ever since its accidental introduction from Europe and there have been many damaging outbreaks, some of which are chronicled by Barnes (1956). Yield losses in Indiana alone, over the period 1929-36, averaged 2 million bushels per year, and similar losses occurred in other states. In Georgia, USA, there was a severe outbreak on winter barley in 1988-89 (Buntin and Raymer, 1992) and M. destructor also caused substantial reduction of forage production from winter wheat (Buntin and Raymer, 1989). Pfadt (1985) records that losses in the USA have gradually decreased as resistant varieties have become available. In 1945, which was the last year of general distribution of susceptible wheat varieties, the overall loss was about $37 million compared with average losses of about $16 million per year in the 1980s. ^p^pSkuhrava et al. (1984) reviewed outbreaks of M. destructor and other gall midge pests of cereals in Europe. They noted that M. destructor was an important pest of wheat in the Soviet Union and Poland after 1918 but decreased after 1940. By 1970 it had practically disappeared from central Europe but continued to be an important pest of wheat in the southern European parts of the USSR, the east Mediterranean, the Transcaucasian region and Soviet Middle East and in Siberia.^p^pA recent assessment of crop loss to this pest in Badajoz, Spain, recorded reduction of grain yields by 14-35% (Moral et al., 1994) and field trials in Morocco in 1987-89 recorded a yield loss of 38% (Amri et al., 1992).

remark: The initial accidental introduction of this pest from Europe to North America was probably in straw carried by Hessian troops at the time of the Revolutionary War - hence its common name of 'Hessian fly'. Transport of diapausing larvae in wheat straw would certainly seem the most likely cause of long-distance transfers and phytosanitary measures should be aimed at preventing this. It is also possible to transport flax-seed cocoons with grain and seed samples.^p^pIn the USA, hydrogen phosphide fumigation has been shown to kill M. destructor puparia in compressed hay for export (Yokoyama et al., 1994b; Yokoyama et al., 1994a). Heat treatment may also be used and research in Canada indicates that pupae mixed with chopped hay are all killed when maintained at 58°C for at least 3 minutes (Sokhansanj et al., 1993).

management_info: Cultural ControlBarnes (1956) reviewed the development of control measures and summarized general practices in the USA for cultural control, which include crop rotation, ploughing-in stubbles, destruction of volunteer wheat plants, good soil preparation with the use of good seed to ensure quick germination, and moderately late sowing of winter wheat to avoid infestation by the autumn generation of adults. Barnes emphasized that these practices must be modified to meet local conditions and noted the emphasis that had always been laid on a thorough knowledge of the local biology and bionomics of M. destructor and the integration of such information with good farming practice on a co-operative basis.^p^pRefinement of these methods has continued in the USA (Chapin et al., 1992; Buntin et al., 1991; Buntin and Bruckner, 1990; Buntin et al., 1990) and in other areas where M. destructor is a persistent pest, such as Spain (Moral et al., 1994) and Kazakhstan (Evdokimov et al., 1986).^p^p^Biological Control^p^pHigh levels of natural parasitism have been recorded in many areas where M. destructor is a pest, and conservation of these natural enemies is important. Classical biological control by introduction of non-indigenous agents has not been attempted in recent years, but some deliberate and some accidental introductions have been made in the past and these account for the presence of non-indigenous parasitoids in North America and in New Zealand (Barnes, 1956). Luck (1981) noted successful introductions of Pediobius metallicus from the UK to the USA in the 1890s and unsuccessful introductions of Platygaster pleuron and Trichasis remulus in the 1930s.^p^pIn North America the egg parasitoid Platygaster hiemalis shows greatest promise as a biological control agent as it attacks the autumn generation of the pest and therefore limits initial attack in the following season (Schuster and Liddell, 1990). ^p^pA novel development in the use of biological control in the USA has involved the inundative release of a dominant avirulent Great Plains biotype to suppress an Indiana population of eastern soft wheat biotypes (Foster, 1977).^p^p^Host-Plant Resistance^p^pPlant breeding for resistance has been the main control strategy used against this pest in North America for many years, and includes the pioneering work by R H Painter and colleagues (Painter, 1951). Barnes (1956) reviewed this and other work. Much new research and development has been completed since then and the extensive literature should be consulted for details. ^p^pIn North America, at least 16 biotypes have been recognized (Patterson et al., 1992) and 25 genes conferring resistance have been identified in wheat (Dweikat et al., 1994). ^p^pThe first source of host plant resistance in durum wheats has been detected in Morocco and is being used by CIMMYT, ICARDA and Moroccan plant breeders to develop resistant durum wheat varieties. El Bouhssini et al. (1998) reported that screening of 347 accessions of Aegilops against M. destructor in Morocco has revealed a number of sources of resistance, expressed as antibiosis against first-instar larvae, which could be exploited by transfer into wheat. Transfer of one resistance gene from Aegilops ventricosa into hexaploid wheat has been reported by Delibes et al. (1997).El Bouhssini et al. (1998) studied larval survival on resistant wheat plants and found that the operation of most genes that condition antibiosis to Mayetiola destructor results in some survival.  Wheats carrying genes H3, H5, H6, H9 and H10 had low survival rates ((dayuhao)15%) and there was no survival on plants carrying gene H13. Genes H1 and H2 allowed the highest levels of larval survival and plants with genes H7 and H8 showed intermediate levels of survival. The authors concluded that resistance genes that allow avirulent genotypes of M. destructor to survive on resistant plants should be used to reduce selection for biotype development.^p^pGenetic mapping of whea

management_info:
Barnes (1956) reviewed the development of control measures and summarized general practices in the USA for cultural control, which include crop rotation, ploughing-in stubbles, destruction of volunteer wheat plants, good soil preparation with the use of good seed to ensure quick germination, and moderately late sowing of winter wheat to avoid infestation by the autumn generation of adults.  Chemical control measures (based on the use of systemic or non-systemic insecticides) against ovipositing females, eggs and first-instar larvae, have been developed, but are not always effective (Buntin and Hudson, 1991; Dur醤 et al. 1992).  High levels of natural parasitism have been recorded in many areas where M. destructor is a pest, and conservation of these natural enemies is important. Classical biological control by introduction of non-indigenous agents has not been attempted in recent years, but some deliberate and some accidental introductions have been made in the past and these account for the presence of non-indigenous parasitoids in North America and in New Zealand (Barnes, 1956). Luck (1981) noted successful introductions of Pediobius metallicus from the UK to the USA in the 1890s and unsuccessful introductions of Platygaster pleuron and Trichasis remulus in the 1930s.

In North America the egg parasitoid Platygaster hiemalis shows greatest promise as a biological control agent as it attacks the autumn generation of the pest and therefore limits initial attack in the following season (Schuster and Liddell, 1990).  In North America, M. destructor attack on wheat has been limited by IPM. This has relied mainly on plant breeding for host-plant resistance, combined with clean cultivation, good management of volunteer wheat and delayed sowing in autumn to escape infestation of overwintering crops (Davidson and Lyon, 1987; Pfadt, 1985).
